> Four separate bugs in live-federation-gate.sh share one shape: a correct, well-logged decline that exits 0 and is therefore indistinguishable from "ran and was fine". The fix is never to remove the decline — it is to make it name itself at the verdict line.

## The shape [Section titled “The shape”](#the-shape) `papercusp-desktop/bin/live-federation-gate.sh` has now produced **four** bugs with one root shape: > A decline to run a leg that is individually correct, cheap, well-logged — and **exits 0**, so it is indistinguishable from “ran and was fine” at every consuming surface. The four, in the order they were found: | # | Decline | Filed as | | - | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | | 1 | `LOAD_GATE` defer | EI-18657324526667507 | | 2 | `MATRIX_TTL_H` cadence window | EI-18657324526667507 | | 3 | §0z rig-busy pre-check skip | EI-18657324526667507 | | 4 | content-matrix red ⇒ local-matrix never runs | EI-18715623477356990 | Each was written by someone who reasoned correctly about the *local* question (“should this heavy leg burn the box right now?”) and not at all about the *global* one (“what does a consumer waiting on this leg’s verdict see?”). ## Why “we already have a staleness detector” is not the answer [Section titled “Why “we already have a staleness detector” is not the answer”](#why-we-already-have-a-staleness-detector-is-not-the-answer) The fix for #1–#3 was a `last-matrix-verdict` stamp plus `check_matrix_staleness()` — a good fix, and it did **not** cover #4. The reason is worth internalising: that detector’s threshold is `MATRIX_STALE_H = MATRIX_TTL_H + 48h`, i.e. **192h ≈ 8 days** by default. So there are two different questions, and a detector for one is not a detector for the other: * **“Has this leg been dark for a week?”** — the staleness clock. Catches chronic suppression. * **“Did it decide THIS window, and if not, why not?”** — what an agent *waiting on the verdict right now* needs. Nothing answered this until EI-18715623477356990. Observed 2026-07-26: content-matrix was red on `incr-B→A`, so every hourly window skipped local-matrix — the only leg that runs `revocation_kcut` (order 90) and `attestation_unattested_device` (order 91). Two agents each waited on a gate run for evidence that *structurally could not arrive*, and neither could have known from the gate’s own output. The staleness detector would have surfaced it — up to eight days later. ## The rule [Section titled “The rule”](#the-rule) When a verification leg declines to run: 1. **Do not remove the decline.** The sequencing rationale is usually right (don’t burn the rig on a window whose cheap smoke already failed). The defect is the silence, not the skip. 2. **Set one reason string, on every decline path.** Not a boolean per path, not a log line per path — *one* variable (`MATRIX_SKIP_REASON`) that every branch assigns, so the reason is always attributable and can never fall through unset. In practice this means turning a compound `if A && B && C` into an `if/elif` ladder: a compound condition **cannot** name which clause closed, which is precisely why all four bugs read identically. 3. **Give a consequential decline its own result token.** `SKIPPED-CONTENT-RED`, not `SKIPPED` — so the verdict `SUMMARY` line carries it. Keep it inside the existing family shape (`SKIPPED*`) so predicates like `is_skip_result()` still treat it as “nothing proven” and the vacuous-pass trap keeps working. 4. **Put it on the human-facing verdict line, every exit path.** An EI in a queue and a line in journald are both easy to miss; `GATE: …` is not. The gate already had `matrix_stale_suffix()` for exactly this reason — `matrix_skip_suffix()` is its sibling and hangs off GREEN, RED, SKIPPED, SKIPPED-STARVATION and SKIPPED-STORM alike. Point 4 has a corollary that is easy to get wrong: **the GREEN path needs it most.** A green gate is the state that best hides a dark leg, because the cheap leg keeps `last-green` fresh on its own. ## Testing this class [Section titled “Testing this class”](#testing-this-class) Both fixes are pinned by tests that **extract the real bash out of the shipping script** and eval it under `bash` against a scratch state dir — see `live-federation-gate-matrix-leg-skip-reason.test.ts` and its older sibling `live-federation-gate-matrix-leg-staleness.test.ts`. That pattern is worth copying for any gate-script change: a static leg pins the structural invariant (every exit line carries the suffix; the chain stays an `elif` ladder), a behavioural leg proves each branch actually names itself, and `bash -n` guards the parse. One gotcha when writing the static leg: `live-federation-gate.sh` echoes `GATE: RED` in **two** places — the §4 verdict and a much earlier assert-core self-test bail. The early one exits before the leg section runs, so it correctly has no leg reason to report; select the verdict line via `${REDS[*]}` rather than a bare `GATE: RED` prefix. ## Where else to look [Section titled “Where else to look”](#where-else-to-look) The same shape lives anywhere a cheap gate guards an expensive one. When you add a “don’t bother running X when Y already failed” condition, ask the second question before you commit it: *what does someone waiting on X’s verdict see this window?* If the honest answer is “nothing distinguishable from success”, you are writing bug #5.

# A workspace package can shadow the root dependency — resolve the binary before you read its source

> In an npm-workspaces monorepo the same dep can exist at two different MAJOR versions. Reading the wrong copy's source produces a confidently-wrong root cause. Resolve which binary actually runs, first.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) This is an **npm workspaces** monorepo, so a dependency can be installed **twice, at different major versions**: once at the root, and again inside a workspace package that pins its own. Node resolves the *nearest* `node_modules` walking up from the importer — so the copy a build actually runs is often **not** the copy you get from the repo root. Nothing warns you. Both copies are real, both are on disk, and `node_modules/<dep>` at the root looks exactly like “the” dependency. Measured, 2026-07-12: 
```bash
node_modules/vite/package.json                    → 7.3.5
apps/operator-vite/node_modules/vite/package.json → 8.0.16   ← what the SPA build runs
```
 ## Why it costs more than a wasted read [Section titled “Why it costs more than a wasted read”](#why-it-costs-more-than-a-wasted-read) Investigating EI-10539 (“a failing build destroys the live bundle”) I needed to know **when** Vite empties `outDir`. I read the source of `node_modules/vite` — v7 — and reasoned from it. The app builds with **v8**, where that logic differs. The failure mode is nasty because *nothing errors*. You get a clean, plausible, internally consistent root cause — from the wrong source tree. Had I not double-checked the version before writing it down, that wrong conclusion would have been committed to a work-item body and an agent-insights doc, where the next agent would have inherited it **as fact**. A confidently-wrong root cause propagates; a missing one just gets re-investigated. This is the [derived-claims class](/internal/docs/agent-insights/derived-claims-carry-their-own-caveat): the read *succeeded*, so nothing signalled that the answer was about a different program than the one you’re debugging. ## The rule [Section titled “The rule”](#the-rule) **Before you read a dependency’s source to reason about runtime behaviour, resolve which copy actually runs.** One command: 
```bash
# What version does THIS workspace package actually resolve?
npm --workspace @papercusp/operator-vite ls vite


# Or ask node, from the package that imports it (the authoritative answer —
# this is the exact resolution the build performs):
npm --workspace @papercusp/operator-vite exec -- \
  node -p "require('vite/package.json').version"
```
 If it disagrees with the root copy, read **that** one: 
```bash
apps/operator-vite/node_modules/vite/...   # not node_modules/vite/...
```
 ## Smells that you are in this trap [Section titled “Smells that you are in this trap”](#smells-that-you-are-in-this-trap) * The source you’re reading doesn’t have the code path the error message mentions. * A flag/option in the docs “doesn’t exist” in the source you have open. * A behaviour you just proved from the source doesn’t reproduce when you actually run it. * `npm ls <dep>` prints the dep more than once, at different versions. When any of those hit, **check the version before you check your reasoning** — the code is usually right and your copy is usually wrong.

# Absorbing-state guards, and why your detector didn't notice

> Six failure instances, four found independently on one day by four agents in different lanes, then recognised as one pattern. Five guard/detector shapes: (A) a guard whose baseline or latch advances ONLY through its own success cannot clear itself — the first failure is permanent; (B) when a component reports its own failure, a detector that infers the same condition from a downstream proxy instead is strictly weaker, because the proxy can be confounded; (C) a detector whose coverage is gated on the success it exists to detect the absence of reports healthy precisely when the thing has failed; (D) a correctly-written detector aimed at an EMPTY set reports a clean pass forever. The headline is the detectors, not the guards: the guard bugs cost hours, the detector bugs cost DAYS — and the Shape D instance had been blind for its entire life.

## Why this doc exists [Section titled “Why this doc exists”](#why-this-doc-exists) On 2026-07-25 two agents in different lanes each hit a multi-day silent outage, within the same hour, in code that shares no call path: **pot-git publishing** (su-a8ea9) and **hyperbee replication liveness** (su-e3b21). Neither was looking for the other’s bug. When one described its root cause in a coordination message, the other recognised it immediately as the shape they had just fixed. Comparing notes surfaced **two more the same day**, in two further lanes — `restart_settle_barrier` (su-48ed7a) and the replication-liveness detector’s call site (su-055ae). **Four independent instances in one day, in four lanes, found by four agents, none of whom was looking for this.** That is a pattern worth a name, not four incident write-ups. ### The headline: it is the detectors, not the guards [Section titled “The headline: it is the detectors, not the guards”](#the-headline-it-is-the-detectors-not-the-guards) The guard bugs (Shape A) are real, but they cost **hours**. What turned each of them into a multi-**day** silent outage was that **every single instance was paired with a detector that structurally could not see it** — Shape B or Shape C. Four for four. That is the claim worth acting on. A guard that wedges and *pages* is an annoyance. A guard that wedges while every dashboard reads green is an outage measured in days, and you find it by accident. **If you change one thing after reading this, change a detector, not a latch.** ## Shape A — the absorbing-state guard [Section titled “Shape A — the absorbing-state guard”](#shape-a--the-absorbing-state-guard) > **A guard whose baseline or latch advances only through its own success cannot clear itself. The first failure is permanent.** This is an [absorbing state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absorbing_Markov_chain): once entered, there is no transition out. It is easy to build by accident, because the code reads as obviously correct — you advance the watermark *when the thing succeeds*, which is exactly what you want, right up until the failure path needs the watermark to move too. ### Instance 1 — the pot-git publish guards (three of them) [Section titled “Instance 1 — the pot-git publish guards (three of them)”](#instance-1--the-pot-git-publish-guards-three-of-them) `own-head-publish.ts` judged the range `(priorSha, head]`, where `priorSha` is the namespace ref — and the namespace ref is written **only after `guard.ok`**: 
```ts
const guardBaseline = priorSha ?? input.genesisBaselineSha ?? null;
// …
if (!guard.ok) return { …, refused: guard };   // ← ref NOT written
await writeNamespaceRef(repoPath, …, headSha); // ← the only advance
```
 So a refusal was terminal *by construction*: the baseline could only move through the publish it was blocking, and every new commit made the refused range bigger. One accidentally-committed 2.26 GB AppImage extraction on 2026-07-20 put the range over the 500 MB cap; five days later the guard was still refusing, and the measured total had grown from 2261 MB to 2415 MB. Deleting the files did nothing — the guard enumerates objects introduced *anywhere* in the range. The same shape, with three different baselines, in three guards: | guard | baseline | advances on | | ------------------ | ----------------- | --------------------------- | | `own_head_publish` | the namespace ref | its own successful publish | | `ref_announce` | sigrefs | its own successful announce | | GitHub egress | `origin/staging` | its own successful push | Because the baselines are *different objects*, unwedging one by hand did not unwedge the others — the manual namespace-ref re-base left `ref_announce` (which reads sigrefs) refusing for hours afterwards. Full incident: [p2p-publish-guard-total-over-cap-wedge](/internal/docs/agent-insights/p2p-publish-guard-total-over-cap-wedge). ### Instance 2 — the replication-liveness alarm latch [Section titled “Instance 2 — the replication-liveness alarm latch”](#instance-2--the-replication-liveness-alarm-latch) `replication-liveness.ts`’s `connected_never_replicated` latch (`alarmedConnectedNever`) was cleared **only on an observed recovery**. On a sustained-offline reset the window was cleared but the latch leaked — and since the fire guard is `!st.alarmedConnectedNever`, a log that had alarmed and then gone offline could never alarm again for the rest of the process lifetime, with `deriveVerdict` reading a stale `no_replicator` off the dead latch. (Found and fixed independently by su-e3b21; regression-tested in `replication-liveness.test.ts`.) ### Where it hides: the reset path and the early exit [Section titled “Where it hides: the reset path and the early exit”](#where-it-hides-the-reset-path-and-the-early-exit) The publish-guard instances were on the obvious **refusal** path. The replication instance was on the **reset** path — much harder to see, because the success path *does* clear the latch and the code looks symmetric at a glance. A third variant turned up in `origin-freshness-watchdog.ts` only because su-e3b21 suggested checking reset paths. Its `of_alerted` latch is cleared in exactly one place — the `verdict === 'ok'` branch — but an **earlier `continue`** skipped the whole verdict block: 
```ts
if (!existsSync(repoPath)) continue;   // ← bypasses the only clear
```
 A pot that alarmed and then lost its bare store (host migration, or a repoKey change like WI-5168’s `slug` → `gh-<id>` move, which relocates that very path) stranded the latch `true` forever and could never alarm again. **So the checklist is not “does the failure path clear the state” but:** * Does the **reset** path clear it, not just the recovery path? * Does **every** early `continue` / `return` / `throw` before the clear leave it stranded? * Can the state advance **at all** without the success it gates? ### The fix shape [Section titled “The fix shape”](#the-fix-shape) Make progress possible without the blocked success: * **Split the range.** Volume/aggregate refusals (“too much at once”) are satisfiable by doing *less*, so publish the longest admissible prefix and let the backlog drain over ticks. The baseline moves; the wedge is self-clearing. * **Attribute precisely.** A hard refusal (a real secret) should stop at the *exact* offending commit with everything before it shipped — never “somewhere in these 358 commits”. * **Budgets, not cliffs.** A scan cap that *blocks* when exceeded is absorbing; a scan cap that *stops and resumes next tick* is not. * **Always ship an escape hatch that reaches every instance.** A runtime exemption existed for one of the three pot-git guards — and not for the one that was actually wedged. ## Shape B — self-report beats inference [Section titled “Shape B — self-report beats inference”](#shape-b--self-report-beats-inference) > **When a component can report its own failure, the detector must consume that report. Inferring the same condition from a downstream proxy is strictly weaker, because the proxy can be confounded.** Shape A is survivable *if something notices*. In both known instances, nothing did — and that was a second, separate bug. There **was** a purpose-built watchdog for the pot-git outage: `origin-freshness-watchdog` (WI-5607), running the whole time, thresholds `aheadCount >= 50` and `tipAge > 3h`, against an outage of **358 commits over 5 days**. It never fired — zero log lines in three days — because it measured against the wrong branch: 
```ts
const branch = entry.github_default_branch ?? 'main';   // ← the INGRESS branch
```
 The bridge *egresses* to `staging`; `main` is the branch it ingests. And `main` is fast-forwarded hourly by the **release pipeline** — a completely unrelated mechanism — so both signals were structurally pinned healthy: | signal | threshold | actual | why | | ---------------- | --------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | `aheadCount` | ≥ 50 | 24 | measured against `main`, kept fresh by the release pipeline | | `originTipAgeMs` | > 3h | \~0 | `main` moved hourly, restarting the clock every sweep | **A detector pointed at a signal kept fresh by an unrelated mechanism is structurally blind.** It does not report a false negative — it reports *correctly, about the wrong thing*, which is much harder to notice. And the part that makes this a *rule* rather than a bug report: the publish leg had been writing 
```plaintext
metadata.own_head_publish.refused = 'total-over-cap'
```
 on **every single tick** for five days, and logging it to the journal. The system stated its own failure out loud, continuously, and no detector consumed it. All that inference was unnecessary. ### The fix shape [Section titled “The fix shape”](#the-fix-shape-1) * **Consume the self-report directly.** A sustained explicit refusal now alarms on its own. * **Do not gate the self-report behind an inferred precondition.** The refusal check deliberately sits *before* the watchdog’s `aheadCount <= 0` “nothing to push ⇒ definitionally healthy” early return — a refusal is true regardless of how any commit count comes out, and in this incident the commit count was the confounded signal. * **Measure the thing you act on.** The watchdog now reads `github_bridge.egress_head` — what egress *actually landed* — not a mirror of a branch it never writes. ## Shape C — the detector that can only observe the healthy case [Section titled “Shape C — the detector that can only observe the healthy case”](#shape-c--the-detector-that-can-only-observe-the-healthy-case) > **A detector whose coverage is gated on the success it exists to detect the absence of will report healthy precisely when the thing has failed.** Shape A is about *state* that cannot advance. Shape B is about a detector consuming a confounded *proxy* instead of a self-report. Shape C is about the detector’s **coverage**: it never runs at all on the failure case, so there is no reading to be wrong. This is the one that produces *zero* log lines and a green dashboard. ### Instance 4 — the replication-liveness detector’s call site (WI-5781) [Section titled “Instance 4 — the replication-liveness detector’s call site (WI-5781)”](#instance-4--the-replication-liveness-detectors-call-site-wi-5781) `sampleReplicationLiveness` has exactly **one** call site — `boot.ts:2400`, **inside the merge pass’s per-remote-log loop**. So the detector can only sample logs it has **already attached**. Read the code and it is entirely reasonable: *iterate the attached logs, sample each one for liveness.* But the failure mode that matters is **a log that never attached** — which is, by construction, not in the loop. Both frames ran on the same host on the same build (run `20260725-153415`), which makes the asymmetry the whole finding: | | frame a (owner path) | frame b (member / join path) | | ---------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | swarm connections | live | live (14 `peer_connected` per harness) | | received the peer’s announce | yes | **yes** — `recv log=5fe26c2e0135` ×7 | | peer log admitted | yes | **no** | | detector lines emitted | 3 | **0** | | detector fired + repaired | yes | — | Frame b is not a false negative. **The detector never executed.** **Why the member and not the owner.** The asymmetry is one line in `classifySameHiveMember` (`boot.ts`): 
```ts
if (memberDevices.includes(devicePubkey)) return 'admit';
return isOwner ? 'admit' : 'miss';   // member BUFFERS
```
 On a membership miss the **owner admits** (a deliberate fix for a different deadlock) and the **member buffers**. A buffered peer then retries every \~5s for up to 30 minutes and is dropped with `announce_rejected` — never once producing a liveness alarm. And it is *circular*: the member needs the owner’s `hive_members` row to admit the log, that row arrives via replication, and replication requires the admission. `memberDevices` only ever advances on success, so this is Shape A feeding Shape C. #### Two traps when you confirm this from banked logs [Section titled “Two traps when you confirm this from banked logs”](#two-traps-when-you-confirm-this-from-banked-logs) Both nearly produced a wrong conclusion here. 1. **`recordBootEvent` writes to an in-memory ring** — not PG, not stdout. So `announce_admitted` / `announce_pending` greps return **zero hits on a PASSING run exactly as on a failing one**, and the restart you are investigating is the event that destroys the buffer. The absence reads as signal when it is an artifact. (Fixed: the sparse forensic kinds are now mirrored to stdout, so they land in the banked serve logs.) 2. **Do not compare runs of different length or scenario scope.** The failing run was a 5-minute `replication_soak`-only run; the runs it was first compared against were \~30-minute full-matrix runs with \~4× the activity. “Zero detector lines” looked damning until the durations were checked — it only survived scrutiny because three *other* runs emitted their first detector line \~45s after start, so 5 minutes was ample. The general rule: before treating **silence** as evidence, prove the detector would have spoken. Silence from a detector that never ran, a buffer that was wiped, or a window too short to alarm are four different things that look identical. **The fix that landed (WI-5781).** Liveness is no longer driven only by the admitted set. The merge pass now also samples `pendingPeers` — precisely “we accepted this peer’s announce, so we are *supposed* to be replicating it, and we have not admitted it” — through a new `expected_never_admitted` axis with the same durable-EI escalation as every other axis. That is the Shape C fix stated concretely: *enumerate the expected set, alarm on the gap.* Note the expected set was already in memory; no roster read or new I/O was needed, which is typical — the expectation usually already exists somewhere, unread. ### Instance 3 — `restart_settle_barrier` (EI-18645423267952485) [Section titled “Instance 3 — restart\_settle\_barrier (EI-18645423267952485)”](#instance-3--restart_settle_barrier-ei-18645423267952485) The same shape one level up, at the harness layer. The barrier PASSes with `order 80 didn't run this session` in **exactly** the case it exists to catch: `restart_durability` had just run and **failed**. Its precondition (“did order 80 run?”) was itself derived from the thing that failed, so absence-of-evidence rendered as PASS. It masked a 25-minute outage. ### Why this is not Shape B [Section titled “Why this is not Shape B”](#why-this-is-not-shape-b) Shape B’s fix is *“consume the self-report instead of inferring.”* That does not help here. **There is no self-report from a log that never attached** — nothing instantiated a reporter for it. Absence does not announce itself. The fix is different in kind: * **Shape B:** the reporter exists; read it instead of guessing. * **Shape C:** the reporter does not exist; you must enumerate the **expected** set and alarm on the difference from the **achieved** set. ### The fix shape [Section titled “The fix shape”](#the-fix-shape-2) * **Enumerate expected, not achieved.** Iterate what *should* be attached / registered / running, and alarm on the gap. A loop over what succeeded can never see total failure. * **Never derive a barrier’s precondition from the thing it guards.** If “did X run?” is answered by X’s own output, a failed X reads as “not applicable” rather than “failed”. * **Make absence loud.** `0 of N sampled` is a finding. A detector that emits nothing must be distinguishable from a detector that emits nothing *because everything is fine*. ## Shape D — the detector pointed at an empty set [Section titled “Shape D — the detector pointed at an empty set”](#shape-d--the-detector-pointed-at-an-empty-set) Shapes A–C are all about a detector that *runs* over the right population and still cannot see the failure. Shape D is nastier and simpler: the detector is written correctly, enumerates exactly the right kind of thing, and is pointed at a population that is **empty**. It then reports a clean pass forever. This is distinct from checklist question 6. Question 6 asks whether you enumerate the EXPECTED set or the ACHIEVED set. Shape D enumerates the expected set — it just enumerates it *somewhere nothing lives*. ### Instance 5 — `origin-freshness-watchdog` swept the wrong workspace (WI-5791) [Section titled “Instance 5 — origin-freshness-watchdog swept the wrong workspace (WI-5791)”](#instance-5--origin-freshness-watchdog-swept-the-wrong-workspace-wi-5791) The watchdog resolved its own scope as: 
```ts
const workspaceId = opts.workspaceId ?? DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID;
const projects = (await loadHarnessRegistry(workspaceId)).projects;
```
 No caller has ever passed `opts.workspaceId` — the boot path is `startOriginFreshnessWatchdog(sql)`, which forwards empty opts. And `DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID` is the literal `'default'`: on this install a scratch workspace holding 14 unrelated pots and **zero** bridged hives. Every real pot lives in `'papercusp-workspace'`. So every sweep since the watchdog shipped returned `checked: 0`. It never entered the per-entry body, never wrote `of_origin_sha`, never aged a tip, and therefore could never fire `tipAgeStale`. Measured, not inferred: a write-intercepting `sql` proxy over the real registry returned `{checked: 0, writes: 0}`, and `of_origin_sha` was NULL on all 21 `system:git-sync` routine rows fleet-wide — every pot, not just the one under investigation. The watchdog built to catch a silently-stalled egress was itself silently stalled for its entire life. It was written *in response to* a five-day egress outage, and it would not have caught that outage. **Why nothing noticed.** `{alarmed: [], recovered: [], checked: 0}` is success-shaped. There is no error, no throw, no warning — and no surface read `checked`. “Covered everything, all healthy” and “covered nothing” were the same value. **Why the tests didn’t notice.** `origin-freshness.test.ts` covered the pure verdict functions (`evaluateOriginFreshness`, `selectOriginWatermark`) thoroughly, and was green the whole time. `checkOriginFreshness` — the wiring that decides *what gets judged* — had no test at all. A well-tested predicate over an untested selection. Unit tests structurally cannot catch this, because a test always injects an explicit `workspaceId`: the path under test is never the production path. **It is a class, not an instance.** At least four occurrences of `?? DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID` silently scoping work to the wrong or empty workspace: this one; EI-10103 (the sibling main-behind watchdog, whose escalation INSERT then violated a NOT NULL constraint and was swallowed by its own outer catch); an in-code comment at `agent-tools/plans/revisions.ts` recording that it read the wrong workspace’s plan spine; and `host-bootstrap`’s stall-waker looping only the registry’s first entry and no-op’ing the other 16. Tracked as EI-18660454282479136. ### The fix shape [Section titled “The fix shape”](#the-fix-shape-3) 1. **Enumerate the scope, don’t default it.** `listRegistryWorkspaceIds(sql)` over `harness_shared.harness_registry`, sweeping all of them. 2. **Do not fall back to the default on a failed enumeration.** That fallback *is* the bug. Return empty and let the guard below report it. 3. **Self-report zero coverage.** Ask a cheap, INDEPENDENT question — “were there bridged pots that a covering sweep must have checked?” — and if the answer is yes while `checked === 0`, set `blind: true` and say so at the same volume as a real alarm. The guard has to come from a different source than the sweep, or it inherits the same blindness. The general form of (3): **any sweeper that can legitimately process zero units needs a second, independent opinion about whether zero was the right answer.** ## Shape E — the detector switched off by the aggregate’s health [Section titled “Shape E — the detector switched off by the aggregate’s health”](#shape-e--the-detector-switched-off-by-the-aggregates-health) Checklist question 4 below already states the rule in its “contaminated signal” form: a signal kept fresh by something *other* than the mechanism you are watching cannot tell you about that mechanism. This shape is its nastier variant — the aggregate does not merely *contaminate* the detector’s input, it **gates whether the detector runs at all**. ### Instance 6 — the live-federation gate’s `local-matrix` leg (EI-18657324526667507) [Section titled “Instance 6 — the live-federation gate’s local-matrix leg (EI-18657324526667507)”](#instance-6--the-live-federation-gates-local-matrix-leg-ei-18657324526667507) `live-federation-gate.sh` has a `check_staleness()` that files a loud EI when no GREEN run has happened in `GATE_STALE_DAYS`. It opens with an early return while the gate-wide `last-green` is fresh — reasonable in isolation. But the gate is several legs, and the *cheap* `content-matrix` leg keeps `last-green` fresh on its own. The heavy `local-matrix` leg had three independent suppression paths (a `LOAD_GATE` defer, the `MATRIX_TTL_H` 144h cadence window, and a rig-busy pre-check) that each **exit 0**. So the leg could stop deciding anything, indefinitely, and the one detector that might have said so was *switched off by the sibling leg’s success*. Measured live: `last-matrix-green` ABSENT — the leg had never once produced a verdict — while `last-run` was minutes old and 205 skip banks had accumulated. A verification waiting on it stalled for days behind an all-green gate. Note the asymmetry that makes this hard to see in review: the detector was correct on every RED path (it is called from all of them) and blind on exactly the GREEN one — the state nobody investigates. ### The fix shape [Section titled “The fix shape”](#the-fix-shape-4) 1. **Give the unit its own clock.** A `last-matrix-verdict` stamp — “when did this leg last DECIDE anything” — kept deliberately separate from `last-matrix-green` (“when was it last GOOD”). They differ in both directions: a leg that only ever FAILs is still *running*, and a leg green last week but suppressed ever since is stale. Do not reuse the success stamp as the liveness stamp. 2. **Only a real verdict clears it.** A downgrade that means “nothing was proven” (here `SKIPPED-STARVATION`) must NOT stamp the clock, and a green *aggregate* must not clear the unit’s dedup file. Otherwise the aggregate re-acquires the power to silence the unit. 3. **Call it on the healthy path too — that is the load-bearing call.** Wiring it into the paths that already report is free but proves nothing; the GREEN exit is the one that was hiding the failure. 4. **Derive the threshold from the cadence it watches.** `MATRIX_STALE_H = MATRIX_TTL_H + grace`, not a second independent constant — otherwise raising the cadence silently disarms its own detector, which is the same drift this doc’s Shape A warns about one level up. General form: **a detector scoped to an aggregate cannot report a unit inside it going dark.** Any unit with its own suppression paths needs its own liveness clock, checked on the aggregate’s success path. ## The checklist [Section titled “The checklist”](#the-checklist) When you write or review a guard, latch, watchdog, or watermark: 1. **Can this state advance without the success it gates?** If no, the first failure is permanent. Split the work, or add a path that advances on partial progress. 2. **Is the clear reachable from every path?** Check reset, and every early `continue` / `return` before it. 3. **Does the thing being watched report its own health?** If so, consume that report — do not infer it. 4. **Is the signal you measure kept fresh by anything OTHER than the mechanism you are watching?** If yes, it cannot tell you about that mechanism. And its sharper form (Shape E): does that signal *gate whether your detector runs at all*? A detector scoped to an aggregate goes blind to any unit inside it that stops running while a sibling keeps the aggregate healthy. 5. **Does the escape hatch cover every instance of the guard?** An escape hatch present on two of three guards is absent from the one that wedges. 6. **Does the detector enumerate the EXPECTED set or the ACHIEVED set?** If it iterates things that already succeeded, it is structurally blind to total failure — the case you most need it for. 7. **Is the set it enumerates actually non-empty in production?** A correct enumeration pointed at the wrong scope reports a clean pass forever. If a zero-unit pass is possible, get a SECOND, independent opinion on whether zero was right — and make a wrong zero as loud as an alarm. **Question 6 is the highest-yield of the six.** State it as a test you can apply without reading the implementation: > **“If this never worked even once, would this detector produce a single line?”** If the answer is no, the detector cannot detect its own primary failure mode. That one question catches instances 3 and 4 directly. It also catches the `origin-freshness-watchdog` early-`continue` in Shape A above — a pot that lost its bare store was dropped from the enumerated set entirely, which is the same blindness arriving by a different route. **Question 7 has its own version of that test**, and it is the one that catches Shape D: > **“If this detector were pointed at nothing at all, would its output differ from a clean pass?”** For instance 5 the answer was no, for the entire life of the watchdog. Note that question 6’s test does NOT catch it: if origin-freshness “never worked even once” it would still have produced a line — for a pot in the wrong workspace. The enumeration was the right shape, aimed at an empty room. ## Provenance [Section titled “Provenance”](#provenance) Four instances, four agents, four lanes, one day: | # | Instance | Shape | Found by | | - | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | --------- | | 1 | pot-git publish guards (×3) | A | su-a8ea9 | | 2 | replication-liveness alarm latch | A (reset path) | su-e3b21 | | 3 | `restart_settle_barrier` (EI-18645423267952485) | C | su-48ed7a | | 4 | replication-liveness call site (WI-5781) | C | su-055ae | | 5 | `origin-freshness-watchdog` swept workspace `'default'` (WI-5791) | D | su-a8ea9 | Shape B and the `origin-freshness-watchdog` latch leak: su-a8ea9. Shape D was added the day after, from WI-5791 — which is the sharpest evidence for this whole doc’s thesis. WI-5791 was filed as a cautious follow-up to the Shape A/B fixes, with an explicit note not to assume the benign explanation. The benign explanation was wrong: the watchdog those fixes had just hardened had never once looked at a real pot. Every repair in Shape A and Shape B above was made to a detector that was, at that moment, still pointed at an empty room — and nothing in the fix-and-verify loop surfaced that, because a zero-coverage pass is success-shaped. None of this was written by one agent. The general statement came out of a coordination exchange: su-e3b21 asked whether the **reset path** had been checked, which is the only reason the `origin-freshness-watchdog` latch leak was found; su-e3b21 then rejected the first draft’s two-instance framing, supplied instances 3 and 4, and argued Shape C and checklist question 6 into existence — including the observation that the *detector* failures, not the guard failures, are the real headline. The run evidence for instance 4 is su-055ae’s.

# Acceptance rubrics on every plan — authoring + grading runbook

> Runbook for the plan-completion acceptance gate: every plan ships with a kind:'acceptance' rubric authored AFTER implementation and graded by a non-implementer; covers the rubric kind field, the propose/grade/ship flow, gate refusal codes, exemptions, and the four plan-class rubrics.

## The model (owner-ruled 2026-08-11) [Section titled “The model (owner-ruled 2026-08-11)”](#the-model-owner-ruled-2026-08-11) Every plan carries a gradeable definition of done as a REAL rubric — a `template:'rubric'` plan whose `template_data.kind` is `'acceptance'` — not an embedded plan section and not a parallel grading mechanism. The one enforcement point is COMPLETION: `plans:set-plan-status → 'shipped'` (and its `done` alias) refuses without a graded acceptance rubric. There is deliberately NO gate at `plans:new` / `plans:start`. Timing is post-implementation BY DESIGN (plan D-007, superseding the TDD-style instinct): the rubric does not exist until the work is done, so it is authored against as-built reality — better informed, and no tokens are spent on criteria a mid-implementation redesign would invalidate. The honesty guard is at grading, not authoring: the GRADER must not be the rubric’s author (D-005), and the grader’s first check is coverage — criteria must trace to the plan’s stated GOAL + Decisions, never merely describe the diff. ## The kind field [Section titled “The kind field”](#the-kind-field) `rubric-template.ts` validates `kind: 'standard' | 'acceptance'` (absent = `standard`; every pre-kind rubric is unchanged). | | standard | acceptance | | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | semantics | reusable shared-standards library entry | one-shot per-plan definition of done | | default `rubrics:list/search` | ✅ shown | hidden (`kind:'acceptance'`/`'any'` opts in) | | ratification | Queen ratifies (propose → draft) | none — ACTIVATES on propose (D-008) | | staleness watchdog / releaseGating | watched / allowed | exempt / refused | | links | none | `subjectPlan` REQUIRED (validated to exist); optional `classRef` to a standard class rubric | | criteria | ≥1, full model/method/driftMarkers | 3–7 light criteria (model/method optional); may be EMPTY with a `classRef` (D-009) | | lifecycle | until retired | auto-retired when the subject plan ships | `getRubric(id)` resolves ANY kind (an explicit id is an explicit opt-in), so the shared grading path (`scorecards:emit` → `listScorecards`) works unchanged (D-010). `getAcceptanceRubricForPlan(planSlug)` is the subject-plan lookup the gate and `plans:get` use — `plans:get` (sections/full) surfaces `acceptanceRubric` when one exists. ## The flow (implementer, then grader) [Section titled “The flow (implementer, then grader)”](#the-flow-implementer-then-grader) 1. Implement the plan; verify it for real. 2. **Author** (implementer, post-implementation): `rubrics:propose { kind:'acceptance', subjectPlan:'<plan-slug>', classRef:'plan-class-feature-ship'|'plan-class-bugfix'|'plan-class-migration'|'plan-class-investigation', criteria:[3–7 OUTCOME criteria tracing to the plan's goal + Decisions] }`. Dangling `subjectPlan` is refused; a rubric-template plan as subject is refused (no rubric-of-a-rubric). Investigation-only plans may pass `criteria: []` with `classRef:'plan-class-investigation'`. 3. **Grade** (a NON-implementer — different agent or the owner): `scorecards:emit { rubricRef:'<the acceptance rubricId>', ratings:{ <every criterion key>: { rating, evidence } } }`. A complete, non-synthesized scorecard whose `createdBy` ≠ the rubric’s `proposedBy` satisfies the gate. 4. **Ship**: `plans:set-plan-status { slug, status:'shipped' }` — on success the acceptance rubric is auto-retired (`acceptanceRubricRetired` in the result). ## Gate refusal codes (evaluatePlanAcceptanceGate) [Section titled “Gate refusal codes (evaluatePlanAcceptanceGate)”](#gate-refusal-codes-evaluateplanacceptancegate) * `acceptance_rubric_missing` — no acceptance rubric names this plan; the message carries the propose recipe. * `acceptance_ungraded` — rubric exists, no complete scorecard. * `self_graded_only` — only the author has graded it (the self-graded-homework guard). Exemptions (satisfied without a rubric): flag `ACCEPTANCE_RUBRIC_COMPLETION_GATE` off; the plan IS a rubric-template plan; scheduled template instances (`template_slug` set). ## The four class rubrics [Section titled “The four class rubrics”](#the-four-class-rubrics) Seeded first-party (repo `rubrics/plan-class-*`, standard-kind, characteristic `plan-acceptance`): `plan-class-feature-ship`, `plan-class-bugfix`, `plan-class-migration`, `plan-class-investigation`. They encode the shared invariants ONCE (tests-with-feature, flag-ON default, gate-green shipped, root-cause + recurrence guard, migration hygiene, writer-read findings) so per-plan bespoke criteria stay short — reference one via `classRef` instead of restating them. ## Amending [Section titled “Amending”](#amending) `rubrics:amend` round-trips kind/subjectPlan/classRef (dropping them would flip an acceptance rubric to standard — the WI-4287 loss class on identity fields). `rubrics:ratify` REFUSES acceptance rubrics with a teaching error.

# Adding a derived plan frontmatter scalar (mirror `owner`)

> The full edit-site set for a new harness_plans frontmatter column (e.g. `initiative`) — incl. the 3 federation re-derive sites and the integration-test STUBS that unit tests won't catch.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) Adding a new plan-frontmatter scalar that must reach the client (a filter facet, a badge) means adding a **derived index column** on `harness_plans`, mirroring `owner` — NOT parsing the content blob in the resolver. `plans:list` is deliberately parse-free (audit P-042): it reads `listPlanIndexRows` (index columns only, content never leaves PG). Parsing for your field reintroduces the exact per-request-parse regression P-042 removed. Worked example: `initiative` (shared-pot-collaboration P-015 / D-015). The same edit-site set was reused verbatim for `template`/`promote_policy`/`template_data` (mig 329/331, plan-template provenance + auto-promote policy) — `template` is a plain frontmatter-derived TEXT scalar (mirrors `initiative`, see the comments in `with-plan-lock.ts` and `source.ts`), confirming the pattern below holds across more than one addition. ## Why it’s a trap [Section titled “Why it’s a trap”](#why-its-a-trap) Two things bite you AFTER unit tests are green: 1. **The federation hand-written stubs.** Three integration tests build a *column-faithful* `harness_plans` via raw `CREATE TABLE` (not the migration set): `sync/hyperbee/__tests__/plan-part-federation-cutover.integration.test.ts` and `ei117-replay-revert-guard.integration.test.ts` mirror the real columns — you MUST add your column to their stub or they red with `column "<x>" of relation "harness_plans" does not exist` (the projection INSERT now binds it). (`backfill-local-state.integration.test.ts` uses a *subset* stub that omits `owner`/`supersedes` too — leave it; it never runs the full INSERT.) Unit tests + tsc are all green; only the integration tier catches this, so it lands as a green-checkpoint red unless you run the federation integration tests locally. 2. **Federation needs NO wire redesign** — and reasoning otherwise wastes time. The scalar is derived from `content`, and `content` always federates. The per-part recompose re-derives scalars from the recomposed frontmatter; the whole-blob projection carries them on the wire. So this is NOT the heavy “federated-schema migration” category — keep the wire validator *tolerant* (optional field) and you’re done. ## The edit-site set (all mirror an existing `owner` line) [Section titled “The edit-site set (all mirror an existing owner line)”](#the-edit-site-set-all-mirror-an-existing-owner-line) * **Parser** `libs/generic/plan-parser/src/parser.ts`: add to `PlanFrontmatter` * `if (typeof raw.<x> === 'string') out.<x> = raw.<x>;` * **Migration**: reserve the number via `db:next-migration` (NOT a hand-picked one — they collide), then a single `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS … text;`. Files ≥215 carry **no** top-level `BEGIN;/COMMIT;` (the runner wraps each file — `lint:migrations` enforces it). * **source.ts**: `PlanRow`, `PlanDbRow`, `PlanIndex`, `rowFromDb`, `deriveIndexFromContent`, and **all five SELECT lists** (getPlanRow / listPlanRows / listPlanIndexRows / listPlanRowsMatchingAnyToken / `listPlanIndexRowsForWorkspace` — added 2026-06-30 for the scheduled-recurring-plans work; it carries its own column-not-exist fallback query, so both its SELECTs need the new column too). * **with-plan-lock.ts**: the INSERT column list + VALUES + the `DO UPDATE SET`. * **Federation (3 sites)**: `projections/harness-plans.ts` (wire type — make it optional/tolerant in `isHarnessPlanRow` — plus both INSERT paths), `projections/harness-plan-parts.ts` `defaultRecomposeSink`, `feature-issue-op-keys.ts` `toPlanValue`. * **list.ts** (`plans:list`): `ListRow` + the pushed row. * **Client**: `plans-api.ts` `PlanListRow`; `plan-filtering.ts` (state + predicate); `PlanFilters.tsx` (nuqs key + facet + active-token + clearAll) and the readers `PlanRail.tsx` / `PlanBucketTabs.tsx` that construct `PlanFilterState` (+ their test fixtures). * **A write verb** (optional): mirror `plans:transfer-owner` — reuse its exported `setFrontmatterScalar`; register in `agent-tools/index.ts`; run `tools-md-sync`. ## generated.ts [Section titled “generated.ts”](#generatedts) The drizzle `generated.ts` models `harness_plans`. `pull-schema` regenerates it from a *migrated* DB — which the dev box’s live PG won’t be until boot-apply runs. Add the one convergent column line by hand (`<x>: text(),` after `owner`); the drizzle-drift CI check is **informational/non-gating**, and a post-deploy `pull-schema` yields the identical line. ## Verify [Section titled “Verify”](#verify) `vitest run` the federation integration tests above + the `baseline-schema-globalsetup` test (proves your migration applies via the real runner), plus the parser, `plan-buckets` (filter predicate), and `tools-md-sync`.

# Adding a reactive table — the consolidated pattern

> How to make a new PG table push live updates to the UI. PG trigger → sync_invalidate → existing /api/zero-harness/sse → libs/sync invalidates the matching useSyncQuery.

Superseded — the trigger→camelCase bridge is now LIVE The section below titled **“Two name conventions exist — they don’t talk to each other yet”** is out of date. Its central forward-looking claim — that PG-trigger `<schema>.<table>.changed` events are **“broadcast no-ops for existing clients today”** and that a name-translator bridge is **“Bridge work pending”** / a dormant safety net “until that lands” — no longer holds. The **P-067 bridge shipped** (plan `papercusp-dogfood-v5-2026-05-23`). Current behavior: * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts:49-51` constructs the invalidation bus with `bridge: (name) => queryNamesForTriggerEvent(name)`. * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts:189` exports `queryNamesForTriggerEvent`, backed by the reverse map `TABLE_TO_QUERY_NAMES` (e.g. `table-to-query-names.ts:43` maps `'harness_shared.harness_text_artifacts' → ['harnessTextArtifact.byHarness']`). So a `harness_shared.harness_text_artifacts.changed` trigger event is **now translated** into the camelCase `harnessTextArtifact.byHarness` name that existing `useSyncQuery` consumers subscribe to. Trigger events are **no longer inert for existing clients** — they reach the documented camelCase consumer surface automatically. To add coverage for a new table, add its `'<schema>.<table>' → ['camelCase.scope']` entry to `TABLE_TO_QUERY_NAMES`. Two further point-in-time notes (not contradictions): the generic mechanism now lives in `libs/generic/sync/src/server/invalidation-bus.ts` (`@papercusp/sync/server`) — `sync-sse.ts` is operator wiring + re-export, but still exports `notifySyncInvalidate` / `subscribe` / `backfillSince` / `SyncEvent`, so the import examples below remain valid. And the 90-second dedupe window is correct (`DEFAULT_DEDUPE_WINDOW_MS = 90_000`), distinct from a separate 60s ring-buffer replay window (`DEFAULT_HISTORY_WINDOW_MS = 60_000`). The recipe and payload contract below are otherwise still accurate — the historical narrative is preserved as-is. ## What [Section titled “What”](#what) Papercusp’s UI gets live updates from PG through **one channel, two producers**: 
```plaintext
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Application code     │── notifySyncInvalidate(name, args, data?) ─┐
  └──────────────────────┘                                            │
                                                                      ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐                              pg_notify('sync_invalidate', ...)
  │ PG trigger           │── emit_change_notify() ─────────┘          │
  │ (auto, every row)    │                                            │
  └──────────────────────┘                                            ▼
                            packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts → /api/zero-harness/sse
                                                                      ▼
                              libs/sync SSEAdapter → @tanstack/react-query
                                                                      ▼
                                                useSyncQuery refetches matching query
```
 Both producers emit the same payload shape; consumers don’t care which fired. The 90-second dedupe window in `sync-sse.ts` collapses identical `(name, args)` notifies — so an app-code notify followed by a trigger-driven one for the same row hits the wire once. ## When to use which producer [Section titled “When to use which producer”](#when-to-use-which-producer) | Choice | Use it for | | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `notifySyncInvalidate(name, args, data?)` in app code | Fine-grained, intentional notifies after a meaningful write. Optional `data` payload pushes the new rows directly, saving the client a refetch. Used by 20+ writers. | | `emit_change_notify` PG trigger | Coarse, automatic, fires on EVERY INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Catches writes that bypass app code — raw SQL from migrations, MCP-tool direct writes, agent-direct edits. | You usually want **both**: app code fires the targeted notify on the happy path; the trigger covers everything else. ## Recipe — add a reactive table [Section titled “Recipe — add a reactive table”](#recipe--add-a-reactive-table) ### Step 1: define the table [Section titled “Step 1: define the table”](#step-1-define-the-table) In a `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/NNN-<name>.sql` migration (≥ `107`). **Update:** the old runtime-ensure path (`ensure-schema*.ts`, lazy-`CREATE TABLE`) is **removed** — schema is migrations-only now (`self-contained-migration-baseline-2026-06-02`). Add a migration; do not add an `ensureXxx()`. ### Step 2: attach the trigger [Section titled “Step 2: attach the trigger”](#step-2-attach-the-trigger) 
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER emit_change_notify_trg
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE
  ON harness_shared.your_new_table
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION harness_shared.emit_change_notify();
```
 **Update:** the old runtime `wireDogfoodTriggers()` helper (in the removed `ensure-schema-dogfood.ts`) is gone. The dogfood trigger wiring now lives in a migration — `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/107-dogfood-reactivity-triggers.sql` attaches `emit_change_notify` to the reactive tables. Add your new table’s `CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER` line to a migration alongside those. Idempotent (`CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER` is PG 14+), so re-applying the migration is safe. ### Step 3: in app code, also call `notifySyncInvalidate` after writes [Section titled “Step 3: in app code, also call notifySyncInvalidate after writes”](#step-3-in-app-code-also-call-notifysyncinvalidate-after-writes) After your route handler writes to the table: 
```ts
import { notifySyncInvalidate } from '@papercusp/operator-core/lib/sync-sse';


// After the successful write:
void notifySyncInvalidate('your_table.changed', { workspace_id, op }).catch(() => {});
```
 Best-effort — never let a notify failure break the write itself. ### Step 4: on the client, subscribe with `useSyncQuery` [Section titled “Step 4: on the client, subscribe with useSyncQuery”](#step-4-on-the-client-subscribe-with-usesyncquery) 
```tsx
import { useSyncQuery } from '@papercusp/sync';


const { data, loading } = useSyncQuery<YourRow>({
  // ...
});
```
 `useSyncQuery` reads the SSE invalidate stream and refetches whenever a matching `name` arrives. ## Payload shape — never break this [Section titled “Payload shape — never break this”](#payload-shape--never-break-this) Both producers emit on `sync_invalidate` channel with: 
```json
{
  "name": "<event-name>",
  "args": { "workspace_id": "<id|null>", "op": "INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE" }
}
```
 Consumers filter on `name`. The format is the established `SyncEvent` contract in `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` — don’t invent a parallel channel; the trigger function was rewritten in commit `20609bb` to stop doing exactly that (was emitting on a new `papercusp_changes` channel; consolidated onto `sync_invalidate` for the 20+ existing consumers). ### Two name conventions exist — they don’t talk to each other yet [Section titled “Two name conventions exist — they don’t talk to each other yet”](#two-name-conventions-exist--they-dont-talk-to-each-other-yet) | Producer | Name shape | Example | | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | Application code via `notifySyncInvalidate(name, args)` | camelCase noun + scope | `plans.list`, `toastLog.recent`, `harnessTextArtifact.byHarness` | | PG trigger `emit_change_notify` (this insight’s recipe) | `<schema>.<table>.changed` | `harness_shared.plan_runs.changed` | Today’s existing `useSyncQuery` consumers subscribe with `queryName: 'harnessTextArtifact.byHarness'` (camelCase). My PG-trigger events fire with `harness_shared.harness_text_artifacts.changed` — clients filter on name, see no match, refetch nothing. Trigger events are **broadcast no-ops for existing clients today.** **What this enables**: future code subscribing to `<schema>.<table>.changed` (the catch-all name shape) gets free coverage of any write to that table, including raw-SQL or MCP-tool writes that app code never notified about. **Bridge work pending**: a future item should add a translator — “when `harness_shared.harness_text_artifacts.changed` arrives, also invalidate any subscriber to `harnessTextArtifact.*`.” That ties the trigger producer to the existing consumer surface. Until that lands, app-code `notifySyncInvalidate` calls remain the active path for known consumers; the trigger is the dormant safety net. ## Verifying it works [Section titled “Verifying it works”](#verifying-it-works) Live test that brings its own embedded PG, no shared-state risk: 
```bash
node apps/operator/scripts/verify-trigger-consolidation.mjs
```
 Runs in \~2s. Asserts the trigger fires on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, the payload shape is correct, the GUC workspace\_id is captured, and a coexisting trigger on the same table doesn’t block this one. ## Why it matters [Section titled “Why it matters”](#why-it-matters) Before the consolidation, agents were tempted to invent a new channel per concern (e.g., a new `/api/sync/stream` endpoint for a new feature). That fragments the SSE consumer surface (one EventSource per channel — and browsers cap HTTP/1.1 connections per host at 6). One channel + payload-filtered topic gives sub-second invalidation across the whole UI without exhausting the connection pool. See the [connection-pool insight](/internal/docs/agent-insights/webkit-connection-pool-exhaustion) for the failure mode if you stack multiple long-lived connections. ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` — `notifySyncInvalidate` + `subscribe` * `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/zero-harness/sse.ts` — the SSE endpoint * `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/000-baseline.sql` — the `emit_change_notify()` trigger function (originally `archive/078-emit-change-notify.sql`) * `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/107-dogfood-reactivity-triggers.sql` — the trigger-attach migration (replaced the removed `wireDogfoodTriggers()` runtime helper) * `apps/operator/scripts/verify-trigger-consolidation.mjs` — the live verifier

# Adding a query to the Zero-free sync resolver

> How to add a new useSyncQuery name to the v2 dispatcher. ~15 LOC drizzle entry, registry-style, no ZQL. Pairs with the reactive-table insight.

Superseded — Step 4 is stale Step 4 below tells you to bump exact-count `toHaveLength(N)` assertions in two test files. **Those assertions no longer exist** — both were deliberately deleted and replaced with non-shrinking floor checks specifically *because* bumping them on every add/remove flapped CI red. There is no count to bump. * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.test.ts` now asserts `expect(names.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(61)` (grep for it — the adjacent comment calls the old `toHaveLength(63)` a “brittle exact-count that flapped red”). * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.test.ts` now asserts `expect(names.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(45)` (the adjacent comment calls the old exact count of 56 “brittle” and states the floor is “set WELL BELOW the current count … so a routine add/remove doesn’t flap it red”). (Line numbers deliberately omitted — they drift on every edit; grep the assertion text instead.) **What to actually do for a registry add today:** add your new name to the relevant `toContain(...)` family assertion(s) in `index.test.ts` (the exact-set assertions are what catch real drift now) and, if it’s bridged, to the corresponding membership assertion in `table-to-query-names.test.ts`. The floor checks (`toBeGreaterThanOrEqual`) only fire if the registry *shrinks* below the floor — leave them alone. The `FORWARD_DEFINED` guidance later in Step 4 is still correct. ## What [Section titled “What”](#what) The operator serves `useSyncQuery({ queryName: '<name>' })` reads through a switch-on-name dispatcher at `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts`. Each entry is a small async function that takes validated args and returns a flat row array. Adding a query is purely additive — \~15 LOC, no client-side changes needed for the dispatcher itself. This replaced the legacy `@rocicorp/zero`-coupled ZQL resolver in P-022 (cutover commits `164671ed` + earlier batches). The legacy resolver is gone; this dispatcher is the only path. ## When to use it [Section titled “When to use it”](#when-to-use-it) Add an entry when: * A UI component needs to subscribe to a PG-backed read with `useSyncQuery` and the queryName isn’t already registered. * You’re moving a route from manual fetch + setInterval polling to push-driven reactivity. Don’t add an entry for: * One-shot reads that don’t need invalidation. Use a regular fetch * `useAsyncJson` or similar. * Writes. The dispatcher is read-only; mutations stay on `POST /api/...` routes and fire `notifySyncInvalidate(...)` after the write succeeds. ## Recipe [Section titled “Recipe”](#recipe) ### Step 1: confirm the table exists in drizzle’s generated schema [Section titled “Step 1: confirm the table exists in drizzle’s generated schema”](#step-1-confirm-the-table-exists-in-drizzles-generated-schema) The dispatcher uses `@papercusp/db-org`’s `generated` table registry for column → camelCase conversion. Check that your table is there: 
```bash
grep "^export const yourTableNameInHarnessShared" \
  libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/schema/generated.ts
```
 If missing: regenerate the schema via the drizzle generator, or add the table via `ensure-schema.ts` / a SQL migration first. ### Step 2: add a registry entry [Section titled “Step 2: add a registry entry”](#step-2-add-a-registry-entry) Open `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts`. Each entry has this shape (mirrors the legacy ZQL chain): 
```ts
'yourQueryName.byScope': {
  argsSchema: z.object({
    harnessSlug: z.string(),
    limit: z.number().int().positive().max(500).default(50),
  }),
  resolve: async (args) => {
    const { harnessSlug, limit } = args as { harnessSlug: string; limit: number };
    const { getOrgPg, generated } = await import('@papercusp/db-org');
    const { desc, eq } = await import('drizzle-orm');
    const t = generated.yourTableNameInHarnessShared;
    const { db } = getOrgPg();
    return (await db
      .select()
      .from(t)
      .where(eq(t.harnessSlug, harnessSlug))
      .orderBy(desc(t.updatedAt))
      .limit(limit)) as unknown[];
  },
},
```
 Key points: * **`argsSchema`**: a zod schema. Validation runs before `resolve`. Bad args throw → route handler returns 400. * **`resolve`** returns `unknown[]` — a FLAT row array. If your existing data helper returns `{rows: [...]}`, unwrap it here. * **Dynamic `import()`** of `@papercusp/db-org` + `drizzle-orm` keeps the registry module lightweight and avoids cycles. The lazy import is per-call but the loader caches; no perf cost in practice. * **`as unknown[]`** at the return — drizzle’s `select()` returns rich types; the dispatcher contract is `unknown[]`. The cast is intentional. ### Step 3: add the bridge entry (P-067) [Section titled “Step 3: add the bridge entry (P-067)”](#step-3-add-the-bridge-entry-p-067) Open `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts`. Add a line in `TABLE_TO_QUERY_NAMES` mapping your PG table to the new queryName: 
```ts
'harness_shared.your_table_name': ['yourQueryName.byScope'],
```
 This makes the PG trigger producer (P-018 `emit_change_notify`) fire your camelCase invalidation when ANY write touches the table — including raw SQL, MCP-tool writes, or migrations that bypass app code. Without this bridge, only app-code `notifySyncInvalidate` calls reach your subscribers. If multiple queries scope on the same table (e.g. `byHarness` + `byFeature` over the same chunk plans), list both: 
```ts
'harness_shared.harness_chunk_plans': [
  'chunkPlans.byHarness',
  'chunkPlans.byFeature',
],
```
 ### Step 4: update the registry-count assertion [Section titled “Step 4: update the registry-count assertion”](#step-4-update-the-registry-count-assertion) Open `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.test.ts`. Bump the running-count assertion (`expect(knownQueryNamesV2()).toHaveLength(N)`) and add the new name to the closest batch assertion. The count assertion exists so future drift surfaces: a registry entry added without the corresponding test update is treated as suspicious. Same in `table-to-query-names.test.ts` — bump the `allBridgedQueryNames()).toHaveLength(N)` assertion. **If the name you’re migrating is in the `FORWARD_DEFINED` set** (advance-mapped before its v2 entry existed — see [forward-defined-registry-entries insight](/internal/docs/agent-insights/forward-defined-registry-entries)), **remove it from `FORWARD_DEFINED` in the same commit**. The sanity assertion (“forward-defined names are NOT in v2”) will fail otherwise and tell you to do this; doing it as part of the migration commit keeps the drift signal accurate. ### Step 5: verify [Section titled “Step 5: verify”](#step-5-verify) 
```bash
cd packages/operator-core
npx vitest run lib/sync-resolver/    # 33+ tests
npx tsc --noEmit                     # check for type regressions
```
 Optional live verification against running operator: 
```bash
curl "http://127.0.0.1:3070/api/zero-harness/rest-query?name=yourQueryName.byScope&args=$(python3 -c 'import json,urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote(json.dumps({\"harnessSlug\":\"sheets\"})))')"
```
 You should see `{"rows":[...], "version":"..."}` with the expected row shape. ## Why this design (not just calling notifySyncInvalidate on each write) [Section titled “Why this design (not just calling notifySyncInvalidate on each write)”](#why-this-design-not-just-calling-notifysyncinvalidate-on-each-write) Two complementary producers run side by side: | Producer | Trigger | Use it for | | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `notifySyncInvalidate(name, args, data?)` in app code | Application write paths | Fine-grained intentional notifies with optional row payload | | PG `emit_change_notify` trigger | Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on attached tables | Catch-all for raw SQL, MCP-tool writes, agent-direct edits, migrations | Together they cover both planned writes (app code) and any other write (trigger). The 90s source-side dedupe window (`DEFAULT_DEDUPE_WINDOW_MS` in the generic `@papercusp/sync/server` invalidation bus, `libs/generic/sync/src/server/invalidation-bus.ts` — `sync-sse.ts` just wires the operator’s PG LISTEN/pg\_notify plumbing into it) collapses the inevitable overlap so subscribers see one event per (name, args) per dedupe window. The bridge (P-067, `table-to-query-names.ts`) is what makes the trigger producer reach the camelCase consumers. Without it, the trigger fires `harness_shared.your_table.changed` and clients subscribed to `yourQueryName.byScope` see no match. ## When to NOT add to this dispatcher [Section titled “When to NOT add to this dispatcher”](#when-to-not-add-to-this-dispatcher) Some reads don’t fit the registry shape: * **Multi-table joins / aggregates**: legacy ZQL had limited join support too. Build a regular REST endpoint (e.g. `/api/admin/...`) and fire `notifySyncInvalidate` from the route. * **File-system reads** (e.g. plans-admin’s markdown loading): these aren’t PG rows; the dispatcher’s `getOrgPg` shape doesn’t apply. Use `useAsyncJson` + push invalidation via `notifySyncInvalidate('plans.list', ...)` from the file-watcher. * **Per-row scoped reads** (`one()` instead of an array): drizzle’s `.limit(1)` returns a single-element array, which matches the dispatcher contract. The client unwraps `rows[0]`. Don’t try to return a non-array — the SSE adapter expects `unknown[]`. ## Gotcha: invalidation args must match the subscription’s args (or be name-only) [Section titled “Gotcha: invalidation args must match the subscription’s args (or be name-only)”](#gotcha-invalidation-args-must-match-the-subscriptions-args-or-be-name-only) The single most common reason a write “saves but the UI doesn’t update”: **`notifySyncInvalidate(name, args)` with an `args` object does an EXACT-key invalidation on the client**, and it only matches a subscription whose `args` are structurally equal. In the SSE client (`SSEAdapter.tsx`): * `notifySyncInvalidate('q')` — **name-only** → `invalidateQueries({ predicate })` invalidates **every** cached entry under `q` (all arg variants). Refetches. * `notifySyncInvalidate('q', { workspaceId })` — **args-scoped** → `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['sync','q',{ workspaceId }] })`. This matches **only** a subscription whose key is exactly `['sync','q',{ workspaceId }]`. A component that calls `useSyncQuery({ queryName: 'q' })` (no args) has the react-query key `['sync','q',{}]`. An args-scoped invalidate for `{ workspaceId }` will **never** match `{}` → no refetch → the write lands in PG but the surface looks frozen until the 180s drift-repair poll. **Rule of thumb:** the invalidate `args` must equal the consumer’s `useSyncQuery` args. * Resolver reads `activeWorkspaceId()` internally and the client subscribes with **no args** (workspace-singleton: `autonomy.policy`, `plans.list`, `decision.ledger`) → emit **name-only** `notifySyncInvalidate('q')`. Do NOT pass `{ workspaceId }` — it’s not part of the key and silently breaks the match. * Client subscribes WITH args (`voiceLease.current` → `{ workspaceId }`, `planItems.byPlan` → `{ planSlug }`) → pass those **same** args. This bit the Mug-autonomy settings page: the ceiling slider wrote to PG but the dot never moved because the route/tool emitted `{ workspaceId }` against a no-arg subscription. Fixed by switching those emits to name-only. (Belt-and- suspenders on the consumer side: an optimistic local overlay reconciled against the refetch makes a control move on click regardless of invalidation latency.) ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts` — the dispatcher * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts` — the P-067 bridge * [Adding a reactive table](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-reactive-table) — the producer side (PG trigger + `notifySyncInvalidate`) * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` — the LISTEN handler + SSE fan-out

# A coordination WRITE tool hangs forever — the admin pool has no statement_timeout

> When work_items:comment (or any getOrgPg()-based mutating tool) HANGS indefinitely instead of failing, the cause is that the harness_admin pool has a role-default lock_timeout (15s) but NO statement_timeout — so a query that stalls for any non-lock reason runs unbounded. A JS/AbortController watchdog can't cancel an in-flight postgres-js query; only a DB-side statement_timeout can. Fix interactive admin-pool writes with boundedOrgTxn (SET LOCAL statement_timeout + atomic txn); leave migrations unbounded.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) An agent reports a coordination **write** tool — `work_items:comment` is the one that surfaced this — **hung** (never returned), then **timed out on a bounded retry**, and a follow-up `work_items:get detail:true` shows **no new row landed**. It reads like a flaky transport; it is not. It is an *unbounded database query* on a write path that has no per-statement time budget. ## Root cause [Section titled “Root cause”](#root-cause) `work_items:comment` → `commentWorkItem` → `commentIssue` (issue family) or the feature branch of `commentWorkItem` runs its queries (`getIssue`, `getOrCreateThread`, `addPost`, the fan-out) directly on the **`harness_admin`** pool (`getOrgPg().sql`). That pool’s role defaults are: 
```plaintext
harness_admin → lock_timeout=15s, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=60s
```
 There is **deliberately NO `statement_timeout`** — migrations and long maintenance tooling share this same pool and must be allowed to run unbounded (see `connection.ts`; the GUC is set per-session, not on the role). The cost of that omission falls on *interactive* writes: * A query that **lock-waits** fails at 15s (`55P03`) — slow, but bounded. * A query that stalls for **any non-lock reason** — a CPU-starved / event-loop-blocked operator, a slow scan, a buffer wait — runs **UNBOUNDED** and hangs the MCP call until the client transport gives up. A JS watchdog cannot save you here The route stack arms a 30s `AbortController` watchdog (`route-stack.ts`), but **postgres-js does not cancel an in-flight query when the signal aborts** — the 408 only materializes once the handler finally returns. The ONLY thing that actually unblocks a wedged query is a DB-side `statement_timeout` (PG `57014`). Reach for the DB timeout, not a `Promise.race`. Two aggravating factors on the same path: 1. **Non-atomic durable write.** `PgThreadStore.addPost` did `INSERT … coord_thread_posts` then a *separate* `UPDATE coord_threads SET post_count = post_count + 1` as two auto-commit statements. A stall between them half-writes; worse, if the INSERT commits and the call then appears to fail, a client retry **duplicates** the comment. 2. **Best-effort fan-out that could still hang.** `fanoutForObject` was documented “best-effort — a delivery failure cannot break the caller’s write” and caught *errors*, but did not bound *slowness*: a stalled subscriber-resolve / `appendLine` hung the caller. ## Fix — `boundedOrgTxn` + atomic write + bounded fan-out [Section titled “Fix — boundedOrgTxn + atomic write + bounded fan-out”](#fix--boundedorgtxn--atomic-write--bounded-fan-out) `packages/operator-core/lib/pg-bounded-txn.ts` adds `boundedOrgTxn(fn, opts)` — the interactive-WRITE counterpart to `pg-read-query`’s bounded READ ONLY txn, and a lighter sibling of `locks/inWorkspaceTxn` (no per-workspace advisory lock). It wraps a unit of admin-pool writes in ONE transaction with `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` (15s) + `lock_timeout` (8s), so the work is: * **ATOMIC** — partial writes can’t half-land and a post-stall retry can’t duplicate; and * **BOUNDED** — a stall surfaces as a typed `OrgTxnTimeoutError` (mapped from PG `57014`/`55P03`) that the caller turns into a clean `{ ok:false, error }` (bulk tools get this for free via `runBulk`), instead of an indefinite hang. `commentIssue` and the feature comment path now run get-or-create-thread + add-post inside `boundedOrgTxn` via a **tx-bound `PgThreadStore`** (`new PgThreadStore({ ...coordOpts, getSql: () => tx })`) — reusing the exact tested store SQL, atomic and bounded. The fan-out runs *after* the durable write commits and is wrapped in a wall-clock `withDeadline` so the best-effort contract holds for slowness, not just errors. Migrations keep calling `getOrgPg()` directly and stay unbounded. `createIssue` (`issues-engineer.ts`) was also converted: its `nextIssueId` advisory-lock read + INSERT now run together in a single `boundedOrgTxn` — id allocation and row creation are atomic (no half-write a retry would duplicate) and bounded by the same 15s statement\_timeout. `conversations:post` / `conversations:answer` carried the **same class** and are now closed the same way (WI-766). Because `appendPost` lives in a **pure core** (`conversations-core.ts`) over injected deps — not a binding-layer function like `commentIssue` — the tx-bound store is threaded through a `threadTxn` seam on `ConversationDeps`: prod binds `threadTxn: (fn) => boundedOrgTxn((tx) => fn(new PgThreadStore({ ...storeOpts, getSql: () => tx })))`, and the PG integration tests bind the *same* `boundedOrgTxn` over their throwaway client so the real atomic path is asserted (`post_count` never drifts from the row count). The seam pattern is the reusable way to bound a pure-core write without coupling the core to `getOrgPg` / `PgThreadStore`. ## When you hit this again [Section titled “When you hit this again”](#when-you-hit-this-again) * A `getOrgPg()`-based **mutating** tool that can hang → route its durable write through `boundedOrgTxn` (don’t reach for `getOrgPg().sql` raw on an interactive write path). * Don’t try to fix a DB hang with an `AbortController` / `Promise.race` alone — add the `SET LOCAL statement_timeout`. The JS race is only a secondary guard for best-effort, fire-and-forget work (like a fan-out). * A pure **core** (deps-injected, no `getOrgPg`) that needs a bounded write → add a `threadTxn`-style seam to its deps and bind `boundedOrgTxn` + a tx-bound store in the binding layer (see `conversations-core.ts` ↔ `conversations.ts`). Don’t import `getOrgPg` into the core — it breaks the integration-test-without-prod-singletons split. * The known per-tool offenders are now closed (`work_items:comment`, `conversations:post` / `conversations:answer`, `issues:create`). **WI-832** landed a DI seam in `connection.ts` (`setAdminPoolStatementTimeoutProvider`) — **now wired** at boot by `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/locks/configure.ts` → `adminPoolStatementTimeoutMs()` from `txn-timeouts-config.ts`. The default is **0 (no timeout)**: the admin pool stays deliberately unbounded unless a non-zero value is set at runtime via the `db:txn-timeouts` tool (`adminPoolStatementTimeoutMs` field; kill-switch: `papercusp-txn-timeouts-config`). When set to a non-zero value, every new pooled connection gets that per-statement cap, bounding the whole interactive-write class at the source; the migration runner opts out per-txn (`SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 0`). Until `adminPoolStatementTimeoutMs` is configured to a non-zero value, wrap any new interactive admin-pool write in `boundedOrgTxn` yourself.

# A proxied tool going BULK blanks its admin-UI consumers — unwrap results[0]

> When a defineTool the /admin route proxies is migrated to the _bulk { ok, results, counts } envelope, the route's generic unwrap() forwards the envelope verbatim and any single-object UI consumer (e.g. the Plans editor reading data.raw/prose) gets undefined → renders BLANK with no error. Fix: unwrap results[0] in the route; if a payload-diet also dropped a field the UI round-trips (raw), restore it behind an opt-in flag that's also in the SWR cache key.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) Select a plan in the Plans admin tab and the **detail body renders BLANK** — the header (title/tabs) shows, but the markdown pane has zero height, zero children, zero text. No error toast, no spinner, no “Couldn’t load the markdown renderer” fallback. It looks like “selection works but the content vanished.” The give-away in a live DOM probe: `.pc-md-preview` exists but `h:16, childCount:0, textLen:0`, and the value React handed `<MarkdownPreview>` is the empty string — while the plan’s body (30 KB+) is sitting un-read one level down in the server response. ## Root cause — a proxied tool quietly became BULK, and the route still passthrough-unwraps [Section titled “Root cause — a proxied tool quietly became BULK, and the route still passthrough-unwraps”](#root-cause--a-proxied-tool-quietly-became-bulk-and-the-route-still-passthrough-unwraps) Two independent server changes compounded: 1. **`plans:get` was migrated to the bulk envelope.** Per [bulk-tool-contract-2026-06-22](/internal/docs/agent-insights/bulk-tool-contract-2026-06-22), it now runs through `runBulk` → `bulkContent` and returns `{ ok, results: [plan], counts }` — **even for a single slug**. The plan object moved from the top level into `results[0]`. 2. **The admin route proxy didn’t unwrap it.** The [admin-route-tool-proxy](/internal/docs/agent-insights/admin-route-tool-proxy) shape ends in a generic `unwrap(result)` that just extracts the tool’s `content[].text` and `JSON.parse`s it — a **verbatim passthrough**. So `/api/admin/plans/get` started returning the whole `{ ok, results, counts }` envelope to the browser. The UI consumer is single-plan: `usePlan` → `fetchPlan` (`plans-api.ts`) types the response as one `PlanGetResult`, and `PlanDetail` reads `data.raw ?? data.prose` straight off it.
