failure → doc pointer | `tutorial-runner.mjs` (`buildQaCommand`/`buildQaPrompt`) | | Tutor brief | \`GET /api/desktop/onboarding-launch-context?agent\&mode=first-run | tutorial\` renders the tutor prompt to a file | | Tutor prompt | `onboarding-tutor.md` + token splice (`{{PACK_INDEX}}`, `{{GUI_TAB_TOUR}}`, setup snapshot, OS, agent…) | `apps/operator/prompts/onboarding-tutor.md` + `…/lib/onboarding/launch-context.ts` | | Content pack | `apps/operator/prompts/tutorial/<ch>/<nn>-<slug>.md` (frontmatter `id/chapter/order/title/docSlugs`, `## Brief` + `## Details`) + loader/registry | `packages/operator-core/lib/onboarding/` | | GUI finale | `GUI_TAB_TOUR` mirrors `ADV_TABS` — tutor drives tabs via `ui:dispatch {intent:'set_url', args:{path:'/adv', params:{tab}}}` | `…/lib/onboarding/gui-tab-tour.ts` | | Re-entry | `papercusp tutorial` / desktop icon → `onboard-launcher --tutorial` → the unified Tutorial\|Setup shell, opening on the **Setup tab** (owner 2026-07-06: “the setup page should be the first thing, not the tutorial” — `defaultTab` returns `setup` for `--tutorial` even on a set-up box; the tour is one Tab away). `papercusp setup` AND `papercusp tutorial` both route STRAIGHT to the shell now (the old concierge→runner double-layer is dropped — it jumped past setup on a machine with an agent already installed); only the auto first-boot `papercusp onboard` (no flags) still runs the linear concierge. | launcher + `…/lib/desktop-install/papercusp-files.ts` | | Graduation | tutor calls `setup:complete` → `finished_at`; all stages re-derive statelessly (resumable by construction) | `setup:*` tools | | Wizard fallback | Settings → Advanced → “Setup Wizard (classic)” + `/setup?force=1` | `apps/operator/app/settings/layout.tsx` | ## Test coverage — where to add yours [Section titled “Test coverage — where to add yours”](#test-coverage--where-to-add-yours) * **Stage machine**: unit tests beside `stage-resolver.ts`. * **Concierge helpers**: `apps/operator/scripts/__tests__/onboard-launcher.test.ts`. * **Scripted concierge → handoff (CI, fake binaries)**: `apps/operator/scripts/__tests__/onboard-launcher-flow.integration.test.ts` — spawns the REAL launcher against a stub operator API (node:http); asserts install streaming, done-stage no-spawn, and that the handoff now **launches the deterministic runner** (an empty `tutorial-script` pack makes it exit 0 fast) in both first-run and `--tutorial` re-entry. * **Deterministic runner, end to end**: `apps/operator/scripts/__tests__/tutorial-runner-flow.integration.test.ts` — spawns the REAL `tutorial-runner.mjs` against a stub `tutorial-script` + `setup-wizard-state`, answering `@inquirer` prompts one at a time over a pipe (send-on-quiet debounce — @inquirer consumes one line per prompt). Asserts verbatim Brief delivery, `[1]` advance + progress checkpoint, `[2]` details, a free-form question one-shotting a FAKE agent binary, finale narration, and graduation (`finished_at`). Drive only the `input`-only path (empty optionalSetup + no progress ⇒ no `select`/`confirm`, which can’t be driven over a pipe). * **Runner navigation logic (unit)**: `apps/operator/scripts/__tests__/tutorial-runner.test.ts` — `interpretReply` (`1`/`2`/`m`/`f`/question), `buildQaCommand`/`buildQaPrompt`, resume math. * **Preview-flag filtering (unit)**: `packages/operator-core/lib/onboarding/optional-setup-items.test.ts` — a default install never sees telemetry / mobile-pairing / auto-update; a tester (flag on) sees all. The dark flag itself is guarded by `libs/flags/src/production-defaults.test.ts`. * **First-run routing + console surface**: `apps/operator/e2e/onboarding-first-run.spec.ts` — hermetic via `page.route` mocks of `setup-wizard-state` + `flags/bootstrap`. * **Tutor behavior (LLM)**: target `onboarding-tutor` + scenarios OT1–OT3 in `packages/operator-core/lib/llm-testing/`; hermetic wiring test in `__tests__/onboarding-tutor-target.test.ts`. * **Pack ↔ docs sync**: the registry test fails if any pack `docSlug` doesn’t resolve to a live `/internal/docs` page — the tutorial doubles as a docs coverage audit. Write the missing doc, don’t drop the slug. * **Tab-tour drift**: `gui-tab-tour.test.ts` parses `AdvShell.tsx` source and fails if `ADV_TABS` and `GUI_TAB_TOUR` diverge (order, ids, labels). ## Traps [Section titled “Traps”](#traps) 1. **A browser never shows the real console.** `isTauriNative()` false → the fallback card. Playwright therefore verifies the card + routing only; the real pty console is verified in the Tauri shell per [testing/agent-e2e](/internal/docs/testing/agent-e2e). 2. **Stage resolution is server-side on purpose.** The `.mjs` concierge must not grow stage logic — quit-anywhere resumability depends on every stage re-deriving from `onboarding-status`. Thread new session choices through query params, like `embeddingsSkipped`. 3. **The handoff env seam**: `PAPERCUSP_ONBOARD_LAUNCH_CONTEXT` / `PAPERCUSP_ONBOARD_HARNESS` are read by `buildHandoffArgs` at spawn time. Tests must scrub them from the child env (the dev box may carry them). 4. **The tutor prompt renders at launch**, not live: token changes need a fresh launch-context render; `{{GUI_TAB_TOUR}}` lines embed `ui:dispatch` calls verbatim — the `set_url` handler’s `path` arg exists for exactly this (added with P-018; older `params:{url:…}` guidance was silently broken — EI-7263). 5. **Cutover flag**: `papercusp-onboarding-agent-first` default ON; OFF must stay byte-identical to the pre-plan behavior (`/setup` first-run). The e2e spec pins both directions — keep it green when touching routing. 6. **`/onboarding` is deliberately un-gated** (no `requireFlag`): tutorial re-entry deep-links to it after first-run. Don’t “fix” that. 7. **Setup is the FIRST tab, not the tutorial (owner 2026-07-06, extended 2026-07-07).** `defaultTab(args, { setupComplete })` in `tutorial-runner.mjs` opens the unified shell on **Setup** whenever required setup (agent backend * sign-in + mem0 key) is unfinished, OR `args.tab === 'setup'`, OR `args.tutorial` is set (a `papercusp tutorial` re-entry shows Setup first even on a set-up box — the tour is one Tab away). As of 2026-07-07 the **first-run concierge handoff ALSO lands on Setup**, not Tutorial: the concierge’s `buildTutorialRunnerArgs` (`onboard-launcher.mjs`) now passes `--tab=setup` on first-run handoff (only a `papercusp tutorial` re-entry passes `--tutorial` instead), so `defaultTab`’s Tutorial-tab fall-through is reached only by a bare `tutorial-runner.mjs` invocation with neither flag — no production entry point does that anymore. `setupComplete` is computed off the same `setupChecklist` as `runSetupTab`; on any fetch error it defaults to `false` (err toward showing Setup). Don’t “fix” `papercusp tutorial` (or the first-run handoff) back into opening the tour directly. 8. **The `finished_at` redirect loop (WI-3281).** The root route (`/`) hard-redirects to `/onboarding` whenever `setup-wizard-state.finished_at` is unset, so navigating home from the embedded onboarding pane WITHOUT stamping it just reloads the tutorial — the mac-GUI “no way past the tutorial” loop. `OnboardingConsole.markSetupFinished()` PATCHes `/api/desktop/setup-wizard-state { finished_at }` (idempotent merge, best-effort, never throws) before navigating home; graduation via `setup:complete` also stamps it. If you add another exit from the pane, stamp `finished_at` first or the gate bounces the user back in.

# Agent-mcp routes slow but /health fast = main-event-loop saturation (not a leak/pool/DB issue)

> When :3070 agent-mcp routes degrade to many seconds and MCP clients time out while /api/health stays fast, the cause is sustained main-thread CPU saturating the event loop — every await hop pays the loop delay, so hop-heavy routes degrade ~Nx while health (~2 hops) barely moves. Read the event-loop-lag gauge first, not the PG pool.

## The signature [Section titled “The signature”](#the-signature) `:3070` agent-mcp routes (psu / fleet MCP, `/api/agent-mcp/*`, `/api/harness/*`) degrade to **12–30s/req and MCP clients time out**, but `/api/health` stays **\~sub-second**. It may worsen over \~1h after boot and “recur after restart”. Memory may spike separately — don’t be misled into chasing a leak. This is **main-event-loop saturation**, not what it looks like. The discriminator chain (EI-79, a multi-day forensic slog precisely because nothing reported it): * **Not a leak / fd / conn exhaustion** — fd and conn counts are normal. * **Not the PG pool** — PG is healthy (sub-second queries, no blockers); N parallel requests finishing *together* at \~the same long time = no pool staircase, they’re all waiting on the same shared resource (the loop). * **Not CPU priority** — changing CPUWeight does nothing. * **The tell**: trivial agent-mcp routes (one settings read) are as slow as heavy ones, while `/health` is fine. Hop-heavy routes (auth→identity→roles→telemetry→PG) pay the per-await **loop delay** dozens of times; `/health` (\~2 hops) pays it \~twice. Sustained host CPU (`node` \~165%+ steady) is the burden; every `await` hop is where it’s felt. ## Diagnose it in one read [Section titled “Diagnose it in one read”](#diagnose-it-in-one-read) A standing **event-loop-lag gauge** exists for exactly this — read it before touching the PG pool: * `packages/operator-core/lib/event-loop-lag-monitor.ts` — `perf_hooks` `monitorEventLoopDelay()`, wired at boot in `apps/operator/bin/hono-host.ts`. * It logs `[event-loop-lag] high loop delay — host is CPU-bound on the main thread` (with p50/p95/p99/max) **only** when p95 over a 10s window ≥100ms; silent on a healthy host. Grep the `papercup-dev-api.service` journal for it. To name the on-loop consumer: a 60s CPU profile of the live host (`node --cpu-prof` / inspector). EI-79’s was the hyperbee P2P read-merge driver (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/boot.ts` `mergeNow`, 1Hz poll) re-decoding **every op from index 0 in every admitted peer log every second** — O(total-history) per tick. Fix was an incremental merge cursor reading only `[cursor,length)` + a steady-state change-detection skip + PG-level `fed_ts` ts-guarded LWW writers (mig 181). ## On a busy box: separate loop work from scheduler preemption [Section titled “On a busy box: separate loop work from scheduler preemption”](#on-a-busy-box-separate-loop-work-from-scheduler-preemption) Caution `monitorEventLoopDelay()` measures wall-clock delay between timer fires, which **includes time the OS descheduled the process**. On an oversubscribed box (high load average), the gauge can sit at p95 \~100–150ms from **scheduler preemption alone**, not host on-loop work. Discriminator: time a **hop-heavy** agent-mcp route. If the loop genuinely carried \~Xms of on-loop work *per hop*, a dozens-of-hops route would be multi-second. If hop-heavy routes are **sub-second** while the gauge reads \~100ms, the floor is mostly scheduler noise (external box load) — a real but *different* problem from a host on-loop regression. Latency on the actual routes is the ground truth; the gauge p95 is the alarm, not the verdict.

# Injecting precomputed state into an agent's prompt (the wake-brief pattern)

> Six load-bearing rules for prompt-state injection — tail-not-prefix, delimiter stripping, skip-set parity, when stateless digests need no watermark, generation plus full resync for warm sessions, and fail-soft fallback.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) When you precompute state and hand it to an agent **in its prompt** (so its first turn is a decision, not 5 survey tool calls), you are doing *prompt-state injection*. The Mug wake-brief (\[\[mug-brief-cache-assembly-2026-06-13]]) is the reference implementation. The pattern is reusable for any agent — but it has six non-obvious traps. All six were live bugs or near-bugs in production paths. ## The five rules [Section titled “The five rules”](#the-five-rules) 1. **Volatile state goes in the TAIL, never the cached prefix.** Prompt caching is a strict prefix match — any byte change before a breakpoint invalidates the cache for everything after it. A per-wake snapshot changes every wake, so splicing it into the persona/system prefix yields a 0% hit rate on the most valuable block. Render it as a `<system-reminder>` appended to the **volatile tail** (`buildPrompt({ queenBrief })` → `prompt-build.ts`), after the cached preamble. **Verify with a preamble-byte-stability test**: build two prompts that differ ONLY in the injected content and assert `wake1.preamble === wake2.preamble` (see the MUG preamble test in `prompt-build.test.ts`). 2. **Strip the framing delimiter from embedded content (breakout defense).** The injected block wraps free-text the agent or *other* agents authored — a carry-note, ranked work-item titles, change-feed/escalation summaries. A literal `</system-reminder>` anywhere in that content closes the wrapper early and the following text reads as un-framed operator instructions. Strip it before wrapping — mirror the existing `wrapUntrusted` `DELIMITER_RE` defense (`SYSTEM_REMINDER_RE` in `prompt-build.ts`). This is content-confusion even when the content isn’t “remote”: a work-item title is semi-untrusted. 3. **Only tell the agent to skip a read whose content is ACTUALLY in the brief.** The big win is the agent NOT re-running the tools the brief replaces — so you teach “don’t call `pot:survey` / `coord:inbox` / … to gather this.” But if a read is listed in that skip-set while its content is **not** folded into the brief, the agent goes **blind** to it. This was a real bug: the brief told the Mug to skip `coord:inbox`, but the floor didn’t carry the inbox → handoffs/acks/plan-events invisible. Keep the skip-set and the actually-injected set **identical**; carve out anything not folded in, or fold it in (we folded it in — D-021). 4. **Fresh-per-wake makes a read-only “recent” digest of a stateful source safe — no watermark needed.** Folding a delta-shaped source (an inbox) looks hard: “new since last wake” implies a per-agent watermark, and advancing it at precompute time risks marking items seen on a wake that then fails. But if the consuming agent is **fresh-per-wake / stateless** (no memory of last wake), it already re-reads the source from scratch every wake with no unread-tracking — so a read-only *recent* digest in the brief is **equivalent** to its own tool call. Skip the watermark; just cap a recent window. (If the agent were a long-lived session, you’d need the watermark.) 5. **A warm-session delta needs a generation and an explicit full resync.** A long-lived agent already holds a base, so a delayed wake or two mutations before its next turn can make the newest delta impossible to apply safely. Stamp every transition with `previousGeneration` + `generation`, and track the last delivered generation at the server. Apply only when `previousGeneration === deliveredGeneration`; otherwise reject the pending payload and inject a bounded full replacement from the current authoritative state. Schema mismatch and missing base take the same resync path. The P-014 CTRL anchor is the reference: the turn-start hook atomically consumes one generation, stale transitions never merge, and `coord:orient { afterCompaction: true }` is the named recovery verb. 6. **Fail-soft to the tools, and teach the whole-brief-absent fallback.** The precompute must degrade to `null`/empty on any error so the launch still fires and the agent falls back to gathering state itself. Each sub-gather should fail independently (one flaky read drops its section, not the brief). And the persona must say: *“if the brief is absent, gather it yourself”* — otherwise a best-effort failure leaves a skip-instructed agent with nothing. ## Why it matters [Section titled “Why it matters”](#why-it-matters) Rules 2, 3, and 5 are silent correctness bugs (breakout / blindness / stale overwrite) that pass every happy-path test — the kind a “marked done” feature hides. Rule 1 is the entire point of the feature (a leak into the prefix destroys the cache it exists to build). Rule 4 is the difference between “this is a hard deferred design task” and “this is a 20-line read-only digest.” Rule 5 prevents a generation-behind wake from undoing newer control state. When you build (or review) any prompt-state-injection feature, walk these six explicitly. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * \[\[mug-brief-cache-assembly-2026-06-13]] — the reference build (D-001 tail-not-prefix, D-015 breakout strip, D-017/D-021 skip-set consistency + inbox fold). * `agent-insights/pot-mug-fresh-per-wake` — why the Mug is stateless per wake (rule 4’s precondition). * `agent-insights/mcp-tool-surface-prompt-cache` — the prefix-cache mechanics this rides on.

# A script that imports the agent-tools registry never exits — call process.exit

> Importing '@papercusp/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/index.ts' (the defineTool registry barrel) opens keep-alive handles, so a one-shot tsx script hangs after finishing instead of exiting — and a spawnSync caller blocks forever. End such scripts with an explicit process.exit.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) A one-shot `tsx` script that imports the agent-tools barrel (`import '@papercusp/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/index.ts'` — e.g. to call `listAllProjectedTools()`) **prints its final output and then never exits**. Run standalone you may not notice (Ctrl-C, or a `timeout`/pipe masks it: a `timeout 180 npx tsx … | tail` pipeline still exits 0 because the *pipeline’s* last command succeeds). But any caller that **waits for the child** — `spawnSync`, a CI step, another script — blocks until an external timeout kills it. In `starlight-projection-generators-2026-06-05` this wedged the `gen:doc-projections` umbrella: the tool-catalog child printed its ✓, never exited, and the projectors queued behind it never ran (the outer `timeout` returned 124, which looked like the *next* script hanging). ## Root cause [Section titled “Root cause”](#root-cause) Importing the registry barrel side-effect-registers \~300 tools, and that import chain opens **keep-alive handles** (connection pools, timers), so Node’s event loop never drains. The script’s top-level code finishes; the process stays alive. ## Fix [Section titled “Fix”](#fix) End any one-shot script that imports the registry (or anything else that opens pools — e.g. a PG read via `withWorkspace`) with an explicit `process.exit(0)` (after your `--check` logic’s `process.exit(1)` paths). Both `scripts/gen-tool-catalog.ts` and `scripts/gen-doc-tool-catalog.ts` do this now; `scripts/gen-doc-plans-index.ts` always did (why it was wrongly cleared as the hang suspect first — it exits in \~1.4s). Defense in depth for orchestrators: give `spawnSync` a `timeout:` + `killSignal: 'SIGKILL'` per child (see `scripts/gen-doc-projections.ts`) so one wedged child can never hang the whole run.

# Turn-lifecycle control: always-arm wake + turn-interrupt

> The two halves of turn-lifecycle control. WAKE: arming your inbox-wake watch is automatic at SessionStart — you are wakeable even if you never call coord:await-inbox (standing-row model, the woken:0 warning, the migration-183-rides-the-deploy hazard, why you still must not poll). INTERRUPT: turn:interrupt ends a RUNNING peer's turn — cooperative yield (glyph |) vs force, operator-mediated + audited + storm-limited.

Superseded — the wake API was redesigned (directed-wake-honesty) Two parts of this runbook’s wake surface no longer match the code. The always-arm wiring, the standing-row upsert + migration 183, the `await-inbox` annotation, the full `turn:interrupt` dual, and both EI-151 owner-scoping rungs all still verify — only the `coord:send` wake API drifted. * **No more `wake.warning` / `woken:0` warning.** The “woken:0 warning” section below used to quote a `wake.warning` string for the fired-but-woke-nobody case. That field is gone. A `required` wake, or an `optimistic` wake without a declared backstop, now reports the miss via `wake.recipient_absent: true` plus a `wake.note` — see the loud-miss branch in `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/coordination/tools/send.ts`. The miss is still auditable, but the surface is now `recipient_absent`, not a `warning` field. * **`wake` is a union, not a boolean.** The body used to write the API as `coord:send {wake:true}`. `wake` is now `boolean | 'required' | 'optimistic'` on the `send` schema, coerced to the internal wake mode (`true → 'required'`, `false`/omit → no wake). Legacy `{wake:true}` still functions, but the documented intent surface is `wake:'required'` for a loud required wake or `wake:'optimistic'` when a durable `backstop:` will re-dispatch a miss. Without a declared backstop, an optimistic miss is reported loudly too. See plan `directed-wake-honesty-and-spawn-handoff-2026-06-14`. The original narrative below is preserved. ## What changed [Section titled “What changed”](#what-changed) You no longer have to *remember* to make yourself wakeable. The operator now **arms your inbox-wake watch automatically at SessionStart** — server-side, in the lifecycle endpoint that `~/.papercusp/hooks/cc/lifecycle-report.sh` already POSTs to (`activity:report`, `kind:lifecycle`). It is client-agnostic (claude / omp / codex) and armed for the whole session, not just between turns. So every psu/Mug-launched agent is re-invokable on a `coord:send {wake:'required'}` (legacy `wake:true`) **even when it has no idea it will ever be woken**. Plan: `turn-lifecycle-control-2026-06-08` (Phase 1, D-001). The old rule — “call `coord:await-inbox` when you go idle or you won’t be wakeable” — is dead. Forgetting to arm no longer strands you. ## The model: one standing row per agent [Section titled “The model: one standing row per agent”](#the-model-one-standing-row-per-agent) Your watch is a single row in `harness_shared.event_awaits`, keyed `(workspace_id, subscriber_id, event_key)` with `event_key = coord:inbox-wake:<you>`. * **Idempotent (D-002).** SessionStart re-arms by **upsert** (`upsertInboxWakeAwait`, `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE`): re-arming refreshes the captured wake-handle + idle note + floor on the one row — it never inserts a duplicate. A partial unique index (migration 183) enforces exactly one live standing inbox-wake await per agent. * **The rendezvous.** `coord:send {wake:'required', to:[you]}` (legacy `wake:true`) and `coord:message-agent` fires exactly `coord:inbox-wake:<you>` — a key only you watch. It is targeted, never a broadcast; `*`/`human` are not wakeable (no thunder-herd). * **SessionEnd cancels it (D-003).** A clean session end cancels your standing watch, so a wake can’t race a just-exited session and phantom-resume it. If work arrives later, a fresh session is spawned by whoever needs it. ## `coord:await-inbox` is now just an annotation (D-005) [Section titled “coord:await-inbox is now just an annotation (D-005)”](#coordawait-inbox-is-now-just-an-annotation-d-005) Because arming is automatic, `coord:await-inbox` is **no longer the gate** that makes you wakeable. It survives as an *annotation*: it refreshes the “why I’m idle” note on your already-armed standing row (the note rides your wake turn) and lets you tune your `min_sleep_sec` floor. Call it to explain your idle state if you like — but forgetting to no longer makes you unwakeable, which was the whole point. ## You still must not poll [Section titled “You still must not poll”](#you-still-must-not-poll) Always-arm makes you *reliably wakeable*; it does not make polling OK. When you have no queued work: **end your turn.** You are re-invoked when someone `coord:send`s you with `{wake:'required'}` (legacy `wake:true`; bursts inside your floor coalesce into one wake). For a specific one-shot readiness (a lock grant, a peer’s artifact, a plan-run finishing) use `events:await` on that exact key and end the turn. A wake costs a whole turn — await only what genuinely blocks you; ambient interest stays a `topics:subscribe`. ## The woken:0 warning — don’t trust a silent ok (D-010) [Section titled “The woken:0 warning — don’t trust a silent ok (D-010)”](#the-woken0-warning--dont-trust-a-silent-ok-d-010) `coord:send {wake:'required'}` now reports a loud miss when it fired but woke **nobody**: 
```plaintext
required wake reached no awake/watching session for the addressee(s) — the
message was injected to their inbox (seen on their next natural turn) but the
recipient was not re-invoked now.
```
 This is the exact gap that once made a wake *look* successful when nothing was listening. Always-arm makes a required miss rare for fleet agents, but the `recipient_absent` surface still catches a not-yet-armed / non-fleet / dead-handle target. If you see it, the wake degraded to a plain inbox inject — the addressee sees it on their next natural turn, not now. ## The one deploy-time hazard: migration 183 rides the deploy (D-012) [Section titled “The one deploy-time hazard: migration 183 rides the deploy (D-012)”](#the-one-deploy-time-hazard-migration-183-rides-the-deploy-d-012) If you are deploying or debugging the live DB: **never manually apply migration 183 (the partial unique index) to the shared `papercusp` database.** The green-main operator (`:3070`, the live fleet) still *plain-inserts* `coord:inbox-wake:*` rows (no `ON CONFLICT`) until the Phase-1 upsert code is deployed. Applying the unique index first would dedup to one row/agent and then make green-main’s next idle insert throw a `unique_violation` → live-fleet idle-arm regression. The index is correct and applies clean empty→head; it must land **coupled with the upsert code**, which only happens through the green-main deploy (green-checkpoint → release-trigger → `deploy-cli applyStagedMigrations`). It is not triggerable by accident: boot-migrate is gated off on `:3170`, and `:3070` reads the release SQL dir. So “apply 183 to live PG” is a no-op-by-design that rides the deploy — not a pending manual step. ## Where it lives [Section titled “Where it lives”](#where-it-lives) * `armInboxWake` / `cancelInboxWake` — `packages/operator-core/lib/events/await/inbox-wake-arm.ts` * `upsertInboxWakeAwait` / `cancelInboxWakeAwaits` + the standing-row SQL — `packages/operator-core/lib/events/await/store.ts` * SessionStart→arm / SessionEnd→cancel wiring — `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/activity/report.ts` * The `woken:0` warning — `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/coordination/tools/send.ts` * `coord:await-inbox` (annotation) — `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/coordination/tools/await-inbox.ts` * Migration — `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/183-event-awaits-inbox-wake-one-per-agent.sql` ## Cross-owner discovery safety (EI-151) [Section titled “Cross-owner discovery safety (EI-151)”](#cross-owner-discovery-safety-ei-151) A wake / `turn:interrupt` resolves a peer’s LIVE interactive session via `findLiveHost(ownerId)`, which reads a discovery file at `~/.papercusp/psu-pty/<sanitizeKey(ownerId)>.json`. `sanitizeKey` is **lossy** (every char outside `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]` → `_`, truncated to 200), so two *distinct* coord owner ids can resolve to the **same** filename (a structured pot id vs a colliding one; a stale file left at a reused key during a `/loop` re-host). The filename alone is therefore NOT proof of ownership: `findLiveHost` also requires the file’s **recorded `ownerId`** to equal the one asked for, else it returns null (→ park/inbox, never the wrong session). Without that check, agent A’s inbox-wake (or a force-interrupt) would inject into agent B’s live session — the third member of the cross-agent-wake-misroute family (EI-152 / EI-153 / EI-151). The guard lives in the ONE shared discovery function so it covers both the wake-executor’s `psu-socket-inject` rung and `turn:interrupt`’s pty-force leg. Regression: `psu-pty-discovery.test.ts` “EI-151 … recorded ownerId differs from the requested key”. ### The second rung: recycled-pid managed-pty inject (EI-151, Channel 1) [Section titled “The second rung: recycled-pid managed-pty inject (EI-151, Channel 1)”](#the-second-rung-recycled-pid-managed-pty-inject-ei-151-channel-1) The discovery-file check above guards the `psu-socket-inject` rung. The wake-executor has an EARLIER rung — Channel 1, `findPty(pid)` — for sessions that are one of OUR managed ptys (`/adv`-spawned). It matched on **pid alone**, but the OS **recycles a pid** to a *different* agent’s live managed pty after a session exits uncleanly (its `adv_sessions` row never marked ended). So the recorded pid for sleeping agent A could now belong to agent B’s live pty, and A’s wake turn would inject into B’s session — the same cross-agent misroute, one rung up. Fix: `PtyHandle` captures **`ownerSid`** from `PAPERCUSP_SID` at spawn, and `findPtyByPid(pid, ownerSid)` rejects a handle tagged with a foreign owner. An **untagged** pty (`ownerSid === null` — a shell pane / legacy spawn) still matches, so the guard is never *stricter* than the old pid-only behavior. The wake-executor passes `d.subscriberId` (which is also the `PAPERCUSP_SID` it stamps on resume), and parks on a cross-owner miss instead of injecting. Regression: `pty-bridge.test.ts` “findPtyByPid owner-scoping” + `wake-executor-matrix.test.ts` “EI-151 cross-owner pid-reuse”. **Lesson:** any pid→session routing must be owner-scoped — a pid is not a stable identity. ## The dual: turn-interrupt — ending a RUNNING peer’s turn [Section titled “The dual: turn-interrupt — ending a RUNNING peer’s turn”](#the-dual-turn-interrupt--ending-a-running-peers-turn) Wake re-invokes a *sleeping* agent; **`turn:interrupt`** ends a *running* one’s turn. It is **operator-mediated** (D-008): every fleet agent runs as the same OS user, so authorization / attribution / rate-limit can’t live at the OS socket — they live in the tool. `turn:interrupt { owner, mode, reason }` — `reason` is REQUIRED and audited. **Two modes:** * **`cooperative`** (the polite default) — injects a high-priority `yield` coord message (glyph `|`) into the peer’s `[coord+N]` block mid-turn. The peer follows the yield policy every role’s prompt now carries (the dual clause to this page’s wake guidance): reach a safe checkpoint, persist partial state to the work\_item, release locks, write a one-line successor note, end the turn. It is **not** killed. It **DEFERS** when the target holds file locks (a critical section) — a hard yield mid-edit can orphan a lock or half-write a file, so it lets the atomic edit finish and the lock release first, then you retry. * **`force`** — ends the turn NOW, mid-thinking. A managed-pty session gets Ctrl+C over its control socket (the Phase-3 `interruptViaPty` seam); a headless spawn gets SIGINT to the session pid. The **turn** ends, not the agent — the session stays resumable by id. On a critical section `force` WARNS (orphaned-edit hazard) but proceeds. **Guardrails (D-009):** `reason` required; every call audited (`turn.interrupt_cooperative` / `_force` / `_deferred` / `_rate_limited` / `_failed` in `harness_shared.audit_log`); storm-limited so a confused or looping agent can’t halt the fleet. The base ceiling is `STORM_MAX` (10 / 60s / actor, the audit log is the rate source), but `stormMaxFor(actor)` raises it for trusted SYSTEM recovery actors that legitimately force-ESC many *distinct* owners in one burst — a fleet-wide recovery loop was tripping the flat cap after \~10 different owners (`gateway-mass-outage-storm-guard-2026-07-01`). Self-interrupt refused. **Reach for cooperative first**; use `force` only when cooperative was ignored or there’s no time. To re-invoke an *idle* peer use `coord:send {wake:true}` — interrupt is for a *running* peer. The `yield` glyph + every other line type are sourced from the one `COORD_LEGEND`; see [the coord injection protocol](/internal/docs/agent-insights/coord-injection-protocol). **Known gaps (2026-06-08):** the managed-pty typing-parity feel-check and the default-on flip (`PAPERCUSP_PSU_PTY` is opt-in today), and a full live interactive force-interrupt-mid-thinking e2e, are not yet run — the transport and the logic are each covered separately (`turn:interrupt` unit tests 8/8 + the Phase-3 control-socket e2e). Where it lives: `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/turn/interrupt.ts` (`performInterrupt` is the dep-injected, testable core).

# An empty log reads as a clean run: the three ways a verification silently reports GREEN without running

> grep -c on a file that was never written returns 0, and 0 errors looks exactly like success. Three false-greens hit in a single session while verifying a change — an empty tsc log counted as clean; a vitest that never started (a reporter that failed to LOAD) reporting exit 0 because $? captured the wrong command; and a raw `npx vitest run <dir>` sweeping in DB-dependent integration tests whose 241 timeouts said nothing about the change. Before believing any '0 errors / all passed', prove the run HAPPENED: non-empty output, the runner's OWN exit code, a plausible test count. A verification that cannot fail is not a verification.

## The shape of the bug [Section titled “The shape of the bug”](#the-shape-of-the-bug) A verification is supposed to be the thing that *cannot* lie to you. But every verification is really two claims stacked: 1. the run happened, and 2. the run found nothing. Almost every tooling convention we use collapses those into one number — and when the number is **zero**, the two claims become indistinguishable. `grep -c ' error TS' log.txt` returns `0` when the compiler found no errors. It also returns `0` when the compiler never ran and `log.txt` is an empty file. This is the same failure class as the `ok:true`-but-every-field-blank tool result that [EI-10892’s shape-hint](/internal/docs/agent-insights/) exists to catch — a call that *succeeds* and returns nothing usable — turned around and pointed at the verifier itself. It is more dangerous there, because the whole point of the verifier is that you stop looking once it says green. All three forms below were hit in a **single session** (2026-07-13), while verifying a change whose blast radius was every tool in the tree. Each produced a confident, specific, *wrong* “green”. ## Form 1 — the empty log counted as clean [Section titled “Form 1 — the empty log counted as clean”](#form-1--the-empty-log-counted-as-clean) 
```bash
npx tsc --noEmit > /tmp/out.txt 2>&1
echo "TOTAL=$(grep -cE ' error TS[0-9]+' /tmp/out.txt)"   # → TOTAL=0  "clean!"
```
 `/tmp/out.txt` had **zero lines**. The run had been killed. `TOTAL=0` was not a measurement of the code; it was a measurement of an empty file. **Guard:** never derive a verdict from a count alone. Print the evidence that the run *happened* next to the count: 
```bash
npx tsc --noEmit > /tmp/out.txt 2>&1; code=$?
echo "EXIT=$code LINES=$(wc -l < /tmp/out.txt) ERRORS=$(grep -cE ' error TS[0-9]+' /tmp/out.txt)"
```
 `EXIT=0 LINES=0 ERRORS=0` is a clean run. `EXIT=137 LINES=0 ERRORS=0` is a killed one. The count is identical; only the other two columns tell them apart. ## Form 2 — `$?` captured the wrong command, and the runner never started [Section titled “Form 2 — $? captured the wrong command, and the runner never started”](#form-2---captured-the-wrong-command-and-the-runner-never-started) 
```bash
npx vitest run --reporter=basic <dirs> > /tmp/v.txt 2>&1
echo "exit=$?"      # ← FINE here…
tail -35 /tmp/v.txt
```
 Two bugs compounded: * `--reporter=basic` **does not exist** in this repo’s vitest. The reporter failed to *load*, so vitest never ran a single test — it died in startup with `ERR_LOAD_URL`. * The harness reported the *chain’s* exit status. Put anything between the runner and the `echo` — or let a wrapper report the last command’s status — and `$?` is no longer the runner’s. The result: a “completed (exit code 0)” notification for a test run **that executed zero tests**. **Guard:** capture the runner’s status into a variable on the very next statement, and never let anything sit between: 
```bash
npx vitest run <dirs> > /tmp/v.txt 2>&1; code=$?    # ← nothing between
echo "VITEST_EXIT=$code"
grep -E "Test Files|Tests  " /tmp/v.txt              # ← and a plausible test COUNT
```
 A test count is the cheapest possible proof the suite ran. “Tests 711 passed” cannot be faked by a startup crash. ## Form 3 — the run was real, but it was the wrong run [Section titled “Form 3 — the run was real, but it was the wrong run”](#form-3--the-run-was-real-but-it-was-the-wrong-run) 
```bash
npx vitest run libs/generic/tooldef packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools
# → 256 failed | 6555 passed
```
 Real run, real failures, **zero signal**. A raw `vitest run <dir>` globs in `*.integration.test.ts`, which need a database the plain shell never provides. 241 of the 256 “failures” were 5000 ms timeouts; the rest were `admin is not a function` and `Invalid URL`. None of it said anything about the change under test — but it *looked* like a catastrophic regression, and the temptation to “investigate the 256 failures” would have burned an hour. The project’s own runner deliberately splits these: * `npm test` → `scripts/affected-tests.mjs` → each workspace’s **unit** suite. * `--integration` → additionally runs `npm run test:integration` where defined. **Guard:** verify through the path the project actually uses — per-workspace `npm test`, not raw vitest over a directory. If a failure set is dominated by timeouts and connection errors, you are looking at your own environment, not the code. ## The rule [Section titled “The rule”](#the-rule) Before believing any “0 errors / all passed”, **prove the run happened**: * **non-empty output** (`wc -l`) — an empty log is not a clean log; * **the runner’s OWN exit code**, captured immediately (`cmd; code=$?`); * **a plausible count** — tests executed, files checked. Zero of everything is a smell, not a pass. And the general form, which is worth carrying beyond this repo: > **A verification that cannot fail is not a verification.** If there is no input that would make your check report red, it is not checking anything — it is printing `0`. The corollary is the one that bites hardest in an autonomous loop: a green you did not earn is strictly worse than a red, because a red gets investigated and a green gets *shipped*.

# The .AppImage leaks a clean source — the culprit is tauri's release resource-STAGING dir, not the AppDir

> A perfectly clean sidecar can still leak in the shipped .AppImage while the .deb of the SAME build is clean. tauri stages each `resources` glob into target/release/<name>/ next to the release binary and BUILDS THE APPIMAGE FROM THERE — that staging dir is copied-into-never-deleted, so it accumulates the union of every past cut (dropped code-server/meridian-host, pre-prune docs, old identity-baked SPA). Wiping the AppDir does NOT fix it (tauri just refills the AppDir from the stale staging dir). The deb is immune because dpkg archives fresh from the source. Fix: rm -rf target/release/{sidecar,seed,resources} before the tauri appimage build; a fail-closed --scan-dir gate on the assembled AppDir is the backstop.

> **Correction (2026-07-14):** an earlier revision of this note blamed the *AppDir* (`release/bundle/appimage/<product>.AppDir`) and prescribed `rm -rf "$APPIMG_DIR"/*.AppDir`. That was **wrong** — proven when a mtime-FRESH AppDir (built *after* that wipe) still leaked 339 files. The real accumulation point is one level up: tauri’s **resource-staging** dir `target/release/<name>/`. This note now describes the correct cause + fix. The AppDir wipe is retained as a cheap belt-and-suspenders, but it is not the fix. ## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) The 0.0.9 release cut passed every in-build privacy audit — `build-desktop-sidecar.sh` pruned the internal-build-infra docs out of `src-tauri/sidecar` and its `--scan-dir` gate reported the sidecar **CLEAN** — and the resulting **.deb was genuinely clean**. Yet an independent scan of the assembled **`.AppImage` AppDir FAILED**: 339 files carrying the mac-VM sudo/login credentials + build-box identity (the builder’s home path, hostname, build-box email) — a long-dropped `code-server` tree (\~447 MB), a `meridian-host` tree, pre-prune `operator-docs`, a stale `seed/corestore/db/LOG`, and old identity-baked SPA assets. Same build, same commit, same `sidecar/**/*` resources glob — one bundle clean, the other leaking. ## Why the two bundles differ despite one clean source [Section titled “Why the two bundles differ despite one clean source”](#why-the-two-bundles-differ-despite-one-clean-source) The tell: the leaking trees in the AppDir (`code-server`, `meridian-host`, the un-pruned docs) were **absent from the current `src-tauri/sidecar`** — yet present in an AppDir whose files had a **fresh (this-cut) mtime**. A fresh AppDir built from a clean source cannot contain trees the source lacks. So the AppDir was *not* built from `src-tauri/sidecar` directly. It was built from an intermediate. Root cause: **tauri stages the bundle `resources` into a persistent per-profile directory next to the release binary, and the AppImage is assembled FROM that staging dir.** For each glob in `tauri.conf.json` `bundle.resources` (`sidecar/**`, `seed/**`, `resources/*`), the build copies the current tree into `target/release/<name>/` (e.g. `~/.cargo-target/release/sidecar`). That copy is **copy-into-never-delete** — it never removes files absent from the new set — so each dir accumulates the **union of every past cut**: * `code-server` / `meridian-host` from cuts *before* they were dropped (owner directive 2026-07-07) → still there (observed: `code-server` mtime **2026-06-17**, a month stale, in a **11 GB** `release/sidecar` — vs a \~1.2 GB clean source); * pre-prune internal docs from before the doc-prune existed → still there; * a stale `seed/corestore/db/LOG` in `release/seed`; old identity-baked SPA in `release/resources`; * all of it **coexisting** with the current cut’s freshly-copied files (same dir, mixed mtimes). The AppImage’s AppDir is then populated from these stale staging dirs → it ships the union. **The deb is immune** because `dpkg-deb` archives a **fresh** tree straight from the clean `src-tauri/sidecar` each build — there is no persistent staging dir to accumulate into. That asymmetry is the whole bug: deb reflects the clean source; AppImage silently does not. ## Why wiping the AppDir does NOT fix it [Section titled “Why wiping the AppDir does NOT fix it”](#why-wiping-the-appdir-does-not-fix-it) The intuitive fix — `rm -rf "$APPIMG_DIR"/*.AppDir` before `tauri build --bundles appimage` — **fails**, because after the wipe tauri rebuilds a *fresh* AppDir but **refills it from the still-stale `target/release/<name>/` staging dir**, not from `src-tauri/sidecar`. Proven 2026-07-13/14: a cut whose AppDir was purged still produced a fresh-mtime AppDir carrying 339 leaking files. You must purge the **upstream** staging dir, not the downstream AppDir. ## Why the in-build audit missed it [Section titled “Why the in-build audit missed it”](#why-the-in-build-audit-missed-it) `build-desktop-sidecar.sh`’s `--scan-dir` gate scans the freshly-assembled sidecar (a temp `sidecar.tmp.<pid>` that is then atomically swapped into `src-tauri/sidecar`) — the **source**, which was correctly pruned and genuinely clean. It never looked at tauri’s `target/release/*` staging dirs or the assembled AppDir. A gate that scans the source instead of the shipped artifact reports green while the artifact leaks — the same lesson `audit-release-bundle.py`’s header already states for `source.tar.zst` (“scan the artifact, not the repo”). ## Fix [Section titled “Fix”](#fix) 1. **Purge tauri’s release resource-staging dirs before the appimage build** — the root-cause fix (`build-appimage.sh` step 0b): 
   ```bash
   # $CT = cargo target dir (cargo metadata → target_directory)
   rm -rf "$CT/release/sidecar" "$CT/release/seed" "$CT/release/resources"
   ```
 tauri then restages **only** the current (pruned, clean) resources, so the AppDir’s sidecar equals the clean deb sidecar. (Bonus: reclaims \~15 GB on a disk-pressured builder.) Verify tauri actually restages (the AppDir sidecar is non-empty) — the appimage bundle step copies resources at bundle time, so it does. 2. **A fail-closed `--scan-dir` gate on the assembled AppDir**, right before `appimagetool` packages it — scans *the bytes that ship*, so any future regression reds the build instead of shipping silently: 
   ```bash
   python3 bin/audit-release-bundle.py --scan-dir "$APPDIR" || exit 1
   ```
 (Also relativize any absolute symlink whose target points inside the AppDir — `grep` never follows a symlink target, so `--scan-dir` cannot see a build-box path hidden in a `.DirIcon` / `.desktop` symlink; rewrite them relative.) 3. The pre-existing `rm -rf "$APPIMG_DIR"/*.AppDir` is kept as a cheap belt-and-suspenders, but it is NOT the fix — see “Why wiping the AppDir does NOT fix it” above. ## Generalize: the accumulator is often UPSTREAM of the artifact you’re staring at [Section titled “Generalize: the accumulator is often UPSTREAM of the artifact you’re staring at”](#generalize-the-accumulator-is-often-upstream-of-the-artifact-youre-staring-at) The bug is the shape “a persistent output directory that is **copied into** rather than **rebuilt fresh**” — but the trap is that the *first* such dir you find (the AppDir) may be a red herring for a *staging* dir feeding it. When a fresh-mtime artifact contains trees its source lacks, walk UP the copy chain to find the dir that is never wiped. Audit every format: * **deb** — dpkg archives fresh each build → structurally safe. * **Windows** (`build-windows-cross.sh`, cross-compiled on Linux — WI-5651 retired the VM-based `build-windows-on-vm.sh` that used to own this) — explicitly wipes its `bundle/inno` output before packing and packs a freshly-tarred pruned sidecar → structurally safe. * **AppImage** — the offender above; safe only after wiping `target/release/{sidecar,seed,resources}`. * **macOS `.app`** — check whether `tauri build --bundles app` restages from a persistent `target/release/*` too. If a cut’s `.app` looks clean only because a disk-reclaim happened to delete the staging dir first, that cleanliness is a side-effect, not a guarantee. Rule of thumb: **prune/scan the assembled artifact that ships, and make sure the assembler — and every staging dir it copies from — starts from empty.** A clean source tree is necessary but not sufficient when an intermediate accumulates.

# Arm-call-site risk tier — use the ceiling, not fail-safe critical

> When planReversibleArm runs without a declared riskTier (the common case — cups never pass decision.riskTier), deriving the risk from the category's effective ceiling is what makes tripwires actually arm. Defaulting to 'critical' silently prevents every tripwire from firing.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) The autonomy system has two separate decider-gate calls for a reversible action: 1. **The chokepoint** — `resolveAutonomyDecision` run by the Mug before dispatching. It has the action’s `riskTier` (from the ranked item’s economics) so it can correctly decide `auto` for a `low`-risk action in `work-prioritization` (ceiling=`low`). 2. **The arm-call-site** — `planReversibleArm` run inside the verb handler after the chokepoint already said `auto`. It calls `resolveAutonomyDecision` **again** — but cups never pass `decision.riskTier`, so the decider’s D-002 fail-safe fires: `critical`. With ceiling=`low`, `critical > low` → gated → `planReversibleArm` returns null → **no tripwire is ever armed** (EI-570: `harness_shared.autonomy_tripwires` was empty for the entire fleet despite 39 policy auto-takes). ## The fix (landed 2026-06-18) [Section titled “The fix (landed 2026-06-18)”](#the-fix-landed-2026-06-18) `planReversibleArm` now derives a risk proxy from the category’s effective ceiling when no `riskTier` is declared: 
```ts
let riskTier = input.riskTier;
if (riskTier == null) {
  const category = categoryForAction(input.action ?? '');
  if (category != null) {
    const policy = await d.decider.getPolicy(category);
    const ceiling = computeEffectiveCeiling(policy);
    if (ceiling !== 'never-auto') {
      riskTier = ceiling; // Exclude<AutonomyCeiling, 'never-auto'> = RiskTier
    }
  }
}
```
 This makes the arm gate agree with the chokepoint: if the policy would auto-decide the action (risk ≤ ceiling), the arm gate uses the same ceiling as the risk and also says `auto` → tripwire arms. Falls through to `critical` only for unmapped actions or `never-auto` ceiling (still correctly gates). ## When you hit this [Section titled “When you hit this”](#when-you-hit-this) * You’re adding a new reversible verb to the arm seam (new `planWorkItemArm`-style wiring). * You see `autonomy_tripwires` empty despite policy being armed and auto-takes happening. * You’re debugging a caller that doesn’t pass `decision.riskTier` and wonder why no tripwires fire. ## What NOT to do [Section titled “What NOT to do”](#what-not-to-do) * **Don’t change `decider.ts`** to fix this — the D-002 fail-safe to `critical` is correct for the chokepoint (where an undeclared risk should be conservatively refused). Only the arm-call-site needs the ceiling-as-proxy logic, because it’s called *after* the chokepoint already approved the action. * **Don’t assume callers will pass `decision.riskTier`** — the arm seam must work correctly even when they don’t. ## Files [Section titled “Files”](#files) * `packages/operator-core/lib/autonomy/arm-reversible-action.ts` — the fix lives here * `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/work_items/arm-reversible-work-item.ts` — the work\_items wiring that calls it

# Arrow loses to JSON on Papercusp sync payloads (and why the estimate said otherwise)

> A measured negative result — Apache Arrow is net slower than JSON for our sync reads. Includes the two estimation mistakes that made it look like a win, both of which generalize.

**Verdict: do not convert Papercusp sync reads to Apache Arrow.** It is \~21ms/wave *slower* end-to-end on real data. This page exists so nobody re-proposes it from first principles, and — more usefully — so the two mistakes that made it look attractive don’t get repeated on the next format decision. Measured 2026-07-26 with `apache-arrow` v21.2.0. Full record: plan `arrow-zero-copy-sync-reads-2026-07-26` D-003. ## The numbers [Section titled “The numbers”](#the-numbers) Three fattest sync payloads, pulled live from `:3070`: 
```plaintext
                        JSON        Arrow      delta
  server encode        11.5 ms      41.3 ms   +29.8 ms
  client decode        11.5 ms       2.5 ms    -9.0 ms
  NET                  23.0 ms      43.8 ms   +20.9 ms   <== Arrow LOSES
  bytes on wire         3.97 MB      3.23 MB      -19%
```
 Arrow’s client decode really is \~4.6× faster and the wire really is 19% smaller. But `tableFromJSON` encode costs 3.6× what `JSON.stringify` does, and that swamps both wins. ## Mistake 1 — the estimate used a synthetic payload [Section titled “Mistake 1 — the estimate used a synthetic payload”](#mistake-1--the-estimate-used-a-synthetic-payload) The figure that motivated the work (55.1ms for the JSON path) came from a hand-built 12,000-row payload of uniform wide rows. Real sync payloads are 153–2,760 rows, and **V8’s `JSON.parse` is optimized C++** — it handles the real ones in 3–9ms, not 20ms. The synthetic number was 2–4× too pessimistic, which was enough to invert the conclusion. > **Generalizes to:** never size a serialization-format decision on synthetic data. Pull the real payload. It is usually one `curl` against the running operator. ## Mistake 2 — our rows are not tabular [Section titled “Mistake 2 — our rows are not tabular”](#mistake-2--our-rows-are-not-tabular) Arrow’s advantage is a columnar layout over flat, typed columns. Ours are nested blobs: | query | rows | size | shape | | ----------------- | ----- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | `plans.items` | 2,760 | 1.64 MB | 3 cols — **92% of bytes is one nested `item` dict per row** | | `plans.attention` | 153 | 1.53 MB | 7 cols — **98% of bytes is a nested `items` list** (\~10 KB/row) | | `plans.list` | 880 | 0.80 MB | 22 cols — the most tabular, and the **worst** result | `tableFromJSON` cannot infer heterogeneous nested structures, so they degrade to JSON-stringified strings held inside Arrow columns. That is still JSON parsing — just deferred to field-access time, after you have already paid Arrow’s encode. Note the shape of the failure: `plans.list`, the *most* column-like of the three, came out exactly break-even client-side (3.3ms vs 3.3ms) while costing +18.9ms to encode. More columns did not help. ## What would have to change before re-measuring [Section titled “What would have to change before re-measuring”](#what-would-have-to-change-before-re-measuring) The resolvers would have to emit **flat, typed, genuinely columnar rows**. That is projection work, not a format change. If that ever lands and payloads are still large, re-measure — but a format swap alone will not rescue this. ## The thing that was actually worth finding [Section titled “The thing that was actually worth finding”](#the-thing-that-was-actually-worth-finding) The measurement’s real value was diagnostic. Those three queries are 65% of a 5.94 MB hydration wave **and** the three slowest resolvers (905 / 620 / 577 ms). Size and latency share one cause: the `plans.*` sync resolvers do no projection at all — they pass through whatever `callPlansRead()` returns, whole nested object per row. Tracked as **WI-5910**. The chokepoint is `callPlansReadRaw` in `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/plans/read-dispatch.ts` (per the 2026-07-19 whole-app payload audit): it is the single in-process dispatch feeding both the `/api/admin/plans/*` REST routes and the `@papercusp/sync` `plans.*` resolvers, and agent/MCP sessions do not reach it — so a display projection there is UI-only and cannot regress the agent-facing payload tier. ## Two adjacent facts established by the same investigation [Section titled “Two adjacent facts established by the same investigation”](#two-adjacent-facts-established-by-the-same-investigation) * **The copy into the webview is 4.6ms per 6.65MB.** So true shared memory — an mmap’d store, or leaving the webview for a native/Electron renderer — is worth \~4.6ms. That is not a performance argument. If webview replacement is ever revisited, argue it on memory footprint (EI-278 records sustained `/adv` fetch load as the dominant workload behind a 16GB webview OOM), not on copies. * **Tauri 2.11.5 supports raw byte IPC bodies.** `InvokeResponseBody` has a `Raw(Vec<u8>)` variant and `Channel::send(data) where TSend: IpcResponse` accepts it. The `"Tauri's IPC serializer is JSON-based"` comment in `ipc-stream.ts` is v1-era and stale; every non-SSE sync response body is currently base64’d out and back (\~12ms/wave). Tracked as **WI-5911** — format-independent, so this verdict does not touch it. ## The pattern worth carrying [Section titled “The pattern worth carrying”](#the-pattern-worth-carrying) Three separate comments in this subsystem asserted constraints that had quietly expired and were being obeyed anyway: the batcher’s 6-connection-per-host justification (webapp-era, dead once desktop moved to IPC), `ipc-stream.ts`’s JSON-serializer claim (Tauri v1-era), and a stale client-side `AttentionKind` mirror. Each cost real time. When a comment states a constraint that is load-bearing for a design decision, **re-verify it before building on it** — especially a comment that predates a platform pivot.

# A source-text assertion cannot tell CONTRACT from DECORATION — and cannot see reachability at all

> Guarding a machine-readable marker line by regex-matching the emitting script's SOURCE reded the fleet's green gate twice on pure copy edits, and left two more pins armed. Why the defect is structural, the worse blind spot (a source pin passes whether the pinned code runs or is dead), the cheap test for executing instead, why the obvious 'ban prose in assertions' lint is the wrong fix (measured), and how to prove such a guard falsifiable without dirtying a tree git-sync sweeps.

## The shape [Section titled “The shape”](#the-shape) A script emits a machine-readable line that callers grep, with a human-readable line directly above it: 
```plaintext
No affected workspaces (and no repo-wide invariant guard matched the changed paths).
AFFECTED_TESTS_RESULT status=passed tasks=0 failed=0 … reason=no-affected-workspaces
```
 The guard for “the marker is emitted on every exit path” was written as a regex over the **source text** of `scripts/affected-tests.mjs`, pinning both lines. Twice, a pure copy edit to the prose — a trailing `.` added to `…none declare a 'test' script.`, then a clarifying tail added to `No affected workspaces` — turned the fleet’s green gate red. Nothing functional changed either time; the marker was emitted correctly throughout. Both times the fix loosened *that one* assertion and wrote a comment explaining why. Neither time did the sibling two feet away get the same treatment. When the class was finally reviewed, the same file still had **two** exact-prose pins armed (`'\nAll affected tests passed.'` and `non-quarantined task(s) failed:`) — a third and fourth recurrence already queued. > A fix applied to the instance instead of the class does not survive contact with the next edit. The tell that you are looking at a class is that the file **already contains a comment explaining the same lesson**. ## Blind spot 1 — contract vs decoration [Section titled “Blind spot 1 — contract vs decoration”](#blind-spot-1--contract-vs-decoration) A source-text regex cannot distinguish the **contract** (the marker a caller greps) from the **decoration** (the prose above it). So every wording edit is a coin flip against a shared gate. The cost is asymmetric and lands on a third party: the editor sees green locally if they skip the suite, and the gate reds for everyone else. > ⚠ This is the counterpoint to [negative assertions rot silently](/internal/docs/agent-insights/negative-assertions-rot-silently), which correctly notes that a POSITIVE literal-pinned assertion “fails loudly when the string is reworded, forcing you to look at it”. True — but on a shared gate, *loudly* means “in someone else’s run, about a change that is not theirs”. Loud is a virtue only when the failure is informative; here it is pure noise, because the pinned bytes were never the contract. ## Blind spot 2 — reachability (the worse one) [Section titled “Blind spot 2 — reachability (the worse one)”](#blind-spot-2--reachability-the-worse-one) A source-text assertion **passes identically whether the code it pins runs or is dead.** It asserts presence, not execution. That is not hypothetical. In this exact file’s subject, an early `process.exit(0)` sat 46 lines above the `REPO_WIDE_INVARIANT_GUARDS` loop, making every repo-wide guard unreachable for any change routing to no workspace — presenting as a healthy `AFFECTED_TESTS_RESULT status=passed tasks=0`. A source-shape guard would have stayed green through the entire bug, because the code it pinned was still *there*. Executing the path closes both holes at once: prose becomes free to change, and a path that stops being reachable fails loudly. ## The decision procedure [Section titled “The decision procedure”](#the-decision-procedure) Before reaching for a source-text regex, ask **“is this path cheap to DRIVE?”** — a question that is rarely asked, because the phrase “a full run needs a real repo tree and real test children” is usually true of the *expensive* path and gets generalised to all of them. Here it was false for exactly the paths that kept breaking. All three early-exit paths `exit(0)` **before** spawning any test child: | path | how to reach it | cost | | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | --------- | | `reason=no-affected-workspaces` | an unrouted path + `--exclude` every workspace in play | — | | `reason=no-test-script` | a routed path + `--exclude` every workspace in play | — | | `status=dry-run` | `--dry` | — | | | **all three combined** | **0.45s** | The assertions that keep breaking are often the cheapest ones to execute, because “emits X and exits early” is exactly the kind of path that has no expensive setup. Keep source-shape assertions only where driving the path is genuinely expensive (here: a real *failing* run needs real vitest children), and pin **code tokens** there — `resultLine('failed')`, `process.exit(1)` — never wording. ## Derive the fixture inputs; do not hardcode them [Section titled “Derive the fixture inputs; do not hardcode them”](#derive-the-fixture-inputs-do-not-hardcode-them) Reaching the empty-task exits requires excluding every workspace that would contribute a task. Today all 17 repo-wide guards live in `@papercusp/operator-core`, so `--exclude @papercusp/operator-core` works — and hardcoding that would reintroduce a staleness trap one level up from the prose pins being removed. Instead, read the script’s own `--dry` task list and exclude what it names: 
```ts
function workspacesInPlay(paths: string): string[] {
  const { stdout } = runAffected(['--changed-paths', paths, '--dry']);
  const names = new Set<string>();
  for (const line of stdout.split('\n')) {
    const m = /^\s+-\s+(\S+)\s+::\s+\S+$/.exec(line);
    if (m) names.add(m[1]);
  }
  return [...names];
}
```
 When an expectation *is* setup-dependent, say so **in the failure message**, so a stale fixture does not read as a broken contract: 
```ts
expect(
  fields.reason,
  `reached a different early-exit path than intended — either the marker contract changed, or this probe's --changed-paths/--exclude inputs went stale. Output:\n${stdout}`,
).toBe(c.reason);
```
 ## Do NOT build the obvious “guard for the guard” — measured [Section titled “Do NOT build the obvious “guard for the guard” — measured”](#do-not-build-the-obvious-guard-for-the-guard--measured) The tempting class fix is a lint banning human prose inside source-text assertions. **Measure the population before encoding that rule.** Across this repo: | | count | | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------ | | test files reading a file | 535 | | binding a var to `readFileSync` | 240 | | with ≥1 assertion pinning 3+ consecutive prose words | **22** | | such assertions | **57** | Bounded — but reading the hits, *most pin prose that genuinely IS the contract*: a generated doc’s `## heading`, a persona’s rule sentence, a projected prompt’s literal body. A lint on the pattern would fire mostly on **correct** assertions and would pressure people to loosen tests that should stay tight. The heuristic cannot separate contract-prose from decoration-prose — which is the same distinction the broken assertions could not make. A guard built on it inherits the defect it was meant to police. > Also: that probe **under-counted** its own target file (it missed the hyphenated `non-quarantined task(s) failed:`). A pattern census is a floor, not a total — state the filter whenever you report one. ## Proving it falsifiable without dirtying the shared tree [Section titled “Proving it falsifiable without dirtying the shared tree”](#proving-it-falsifiable-without-dirtying-the-shared-tree) A guard that has never failed is a guard you have not tested — but the obvious probe is unsafe here. git-sync sweeps the **whole** working tree every few minutes, so a mutation held in place for the length of a suite run can be **committed even when nothing goes wrong and no handler fails**. A `trap` does not fix that; it is a different race. The script resolves its own root (`resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..')`), so a bare `/tmp` copy resolves the wrong root and cannot run. Build a scratch root of **symlinks** instead — every repo entry linked, one real copy of the file under test — plus a test-only env seam pointing at it: 
```ts
const AFFECTED_TESTS = process.env.PAPERCUSP_AFFECTED_TESTS_SCRIPT
  ? resolve(process.env.PAPERCUSP_AFFECTED_TESTS_SCRIPT)
  : resolve(REPO_ROOT, 'scripts/affected-tests.mjs');
```
 Then prove all three directions — and note that the *passing* row is the one that matters: | mutation | expected | observed | | -------------------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | prose completely rewritten | **PASS** | ✅ 8/8 green | | marker emission deleted | FAIL | ✅ `expected exactly one marker line, got: []` | | `reason=` token renamed | FAIL | ✅ `expected 'nothing-selected' to be 'no-affected-workspaces'` | A falsifiability probe that only demonstrates failures has not shown the guard is *well-targeted* — only that it is sensitive. The row proving the guard **ignores** the change class that used to break it is what shows the fix actually landed. ## When a source-text assertion is still right [Section titled “When a source-text assertion is still right”](#when-a-source-text-assertion-is-still-right) * The path is genuinely expensive to execute (needs real test children, a real network, a real desktop). * The thing being asserted is a **source-order / structural** property that execution cannot observe — e.g. “the failure announcement and `process.exit(1)` are inseparable”, which is a claim about the code’s shape, not about any one run. * The prose **is** the contract (a generated doc’s heading, a persona rule) — then pin it exactly, and expect it to fail loudly on a reword, because that is the point.

# The attention/importance system (Planning tab)

> How plan-item importance + the unified AttentionItem feed fit together, and two non-obvious gotchas — parseWarnings become lint ERRORS, and (historically) the Plans tab had no in-app chat host (now superseded by the inline PlanChat host).

Superseded — Gotcha 2 no longer holds The “Plans tab has no in-app chat host” gotcha below is **out of date**. The Plans tab now ships a dedicated inline chat host, so Chat there is no longer a no-op: * `apps/operator/app/admin/plans/PlanChat.tsx` creates a harness-scoped chat (`POST /api/harness/:slug/agent-chats`, lines 39–63) and mounts `<ChatPanel slug chatId mode="discuss" />` **inline** (line 84) — exactly the host the original Gotcha 2 said was missing (inbox-cards-unification D-006). * It is wired into the Plans UI: `PlanItemPreview.tsx:192` (`{chatOpen ? <PlanChat harnessSlug={harnessSlug} label={…} /> : null}`) and `DiscussPanel.tsx:75` (`<PlanChat harnessSlug={item.harnessSlug} label={chatLabel} />`). * The no-harness case is handled with a clear message (`PlanChat.tsx:65–71`), not a silent no-op. * `PlanChatModal` and the bespoke `InboxItemActions` toolkit are **retired** (`PlanItemPreview.tsx:15–17`). The plan the original section pointed at as “open work,” `planning-attention-importance-2026-05-31` P-017, is **done**. Gotcha 1 (parseWarnings → lint errors) and the importance axis described in **What it is ¶1** remain accurate. The attention-feed source list in **¶2** has drifted (`plans-awaiting-review` was retired, `types.ts:171`; the feed gained operator-report / improvement / standing-approval / conversation / scout-grade kinds, `types.ts:22–34`) — treat that enumeration and the UI facet labels as point-in-time, not load-bearing. The original narrative is preserved below for history. ## What it is [Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is) Plan items carry an **importance** — a 4th axis orthogonal to status: `urgent | high | normal | low` (default `normal`), written as an `importance:` keyword on the item line and parsed glyph-agnostically like `blocked-by:`. It drives the Planning-tab sort/badges, the orchestrator’s halt-on-`urgent`, and (eventually) the push threshold. Source of truth: `@papercusp/plan-parser` (`IMPORTANCE_LEVELS`, `PlanItem.importance`); spec at [plan-format §Importance](/internal/docs/spec/plan-format#importance); rubric in [agent-policies §18](/internal/docs/agent-policies). The Planning tab also shows a **unified attention feed**: one `AttentionItem` read-model (`packages/operator-core/lib/attention/`) that every “needs the human” surface adapts into — plan items, coord escalations, coord messages-to-human, smoke-test failures, plans-awaiting-review. The `plans:attention` tool unions them (best-effort per source), grouped by plan + a synthetic per-harness “Alerts” bucket, importance-sorted. The UI filter facets are ToDos / Needs Human / Blocked (plan-item statuses) + Escalations / Messages / Smoke / Reviews (the non-plan-item kinds). ## Gotcha 1 — parseWarnings become lint ERRORS [Section titled “Gotcha 1 — parseWarnings become lint ERRORS”](#gotcha-1--parsewarnings-become-lint-errors) `plans:lint` turns **every** `parsed.parseWarnings` entry into a hard `parse_warning` **error** (`lint.ts`). So the parser must NOT push a parseWarning for a recoverable condition like an unknown `importance:` value — that would fail CI on a typo. Instead: * the parser **degrades silently** to `normal` (no parseWarning), and * `plans:lint` re-scans the item’s `rawLine` and emits a soft `unknown_importance` **warning** (never an error). If you add another tolerant item-keyword, follow the same split: degrade in the parser, warn (don’t error) in lint. ## Gotcha 2 — the Plans tab has no in-app chat host [Section titled “Gotcha 2 — the Plans tab has no in-app chat host”](#gotcha-2--the-plans-tab-has-no-in-app-chat-host) The in-app agent chat (`ChatPanel` via `AdvChatPanel`) is hosted **only by the `/adv` HarnessesDock**, opened by an `OPEN_CHAT_EVENT` that the dock listens for (`openFeatureChat` → `POST /api/harness/:slug/agent-chats` → dispatch event). The **Plans admin tab is not inside that dock**, so an `openFeatureChat`-style call there creates a chat that opens nowhere visible. The PlanItemPreview/PlanOtherList “Chat” buttons fall back to `launchAgent` (an external OMP/claude terminal session), which on desktop is invisible/no-op if the agent isn’t configured — hence “Chat does nothing.” To make Chat work in the Plans tab you must add a host (e.g. a modal that creates a chat and renders `<ChatPanel slug chatId />` directly), and a chat needs a **harness** (`agent_chats` is per-harness-schema) — pure SU plans with no harness can’t host one. This is the open work in `planning-attention-importance-2026-05-31` P-017. ## Related: the unified owner Inbox (2026-07-17) [Section titled “Related: the unified owner Inbox (2026-07-17)”](#related-the-unified-owner-inbox-2026-07-17) `owner-inbox-single-pane-2026-07-17` widens this same `AttentionItem` feed with more sources (every kind’s `needs_human`/blocked work-items, registered owner-walls, pending dark-flag ratifications, hook- and transcript-derived owner-gates from any client) and adds reply routing back to a live asker plus a session chat popup on top of the feed described above — see [owner-inbox-single-pane-capture-architecture](/agent-insights/owner-inbox-single-pane-capture-architecture).

> How needs-human / escalation / smoke notifications get delivered — event-driven at the source (notifyAttention), to mobile push + an in-app toast (native desktop OS notification now opt-in). No more 60s poll.

Everything else (the `notifyAttention` two-channel fail-safe, the escalation/smoke-fail/needs-human gating, the importance map for live kinds, the deleted 60s poll) still holds. ## What it is [Section titled “What it is”](#what-it-is) The flip side of [the attention/importance system](/internal/docs/agent-insights/attention-importance-system): how an attention item that needs a human becomes a **push notification** on the user’s devices. Implemented by `planning-attention-importance-2026-05-31` P-020/P-021/D-007 (2026-05-31). This is the map. ## One helper, two channels, event-driven [Section titled “One helper, two channels, event-driven”](#one-helper-two-channels-event-driven) Everything funnels through **`notifyAttention()`** in `packages/operator-core/lib/attention-notify.ts`. Producers call it at the source the moment a ≥high attention item appears; it fans out to two independently fail-safe channels (a delivery error is logged and swallowed — it never propagates into the producer’s write path): 1. **Mobile** — `notifyWorkspace(wsId, payload)` → `packages/operator-core/lib/device-push-dispatcher.ts` → APNs/FCM to devices paired in `harness_shared.mobile_push_tokens`. No-op when none are paired. `data` must be string-valued and `kind` a `PushKind` — the helper coerces/maps. 2. **Desktop-native** — emits an `attention.notify` event on the sync SSE bus (`notifySyncInvalidate`). The webview’s `DesktopAttentionNotifier` (`apps/operator/app/_components/`, mounted once at the root, app-level so `@papercusp/sync` stays domain-free) shows an in-app **sonner toast** always, and in the Tauri shell invokes the **`show_attention_notification`** Rust command (`papercusp-desktop`, `tauri-plugin-notification`) for a native OS notification. Driven from Rust, so no JS-facing notification capability is needed; the command is app-defined → allowed by default. **No 60s poll.** The old `device-intervention-watcher` (a `setInterval(60s)` catch-all that SELECTed the three tables) was **deleted** in P-021 — its triggers now emit at the source. ## Where those rows are written (the producer chokepoints) [Section titled “Where those rows are written (the producer chokepoints)”](#where-those-rows-are-written-the-producer-chokepoints) The fs-watcher mirror for these three tables is **retired** (see the long comment block in `harness-fs-watcher.ts`). They’re now written **at producer time** by three internal endpoints: * `POST /api/internal/escalation-event` → `harness_escalations` * `POST /api/internal/smoke-test-event` → `harness_smoke_test` * `POST /api/internal/plan-review-event` → `harness_plan_review` So an event-driven emit for these has a clean home (those 3 endpoints) — but see the coupling gotcha below. ## The importance map (what the ≥high gate includes) [Section titled “The importance map (what the ≥high gate includes)”](#the-importance-map-what-the-high-gate-includes) P-020 pushes only at importance **≥ high**. The per-kind importance lives in `packages/operator-core/lib/attention/adapters.ts`: | Kind | importance | | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | smoke-fail | `high` (fixed) | | plan-review | `high` (fixed) | | coord escalation | `severityToImportance(sev)` — blocker→`urgent`, question→`high`, advisory→`low` | | coord message-to-human | `normal` | | plan item | the item’s own `importance:` keyword | Note `harness_escalations` (the table the watcher polls) has **no severity column** — it’s a harness-level escalation, distinct from a *coord* escalation. Treat it as inherently high. Net: the watcher’s three triggers are all already high, so the watcher never pushed low-importance noise to begin with. ## The four producer call-sites + their once-per-event gating [Section titled “The four producer call-sites + their once-per-event gating”](#the-four-producer-call-sites--their-once-per-event-gating) `notifyAttention()` is called at exactly the points that *create* a ≥high attention item — there’s no poll, so each must fire **once per genuine event**: | Source | Where | Fire condition | | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | escalation | `endpoint-route/routes/internal/escalation-event.ts` | `escalation != null` (skip notes-only updates) | | smoke-fail | `endpoint-route/routes/internal/smoke-test-event.ts` | **transition** into failing — reads prior `status`, fires only on `pass→fail` / first fail | | plan-review | `internal/plan-review-event.ts` | every call (the producer posts once per completed review) | | needs-human | `plans:set-status` | transition INTO `needs-human` at importance ≥ high (`shouldPushNeedsHuman` + `itemImportance`) | Why this was safe to do at once: each source is its own chokepoint, so there’s **no double-fire** (the poll that used to also push escalation/smoke/plan-review is gone). The gating above prevents re-pushing on idempotent re-writes. The trade vs the old poll: the poll was a catch-all that fired regardless of write path; source emits only fire from these four sites — if a *new* write path for those tables appears, wire `notifyAttention` into it too. ## Extending it [Section titled “Extending it”](#extending-it) * **New attention source:** call `notifyAttention({ kind, title, body, harnessSlug, importance })` at the write site. Add the kind to `AttentionNotifyKind` + `MOBILE_KIND` if it needs a distinct mobile route. * **The desktop native notification needs a cargo rebuild** of `papercusp-desktop` to pick up `tauri-plugin-notification` + the `show_attention_notification` command. The toast + mobile push work without it; the native OS notification is a no-op (caught) until the rebuild. * End-to-end delivery (APNs/FCM, native OS notification) is **not headless-testable** — verify in the desktop shell. The `notifyAttention` fan-out + the gates are unit-tested (`attention-notify.test.ts`, `set-status.test.ts`).

# Attributing a change despite git-sync squash: git blame lies here — search sessions instead

> git-sync squashes every agent's commits under the OWNER'S OWN git identity, so git blame/log/show don't just fail to name the authoring agent — they actively name the owner, on every line, always. An agent that trusts blame gets a confident false 'the owner wrote this' (it has already produced a blocker escalation accusing the owner of an agent's own broken migration — WI-5111). This doc gives the channels that actually work — timestamp-correlated sessions:search — versus the ones that look plausible but dead-end (git blame, change_ledger, audit:list), using a real hunt for the green-checkpoint quiet-cut feature as the worked example.

Blame doesn't return 'unknown' — it returns the OWNER's name, and it is lying This is the part that bites, and it is worse than a dead end. A dead end returns nothing and you move on. **This returns `the owner` — on every line of every file, always** — so an agent that trusts blame doesn’t get *no* answer, it gets a confident **wrong** one: “the owner wrote this.” That reads as strong evidence precisely because blame *is* real evidence in every other repo. It has already caused real harm. On 2026-07-17 a release-fixer triaging a green-checkpoint red ran blame, concluded the owner had made the P-020 `gpt-5.6-luna` role-model migration, and sent the owner a **blocker** escalation opening *“ROOT CAUSE (single, confirmed by git blame): **your** 2026-07-16 migration … **you** updated the orchestrator’s OWN tests”* — then asked him to adjudicate a model-ranking decision an agent had already made and landed. Every clause was false: an agent session executing WI-4640 / plan item P-020 made the change, and simply hadn’t run the operator-core consumers of `roleModelDefault`. An agent’s own incomplete work was escalated to the owner **as the owner’s mistake**, with blame cited as proof. (WI-5111.) So: never write *“your change”* / *“you updated X”* / *“the owner’s migration”* on the strength of git metadata. “Confirmed by git blame” is not a phrase that can be true in this repo. If you cannot name the author from a session transcript or the commissioning work-item, say **“not attributable from the available record”** — never name a person.
