They are NOT harness ops. *apps/desktop/src/lib/local-dbos-wiring.ts* (hypothetical third-party harness, per the note above) launches DBOS (mirrors `operator-core/lib/dbos/bootstrap.ts`: `DBOS.setConfig({systemDatabaseUrl: <embedded PG>, systemDatabaseSchemaName:'dbos', applicationVersion, runAdminServer:false})` → `registerWorkflow` + `registerScheduled` → `launch()`). The cadence seam already existed: the engine drives its loop through an injected `Scheduler` and exposes `TradingEngine.tick()`; the live-loop’s per-cycle work is `createLiveLoopRunner().runCycle()` (factored out of `startLiveLoop`). In **DBOS mode** the wiring DOESN’T start the in-process loop — it BINDS the per-tick fn (`bindEngineTick` / `bindLiveLoopCycle`), and a `DBOS.registerScheduled` workflow fires it on a crontab derived from the loop’s `intervalMs` (`intervalToCrontab`: sub-minute → seconds field). Each fire is a durable, checkpointed workflow; an in-flight tick that crashes is recovered on restart. `SchedulerMode.ExactlyOncePerIntervalWhenActive` SKIPS make-up work for slots missed while the sidecar was down — a restart never replays a backlog of stale trading ticks. **Gate:** `MYAPP_ENGINE_DBOS=1` (default-OFF). OFF ⇒ the engine + live-loop run their existing in-process loops byte-for-byte and DBOS is never imported/launched (D-005 unchanged). ON ⇒ `serve.ts` builds them in `dbosMode`, then `launchLocalDbos` registers a scheduled workflow per ENABLED cadence and launches; the DBOS scheduler is stopped FIRST in the shutdown sequence so no tick fires into a half-torn-down engine. Verified live (`local-dbos-wiring.integration.test.ts`): DBOS boots against a real PG, runs its migrations, and the scheduled `myappEngineTick` workflow fires the bound tick on the crontab.

# Harness tests gate feature approval, and link to plans through the VAL

> The V2 tester writes one black-box test per VAL; the validator runs them as the approval gate. VALs live in harness_plan_assertions (inline plan bullets via plans:promote) — NOT validation-contract.md or a validation_criteria table. The plan↔test link is a rollup join on the VAL.

How the harness testing system fits together after `harness-tests-tab-and-tester-promotion-2026-05-26` (phases A–E + G). If you’re touching the tester, validator, the harness Tests tab, or anything that reads VAL assertions, start here. ## The VAL is the single join key [Section titled “The VAL is the single join key”](#the-val-is-the-single-join-key) A **VAL** (`VAL-{plan-slug}-{NNN}`) is one binding behavioral assertion. It is the only thing that links plans, features, tests, and the validator: * **Plan item** authors VALs as inline `[VAL-…]` sub-bullets (`Verify:` / `Evidence:` / `Status:` / optional `RequiresTest:`). `plans:promote` parses them (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/plans/val-assertions.ts`) and writes them to PG. * **Feature** carries them in `claims[]` (set by `plans:promote`). * **Test** declares `coversVALs[]` in `.papercusp/tests.json`. * **Validator** resolves them by id to decide pass/fail. VALs live in harness\_plan\_assertions Do **not** read `.papercusp/validation-contract.md` (retired by plans-central-harness-ux-2026-05-26 D-005) and do **not** add a `validation_criteria` table (the original plan proposed one; it was dropped). The canonical store is `harness_shared.harness_plan_assertions`, keyed by `(workspace_id, harness_slug, val_id)`, with `plan_slug` / `item_id` / `verify_text` / `evidence_text` / `status` / `requires_test`. Resolve a VAL via `GET /api/harness/:slug/assertion/:valId`. ## The gate: tester writes, validator runs, approval requires green [Section titled “The gate: tester writes, validator runs, approval requires green”](#the-gate-tester-writes-validator-runs-approval-requires-green) The staging loop (`libs/papercusp/.../prompts/staging/`) gates feature approval on tests: 1. A feature is `validating` (worker committed). The orchestrator’s **C0** decision emits `NEXT_TESTER <F> <VAL>` for each claim VAL with no passing covering test. (`NEXT_TESTER` is wired in the **DBOS pipeline** — `packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/orchestrator-decide.ts` dispatches the `tester` role; bash `run.sh` AND the TS run-loop (`main-loop.ts`, archived 2026-06-06 to `_retired/orchestrator-run-loop/`) are both retired. The prompt just needed to start emitting it.) 2. The **tester** (`staging/tester.md`) writes one black-box test per VAL, registers it in `.papercusp/tests.json` with `coversVALs`, exits. 3. Once every test-requiring VAL has a passing test, the orchestrator sends the feature to the **validator** (`staging/validator.md` V2), whose primary gate is **running** the VAL-covering tests. An untested required claim is a FAIL. A VAL with `requires_test: false` (copy, design-spec, judgement) is **exempt** — the gate skips it; the validator verifies it by inspection. Default is `true`. ## The plan↔test link is a rollup, not a new edge [Section titled “The plan↔test link is a rollup, not a new edge”](#the-plantest-link-is-a-rollup-not-a-new-edge) There is **no** `test → plan-item` foreign key. The link is computed by joining through the VAL (`packages/operator-core/lib/harness-test-rollup.ts`, pure + unit-tested): * `/api/internal/test-snapshot` drives `harness_plan_assertions.status` from covering-test outcomes (`deriveAssertionStatus`) and stamps `plan_slug` / `item_ids` onto each test row. * `GET /api/harness/:slug/plan-items-test-status` and `plans:get`’s `planItemTests` both call `computePlanItemTestStatus` → per-plan-item `{ valsTotal, valsRequiringTest, valsCovered, valsPassing }`. * The Plans UI badge (`decoratePlanItemTestBadges`) and the harness Tests tab’s Acceptance view render from that. ## Surfacing tests for a plan that was never promoted [Section titled “Surfacing tests for a plan that was never promoted”](#surfacing-tests-for-a-plan-that-was-never-promoted) The happy path above assumes the plan was promoted (`plans:promote`) so its features + VALs exist in PG. A plan implemented **directly via `plans:set-status`** (no promote — common for infra/refactor work an su drives outside the feature pipeline) has **zero features** in `harness_features_consolidated` and **zero VALs** in `harness_plan_assertions`, so its tests have nothing to link to. Two options: * **Register Built-in tier** — add the test files to `.papercusp/tests.json` with `coversVALs: []`. They show in the Tests tab’s **test list** (`harnessTests.byHarness`) but not the per-VAL Acceptance view (same tier as lint/typecheck). No side effects. * **Promote for the Acceptance link** — author `[VAL-…]` sub-bullets on the plan items, then `plans:promote`. This **mints harness features** from the plan items (a first-time promote on a done plan injects features into the pipeline) — deliberate, not free. Use when you want the per-VAL Acceptance view. harness\_tests is CI-posted — empty on the dev box The Tests tab reads `harness_tests`, written by the **CI / green-checkpoint runner** posting to `/api/internal/test-snapshot` (a replace-all-per- `(harness,phase)` upsert). On the **dev box `harness_tests` is empty** — a local `vitest` run does not populate the tab. Register the test (tests.json + a matching registry glob, enforced by `npm --prefix apps/operator run lint:tests`, else it’s an invisible orphan); the tab fills through CI, not a dev run. ## Where things live [Section titled “Where things live”](#where-things-live) * **`@papercusp/testing-shell`** — `TestingShell` (left-rail + panel host), `DomainTestPanel`, the `universalDomains` registry (Built-in/Universal tier, pure data — `src/registry/universal.ts`), and the `TestingDataSource` interface. The lib↔operator boundary *is* the universal↔Papercusp boundary. * **operator** — `packages/operator-core/lib/testing-domains-registry.ts` (`papercuspRegistry`, \~35 Papercusp domains as of 2026-06-30, composed with the lib’s universal tier into `adminRegistry`), the harness `/testing/*` routes, and the `/adv` `HarnessTestsView` + `AcceptancePanel`. The harness Tests tab is an `/adv` dock panel (`adv:tests`), not a `HarnessDashboard` tab — that monolith was deleted by the `/adv` migration.

# The harness testing:run ad-hoc runner can stamp a test_runs row with a commit sha it never actually ran at

> POST /harness/:slug/testing/run executes vitest against the shared, concurrently-edited working tree and sampled commit sha AFTER the run — a torn read that can misattribute a red to an innocent commit. Fixed with a worktree_dirty flag (EI-18795303393201472, migration 709).

**If you’re diagnosing a `harness_shared.test_runs` row whose named failing test(s) don’t exist in the commit it’s stamped with (`git show <sha>:<file> | grep <test name>` comes back empty at that sha AND its neighbors), suspect a torn read from the harness-scoped ad-hoc runner before you suspect the ledger itself is corrupt** — this is a known, fixed-at-the-source class of misattribution, distinct from [gate-red-on-quarantined-file-phantom-attribution](/internal/docs/agent-insights/gate-red-on-quarantined-file-phantom-attribution) (that one is a log-parsing bug in the isolated green-checkpoint run; this one is a genuine torn read against the live shared tree). ## The signature (incident 2026-07-27, EI-18795303393201472) [Section titled “The signature (incident 2026-07-27, EI-18795303393201472)”](#the-signature-incident-2026-07-27-ei-18795303393201472) A `test_runs` row (`status='fail'`, `source` from the harness Tests-tab path) named test cases that exist in NO commit near its stamped `commit_sha` — only in a LATER commit, once the author’s edit (which was mid-flight when the run executed) finished landing. `git log`/mtimes showed: the test file was written to the tree, the ad-hoc run executed a few seconds later (before the matching implementation was written), and the implementation landed after that. The run observed a state that was never a commit and never will be. ## Root cause [Section titled “Root cause”](#root-cause) `POST /harness/:slug/testing/run` (`endpoint-route/routes/harness/testing.ts`, backing the `testing:run` MCP tool) runs `npx vitest run <files>` **synchronously, `cwd: root`, against the shared, concurrently-edited working tree** — not an isolated checkout (unlike the actual green-checkpoint gate, which per its own header comment always judges a dedicated isolated worktree). It then called `git rev-parse HEAD` to stamp `commit_sha` **after the run finished**. Between the run starting and that sample, a peer’s edit or a git-sync commit can change what’s on disk, so the stamped sha can name a commit whose real content never matches what vitest actually executed. This matters beyond a single false-attribution report: `ledgerFilesForCandidate` / `verifyGateVerdict` (`why-chain.ts`, WI-4533/EI-17603) treat `test_runs` rows matched by `commit_sha` as **first-hand evidence** to cross-check the release gate’s own named failures for the EXACT candidate under verdict. A torn-read row can poison that very cross-check for an unrelated commit that happens to share the stamp. ## The fix (migration 709) [Section titled “The fix (migration 709)”](#the-fix-migration-709) The runner now snapshots `{ commit, git status --porcelain -- <files> }` **both before and after** the vitest run (`computeWorktreeDirty` in `testing-run-store.ts`). Any mismatch — HEAD moved, or the tested files carry uncommitted changes at either snapshot, or either git read failed (fail-safe: unreadable ⇒ treated as dirty) — marks the row `worktree_dirty = true`. `ledgerFilesForCandidate` excludes dirty rows from its commit-scoped first-hand-evidence query (`AND worktree_dirty = false`); the time-windowed proxy `recentFailingFiles` deliberately keeps them, since “something failed recently, somewhere” doesn’t depend on sha precision. Not yet covered by the same fix (filed as follow-up, same failure class): `testing-run-store.ts`’s `persistFallbackRow` (the node/shell admin-suite fallback path) and the in-process vitest reporter used by admin-ui spawns both sample git context after their run finishes too — lower blast radius (their commit\_sha isn’t the primary input to `ledgerFilesForCandidate`’s gate cross-check today) but the same hazard shape.

# Harness Tests-tab domains are harness-owned, not operator-hardwired

> The harness Tests tab's domain nav comes from the harness's OWN contract at <worktree>/.papercusp/testing-domains.json (served by GET /api/harness/:slug/testing/domains), falling back to the generic generalized+Acceptance set. Do not special-case a harness in operator code. Also — harness endpoints resolve against reg.current (the global active workspace), so a CLI curl can silently hit the wrong workspace.

Two things to know before you touch the harness **Tests** tab (`/adv` → `HarnessTestsView` → `@papercusp/testing-shell`, backed by `/api/harness/:slug/testing/*`). ## The domain nav is HARNESS-owned data, not an operator registry [Section titled “The domain nav is HARNESS-owned data, not an operator registry”](#the-domain-nav-is-harness-owned-data-not-an-operator-registry) The operator’s testing API (`/api/admin/testing/*`; the old `/admin/testing` UI route was removed 2026-06-11) reads `adminRegistry` (the 1-domain Universal tier — `routes` only; the former 8-domain “generalized” set was narrowed down as the portable tabs moved to custom-panel domains via `UNIVERSAL_PANEL_DOMAINS` in `@papercusp/testing-shell`, which are appended client-side and are NOT part of `adminRegistry` — plus \~35 Papercusp domains, i.e. `[...operatorUniversal, ...papercuspRegistry]`) from `packages/operator-core/lib/testing-domains-registry.ts` — operator-internal code. The **harness** Tests tab does NOT import that. Each harness declares its own test domains in its contract surface: 
```plaintext
<worktree>/.papercusp/testing-domains.json   ->  { domains: TestDomain[], tierLabels?: {} }
```
 served by `GET /api/harness/:slug/testing/domains` (`endpoint-route/routes/harness/testing.ts` → `loadHarnessDomains(root)`). A harness that declares **no** file falls back to the generic `harnessTestingRegistry` (Built-in *Universal* tier + Acceptance — `[...universalDomains, ACCEPTANCE_DOMAIN]`, in `packages/operator-core/lib/harness-testing-registry.ts`). The frontend fetches that route for its nav; it does not import a static registry. Don't special-case a harness in operator code The wrong fix (rejected) was `isSelfHarness(slug) ? adminRegistry : …` wired into the view/route. That hard-wires the operator’s internal registry into a harness surface. The right place for a harness’s test config is the harness’s own `.papercusp/` contract — the same surface where `tests.json` (tester-created tests) lives. To give a harness more domains, write its `.papercusp/testing-domains.json`; don’t edit operator code. The **papercup dogfood harness** (its worktree IS the operator repo) ships a `.papercusp/testing-domains.json` **generated from `adminRegistry`** (so there’s no hand-maintained drift) — that’s why its Tests tab shows the full `adminRegistry` set while a generic harness shows the sparse Universal tier + Acceptance. Regenerate it the same way (load `adminRegistry` + the Acceptance domain, serialize) if the domains change. Note that several Universal-tier domains are `admin-suite` runners that are non-functional in the harness data-source, and others (`live-web`/`chaos-web`/`routes`) glob operator-internal paths — so for a *non-papercup* harness the Built-in tier is mostly empty; that’s expected, not a bug. Default the nav to the first non-`universal` (content-bearing) tab. The contract DOES drift on the dev box — regenerate it by hand “Generated from `adminRegistry` so there’s no hand-maintained drift” is the *intent*, not the dev-box reality. The only guards that catch a stale `.papercusp/testing-domains.json` (or a test file that matches no domain glob → invisible in the tab) are `gen:contract:check` and `lint:tests` — and those run **only in GitHub Actions CI** (`.github/workflows/test.yml`). git-sync commits the shared tree with `[skip ci]`, and the local green-checkpoint gate runs only `npm run test:affected` (the registry self-tests check structure, not contract↔registry freshness). So on the dev box a stale contract sails straight to `main`/`:3070` and the Tests tab silently shows old domains. Found 2026-06-18: the committed contract was stale and a real test (`gitnexus-bridge/index.test.ts`) was an uncaught orphan. **After ANY edit to `testing-domains-registry.ts`, run `npx tsx scripts/gen-testing-domains-contract.ts` + `npm --prefix apps/operator run lint:tests`** yourself — do not trust the tab to reflect a registry change, and do not trust CI to have caught a stale contract. (Systemic fix tracked separately — wire both gates into green-checkpoint.) ## Harness endpoints resolve against `reg.current` — your curl can hit the wrong workspace [Section titled “Harness endpoints resolve against reg.current — your curl can hit the wrong workspace”](#harness-endpoints-resolve-against-regcurrent--your-curl-can-hit-the-wrong-workspace) `resolvePhasedProject(slug, phase)` resolves the harness from the registry scoped to `activeWorkspaceId()`, which reads `current` from `~/.papercusp-workspaces/registry.json` — a **single global** value, not per-request. The `:3070` host serves whatever `reg.current` is *right now*. This bites hard when debugging: a `curl /api/harness/papercup/...` returns `{"error":"unknown project"}` not because the harness is gone, but because `reg.current` is a workspace that doesn’t contain it (it switches under you — the desktop, or a concurrent agent, flips it). I burned real time concluding “the papercup harness was deleted” when it was simply that `reg.current` had moved from `papercusp-workspace` to `default` mid-session. Corollary: server-side edits to `harness/testing.ts` need a host restart (`systemctl --user restart papercup-dev-api.service`) — the `:3070` host has no hot-reload — and frontend edits to `HarnessTestsView` ship via the operator-vite watch-build + a desktop reload. ## What the harness testing routes expose (current as of 2026-06-30) [Section titled “What the harness testing routes expose (current as of 2026-06-30)”](#what-the-harness-testing-routes-expose-current-as-of-2026-06-30) `endpoint-route/routes/harness/testing.ts` exports these routes: * `GET /harness/:slug/testing/domains` — harness-owned domains + tier labels (the one this page is about). * `GET /harness/:slug/testing/domain-detail` — file list + runners for one domain. * `GET /harness/:slug/testing/file-status` — per-file pass/fail chips (Acceptance domain only; built-in domains render “none”). * `GET /harness/:slug/testing/health-strip` — minimal flake/duration strip. * `POST /harness/:slug/testing/run` — synchronous vitest run. Now also runs the JSON reporter alongside `default`, parses the JSON file via `parseVitestJsonForHarnessRows`, and persists one `harness_shared.test_runs` row per file via `persistHarnessTestRuns` (best-effort, fail-soft — a DB error never changes the run result the panel sees). This is how the pot’s Tests tab renders per-file run history without per-repo scaffolding. * `GET /harness/:slug/testing/file-history` — per-file run history from `harness_shared.test_runs`, scoped to this harness + workspace. Backs the status-chip history sheet in the Tests tab. * `GET /harness/:slug/testing/assertions` — list VAL assertions from `harness_shared.harness_plan_assertions` (optionally filtered by `?plan=`). * `POST /harness/:slug/testing/assertions/:valId` — patch `requires_test` on a VAL. * `GET /harness/:slug/plan-items-test-status` — per-plan-item coverage rollup via `computePlanItemTestStatus` (joins assertions ↔ tests through the VAL). `resolveCtx` also handles `kind:'pot'` harnesses: a repo-less pot harness has its `path` pointing to the pot state dir, so `resolveCtx` now calls `resolveHarnessContentPath` to find the member repo’s worktree for glob walks.

# The 4-kind harness-tree classifier + qualified-slug rule

> When walking a git repo's nested .git entries, classify each as submodule / worktree / standalone / plain-dir, and derive qualified slugs for submodules. Used by the harness-creation flow to decide what becomes a sub-harness.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) When you point the harness-creation flow at an existing git repo (Entries 1, 2, or 3 of the §3 create-harness wizard), it walks the directory looking for nested `.git` entries and decides whether each one becomes a sub-harness, a separate root harness, or part of the parent. The classifier lives at `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/classify-tree.ts` (papercusp-dogfood-v5 P-007). There are **four classified kinds**, plus a fifth rule that derives the sub-harness slug for submodules: 1. **Submodule** — `.git` is a *file* whose contents point into the parent repo’s `.git/modules/<name>/`. → Becomes a **sub-harness**. 2. **Worktree** — `.git` is a *file* whose contents point into the same repo’s `.git/worktrees/<name>/`. → **NOT a new harness** (it’s an additional checkout of the same repo, which is what phases already are). 3. **Standalone** — `.git` is a *directory* with its own `HEAD` etc. → Becomes a **separate root harness**, not a sub-harness. 4. **Plain dir** (no `.git`) — just part of the parent repo. → No harness. 5. **Qualified slug** — a submodule’s slug is path-qualified as `<parentSlug>/<relPath>` (for example `papercup/libs/papercusp`). This is a field on the `submodule` result, not a separate classified kind. ## Why distinguishing matters [Section titled “Why distinguishing matters”](#why-distinguishing-matters) The three “has-nested-.git” cases (1, 2, 3) all look superficially the same: there’s a `.git` somewhere below the root. But they mean completely different things: * **Submodule**: the parent repo deliberately references a separate upstream repo, pinned to a commit. It IS a logical sub-project of the parent. Sub-harness is right. * **Worktree**: the parent repo has multiple checked-out branches living side by side, sharing one object store. Each worktree is the SAME project. Treating it as a sub-harness would duplicate the harness for every phase the user has materialized. * **Standalone**: someone happened to clone an unrelated repo inside the parent’s directory. Not part of the parent’s project at all. Should be a separate root, not a sub of the parent. Getting this wrong creates ghost harnesses, double-counts work, or makes the harness tree feel arbitrary. ## How the rules detect each case [Section titled “How the rules detect each case”](#how-the-rules-detect-each-case) The classifier reads the first line of `<dir>/.git` and pattern-matches: 
```plaintext
.git is a directory          → standalone (rule 3)
.git contents start with
  "gitdir: <abs>/.git/modules/" → submodule (rule 1)
  "gitdir: <abs>/.git/worktrees/" → worktree (rule 2)
  malformed / unknown target → plain (rule 4, conservative fallback)
```
 For directories without `.git`, the walker descends into them. It also descends into submodules by default (`recurseIntoSubmodules: true`) so sub-sub-harnesses can be discovered; callers that only want direct children pass `recurseIntoSubmodules: false`. Worktrees and standalone repos are never recursed into. ## Real-world layout (papercup itself) [Section titled “Real-world layout (papercup itself)”](#real-world-layout-papercup-itself) papercup has (after the 2026-05-31 borrowable-submodule regroup under `libs/generic/`, the `test-config`/`testing-shell` promotions, snapshot-system retirement, and `zero-harness` de-materialization): * 1 tree root: the papercup repo at `/home/dev/papercupai-workspace/papercup` * 6 direct-child submodules under `libs/`: `agent-chat`, `papercusp-db`, `papercusp-shared`, `papercusp`, `test-config`, `testing-shell` (the formerly-direct `git-graph`/`papergrid`/`sync`/`ui-primitives` submodules now live under `libs/generic/`; `zero-harness` is retired and not materialized) * 6 plain dirs under `libs/`: `flags`, `generic`, `holepunch-spike`, `host-platform`, `marketplace-public-ui`, `papercusp-publish-auth` (`generic/` itself is plain at depth 0 — it holds the regrouped borrowable submodules below it) * Many worktrees in siblings of the papercup repo (`papercup-backup`, `papercup-design-migration`, etc.) — those are detected if a future walk starts above papercup, but the classifier never confuses them for new harnesses. Total direct `libs/` count: 12 dirs (6 submodules + 6 plain), exactly what the test asserts against: packages/operator-core/lib/harness/classify-tree.test.ts 
```ts
it('matches the libs/ layout: 6 submodules + 6 plain (borrowable submodules regrouped under libs/generic/)', ...)
```
 ## When you touch this code [Section titled “When you touch this code”](#when-you-touch-this-code) * **Adding a 6th rule** (e.g. `git-annex` repos, fossil repos)? Add to the precedence list and update the test count. The classifier is a pure function over (path, fs) → outcome; tests are cheap. * **Changing the walker boundary**? The current default stops recursion at worktrees and standalone repos, but recurses into submodules unless `recurseIntoSubmodules: false`. If you change that, you’ll change whether nested submodules become visible to harness creation. * **Changing the slug derivation**? Sub-harness slugs are path-qualified relative to the tree root (e.g. `papercup/libs/sync`). Changing this collides with existing harness registry entries. ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/classify-tree.ts` — the classifier * `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/plans/source.ts` — uses `detectPapercupRoot` (same shape) to find the papercup repo for Phase 4 dogfood self-registration (formerly `harness/register-papercup.ts`) * v5 plan §2 — the architectural treatment of harness hierarchy reflecting submodule hierarchy

# Headless desktop testing needs real GL — bare Xvfb gives blank screenshots

> WebKitGTK on a plain Xvfb has no GPU/GL, so it never paints the webview — every screenshot comes back uniformly blank-white regardless of the DOM. Looks like a broken/blank app; it isn't. Use VirtualGL (vglrun -d egl0) on an isolated Xvfb, or run on :0. Verified recipe + the exact gotchas.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) When you drive the Tauri desktop on a headless box by spawning a bare `Xvfb` and screenshotting it (`import -window …`), **every screenshot comes back uniformly blank white — regardless of what the webview’s DOM actually contains.** It looks exactly like a broken or non-rendering app. It is not. The DOM is fine; the *pixels* never render. Why: a plain `Xvfb` is a software framebuffer with **no DRI3 / no GL**. The tell is in the app log: 
```plaintext
libEGL warning: DRI3 error: Could not get DRI3 device
```
 WebKitGTK’s accelerated compositor can’t get a GL context, so it never paints the webview to the framebuffer. The window chrome (titlebar, drawn by the WM) shows up; the webview content area is blank. This burned \~hours in the desktop-ipc Phase-4 packaged smoke (2026-06-01): the “blank window” across every boot was read as a render failure, when it was purely the GL-less Xvfb. The giveaway was that **every screenshot was the exact same byte size** — the framebuffer never changed because nothing ever painted into it. ## Why it’s easy to miss [Section titled “Why it’s easy to miss”](#why-its-easy-to-miss) * On a **release** build there’s no dev bridge (`#[cfg(debug_assertions)]`), so a screenshot is your *only* introspection — and it lies (blank). * On a **debug** build the bridge (`tauri-agent-tools`) reads the **DOM**, not pixels, so it works fine GL-less — which is why DOM-level checks pass while screenshots look broken. The two disagree, and the screenshot is the wrong one. * `WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1` / `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` / `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` do **not** fix it here (NVIDIA box; mesa software paths don’t drive the NVIDIA card). ## The fix — get real GPU GL [Section titled “The fix — get real GPU GL”](#the-fix--get-real-gpu-gl) Two options: 1. **Run on `:0`** (the real GPU X server): `DISPLAY=:0 …`. Simplest, but opens a window on the operator’s actual screen (focus-steal). 2. **VirtualGL on an isolated Xvfb** — *recommended* (no focus-steal, real GPU). `vglrun` routes GL to the GPU’s EGL render node while the app displays to the isolated Xvfb. VirtualGL isn’t in Ubuntu apt; install the GitHub release once: 
```sh
curl -sSL -o /tmp/vgl.deb \
  https://github.com/VirtualGL/virtualgl/releases/download/3.1.4/virtualgl_3.1.4_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/vgl.deb
```
 **Always confirm you got the real GPU, not `llvmpipe`/`swrast`:** 
```sh
Xvfb :90 -screen 0 1920x1080x24 -nolisten tcp & sleep 2
DISPLAY=:90 vglrun -d egl0 glxinfo | grep -i "OpenGL renderer"
# → OpenGL renderer string: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090/...   ✅
# → ...llvmpipe / swrast                                  ❌ still software
```
 Then launch the app **under `vglrun`** so WebKitGTK composites on the GPU: 
```sh
( cd papercusp-desktop && DISPLAY=:90 vglrun -d egl0 npm run dev ) &
DISPLAY=:90 import -window root /tmp/shot.png   # now shows REAL content
```
 ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * Use **`-d egl0`** — the EGL **device index**. Do **not** pass the `/dev/dri/renderD128` path: VGL rejects it with `[VGL] ERROR: Invalid EGL device`. * If you see `libEGL ... failed to create dri2 screen` with `-d egl0`, the mesa loader is fighting NVIDIA; `-d egl0` already selects the NVIDIA EGL device (`EGL_NV_device_cuda` in `eglinfo`), so it still works — the warning is noise as long as `glxinfo` reports `NVIDIA`. * The render node is `/dev/dri/renderD128` (`crw-rw----+ root render`); the invoking user must be in the `render` group (or it’s ACL-granted). See the full cookbook in [testing/agent-e2e §15.4](/internal/docs/testing/agent-e2e#154-xvfb--xdotool--ocr-fallback-cookbook).

# A headless spawn that omits --account silently bypasses the gateway

> Omitting --account on a psu-launcher spawn routes it in 'default' mode (single CLI credential, no failover), which starves a batch spawner into silent all-null cells while the gateway pool sits idle.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) `psu-launcher`’s `--account` selects one of three LLM routing modes (account-routing-3-options, `psu-launcher.mjs` \~L426 / `agent-launch-core.ts`): * `<pool-id>` → hard-pin to that pool account **via the inference gateway** (no failover) * `auto` → route **through the gateway**, auto-select an available pool account **with failover** * `default` (or **omitted**) → **skip the gateway**, use the single shared `~/.claude` CLI-login credential The footgun is the default. A spawner that omits `--account` runs **every** child on the **one** CLI credential, with no failover. A one-off is fine; a **batch** spawner (a benchmark sweep, a fan-out) fills that single account’s rolling usage window and then its children **spawn but land zero API turns** — while the 7-account gateway pool sits completely idle. `cup:spawn` and fleet launch already default to the gateway; **direct `psu-launcher` callers do not** and must opt in. ## Why it’s nasty: silent all-null cells [Section titled “Why it’s nasty: silent all-null cells”](#why-its-nasty-silent-all-null-cells) A starved child still creates its config dir and exits cleanly, so a naive driver records it as `status: 'ok'` with **every metric null** (a zero-hop transcript → `emptyCellMetrics()`). The data looks present but is empty, and the failure **clusters at the tail** of a long run (the credential fills over time) — so the highest-cost / highest-value cells are exactly the ones lost. Traced live 2026-07-17 on the P-025 `maxturn-sweep` (`WI-5003`): ornith mt25k 0/9 null → mt50k 6/9 → mt100k 9/9, and the next chunk started already starved. It reads like “the pool is saturated” but it is the opposite — the pool was never used. ## Detect it at the process level (don’t guess) [Section titled “Detect it at the process level (don’t guess)”](#detect-it-at-the-process-level-dont-guess) A gateway-routed child’s `claude` process has the gateway endpoint in its env; a `default`-mode child has it **blank**: 
```plaintext
# gateway-routed (--account=auto / pool-id):
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8788
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=papercusp-gateway


# default mode (no --account):
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=      # blank
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=    # blank
```
 `tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/<claude-pid>/environ | grep -iE 'ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL|GATEWAY'`. And confirm the pool is healthy with capacity via `gateway:status` (running/queued vs cap) + `accounts:status` (per-account utilization / walls) — if turns stall while the pool is idle, suspect routing, not capacity. ## The fix [Section titled “The fix”](#the-fix) Pass `--account=auto` (or a pool-id) explicitly on the spawn. Make it a **typed, defaulted option** on the spawn interface rather than a bare flag — the sweep now carries `SweepAccountRouting` on `SweepSpawnInput` / the CLI’s `--account`, defaulting to `'auto'`, emitted on **every** spawn so routing is never an implicit fall-through (`maxturn-sweep-live.ts` `buildSweepSpawnArgs`). ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `agent-insights/rate-limit-is-usually-account-routing-not-capacity` * `agent-insights/llm-429-check-the-transport-not-the-account`

# Heavy-command admission control (don't melt the shared box)

> The 128-core dev box is shared by the whole fleet. Each agent's vitest/tsc/test:affected is already per-suite worker-capped, but N agents running their own simultaneously with zero cross-process coordination is what melts the host to load 3000+. A PreToolUse hook now DENIES a new raw heavy command when host load is already past ~1.5x cores; scripts/pc-heavy.sh is the flock counting-semaphore that WAITS for a free slot instead of failing. What every agent needs to know when a heavy command gets denied.

## The problem [Section titled “The problem”](#the-problem) The dev box is a single 128-core host shared by the entire fleet. A single `npm run test:affected` is already well-behaved: `scripts/affected-tests.mjs` caps vitest at 32 workers per suite and runs workspaces sequentially. The danger is **cross-process**: when \~6 agents each launch their own capped run at once, that is \~185 vitest workers, and the box climbs from a healthy \~1x load to 1.9x, then spirals (load 245 → 3000+ happened twice in one week). Nothing coordinated heavy runs *across* agents — until now. ## What changed [Section titled “What changed”](#what-changed) Two cooperating pieces (WI-3821): **1. Admission gate (in the PreToolUse bash hook).** `apps/operator/scripts/hooks/cc/pretooluse-bash-resource-gate.sh` now checks, on every raw agent `Bash` command, whether the command is *heavy* (`vitest` / `tsc` / `npm test` / `test:affected` / `npm run build` / `turbo run test|build|typecheck`) and whether host `load1` is already over the threshold (default `1.5 × cores` = 192 here). If so, it **denies** the command with a message telling you what to do. It is the only place that transparently sees every raw heavy command, but a PreToolUse hook can only allow/deny — it exits before the command runs, so it cannot hold a slot. Hence piece two. **2. `scripts/pc-heavy.sh` — the “run it anyway, politely” path.** A flock **counting semaphore**: it waits for one of N free build slots (default `cores / 32` ≈ 4), runs your command `nice`/`ionice`’d, and releases the slot when the command exits (kernel-backed, so a crash never leaks a slot). It sets `PC_HEAVY_BYPASS=1` for the child, so the admission gate does not also deny it — the wrapper already self-limits. ## What to do when a heavy command is denied [Section titled “What to do when a heavy command is denied”](#what-to-do-when-a-heavy-command-is-denied) You have three options, in order of preference: 
```sh
# 1. Preferred: run it under the semaphore — it queues for a slot instead of
#    failing, and runs at lowered priority so it yields to critical services.
scripts/pc-heavy.sh -- npm run test:affected
scripts/pc-heavy.sh -- ./node_modules/.bin/vitest run lib/x.test.ts


# 2. Just wait ~30-60s and re-run — the gate clears itself as load drops.


# 3. Verify via the sanctioned MCP tool instead of raw bash. capability:inspect
#    (npx tsc --noEmit / npm run test:affected / npx vitest run) runs
#    server-side and never hits this hook, so it is never gated.
```
 ## Who is exempt (by construction) [Section titled “Who is exempt (by construction)”](#who-is-exempt-by-construction) * **The green-checkpoint gate** and **`capability:inspect`** run server-side / as MCP tools and never reach the bash hook — never gated. * **The owner** (a session with no `PAPERCUSP_AGENT_SESSION` marker, working outside the canonical shared tree) — never gated. * Anything already wrapped by `pc-heavy.sh` (`PC_HEAVY_BYPASS=1`). Only raw, uncoordinated **agent** heavy commands get staggered — exactly the load that piles up. ## Tunables & kill-switch [Section titled “Tunables & kill-switch”](#tunables--kill-switch) | Env | Default | Effect | | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | `PC_HEAVY_ADMISSION=off` | on | **Kill-switch** — disables the deny entirely. | | `PC_HEAVY_MAX_LOAD1` | `round(1.5 × cores)` | Load1 above which heavy commands are denied. | | `PC_HEAVY_SLOTS` | `max(2, cores/32)` | Concurrent heavy runs `pc-heavy` allows. | | `PC_HEAVY_TIMEOUT_SEC` | `900` | Max seconds `pc-heavy` waits for a slot before running anyway. | | `PC_HEAVY_NICE` / `PC_HEAVY_IONICE` | `10` / `best-effort 7` | Priority of a wrapped run. | The gate is **fail-open**: any error (can’t read load, bad env, parse failure) allows the command. It lands fleet-wide via git-sync with no review, so a fail-closed bug would wedge every agent’s bash — every path errs toward allowing. The threshold sits well above healthy full-tilt operation (1.0–1.3x), so it only trips during genuine oversubscription. ## Known boundary (follow-ups) [Section titled “Known boundary (follow-ups)”](#known-boundary-follow-ups) Coverage is best-effort, not airtight: a compound `cd <canonical> && vitest` carries the workspace root as its payload `cwd`, so for those it relies on the agent-session marker rather than the tree check. And raw invocations are *denied*, not auto-queued — full transparent queueing (auto-routing heavy commands through `pc-heavy`, an adoption check-guard, or an optional `systemd` slice) is deliberately left as a follow-up rather than rushing a host-wide scheduling change.

# Test agent-dispatch loops hermetically: point PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_BASE at an in-test HTTP server

> Any code path that fires the /invoke route via loopbackFetch (git-sync's merge-resolver, fireLaunchBlueprint callers) can be integration-tested END-TO-END — real blueprint resolution, real POST, observable settle — by setting PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_BASE to an in-test node:http server that plays the invoked agent. Never let a test's dispatch reach a live :3070 (it would spawn a REAL agent). Bonus pattern: two member slugs in one process ≡ two operator stacks for git-sync-style per-slug subsystems.

## The problem [Section titled “The problem”](#the-problem) Code that dispatches agents through the invoke route — `spawnMergeResolver` in `git-sync-action.ts`, anything riding `resolveLaunchTargetForEvent` / `fireLaunchBlueprint` — was effectively untestable at integration level: the dispatch is a `loopbackFetch` POST at `operatorApiBase()`, which defaults to `http://localhost:3070`. On the dev box **that port is the LIVE green operator** — a test that lets the POST through would invoke a *real* merge-resolver agent. `seed-any-pot.integration.test.ts` S4 therefore parked a fake `last_resolver: dispatched` marker to keep the dispatch path from ever running, leaving `spawnMergeResolver` (blueprint resolution, the observe loop, `merge_resolver` pipeline events) uncovered. ## The pattern [Section titled “The pattern”](#the-pattern) `operatorApiBase()` honors **`PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_BASE`** (read per call, not memoized at import). So an integration test can: 1. Stand up a `node:http` server on an ephemeral port (`listen(0, '127.0.0.1')`) that parses `/api/harness/:slug/invoke?role=...`, queues each arrival, and lets the TEST decide when (and with what body) to respond — `{ ok: true, exitCode: 0 }` settles the caller’s observe loop. 2. `process.env.PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_BASE = http://127.0.0.1:<port>` in `beforeAll` (delete in `afterAll`; respond to any still-parked request before closing or the caller’s dangling promise leaks across teardown). 3. Drive the production code path for real: the built-in blueprint event map (`git-sync:conflict` → merge-resolution → role `merge-resolver`) resolves fine under vitest, the POST lands on the test server, and the test plays the invoked agent — including *parking* the response to simulate a long-running agent (that is how the `RESOLVER_INFLIGHT_MS` dedup gets tested for real). Working example with all the trimmings (dispatch queue, parked responses, scripted adversarial resolver, settle polling): `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/git-sync/two-peer-convergence.integration.test.ts`. ## Bonus: two slugs in one process ≡ two operator stacks [Section titled “Bonus: two slugs in one process ≡ two operator stacks”](#bonus-two-slugs-in-one-process--two-operator-stacks) For per-slug subsystems (git-sync’s routine rows, `(slug, phase)` escalation rows, `git-sync:<slug>` lock resources), N “peer machines” can be simulated as N member slugs in ONE process + ONE test PG, each slug owning its own checkout of one shared bare origin: peers share *nothing* but the origin — exactly the real multi-stack topology — while every race interleaving becomes deterministic and scriptable. That is how the P-010 two-peer convergence verification (plan `git-sync-any-pot-2026-06-12` D-007) replaced a “stand up a second isolated operator stack” manual run with a permanent regression suite. Check which state is actually per-slug before reusing this: anything keyed on a process-global singleton (one workspace pin, one registry) is shared and would diverge from the multi-stack reality.

# hive-git P2P ops runbook — mode flip/rollback, integrator/epoch, divergence, sigrefs, drill

> Operational playbook for the per-hive P2P git replication plane (lib/sync/pot-git) — how to flip/rollback hiveGit.mode, what the integrator lease + epoch fencing actually guarantee today, how to triage a github-bridge divergence escalation, the 5 sigrefs rejection reasons, how to re-run the drill, and why the git-sync stall watchdog does not false-alarm under commit-only mode.

## What this covers [Section titled “What this covers”](#what-this-covers) The P2P git replication plane (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync/pot-git/`, \~30 modules — storage/namespaces, sigrefs, fetch-transport, the integrator, the GitHub bridge, worktree-bridge, gc, secrets-guard) plus its ONE production wiring seam, `lib/harness/git-sync/git-sync-action.ts`. This doc is the day-2 operator playbook: how to flip modes, how to roll back, what the integrator/epoch machinery actually guarantees **today** (vs. what it will once Phase 3 lands), how to triage a divergence escalation, the sigrefs rejection reasons you’ll see in logs, how to re-run the drill, and why the stall watchdog does not need special-casing for commit-only members. Plan: `p2p-git-live-activation-2026-07-09` (P-501). Design doc: `docs/plans/p2p-git-research-2026-07-01.md`. ### Where things actually stand (updated 2026-07-17 — every Phase-2 leg is now wired) [Section titled “Where things actually stand (updated 2026-07-17 — every Phase-2 leg is now wired)”](#where-things-actually-stand-updated-2026-07-17--every-phase-2-leg-is-now-wired) **All of P-201..P-205 have landed.** `git-sync-action.ts::handleGitSync` runs the following legs, in this order, on every tick of any non-`legacy` hive (`gate.hiveGitMode` truthy) — each is its own `runCheckpointedStep` so a resumed fire never re-runs a leg it already completed this tick: 1. **bootstrap** (`runBootstrapLeg`, G-8, P-205/WI-3591) — a genuinely cold local mirror (zero `refs/namespaces/*`) seeds every namespace a peer holds over a real socket duplex, before anything below needs to read local state. Self-gates to a fast no-op the instant ANY namespace exists locally — safe across repeated mode flips, no re-seed ever re-attempted. 2. **own-head-publish** (`runOwnHeadPublishLeg`, G-2a, WI-5146) — publish this device’s own worktree branch head into its own namespace (the `git push rad` analogue). The G-10 **secrets-guard publish gate** (`publish-guard.ts` → `secrets-guard.ts`’s `scanForSecrets`) runs INSIDE this leg, before the ref write makes the objects servable — a planted credential in a new text blob is refused here, not downstream. 3. **ref-announce** (`runRefAnnounceLeg` → `runRefAnnouncePublishTick` + `runRefAnnounceReceiveTick`, P-202) — publish this device’s own namespace advance hive-wide (sigrefs-signed), then ingest any pending peer ref-announcements into the local mirror (verify via `acceptFetchedSigrefs`, see the rejection-reasons table below) — this is the **live announce→fetch driver** the 2026-07-09 draft of this doc said didn’t exist yet. 4. **integrator** (`runIntegratorLeg` → `runIntegratorTick`, P-203) — the lease holder merges member namespace heads into `staging` + announces the advance fed-wide; every other member’s tick is a fast, correct no-op (`skipped: 'not-integrator'`). See “Integrator lease + epoch semantics” below — the **lease-holder gate landed** since the 07-09 draft; the epoch-**granting** protocol has not. 5. **worktree-bridge** (`runWorktreeBridgeLeg` → `runWorktreeBridgeTick`, P-204) — every member (including the integrator’s own machine) consumes pending `hive-git:staging-advance` announcements and ff-advances its local worktree (G-7c: never `reset --hard`; G-7b: refuses when dirty ∩ incoming ≠ ∅). This is the **live worktree-bridge driver** the 07-09 draft said had no consumer yet. 6. **github-bridge** (`runGithubBridgeLeg` → `runGithubBridgeTick`) — still gated on `hiveGit.mode === 'bridged'` AND `FLAGS.GITHUB_BRIDGE` (default ON); unchanged from the original draft. Additionally, **serve plane** (`serve-wiring.ts::wireHiveGitServe` / `serveUploadPack`, P-201) is wired onto the live hive-swarm Protomux connection via `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/swarm.ts` + `peer-dial-registry.ts` — a peer’s fetch duplex is now actually served, not just unit-tested in isolation. **gc** (`gcHiveGitRepo`, G-9) runs as a scheduled `tier:ephemeral` `system:hive-git-gc` routine (`hive-git-gc-action.ts`), armed automatically the moment a hive flips off `legacy` (`hive-git-gc-routine.ts`, called from the mode-flip path in `hive-git-mode.ts`) — not a bare `setInterval`, and self-gates to a no-op on a `legacy` hive. So today, flipping a hive’s `hiveGit.mode` to `bridged` (or `p2p-only`) gets you the **full single-authority replication loop**: commit → own-head-publish (secrets-scanned) → sigrefs-signed announce → peer fetch+verify → integrator merge (lease-gated) → staging-advance → every member’s worktree ff-advances → gc bounds the namespace-ref growth. `p2p-only` mode is **no longer a bare no-op beyond commit-only** — it now drives real peer replication; only the GitHub bridge leg additionally requires `bridged` mode. **What is still NOT proven live**, per the plan’s Phase 3 drill (`p2p-git-live-activation-2026-07-09`, `## Now`): the mechanics above are proven in-process (drill LEGS MODE/A/B/C/D/F all green, single-box) and, as of P-302 (2026-07-17), the cold-join bootstrap leg (G-8) has been proven on the REAL 2-machine rig too. Still open: **Leg E (P-306)** — flip a real hive to `bridged` and confirm the commit-only watchdog analysis below holds under genuine multi-machine wall-clock/network timing (currently only static-verified); **Leg G (P-308)** chaos (integrator-kill mid-advance, PG blip, lease failover) — needs legs A-F live under one genuine multi-machine run first. Re-verify this section against `git log -p -- packages/operator-core/lib/harness/git-sync/git-sync-action.ts` and the plan’s `## Now` before trusting it; the remaining gap is REAL-RIG proof, not missing wiring. ## Mode flip + rollback [Section titled “Mode flip + rollback”](#mode-flip--rollback) The mode lives in the **federated `hive_settings` store**, key `hiveGit.mode`, one owner-side write reaches every member machine’s next tick (no re-seed needed — `git-sync-action.ts` re-consults it every fire, per-tick, not just at routine-seed time). 
```ts
import { setHiveGitMode, getHiveGitMode } from 'packages/operator-core/lib/harness/git-sync/hive-git-mode';


await setHiveGitMode(workspaceId, hiveHomeSlug, 'bridged');   // flip on
await setHiveGitMode(workspaceId, hiveHomeSlug, null);        // ROLLBACK: delete the row → reads as 'legacy' again
```
 **Rollback is a single delete, and it is safe by construction:** `getHiveGitMode` is **fail-open** — an absent row, a malformed value, AND a settings-store read error all coerce to `'legacy'` (never throws). So: * `mode → null` (or any settings-store outage) instantly restores **today’s behavior byte-for-byte**: every member’s git-sync pushes origin directly again per `decideGitSyncPush`’s existing rules, no bridge, no integrator pass. Legacy hives are provably unaffected by this whole plane (they never read a truthy mode). * **Do not “fix” the fail-open by making it fail-closed.** A PG blip on a BRIDGED hive briefly re-enabling member push is an *accepted risk* (`hive-git-mode.ts` header comment) — both the member and the bridge writer push FF-only + CAS, so at worst one push wins and the other is rejected noisily (a divergence signal, see below), never silent corruption. Failing closed would silence a healthy legacy hive’s pushes on the same blip — a strictly worse failure mode. **Verifying a flip took effect:** read `harness_shared.routines.metadata` for the hive’s `system:git-sync` row — each leg writes its own key, all only populating once a tick has actually run that leg: `metadata->'bootstrap'` (`{ok, namespaceCount, skippedExisting, at}`), `metadata->'own_head_publish'` (`{changed, branch, sha, refused, at}` — a non-null `refused` is the G-10 secrets-guard refusing a publish), `metadata->'ref_announce'` (`{lastEventId, budgetStates, at}`), `metadata->'integrator'` (`{epoch, seq, at}`), `metadata->'worktree_bridge'` (`{lastEventId, epochSeq, stagingSha, at}`), and `metadata->'github_bridge'` (bridged mode only). No leg activity within \~2 routine intervals after a flip means the routine hasn’t fired yet, not that the flip failed — check `metadata->>'last_synced_at'` first. ## Integrator lease + epoch semantics — what’s real today, what’s a known simplification [Section titled “Integrator lease + epoch semantics — what’s real today, what’s a known simplification”](#integrator-lease--epoch-semantics--whats-real-today-whats-a-known-simplification) The integrator (`lib/sync/pot-git/integrator.ts`, called by `runIntegratorLeg`/`runIntegratorTick`) is the mechanism that turns N member namespace heads into one `staging` ref: * **Who runs it — the lease-holder gate IS wired:** `runIntegratorTick`’s `isIntegrator` check (default `lockAuthorityForHive(potHomeSlug).isSelf` — `lib/authority/lock-authority.ts`) decides, every tick, whether THIS machine is the current integrator. That authority resolution is a **deterministic election** (lowest live `device_pubkey`, or HRW rendezvous when that mode is on) over the hive’s live Swarms/presence rows — not a held token. A non-integrator’s tick returns `{ skipped: 'not-integrator' }` and does nothing; only the elected machine actually merges + publishes. On a single machine (no remote Swarms in presence) the check is a no-op-to-self (`isSelf: true` always), which is why a solo dev-box run never notices this gate exists — it matters once a second machine’s presence is visible. * **Merge policy** (`integrateMemberHeads`, deterministic by device-hex sort): a member head already an ancestor of staging → skip; staging behind the head → fast-forward; heads diverged → bare-repo 3-way merge (`git merge-tree --write-tree`, no worktree) → clean merge commit (2 parents) or, on conflict, **skip that head and report it** — a conflicting member’s own next publish must rebase onto the new staging. One bad/ conflicting head never blocks integrating the others. * **Epoch fencing (G-5d) IS wired**: every staging-advance announcement carries `{epoch, seq}`, monotonically increasing, so a stale/duplicate advance is fenced by strict `(epoch, seq)` order at the receiving end. * **Epoch GRANTING (the lease handoff itself) is NOT wired yet** — this is a **known simplification** flagged directly in `runIntegratorLeg`’s doc comment: today’s `epoch` is persisted once per `(hive, repo)` for the life of the routine’s own metadata row and only `seq` advances within it. That is correct and safe for a **single-authority dev-box run** (only one epoch is ever in play), but a genuine multi-machine lock-authority HANDOFF (via the G-0 handoff-token library) must be wired in **before** the Phase 3 live 2-machine drill (P-301+) — otherwise two machines can each believe they hold epoch 1 and both integrate independently with no fence between them. **Do not treat today’s epoch as proof of single-writer safety across machines** — it only fences a single machine’s own re-announcements. * **Storage note:** the integrator publishes to `refs/namespaces/<integratorDeviceHex>/refs/heads/staging` — its OWN namespace, not a shared top-level ref. Now that the lease-holder gate is wired, only the elected machine’s namespace carries a *live* staging ref at any moment — a prior integrator’s namespace ref simply stops advancing once the election moves off it (no ref is deleted or rewritten on handoff). Every member’s worktree-bridge leg (P-204) follows the `hive-git:staging-advance` fed-event, which names the emitting device’s namespace explicitly, so a stale-authority’s namespace is never mistakenly fetched from once a newer advance has fired. This becomes a real correctness question only in a genuine multi-machine authority HANDOFF mid-flight — see the epoch-granting gap immediately below. ## Divergence triage (github-bridge mode only) [Section titled “Divergence triage (github-bridge mode only)”](#divergence-triage-github-bridge-mode-only) The bridge (`bridged` mode) writes ONE `harness_escalations` row per hive on phase `github-bridge`, kind `github-bridge-divergence` (`classifyDivergence` in `github-divergence.ts`). **GitHub is never treated as authority and the bridge never force-pushes** — every signal is reported-not-applied. Four signal kinds, each with its own resolution lever: | signal | meaning | lever | needs owner? | | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | | `egress-non-ff` | origin diverged from hive canonical (a human pushed / an old merge landed on GitHub) | self-heals: next ingress brings the origin head into the synthetic github-origin namespace, the integrator merges it like any member head, egress FFs cleanly once canonical descends from it | no | | `ingress-non-ff` | origin REWROTE history (would rewind the synthetic namespace) | owner-authorized `allowNonFF` ingress — explicit, audited, **never automatic** | **yes** | | `admission-blocked` | a revoked contributor’s commits (or a fail-closed admission error) sit in the origin range | revocation review / re-run admission | **yes** | | `egress-secret-block` | the secrets gate refused to publish a ref (nothing left the machine) | scrub the secret + re-egress | no | Triage steps: 1. Read `metadata->'github_bridge'` on the hive’s `system:git-sync` routine row (`divergence`, `needs_owner`, `errors`) — written every bridged tick. 2. `needs_owner: true` → surface to the owner; do not attempt an automatic fix. `needs_owner: false` (`egress-non-ff` / `egress-secret-block` only) → the next clean tick usually clears it on its own (a clean pass clears the escalation, same idiom as git-sync’s own conflict/error rows); a `egress-secret-block` needs a scrub first. 3. A clean bridge pass (`signals.length === 0`) writes `action: 'clear'` and clears the escalation — do not manually clear an open row while a real signal is still active. ## sigrefs rejection reasons (`acceptFetchedSigrefs`) [Section titled “sigrefs rejection reasons (acceptFetchedSigrefs)”](#sigrefs-rejection-reasons-acceptfetchedsigrefs) When a fetched device’s sigrefs blob is checked, exactly 5 outcomes exist — all of them REFUSALS except `{ ok: true }`: * **`malformed`** — doesn’t even parse as a `SignedSigrefs` shape. * **`wrong-device`** — the blob’s `device_pubkey` doesn’t match who you fetched it from (a relay handed you someone else’s signed blob under the wrong namespace). * **`bad-signature`** — Ed25519 verify failed against the claimed device key (tamper, or a stale/rotated key). * **`rollback`** — the blob’s `version` does not strictly exceed the last *accepted* version for that device (G-4b monotonic guard — replay/rollback attack, or a relay serving a stale cached copy). * **`origin-claim-outside-scope`** — the blob carries a v2 origin-claim entry but the caller didn’t pass `allowOriginClaims: true` (the hive-wide integrator always refuses these; only a scope-repo integrator accepts them, D-017 n2 confinement). Separately, `reconcileFetchedHeads` cross-checks a fetched namespace’s **actual post-fetch head shas** against what the verified sigrefs claimed — any mismatch (missing, wrong, or an unsigned extra ref) means don’t trust that ref even though the signature itself verified; the integrator only trusts refs that reconcile cleanly. A relay lying about a peer’s head shows up here, not as a signature failure (transport auth ≠ per-namespace content authenticity — this is exactly the gap sigrefs-lite closes, see the research doc §3.3). ## Drill re-run instructions [Section titled “Drill re-run instructions”](#drill-re-run-instructions) The repeatable acceptance drill lives at `papercusp-desktop/bin/hive-git-drill.sh` (P-301 scaffold, mirrors `bin/work-distribution-drill.sh`’s shape). Every leg is either a **live assert** (wiring has landed) or an explicit **SKIP-with-reason** (never a silent green) — the SKIP census IS the release evidence for what’s still unproven. Run it locally against a throwaway test hive: 
```bash
cd papercusp-desktop
bin/hive-git-drill.sh                 # uses the newest built .deb by default
KEEP_UP=1 bin/hive-git-drill.sh        # leave the sidecar(s) up for inspection after
```
 **Current leg census (2026-07-17):** | leg | plan item | status | proves | | ---- | --------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | MODE | — | live | `hiveGit.mode` round-trip legacy → bridged → rollback → legacy (the fail-open delete) | | A | P-302 | live | G-8 cold-clone bootstrap: a fresh joiner seeds every namespace a peer holds, over a real socket duplex | | B | P-303 | live | G-3 announce-driven fetch: announce → fetch → sigrefs accept → heads reconcile, over a real socket duplex | | C | P-304 | live | trust/tamper drill: relay-lie detection, rollback refusal (G-4b), non-member scope-serve-gate refusal | | D | P-305 | live | integrator computes + publishes canonical staging; a non-steer head lands in the real PG integration-requests queue; the other machine’s worktree ff-advances | | E | P-306 | **SKIP** | GitHub bridge live under REAL multi-machine wall-clock/network timing — needs the 2nd rig machine; the commit-only watchdog analysis below is static-verified only | | F | P-307 | live | G-9 gc keep-work/last-N/departed-member archival + G-10 secrets/oversized-blob guard, real bare repos | | G | P-308 | **SKIP** | chaos (integrator-kill mid-advance, PG blip, lease failover) — needs A-F live under ONE genuine multi-machine run first | Legs MODE/A-D/F run **single-box, in-process** (real production code paths, fake/local transport) — sufficient to prove the mechanics, not sufficient to close E/G, which need the actual 2-machine rig (`docs/plans/LIVE-1-rig-runbook-2026-07-02.md`). As of P-302 (2026-07-17) leg A’s underlying mechanism (G-8 cold-join) has ALSO been proven on the real rig — see the plan’s `## Now` for the live-rig evidence trail; that proof lives on the plan, not duplicated into this drill script. Do not hand-author a second drill script for a leg this one already scaffolds — flip its SKIP to a live assert in this same file as rig proof lands. ## Watchdog interplay under commit-only mode — verified, no fix needed [Section titled “Watchdog interplay under commit-only mode — verified, no fix needed”](#watchdog-interplay-under-commit-only-mode--verified-no-fix-needed) A `bridged`/`p2p-only` hive’s members go **commit-only** (git-sync stops pushing origin; the bridge writer alone pushes). The natural worry: will the `git-sync-stall-watchdog` (`packages/operator-core/lib/release/git-sync-stall-watchdog.ts`) false-alarm on members that (correctly) never push? **No — verified by reading `evaluateGitSyncStall`.** Its primary signal, `commitStale`, is **HEAD-movement-based, not push-based**: it fires only when the tree’s committed HEAD hasn’t advanced for `headStaleMs` **while the last recorded status is NOT `'nothing'` and NOT `'skipped'`** (i.e. there was actually work to commit and it didn’t land). A commit-only member still commits locally every tick exactly as before — only the *push* leg is disabled — so `commitStale` is entirely unaffected by commit-only mode. The other three fault classes (`fireStale`, `errorStall`, `persistentReap`) are about the routine firing/erroring at all, likewise orthogonal to push-vs-commit-only. **Conclusion: no watchdog code change is needed for commit-only mode; this is a documentation/verification item, not a bug.** If a false alarm is ever observed on a bridged hive, it is a NEW bug distinct from this analysis — re-open, don’t assume this note covers it forever. ## Kill-switch / rollback summary (one-line version) [Section titled “Kill-switch / rollback summary (one-line version)”](#kill-switch--rollback-summary-one-line-version) `setHiveGitMode(ws, hive, null)` → immediate, fail-open, byte-for-byte revert to legacy behavior on every member’s next tick. No flag exists for the P2P drivers themselves (by design — same pattern as `FLAGS.GITHUB_BRIDGE`: activation is **structural**, gated by `hiveGit.mode`, not a separate default-off flag; see `libs/flags/src/types.ts` comment above `FEDERATED_SCOUT_LEARNING` for the precedent). `FLAGS.GITHUB_BRIDGE` (default ON) is a secondary instant off-switch for the bridge leg specifically, on top of the mode. ## Live-rig diagnostic gotchas (from the 2026-07-06→09 fed-plane outage) [Section titled “Live-rig diagnostic gotchas (from the 2026-07-06→09 fed-plane outage)”](#live-rig-diagnostic-gotchas-from-the-2026-07-0609-fed-plane-outage) Hard-won during the WI-1729 root-cause hunt (su-4dc3befd + su-63834d42, 2026-07-09); three STACKED environmental root causes (Mac zombie stack, ufw drop, wedged DHT bootstrap) meant no single fix showed green — verify each layer independently: * **hyperswarm is UDX/UDP** — `ss -tnp` / TCP socket lists NEVER show its connections. Absence there is not evidence of no connectivity; probe the swarm itself. * **The isolated DHT bootstrap can wedge across a host reboot while the unit stays `active`** (`papercup-isolated-dht.service`, 172.31.44.1:49838, wedged from the tower’s 2026-07-06 23:02 reboot). `systemctl status` is not a health check — verify with a RAW hyperswarm announce+lookup probe (two fresh instances, fresh topic, tower-local). A wedged bootstrap = zero connections fleet-wide. * **`dev:dogfood_substrate_status` lies on clustered hosts** — it can hit a non-substrate-owner cluster worker and report `bootedCount:0` (EI-8816). Don’t trust a zero from it. * **Mac server logs** live at `~/.papercusp/logs/serve.log` (launchd `StandardOutPath` was `/dev/null` until 2026-07-09 — older incidents have no Mac-side logs at all). * **Fed-plane liveness watermark** (the discriminant for “arrivals dead”): `SELECT origin, count(*), max(ts) FROM harness_shared.coord_event_log GROUP BY origin` — `origin='remote'` max(ts) is the tower←peer arrival watermark; local advancing while remote is pinned = the inbound leg is dead. After a DHT/bootstrap fix, allow one periodic swarm re-announce cycle (\~10–15 min) before judging the fix red. ## Named-hop pipeline observability (P-012, fleet-reliability-verification-2026-07-10) [Section titled “Named-hop pipeline observability (P-012, fleet-reliability-verification-2026-07-10)”](#named-hop-pipeline-observability-p-012-fleet-reliability-verification-2026-07-10) WI-3619’s fix (send-side drain, `outbox-drain.ts`) proved a pattern worth generalizing: when a pass-level watchdog (like `DRAIN_PASS_TIMEOUT_MS` above) can name that a hop HUNG, but not WHICH internal await hung, wrap every await inside that hop with a one-shot stall logger. If the await is still pending after a threshold, it logs a loud, grep-able line naming the exact stage — turning “the pipeline went quiet” into “THIS specific await, on THIS scope, has been hung for THIS long”, diagnosable from the journal alone even when the await never settles. This is now a **shared primitive**, not a one-off: `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/stage-stall-log.ts` exports `logIfStageStalls(scope, stage, promise, thresholdMs?)` (default threshold `STAGE_STALL_LOG_MS` = 15s). It never times out or rejects the wrapped promise — it’s purely an observability side-channel; the promise’s own resolve/reject is untouched. **Current adopters** (capture → drain → replicate → **merge** → member-guard → project — the federation hop chain this item names): * **`outbox-drain.ts`** (drain stage, the original WI-3619 site) — every await inside a drain pass (GC delete, the undrained-batch SELECT, epoch-encrypt, the Hypercore `append`, the fan-out, the `mark-drained` UPDATE) is wrapped; scope = `${workspaceId}::${harnessSlug}`. * **`read-merge.ts`** (merge stage, P-012) — `applyRecordingWinner`’s `apply(env)` call is an **unbounded PG write** (the projection writer) with the exact same hang shape as the drain’s `append()` (a wedged connection/lock never resolves) — unlike `readOpBoundedDetailed`, which already has its own per-op timeout on the read side, nothing bounded the write side before this. Scope = the source peer log’s `keyHex`; stage = `merge-apply (${table}::${hbKey})`. Tests: `read-merge-stage-stall.test.ts` (a hung apply logs the named line; a fast apply logs nothing) + `stage-stall-log.test.ts` (the shared primitive itself: silent-on-fast-settle, logs-on-stall, never swallows a reject, respects an explicit threshold override). **Not yet adopted** (deliberately scoped out of this pass — a candidate list for a follow-up, not a silent gap): * **capture** (Stage 1) — a synchronous PG trigger; no long-lived await to name. * **replicate** — Hypercore’s own internal replication machinery; not this codebase’s await to wrap. * **member-guard / project** (`github-ingress-admission.ts`, `contribution-admission.ts`, the per-table projection writers other than the merge-pass caller above) — worth instrumenting once a LIVE wedge is actually observed there, per this pattern’s own philosophy: name the failure class you’ve actually seen, don’t pre-emptively wrap every await in the repo speculatively. **To add it to a new hop:** identify the hop’s serialized, single-flight- per-tick await loop; pick a `scope` string that identifies the pipeline instance (workspace+harness, or a peer/log key); wrap each await with `logIfStageStalls(scope, '<stage-name>', theAwaitedPromise)`. The stage name should be specific enough to be immediately actionable (include a row/op id or key, not just a generic verb). ## Refs [Section titled “Refs”](#refs) Plan `p2p-git-live-activation-2026-07-09`; design doc `docs/plans/p2p-git-research-2026-07-01.md`; the drill `papercusp-desktop/bin/hive-git-drill.sh` (P-301); `hive-git-mode.ts`, `integrator.ts`, `integrator-tick.ts`, `ref-announce-tick.ts`, `worktree-bridge-tick.ts`, `serve-wiring.ts`, `gc.ts`, `publish-guard.ts`, `sigrefs.ts`, `github-divergence.ts`, `lock-authority.ts` (the `lockAuthorityForHive` integrator-lease election), `git-sync-stall-watchdog.ts`; `stage-stall-log.ts` (P-012, named-hop pipeline observability), plan `fleet-reliability-verification-2026-07-10`.

# The pot:* tool namespace — local pot lifecycle

> The pot:* namespace is the full LOCAL pot lifecycle (a kind:'hive' harness + its Mug/cups) — list/get/create/dissolve/update plus the Mug run-loop verbs (start/pause/wake/declare-wake/status/survey). Gotchas — create/dissolve/update are root-only; create must stamp harness_kind:'hive' (harness:create doesn't); deploy:pot is a DISTINCT cloud step; cup placement stays fleet:*.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) `pot:*` (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/hive/`) is the **local pot lifecycle** surface — the verbs that manage a pot on this machine: * **`pot:list`** — workspace-local pots (kind:‘hive’ harnesses) + a live-agent count (one batched fleet read, no per-pot fan-out). * **`pot:get`** — one pot in depth: wake schedule + cups `{doing,queued,load}` + todo frontier depth. A pure aggregator. * **`pot:create`** / **`pot:create_from_repo`** — stand up a new pot (home harness + the `hive` blueprint + optional Mug wake), transactional with rollback; the `_from_repo` variant onboards a GitHub URL. * **`pot:dissolve`** — tear one down (clear the wake, cancel cups, delete `hive_members`, tear down the learning loop + sandbox desktop, deregister; optional schema drop), confirm-gated + owner-tier-gated. * **`pot:update`** — edit deployment target / per-instance config overrides. * **`pot:start`** / **`pot:pause`** / **`pot:wake`** / **`pot:declare-wake`** / **`pot:status`** / **`pot:survey`** / **`pot:set-steering`** — the Mug run-loop control surface (start/pause the pot, fire or schedule the next wake, read status, the placement survey, owner steering). It **composes** existing primitives (`fleet:*`, `coord:*`, `harness:create` internals) rather than reinventing them. A pot is read through one seam, `resolveHive` (`_resolve.ts`), which now points onto the first-class Hive entity (`shared-hive-federation`) — the verbs didn’t have to change. (The same `pot:*` namespace also carries the **shared-pot** surface — membership/approval, moderation, and cross-pot ask/grant — covered in the [shared pots guide](/system/shared-pot-guide/).) ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * **Create/dissolve/update are ROOT-ONLY.** They refuse a parented cup (a `cup:spawn` child — `resolveAgentIdentity(ctx).source === 'fleet-spawn'`) up front; the `assertNotNestedHive` guard in `fireLaunchBlueprint` is the runtime backstop. Pots are peers, never nested — a cup that needs structure spins a `kind:'harness'` subharness, never a pot. * **`pot:create` must stamp `harness_kind:'hive'` itself.** `harness:create` never sets `harness_kind`, and `resolveHive`/`pot:list` filter on it — so a pot home harness created any other way (or a pre-existing plain harness) is **invisible** to the namespace until stamped. `createHiveHarness` sets it; that’s the one non-negotiable difference from a plain `harness:create { blueprintId:'hive' }`. * **`deploy:pot` / `deploy:teardown_pot` are DISTINCT** — they are the *cloud execution-plane* (provision/destroy frames for an already-existing pot), not local lifecycle. `pot:create` does NOT deploy; `pot:dissolve` does NOT destroy a cloud frame. Order: `pot:create` → (later) `deploy:pot`; `deploy:teardown_pot` → `pot:dissolve`. * **The Mug run-loop verbs live under `pot:*`.** `pot:start` / `pot:pause` (the pot on/off switch), `pot:wake` / `pot:declare-wake` (fire or schedule the next Mug wake; pause-without-stopping = `pot:declare-wake { mode:'none' }`), and `pot:status` / `pot:survey` are all in the namespace. Cup placement stays `fleet:*`; per-loop error/backoff control is `autoloop:control`. * **`pot:dissolve` leaves workspace-scoped event-wake subscriptions.** The pot time-wake routine is per-home-slug (cleared cleanly), but the pot’s event-wake subscriptions are one row per *workspace* today — so dissolve clears only the time wake to avoid clobbering sibling pots (`dissolve.ts` step 1). The first-class Hive entity makes event subs per-pot. ## Tests [Section titled “Tests”](#tests) `agent-tools/hive/{_resolve,_create,dissolve}.test.ts` + `guard.integration.test.ts`: descriptor shaping, `harness_kind` stamping, create rollback-on-failure, dissolve unwind (incl. the membership / learning-loop / desktop teardown legs), and the root-only + owner-tier refusals — all PG-free (deps mocked). The live create→wake→dissolve path (a real Mug spawn on shared infra) is a manual smoke, not auto-run.

# HLC merge order must match the PG fed_ts LWW guard (or cells diverge)

> Why two federated cells can "converge" to DIFFERENT values — the merge winners-fold orders by HLC (P-010) but the projection PG LWW guard orders by fed_ts, and HLC stamped at DRAIN disagrees with fed_ts stamped at WRITE. Fix - seed the HLC from the op's own write-time `ts`.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) A federated write goes through **two** ordering decisions, and they must agree: 1. **The merge winners-fold** (`read-merge.ts` `mergeAdmittedLogs`, whose `beatsStored` comparator — defined in `read-merge.ts` as a hand-mirror of `projection.ts`’s `lwwPick` — decides winners) — since P-010 this orders by the op’s **HLC** when both ops carry one, else falls back to wall-clock `ts`. 2. **The PG projection LWW guard** (`harness-features.ts` etc.) — the `INSERT … ON CONFLICT … WHERE stored.fed_ts IS NULL OR EXCLUDED.fed_ts >= stored.fed_ts` clause — orders by **`fed_ts`**. If these two disagree under same-key contention, the system **silently diverges**: the merge picks op X as the winner and hands it to `apply`, but the PG guard rejects X (its `fed_ts` lost) → no write → the cell keeps its own value. Each cell keeps its own → the two cells “converge” (no more ops to drain, `fixedPoint=true`) to **different** values. The tripwire was `split-brain-mug.integration.test.ts` (both Mugs steer opposite orders; cell A ended with a mix, cell B with all-its-own). ## Why they disagreed [Section titled “Why they disagreed”](#why-they-disagreed) * **`fed_ts`** is stamped at the **local write** (migration 214 `stamp_local_federated_write`, `clock_timestamp()`). * **HLC** was stamped at **DRAIN** (`stampOpHlc` in `hlc-stamp.ts` called from `boot.ts`’s `handle.append`, using a bare `clock.now()` = wall-clock-at-drain). Drain happens later than — and in a different order than — the writes (the CDC outbox drains in batches, concurrently across cells), so the HLC ordered ops by **drain-interleave** while `fed_ts` ordered them by **write time**. An op could win the HLC fold but lose the `fed_ts` guard. ## Fix [Section titled “Fix”](#fix) Seed the HLC’s physical component from the op’s **own recorded write-time `ts`** (the outbox row’s capture `ts`, ≈ `fed_ts`), not the wall clock at stamp time: hlc-stamp.ts 
```ts
export function stampOpHlc(op, clock = processHlc()) {
  if (op.hlc) return op;
  return { ...op, hlc: encodeHlc(clock.now(op.ts)) }; // was clock.now()
}
```
 `HlcClock.send(physicalNow)` is built for exactly this (“seed from an event’s own recorded ms”) and stays monotone via `bumpCount` when `ts` is in the past, so causality (the RECV-seam `observeRemoteHlc` advance) is preserved. The merge’s HLC order matches the PG guard’s `fed_ts` order → no silent rejection **FOR THE DRAIN-INTERLEAVE CASE**. > ⚠️ **This 2026-06-14 patch was INCOMPLETE (it closed only the drain-interleave trigger) and was later REOPENED then fully RESOLVED — see ”## REOPENED (D-001)” and ”## RESOLVED” below.** Seeding the HLC from `op.ts` only guarantees `HLC.physical ≥ op.ts` for the SAME op. It does NOT make the HLC ORDER of two CONCURRENT ops match their `fed_ts` order, because the RECV-seam advance this patch DELIBERATELY PRESERVES raises a peer’s clock ABOVE a later write’s `ts` (`send(ts)` returns `max(clock.physical, ts)`). The split-brain was still reachable until the D-001 ordering-key fix shipped. ## Gotchas when reproducing in a rig [Section titled “Gotchas when reproducing in a rig”](#gotchas-when-reproducing-in-a-rig) `composition-rig.ts` simulates **two swarms in ONE process**. Real swarms are separate processes with **independent** HLC clocks, but the rig shared the process-global `processHlc()` singleton — so the two cells’ concurrent drains raced the same counter and decided cross-swarm LWW by drain-interleave. Give each cell its **own** `HlcClock` (gated `hlcClock` seams on `boot.ts` `BootHarnessOpts`, `projection.ts` `ApplyOpOpts`, `hlc-stamp.ts`; default `processHlc()` so production is unchanged). See \[\[substrate-hlc-and-capture-coverage]] and \[\[two-federation-paths-cannot-share-one-fed-ts]]. ## Smell test [Section titled “Smell test”](#smell-test) If two federated cells end a converge() with DIFFERENT values for the same key (and `fixedPoint=true`), suspect an ordering-key mismatch between the merge fold and a projection’s PG LWW guard — they must use the SAME key. ## REOPENED (D-001, 2026-06-19, shared-pot-release-testing Brief D) [Section titled “REOPENED (D-001, 2026-06-19, shared-pot-release-testing Brief D)”](#reopened-d-001-2026-06-19-shared-pot-release-testing-brief-d) The 2026-06-14 fix closed the **drain-interleave** trigger but NOT the root cause: the merge fold orders by **HLC** and the PG guard orders by **fed\_ts = op.ts**, and these are still two different clocks. Seeding HLC from `op.ts` makes `HLC.physical ≥ op.ts` for one op, but the RECV seam (`observeRemoteHlc`, kept on purpose) advances a peer’s `HlcClock` ABOVE a later write’s `ts`. Then: * Winner **W**: its author observed a remote op at HLC.physical = 9000 (recv advance), then wrote KEY at wall `ts = 1000` → HLC `(9000,·)`, **fed\_ts 1000**. * Loser **L**: a fresh-clock peer wrote KEY at `ts = 5000` → HLC `(5000,0)`, **fed\_ts 5000**. `lwwPick`/`beatsStored` pick W (higher HLC); the PG guard prefers L (higher fed\_ts). The merge SUPPRESSES the HLC-loser once the HLC-winner is the standing winner, and the PG guard REJECTS the HLC-winner when its fed\_ts lost — so the two authors materialise different rows and never reconcile: * W’s author folds W first → PG = W; L arrives, beatsStored(L,W)=false → suppressed. * L’s author folds L first → PG = L; W arrives, handed to apply → `WHERE EXCLUDED.fed_ts(1000) >= stored.fed_ts(5000)` is FALSE → rejected → PG stays L. **Reachability:** HLC.physical is monotone and propagates the GLOBAL-max wall-ts seen anywhere (recv takes `max`). A single forward clock excursion on ANY peer (NTP overshoot, fast VM, manual set) raises the HLC floor for everyone permanently; thereafter any concurrent same-key writes whose wall-`ts` order differs across peers can diverge.
