They enter through `/console/launch`, which validates the request and delegates the actual OS-window spawn to the shared `spawnConsole` primitive. ## Selection heuristic [Section titled “Selection heuristic”](#selection-heuristic) * If the subject is an **agent**, start with `capability:launch-agent`. * If the request is specifically **N agents on a plan**, use `fleet:launch-on-plan`. * If the subject is a **command**, use `capability:terminal`. * If the action came from the desktop console UI, follow `/console/launch` → `spawnConsole`. ## Per-member config + runtime reconfigure (per-member-declarative-launch-specs) [Section titled “Per-member config + runtime reconfigure (per-member-declarative-launch-specs)”](#per-member-config--runtime-reconfigure-per-member-declarative-launch-specs) A multi-agent launch is **declarative**: pass `members: MemberSpec[]` to either `capability:launch-agent` or `fleet:launch-on-plan`. Entry `i` configures agent `i` (index-aligned to `count`); each set field OVERRIDES the flat top-level arg for that agent only, an unset field falls through to the flat arg then the system default, and a shorter array is fine (`count` defaults to `members.length`). `MemberSpec` carries `model`, `effort`, `account`, `carry`, `contextSize`, `compactionLimit`, `role`, `agent`, `brief`, `claimKinds`, `headless`, and more (see `agent-launch-core.ts`). Door note: `carry` / `claimKinds` seed a **self-pulling fleet** member’s baseline + per-member claim spec, so they are honored ONLY by `fleet:launch-on-plan`. The general `capability:launch-agent` door opens raw agents — it IGNORES those two fields (and warns), so use `fleet:launch-on-plan` when a member needs a carry mode or a claim-kind lane. Once a fleet is running, reconfigure ONE member without re-authoring the whole launch — the setting’s nature picks the tool (D-003): | Setting | Fixed at launch? | Tool | | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | compaction limit, claim spec, next-wake brief | no — runtime | `fleet:reconfigure-member` (adjusts in place, no respawn) | | model, effort, account, contextSize, agent, compactionLimit | yes — boot-baked | `fleet:respawn-member` (drains + relaunches with the new spec) | `fleet:reconfigure-member` applies each lever directly — compaction limit via the cross-session setter (clamped to the member’s own spec+role ceiling), claim spec under the member’s cupId (applied on its next `scheduler:get_next`), and the brief as a next-wake coord message. `fleet:respawn-member` KILLS the old session (releasing its claims via `fleet:kill`) then fresh-launches a replacement into the same fleet — a new identity that inherits the fleet claim lane; it ABORTS the relaunch if the kill fails, so a lane is never double-run. Both default `fleet` to the single fleet you lead and are authorized to the fleet’s leader, the queen, or the owner. Deep dives: [desktop fleet vs. loop cup](/internal/docs/agent-insights/desktop-fleet-vs-loop-cup), [launching, resuming and forking agents](/internal/docs/agent-insights/launching-resuming-and-forking-agents), and [native console](/internal/docs/desktop/native-console).

# Launching, resuming and forking agents — capability:launch-agent

> The one tool for putting an agent on work that is NOT a plan-fleet: an ad-hoc brief, bringing a DEAD agent back mid-thread (resume), or branching a LIVE one (fork). Covers the account-pin login trap, why a live source must be forked, and how the first turn actually gets delivered.

## What this tool is for [Section titled “What this tool is for”](#what-this-tool-is-for) `capability:launch-agent` puts an agent on work in the three cases a **plan-fleet launch cannot express**: | You want | Call | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | An agent on an **ad-hoc brief** (no plan, no fleet ceremony) | `capability:launch-agent { brief }` | | A **dead** agent back, mid-thread, with its context intact | `capability:launch-agent { resume: { agentId }, brief }` | | To **branch** a live agent’s thread without disturbing it | `capability:launch-agent { resume: { agentId }, fork: true, brief }` | It is NOT a replacement for `fleet:launch-on-plan` — that stays the right tool for “open N members and work this plan”. The routing rule: > **Work is a plan** → `fleet:launch-on-plan`. **Work is a brief, or the agent already exists** → `capability:launch-agent`. **Headless, no desktop window** → `fleet:launch-on-plan { headless: true }` (see [desktop-fleet-vs-loop-cup](/internal/docs/agent-insights/desktop-fleet-vs-loop-cup)). All three sit on ONE shared core (`agent-launch-core.ts`) — command construction, fleet/launched-by/account injection, resume resolution. There is deliberately no second spawn path to drift out of sync. ## Trap 1: a scripted resume that does not pin an account stops on the login picker [Section titled “Trap 1: a scripted resume that does not pin an account stops on the login picker”](#trap-1-a-scripted-resume-that-does-not-pin-an-account-stops-on-the-login-picker) This is the owner-visible bug that motivated the whole thing — *“why is it asking me to log in?”* `psu`’s `resumeAccountPlan` shows an **interactive account picker** when a resume carries neither `--account` nor `--no-picker`. A human typing `psu --resume` picks an account and moves on. A *scripted* launch has nobody to pick, so the agent sits on a login prompt forever, looking hung. Both `capability:launch-agent` and `capability:terminal` now inject `--account=default` into any `--resume` command that lacks one, and `buildAgentLaunchCommand` always emits `--no-picker --account=<acct>`. **If you construct a psu resume command by hand anywhere else, pin the account yourself.** On **macOS the default is `--account=auto`**, not `default`: a per-session config dir cannot reach the Keychain login, so darwin routes through the gateway account (`defaultLaunchAccount`). ## Trap 2: resuming a LIVE agent is not what you want — fork it [Section titled “Trap 2: resuming a LIVE agent is not what you want — fork it”](#trap-2-resuming-a-live-agent-is-not-what-you-want--fork-it) An in-place resume **re-attaches the original coord `ownerId`**. Do that to an agent that is still alive and you now have two processes answering to one identity: wakes, claims and messages land in a coin-flip. (This is WI-3882.) So: `resolveResumeTarget` detects a live source and the tool **auto-forks it**, with a loud note in the report. A fork gets a **fresh identity** — which is the other half of the trade: > A forked agent is a NEW ownerId that nobody — not you, not the fleet — can address until it boots and registers presence. You cannot pre-wake it, and you cannot hand it work by id in the same turn you launch it. That is exactly why the brief matters (below). ## How the first turn actually gets delivered [Section titled “How the first turn actually gets delivered”](#how-the-first-turn-actually-gets-delivered) A launched agent that opens IDLE is useless — someone has to give it its first turn, and the seam differs by mode: * **Fresh launch** → the brief rides the spawn-safe env var `PAPERCUSP_KICKOFF_PROMPT`, and `psu-launcher` turns it into the CLI’s positional prompt (`kickoffPositionalArgs`, gated on `--no-picker`, suppressed by `--no-kickoff`). Free-form text must NOT be passed as `--kickoff=<text>` inside a console greeting one-liner — it gets double-quoted and breaks the shell. * **Resume / fork** → there is no CLI seam at all (`claude --resume <id> "<prompt>"` is not a supported form, and a fork’s fresh ownerId is unaddressable from outside). Instead **psu’s own managed pty host injects the first turn**: it waits for the agent to settle at its prompt, writes the turn, and *verifies submission* (`injectTurnAtPrompt` in `psu-pty-host.mjs`). This is the same wait-at-prompt + submit-verify machinery the WI-1941 recycle carry-note already used — one delivery path, guaranteed or **loudly dropped**, never silently lost. **Always pass a `brief`.** Without one the agent boots and sits there; the tool warns you, but a warning is not a turn. ## Cross-backend resume is a port, not a shared native thread [Section titled “Cross-backend resume is a port, not a shared native thread”](#cross-backend-resume-is-a-port-not-a-shared-native-thread) `psu --resume=<tracked Claude row> --agent=codex|omp` uses the session-port protocol. The distinction matters: * A same-backend resume reopens the original backend’s native transcript. * A cross-backend port snapshots the source, creates a **new** target session, carries history as a managed seed, waits for native persistence, and then lets every later resume use the target backend normally. OMP can appear to resume across models more simply because an OMP thread is already provider-neutral: OMP owns one conversation representation and sends the next request to whichever model/provider is selected. That is a good pattern inside a single host runtime, but it does not make Claude Code JSONL, Codex rollouts, and OMP thread storage mutually readable. `psu` coordinates those independent native CLIs, so pretending they share one thread would produce false lineage and targets that cannot resume natively later. What the port deliberately copies from OMP’s strategy: * a versioned, provider-independent conversation contract; * explicit model/provider selection separate from history; * deterministic history fitting before the target request; * preserving tool-call/result relationships while normalizing backend syntax. What it deliberately does not copy: * relabeling a provider switch as the same native session; * replaying unbounded history and hoping the target truncates it safely; * persisting full normalized transcript text in coordination/audit metadata; * importing source control state, permissions, claims, or prompt authority; * treating terminal output as proof that the target recorded the seed. The extra ceremony is the value: inspect is read-only, prepare occurs only after an egress preview/confirmation, delivery is idempotent, the artifact is one-use, and `delivered` means the native target transcript contains the managed seed. Protocol/transform skew and a missing migration fail closed. A stale prepared or pending port is expired by the existing telemetry-retention routine, which ends the target, removes the seed, and emits content-free failed-delivery telemetry. V1 is intentionally narrow: tracked plain Claude sources, Codex/OMP targets, no native fork combination, and no transfer from an active fleet/loop/claim-bearing source. That boundary keeps the first implementation auditable while leaving the contract extensible for future source adapters. ## Trap 3: a launched agent that “never wakes up” is usually not rate-limited [Section titled “Trap 3: a launched agent that “never wakes up” is usually not rate-limited”](#trap-3-a-launched-agent-that-never-wakes-up-is-usually-not-rate-limited) Two failures on this box make a perfectly-launched agent sit at a dead prompt forever, with **no error anywhere**. Both were found by live-verify on 2026-07-12, and both were misread as “the model hung” / “we got rate limited” before the real cause turned up. Check these before you blame the API: **(a) claude’s first-run wizard.** Every psu session gets a per-session `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` that **symlinks the global `~/.claude.json` in** — and that file carries `hasCompletedOnboarding`. If it is ever `false`, claude boots the first-run **theme picker** instead of a session: the agent never reaches a prompt, so the kickoff can never land. It also *self-propagates* — the symlink is write-through, so a session wedged in the wizard writes its not-yet-onboarded state straight back to the global file and re-arms the trap for the next launch. `writeInteractiveClaudeConfig` now **asserts** the flag on every materialize (`ensureOnboardingComplete`), so this self-heals; if you ever see a launched agent parked on a theme menu, that guard is what failed. **(b) `--harness` is what makes it a papercusp agent at all.** A fresh launch without `--harness` boots a *plain* claude: psu skips the su bootstrap, the per-session config dir is never seeded, and you get (a) as a side effect. The tool now always harness-scopes a fresh launch. Symptom to recognise: the session’s config dir holds a small *real* `.claude.json` that claude wrote itself, instead of the \~87-key symlink farm every healthy session has. ## Trap 4: `psu` may not be running the launcher you just edited [Section titled “Trap 4: psu may not be running the launcher you just edited”](#trap-4-psu-may-not-be-running-the-launcher-you-just-edited) `~/.papercusp/bin/psu` is a shim that hardcodes an **absolute path** to one `psu-launcher.mjs`, and **every operator boot rewrites it to point at that operator’s own tree** — the green operator (`:3070`) stamps in `papercup-release/…`, the staging operator (`:3170`) stamps in the shared integration tree. On the dev box both run, so the last boot silently wins. The consequence is nasty and near-invisible: you edit `apps/operator/scripts/psu-launcher.mjs` in the shared tree, launch through `psu`, and may silently exercise the **release** copy of your file — then conclude your code does not work. (That is precisely what happened while verifying the resume/fork kickoff seam: the same command dropped its kickoff at 20:08 and delivered it at 20:19, with no code change in between.) Note this also punches a hole in the “guaranteed or loudly dropped” promise above — a launcher that *predates* the seam cannot warn about a kickoff it has never heard of. To test a launcher change, **bypass the shim** and run the tree’s launcher directly: 
```bash
node apps/operator/scripts/psu-launcher.mjs --no-picker --account=default …
```
 (with the `PAPERCUSP_*` env the console wrapper exports). Tracked as WI-4440. ## No “resume the fleet” verb — and why [Section titled “No “resume the fleet” verb — and why”](#no-resume-the-fleet-verb--and-why) There is deliberately no one-shot fleet revival. Any single verb has to *guess* which dead members to bring back (all of them? only the ones that died this hour? not the one you killed on purpose yesterday?) and every guess is wrong for someone. Instead `fleet:status` hands the leader the **facts**, per ended member: * `endedAt` — when it died * `resumable` / `resumableSessionId` — whether a native session actually exists * `resumeHint` — when it does not (an omp thread, or a row predating native-id tracking → launch that lane fresh instead) The leader then composes the revival *per member* — resume, fork, or fresh. ## Odds and ends [Section titled “Odds and ends”](#odds-and-ends) * **Idempotency.** Pass `idempotencyKey` and a retry/duplicate call returns “Already launched (deduped)” instead of spawning a second agent (`agent_launch_idempotency`, migration 586). A PG failure never blocks a launch — it warns and launches unguarded. * **Shell safety.** `buildAgentLaunchCommand` *validates* rather than quotes: every value must match `/^[A-Za-z0-9._:=@/,+-]+$/` or it throws. Free-form text (the brief) never goes on the command line at all — it rides the env. * **Headless.** `headless: true` launches with no window. Note EI-9748: headless children are reaped by the service cgroup on a `:3170` restart. * **Fleet.** An explicit `fleet` wins; otherwise the launch inherits the *caller’s* fleet (WI-4234), so a leader’s ad-hoc launches join its own fleet by default.

# Lazy-import coord/presence into registry-loaded files (avoid load-time cycles)

> A top-level import of a coordination/presence module into a file the system-action or endpoint registry side-effect-imports (e.g. git-sync-action) forms a require cycle that 500s an unrelated route. Use a call-time `await import()`.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) You add a top-level `import { listPresence } from '../../agent-tools/coordination/presence'` (or any coordination/identity module) to a file that the **registry loads as a side effect** — `git-sync-action.ts`, another `*-action.ts`, or a `defineTool` file. Suddenly an **unrelated** route/tool returns **500** instead of 200, even though your code never touches it. The `composed-app-shadowing` / route-shadowing tests catch it (e.g. `/harness/projects must hit the defineTool … expected 500 to be 200`). ## Cause [Section titled “Cause”](#cause) A load-time **require cycle**. The registry imports your module to register its handler: 
```plaintext
register-system-actions → git-sync-action → agent-tools/coordination/presence
  → coordination/identity → … → agent-tools/index → register-system-actions  ← cycle
```
 During the cycle one module’s exports are still partial (`undefined`) when another reads them, so a handler throws at request time → 500. It is intermittent-looking because it depends on import order, but it is deterministic per build. ## Fix [Section titled “Fix”](#fix) Import the coordination module **lazily, at call time** — never top-level — in files the registry side-effect-imports: 
```ts
// inside the handler / closure, only when actually needed:
const { listPresence } = await import('../../agent-tools/coordination/presence');
```
 This defers the import until after every module has finished initializing, so the cycle never forms. It matches the existing idiom in `git-sync-action.ts`, which already lazy-imports `@papercusp/db-org`, `@papercusp/flags/server`, `attention-notify`, etc. for the same reason. ## Rule of thumb [Section titled “Rule of thumb”](#rule-of-thumb) In any file the **system-action registry** or an **endpoint `defineTool`** pulls in, import sibling `agent-tools/coordination/*` (and other registry-adjacent) modules with a call-time `await import()`, not a static top-level import. A new static import into one of these files + a fresh 500 in an unrelated tool = suspect a cycle first.

# Lazy substrate boot (LAZY_SUBSTRATE_BOOT) + why the sidecar (SUBSTRATE_SIDECAR) stays dark

> How the LAZY_SUBSTRATE_BOOT eviction reaper works (v1 evicts only inert private engines; the swarm-presence keepalive for idle SHARED harnesses is v2), and the evidence that SUBSTRATE_SIDECAR is a pervasively-coupled multi-session re-architecture that must NOT be flipped on.

## TL;DR [Section titled “TL;DR”](#tldr) * **`papercusp-lazy-substrate-boot` is DEFAULT-ON (v1, WI-596).** A 60s reaper (`substrate-eviction-reaper.ts`) tears down idle, **inert private** (swarm-less, peerless) harness substrate engines via the pure `planSubstrateEviction` policy, bounding operator RSS sub-linearly in harness count. OFF is byte-identical eager boot. * **`papercusp-substrate-sidecar` stays DEFAULT-OFF (genuinely incomplete, WI-604).** P-009 was dropped; the substrate is pervasively coupled to the main process. Flipping it on is a no-op-but-wasteful spawn, or — if naively cut over — breaks federation. Do **not** flip it without the full re-architecture. ## Lazy boot: the safety boundary that makes v1 flippable [Section titled “Lazy boot: the safety boundary that makes v1 flippable”](#lazy-boot-the-safety-boundary-that-makes-v1-flippable) The eviction RULE (`substrate-eviction-policy.ts`, a pure tested function) never evicts an `active-peer`, `pinned`, or `hot` harness. The **v1 wiring** (`boot-all.ts` `gatherBootedHarnessFacts`) tightens this further: a harness with a **live swarm** (`handle.swarm != null`) or **any admitted remote peer** (`handle.admitted.size > 1`) is reported `pinned`/`hasActivePeer`, so it is **never** evicted. Why that is safe-by-construction: a **private** (swarm-less) harness’s substrate engine is *pure overhead* — it merges nothing (no peers) and its local writes go **PG-direct**. Tearing it down loses no federation state, so the EI-126 fleet-divergence class is off the table for v1. Consumers null-handle an evicted engine gracefully (`feature-queue` → `substrate-off`, claims → legacy single-writer — never data loss), and an evicted engine **re-boots on access** (`getBootedHarness` fires a background `bootSingleHarness` for a key in the `evicted` set) or on the next boot-all reconcile. The race between the reaper’s fact snapshot and the close is closed by `evictBootedHarnessEngine` **re-checking** freshness + swarm/peer state *immediately before* `closeBootedHarness` — if the harness got hot or gained a peer since the snapshot, the eviction is skipped. The whole path is gated by `enableSubstrateEvictionTracking()` (called only when the reaper starts, i.e. the flag is ON), so the **OFF path is byte-identical** — `getBootedHarness` does no extra work, no reaper runs. ### Current-fleet reality (why v1 is correct but currently inert) [Section titled “Current-fleet reality (why v1 is correct but currently inert)”](#current-fleet-reality-why-v1-is-correct-but-currently-inert) `dev:dogfood_substrate_status` on the live operator shows **one** booted harness (an internal reference harness), which is **shared + peered** → the reaper correctly evicts nothing today. The path-liveness filter in `boot-all` (skip registry entries whose project path is gone) already bounded the original O(harness-count) RSS problem. v1 is ready to act when idle *private* harnesses exist; the real at-scale win is v2. ### v2 (WI-662, NOT done): evict idle SHARED harnesses [Section titled “v2 (WI-662, NOT done): evict idle SHARED harnesses”](#v2-wi-662-not-done-evict-idle-shared-harnesses) The value-at-scale slice is evicting idle **shared-but-currently-peerless** harnesses while a **lightweight swarm-presence keepalive** (D-004) re-boots them on a later peer connection / a `substrate_outbox` NOTIFY / an access. This is divergence-critical and **cannot be verified on a single box** — it needs a real 2-machine federation peer rig. It is the SAME flag (no new flag); it only widens the `pinned = swarm != null` boundary + adds the keepalive + a swarm peer-connection reboot hook. ## Why SUBSTRATE\_SIDECAR cannot just be flipped on [Section titled “Why SUBSTRATE\_SIDECAR cannot just be flipped on”](#why-substrate_sidecar-cannot-just-be-flipped-on) The substrate engine is **pervasively coupled** to the main operator process: * **5+ hot-path consumers call `handle.append()` in-process, synchronously:** feature-queue enqueue/dequeue, distributed-claim, work-item-claim-lease, authority lock-events, presence. Routing these over IPC adds 10–50 ms/append and loses append-atomicity (PG write then a racing IPC append). * **2 in-process background loops bound to the live handle:** the outbox-drain (`LISTEN substrate_outbox` → `handle.append` per row) and the 1 s merge-poll driver (→ PG projections). * **The sidecar bin only built the socket-handoff replication spike.** `apps/operator/bin/substrate-sidecar.ts` stubs `bootHarness`, swarm-join, the merge loop, admission, and the PG projection writers (“later phase”). * **The wrapper never actually cuts over.** `bootSubstrateWithFallback` spawns the sidecar + healthz, then **falls back to in-process boot** — so even ON it is a no-op-but-wasteful spawn. A real cutover means the sidecar must HOST the full `bootHarnessSubstrate` (corestore + swarm + merge loop + PG projections) and the main process must route every `handle.append()` over IPC and read PG-only — or a narrower “replication-offload” design (main keeps the engine, hands raw swarm sockets to the sidecar for `corestore.replicate`, the part already built) that offloads only the merkle-verify CPU/RSS. Either is a tracked multi-session feature, never an overnight flip. (Orthogonal to lazy boot per D-018/D-019.)

# Leading a fleet without polling — the composed await that replaces the monitor loop

> A fleet leader's monitor loop was the exact clock-driven anti-pattern the plan it supervised existed to eliminate: ~14 wakes in one run, mostly near-noops, and still up to 3 minutes to notice a member had dropped its last claim. Leading is now PUSH-based — park on one composed events:await over the fleet transition keys, and demote loop:arm to a long fallback heartbeat. Includes the ready-to-paste spec, why two of the five transitions could NOT be served by the keys that already existed, and the id-scoped-vs-scope-keyed distinction that makes the difference.

## The thing to change [Section titled “The thing to change”](#the-thing-to-change) If you are leading a fleet and your monitor is `loop:arm { intervalSec: 60 }` plus a `fleet:leader-brief` every wake, **you are polling.** Replace it with one composed `events:await` and a long fallback heartbeat. That is not a stylistic preference. It was measured on the `push-not-poll` run of 2026-07-26: a leader supervising 6 members through a 17-item plan burned **\~14 wakes, most of them near-noops**, and still took **up to 3 minutes** to notice that the last item’s claim had dropped. The plan that leader was supervising existed to eliminate clock-driven waiting. Its own monitoring loop was the anti-pattern. ## Ready-to-paste [Section titled “Ready-to-paste”](#ready-to-paste) Substitute your fleet slug and plan slug. Then **end your turn** — the wake carries the payload. 
```plaintext
events:await {
  any: [
    { event: "fleet:member-dead:<my-fleet>" },
    { event: "fleet:context-critical:<my-fleet>" },
    { event: "fleet:claim-released:<my-fleet>" },
    { event: "fleet:item-completed:<my-fleet>" },
    { event: "work-item:claimable", payload_filter: { plan: { eq: "<my-plan>" } } },
    { event: "fleet:drained:<my-fleet>" }
  ],
  timeout_sec: 900,
  on_timeout: "wake"
}
```
 Then, and only then, a **long** heartbeat for what is genuinely not event-shaped: 
```plaintext
loop:arm { intervalSec: 900, goal: "fallback heartbeat for fleet <my-fleet>" }
```
 `loop:arm` is no longer the monitor. It is the backstop for the case where a push was missed — see *Why the heartbeat stays* below. On each wake: `fleet:leader-brief` to SEE the fleet, act, re-register the await, end the turn. The brief is how you look at the fleet; it is not how you watch it. ## What each key buys you [Section titled “What each key buys you”](#what-each-key-buys-you) | key | you are woken when | replaces | | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | | `fleet:member-dead:<slug>` | a member reaches a CONFIRMED-dead verdict | polling the brief for liveness | | `fleet:context-critical:<slug>` | a member crosses into critical context pressure | polling every member’s `contextPressure` | | `fleet:claim-released:<slug>` | a member’s claim returns to the pool | polling `fleet:assignments` for a dropped claim | | `fleet:item-completed:<slug>` | a member settles an item | polling the brief for burn-down delta | | `work-item:claimable` + `payload_filter {plan}` | work exists for an idle member | the idle re-poll of `scheduler:get_next` | | `fleet:drained:<slug>` | every claimable lane is done | polling to know when to `loop:end` | `fleet:context-critical` pairs directly with `fleet:require-checkpoint { member, itemId }`: you are woken *before* the member compacts, while forcing a checkpoint still helps. ## The distinction that makes this work — and that fooled me first [Section titled “The distinction that makes this work — and that fooled me first”](#the-distinction-that-makes-this-work--and-that-fooled-me-first) Surveying the catalogue before building these, I matched the five transitions a leader reacts to against existing key names and concluded three already fired. That was wrong, and wrong in the expensive direction — it argued for not building something that was missing, with apparent evidence. **Name-matching is not capability-matching.** Awaitable keys come in three populations, and the catalog does not currently distinguish them: * **id-scoped** — `work-item:done:<id>`, `claim:released:<id>`. These fire for ONE known id. They are correct for a **delegator** awaiting a SPECIFIC child. * **global / payload-filtered** — `work-item:claimable`, `work-item:created`. Usable by anyone; narrow with `payload_filter`. * **scope-keyed** — `fleet:drained:<slug>` and the four above. Usable by anyone who knows a scope they already own. A **leader** does not know, in advance, which of its fleet’s items will be released or completed next. So the id-scoped keys are unusable for it: using them means registering N awaits and re-registering every time the set changes — a subscription treadmill driven by polling the item set, which is the very thing being removed. `claim:released:<id>` and `work-item:done:<id>` keep firing unchanged; they are simply not a fleet feed. Of the five transitions, exactly one (`work-item:claimable`) was genuinely already usable. The other four had to be published. > If you are ever surveying “does this event already exist?”, ask **who can subscribe without already knowing the answer.** That question, not the key name, is the one that decides whether a family is usable. (Filed as EI-19299170840541307 — the catalog should carry this as an explicit field rather than leaving it to be inferred.) ## Why the heartbeat stays [Section titled “Why the heartbeat stays”](#why-the-heartbeat-stays) Two of the four transitions have no transition site at all. **Death is the ABSENCE of a write** — nothing happens at the moment a member dies; a verdict merely becomes derivable. Context pressure is derived from self-reported token counts, so the bucket changes with no event of its own. Both are therefore produced by a periodic sweep (`system:fleet-transition-sweep`, every 60s) that diffs against the previous observation. That sweep is still push, not poll, in the sense that matters: **one sweep for the whole box replaces N leaders each burning a turn to look.** The leader sleeps; the substrate looks. But its previous-observation snapshot is in-process, so a restart costs at most one missed edge, once. That is the whole reason `loop:arm` stays: **push-primary with a backstop.** Size it in the 15-minute range — long enough that quiet wakes are rare, short enough that a missed edge is not a lost one. Do not delete it, and do not shorten it back toward a minute; that just reinstates the poll with extra steps. ## The two false alarms deliberately NOT sent [Section titled “The two false alarms deliberately NOT sent”](#the-two-false-alarms-deliberately-not-sent) A monitor that cries wolf is worse than no monitor, because the leader learns to ignore it. Two suppressions are load-bearing: 1. **`draining` and `suspect` do not count as dead.** Both read as “dead” in the orphaned-claim arithmetic, but per WI-4400 they require a wake confirmation first. Only `ended` fires `fleet:member-dead`. 2. **A member DISAPPEARING is not a death.** A row reaped on its TTL and a member that left the fleet are indistinguishable to the sweep, so it stays silent rather than guessing. Likewise the detector never fires on a **first sighting** (or the first sweep after an operator restart would wake every leader for every historically-dead row), and never **re-fires while a state persists** (`ended` and `critical` last many sweeps; re-firing would be a wake storm). ## Key shape, if you add another one [Section titled “Key shape, if you add another one”](#key-shape-if-you-add-another-one) Use `fleet:<transition>:<slug>` — **slug last**, uniform with `fleet:drained:<slug>`. This is not cosmetic. `familyKeyPrefix` truncates a catalog template at its FIRST placeholder, so a slug-first template like `fleet:<slug>:member-dead` registers the bare prefix `fleet:` — and `keyMatchesCatalog` then matches EVERY `fleet:*` key ever awaited, typos included, silently disarming the EI-10870 orphan guard for the whole namespace. The plan text that commissioned these keys sketched the slug-first shape; it was caught during implementation, not review. ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `events:catalog` — the discoverable list; every family above carries a `replacesPoll`. * `fleet:require-checkpoint` — the lever to pull on `fleet:context-critical`. * `fleet:bench { member, wakeEvent }` — park a member that is blocked-waiting, so it too stops burning wakes.

# The lexical leg is `ts_rank_cd` (cover density), not BM25 — and four tuning fixes died on that

> Papercusp's hybrid search called its lexical leg `bm25` for months. It never was BM25. `ts_rank_cd` is COVER DENSITY — it scores how tightly the query lexemes cluster — so on a single-lexeme query it has nothing to measure and collapses hundreds of matches onto a handful of tied scores. It is also called with no normalization argument at every call site, so there is no document-length term at all. Four independent fix directions for a recall complaint were measured and all died on this one fact: a wider rerank pool, a Stage B re-rank, every other built-in PG ranker, and length normalisation (which had nothing to correct). Read the ranker before you tune the ranking.

## The one-line version [Section titled “The one-line version”](#the-one-line-version) The lexical leg of hybrid search is PostgreSQL’s **`ts_rank_cd`** — *cover density* ranking. It was called `bm25` in the type system until P-013 renamed it. **It was never BM25, and the two behave nothing alike.** If you are about to tune lexical relevance, tune the thing that is actually running. ## What `ts_rank_cd` actually computes [Section titled “What ts\_rank\_cd actually computes”](#what-ts_rank_cd-actually-computes) Cover density scores **how tightly the query’s lexemes cluster together** in the document — a “cover” is a span containing all of them. That is a genuinely useful signal for a multi-word phrase query. It has two properties that matter enormously here, and neither is what “BM25” would lead you to expect: **1. On a single-lexeme query it has nothing to measure.** There is no span between one term and itself, so the score degenerates toward a function of raw occurrence, and huge numbers of documents tie. Measured on this corpus (plan `semantic-search-fingerprint-coverage-2026-08-03`): a single-lexeme query returning **913 matches produced 7 distinct scores.** A leg that emits 7 buckets for 913 rows contributes almost no ordering information to the fusion — most of the “ranking” downstream of it is tie-breaking by whatever comes next. **2. There is no document-length normalization. At all.** `ts_rank_cd` takes an optional integer `normalization` argument controlling length division; **omitted, it defaults to `0` — no normalization.** Every call site in this repo omits it: 
```ts
// packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/search/sources.ts — all legs, no 3rd argument
rank: sql`ts_rank_cd(${tsv}, q.andq)`,
rank: sql`ts_rank_cd(${tsv}, q.orq)`,
ts_rank_cd(body_tsv,    plainto_tsquery('english', ${query})) AS rank,
ts_rank_cd(content_tsv, plainto_tsquery('english', ${query})) AS rank,
```
 BM25, by contrast, is *defined* by its length normalization (the `b` parameter) and its saturating term-frequency (`k1`). Neither exists here. Calling this leg `bm25` did not merely mislabel it — it implied a tuning surface that is not present. ## Why this matters: four fix directions died on it [Section titled “Why this matters: four fix directions died on it”](#why-this-matters-four-fix-directions-died-on-it) A recall complaint (“theory” scoring 2/9 at recall\@30) generated four independent fix directions. **All four were measured and all four were dead**, and in hindsight every one of them was refuted by the paragraph above: | direction tried | measured outcome | why it was doomed | | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Length normalisation** | on-topic turns average 2499 chars vs 2670 overall — no length skew to correct | there is no length term in the score to begin with | | **A wider rerank pool** | 13.5s at 45ms/pair — cost-prohibitive | a wider pool re-ranks more *ties*; the input ordering carries no signal to widen | | **Stage B re-rank** | recall 0.333 → 0.333, exactly unchanged | same reason — reordering a tied set | | **Other built-in PG rankers** | `ts_rank_cd` is cover density; `ts_rank` differs but is still not BM25 | no built-in PG ranker implements BM25 | The transferable point is not “these four ideas were bad.” Each is a sensible thing to try against a lexical ranker. **They were refuted by a property of the ranker that nobody had read** — and the ranker’s *name* actively pointed away from reading it. A day of measurement substituted for ten minutes with the source. ## Reading a score: native vs fused [Section titled “Reading a score: native vs fused”](#reading-a-score-native-vs-fused) Two scores travel with a hit and they are **not comparable**: * **`SearchHit.rankerScores`** — the *native* per-ranker score (P-001/WI-7505). A `ts_rank_cd` value is unbounded-positive and typically small; a cosine similarity is bounded `[-1, 1]`. * **the fused RRF score** — reciprocal-rank fusion, whose value depends only on *rank position*, not on either native scale. Comparing a fused score against a cosine threshold is meaningless, and it has produced a confidently-wrong report here before: a post-fusion RRF score whose ceiling is \~`0.0328` was read against a `0.45` cosine floor and reported as “99.9% of injections fall below the floor.” **A suspiciously round rate over thousands of samples is usually a definitional artifact, not a finding.** `min-score.ts` documents the per-leg scales; read it before setting any threshold. ## The naming, and why `bm25` still appears [Section titled “The naming, and why bm25 still appears”](#the-naming-and-why-bm25-still-appears) P-013 renamed the leg `bm25` → `lexical` in `@papercusp/search`. **The string `bm25` is still accepted as INPUT and that is deliberate — it is not a deprecation alias** (which this repo otherwise bans). `provenance.ts` spells out why: a *host* may name its own lexical source `bm25`, and such a source must still classify as lexical rather than be silently dropped: 
```ts
return ranker.startsWith('lexical') || ranker.startsWith('bm25');
```
 So: `bm25` surviving in the predicate is a compatibility surface for foreign inputs, not a leftover. Do not “finish the rename” by deleting it. ## What to do instead [Section titled “What to do instead”](#what-to-do-instead) * **Want real BM25?** It has to be built — no PostgreSQL built-in provides it. That is the one remaining live route for the recall complaint above (tracked as P-035, owner-gated). * **Before tuning any ranker**, open the SQL and check (a) which ranking function, (b) its normalization argument, (c) whether the query is single- or multi-lexeme. Those three facts determine which tuning ideas are even coherent. * **Never infer a ranker’s behavior from its identifier.** This is the general form, and it cost four measured experiments: a name is documentation, and documentation drifts. The function call does not. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * [A guard can be ENFORCED and still be too late](/internal/docs/agent-insights/a-guard-can-be-enforced-and-still-be-too-late) — the same “read the writer, not the label” failure in the guard/lint domain. * `libs/generic/search/src/min-score.ts` — the per-leg score scales, and why one floor cannot serve both legs.

# Linux-VM desktop testing — the test VM already exists, plus the seeded-.deb recipe

> The Linux clean-room test VM already exists at /mnt/data/offload/papercup-linux-test-vm (do NOT provision a new one). How to boot it, SSH/SPICE in, install and launch a seeded release .deb, and drive its GUI headlessly on DISPLAY=:0 via SPICE — plus the E2E findings from the first seeded-.deb run (2026-07-05).

## The one thing to know first: the Linux test VM ALREADY EXISTS [Section titled “The one thing to know first: the Linux test VM ALREADY EXISTS”](#the-one-thing-to-know-first-the-linux-test-vm-already-exists) **Do NOT provision or download a fresh Ubuntu image.** A ready, provisioned Linux clean-room test VM lives **outside** the repo (the heavy disk images are never committed) at: * **`/mnt/data/offload/papercup-linux-test-vm/`** (symlinked as `~/papercup-linux-test-vm`), on the 7.3T `/mnt/data` disk — **not** under `/home`, `/var/lib/libvirt`, `/tmp`, or `/srv`. A name-filtered search of the usual dirs misses it; this cost su-bf97d a wrong “no VM exists, I’ll provision one” conclusion on 2026-07-05 until the owner corrected it. If you’re about to provision a Linux VM, **stop and look here first.** Layout: `images/golden.qcow2` (the provisioned desktop image) + `images/ubuntu-24.04-base.img`; `run/<instance>/` holds each running instance’s `overlay.qcow2`, `qemu.pid`, `serial.log`. The default instance is **`clean`**. ## Boot / access [Section titled “Boot / access”](#boot--access) * **Launcher**: `papercusp-desktop/scripts/linux-test-vm/boot-vm.sh <instance>` (helpers in `lib/common.sh`). Raw QEMU/KVM, headless (`-display none`), SPICE for pixels, slirp `hostfwd` for SSH — the same box convention as the Mac/Windows build VMs. It no-ops if the instance is already running. * **Per-instance ports** (`ports_for()` in `common.sh`): instance `clean` → **SSH `2224`, SPICE `127.0.0.1:5932`, operator-forward `3090`**. (`fed-a`/`fed-b` are +1/+2 for federation runs, each on a distinct slirp subnet so hyperswarm holepunching doesn’t dial itself.) The operator-forward base moved off `3072`→`3090` (EI-495): `3072-3074` sat inside the green release operator’s own `:3070`/`:3073` listener neighborhood, so fed-a’s default forward (`3073`) collided with it and FATAL’d `vm-federation.sh` boots whenever a green operator was running. * **SSH**: user **`tester`** (`VM_USER` default), key **`~/.ssh/papercup-vm-linux`**. One-liner: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-linux -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -p 2224 tester@127.0.0.1` (host keys are intentionally unpinned — a fresh overlay re-presents golden’s key). Passwordless `sudo` works. * **Show it on the owner’s real desktop**: the guest renders to qxl → SPICE 5932. From the host, on the owner’s X display: `DISPLAY=:1 nohup remote-viewer spice://127.0.0.1:5932 &`. Whatever is on the guest’s `:0` is what the owner sees. ## Driving the GUI headlessly (no owner needed) [Section titled “Driving the GUI headlessly (no owner needed)”](#driving-the-gui-headlessly-no-owner-needed) The guest runs an Xorg on **`:0`** (tty1, user `tester`). Its auth file is the `-auth /tmp/serverauth.XXXX` from the Xorg cmdline (grep `ps -eo args | grep -oE '\-auth /tmp/serverauth[^ ]*'`). With `DISPLAY=:0 XAUTHORITY=<that file>` you can, over SSH: * launch the app detached: `setsid env DISPLAY=:0 XAUTHORITY=$XA '/usr/bin/papercusp-desktop' >/tmp/app.log 2>&1 </dev/null &` * screenshot: **`scrot /tmp/shot.png`** (ImageMagick `import` is NOT installed; `scrot` is). `scp` it out and view it. * click / type: `xdotool` (install via `sudo apt-get install -y xdotool` — the VM has slirp outbound internet). `/usr/bin/papercusp-desktop` is the Tauri binary. `/usr/bin/papercusp` is only a thin `setup`/`tutorial` onboarding wrapper — not the app. ## Installing + testing a seeded release .deb [Section titled “Installing + testing a seeded release .deb”](#installing--testing-a-seeded-release-deb) 1. **Build the .deb on Tower** (the owner box — the seed cut MUST happen there; see below). Output lands at `${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-~/.cargo-target}/release/bundle/deb/` named `Papercusp GUI_<ver>_amd64.deb` (note the **space** in the productName — the old in-tree `Papercusp_*` glob silently resolved 18-day-stale artifacts; `default_deb()` in `common.sh` now searches both locations + name shapes and warns on a stale mtime). 2. **Copy in** (loopback scp is fast — 4GB in \~20s): `scp -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-linux -P 2224 "<deb>" tester@127.0.0.1:~/`. 3. **Clean first-boot**: stop any lingering services (`sudo pkill -f 'Papercusp GUI/sidecar'; pkill -f 'papercusp-desktop|embedded-postgres|code-server'`) and **wipe `~/.papercusp` + `~/.papercusp-workspaces`** — otherwise the fresh seed-restore path is skipped. (No systemd/autostart supervises the sidecar — it daemonizes with ppid 1, so a `pkill` sticks.) 4. **Install**: `sudo dpkg -i ~/<deb>` (works even reinstalling the same version; extracting the \~3.6GB seed takes \~2 min). 5. **Verify the seed bundled** at `/usr/lib/Papercusp GUI/seed/`: expect `manifest.json` + `git/super.bundle` (\~1.86GB) + `git/submodules/` + `corestore/` (\~1.8GB). A seed dir with only `.gitignore`+`README.md` means you installed the **non-seeded** build. 6. **Launch** on `:0` (per above) and watch `~/.papercusp-workspaces/default/.papercusp/logs/gui.log` + `~/.papercusp/logs/serve.log`. ### Querying the guest’s embedded Postgres [Section titled “Querying the guest’s embedded Postgres”](#querying-the-guests-embedded-postgres) **Builds since 2026-07-07 ship real, self-contained client tools** at `/usr/lib/Papercusp GUI/sidecar/bin/` — `psql`, `pg_dump`, `pg_dumpall`, `pg_restore`, wrapper-wired to the embedded libpq (+ its own openssl), so they run on a clean machine with no host PostgreSQL packages. Just use them (`fed.sh <a|b> sql` does automatically): 
```plaintext
"/usr/lib/Papercusp GUI/sidecar/bin/psql" \
  'postgresql://harness_admin:harness_admin_pwd@127.0.0.1:<port>/papercusp'
# conn URL is in ~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json
```
 **Installs from builds BEFORE 2026-07-07** shipped a broken `bin/psql` (a Debian `pg_wrapper` perl shim that dies with `Can't locate PgCommon.pm` — root cause below). On those, reinstall a fresh .deb, or fall back to the bundled `node` + `pg` module: 
```plaintext
NODE="/usr/lib/Papercusp GUI/sidecar/bin/node"
PG="/usr/lib/Papercusp GUI/sidecar/node_modules/@papercusp/embedded-postgres-server/node_modules/pg"
```
 Write a tiny `.cjs` that `require(PG)`, connect with that URL, run your SELECTs. **Root cause of the old breakage (traced + FIXED 2026-07-07):** `papercusp-desktop/bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` needs client tools for the snapshot subsystem, but embedded-postgres ships server-only — so it fell back to copying whatever `command -v psql` resolved to on the **build host**. On Debian/Ubuntu that is `/usr/bin/psql` = postgresql-common’s **perl `pg_wrapper` dispatcher**, not a real binary. It works on the build host (wrapper + versioned client both installed there), so every build-time probe passed — then died on any clean machine. All FOUR tools shipped as the same \~9.5K wrapper (see `sidecar/bin/.pg-tools-source`), which also silently disabled the PG half of the **snapshot subsystem** — `packages/backup/src/hook.ts` degrades to a dump-less snapshot on spawn failure, so backups “succeeded” with no DB state. The fix vendors the real `/usr/lib/postgresql/<major>/bin/` binaries (major matched to the embedded server) behind LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH wrappers pointing at the bundled libpq, and the build now hard-fails if any vendored tool is a `#!`-script or fails a `--version` probe as-installed. The lesson that generalizes: **a tool copied off the build host can be a dispatcher/shim that only works there — verify what a copied binary IS, not just that it runs on the host that built it.** ## Seed-cut identity rule (do not violate) [Section titled “Seed-cut identity rule (do not violate)”](#seed-cut-identity-rule-do-not-violate) The seed’s git half is encrypted with `deriveEpochKey(pot, epoch)` — deterministic per the pot’s PRIVATE key, held only in **Tower’s live pot keychain** (Tower = the owner box that owns the Papercusp GitHub identity). `cut-seed-cli` fails-closed off-Tower (`--allow-mint-epoch-key` is the only bootstrap hatch). **Never cut a seed on a build VM** — get-or-CREATE would mint a divergent, unwrappable key and the installed app could never decrypt the seed post-admission. ## E2E findings from the first seeded-.deb run (2026-07-05, WI-2902) [Section titled “E2E findings from the first seeded-.deb run (2026-07-05, WI-2902)”](#e2e-findings-from-the-first-seeded-deb-run-2026-07-05-wi-2902) What the seeded Linux GUI .deb actually does on a clean first boot: * ✅ **Installs + boots cleanly.** Self-hosts the operator sidecar (`no Server reachable — self-hosting … (single-bundle Linux)`), applies the pre-migrated PG snapshot (`pg: seed applied — skipping … full migration replay`), spawns code-server + ghostty terminal + embedded Postgres. The PUI terminal (Zellij `network`/`plans` tabs) renders and shows the expected pre-sign-in empty network board. * ⏸️ **Pot seed git-restore is gated on GitHub sign-in.** `[papercusp-pot] not created this boot: join awaiting GitHub sign-in`. The encrypted git half only decrypts **post-admission**, so a fully-offline first boot cannot restore the repo until the owner signs in (an interactive, owner-gated step — do not attempt to enter credentials). * 🐛 **A release .deb built before a migration lands ships the pre-fix schema.** This run’s .deb predated migrations 505/506 (`db-sql/` + the baked `db-seed.tar.gz` both stop at `503`), so `agent_facts` shipped with `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` + a stored generated column (`fed_key`) + membership in the `zero_harness` publication and **no primary key** → every 30s the sweep fails with `cannot delete from table "agent_facts": Replica identity must not contain unpublished generated columns` (the WI-2914 bug that mig 505 fixes). The db-seed snapshot and the shipped migration SQL are internally *consistent* (both 503) — this is **staleness, not a runtime migration bug**. **Cut releases from a tree that includes every intended migration**, and treat the on-VM sweep log as a schema-freshness check. **Now guarded (WI-3047):** `release-local.sh` fetches and compares the `libs/papercusp` submodule against `origin/<branch>` before cutting — a stale (behind-remote) submodule **fails the build on stable/beta** and **warns on alpha** (mirroring the dirty-tree channel split). That closes the exact root cause here: `build-desktop-sidecar.sh` bakes `db-seed.tar.gz` from whatever is checked out under `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/`, so a lagging submodule pointer silently shipped pre-505/506 SQL. * ⚠️ **`native-terminal: could not establish X11 glue session`** → the ghostty terminal floats as a separate window instead of embedding in the webview. Suspected to be a VM-environment artifact: this barebones test VM runs an Xorg with **no window manager** (only `at-spi2-registryd`; no mutter/gnome-shell), so X11 reparenting/embedding can’t work. Verify on a full DE before filing as an app bug. * ℹ️ The first webview frame briefly hit a React error boundary worded for dev (“the app was rebuilt underneath the page — the dev build watcher rewrote the bundle”); a reload cleared it. That copy is misleading in a release build and should be conditioned on dev mode. ## Build-speed notes (release-local.sh) [Section titled “Build-speed notes (release-local.sh)”](#build-speed-notes-release-localsh) * The deb already uses **gzip** (`data.tar.gz`), not xz — that lever is pulled; Tauri 2’s deb bundler exposes no compression knob to tune further. * The dominant, **re-incurred** cost is `cut_release_seed()` (runs *unconditionally* at every build, line \~224): full-history git bundle (superproject + \~40 submodules) + 1.8GB corestore snapshot + chacha20 encryption of the \~1.86GB git half. For **iterative rebuilds where HEAD/seed is unchanged**, `PAPERCUSP_SKIP_SEED_CUT=1` reuses the existing `src-tauri/seed` and is the single biggest time saver. (A real *release* cut still needs a fresh seed matching HEAD.) * `PAPERCUSP_BUILD_ROLES="gui"` builds only the GUI role (skips the server bundle); cargo incremental compile is \~3 min. The AppImage is built separately via `bin/build-appimage.sh` (Tauri’s appimage target crashes linuxdeploy on the sidecar tree — WI-2918). That script also **overwrites linuxdeploy’s compiled `AppRun` with a robust shell `AppRun`** (WI-2902): the ELF AppRun NULL-derefs in libc on some hosts (`segfault at 0 … in libc.so.6`) and crashes the launch before the app starts, even though the binary runs fine given `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` * the WebKitGTK env; the shell AppRun sets that env off `$APPDIR` (pixbuf/gio/ gstreamer/webkit helper paths) and execs `usr/bin/papercusp-desktop`. * `scripts/linux-test-vm/boot-vm.sh` now guards the `reset→up` / port-collision race (WI-2902): qemu treats a SPICE **or** hostfwd bind failure as FATAL and boots no VM. It waits (bounded) for a just-killed VM to release the deterministic SSH/SPICE ports, and **drops just the operator hostfwd** (`host:$OP_PORT → guest:3070`) when that port is held by a live host service, booting anyway — the in-guest tests (SSH + in-guest curl + screendump) never use the forward. Set `VM_OP_BASE` to a free base to reclaim it; `VM_VGA` overrides the default `qxl`.

# Live 2-machine K-CUT re-key witness — the working recipe + the federation gaps (WI-560)

> How to run the live fed-a/fed-b K0→K1→K-revoke→K-CUT re-key cut-off witness on the linux-test-vm rig, what actually works, and the remaining live blocker for JOINER-side epoch-key receipt: live announce→admit still needs a gh-ATTESTED device announce, absent on the gh-unauthed VMs — so admit fed-b via the owner approval path (seed the pending-join + pot:membership_decide). Current joinHiveAsView now records the owner's pot pubkey and re-keys joined member substrates in place, so post-startup view joins no longer require a joiner restart just to move member substrates onto the pot topic. Owner-side K-CUT is fully verifiable on fed-a regardless. Discovered 2026-06-24 running WI-560; refreshed 2026-06-25 after EI-681 join-pot fixes.

The C-001 read-plane re-key flip (`papercusp-pot-rekey`) is owner-gated on a **live 2-machine K-CUT witness** (WI-560; see [pot-rekey-flip-readiness](/internal/docs/agent-insights/pot-rekey-flip-readiness)). This page is what running it on the `scripts/linux-test-vm` rig actually taught: the re-key **mechanism** is green end-to-end at the authoritative OWNER layer, and the only thing standing between that and the joiner-side confirmation is **federation transport**, not the re-key code. ## The witness, owner-side (this part WORKS, fully on fed-a) [Section titled “The witness, owner-side (this part WORKS, fully on fed-a)”](#the-witness-owner-side-this-part-works-fully-on-fed-a) Mechanism map (all gated on `papercusp-pot-rekey`, ON on the rig): * **K0 admit/grant** — owner admits a member ⇒ `upsertHiveMember` ⇒ `grantEpochKeysToMembers` wraps epoch `[0..current]` to the new device (owner-self-gated on `loadHivePubkey`). `pot-membership-admission.ts` + `pot-epoch-boundary-wiring.ts`. **Reconnect path (BUG B, D-028 layer 3):** `ownerAdmitOrPend`’s `already_member` branch now also calls `reconcileEpochKeysForCurrentMembers({ refederate: true, onlyDevices: <this member's devices> })` on reconnect — a member that missed its original federated grant (joined-after-grant, forward-only cursor, or re-session) has its keys re-sent automatically. Best-effort (a re-grant hiccup never fails admission). * **K1 owner re-key** — a benign boundary that KEEPS everyone: `pot-set-listing.ts` go-private ⇒ `advanceEpochOnHiveBoundary` with **no cutOff** ⇒ epoch++ wrapped to ALL current members. * **K-revoke** — `pot:ban_member` ⇒ `pot-revoke-contributor.ts` `revokeHiveContributor` ⇒ `advanceEpochOnHiveBoundary(cutOffPubkeys=[target device])` ⇒ epoch++ wrapped to **remaining members only**. Ban is Pot-native (owner = holds the pot key via `loadHivePubkey`), **NOT gh-repo-admin** — no GitHub token needed to ban. * **K-CUT** — the revoked device simply has no row at the new epoch; no such row exists to author or federate, so it can never reach the cut member. Verified live on fed-a (fresh isolated pot `wi560k-pot`, member ← a public repo), epoch × device wrap matrix: | epoch | owner device | revoked device | event | | ----- | ------------ | -------------- | ------------------------- | | 0 | ✓ | ✓ | admit/grant | | 1 | ✓ | ✓ | owner re-key (go-private) | | 2 | ✓ | **✗** | ban → cut | The owner-side cut is the thing the flag actually gates, and it composes with the already -green hermetic content read-cut witness (`pot-epoch-read-cut-witness.test.ts`). ## Gap 1 — admitting the joiner: the live announce→admit needs gh attestation [Section titled “Gap 1 — admitting the joiner: the live announce→admit needs gh attestation”](#gap-1--admitting-the-joiner-the-live-announceadmit-needs-gh-attestation) On the rig **both VMs are gh-unauthed**, so a joiner cannot produce the attested device announce that the owner’s substrate admission (`admitAnnouncedPeerAsOwner` / `drainAdmissionQueue`) consumes — the joiner materializes only as a read-only VIEW (`joinHiveAsView`), never a crypto member (this is the long-standing “fed-b is a view-joiner but has 0 epoch rows” symptom). **Recipe that works** — drive the owner approval path the WI explicitly allows. Seed the pending-join on the OWNER (the part the gh gap blocks) then admit through the real verb: 
```sh
# on fed-a (owner): seed fed-b's pending join with its real device pubkey
fed.sh a sql "INSERT INTO harness_shared.hive_pending_joins
 (workspace_id,harness_slug,github_user_id,github_username,device_attestations,status,
  requested_at,origin,created_at,updated_at)
 VALUES ('default','<pot-home>',<joiner_gh_id>,'<login>',
  '[{\"device_pubkey\":\"<joiner_device_b64>\",\"gist_id\":\"manual\",\"gist_url\":\"\",
     \"device_label\":\"fed-b\",\"created_at\":0,\"signature_by_device\":\"\"}]'::jsonb,
  'pending',(extract(epoch from now())*1000)::bigint,'local',
  (extract(epoch from now())*1000)::bigint,(extract(epoch from now())*1000)::bigint)"
# admit through the PRODUCTION verb (runs approvePendingJoin → upsertHiveMember → grant)
fed.sh a mcp pot:membership_decide '{"pot":"<pot-home>","githubUserId":<id>,"decision":"approve","workspace":"default"}'
```
 The grant/cut path is 100% production code; only the *discovery* of the device is shortcut (the gh-attestation concern is orthogonal to the re-key mechanism). The real fix for live admission is restoring gh auth on the VMs (WI-757). ## Current behavior (2026-06-25) — join-pot now re-keys members in place [Section titled “Current behavior (2026-06-25) — join-pot now re-keys members in place”](#current-behavior-2026-06-25--join-pot-now-re-keys-members-in-place) The original WI-560 witness found that a view-join performed after operator startup left joined member substrates on their per-repo `gh:<repo_id>` topics while the owner served the pot on the pot-pubkey topic. That part is now fixed in `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/join-hive.ts`: * `joinHiveAsView` accepts or resolves the owner’s `hivePubkey` from discovery. * It writes a remote pot identity with `upsertRemoteHiveIdentity`, using a non-signing `remote:<hiveId>` keychain id so the joiner can resolve the same pot topic without pretending to own the pot. * After stamping `hive_slug` on the joined members, it calls `rekeyHarness(workspaceId, memberSlug)` for each successful join. That re-resolves the substrate binding in place onto the owner’s pot-pubkey topic; a joiner operator restart is no longer required solely to move post-startup joins onto the pot topic. The remaining live-rig blocker is therefore narrower: the owner still has to announce the pot/home identity on the shared topic, and the gh-unauthed VMs still cannot produce the attested live announce path. Use the owner approval path below for membership grant/cut testing until VM gh auth is restored. ## Gap 2 — historical note: repo-LESS homes did not federate without gh + a boot [Section titled “Gap 2 — historical note: repo-LESS homes did not federate without gh + a boot”](#gap-2--historical-note-repo-less-homes-did-not-federate-without-gh--a-boot) This was the second blocker observed on 2026-06-24 before EI-681 landed: * **Repo-bound MEMBER harnesses federate fine without gh auth** — they rendezvous on the public repo topic (`shared_repo_binding_cache.harness_topic`). On the rig fed-b actively peers hello-world / fixawitness / spoon-knife members + a freshly-joined member clone. * **The repo-LESS pot HOME needs the gh-auth-bound announce** (`local-announce-identity` → `resolveLocalAnnounceIdentity` throws when gh-unauthed ⇒ `boot.ts` keeps it local-only; see [substrate-swarm-self-heal-no-restart](/internal/docs/agent-insights/substrate-swarm-self-heal-no-restart) * the [restart runbook §6](/internal/docs/agent-insights/federation-rig-restart-runbook)). * **`hive_epoch_keys` (and `hive_members`) federate over the HOME log** (the A-003 pot-home seam), NOT the member topic. So even when the joiner peers the member, the epoch keys never arrive. * **A joiner only peered a HOME its operator booted at STARTUP.** Before EI-681, `joinHiveAsView` cloned the member harnesses but did not materialize the remote pot identity or re-key member substrates after stamping `hive_slug`, so a pot view-joined after startup stayed on member repo topics until a restart. ### To complete the live joiner-side receipt [Section titled “To complete the live joiner-side receipt”](#to-complete-the-live-joiner-side-receipt) 1. Restore gh auth on the OWNER VM with its **correct historical identity** (host `gh auth token` piped over ssh — runbook §6; reversible, no restart) so the home announces. 2. Re-publish the pot (a go-private K1 WITHDRAWS it — re-`discovery:set_pot public` after). 3. Re-run the join/discovery path with the current driver. `joinHiveAsView` now records the remote pot identity and calls `rekeyHarness` for joined members in place; only restart the joiner if you need to recover from an already-wedged old run or to pick up a new deploy. Then the joiner replicates the owner’s home log and ends up holding epoch 0..K-1 (the keys it legitimately had) but **never the post-ban epoch** — the live K-CUT, and (with content encryption on) the AEAD content read-cut. ## Gap 3 — fresh-joiner bootstrap-admission deadlock (WI-779/WI-780, both resolved) [Section titled “Gap 3 — fresh-joiner bootstrap-admission deadlock (WI-779/WI-780, both resolved)”](#gap-3--fresh-joiner-bootstrap-admission-deadlock-wi-779wi-780-both-resolved) Two DEEPER transport-layer findings from the same fed-a/fed-b rig session, upstream of Gaps 1-2 (both fixed; captured here so the next agent hitting “peers connect but nothing merges” doesn’t have to re-diagnose from scratch). If you’re chasing this on a fresh rig session and instead hit `superuser_invalid_bearer` or `no_owner_identity` with no VM reset in between, that’s the separate, upstream **D-007** operator-workspace-scoped-`HOME` gotcha (one session earlier in this same investigation) — see [federation-rig-restart-runbook §8](/internal/docs/agent-insights/federation-rig-restart-runbook#8-operator-workspace-scoped-home-silently-breaks-both-the-superuser-token-and-gh-auth-d-007), not a re-run of the bootstrap deadlock below. **WI-779 — substrate boot timeout under concurrent multi-harness load.** The swarm/DHT layer peers fine (`peer_connected` fires on the pot topic) but `sync/hyperbee/boot.ts`’s per-harness hyperbee-substrate boot (log-replication layer) hit its 30s timeout and never came up when many cross-workspace harnesses booted at once (a healthy baseline was 2 harnesses in \~6.1s). Roster + features never merge because the substrate that would carry them never finishes booting. Root-caused as a boot-concurrency / serialization issue in `boot-all.ts`’s per-harness boot fan-out, not a DHT reachability problem — fixed as part of the same investigation that unblocked WI-780 below. **WI-780 — owner-log bootstrap-admission deadlock (the actual “roster never arrives” cause).** Even once WI-779’s substrate boot succeeded and swarm peering was bidirectional, a **fresh joiner’s `hive_members` roster is empty**, and `boot.ts`’s `resolveSameHiveMember` → `classifySameHiveMember` only admits an announcing peer’s frame if `memberDevices.includes(devicePubkey)` — i.e. it needs the roster to already contain the announcer. For the OWNER’s own announce this is circular: the roster that would admit the owner lives in the owner’s own log, which the joiner will never merge until it admits the owner. Every owner announce buffers in `pendingPeers` and retries forever — a genuine bootstrap deadlock, not a crypto/admission/cursor bug (crypto, epoch-K0 wrap, and admission were all separately verified working on the rig before this was isolated). Fix (security-scoped, landed via WI-797): bootstrap-admit the OWNER’s home log via the existing `hive-announce.ts` binding of `owner_device_pubkey` ↔ `hive_pubkey`. At join time the joiner already has the hive\_pubkey; persist the matching owner device as the hive’s trusted bootstrap identity, then add a pre-check in `resolveSameHiveMember`: if the frame’s `device_pubkey` matches that hive’s stored owner device AND the frame’s hive matches the joined `hive_pubkey`, admit unconditionally — **scoped to exactly that one owner device**, never widened to arbitrary peers (widening it would reopen the WI-259 membership guard as an over-admission hole). Adversarial coverage added alongside the fix: an owner bootstrapping on an empty roster, a non-owner peer with an empty roster still correctly `miss`-buffering, and a peer that spoofs the owner’s `github_user_id` on a different device still correctly refused. A second, unrelated bug was masking the fix’s effect during verification: **WI-808** — the peer-log wire envelope was dropping the new epoch op field, so federated content arrived with `epoch=NULL` and was silently passthrough-dropped even after roster+epoch-K0 legs went green. See [peerlogop-wire-envelope-drops-new-opfields](/internal/docs/agent-insights/peerlogop-wire-envelope-drops-new-opfields) for that finding in full. Both are **resolved and live-verified** (2026-06-25, on the gh-attested fed-a/fed-b rig: `WI-21` created on fed-a federated to fed-b end-to-end — `epoch_gate_seen → epoch_applied → work_items WI-21 origin=remote` on the joiner). Full history: `shared-hive-public-release-2026-06-22` plan, decisions D-008/D-009/D-013. ## WI-887: epoch key reconcile self-heal [Section titled “WI-887: epoch key reconcile self-heal”](#wi-887-epoch-key-reconcile-self-heal) A member admitted while `papercusp-pot-rekey` was dark — or admitted after an epoch advanced before they were known to the owner — permanently lacks the epoch keys minted before them unless explicitly healed. `pot-epoch-boundary-wiring.ts` now has two complement paths: * **`reconcileEpochKeysForCurrentMembers`** — wraps epochs `[0..current]` to every LIVE (non-revoked) member device. Called via the `onMemberApplied` hook (pot-members projection) to heal the moment a membership op lands. ‘no-fresh-members’ when the pot has no live device. **New params (BUG B, D-028 layer 3):** `refederate?: boolean` re-stamps existing rows so the mig-411 AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE capture trigger re-federates them (vs default write-once gap-fill); `onlyDevices?: readonly string[]` restricts the re-grant to a specific device set (the reconnecting member’s devices) rather than the whole pot — used by `ownerAdmitOrPend`’s reconnect path. * **`reconcileOwnedHiveEpochKeys`** (WI-887 sweep) — GAP-AWARE: enumerates every pot the box knows (`harness_shared.pots`), checks whether any live device is missing the current epoch key, and only then calls `reconcileEpochKeysForCurrentMembers`. NO crypto on the steady state (the perf-anti-pattern guard). Owner-only (self-gates via `loadHivePubkey` null check), C-001-safe (revoked devices excluded), idempotent. Host on in-process periodic checks or call once at owner boot. **On the rig:** after seeding `hive_members` via the owner approval path (Gap 1 recipe), call `reconcileOwnedHiveEpochKeys` on fed-a if any member device shows missing epoch rows. It backfills without advancing the epoch — safe to call even mid-witness. ## Adjacent bug observed (historical — fixed 2026-06-26) [Section titled “Adjacent bug observed (historical — fixed 2026-06-26)”](#adjacent-bug-observed-historical--fixed-2026-06-26) **FIXED by WI-892:** All 11 pot write-tools (`create`, `create_from_repo`, `ban_member`, `add_member`, `membership_decide`, `leave`, …) now route through `resolveConcreteWorkspaceId` (skips `'*'`/blank, falls back to `activeWorkspaceId()` = `'default'`). The `workspace_id='*'` papercup no longer leaks into hive\_members writes, so the MCP path and the HTTP route are now equivalent. No `workspace:"default"` workaround needed for these tools. *Original finding (2026-06-24):* `pot:create_from_repo` via the **superuser MCP** failed `member_create_failed / hive_not_found` because the MCP session resolved `ctx.workspaceId='*'` while pots live in `default`; the HTTP route (`activeWorkspaceId()='default'`) worked. Same EI-3409 class. The versioned `fed.sh` driver sets `FED_MCP_WS=default` as a safety net for any non-pot tools not yet using `resolveConcreteWorkspaceId` — keep it in place for non-pot MCP calls.

# Pair every schema-ensure module with a live-PG regression papercup

> Unit tests can't catch CREATE TABLE typos, missing CHECK constraints, or PG-side DDL incompatibilities. A 2-second live verifier (boot embedded PG → call your ensures → assert the resulting schema) catches them all and gives you a one-line pre-commit gate.

Update: the dogfood-ensure example is gone; the principle lives on as the fresh-migrate gate The concrete subject of this page — `ensure-schema-dogfood.ts`, `ensureAllDogfoodTables()`, `DOGFOOD_REACTIVE_TABLES`, and `apps/operator/scripts/verify-dogfood-schema.ts` — has been **removed** (plan `self-contained-migration-baseline-2026-06-02`). Schema is now migrations-only (`libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/000-baseline.sql` + `107+` incrementals), so there is no runtime ensure module to pair a verifier with. The *general principle* (boot real PG → apply the DDL → assert the resulting schema) is now realized by the **`empty → head` gate**: `apps/operator/test/fresh-migrate.integration.test.ts` + `packages/operator-core/lib/db-tools/verify-baseline.ts` (zero skip-tolerance). Read the examples below as the historical pattern; for DDL changes today, that integration test is the papercup. ## The gap unit tests can’t fill [Section titled “The gap unit tests can’t fill”](#the-gap-unit-tests-cant-fill) `ensure-schema-dogfood.ts` has \~600 lines of `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` strings. Its unit test (`ensure-schema-dogfood-binding.test.ts`) asserts on the exported `DOGFOOD_REACTIVE_TABLES` array — useful, but the array could match the spec exactly while the SQL strings have: * A typo in a CHECK constraint name * A missing column in the `INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET` clause * A `BIGINT[]` default value that PG18 parses differently than your shell does * A primary key that mentions a column not in the CREATE TABLE body The unit test passes. The DDL fails at first runtime. The error surfaces somewhere downstream — usually in a user-facing flow at 2am. ## The pattern [Section titled “The pattern”](#the-pattern) Write a `verify-<schema>.ts` script that: 1. **Boots embedded PG18** on a non-default port (e.g. 16781) with a fresh `tmpdir`. Does NOT touch the user’s running operator or any live PG. 2. **Points the module’s PG accessor** at the test instance via the override env var your connection layer reads (here: `HARNESS_ADMIN_DATABASE_URL`). 3. **Dynamic-imports the module AFTER the env is set** so the cached `getOrgPg()` resolves to the test PG. 4. **Calls the module’s batch ensure** (`ensureAllDogfoodTables()`). 5. **Asserts the resulting schema** against a declarative list of expected `(table, required-columns, CHECK constraints)` tuples. 6. **Tests idempotence** — second call short-circuits via the globalThis flag in `<200ms`. 7. **Cleans up** — drops the tmp PG, removes the data dir. Example (`apps/operator/scripts/verify-dogfood-schema.ts`): 
```ts
process.env.HARNESS_ADMIN_DATABASE_URL = 'postgres://...:16781/papercusp';
const { ensureAllDogfoodTables } = await import('../lib/ensure-schema-dogfood.js');
await ensureAllDogfoodTables();


// Then query information_schema and assert.
const tables = await checkSql<{ table_name: string }[]>`
  SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables
   WHERE table_schema = 'harness_shared'
   ORDER BY table_name
`;
for (const expected of EXPECTED_TABLES) {
  expect(tableSet.has(expected.name), 'table ' + expected.name + ' exists');
}
```
 Total: \~180 LOC. Runs in \~2s wall-clock. Catches the entire class of bugs unit tests can’t. ## What it catches that unit tests don’t [Section titled “What it catches that unit tests don’t”](#what-it-catches-that-unit-tests-dont) | Bug class | Unit test | Live-PG papercup | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------------------ | | Column missing from CREATE TABLE | ❌ | ✅ | | CHECK constraint syntax error | ❌ | ✅ (PG rejects on CREATE) | | Wrong column count in array default | ❌ | ✅ | | `BIGINT[]` vs `BIGINT` typo | ❌ | ✅ | | PG18 incompatibility (e.g. `IF NOT EXISTS` on a syntax that PG14 accepted) | ❌ | ✅ | | Trigger function reference to nonexistent table | ❌ | ✅ | | `ON CONFLICT` target column not in PK | ❌ | ✅ | | Idempotence broken by a missing flag | partial | ✅ (timing assertion) | | Renamed column not propagated to a partial index | ❌ | ✅ | ## Wire it as a discoverable script [Section titled “Wire it as a discoverable script”](#wire-it-as-a-discoverable-script) Add a `verify:<name>` entry to `package.json` so it surfaces under `npm run`: 
```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "verify:dogfood-schema": "tsx scripts/verify-dogfood-schema.ts",
    "verify:all-dogfood": "npm run verify:dogfood-schema && npm run verify:dogfood-bootstrap && npm run verify:trigger-consolidation"
  }
}
```
 Now `npm run verify:` tab-completes the full surface. A future agent who’s about to touch the ensure module sees the papercup exists + runs it before committing. ## Pre-condition setup [Section titled “Pre-condition setup”](#pre-condition-setup) Two things the papercup needs but the production code doesn’t: 1. **The schema** (`CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS harness_shared`) — the embedded PG starts empty; the ensure functions assume the schema exists. 2. **Required roles** (`CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS harness_app / harness_admin`) — only needed if downstream `GRANT` statements reference them. Some ensure modules don’t issue GRANTs; sniff the module before adding the role setup. Wrap both in `DO $body$ BEGIN IF NOT EXISTS ... END $body$` so re-runs are clean. ## When the unit test is enough [Section titled “When the unit test is enough”](#when-the-unit-test-is-enough) For modules whose only PG interaction is `SELECT` or `UPDATE` (no DDL), the unit test surface IS the regression papercup. The live verifier pattern matters specifically for DDL-shipping modules: ensure-schema, migration files, trigger function definitions. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * `apps/operator/scripts/verify-dogfood-schema.ts` — **removed** (see the Update banner); was the canonical example. * `apps/operator/test/fresh-migrate.integration.test.ts` + `packages/operator-core/lib/db-tools/verify-baseline.ts` — the current `empty → head` schema gate that replaces it. * `apps/operator/scripts/verify-trigger-consolidation.mjs` — sibling pattern for trigger behavior (vs DDL shape); still present. * [`idempotent-pg-ensure`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/idempotent-pg-ensure/) — the module-side pattern this papercup verifies. * [`pg-migrations-dollar-quote`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/pg-migrations-dollar-quote/) — the shell-quoting hazard the papercup also catches as a side effect.

# A liveness check keyed on an entrypoint NAME fails silently and totally — the desktop IPC transport was dead for exactly this reason

> discovery_pid_alive answered 'is our operator running?' by grepping the process cmdline for serve.mjs/serve.ts. But the process that owns the IPC socket is hono-host, not serve — so it returned false for 9 of 9 live operators on the dev box. Once that check was wired into the endpoint-ipc advertisement path, /api could never dial IPC at all: every advertisement read as a restart orphan, every stream fell back to the webview's ~6-socket HTTP pool, and the only symptom the owner saw was 'clicking an agent takes several seconds'. Nothing logged an error.

## The shape of the bug (WI-6512) [Section titled “The shape of the bug (WI-6512)”](#the-shape-of-the-bug-wi-6512) 
```rust
fn cmdline_looks_like_serve(cmdline: &str) -> bool {
    let lower = cmdline.to_ascii_lowercase();
    lower.contains("serve.mjs") || lower.contains("serve.ts")
}
```
 `discovery_pid_alive(pid)` = *the pid exists* **AND** *its cmdline passes the predicate above*. It was written (WI-3282) to stop a stale `operator.json` pid from false-**positively** matching after the OS recycled it onto an unrelated process. Reasonable goal, and the recycled-pid risk is real — this box wraps pids roughly daily under fleet load. The defect is which process it names. `serve.mjs` / `serve.ts` is the **supervisor**: it owns embedded-PG startup and migrations, and then runs the actual HTTP/IPC host, `hono-host`. **The host is the process that writes `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc*.json` and owns the IPC socket.** The check was asking about the wrong process. Measured on the dev box, 2026-07-28 — every operator that had published a live advertisement, versus the predicate: | advertisement | real `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` | matches? | | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | `endpoint-ipc.3070.json` (release) | `node …/papercup-release/apps/operator/dist-host/hono-host.mjs` | **no** | | `endpoint-ipc.3170.json` (staging) | `node dist-host/hono-host.mjs` | **no** | | `endpoint-ipc.3270.json` (dev) | `node --require tsx/dist/preflight.cjs --import tsx/dist/loader.mjs bin/hono-host.ts` | **no** | | …6 further dev instances | same tsx-wrapped form | **no** | **9 of 9.** Not a sampling artifact — the predicate could not match any operator this repo actually runs. ## Why it stayed invisible for so long [Section titled “Why it stayed invisible for so long”](#why-it-stayed-invisible-for-so-long) Two properties combined, and neither is specific to this codebase. **1. The failure direction was a false NEGATIVE, and a false negative reads as ordinary absence.** `discovery_pid_alive` returning `false` is indistinguishable, at every call site, from “the operator genuinely isn’t running yet” — which is a completely normal state during boot. There is no error to log because, as far as the code is concerned, nothing went wrong. **2. There was a working fallback underneath.** When IPC could not resolve a socket, `/api` quietly fell back to the webview’s native HTTP transport. That works. It is merely *slow*, because WebKitGTK/libsoup allows \~6 connections per host and five long-lived SSE streams eat five of them, leaving one socket for everything else. Same URL: **9 ms via curl, 2542 ms in-webview.** The owner experienced this as “clicking an agent in the agents-running dropdown takes several seconds”, and reported it as a database problem. The database was answering in 75 ms. A silent false-negative plus a degraded-but-functional fallback is the recipe for a defect that survives months of use. The system never says it is broken; it just quietly stops being fast. ## The trigger that turned it fatal [Section titled “The trigger that turned it fatal”](#the-trigger-that-turned-it-fatal) The name check existed for a while without touching IPC.
