Decide this first. ### Implementation status (landed 2026-06-23, plan `loop-wake-rate-limit-robustness-2026-06-23`) [Section titled “Implementation status (landed 2026-06-23, plan loop-wake-rate-limit-robustness-2026-06-23)”](#implementation-status-landed-2026-06-23-plan-loop-wake-rate-limit-robustness-2026-06-23) **DECISION: shape (b)** (capture-and-watch) — minimal blast radius on the now-LIVE pump (claim/floor/coalesce/recover untouched) — UNIFIED with the existing `reconcile-loop-routines` signals: completion (lifecycle/presence) = success → `recordFire('ok')`, stuck-park backstop = channel-agnostic failure → `recordFire('error')`, plus a fast/precise resume-exit observer for the common resume path. (Loop wakes are NOT re-opened/immediately-retried — the right “retry” for a loop is the fire-gate backoff + the 429-aware re-arm, not thundering the same wall.) * **✅ P0a** — `resume-turn-outcome.ts` `classifyResumeTurnExit` (pure, reuses `turn-error.ts`: exit 0 = success without the empty-output false-positive; non-zero scans stdout+stderr — the CLIs print 429s to STDOUT). `wake-executor.ts` captures BOUNDED stdout/stderr tails (actively drained — no pipe-backpressure deadlock; integration-tested with a 250KB flood) and fires a new `ExecuteWakeDeps.onResumeTurnExit` on the detached turn’s close; byte-identical when no observer is wired. Migration 387 adds `event_wake_deliveries.source` (threaded emit→insertDeliveries→DeliveryWork) for precise loop attribution. * **✅ P0b** — `loop-turn-outcome.ts` (registered into the pump via `registerResumeTurnOutcomeHandler`, a seam avoiding the harness/routines→engine import cycle) routes a loop-sourced resume DEATH to `recordFire(installSlug, name, …, 'error')` so the EXISTING autoloop circuit engages. `fireLoopWake` enqueue now records `'attempt'` not `'ok'` (the turn outcome owns ok/error, so consecutive\_errors accumulates → the circuit opens at 8). `reconcile-loop-routines` records `'ok'` on completion / `'error'` on the stuck-backstop (channel-agnostic — covers inject-path deaths the resume-exit observer can’t see). * **✅ P1a** — the same handler re-arms `next_fire_at` by the 429 `retry-after` (or `resetAt-now`), floored at the interval + capped at 1h, ONLY while still parked at `'infinity'` (idempotent, never-backwards). * **✅ P1b** — new `WatchdogSource 'loop-stalled'` + `collectLoopStalledSignals` (`watchdog.ts`): a parked-stalled loop with a dead/undelivered turn surfaces EARLY (before the ≥30min backstop). * **✅ P2a** — optional `maxFires` / `maxDurationSec` dead-man guard (`loop-dead-man.ts`, Guard 3 in `fireLoopWake`, exposed on `loop:arm`). Config rides `payload_template` + a `metadata.fire_count` counter — NO migration (reuse-first, mirrors `costCapCents`). * **✅ P2b** — `loop:status` now reports `stalled` / `stalledSinceMs` / `lastDeliveryOutcome` / `consecutiveErrors` / dead-man bounds (`getLoopStatus` + pure `computeLoopStall`). * **✅ P2c** — `fireLoopWake` now auto-ends an orphaned loop when a fire reaches **no wakeable/resumable session at all** (`woken=0`, `staged=0`, `no-session-now`) instead of leaving the routine parked at `next_fire_at='infinity'` for the stuck-backstop to rediscover. This closes the clean-session-end orphan class proven on 2026-07-02: the owner’s session had ended and its inbox-wake was correctly canceled, but the loop row stayed active and kept re-parking itself on every retry. The branch now deactivates the routine immediately and records `no-session-now:auto-ended` as an error, so the watchdog sees the terminal cause once instead of chasing a permanent parked row. * **✅ P3** — FIXED (the deferred blocker, resolved). Root cause: `interactive-usage/ingest-claude-transcripts.ts` wrote the native session UUID (the transcript filename) into `agent_usage_samples.run_id` and left `session_id` **NULL** — so `readLoopSpendCents`’s owner→`adv_sessions.session_id`→`agent_usage_samples.session_id` join always found 0 and the cost-cap never bound a warm-session loop. The native UUID *is* the session id (= the value `adv_sessions.session_id` carries), so the ingestion now also populates `session_id` — a ONE-LINE additive change, no schema change, the existing join now works. Proven against real PG (`ingest-claude-transcripts.session-attribution.integration.test.ts`): interactive spend is now summed by `session_id`. Cap still fail-open on genuinely uncertain data (no tracked session / read error). **DEPLOYED + LIVE-VERIFIED (2026-06-23):** the fix is `deployed ✓` on `:3070`, and live PG confirms `agent_usage_samples.session_id` flipped from NULL (all pre-cutover `source='interactive'` rows) to populated (= the native session UUID) for rows ingested after \~11:30 EDT — see the Gating note’s Live-Verification section. The original per-file roadmap (kept below for provenance): * **P0a — observe the resume turn.** Stop `stdio:'ignore'`; capture exit code + a bounded stderr tail. Add a pure `classifyResumeTurnExit(code, stderrTail)` (reusing `turn-error.ts`). Files: `wake-executor.ts` (the `spawnDetached` default + a new injected outcome callback), `engine.ts` (wire the callback), `store.ts` (the re-open/fail transition). * **P0b — open the circuit on dead turns.** Route a classified rate-limit/non-zero turn death to `recordFire(installSlug, routineName, reason, 'error')` so the EXISTING autoloop backoff engages. Requires the wake delivery to durably carry the loop’s fire-gate key (installSlug + routineName) so the async exit handler can reconstruct it — today the wake only carries `source: 'loop:<routineId>'`. Files: `loop-fire.ts` (enrich the wake payload), the P0a outcome handler, `autoloop.ts` (no change — just fed correctly). * **P1a — rate-limit-aware re-arm.** Back off `next_fire_at` by the 429’s `retry-after` instead of the blind interval. Files: `reconcile-loop-routines.ts`, `loop-fire.ts`. * **P1b — watchdog visibility.** New `WatchdogSource` (e.g. `loop-stalled`): a loop `active` + parked at `'infinity'` for ≥`stuckParkMs` with no post-fire lifecycle marker → surface a signal. File: `harness/improvements/watchdog.ts`. * **P2a — dead-man guard.** Optional `maxFires` / `maxDurationSec` on the routine row + `loop:arm`; auto-pause when exceeded (mirror `autoPauseLoopRoutine`). Files: `loop/arm.ts`, `loop.ts`, `loop-fire.ts`, a new migration. * **P2b — `loop:status` stall state.** Distinguish “parked, healthy in-flight” from “parked, last fire produced no completion in N×interval”; add `stalledSinceMs` / `lastDeliveryOutcome`. File: `loop.ts`. * **P3 — cost-cap attribution.** Land the direct owner→cost rollup so the cap actually bounds a warm-session loop. File: `loop-cost-cap.ts`. ## Gating note [Section titled “Gating note”](#gating-note) `papercusp-loops` is FLAG-ON at runtime (owner-flipped 2026-06-23) — its `FLAGS.LOOPS` *default* was `false` (KNOWN\_DARK) at the time this doc was written; see the note above for the current state. **P0/P1/P2/P3 have all LANDED + are unit/integration-tested** (see the implementation-status section above). ### LIVE VERIFICATION (2026-06-23 \~13:30 EDT, deployed sha b40cff17d) — gate effectively satisfied [Section titled “LIVE VERIFICATION (2026-06-23 \~13:30 EDT, deployed sha b40cff17d) — gate effectively satisfied”](#live-verification-2026-06-23-1330-edt-deployed-sha-b40cff17d--gate-effectively-satisfied) The previously-”unverified-live” turn-outcome path is now **production-verified on real loops**, not just unit tests: * **Death-path accounting + circuit (the most important leg) — CONFIRMED LIVE.** Several warm-session loops whose detached resume turns produced *no completion* (sessions long-exited; the exact delivered-but-didn’t-survive case this doc is about) had the `reconcile-loop-routines` stuck-park backstop fire and `recordFire(..., 'error')` — observed in `harness_shared.autoloop_state`: `last_status='loop-stuck-backstop'` with `consecutive_errors` climbed to **12** (≥8 → the per-loop circuit OPENS, throttling them off the every-30-min blind-retry cadence). **Pre-fix these stayed `consecutive_errors=0` forever** — that 0→12 swing IS the bug being fixed, observed in production. This is the channel-agnostic reconcile death-path (covers inject- AND resume-path deaths). * **P3 cost-cap attribution — CONFIRMED LIVE.** After the `ingest-claude-transcripts.ts` fix deployed (\~11:30 EDT, sha confirmed `deployed ✓`), `agent_usage_samples.session_id` is now POPULATED for `source='interactive'` rows (it was NULL for every row before the cutover — directly observed in PG). `readLoopSpendCents`’ owner→`adv_sessions.session_id`→`agent_usage_samples.session_id` join now resolves, so the warm-session loop cost-cap can actually bind. **The only un-exercised sliver** is the FAST `onResumeTurnExit` resume-exit observer firing *specifically* on a detached-resume 429 — vs. the reconcile stuck-backstop catching the same death a beat later. Both routes end in the identical `recordFire('error')` + circuit-open + re-arm outcome, so this is a precision/latency refinement, **not a correctness gap**: the gate’s real risk (a dead turn silently recorded as a successful delivery, circuit never opening) is now disproven in production. **Recommendation:** the flip-dark-flags effort can flip the `FLAGS.LOOPS` default ON. The default flip remains owned by that effort (not this fix); this section is the live-verify evidence they were gating on. **✅ Done.** `FLAGS.LOOPS` now defaults ON (see the note at the top of this section) — the recommendation this doc made has been executed. ## Also since this doc (2026-07-03) — cold-auto loops are a new, separate capability [Section titled “Also since this doc (2026-07-03) — cold-auto loops are a new, separate capability”](#also-since-this-doc-2026-07-03--cold-auto-loops-are-a-new-separate-capability) A follow-on effort (`su-cold-auto-mode-2026-07-03`) added a **second loop wake mode** on the same `wake-executor.ts` / `engine.ts` path this doc analyzes: a loop armed with `loop:arm { carry: 'cold' }` can RESET-CONTEXT / periodically recycle to a carry-note instead of resuming the warm in-place turn this doc describes throughout. It is gated by its own master flag, `FLAGS.SU_COLD_AUTO` (`papercusp-su-cold-auto`, default ON but only an *availability* switch — nothing goes cold until a loop is explicitly armed `carry:'cold'` AND a carry-note exists via `decideColdWake`). The turn-death-recorded-as-delivered failure mode this doc documents is about the WARM resume path specifically; cold-auto wakes are a distinct code path and are out of scope here — see the code at the `coldAutoEnabled` dep in `engine.ts` if you’re chasing a cold-loop issue instead of a warm one. **Same day, later commit:** `injectPsuHostWake`’s cold branch (`wake-executor.ts`) no longer injects the raw `carryNote` — it now wraps it with `su-cold-loop.ts`’s new `renderColdWakeInjection(carryNote)`, which frames the note as the woken agent’s entire reconstructed working state and appends a standing mandate to refresh it (`loop:checkpoint`) before ending the turn, or call `loop:end` if done/blocked — otherwise a cold loop’s anchor goes stale after one wake. Still entirely inside the cold-auto branch this section already scopes out of the warm-path failure mode; noted here only so the `wake-executor.ts` anchor stays precise. ## Also since this doc (2026-07-03) — `reconcile-loop-routines.ts` gets a cold-aware settle ladder + a circuit-open terminal route [Section titled “Also since this doc (2026-07-03) — reconcile-loop-routines.ts gets a cold-aware settle ladder + a circuit-open terminal route”](#also-since-this-doc-2026-07-03--reconcile-loop-routinests-gets-a-cold-aware-settle-ladder--a-circuit-open-terminal-route) Two more robustness gaps in the SAME re-arm module this doc analyzes (`completionSignal` / `reconcileLoopRoutines`), both found live the same day as the cold-auto rollout above: * **Cold loops need their OWN settle signal — bare quiescence lies.** A cold (`carry:'cold'`) wake resets/recycles the session: the dying child emits a lifecycle ‘ended’ and the fresh child a lifecycle ‘started’ back-to-back at delivery, then (if the carry-note inject is deferred) sits **booted-but-idle** until it actually runs its iteration. The old warm-style fallback (presence went quiet after the fire ⇒ settled) read that idle boot itself as “turn settled” and re-fired \~91s later into a still-booting host (live: wake #5036 re-fired on top of #5033, the “stale-note-treadmill” finding). `completionSignal` now branches on `row.carry`: a cold loop settles ONLY on (a) the turn’s own `Stop`-hook ‘ended’ marker **newer** than the post-fire ‘started’ boundary (i.e. the session booted *and* finished its turn), or (b) a carry-note refresh after the fire (the cold protocol’s own completion receipt — a cold turn is required to `loop:checkpoint` before ending) — taking whichever is later. Neither present ⇒ no settle at all; the loop stays parked for the stuck-park backstop to retry (which safely re-delivers the same note). This adds `lifecycle_started_at`, `carry`, and `note_updated_ts` to the per-row query and a new `RebaseVia: 'note-refresh'`. * **The warm ladder also gained a reset-boundary guard.** Even on the non-cold path, an ‘ended’ marker is now only accepted as a settle when it is NOT older than a newer post-fire ‘started’ marker (`lc != null && (ls == null || ls < lc)`) — defensive hardening against the same reset-boundary confusion, though genuinely warm loops are unaffected in practice (their ‘started’ fires once at process boot, before `last_fired_at`, so it falls outside the post-fire SQL window). * **Circuit-open loops now reach the WI-1399 terminal guard WITHOUT waiting on the stuck-park dwell window (EI-7006).** Previously the dead-owner terminal guard (auto-pause a permanently-unreachable loop) was reachable only via the stuck-park branch (`now - last_fired ≥ max(30min, 4×interval)`). But a loop whose fire-circuit is already open (`consecutiveErrors ≥ circuitThreshold()`) gets an \~hourly probe fire that keeps refreshing `last_fired_at` — so the stuck-park dwell almost never elapses, and even when it eventually does, the terminal guard’s own 2h window still exceeds the inter-probe gap. Dead loops climbed to a permanently fire-circuit-open state (55→∞ open-circuit EIs observed) and never terminated. `reconcileLoopRoutines` now takes an injected `circuitThreshold` (default `autoloop.ts` `circuitThreshold()`) and routes a **parked, quiet, circuit-open** loop into the SAME terminal guard as a stuck-park loop — `checkUnreachableTerminalGuard` now also receives a `circuitOpen` flag, and the `stuckFireCount` it uses is `consecutiveErrors` as-is on the circuit-open path (vs. `consecutiveErrors + 1` on the classic stuck-park path, preserving that path’s original contract). A circuit-open-but-not-yet-guard-breached loop that hasn’t reached the stuck-park dwell is left alone — the fire-gate’s own backoff owns its cadence; reconcile no longer fights it by re-arming early. ## Also since this doc (2026-07-07) — the OPEN-WALLS wake block (P-006, new file `loop-wall-nag.ts`) [Section titled “Also since this doc (2026-07-07) — the OPEN-WALLS wake block (P-006, new file loop-wall-nag.ts)”](#also-since-this-doc-2026-07-07--the-open-walls-wake-block-p-006-new-file-loop-wall-nagts) `loop-fire.ts` and `loop-turn-outcome.ts` gained a **carry-note “walls”** feature (new module `harness/routines/loop-wall-nag.ts`) that is orthogonal to the turn-death failure mode this doc analyzes — noted here only so those two anchors stay precise. It is a wake-diet correctness fix, not part of the rate-limit robustness thread: * `fireLoopWake` now `splitCarryNoteWalls(note)` — open owner-gated commitments (“walls”) are parsed OUT of the truncatable checkpoint body and rendered by `renderLoopWallsBlock` as their own **un-truncatable `⛔ OPEN WALLS` block** in EVERY wake form (full and short), so a capped note can never clip a standing commitment off the end. An agent clears a resolved wall via `loop:checkpoint { walls }`. * `loop-turn-outcome.ts` `detectOwnerAsk` + `stashLoopWallNag`: when a loop turn ends on a row-less owner-ask, a one-shot **turn-settle nag line** (`renderWallNagLine`, read-and-cleared by `takeLoopWallNag` on the next fire) rides the following wake. Both hang off the same `target_owner_id` scope the carry-note uses. None of this touches the delivered-vs-survived accounting, the resume-exit observer, or the autoloop circuit — the warm-turn-death analysis above is unchanged. ## Also since this doc (2026-07-09) — the exact `infra_loss` error string from the original incident now gets its own watchdog signal [Section titled “Also since this doc (2026-07-09) — the exact infra\_loss error string from the original incident now gets its own watchdog signal”](#also-since-this-doc-2026-07-09--the-exact-infra_loss-error-string-from-the-original-incident-now-gets-its-own-watchdog-signal) Item #7 above (“Observability is near-zero … the 429 itself is in the discarded subprocess stderr — logged nowhere”) is partially closed on the **failed-spawn** side (a related but distinct signal source from the loop-delivery path this doc analyzes). `watchdog.ts` `classifySpawnError` gained a new `'infra-loss'` class (EI-8667) that explicitly matches `infra_loss:` / `"returned HTTP <n> but the agent produced no turn"` / `"API Error: Request rejected"` — the *literal* error string quoted in this doc’s opening paragraph (`infra_loss: …/<role> returned HTTP 200 but the agent produced no turn (exitCode=1)`, from the 2026-06-23 429-storm incident). Previously that string fell through to the generic `'other'` class, burying a diagnosable gateway/rate-limit-stall pattern inside unrelated noise. It now keys its own `failed-spawns:infra-loss` watchdog signal instead. This is the spawn-tracking (`harness_shared.spawned_agents`) surface, not the loop wake-delivery surface `resume-turn-outcome.ts`/`loop-turn-outcome.ts` cover — the two overlap in the failure mode they both ultimately trace to (an upstream 429/gateway stall) but are separate collectors. ## Also since this doc (2026-07-10) — `executeWake` gained rematerialize-on-miss for archived session files [Section titled “Also since this doc (2026-07-10) — executeWake gained rematerialize-on-miss for archived session files”](#also-since-this-doc-2026-07-10--executewake-gained-rematerialize-on-miss-for-archived-session-files) `wake-executor.ts` gained a **third, unrelated** pre-resume step (plan `session-db-archive-retire-dirs-2026-07-10` P-008, new module `session-archive.ts`) — noted here only so the `wake-executor.ts` anchor stays precise; it does not touch the delivered-vs-survived accounting this doc analyzes: * Since that plan’s P-002/P-003, PG (`harness_shared.session_archive_files` + `session_archives`) is the **canonical** archive of an ended CLI session’s on-disk files (zstd-compressed, sha256-verified) — `deleteArchivedSessionFiles()` may remove the local copy once the archive stamp is committed. * `executeWake` now checks, **immediately before** building the `resumeCommandFor(...)` invocation, whether the target session’s local files are still on disk and, if not, calls `rematerializeSession(...)` to pull them back byte-exactly from the PG archive before `claude --resume <uuid>` / `codex resume <uuid>` / the omp thread-resume runs. Wired for all three resume agents: `codex` (`codexHomeForAdvSession`, falling back to `findArchivedSessionIdForAdv` when no local session id is known), `omp` (`ompSessionsRoot()`), and `claude` (`sessionClaudeConfigDir(owner)`). Each check is FS-only (a no-op) when the file is already on disk; a miss costs one PG read + a decompress-and-write. * This closes a **different** turn-death class than the 429-storm this doc is about: a resume that would previously fail outright with “session not found” (because archive-at-death had deleted the local transcript) now transparently restores it first. It does not change when a delivery is marked `delivered` (still on `spawnDetached` returning a PID — see step 1 above), does not feed the turn-error taxonomy or the autoloop circuit, and is orthogonal to the resume-exit observer / reconcile stuck-park path this doc’s remediation roadmap covers. ## Also since this doc (2026-07-14) — ordinary event wakes now reuse the captured outcome [Section titled “Also since this doc (2026-07-14) — ordinary event wakes now reuse the captured outcome”](#also-since-this-doc-2026-07-14--ordinary-event-wakes-now-reuse-the-captured-outcome) WI-4779 found the remaining scope hole in the capture-and-watch design: the registered `onResumeTurnExit` handler only acted when `source` was `loop:<routineId>`. An ordinary `events:await` delivery still captured the detached child exit, but the loop handler returned `handled:false` and discarded it. Live evidence was await 19350: `release:green:papercusp` fired at 05:20, delivery 18970 was marked `delivered/resume-headless` when its PID spawned, the session produced no turn, and only the paired red-key timeout woke it at 06:09. The pump now observes every detached resume and splits the existing capture-and-watch policy by source: * **Loop-sourced delivery:** unchanged. `loop-turn-outcome.ts` owns circuit accounting and retry-after-aware re-arm; the delivery is not reopened, avoiding a duplicate loop iteration. * **Ordinary event delivery:** a non-zero/signalled exit is classified by the shared `classifyResumeTurnExit` taxonomy, then `reopenDeliveredAfterResumeDeath` atomically moves every still-delivered row from that coalesced wake back to `pending` (or `dead` after the existing eight-attempt ceiling). It clears the optimistic channel/timestamp and reuses the delivery ladder’s exponential backoff. * **Fast child exit:** buffered until `markDeliveryDelivered` plus sibling coalescing finish, so a child that dies immediately cannot be reopened and then overwritten back to delivered. * **Late/duplicate exit callback:** ignored unless the row is still `delivered`, preventing a stale observer from clobbering a row another recovery path already moved. The recurrence lives in `events/await/engine.test.ts` (fast-exit + coalesced rows + loop exclusion) and `events/await/await-store.integration.test.ts` (real-PG delivered→pending, metadata clearing, duplicate callback guard). This closes the generic event half of the same delivered-vs-survived defect without changing live injection channels or loop semantics.

# The fed_hlc LWW comparator is non-transitive under MIXED HLC presence

> lwwPick / the fed_hlc PG guard used to use "both-HLC → compare HLC, else → compare ts" — a rule that CYCLED when a no-HLC (pre-314) op sat between two skewed HLC ops, so the fold winner became order-dependent and peers could diverge (EI-1698). FIXED as of 2026-07-02 (compare in one HLC space, everywhere) — plus a follow-up exact-tie/node-id fix (WI-1672, mig-459) and a THIRD hardening, the HlcClock recv ratchet ε-bound (maxDriftMs) that stops one absurd remote stamp from poisoning a node's (and, re-propagated, the pot's) clock.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) `lwwPick` (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/projection.ts`) and the PG `fed_hlc` guard (each mutable projection’s `ON CONFLICT … WHERE` / `DELETE WHERE`, mig-314) decide the LWW winner with the SAME rule: > if **both** ops carry an `hlc` → compare HLC; **else** → compare `ts` (wall clock). That rule is **NOT transitive** when HLC presence is *mixed* (some ops carry an HLC, some don’t) AND clocks are skewed (an HLC op’s HLC order inverts its `ts` order — the recv-advance case HLC was built for). A non-transitive comparator makes the reduce-fold winner depend on **delivery order**, so two peers folding the same ops in different orders **diverge** on a contended key. This is **EI-1698** (filed 2026-06-19, severity minor/**latent**). ## The cycle (deterministic minimal repro) [Section titled “The cycle (deterministic minimal repro)”](#the-cycle-deterministic-minimal-repro) 
```plaintext
X = { hlc: HIGH, ts: 100 }   // upgraded peer, recv-advanced HLC, low ts
Y = { hlc: none, ts: 150 }   // pre-314 peer, NO hlc, mid ts
Z = { hlc: LOW,  ts: 200 }   // upgraded peer, low HLC, high ts


lwwPick(X, Y) = Y   // mixed → ts fallback: 150 > 100
lwwPick(Y, Z) = Z   // mixed → ts fallback: 200 > 150
lwwPick(X, Z) = X   // both HLC  → HIGH > LOW
⇒ X > Z, Z > Y, Y > X   — a 3-cycle.


reduce(lwwPick, [X,Y,Z]) = Z     // but
reduce(lwwPick, [Z,Y,X]) = X     // ⇒ order-dependent winner = divergence
```
 ## Why it’s LATENT (don’t panic, but don’t leave it for the re-key) [Section titled “Why it’s LATENT (don’t panic, but don’t leave it for the re-key)”](#why-its-latent-dont-panic-but-dont-leave-it-for-the-re-key) The cycle needs a no-HLC op with `ts` **between** two HLC ops. Post-P-010, `stampOpHlc` stamps **every** LWW write, so no-HLC LWW ops are only **pre-P-010 history = the OLDEST `ts`** on a key. An oldest no-HLC op sits at the *bottom* of the key’s `ts` order (loses every mixed comparison on `ts`), so the comparator degenerates to a transitive HLC-ordering among the newer ops → it converges. The divergence is reachable only if a no-HLC op has a mid/recent `ts` — which the production “no-HLC = oldest” distribution does not produce. So: a proven defect, not an active incident. It still matters because the same comparator is **load-bearing for the C-001 re-key** (a member needs epoch-N’s key before epoch-N content, ordered by `fed_hlc`). Adding epoch complexity on top of a non-transitive mixed comparator is risk worth removing first. ## The fix — LANDED [Section titled “The fix — LANDED”](#the-fix--landed) Compare in **one order space**: synthesize an HLC from `ts` for a no-HLC op at compare time, in BOTH `lwwPick` and the PG guard: 
```ts
const key = op.hlc ?? encodeHlc({ ms: op.ts ?? 0, count: 0 }); // missing hlc → ts-as-HLC
```
 Then every comparison is HLC-space → a single total order → transitive → order-independent for ANY HLC-presence mix. **Both halves have now landed:** `lwwPick` (`projection.ts`) does the compare-time synth inline (2026-06-20); mig-458 (`libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/458-fed-order-key-transitivity-fix.sql`, 2026-07-02) gave the PG-level guard the SAME fix via a small immutable SQL function, `harness_shared.fed_order_key(hlc, ts)`, and swept EVERY mutable projection’s `ON CONFLICT … WHERE` / `DELETE WHERE` guard onto it (32 projection files as of 2026-07-03, and growing as new mutable projections land — `grep -rl fed_order_key packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/projections/ | wc -l`) — so the guard now compares in the *exact* order space `lwwPick` does, on every table, not just in `lwwPick` alone. This is **verified**, not argued — see `__tests__/fed-hlc-transitivity-fix-proof.test.ts`: a 600-run sweep shows the synth-HLC comparator is ALWAYS a strict total order (`win-counts {0,1,2}`) while the broken “both-HLC → HLC, else → ts” rule cycles (`{1,1,1}`). (The test still models both comparators locally rather than importing the real ones — that’s a test-hygiene follow-up, not a sign the fix is unapplied; the code cited above is the actual load-bearing path.) ## Update 2026-07-02 — a SECOND, related defect: exact-HLC ties (WI-1672) [Section titled “Update 2026-07-02 — a SECOND, related defect: exact-HLC ties (WI-1672)”](#update-2026-07-02--a-second-related-defect-exact-hlc-ties-wi-1672) Fixing transitivity did not fix everything in this area. Federation testing (P-015) found a **live split-brain on an EXACT `fed_hlc` tie**: two peers whose HLC clocks sit at the same wall-ms frontier (routine after any transient fast-clock episode — `hlc_recv` ratchets every peer to the max ms ever witnessed) can mint the IDENTICAL HLC for two DIFFERENT concurrent writes to the same key. Every guard’s tie-ACCEPTING compare (`fed_order_key(EXCLUDED…) >= fed_order_key(stored…)`) then lets the incoming remote op overwrite the local row on BOTH peers — the two peers stably SWAP winners instead of converging. Live-reproduced on the wi1544 rig: both frames independently minted the same `001783025829985:00417` stamp for different content. **The fix (mig-459, `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/459-hlc-node-id-total-order.sql`):** make the ordering key total *by construction* — append a per-clock node-identity segment, so an HLC string is `"<15-digit ms>:<5-digit count>:<16-hex node>"`. A genuine full tie can then only be the SAME stamp replayed (where tie-accept is correct/idempotent). `harness_shared.hlc_now()` mints the node-carrying 3-segment form; `hlc_recv()` parses both 2- and 3-segment encodings; the `@papercusp/locks-core` HLC type gained an optional `node` field (`compareHlc`/`encodeHlc` in `libs/generic/locks-core/src/hlc.ts`) that breaks `(ms, count)` ties by node — absent ⇒ `''`, so a legacy (pre-459) stamp always loses a tie to any node-carrying stamp, on every peer, identically. No comparator code changed: `fed_order_key` passes the HLC through verbatim and `lwwPick` already does a plain string compare, so a 3-segment stamp just sorts correctly through the existing machinery. ## Update 2026-07-02 (later) — a THIRD hardening: bound the recv ratchet (ε drift clamp) [Section titled “Update 2026-07-02 (later) — a THIRD hardening: bound the recv ratchet (ε drift clamp)”](#update-2026-07-02-later--a-third-hardening-bound-the-recv-ratchet-ε-drift-clamp) Node-id (previous section) makes an exact tie total-orderable, but a SEPARATE risk in the same family is the recv ratchet itself: `HlcClock.recv()` always advanced the local clock’s `ms` up to `max(local, remote, physical)`. One absurd remote stamp (a bad clock, a corrupted/adversarial payload, a far-future `ms`) would permanently pin the receiving node’s clock years ahead — and because every subsequent local `send()` re-stamps at that poisoned `ms`, a re-propagated event ratchets every OTHER peer the same way, so a single bad stamp can drag the whole pot’s clocks forward (the same “amplifier” shape as the WI-1672 exact-tie bug, just via the physical component instead of the tie-break). **The fix (`libs/generic/locks-core/src/hlc.ts`, `HlcClock`):** `recv()` now clamps the ratchet to an ε bound — `maxDriftMs` (constructor option, default `600_000` = 10 minutes, 2× the announce-admission skew window so any legitimately-admitted peer still ratchets us normally). A remote `ms` more than `maxDriftMs` ahead of the local physical clock is treated as absent for ratchet purposes (`remote = { ms: 0, count: 0 }` before the `max()`) — the poisoned stamp still applies to the DATA it was attached to, it just doesn’t advance THIS node’s clock. `processHlc()` (the process-wide federation clock) uses the default bound; tests cover both the clamp firing and a legitimate in-bound skew still ratcheting normally (`hlc.test.ts` → `describe('HlcClock recv drift clamp')`). No comparator or encoding changed here — this is a clock-input guard, not an ordering-key change, so it composes with both the transitivity fix (first section) and the node-id tie-break (previous section) without touching them. ## How to test / reproduce [Section titled “How to test / reproduce”](#how-to-test--reproduce) * Comparator + cycle: `fed-hlc-transitivity-fix-proof.test.ts` (PG-free, the proof-of-fix). * End-to-end through the real merge + `fed_hlc` guard: `version-skew-mixed-hlc-backcompat.test.ts` (Brief Y / AC scenario 6). Note MONOTONE-clock mixed universes DO converge (rolling-upgrade back-compat holds in the normal case); only SKEW + mixed reaches the cycle. * Recv ratchet ε-bound: `libs/generic/locks-core/src/hlc.test.ts` → `describe('HlcClock recv drift clamp')` (an absurd-future remote does not ratchet; an in-bound skew still does; `maxDriftMs` is configurable). ## Gotcha for new work [Section titled “Gotcha for new work”](#gotcha-for-new-work) Any new comparison or LWW path that treats “has HLC” and “no HLC” with *different* comparison **modes** (rather than mapping both into one order) re-introduces this non-transitivity. Map a missing HLC into HLC-space (synth from `ts`) instead of switching to a `ts`-mode branch. Separately (WI-1672): any new comparator built directly on `(ms, count)` without the `node` segment re-introduces the exact-tie split-brain — always compare via the full encoded HLC string (or `compareHlc`), never hand-roll a `(ms, count)`-only compare. And any new caller that merges a REMOTE HLC into a local clock should go through `HlcClock.recv()` (or its `maxDriftMs` bound) rather than a bare `Math.max` — an unbounded ratchet re-introduces the same amplifier one absurd stamp can poison the whole pot with. ## Refs [Section titled “Refs”](#refs) * EI-1698 (the finding + the proof-of-fix comment) · `shared-pot-release-testing/findings-Y.md` * WI-1672 (the follow-up exact-tie/node-id finding, found in P-015 federation testing) · mig-459 `hlc-node-id-total-order.sql`. * The recv ratchet ε-bound (`maxDriftMs`) hardening in `HlcClock.recv()` — same WI-1672 amplifier family, landed as defense-in-depth after the node-id fix. * Adjacent: D-001 `fed_hlc` ordering (`lww-hlc-fedts-divergence.test.ts`), mig-314, mig-458 (`fed_order_key()`), `hlc-stamp.ts`, `@papercusp/locks-core/hlc.ts`. * Adjacent but DISTINCT (not an ordering bug — do not expect node ids to fix it): WI-1684, local-del resurrection under skipOwnOps (no tombstone) — see `agent-insights/federation-public-release-known-limitations` §4a; pinned by the WI-1684 teeth test in `convergence-fuzz.test.ts`.

 All verified against the QEMU macOS 14.8.5 x86\_64 build VM (`ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -p 2222 aviweiss@127.0.0.1`), builds around sha `2ae833a3a1`. `mac-vm-verify-build.sh` runs from the tower/monorepo checkout and rsyncs+builds remotely; every other `mac-vm-*.sh` here runs **on the VM itself** — copy it over (it’s already carried by `mac-vm-verify-build.sh`’s rsync into `papercup-build-mac/papercup/…`) or pipe it directly: `ssh … 'bash -s' < papercusp-desktop/bin/mac-vm-X.sh`. ## Why visual/pixel checks are excluded [Section titled “Why visual/pixel checks are excluded”](#why-visualpixel-checks-are-excluded) **This QEMU VM has no GPU, so WKWebView cannot paint** — a `screendump` during boot shows a black/blank frame even when the app is fully healthy underneath. Actual pixel/visual verification needs real Mac hardware (or a VM with GPU passthrough) — track that gap separately, don’t assume this battery covers it. ## The 5 verified dimensions (first thorough pass, 2026-07-05, all green) [Section titled “The 5 verified dimensions (first thorough pass, 2026-07-05, all green)”](#the-5-verified-dimensions-first-thorough-pass-2026-07-05-all-green) 1. **Visual** — webview loads + renders (VM-GPU-blank pixels only; see above). 2. **HTTP routes** — `/api/health`, `/api/desktop/*`, `/internal/docs`, SPA root shell. 3. **Embedded PG** — full migrated schema (hundreds of tables/migrations) provisions on fresh install. 4. **Real gateway model call** — a live `/v1/messages` round-trip through the app’s auto-supervised `:8788` gateway sidecar. 5. **Lifecycle relaunch** — quit + relaunch reuses the same physical DB (`system_identifier` unchanged), doesn’t re-provision. ## Backlog depth dimensions (WI-3133) [Section titled “Backlog depth dimensions (WI-3133)”](#backlog-depth-dimensions-wi-3133) 6. All-logs error scan — `mac-vm-log-scan.sh` now covers this. 7. It discovers the packaged operator’s dynamic `/api/health` port, writes a synthetic working-set row via `POST /api/harness/papercusp/working-set/F-AUDIT-001/set-active`, polls `GET /api/harness/papercusp/working-set` until the Hyperbee append projects into PG, then `clear-active`s and verifies the row disappears. Prior manual pass observed \~3-8s projection lag, so the script polls instead of asserting immediate read-after-write visibility. 8. code-server bundled IDE health — retired 2026-07-07 with the code-server bundle and vscode-server plugin. # Mac VM isolated packaged-app testing: bypass `open`, exec the binary directly

> The durable fix for EI-14941-style shared-sidecar collisions when testing a packaged macOS Papercusp .app in isolation — launch the Mach-O binary directly instead of `open -a`, sidestepping the launchd env-cache race entirely.

# Mac VM isolated packaged-app testing: bypass `open`, exec the binary directly [Section titled “Mac VM isolated packaged-app testing: bypass open, exec the binary directly”](#mac-vm-isolated-packaged-app-testing-bypass-open-exec-the-binary-directly) ## The problem (EI-14941) [Section titled “The problem (EI-14941)”](#the-problem-ei-14941) Testing a packaged macOS Papercusp `.app` (GUI or Server) “in isolation” — its own `$HOME`, its own embedded PG, its own ports — normally means: `launchctl setenv PAPERCUSP_HOME /some/isolated/dir` (+ the other overrides), then `open -a "/path/to/App.app"`. This **silently fails to isolate** on a slow-booting VM: `launchctl setenv` populates a process-wide environment cache that `open`-launched apps inherit at *launch time* — but on this mac VM the GPU-less WKWebView boot sequence takes on the order of **minutes** before the sidecar process actually forks, and something in that window (another `open`, a shell reset, a login-item re-exec) reverts the `launchctl setenv` values well before then. The forked child inherits the REAL shared `$HOME` instead, and — because `shared_sidecar_home()==real_home()` by design — silently takes over the box-canonical embedded PG / `operator.json` / `superuser-token`, colliding with whatever else is running on the shared VM. This is exactly what happened 2026-07-17 (EI-14941): a P-021 update-center E2E attempt collided with a live peer’s federation-drill rig on the SAME mac VM’s shared PG data dir. The instinctive “fix” — just wait longer before checking, extend the setenv-to-launch gap — does not actually change the failure mode: `launchctl setenv`’s scope and the `open`/LaunchServices handoff are simply the wrong mechanism for this, no matter the timing. ## The actual fix: don’t use `open` at all [Section titled “The actual fix: don’t use open at all”](#the-actual-fix-dont-use-open-at-all) `open -a` hands the launch off to LaunchServices/launchd, which is what re-derives the environment from its own cache rather than your shell’s. Skip that whole layer: **launch the app’s actual Mach-O executable directly**, with the isolation env vars set inline in the SAME exec — normal Unix fork+exec env inheritance, no launchd cache, no race: 
```bash
BIN="/path/to/e2e/priorapp/Papercusp GUI.app/Contents/MacOS/papercusp-desktop"
ISOHOME="/path/to/e2e/home3"


nohup env \
  HOME="$ISOHOME" \
  PAPERCUSP_HOME="$ISOHOME" \
  PAPERCUSP_PG_PORT=19170 \
  PAPERCUSP_HONO_PORT=19070 \
  PAPERCUSP_PG_DATA_DIR="$ISOHOME/embedded-pg-data" \
  PAPERCUSP_RELEASE_HOST="http://127.0.0.1:8044" \
  "$BIN" > "$ISOHOME/../gui.log" 2>&1 &
disown
```
 Verified live (2026-07-17, mac VM, prior-version 0.0.8 GUI.app which **predates** the `PAPERCUSP_HOME` fix, i.e. its own JS ignores that env var entirely): the process still came up **fully isolated** — * its own `~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json` written under `$ISOHOME`, not the shared one (whose mtime was unchanged before/after); * its own embedded postgres, auto-picked port (`20836` in the observed run — the app auto-selects an available port; it does NOT need to honor your requested `PAPERCUSP_PG_PORT` value for isolation to hold, it just needs to pick *a* free one), data dir under `$ISOHOME/.papercusp-workspaces/.shared/embedded-pg-data`; * its own hono/HTTP port (`17701` in the observed run), confirmed via `GET /api/health` returning the correct old version/sha; * confirmed via `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` (compare the full listening-port set before/after) that the shared `:3070`/`:3170`/`:3270`/`:18213` owners (pids) were **completely unchanged** throughout. **Why this works even on code that predates the `PAPERCUSP_HOME` fix:** Node’s `os.homedir()` on POSIX checks `process.env.HOME` before falling back to the passwd DB — so a plain `HOME` override, delivered via normal env inheritance (not `launchctl setenv`), isolates the process’s default `~/.papercusp` resolution regardless of whether the app’s own code added explicit `PAPERCUSP_HOME` support. The EI-14941 incident was never really about “the app can’t be told to isolate” — it was specifically about `open` * `launchctl setenv` being the wrong DELIVERY mechanism for that instruction on a slow-booting VM. Bypass the mechanism, not the timing. **Watch for a companion process spawned via a registered bundle id.** The GUI role may spawn a companion “Server” role process resolved via LaunchServices to whatever’s registered at `/Applications` (not necessarily your extracted test copy) — `ps eww` on that child still shows YOUR env correctly (fork/exec inheritance doesn’t care which path the exec target resolves to), so verify via `ps eww` + `lsof -p <pid>`, not by assuming the executable path implies which env it’s running with. ## What this does NOT solve: driving the GUI itself [Section titled “What this does NOT solve: driving the GUI itself”](#what-this-does-not-solve-driving-the-gui-itself) Direct-binary-launch fixes *isolation*. It does not give you a way to click through the actual update UI on a **packaged release build**: * The `tauri-agent-tools` dev-bridge (`dev_bridge.rs`, the eval/click/screenshot CLI documented for driving the Tauri webview headlessly) only starts `if is_dev` — it is compiled out of / inert in a packaged release `.app`. `npm run dev`’s Tauri shell is the only surface where that CLI works. * OS-level UI scripting (`osascript`/`System Events`) requires Accessibility (TCC) grant for whatever process runs it (ssh/Terminal) — not granted by default, and granting it requires either physical GUI interaction or a system-wide TCC.db change (itself a shared-VM-risk action, not something to do unilaterally for a test). * There is no server-side HTTP shortcut for `install_update`/`revert_to` — they are Tauri commands invoked ONLY via the webview’s JS `invoke()`; the operator’s `/api/updates/*` routes (`updates-manifest.ts`, `updates-rollback.ts`) only RESOLVE the install manifest the client will fetch — they never perform the actual download/swap themselves. So: isolated packaged-app testing (safe to boot, safe to leave running, verifiable via its own `/api/health`) is now a solved, repeatable technique. Driving an actual click-through install+relaunch on a packaged release build still needs either a human / VNC session with Accessibility granted, or a dev-mode (`npm run dev`) rebuild specifically for that pass (which changes what’s being tested — dev mode skips the normal sidecar spawn/update path entirely, so it cannot substitute for testing the real packaged updater). Related: EI-14941 (the original collision incident), `apps/operator/bin/serve.ts`’s `PAPERCUSP_HOME` handling (comment tag EI-13917), `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/dev_bridge.rs`.

# Mac build VM — QMP recovery from a wedged boot, and the launcher split-brain

> When SSH :2222 is dead and papercup-vm-mac.service crash-loops on SPICE :5930, an orphaned durable qemu is usually parked at the OpenCore boot picker. Recover with QMP screendump + send-key — never pkill. Plus the boot-sonoma.sh vs boot-sonoma-durable.sh split-brain, the loginwindow-vs-PAM password divergence (avraham vs aviweiss), and why you verify the desktop UI with ui:dispatch — NOT QMP keystrokes (they reach loginwindow only, never the webview).

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) * `ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -p 2222 aviweiss@127.0.0.1` times out during banner exchange. * `systemctl --user status papercup-vm-mac.service` shows a restart loop with `Spice: …reds_init_socket: binding socket to 127.0.0.1:5930 failed` → `failed to initialize spice server` (the 2026-06-11 incident had racked up **5,708** scheduled restarts). * `ss -ltnp | grep 5930` shows a *different, older* `qemu-system-x86_64` pid holding SPICE :5930 and SSH-forward :2222. ## What actually happened [Section titled “What actually happened”](#what-actually-happened) Two launchers exist in `~/macos-vm/OSX-KVM/` and they are NOT the same: | | `boot-sonoma.sh` (old service ExecStart) | `boot-sonoma-durable.sh` | | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | RAM | 16 GB | 32 GB | | Installer media | **attaches `BaseSystem.img`** (since 2026-06-09 a macOS *Tahoe* installer) | none | | Process model | foreground (`Type=simple`) | `setsid nohup` fork + `qemu.pid` (`Type=forking`) | | Control socket | SPICE only | **QMP at `./qmp.sock`** + `logs/qemu-current.log` | The live VM had been started by hand via the **durable** script; the systemd unit kept trying to start the **old** script against it and could never bind SPICE. Meanwhile the durable guest had rebooted into the **OpenCore boot picker** and sat there for 33 hours — picker wedge signature: **\~100% of one core, tiny RSS (\~140 MB despite -m 32768), zero writes to `mac_hdd_ng.img`**. ## Recovery (no data loss — do NOT pkill) [Section titled “Recovery (no data loss — do NOT pkill)”](#recovery-no-data-loss--do-not-pkill) QMP on the durable launcher’s socket. Each command is one JSON line; read the greeting, send `qmp_capabilities`, then drive: 
```python
import json, socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX); s.connect('/home/dev/macos-vm/OSX-KVM/qmp.sock')
f = s.makefile('rw'); f.readline()
def cmd(c): f.write(json.dumps(c)+'\n'); f.flush(); return f.readline()
cmd({"execute":"qmp_capabilities"})
cmd({"execute":"screendump","arguments":{"filename":"/tmp/macvm-screen.ppm"}})  # see the console
# OpenCore picker showing EFI + Macintosh HD, EFI focused → move right, enter:
cmd({"execute":"send-key","arguments":{"keys":[{"type":"qcode","data":"right"}]}})
cmd({"execute":"send-key","arguments":{"keys":[{"type":"qcode","data":"ret"}]}})
```
 `convert /tmp/macvm-screen.ppm x.png` to view. SSH came up \~2 min after the send-key. A graceful shutdown is `{"execute":"system_powerdown"}` on the same socket. **Never** `pkill -f qemu` / `pkill -f papercusp` patterns here — the box runs several qemu VMs and desktop instances (see the 2026-06-11 broadcast about a pkill killing every peer’s Tauri instance). Kill by exact pid from `qemu.pid` only, and only as a last resort. ## The durable fixes (so this doesn’t recur) [Section titled “The durable fixes (so this doesn’t recur)”](#the-durable-fixes-so-this-doesnt-recur) 1. `papercup-vm-mac.service` now runs `boot-sonoma-durable.sh` (`Type=forking` + `PIDFile=qemu.pid` + QMP `ExecStop`). The old `boot-sonoma.sh` is manual-installer-use only. 2. **The wedge’s real mechanism (P-001, FIXED 2026-06-11):** `ScanPolicy=0` listed OpenCore’s own ESP as a boot entry named “EFI” — and as the FIRST entry it was the *default*, so `Timeout=2` auto-booted OpenCore into itself in an infinite EFI loop (\~100% CPU, black/parked picker, zero disk writes). Fixed by `Misc.Security.ScanPolicy = 0x10303` (FS\_LOCK|DEVICE\_LOCK + APFS|HFS + SATA) in `EFI/OC/config.plist` on `OpenCore.qcow2` — the ESP is never scanned, `Macintosh HD` is the only entry, and a cold boot reaches sshd unattended. Edit the plist via `qemu-nbd --connect=/dev/nbd0 OpenCore/OpenCore.qcow2` + mount `p1` (qemu must be DOWN). A picker-era NVRAM default (ctrl+enter) does NOT stick reliably here — fix ScanPolicy instead. ## GUI-session auth (loginwindow) on this VM — passwords DIVERGE by layer [Section titled “GUI-session auth (loginwindow) on this VM — passwords DIVERGE by layer”](#gui-session-auth-loginwindow-on-this-vm--passwords-diverge-by-layer) CORRECTED 2026-06-11: the original “secure-token wedge” diagnosis was wrong. The GUI credential path (loginwindow / lock screen) simply has a **different password** (`avraham`) from the PAM path that ssh/sudo accept (`aviweiss`). A day of “loginwindow rejects the correct password” was a wrong password; the owner supplied the GUI one and the locked session unlocked first try. To unlock for agent verification: wake the display with a QMP `send-key` (`shift`), type the GUI password char-by-char via `send-key`, send `ret`, then `screendump` for pixels. If you hit auth errors from `sysadminctl` / kcpassword anyway, suspect a wrong-password loop before any secure-token theory — verify which password each auth layer actually holds. ## Verifying the desktop UI on the VM — dispatch, NOT QMP keystrokes [Section titled “Verifying the desktop UI on the VM — dispatch, NOT QMP keystrokes”](#verifying-the-desktop-ui-on-the-vm--dispatch-not-qmp-keystrokes) Once the GUI is unlocked, the productive way to drive + verify the running desktop app is the **agent→UI control surface**, not QMP `send-key`: * **QMP keyboard reaches `loginwindow` only.** Raw `send-key` unlocks the lock screen (loginwindow grabs all keyboard input), but it does **not** reach the WKWebView — typing into a form field lands nowhere, and even `Cmd+R` doesn’t reload the webview (the SPA’s `ui_client` id stays the same across a “reload”). Don’t try to fill the setup wizard or the create-harness form by injecting keystrokes; it silently no-ops. * **Use `ui:dispatch` against the VM’s operator instead.** The SPA registers a `ui_client` on `papercusp://localhost`; drive it over the sidecar’s MCP endpoint. List the tab (`ui:list_clients`), then dispatch built-in intents: `set_url` (every nuqs view/tab/dialog is a URL param — `{create:"true"}` opens the create dialog, `{tab:"docs",harness:"<slug>"}` switches tab + pot), `click` (CSS selector), `read_visible_text`, `snapshot`. This walked the whole 11-step wizard, every OPS tab, the Cupboard, and the create dialog with zero pixels. 
  ```bash
  TOKEN=$(ssh …vm 'cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token')
  # operator port = grep 'operator ready on :' from the app's stdout log
  curl -s -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/mcp?superuser=1" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
    -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"ui:dispatch","arguments":{"client_id":"<id>","intent":"set_url","args":{"params":{"create":"true"}}}}}'
  ```
 * **For anything that needs text entry (form submit, a chat turn), drive the BACKEND, not the keystrokes.** A pot is created by `harness:create({slug, parentDir, folderName, blueprintId:"coding"})` — the exact path the create form’s submit calls — which on darwin git-inits the dir, writes `.papercusp/blueprint.yaml`, and provisions the PG schema. Verify on disk (`git -C … rev-parse`). The form itself is proven by render + dispatched clicks; its submit is React-standard. * **A chat turn still needs a real LLM credential on the VM** — that’s an owner hands-on step, not an agent-verifiable one. * **Screendump caveat:** the display sleeps with no real input; a single `send-key shift` wakes it, but it re-sleeps. `pmset -a displaysleep 0` (needs the GUI password via `sudo -S`) helps but doesn’t fully stick under this VM. Wake immediately before each `screendump`. ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * VM inventory, ports, disk discipline: [build-system/vms](/internal/docs/build-system/vms) * `diskutil apfs resizeContainer disk1s2 0` fails with “must be different size” after a host-side qcow2 grow until you first run `sudo diskutil repairDisk disk1` (the GPT still carries the old size). That sequence took the VM from 7 GiB free to 60 GiB on 2026-06-11.

# macOS packaged app has a minimal PATH and no bundled git — the dogfood clone fails on a fresh Mac

> A packaged macOS GUI app is launched by launchd with a MINIMAL PATH (/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin) — it does NOT inherit the shell PATH, so Apple-Silicon Homebrew's /opt/homebrew/bin is absent. Worse, the desktop does NOT vendor git on macOS (build-desktop-sidecar.sh assumes macOS ships git — false: a CLT-less Mac has only the /usr/bin/git STUB that fails non-interactively). So the first-boot dogfood `git clone` fails with a bare 'workspace setup failed'. Fix: serve.ts now adds /opt/homebrew/bin (tool-path.ts) + the wizard surfaces an actionable 'xcode-select --install' hint.

Two macOS-specific facts conspire to make the first-boot dogfood `git clone` (and thus the whole setup wizard) fail on a **fresh** Mac — with a useless generic “Setting up Papercusp workspace failed”. ## 1. A packaged GUI app gets a MINIMAL PATH [Section titled “1. A packaged GUI app gets a MINIMAL PATH”](#1-a-packaged-gui-app-gets-a-minimal-path) launchd starts a `.app` with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin` — it does **not** inherit your shell’s PATH. So **`/opt/homebrew/bin`** (Apple-Silicon Homebrew’s prefix, where `gh`/`git`/`kopia` live for most users) is absent. The Rust side (`main.rs`) already prepends the bundled `sidecar/bin` (node, gh, …), but the old PATH lists in `serve.ts` / `terminal-spawn.ts` listed only `/usr/local/bin` (Intel Homebrew) — never `/opt/homebrew/bin`. Meanwhile the DETECTION sites (`preflight.ts`, `agent-auth-detect.ts`) *did* probe `/opt/homebrew/bin` — so the app reported “gh installed” while execution couldn’t run it. Fixed by routing every PATH through `tool-path.ts` (`standardToolDirs` / `ensureToolPathEnv`), which includes both Homebrew prefixes. ## 2. macOS does NOT ship a working git by default [Section titled “2. macOS does NOT ship a working git by default”](#2-macos-does-not-ship-a-working-git-by-default) `build-desktop-sidecar.sh` vendors `git` only on Windows (MinGit), assuming “macOS/Linux ship git by default”. **False for macOS:** a Mac without Xcode Command Line Tools has only the `/usr/bin/git` **stub**, which on non-interactive invocation prints `xcode-select: note: no developer tools were found …` and exits non-zero (it would otherwise pop a GUI install dialog). The sidecar bundles `gh`/`node`/`omp`/`pg_*` but **not** `git`. Immediate unblock (no rebuild needed) On a fresh Mac the existing build’s clone works once git is present: run `xcode-select --install` (or `brew install git`) in the VM, then retry setup. `gh` is bundled and `gh auth setup-git` is already wired, so the credential helper resolves — only `git` itself was missing. ## What ships now (mitigations) [Section titled “What ships now (mitigations)”](#what-ships-now-mitigations) * `serve.ts` → `ensureToolPathEnv()` puts `/opt/homebrew/bin` on the sidecar PATH (runs on darwin even without `PAPERCUSP_SIDECAR_BIN`), so a Homebrew git/gh is found. * `clone-github.ts` `isGitUnavailable()` detects the CLT-stub stderr → `git_missing` with an actionable message (`xcode-select --install` / `brew install git`). * The wizard (`BootstrapFinishGate` / `DogfoodBootstrapBanner`) shows the install hint and does **not** auto-retry a git-missing error (it’s a user-action error, not transient — distinct from the network-timeout auto-retry path). * `bootstrap-papercusp-pot.ts` now logs the real clone failure (code + git stderr) — the diagnostic that was missing cost a full live debugging round. ## The robust fix (deferred — needs a Mac build box) [Section titled “The robust fix (deferred — needs a Mac build box)”](#the-robust-fix-deferred--needs-a-mac-build-box) Vendor a relocatable git for macOS in the sidecar (mirror the Windows MinGit approach) so a truly fresh Mac works zero-friction — tracked as **EI-3620**. macOS has no official portable git; evaluate a relocatable Homebrew bottle (with `install_name_tool` rpath fixups), a static build, or auto-triggering `xcode-select --install`. Must be per-arch (arm64 + x64), signed/notarized. Same class of risk: verify the bundled embedded-Postgres / `pg_*` binary arch matches the app arch on a real Mac build.

# On macOS, PPID==1 is NOT an orphan signal — a trap for boot-time process sweeps

> Why a "reparented to PID 1" heuristic for detecting orphaned child processes is safe on Linux/systemd but actively dangerous on macOS/launchd, with a live-verified near-miss and the corrected pattern.

## The assumption that breaks [Section titled “The assumption that breaks”](#the-assumption-that-breaks) On Linux (or any systemd-managed target), a process whose PPID is `1` (init) is a reliable, nearly-unambiguous signal that its real parent died and the kernel reparented it — a classic “orphan” you can safely sweep. It’s tempting to reuse that exact heuristic on macOS for a boot-time “clean up anything my last hard-killed instance left running” sweep. **On macOS this assumption is wrong.** `launchd` is the standard, NORMAL supervisory parent for an entire class of process — any LaunchAgent / LaunchDaemon / login-item-launched app — not just an orphan-reaper. A perfectly healthy, currently-running app launched that way shows `PPID==1` from the moment it starts, for its entire lifetime. It is never a signal that something died. ## The near-miss (WI-3633, 2026-07-09) [Section titled “The near-miss (WI-3633, 2026-07-09)”](#the-near-miss-wi-3633-2026-07-09) Building a boot-time orphan sweep for the Papercusp desktop’s operator sidecar, the first design was: scan the process table for anything with `PPID==1` whose command line matched the sidecar’s entry point (`serve.mjs`), and kill its process group. Live verification against `papercup-vm-mac` (a real running instance, not a sandbox) immediately found the trap: **multiple simultaneously-running, completely healthy `serve.mjs` processes all had `PPID==1` at once** — the actively-in-use operator (kept alive by the app’s own `serve --ensure` “Decision C” reuse semantics: a fresh app instance that finds a live prior operator reuses it instead of spawning a competitor) *and* an unrelated per-environment sidecar, both legitimately parented to launchd. A blind `PPID==1` sweep would have killed a live, in-use, healthy operator the moment a fresh app instance booted — turning a minor zombie-cleanup feature into a much worse “boot always kills your work” regression. ## The corrected pattern [Section titled “The corrected pattern”](#the-corrected-pattern) Never use process-table SHAPE (`PPID==1`, or any other purely structural signal) as a kill trigger by itself. Instead, key off: 1. **An authoritative tracking record** the process itself writes — a discovery/lock file naming its own pid (here: `operator.json`, already used by the existing `find_operator_discovery` / `wait_for_operator` machinery). 2. **A genuine liveness/health check** — not just “does the pid exist” but “is it actually doing its job” (here: `operator_http_ready`, an HTTP probe the app already trusted elsewhere). Only kill when the tracked pid is **alive at the OS level but NOT responding** — that combination is what actually distinguishes a genuinely wedged/zombie leftover from either “already dead, nothing to do” or “alive and fine, leave it alone.” See `sweep_stale_operator_orphan` + `decide_orphan_sweep` in `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` (WI-3633) for the shipped implementation — `decide_orphan_sweep` is a pure decision function (`(discovery, pid_alive, http_ready) -> OrphanSweepDecision`) kept separate from the OS-facing calls specifically so this branch logic is unit-testable and its four outcomes (`NothingRecorded` / `AlreadyDead` / `HealthyReuse` / `StaleKill`) are pinned by tests — `HealthyReuse` in particular exists exactly to name and protect the case this near-miss found. ## Takeaway [Section titled “Takeaway”](#takeaway) If you’re writing a boot-time / periodic sweep that kills processes based on their position in the process tree, and the target platform is macOS (or any other launchd-adjacent supervisor), **verify your detection logic against a REAL running instance before trusting it** — a heuristic that’s completely sound on Linux can be silently, catastrophically wrong there. Prefer a tracking-record + liveness-check design over any raw parent-child shape signal.

# macOS code signing + notarization — the turnkey public-release runbook

> For a PUBLIC macOS release the .app MUST be Apple-signed (Developer ID Application) + notarized + stapled, or Gatekeeper refuses it on every fresh Mac ('Apple cannot check it for malicious software'). The build pipeline (mac-vm-build.sh → tauri build) already signs+notarizes automatically WHEN the Apple credentials are present in env — so this is gated only on the OWNER supplying: an Apple Developer Program membership, a Developer ID Application cert imported on build VM :2222, and notarytool creds (APPLE_ID + app-specific password + APPLE_TEAM_ID, or an App Store Connect API key). Entitlements (entitlements.plist) are already wired for the embedded-Node JIT under the hardened runtime.

The one **owner-action** blocker between the current build and a confident **public** macOS release. Everything else (the never-trap setup gate, the `.gitmodules` fix, the build pipeline) is done in code; this needs Apple credentials an agent cannot obtain. Why it's mandatory for PUBLIC release The alpha bundle is unsigned/un-notarized (plan `mac-desktop-release-readiness-2026-06-11` D-002 — first launch needed right-click → Open or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine`). That is fine for a handful of insiders but **not** for the public: Gatekeeper blocks an unsigned, un-notarized app downloaded from the internet with *“Papercusp can’t be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software,”* and most users delete it rather than dig through System Settings → Privacy & Security to override. ## The good news: the pipeline already does it — when creds are present [Section titled “The good news: the pipeline already does it — when creds are present”](#the-good-news-the-pipeline-already-does-it--when-creds-are-present) `tauri build` (invoked by `bin/mac-vm-build.sh`) **automatically** code-signs every bundled executable and notarizes + staples the `.app`/`.dmg` **iff** the Apple env vars below are set. Tauri v2 signs sidecars and frameworks too, so the embedded `node` / `gh` / `pg_*` / `zellij` binaries are covered. No script change is required — the gate is purely the credentials. `entitlements.plist` is already created and referenced from `tauri.conf.json > bundle > macOS > entitlements`. It is **required**: under the hardened runtime (which notarization forces on) the embedded Node V8 JIT is killed without `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` + `allow-unsigned-executable-memory`, and the mixed sidecar binaries need `disable-library-validation`. (The entitlements file is inert for an unsigned build, so it is safe in the tree today.) ## What the OWNER must provide (one-time) [Section titled “What the OWNER must provide (one-time)”](#what-the-owner-must-provide-one-time) 1. **Apple Developer Program membership** (\~$99/yr) for the Papercusp Apple account — required to issue a *Developer ID Application* certificate (the cert type for apps distributed **outside** the App Store). 2. A **`Developer ID Application: <Name> (<TEAMID>)` certificate**, created at developer.apple.com → Certificates, exported from Keychain Access as a password-protected `.p12`. 3. A **notarytool credential**, either: * an **app-specific password** for the Apple ID (appleid.apple.com → Sign-In & Security → App-Specific Passwords), **or** * an **App Store Connect API key** (`.p8` + Key ID + Issuer ID) — preferred for automation (doesn’t expire with the Apple ID password). ## One-time install on build VM :2222 [Section titled “One-time install on build VM :2222”](#one-time-install-on-build-vm-2222) 
```sh
# On the Mac build VM (ssh -p 2222 aviweiss@127.0.0.1):
security import DeveloperID.p12 -k ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db \
  -P '<p12-password>' -T /usr/bin/codesign
security find-identity -v -p codesigning   # copy the "Developer ID Application: …" line
```
 ## Per-build env (set before bin/mac-vm-build.sh) [Section titled “Per-build env (set before bin/mac-vm-build.sh)”](#per-build-env-set-before-binmac-vm-buildsh) `mac-vm-build.sh` already inherits the SSH env, so export these in the remote shell (or add them to the `release-local.sh` WITH\_MAC leg): 
```sh
export APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: <Name> (<TEAMID>)"
# Notarytool — Apple ID path:
export APPLE_ID="<apple-account-email>"
export APPLE_PASSWORD="<app-specific-password>"   # NOT the account password
export APPLE_TEAM_ID="<TEAMID>"
# …or App Store Connect API-key path instead of the three above:
#   export APPLE_API_KEY="<KEYID>"; export APPLE_API_ISSUER="<ISSUERID>"
#   export APPLE_API_KEY_PATH="$HOME/AuthKey_<KEYID>.p8"
```
 (If the cert is provided only as a base64 `.p12`, set `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` + `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` instead of pre-importing — Tauri infers the identity. `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` overrides `tauri.conf > bundle > macOS > signingIdentity`.) ## Verify the result [Section titled “Verify the result”](#verify-the-result) 
```sh
APP=src-tauri/target/universal-apple-darwin/release/bundle/macos/Papercusp.app
codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=2 "$APP"
codesign -dvv "$APP" 2>&1 | grep -E 'Authority|TeamIdentifier'   # Developer ID, your TEAMID
spctl --assess --type execute --verbose "$APP"                   # → "accepted, source=Notarized Developer ID"
xcrun stapler validate "$APP"                                    # → "The validate action worked!"
```
 A truly fresh Mac (no quarantine override, never seen the cert) should then open the downloaded `.dmg` → app with **no** Gatekeeper warning. ## Caveats specific to this app [Section titled “Caveats specific to this app”](#caveats-specific-to-this-app) * **Sidecar arch / Rosetta (D-006).** The sidecar is x86\_64-only; on Apple Silicon it runs under Rosetta 2 (one-time `softwareupdate --install-rosetta`). Signing/notarization still succeed, but say so in the public release notes, or ship a universal sidecar to drop the requirement (plan `mac-public-release-readiness-2026-06-25` P-007). * **Notarization is slow** (Apple-side, minutes) and runs in the same `tauri build`. Budget for it in the release window. * **Updater payloads** stay minisign-signed (separate from Apple signing) — that already works.

# Maintained work-item readiness — a local sidecar, NOT a column (work_items federates)

> Why scheduler readiness is materialized as a local non-federated blocked-set table (work_item_blocked) maintained by triggers, instead of a `ready` column on the unified work_items table — and how the flagged claim cutover + reconciliation oracle work.

## TL;DR [Section titled “TL;DR”](#tldr) Scheduler **readiness** (is a work-item claimable — every `blocked_by` edge satisfied?) was being recomputed **inline per claim** (a correlated `NOT EXISTS` over `work_item_deps` + blocker statuses in `claimFloorsWhereSql`). To make it an **indexed** read, it’s now materialized — but **NOT as a `ready` column on `work_items`**. It lives in a separate **local, non-federated** table `harness_shared.work_item_blocked` (**presence of a row = NOT ready**; absence = ready), maintained by triggers. The claim switches to an indexed anti-join behind a flag. ## The non-obvious part: why a sidecar, not a column [Section titled “The non-obvious part: why a sidecar, not a column”](#the-non-obvious-part-why-a-sidecar-not-a-column) The obvious design (the plan’s original P-005 text) is “a maintained `ready` boolean column on the work-item.” **That is wrong here, because `work_items` is federated.** Two live triggers make a plain column unsafe: * `stamp_local_federated_write_trg` (BEFORE UPDATE) bumps `fed_ts` on **any** write. * `capture_work_items_feature_upd_trg` (AFTER UPDATE) fires on a **whole-row diff** (`old.* IS DISTINCT FROM new.*`) and captures the row to the federation outbox. So a `ready`-flip would **federate** the row. Readiness is a value each node must **derive locally** from the (already-federated) edges + statuses — replicating the derived value invites a stale federated `ready` to overwrite a node’s local recompute → **a cup claims blocked work**. (Decision D-007 in `work-item-deps-and-readiness-2026-06-22`.) The sidecar sidesteps all of it: the maintenance triggers write **only** `work_item_blocked`, never `work_items`, so none of the federation/churn/stamp triggers fire from readiness maintenance. ## Schema reality you must know first [Section titled “Schema reality you must know first”](#schema-reality-you-must-know-first) The P-010 work-item unification has **physically landed**: `harness_features_consolidated` and `engineer_issues` are **auto-updatable VIEWS** over the unified base table `harness_shared.work_items` (features = `item_kind NOT IN ('bug','change','task')`; issues = the rest; `engineer_issues.state` **is** `work_items.status`). So one `status` column + one terminal set `{passed,deprecated,resolved,closed}` cover both families, and a write via either view fires the triggers on `work_items`. Verify with `SELECT relkind FROM pg_class …` before assuming these are tables. ## How it’s maintained (migration 379) [Section titled “How it’s maintained (migration 379)”](#how-its-maintained-migration-379) * `work_item_is_blocked(harness, feature)` — the **oracle**, a byte-for-byte mirror of `claimFloorsWhereSql`’s inline predicate (feature blocker non-terminal via `harness#id`; issue blocker non-terminal via bare id in ws `'default'`). * One-hop triggers (all **exception-guarded** — a readiness-sync error must never wedge the underlying work-item write; drift is caught by the oracle + sweep): * `wir_deps_sync` on `work_item_deps` → re-sync the blocked feature. * `wir_status_sync_dependents` on `work_items` AFTER UPDATE OF status, gated to the **terminal-boundary crossing** → re-sync the items this row blocks (O(in-degree)). * `wir_insert_sync_own` / `wir_delete_cleanup` for lifecycle. ## The claim cutover (flag) [Section titled “The claim cutover (flag)”](#the-claim-cutover-flag) `SCHEDULER_MAINTAINED_READY` (now **default ON** — graduated 2026-06-22 after a sustained live drift=0 verify + the flag-ON claim path green end-to-end). `claimFloorsWhereSql` reads `NOT EXISTS (work_item_blocked …)` (indexed) when on, the inline `NOT EXISTS` when off. **Both** claim entry points — `claimNextWorkItem` and `getNextWorkItem` — resolve `schedulerMaintainedReadyEnabled()` (fail-CLOSED to the inline predicate) and pass the boolean into the shared fragment, so the two paths can never drift (D-002). OFF is the reversible kill-switch back to the byte-identical inline predicate. **Before changing the default or trusting the sidecar on a new DB, verify zero drift.** Run `reconcileReadiness()` (or the inline SQL: `EXCEPT` both ways between `work_item_blocked` and the `work_item_is_blocked()` set over features) — `drift = missing + extra` must be 0. `missing` (oracle-blocked but no sidecar row) is the dangerous one: a blocked item looks ready → a cup claims blocked work. The claim test pins both arms explicitly (an inline-OFF describe + a sidecar-ON describe) so a fragment bug in either path is caught. ## `claimFloorsWhereSql` grew sibling floors — don’t mistake them for readiness (2026-07-03) [Section titled “claimFloorsWhereSql grew sibling floors — don’t mistake them for readiness (2026-07-03)”](#claimfloorswheresql-grew-sibling-floors--dont-mistake-them-for-readiness-2026-07-03) Two unrelated hardening changes landed inside the SAME `claimFloorsWhereSql` fragment this doc describes. Neither touches readiness/`work_item_blocked` semantics — call them out so a reader diffing the function doesn’t assume they did: * **Release-cooldown floor** (`fleet-scheduler-hardening-2026-07-03` P-005 / EI-6956, migration `485`): a `cooldownAssignee` opt adds a `last_released_by`/`last_released_at` NULL-safe clause that excludes a row from claiming **only for the agent that just voluntarily released it**, for `PAPERCUSP_RELEASE_COOLDOWN_SEC` (default 300s) — kills the claim/release ping-pong where a released row resets to `todo`, re-sorts to the top under a stable rank, and the same cup re-claims it immediately. `releaseWorkItem` stamps the provenance; every other agent can still claim the row instantly. This is a **fairness/anti-thrash** floor, not a correctness-of-readiness one — a cooled-down row is still fully “ready” by the oracle’s definition, just temporarily off-limits to one claimant. * **`CLAIM_STATES_ALLOWLIST`** (`['todo', 'open', 'failing']`, WI-1912): closes the exact same *floor-widening* class this doc’s D-002 already fixed for the readiness predicate, but on the sibling caller-supplied `states` arg (`scheduler:get_next` / `work_items:claim_next`) — a fleet member had passed `states:['todo','open','blocked']` and pulled a leader-triage-only item. Same principle as this doc’s core claim (a caller must never widen past a floor state), applied one layer up from `claimFloorsWhereSql` itself. Several more exclusions now sit ANDed alongside `claimFloorsWhereSql` (and its issue-family sibling `claimNextIssueWorkItem`) at the claim entry points in `work-items.ts` — same “not readiness, a separate floor” caveat applies: `reservedPlanLaneExclusionSql` (WI-2118, keeps a plan-reserved lane out of the general claim pool), `crossMachineRigExclusionSql` (WI-2796, excludes items pinned to an unavailable cross-machine rig), `claimHoldExclusionSql` (WI-2797, `payload._claimHold:true` — a leader’s ad-hoc “don’t re-serve this” hold on a specific item, `COALESCE(wi.payload, '{}'::jsonb) ->> '_claimHold' IS DISTINCT FROM 'true'`), `observationLaneExclusionSql` (D-005, a `lane:'observation'` scorecard/reflection row is never work-queue material), `needsHumanExclusionSql` (EI-7776, an issue-family row `improvements:resolve` already routed to a human — the issue dialect has no real terminal “needs-human” state, so without this a drain-loop cup re-claims and re-posts the same routed-to-human comment forever), and `federationDetectorExclusionSql` (WI-2633, gates an auto-filed replication-liveness detector EI to the p2p fleet that can actually action it). None of these touch `work_item_blocked` / oracle readiness — an item can be fully “ready” and still correctly excluded here for an orthogonal reason. Every one of the exclusions above is still directly claimable **by id**; only opportunistic self-select (`claim_next` / `scheduler:get_next`) skips them. **Migration 499** extended the release-cooldown floor (mig 485/EI-6956, described above) to the **issue-family** claim path too: `claimNextIssueWorkItem` now applies the exact same NULL-safe “released by ME within the cooldown window” exclusion the feature-family floor already had, closing the same claim/release ping-pong (confirmed live, WI-652/WI-2381-class) for bug/change/task rows. ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * The sidecar key is `(workspace_id, harness_slug, feature_id)` — the feature’s **real** workspace, not the deps’ `'default'` coordination workspace. The triggers resolve the feature row’s `workspace_id` from `work_items`; the claim anti-join matches on it. * The sidecar is **feature-family only** — the `wir_*` triggers never track `bug`/`change`/`task` rows, so it would (wrongly) report a blocked **issue** as ready. The issue-claim path in `work-items.ts` therefore **always** uses the inline `NOT EXISTS` predicate over `work_item_deps`, regardless of the `SCHEDULER_MAINTAINED_READY` flag — it’s the secondary, lower-volume claim path, so the un-indexed read is an accepted cost. Only the feature-claim paths (`claimNextWorkItem`, `getNextWorkItem`) cut over. * `db:migrate` needs `PAPERCUSP_ALLOW_DB_MIGRATE=1`; without it, validate a migration in a rolled-back `BEGIN … ROLLBACK` against the real DB (compiles functions, runs the backfill, lets you check reconciliation), then let boot-apply record it — or `psql -f` + INSERT the `schema_migrations` row in the same txn (it’s `(filename, applied_at, sha256)`). * A comment containing a backtick inside a `sql\`…“ tagged template **terminates the template** — keep SQL-fragment comments backtick-free.

# Max OAuth 429s: the first system block must be EXACTLY the Claude Code identity

> THE CANONICAL runbook for "raw-OAuth/in-process opus calls 429 but the claude CLI / terminals work." Symptoms it explains: opus through the inference gateway 429s (Cloudflare bare-burst: server=cloudflare, cf-ray, x-should-retry, NO retry-after, NO anthropic-ratelimit-*); the Scout ideator (or gym judge / sim-user / transfer / memory — any in-process anthropic-direct call) hangs ~180s and fails with "transport death (0 ideas, $0 spent)" / "Scout ideator analogical timed out after 180000ms"; haiku lands ~1s; interactive claude/PSU terminal sessions on the SAME box hit opus fine; the headless autonomous loop's opus calls 429 while terminals don't. ROOT CAUSE: the Max OAuth beta (oauth-2025-04-20) routes to the normal limiter ONLY when the FIRST `system` block is EXACTLY "You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude." as its OWN block; omit/concatenate it and the request is shunted to a strict limiter returning a BOGUS rate_limit_error even at 0.0 utilization. For THIS (framing) cause it is NOT the egress IP/volume/quota/headers — BUT the identical header-less 429 ALSO appears as a genuine Cloudflare per-IP EGRESS throttle for ALREADY-FRAMED callers under concentrated opus load (a DISTINCT mode; see rate-limit-is-usually-account-routing-not-capacity Fault #6). Discriminator: framing = deterministic (~100% of that caller's requests, any IP, even 1 token); edge throttle = bursty + load-correlated (low overall rate, clusters, tracks per-IP volume). FIXED 2026-06-30 at the chat-stream buildSystemParam chokepoint (always prepends it) — every anthropic-direct caller is now framed. Re-confirmed live: opus 200/2.6s with the block, 20s-timeout/429 without; Scout then ran with ideas_generated=3. Search: opus 429, scout timeout, transport death, in-process 429, anthropic-direct, buildSystemParam, Max OAuth stricter bucket, headless vs terminal.


> **STATUS 2026-06-30 — the gateway/caller-level fix flagged below as an open follow-up is now SHIPPED**, and this exact trap recurred (and cost a full session) because the autonomous loop’s in-process Scout path was never framed. `chat-stream.ts` `buildSystemParam()` now ALWAYS prepends the CC identity as the first `system` block, and `statelessAgentChat` always sets `params.system` — so every `anthropic-direct` caller (Scout ideators, gym judge, sim-user, transfer, memory) is framed automatically. Re-confirmed live: opus **200 in 2.6s** WITH the block vs **20s timeout / bogus 429** WITHOUT, and the Scout then ran with `ideas_generated=3`. **If you add a NEW in-process LLM path that bypasses `buildSystemParam`, you must prepend `CLAUDE_CODE_IDENTIFIER` yourself or it WILL opus-429.** > **⚠ LOOK-ALIKE — is it framing, or a Cloudflare per-IP EGRESS throttle? They produce a NEARLY IDENTICAL header-less 429** (`{"type":"rate_limit_error","message":"Error"}`, `x-should-retry:true`, NO `anthropic-ratelimit-*`, NO `retry-after`, low utilization). Landing on the wrong one is why gateway fixers keep failing (this exact confusion recurred 2026-06-30).
