If you’re auditing “which mem0 internals does this repo monkey-patch”, it’s now three: `VectorStoreFactory`, `EmbedderFactory`, `LLMFactory` — check all three when mem0ai bumps its version. ## Prove the full path actually works [Section titled “Prove the full path actually works”](#prove-the-full-path-actually-works) Don’t trust a passing tsc or a mocked unit test — round-trip the real store. Decrypt the OpenAI key from `operator_credentials` via pgcrypto (`pgp_sym_decrypt(payload_ct, <~/.papercusp/db-encryption-key>)`), `configureMemory()` with `getAdminUrl`/`getCredentials`/`resolveEmbedder`, then `getMemoryClient()` → `add()` → `search()` → `getAll()` → `delete()`. A real OpenAI-backed round-trip against the canonical pgvector store takes seconds and is the only thing that proves cause 4 is clear. To exercise just the storage layer **without** an LLM, drive `CanonicalVectorStore` directly (it needs only PG + a pre-computed 384-dim vector) — see [`embedded-pg-discovery`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/embedded-pg-discovery/) for how `getHarnessAdminUrl()` resolves (the native fallback PG may be fully provisioned even with the desktop down). `memory_canonical.id` is a UUID column — use a valid UUID, scope to a throwaway `user_id`, delete after. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * [`live-pg-regression-papercup`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/live-pg-regression-papercup/) — the broader “verify against live PG, not just unit tests” pattern. * [`embedded-pg-discovery`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/embedded-pg-discovery/) — PG URL resolution + the native fallback.

# Memory topology — one PG store, two legs, papercusp-owned injection

> The post-2026-07-13 memory architecture — hybrid-pg (RRF of a PG lexical leg + the mem0 cosine leg over ONE memory_canonical table), why ~/.claude topic files stopped being load-bearing, and the cutover/rollback levers.

Plan: `memory-pg-lexical-own-injection-2026-07-13`. Owner mandate: the lexical leg must be papercusp code over papercusp storage, and ambient injection must be papercusp-controlled — no dependency on Claude’s file-memory implementation. ## Update 2026-07-28 — hybrid-pg is now the DEFAULT, and the \~/.claude backends are gone [Section titled “Update 2026-07-28 — hybrid-pg is now the DEFAULT, and the \~/.claude backends are gone”](#update-2026-07-28--hybrid-pg-is-now-the-default-and-the-claude-backends-are-gone) `memory-declaude-and-defaults-2026-07-28` finished the job this plan started. Three changes to what is written below: * **`hybrid-pg` is the default backend**, not `mem0` — `DEFAULT_MEMORY_BACKEND` in `backend-selection.ts`. Until then a fresh install silently got the 53%-recall backend, and the 98% one was reachable only by knowing to flip a dropdown. * **`claude-file` and `hybrid` are NO LONGER REGISTERED** and cannot be selected. The “Cutover / rollback” section below says the old `hybrid` “stays registered as the rollback” — that is no longer true, and deliberately so: rolling back onto a frozen file store is not a rollback, it is a data-visibility regression. The rollback for `hybrid-pg` is `mem0` (same rows, cosine leg only). ⚠ A persisted `memory_backend` row or `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_BACKEND` still naming a retired backend is **coerced to the default with a one-time warning** rather than throwing `unknown memory backend` on every call — `RETIRED_MEMORY_BACKENDS` in `backend-selection.ts`. Unregistering a backend without that coercion is a live outage for anyone who had legitimately selected it. * **`HybridBackend` takes its `name` from options** instead of hardcoding `'hybrid'`. The canary’s flip-reseed guard below (`set.backend !== backend.name`) compares exactly that string, so while both wirings answered `'hybrid'` a flip between them skipped the reseed and scored against a baseline from the *other* backend. * The settings page’s stale “Memory index over capacity” banner (which counted \~/.claude topic files and told you to curate them, \~2 weeks after the generator that consumed them was retired) is deleted, along with `claude-hygiene.ts` — the last unconditional \~/.claude read in the operator. `ClaudeFileMemoryBackend` still exists as a lib class: the offline bench constructs it directly to reproduce the A/B numbers below. It is unreachable from the product. ## The shape [Section titled “The shape”](#the-shape) **One canonical store**: `harness_shared.memory_canonical` (payload jsonb) + one `memory_vec_<mode>` table per embedding space (`vec-write.ts` `VEC_TABLE` / `MODE_DIMS` are the single source of truth for that set — derive from them, never hand-copy the list). **Two recall legs, same rows** (`hybrid-pg`, registered in `configure.ts`): * **Cosine leg** — `Mem0Backend.search`: pgvector distance over the active embedder mode’s vec table, per-scope fan-out, decay + diversity rerank. * **Lexical leg** — `Mem0Backend.searchLexical` → `CanonicalVectorStore.lexicalSearch`: embed-free, field-weighted token match (`payload->>'name'` ×3 > `'description'` ×2 > `'data'` ×1, normalized by tokens×3 — parity with the claude-file scoring that benched best on exact-identifier recall), min-2-char identifier-preserving tokenizer (`lexicalTokens`, which emits a compound like `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_TIMEOUT` whole *and* its `_`/`-` subtokens). **The score is computed IN SQL and the `ORDER BY` is the score** — see the ranking trap below. * Fusion: `HybridBackend` RRF (floored-union). Both legs return the SAME canonical ids, so fusion dedupes by construction. `LexicalLegBackend` (`lexical-leg.ts`) presents the lexical capability as a standalone `MemoryBackend` for the hybrid’s constructor. **Its `remember()` is a deliberate no-op** — `HybridBackend.remember` write-through-projects into its lexical leg, which is correct for two SEPARATE stores (the old `hybrid`: claude topic files + PG) but would double-write when both legs share `memory_canonical`. ## Why (the evidence) [Section titled “Why (the evidence)”](#why-the-evidence) * Frozen-corpus bench: lexical wins exact-identifier recall (MRR 0.99 vs 0.87 cosine); cosine wins paraphrase. Complementary failure modes → hybrid. * Live A/B (2026-07-13, 40 known-item pairs from post-June memories, `bench/ab-live-recall-cli.ts`, **post-token-cap-fix**): | backend | recall\@10 (admitted) | retrieval\@10 | p50 | | --------------- | --------------------- | ------------- | ------ | | mem0 | 21/40 (53%) | 63% | 1023ms | | old `hybrid` | 22/40 (55%) | 63% | 1061ms | | **`hybrid-pg`** | **39/40 (98%)** | **100%** | 1288ms | The old hybrid’s file leg only saw write-through projections; the PG lexical leg sees every canonical row. **Read the p50 honestly**: hybrid-pg is the *slowest* of the three (+21% over hybrid), not the fastest — it buys \~78% more recall for that. An earlier draft of this page cited 83% recall and “p50 816ms (fastest)”; those were **pre-fix** numbers measured while `LEXICAL_MAX_TOKENS` was still mangling long queries (see the cap trap below) — they are superseded, and the speed claim did not survive. ## The latency fix: an indexable pre-filter + concurrent legs (EI-10931) [Section titled “The latency fix: an indexable pre-filter + concurrent legs (EI-10931)”](#the-latency-fix-an-indexable-pre-filter--concurrent-legs-ei-10931) Two independent bugs made `hybrid-pg` slower than the backend it replaces (bench p50 1182ms vs 821ms). Both are fixed; both are worth knowing, because each is a trap that reads as a virtue. ### 1. The score expression WAS the filter — so no index could ever be used [Section titled “1. The score expression WAS the filter — so no index could ever be used”](#1-the-score-expression-was-the-filter--so-no-index-could-ever-be-used) Every ILIKE lived in the **SELECT list** (the field-weighted `CASE` score), and `lex_raw > 0` was applied in an **outer** query. The inner scan’s only predicate was `invalid_at IS NULL` — so Postgres read and **scored every row**, every search: 
```plaintext
Seq Scan on memory_canonical (actual time=1.368..774.428 rows=1287 loops=1)
Execution Time: 775.674 ms          -- 13,594 active rows, 12-token query
```
 This was *deliberate*, and the code said so: “each ILIKE is evaluated exactly once: the score expression IS the filter, so there is no separate OR pre-filter.” It saves re-evaluating a handful of ILIKEs on the few rows that match — at the cost of a **full scan on every single search, forever, growing with the store.** ⚠ **The trap for the next person: adding a `pg_trgm` GIN index alone does NOTHING here.** There is no predicate for it to serve. (An earlier version of this page recommended exactly that — it was wrong, and it would have been a day wasted staring at an index the planner never touches.) The index only works *together with* an indexable `WHERE`. The fix is both halves: `lexicalSearch` now also emits an **OR pre-filter** into the inner `WHERE` (`name/description/data ILIKE $t OR …` across the tokens), which is **logically identical** to `lex_raw > 0` — a row scores > 0 iff ≥1 token hits ≥1 field — so **recall cannot change by construction**; only the plan changes. Plus migration **594**: `pg_trgm` + GIN `gin_trgm_ops` indexes on the three payload expressions. Result — the plan flips to a `BitmapOr` over the trigram indexes: | query class | before | after | | ---------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------- | | **rare identifier** (this leg’s whole purpose) | 775ms | **1.2ms** | | broad common-token paraphrase | 776ms | \~630ms | Common tokens genuinely match \~9.5% of the store (1287 rows), and each survivor still re-ILIKEs a large `data` field — an index cannot shrink a candidate set that is really that big. That residue is what fix #2 hides. ⚠ **Still do NOT reach for a weighted `tsvector`.** It looks like the perfect fit (`setweight` A/B/D maps straight onto the 3/2/1 weights) — but `to_tsvector('english', …)` stems and drops stop-words, which **mangles identifiers** (`PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_TIMEOUT`, `WI-4522`, camelCase tool names). Exact-identifier recall is the entire reason this leg exists (MRR 1.00 vs cosine’s 0.87), so a tsvector migration would silently destroy its purpose while looking like a clean optimization. `gin_trgm_ops` accelerates `ILIKE '%x%'` with *identical* semantics — no stemming, no tokenization change, no recall risk. ### 2. The two legs ran SERIALLY [Section titled “2. The two legs ran SERIALLY”](#2-the-two-legs-ran-serially) `HybridBackend.search` did `await cosine` **then** `await lexical`. The legs are **independent** — two rankings of the same rows, neither’s input depending on the other’s output — so sequencing them put the lexical leg’s whole cost on the critical path: `total = cosine + lexical` instead of `max(cosine, lexical)`. That was free to ignore while the lexical leg was a local file scan (\~0ms). It became the **dominant** term the moment the leg became a PG query. The cosine leg is embed-bound (a network round-trip); the lexical leg is embed-free and DB-bound. Overlapping them hides the cheaper one entirely behind the one we cannot avoid. Floored-union mode (the default, and what `hybrid-pg` runs) now starts the lexical leg **before** awaiting cosine. ⚠ `cosine-gated` mode still short-circuits deliberately — an empty cosine set must skip the lexical work entirely — and a test pins that contract (*“cosine-gated early-return short-circuits the lexical leg entirely”*). The first cut of this fix broke it; the suite caught it. Guard: `hybrid-backend.test.ts` → *“floored-union runs BOTH legs concurrently”* asserts the lexical leg is **started before cosine resolves**. A refactor that innocently rewrites it back to `await; await;` would restore the regression with every other test still green. ## \~/.claude topic files are NOT load-bearing anymore [Section titled “\~/.claude topic files are NOT load-bearing anymore”](#claude-topic-files-are-not-load-bearing-anymore) * All pre-existing topic-file memories were imported into the canonical store (`claude-import-cli.ts`, P-004): 71 net-new of 1,806 active files — 1,630 were already write-through projections (`extra.link_id` = the canonical id), 26 were ghosts of canonical deletes (deliberately NOT resurrected), 79 exact dups. `archive/` was excluded (plan D-005 — evictions stay evicted; backup tar at `~/.papercusp/backups/p004-memory-import/`). * Idempotency: imported rows carry `payload.imported_from = 'claude-file:<basename>'`; re-runs no-op. * `MEMORY.md` is now a static **pointer stub** (P-008), and the `memory-compact.mjs` SessionStart generator that used to rebuild it is retired to `~/.claude/scripts/retired/` (P-009). Ambient recall is papercusp-owned: the MCP initialize prelude (`mcp-prelude.ts`), `coord:orient` memory folds, work-item claim injection, and the post-compaction re-prime. * ⚠ **The generator had already stopped running before we retired it** — its hook wiring was silently dropped by the 2026-07-12 managed-hooks migration, and *nothing alarmed*. `MEMORY.md` sat frozen for weeks while still advertising itself as “AUTO-GENERATED … regenerated at each session start” — a stale snapshot confidently presenting itself as current. It was found by accident. The missing **detector** (a liveness assertion on each declared hook’s last-fire) is the real defect and is filed as **EI-10907**; retiring the files only removed this one instance. ## Cutover / rollback [Section titled “Cutover / rollback”](#cutover--rollback) * The switch is the persisted `memory_backend` operator setting (`backend-selection.ts`, 15s SWR so all processes converge without restarts). `hybrid-pg` ↔ `hybrid` is runtime-reversible; the old `hybrid` stays registered as the rollback. * ⚠ A process running code WITHOUT the `hybrid-pg` registration throws `unknown memory backend` on every memory call if the setting is flipped early — deploy the code first, flip second. * Watchdogs: the live recall canary (`recall-canary.ts`, EI-10047) auto-reseeds its pair set on a backend flip, and its P-010 probe measures the LEXICAL leg separately every run — a blind leg (zero lexical retrieval while the fused product serves rows) alarms as `degraded` even when cosine carries recall. ## Traps this replaced (don’t re-learn them) [Section titled “Traps this replaced (don’t re-learn them)”](#traps-this-replaced-dont-re-learn-them) * **Never rank a lexical candidate pool by RECENCY and then score it.** The first cut of `lexicalSearch` pulled `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT max(topK*5, 50)` and did the field-weighted scoring in JS over the survivors. That truncates the pool *before* anything is scored, so the best lexical match is dropped without ever being scored whenever it loses a recency race to rows that merely share a common word. It cost lexical-gap MRR on the frozen bench (0.68 vs the file leg’s 0.75 — the paraphrase queries reach their answer only through a couple of generic words), and on a live store it silently breaks **exact-identifier recall**, which is the whole reason this leg exists: a rare identifier sitting in an old row never enters the candidate pool at all. A small bench corpus HIDES this — with 114 rows a cap of 50 still admits most of the corpus. The fix is structural: the per-token `CASE` weights are computed in SQL, `WHERE lex_raw > 0 ORDER BY lex_raw DESC LIMIT topK` — ranking over the whole matching set, each ILIKE evaluated once (the score expression *is* the filter). Guard: `canonical-lexical-search.integration.test.ts` → “ranks an OLD strong match above many NEWER weak ones” (60 newer common-word rows vs one old identifier row), which fails if a recency-ordered candidate cap is ever reintroduced. * **A cap is a SAFETY bound on pathological input — never a relevance knob.** `LEXICAL_MAX_TOKENS` was `12`, while real recall queries run \~20 tokens (gold-set v1: p50 10, **p95 24, max 28**). So the cap silently discarded \~40% of every long query — and it discarded the *tail*, which is where the discriminative terms live (a paraphrase query front-loads common words and reaches its answer through the rare ones at the end). Worse, the score was then normalized by the **truncated** token count, so a mangled query still looked confidently scored. Measured on the lexical leg alone (lexical-gap MRR): cap 12 → **0.432**, 16 → 0.428, 24 → 0.544, 32 → **0.546**, uncapped → 0.546 (the claude-file leg: 0.552). Fixed at 32 — comfortably above p95, still a real bound on a runaway input. **Why it hid for two whole diagnostic rounds:** *exact-identifier MRR is 1.000 at EVERY cap* — those queries are short, so they never hit it. Only the paraphrase class regressed, which made a **tokenizer** bug present as a *fusion/ranking* bug, and sent two plausible ranking “fixes” through the acceptance gate before the real cause was isolated. When one query class regresses and another is untouched, suspect the INPUT PATH the two classes don’t share (here: query length) before you re-litigate the scorer. Guard: `canonical-store.test.ts` → “does NOT truncate a real natural-language query” (a 28-token query must survive intact). * The bench’s isolated `bench_memory` schema used to hand-mirror production DDL and drifted TWICE in one day (missing `memory_vec_harrier`, then missing the temporal-lite columns) — every PG backend benched at literal zero (EI-10793). `ensureBenchSchema` now clones live tables (`LIKE harness_shared.* INCLUDING ALL`), and **drops + recreates at run START** — a killed run used to leave rows behind that contaminated the next run’s corpus (and two concurrently-launched runs cross-seeded the same schema, garbaging both; EI-10854). * Unscoped topic files used to surface under ANY scope via the claude-file backend’s visibility-first trick. The import maps them to the OWNER’S USER POOL because the live `memory:search` fan-out queries `[user.id, harness:*…]` — never `'local'`.

# Grading memory-recall-health: the system-side telemetry reads (runbook)

> Runbook for grading the memory-recall-health rubric: per-surface liveness, admission floors, injection budgets, and dedup-ledger identity — the canonical queries, the identity model, and the score-scale trap (RRF vs cosine).

The rubric-level runbook `memory-recall-health` points at via `methodRef`. This rubric grades the SYSTEM half of recall quality from its own telemetry; the agent half is `su-agent-behavior`’s `recall-utilization` (see its runbook). The deterministic teeth are in Vitest — this page is the LIVE read layer. ## Surface liveness (criterion: per-surface-telemetry-liveness) [Section titled “Surface liveness (criterion: per-surface-telemetry-liveness)”](#surface-liveness-criterion-per-surface-telemetry-liveness) 
```sql
SELECT surface, count(*) AS n,
       max(created_at) AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York' AS last_edt
FROM harness_shared.memory_recall_stats
WHERE created_at > now() - interval '8 hours'
GROUP BY surface ORDER BY n DESC;
```
 Columns are `hit_count` / `top_score` (NOT `hits`). Expected-active surfaces on a busy fleet: `search`, `initialize`, `claim`, `create`, `compact`, `brief` — plus `orient` and `turn-start` once those paths are healthy (both were the silent/broken ones found 2026-07-12). ⚠ Liveness by COUNT alone can mask a whole population getting nothing: 68 initialize recalls/8h looked healthy while every one belonged to a stateless client and zero reached a real agent — always cross-check the ledger’s identity kinds (below). ## The score-scale trap (criteria: admission-floor-integrity + the orient fold) [Section titled “The score-scale trap (criteria: admission-floor-integrity + the orient fold)”](#the-score-scale-trap-criteria-admission-floor-integrity--the-orient-fold) The hybrid backend returns **reciprocal-rank-fusion scores**: rank-1 on one leg ≈ `1/61 ≈ 0.0164`, on both legs ≈ `0.0328`. Pure-vector paths return cosine (≈0.5–0.9). A floor calibrated for one scale silently zeroes the other — the 2026-07-12 live incident: orient’s blanket 0.05 floor emptied every fold (`hits: [], filteredLowScore: 5`) while `search`’s p50 looked fine. When a surface’s `top_score` p50 sits near 0.016–0.033, that is the RRF signature, not “bad memories.” ## Dedup-ledger identity (criterion: dedup-ledger-integrity) [Section titled “Dedup-ledger identity (criterion: dedup-ledger-integrity)”](#dedup-ledger-identity-criterion-dedup-ledger-integrity) 
```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN session_id LIKE 's-%' THEN 'synthetic s-*'
            WHEN session_id LIKE 'su-%' THEN 'su ownerId'
            ELSE 'other' END AS id_kind,
       port, count(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions, count(*) AS rows
FROM harness_shared.memory_session_surfaced
WHERE surfaced_at > now() - interval '24 hours'
GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 2,1;
```
 The invariant: ONE identity per session across every port — the MCP URL’s `client=` (from `PAPERCUSP_SID`) == the hook owner == the coord ownerId. The `s-*` shape is the transport-id fallback for clients that supplied no `client=`; a port whose stamps are predominantly `s-*`/`other` while agent sessions run is the “identity drift — one end renamed” marker live (this exact query found initialize fully drifted on 2026-07-12; root cause: the psu MCP URL template lacked `&harness=`, fixed in `claude-integration.ts`). Epoch semantics: `bumpSessionEpoch` fires once per compaction via the recovery-brief endpoint; the re-prime stamps the NEW epoch under `port='compact'`. Same memory\_id under two ports in ONE epoch = the double-injection signature. ⚠ Forensics: read the ledger DURING a drill — superseded-epoch rows persist only until the 14-day age sweep (and were bump-deleted before 2026-07-12). ## Live end-to-end probe (the drill-2 protocol, replayable) [Section titled “Live end-to-end probe (the drill-2 protocol, replayable)”](#live-end-to-end-probe-the-drill-2-protocol-replayable) Plant two harness-scoped fixture memories (record ids), launch one visible subject on a plan that requires: (A) report fixture-fact-1 at session start stating the delivery source first; (B) `session:request-compaction` while holding the WI, with a focus that forbids carrying the values; (C) report fixture-fact-2 post-compaction, delivery source first. Grade delivery from the ledger (initialize/claim stamps pre-compaction; epoch+1 `compact` stamps after) and consumption from the completion record. Cleanup: `memory:forget` both ids (they leak into other agents’ folds while they exist), wind down the fleet. Full worked example: plan `recall-drill-2-injection-2026-07-12` + scorecards EI-10406/EI-10407.

# Memory write journal — no write is lost to an embedder outage

> The write-ahead journal under memory:remember/update: journaled failure envelopes, the auto-drain, provenance, and the transcript miner.

Memory writes are embed-synchronous: `memory:remember` / `memory:update` only land if the embedder answers. Before the write-ahead journal (`memory-write-journal-auto-recovery-2026-07-11`), an embedder outage — sidecar down, provider quota, a 300s timeout under load — returned `{ok:false}` and the content was **lost**, surviving only in the calling agent’s session transcript. This happened live on 2026-07-10: a `memory:remember` timed out while a bulk re-embed saturated the embed sidecar, and the fact vanished until a manual transcript-forensics pass dug it back out. ## How it works now [Section titled “How it works now”](#how-it-works-now) 1. **INSERT-first.** The tool INSERTs the write into `harness_shared.memory_write_journal` *before* the embed+store attempt. A plain relational INSERT has no embedder dependency, so loss is structurally impossible while Postgres is up. 2. **Honest envelope.** On failure the tool returns `{ok:false, reason, journaled:true, will_retry:true, journal_id}`. **Do NOT re-fire the write** — the fact is parked, not lost. (A blind retry is also unnecessary after a timeout whose write actually landed: the drain’s near-dup guard closes the journal row against the existing memory.) 3. **Auto-drain.** The 5-minute embed-backfill tick replays pending rows oldest-first once the backend probe passes: bounded batch (25/tick), linear backoff per row, 30-attempt cap. Rows past the cap park as `failed_permanent` and are surfaced in the UI — never silently dropped. 4. **Provenance.** Recovered memories carry `metadata.recovered_from` (`journal` or `transcript-miner`) plus the journal id — visible in `memory:list`/`memory:search` results, so an agent can tell a fact arrived late. 5. **User surfacing.** The Settings → Memory page shows a live “N memories pending embedding” badge, a “Memory recovered: N facts from HH:MM–HH:MM now searchable” banner after a drain, and a retries-exhausted notice (`userMemory.journalStatus` sync resolver; the drain fires the invalidate). ## Agent guidance [Section titled “Agent guidance”](#agent-guidance) * A `journaled:true` failure needs **no action** — continue your work; the fact becomes searchable within \~5 minutes of the embedder recovering. * `journaled` **absent** on a failure means the journal itself was unavailable (pre-migration DB, PG hiccup) — the old lossy behavior. Park the fact somewhere durable yourself (e.g. `facts:assert`, which is DB-backed and needs no embedder) and retry later. * Deliberate refusals (`similar_exists` dedup, `conflict`) are **not** journaled-for-retry: the tool closes the journal row so the drain can never land a write it refused. ## Losses that predate the journal [Section titled “Losses that predate the journal”](#losses-that-predate-the-journal) `memory:recover-from-transcripts` mines session transcripts for failed memory-write tool calls (escape-tolerant `"ok":false` detection; excludes writes the same session retried successfully). Dry-run by default; with `confirm:true` it parks candidates in the journal (`source: 'transcript-miner'`), and the standard drain re-stores them behind the same near-dup guard. ## Ops notes [Section titled “Ops notes”](#ops-notes) * Table: `harness_shared.memory_write_journal` (migration 567). * Tunables: `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_JOURNAL_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (30), `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_JOURNAL_DRAIN_BATCH` (25). * The drain logs `[memory-journal] drain: recovered=… deduped=… exhausted=…` on any non-empty pass. * Text updates journal too (`metadata.__journal_update_of`); the drain replays them as `backend.update`, never as a new add. Metadata-only patches are vec-safe and aren’t journaled.

# METR HCAST time-horizon bench — run it via taskhelper.py, not the private Inspect bridge

> The official inspect-metr-task-bridge (mtb) won't install (6 private METR PyPI deps). Drive the pre-built task images directly with the Task Standard's public taskhelper.py. Plus the human-time-baseline join and the two-arm horizon-lift framing.

The METR HCAST / time-horizon suite (`suite='metr-hcast'`, plan `benchmark-suite-metr-hcast-2026-06-17`) measures a **50%/80%-task-completion time horizon** — the human-expert task LENGTH at which an arm succeeds 50%/80% of the time — and reports the **pot-vs-single-opus horizon LIFT**. Integration lives under `packages/operator-core/lib/external-bench/metr-hcast-*` + the horizon math in `libs/generic/bench-metrics/src/horizon.ts`. ## The load-bearing gotcha: the official Inspect bridge won’t install [Section titled “The load-bearing gotcha: the official Inspect bridge won’t install”](#the-load-bearing-gotcha-the-official-inspect-bridge-wont-install) METR’s README says to run tasks via the **Inspect Task Bridge** (`inspect-metr-task-bridge`, the `mtb` package). **It cannot install on a public box** — its `pyproject` pins six METR-internal packages that are not on public PyPI: `metr-task-artifacts`, `metr-task-assets`, `metr-task-aux-vm-helpers`, `metr-task-legacy-verifier`, `metr-task-protected-scoring`, `metr-task-standard`. `pip install` dies on `metr-task-artifacts`. (`inspect_ai` itself installs fine.) **Drive the task images directly with the Task Standard’s own `drivers/taskhelper.py`** — the public, dependency-free script the bridge merely wraps (vendored in `~/.papercusp/bench-harnesses/metr/task-standard`). That is what `dockerTaskStandardOps` (metr-hcast-live.ts) does. ### The container recipe (validated end-to-end) [Section titled “The container recipe (validated end-to-end)”](#the-container-recipe-validated-end-to-end) Pre-built images: `registry-1.docker.io/metrevals/public-tasks:<family>-<version>` (\~4 GB, anonymous Docker Hub pull). They ship the `TaskFamily` at `/root/<family>.py` + the unprivileged `agent` user (uid 1000) but **NOT** `taskhelper.py` — copy it in. 
```bash
docker run -d --name c --entrypoint sh "$IMG" -c 'tail -f /dev/null'
docker cp task-standard/drivers/taskhelper.py c:/root/taskhelper.py
docker exec -w /root c python taskhelper.py <FAMILY> <TASK> start    # sets up + chowns /home/agent
docker exec -w /root c python taskhelper.py <FAMILY> <TASK> setup    # → {instructions, ...}
#   ...agent works inside as `agent` user, produces a submission string...
docker exec -w /root c python taskhelper.py <FAMILY> <TASK> score -s "<submission>"   # → float
docker rm -f c
```
 Output is the line `SEP_MUfKWkpuVDn9E` then a JSON result (`parseTaskhelperResult`). `score()` returns a float (binary tasks: `0.0`/`1.0`); `resolved = score >= threshold` (default `1.0`). ## The human-time baselines: join the open tasks to runs.jsonl [Section titled “The human-time baselines: join the open tasks to runs.jsonl”](#the-human-time-baselines-join-the-open-tasks-to-runsjsonl) The horizon fit needs a human-time baseline per task. The open `metr/public-tasks` repo ships **31 runnable tasks (10 families)** but the structured baselines live in `metr/eval-analysis-public/reports/time-horizon-1-*/data/raw/runs.jsonl` (field `human_minutes`, keyed by `task_id = <family>/<task>`). Joining the two yields only **18 horizon-eligible tasks** (16 `baseline` + 2 `estimate`), spanning \~2–95 min — the other 13 (clone\_game, complex\_payments, cowthello, crossword, several variants) are newer dangerous-capability families absent from METR’s released horizon dataset. The vendoring step writes `~/.papercusp/bench-results/metr-hcast/tasks.jsonl` with `horizonEligible`. ## The math + the honest framing (don’t skip) [Section titled “The math + the honest framing (don’t skip)”](#the-math--the-honest-framing-dont-skip) `fitHorizon` (bench-metrics) is a faithful port of METR’s reference (`eval-analysis-public/src/horizon`): **weighted logistic regression of success on `log2(human_minutes)`, horizon = `2^((logit(q) − intercept)/coef)`**, reg `1e-5`, hierarchical-bootstrap CIs. The golden test reproduces METR’s published Claude 3.7 Sonnet \~50–60 min horizon (we get p50 ≈ 63 min on their data). **The absolute horizon on \~18 short tasks is illustrative-only — NOT leaderboard-comparable** (METR’s real fit spans seconds→8 h over \~170 tasks). The **defensible headline is the LIFT**: treatment (pot, `papercusp`) vs baseline (single-opus, `baseline-a-ablation`) on the SAME tasks cancels much of the subset bias (plan D-002). `buildMetrHcastReport` emits three mandatory caveats — surface them. ## Running it (host-gated) [Section titled “Running it (host-gated)”](#running-it-host-gated) 
```bash
npx tsx packages/operator-core/lib/external-bench/_xbench_metr_hcast.ts \
  --task-set metr-hcast-horizon --arms baseline-a-ablation,papercusp \
  --samples 5 --account <quiet-acct> --concurrency 2 \
  --out ~/.papercusp/bench-results/metr-hcast/run.json
```
 **Gateway contention is the operational gotcha.** Each arm routes opus-4.8 through the gateway; under concurrent benches (tau2 / agentsnet / the fleet) the shared accounts **429 globally** — every account on both `:8788` and `:8799` returned the same synthetic `rate_limit_error`. `gatewayModelCall` retries transient 429s and supports `--account <id>` (the `x-papercusp-account` header) to pin a quiet account, but a clean multi-sample run still needs a genuinely quiet opus window. The 429→`infra-failed` fairness path (excluded from the fit, never a capability fail) is the same discipline as the rest of external-bench.

# Migrating a bespoke loop to a deterministic / hybrid blueprint

> The established pattern for deterministic-blueprints-migration — a learning loop becomes a program-mode blueprint whose steps are registered step-ops (deterministic capability ops + spawn-roles for agents), fired on a cadence by system:blueprint-run. Reuse the lib logic; don't rewrite.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) The blueprint **program-mode spine** (`spine.steps` + optional `spine.gate`) is the deterministic-step substrate. A “deterministic step” is **not a new engine** — it is a registered typed function (a `CoordOp`: `name` + `argsSchema`/`resultSchema` * `run(args, ctx)`) that the program runner executes as a checkpointed step. The coord-op registry is the step-op registry; coordination ops are one family, deterministic capability ops (wrapping lib logic) are another. (Plan: `deterministic-blueprints-migration-2026-06-13`, P-010/P-011.) Two program shapes, discriminated by the gate (no schema field): * **deterministic pipeline** — `steps`, **NO gate**. Runs every step then resolves `done`. The migrated learning loops (negative-space, neologism, fleet-ekg, …). * **decision program** — `steps` + `gate` (must have a fallback). vote / deliberate. ## How to migrate a loop (the recipe) [Section titled “How to migrate a loop (the recipe)”](#how-to-migrate-a-loop-the-recipe) 1. **Reuse the lib logic — don’t rewrite (D-003).** Extract the loop’s flag → governor → tick orchestration into a shared `run<Loop>Mine`-style fn (one source of truth) with **injectable deps as parameters**. Example: `packages/operator-core/lib/negative-space/mine.ts` (`runNegativeSpaceMine`). The existing `system:<loop>` action then delegates to it (keeps its test seams), and so does the new op — provably behavior-neutral (D-004). 2. **Write the deterministic step-op** under `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint-steps/ops/<loop>.ts`: a `CoordOp` named `<domain>:<verb>` (e.g. `negative-space:scan`), declared `argsSchema`/`resultSchema` (the typed I/O — P-140), a module-level test-deps setter (`setXScanDeps`), and `run(args, ctx)` that calls the shared orchestration using `ctx.workspaceId` / `ctx.harnessSlug`. `registerCoordOp(op)` at the bottom, and `import './ops/<loop>.js'` in `blueprint-steps/index.ts`. The op carries the flag + governor gating (P-012) — so **dark stays dark**. 3. **Write the blueprint** at `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/<loop>/blueprint.yaml`: `extends: base`, a `workItem`, a program spine with the step(s) and `triggers.schedule` (the loop’s existing cron). Pure-deterministic ⇒ **no gate**. Args interpolate `{{ payload.* }}` (an unset whole-string placeholder → `undefined` → the op’s optional arg defaults). 4. **Point the seed routine at the blueprint**: `target: 'system:blueprint-run'`, `payload_template: { blueprintId: '<loop>' }`. Keep the governor-loop registration. `system:blueprint-run` detects program-mode (`isProgramSpine`) and runs the program **inline as its durable step** via `runProgramCore` + `inlineRunOp` (behavior-neutral: the bespoke loops also ran inline in their step). 5. **Hybrid loops** (det → agent → det, e.g. regret / transfer / prompt-ablation / iq-battery): the agent leg stays **INTERNAL to the op** (Option A), NOT an `orchestrator:spawn-roles` step. Two reasons (D-009 / D-013): (a) those loops’ “agents” are governed `llmCall`s (regret/transfer/ablation) or fleet cups that already route through `spawnAgentInHarness → cup:spawn → spawnInvokeOnce` — **the one governed chokepoint** — so there is NO ungoverned second spawn path to “close”; (b) `spawn-roles` is for **role fan-out** (vote’s per-lens voters): its agents take a harness *role/persona*. A loop whose agent takes a *brief* (a corpus case, a transcript continuation) doesn’t fit that contract — keep the spawn inside the op. So “deterministic step” = deterministic *top level* (the gate logic), with internal governed spawns, NOT “no spawns.” iq-battery is the worked hybrid: `iq-battery:gen` op wraps `runIqBatteryGen` (cadence-tick + the gen-0 cup runner). ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * **Before migrating, check it isn’t ALREADY a blueprint role.** The worker chunk loop (`worker-chunk-loop.ts`) looked like a bespoke loop to migrate, but it IS the coding blueprint’s `worker` role body — already blueprint-integrated, running in the `invoke-once` subprocess with the subprocess’s `InvokeContext`. “Migrating” it is a cross-process durability RE-ARCHITECTURE (the op runs in the operator’s program workflow, a different context), not a gap. Don’t re-migrate the already-integrated. * **No top-level throwing computation in a wrapped lib** (the same class as the `__dirname` deploy incident). `change-ledger/scan-loop.ts` did `const x = promisify(execFile)` at module scope; a test that partially mocks `node:child_process` (only `spawn`) made `execFile` undefined → `promisify(undefined)` threw AT IMPORT, poisoning every test whose graph includes the module. Promisify / resolve lazily INSIDE the function. * **Workspace-singleton cadence: there is now a first-class trigger for it (D-018).** A migrated loop is a workspace SINGLETON (one routine per workspace), but the default `materializeBlueprintTriggers` mints one routine PER INSTALL (keyed `(install_slug, name)`) seeded ACTIVE — so naively declaring `triggers.schedule` would N-duplicate into N ACTIVE pulses (the D-010/D-012(b) objection that kept the bespoke SEED scripts as the live materializer). A schedule entry can now declare **`singleton: true`**: materialize upserts EXACTLY ONE routine per workspace, seeded INACTIVE/dark, under the reserved synthetic host-slug `SINGLETON_TRIGGER_HOST_SLUG` (`@singleton`), named `bp-singleton-<blueprintId>-<i>` (blueprint-unique under the shared slug). This is the CAPABILITY only (`packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/materialize-triggers.ts`); rewiring the \~13 loops onto it — retiring each bespoke seed + folding its `registerLearningLoop` governor registration — is the per-loop follow-on (D-018 step 2, reverses D-012(b) one loop at a time under the arming gates), NOT the capability. Until a loop is rewired, its bespoke seed stays the live materializer. * **The live `@singleton` cutover RACES the seed-based arming workflow — sequence it, don’t race it (D-023).** The cutover (`seed-learning-singletons.ts`: materialize the `@singleton` row + delete the legacy `papercup` row) is incompatible-while-concurrent with how loops get ARMED: an arming agent re-runs `seed-<loop>-routine.ts --active`, which RE-CREATES the `papercup` row ACTIVE. Run the cutover during a live frontier-arming campaign and you get a double-state (a dark `@singleton` row beside a re-armed `papercup` row → latent double-fire); this actually happened (calibration/deferral/neologism) and had to be reverted (all rows restored to `papercup`). **Correct sequence: (1) let arming settle; (2) RETIRE the bespoke seeds FIRST so arming can only target the `@singleton` row; (3) then run the cutover.** **DONE (D-026):** the full cutover of all 13 loops then completed cleanly by following exactly this sequence — seeds deleted first → no re-creation path → no collision. 5 dark loops via the dark CLI, 8 active loops via `--active-cutover` (the byte-identical copy: active+payload+timing preserved). NEW ARMING PATH (seeds gone): `UPDATE harness_shared.routines SET active=true WHERE install_slug='@singleton' AND name='bp-singleton-<loop>-0'`; re-materialize is active-preserving. * **Two hardenings the collision forced, now in the capability (D-024):** (a) singleton materialize is RE-RUN-SAFE — `upsertSingletonRoutine` seeds dark + `concurrency:'skip'` on first creation, but on conflict PRESERVES `active`/`next_fire_at`/`concurrency` and MERGES the payload (ensure `blueprintId`, keep owner tuning). The generic `upsertRoutine` overwrites those, so a naive re-materialize would DARKEN an armed loop + DROP tuning — never use it for singletons. (b) the cutover CLI is COLLISION-SAFE — it SKIPS any loop whose `papercup` row is ACTIVE (`skipped:'legacy-active'`) instead of minting a dark duplicate; an active loop needs the owner-watched ATOMIC active cutover (copy active+payload+timing → `@singleton`, delete `papercup`, one transaction), not the dark CLI. * **worker-chunk-loop → operator-hosted op (P-142/D-017, Option A) is NOT a thin op-wrap — it needs a NEW operator-side worker-spawn primitive.** `runChunkLoopCore` is cleanly extracted (stage a) and takes injected `ChunkLoopDeps`, so an op CALLING it is easy. The hard part is the deps: `planChunks` needs the worker’s RAW LLM output, `implementChunk` needs a worker run against a SCRATCH dir reporting its TOUCHED files, and the loop commits per chunk. The existing `ctx.caps.spawnRoles` (the `orchestrator:spawn-roles` op) is a CONVERSATION fan-out — it spawns role agents that post into a thread and exit; it has no cwd/scratch, no raw-output capture, no touched-files report. So an operator-hosted `worker:chunk-loop` op must build a new “run a worker against a scratch checkout, capture output + touched files” spawn primitive (plus repo checkout operator-side). That is the operator↔subprocess topology re-architecture D-015 flags as the coding HOT PATH — staged * owner-watched + monitored over weeks (dark-launch → 25→50→100% ramp → retire), NOT an overnight cutover. Don’t write a mock-only op shell and call P-142 “built”: its substance IS the spawn primitive. * `validateBlueprint` is called WITHOUT `knownOps` at every current call site, so a program op that doesn’t exist is caught at RUN time (`requireCoordOp` throws), not load time. Register your op (import the family index) wherever the program runs. * A deterministic op must **fail loud** on a missing `ctx.workspaceId` (a misconfigured fire), not silently mine the wrong scope. * `runProgramCore` maps a gateless completed run (`no-gate-match` from the generic runner) to a clean `done` — don’t reintroduce a gate just to terminate. * **Gating varies per loop** — replicate the ACTUAL gate: most are flag + learning- governor; change-ledger is flag-only (pure bookkeeping); scout is structural (cadence/fire-gate/claim/budget, no flag); iq-battery is owner-budget (refuse if no `budgetUsd`). Read the action; don’t assume flag+governor. * **A `system:blueprint-run` fire spawns into the FIRING install by default — override via a `launchInstallSlug`-family payload key when the routine must launch work into a DIFFERENT named install/pot than the one whose routine fired.** `handleBlueprintRun` builds its durable-spawn `installSlug` (and the idempotency key) from `ctx.installSlug` unless the routine’s `payload_template` sets one of `launchInstallSlug` / `hiveSlug` / `hiveInstallSlug` / `targetInstallSlug` (checked in that order; first non-blank string wins) — the DBOS no-first-step routineFire requeue guard surfaced this when a routine requeued after a reaper-cancelled fire and the replay needed to keep targeting the same install, not wherever it happened to be re-picked-up. Set the override key in the blueprint’s seeded `payload_template` for any cross-install program-mode blueprint; omit it and the fire targets its own firing install (the common case). * **Editing the seed `.ts` does NOT repoint the LIVE routine row — you MUST re-run the seed (step 4 is a runtime act, not just a source edit).** Changing `target` / `payload_template` in the seed script only affects FUTURE upserts. An already-seeded `harness_shared.routines` row — *especially one an owner ACTIVATED before the migration deployed* — still has `target_role = 'system:<loop>'` (now retired, no registered handler) and the old payload shape, so when it fires it hits a dead target and silently no-ops. After the migration lands, **re-run each loop’s seed against the live workspace DB** (`PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID=<ws> tsx lib/.../seed-<loop>-routine.ts [--active]`); the upsert’s `ON CONFLICT` repoints target + payload (and the well- written seeds preserve owner payload keys — change-ledger keeps `sinceDays`, iq-battery keeps `budgetUsd`). This bit **`iq-battery-gen`, `scout-cycle`, `change-ledger-scan`** — all active, all firing at a retired target (Scout + change-ledger loops were dead) until re-seeded 2026-06-13. **Corollary — the INACTIVE migrated rows are latent traps:** flipping `active=true` in the routines admin WITHOUT re-seeding fires the retired target. Arm a migrated loop by **re-running its seed with `--active`**, never by an admin active-flip alone. (Quick audit: `SELECT name,target_role,active FROM harness_shared.routines WHERE target_role <> 'system:blueprint-run'` — every row whose target isn’t a still-registered action is suspect.) ## Files (pilot A — negative-space, the reference) [Section titled “Files (pilot A — negative-space, the reference)”](#files-pilot-a--negative-space-the-reference) * Schema/validator: `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/blueprint/validate.ts` (gate optional) * Runner: `packages/operator-core/lib/coord-ops/program-runner.ts` (gateless → done) * Scheduled fire: `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint/blueprint-run-action.ts` (`runScheduledProgram`) * Op family: `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint-steps/` * Shared orchestration: `packages/operator-core/lib/negative-space/mine.ts` * Blueprint: `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/negative-space/blueprint.yaml` * Tests: `packages/operator-core/lib/blueprint-steps/negative-space-blueprint.test.ts`

# Migration-number collisions: use the reservation tool; the lint's FS checks are now gated

> Two agents racing `ls | tail` pick the same NNN-*.sql number. db:next-migration prevents this — an MCP agent-tool (also available as `npm run db:next-migration` since 2026-06-20) now open to ALL built-in roles, and (2026-07-03) with its fsMax read moved inside the advisory lock to close a TOCTOU race (EI-6852). lint:migrations catches dups + raw BEGIN/COMMIT + unreserved numbers; since 2026-07-04 (EI-6843) its two PG-free checks are gated — lint-migrations.test.ts runs them against the real sql/ dir on every test:affected / green-checkpoint run, after re-baselining ENFORCED_FROM 215→494 to grandfather already-applied ledgered history. Only the PG-backed reservation check still needs a manual run. Plus a two-dirs footgun: the canonical libs dir vs the gitignored sidecar mirror.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) When several agents add SQL migrations concurrently they collide on the leading `NNN`. While implementing PR-4 (WI↔PR producer, `2026-06-20`) I wrote `319-pr4-feature-pr-producer-identity.sql` and found a peer had **already** taken `319` (`319-pr-review-reports.sql`) and another had taken `320` (`320-autovacuum-high-churn-telemetry.sql`). My file had to be re-numbered to `321`, allocated through the reservation ledger to avoid a third collision. ### What a dup number actually breaks today (verify before you assume “silent dark”) [Section titled “What a dup number actually breaks today (verify before you assume “silent dark”)”](#what-a-dup-number-actually-breaks-today-verify-before-you-assume-silent-dark) `next_migration.ts`’s docstring warns “only one of the colliding files applies, so a table goes silently dark.” That is **not** how the current boot runner behaves: `applyPendingMigrations` (`libs/papercusp/packages/embedded-postgres-server/src/ migration-runner.js`) keys `harness_shared.schema_migrations` by **filename**, so `319-foo.sql` and `319-bar.sql` are distinct keys and **both apply** (in lexicographic filename order). The desktop sidecar path applies the same way (its serve boot runs the same runner over the `db-sql` mirror). So the cited single-apply/silent-dark is path/history-specific, not a property of today’s runner — don’t propagate it as a current fact. The **real**, verifiable damage from a dup number today: * **`lint:migrations` goes red** (its `duplicateNumberGroups` check). Since `2026-07-04` that check IS gated for enforced-era numbers (see gap #3’s resolution below): a new dup ≥494 fails `test:affected` / the green gate immediately; pre-494 historical dups are grandfathered (the runner keys by full filename, so they never collided at runtime). * **Coordination confusion** — two unrelated features both claim “319”; tooling and humans that key on the number get the wrong file. * **Possible loss at git-merge time** — when the two authors’ divergent branches reconcile, a careless merge can drop one of the same-numbered files (a VCS hazard, not a runner one). The fix layers are therefore **prevention at creation** (the reservation tool/CLI) + **detection at PR** (the existing lint dup-check) — NOT a change to boot-apply semantics. ## Why it keeps happening (three compounding gaps) [Section titled “Why it keeps happening (three compounding gaps)”](#why-it-keeps-happening-three-compounding-gaps) 1. **`db:next-migration` is the safe path, but was MCP-only until 2026-06-20.** The atomic allocator (advisory lock + `harness_shared.migration_reservations`, GREATEST(max-on-disk across the serving + staging trees, max-reserved, max-applied)+1) lives in `next_migration.ts` as a `defineTool` agent-tool. ~~There is **no `npm run db:next-migration`** script.~~ **Fixed (2026-06-20)** — see the “How to allocate a number now” section and item #1 in the Recommended fix section. An agent (or human) who isn’t wired into the harness MCP still does `ls | tail` and hand-picks — exactly the racing path the tool was built to replace. The lint error even says “use db:next-migration”, naming a command that (before the fix) didn’t exist as a script. **Role access (2026-06-25):** `db:next-migration` previously used `agentRoles: [...SU_ROLES, 'cup']` — only superuser-role agents and the generic cup could call it. Changed to `agentRoles: [...AGENT_ROLES]`: every built-in role (worker, validator, reviewer, architect, etc.) can now call the MCP tool directly and participate in collision-free allocation without falling back to the npm CLI. **fsMax TOCTOU race fixed (2026-07-03, EI-6852):** even after the advisory lock landed, both allocators read the filesystem max (`maxNumberOnDisk`) **before** entering `sql.begin(...)` — i.e. before acquiring `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. That left a window (a pooled-connection-acquire plus the lock-wait, which can run seconds under a busy fleet) during which a concurrent caller could write a higher-numbered `NNN-*.sql` to disk; the stale `fsMax` then failed to fold it in and the tool could hand out an already-used number. Both `next_migration.ts` (the MCP tool) and `scripts/next-migration.mjs` (the CLI) now compute `fsMax` **inside** the `sql.begin` callback, immediately before the `GREATEST(...)` read and the reservation insert, so all three GREATEST inputs (on-disk, reserved, applied) are read atomically under the same lock. `next_migration.ts` also now `export`s `ALLOC_ADVISORY_KEY` so the regression test (`next_migration.integration.test.ts`, case “EI-6852: the filesystem max is read INSIDE the advisory lock”) can hold the lock itself to reproduce the race. This closes the last remaining collision window in the “supported path” — the collisions this doc otherwise documents are all from agents who bypassed `db:next-migration`/the CLI entirely. 2. ~~**The MCP client is currently dropped.**~~ **Historical note (2026-06-20):** At the time of discovery the harness MCP client was dropped, so even MCP-aware agents couldn’t reach `db:next-migration` and fell back to hand-picking. The npm CLI (`npm run db:next-migration`) was added precisely to fix this (gap #1 fix). The MCP client drop is a session-specific transient; the systematic fix is the CLI + the per-role access expansion (see gap #1 update above). 3. **`lint:migrations` was not gated** (RESOLVED for the PG-free checks, `2026-07-04` — see below). `scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` already detects (a) duplicate `NNN`, (b) raw top-level `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;` (which would end the runner’s per-file wrapper txn early), and (c) numbers ≥`ENFORCED_FROM` absent from the reservation ledger. But it was **only an npm script** — referenced in neither `.github/` (CI) nor `.husky/` / `.git/hooks` — so the guard never ran automatically; the dup-number check (which is PG-free and runs fine in CI) never fired on a PR. As of `2026-06-20`, `node scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` exited **1**: 7 files carried raw `BEGIN/COMMIT` (`299, 300, 306, 307, 308, 312, 317`) and \~10 numbers ≥215 were unreserved (`293, 294, 298, 301, 303–307, 319, 320`). **Re-verified `2026-07-03` — the guard is still ungated and the violation count has grown, not shrunk** (confirming gap #3 is still open): `node scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` still exits **1**, now with **3 duplicate-number groups** (`357`, `375`, `460` — each has two distinct files sharing the same leading `NNN`, exactly the collision this doc is about), **34 files** carrying raw top-level `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;`, and **64 numbers ≥215** on disk with no reservation-ledger row. The tree has been shipping with the linter red for weeks with nothing catching it at PR time — direct evidence that gap #3 (below) remains unaddressed. **Resolved for the PG-free checks (`2026-07-04`, EI-6843):** the duplicate-`NNN` and raw-tx-control scans now run against the REAL `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/` directory inside `packages/operator-core/lib/lint-migrations.test.ts` (the “real … sql/ directory (gate wiring)” describe block), which `npm run test:affected` — and therefore the green-checkpoint gate — runs on every candidate. Because the tree was red (worse than at discovery), enforcement was re-baselined FIRST: `ENFORCED_FROM` moved 215→494, grandfathering the already-applied, ledgered history (editing/renaming an applied file would break its recorded checksum), and `duplicateNumberGroups` now takes an `enforcedFrom` boundary so historical same-number pairs don’t red the gate. A FUTURE violation (≥494) fails the suite immediately. The PG-backed reservation check (c) remains CLI-only — as of `2026-07-05` `node scripts/lint-migrations.mjs` still exits 1 with one live violation (migration `510` on disk with no reservation row), so “clean first, gate second” still applies to that check. ## The two-dirs footgun (bonus) [Section titled “The two-dirs footgun (bonus)”](#the-two-dirs-footgun-bonus) There are **two** migration directories and they are NOT the same role: * **`libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/`** — CANONICAL. The operator auto-applies these on boot (`migration-drift.ts` `resolveSqlDir()`), and `db:next-migration` scans this dir for the on-disk max. **Write new migrations here.** * **`papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/sidecar/db-sql/`** — a build-time MIRROR, and it is **gitignored inside the `papercusp-desktop` submodule** (`git check-ignore` confirms). A file written only here is never committed and never applied. Both are submodules (`libs/papercusp`, `papercusp-desktop`). I initially wrote my migration into the sidecar mirror — it silently did nothing useful. Identical copies of `314–318` in both dirs make the mirror look authoritative; it isn’t. ## How to allocate a number now (the supported path) [Section titled “How to allocate a number now (the supported path)”](#how-to-allocate-a-number-now-the-supported-path) Use the CLI (added `2026-06-20` — works even with the MCP client down): 
```bash
npm run db:next-migration -- --name add-foo-index --intent "what it does"
# → reserves the next free NNN in harness_shared.migration_reservations and prints
#   a DRAFT write-target: libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/<NNN>-add-foo-index.sql.DRAFT
#   (+ arm_path / arm_command — see below)
# Add --dry-run to see the number without reserving it.
```
 It scans BOTH dirs for the on-disk max **inside** the advisory lock (the `2026-07-03` EI-6852 fix — see above), allocates, and records the reservation — the same contract as the MCP `db:next-migration` tool. Then **write + iterate at the printed `.DRAFT` path**, not the bare `.sql` name (`2026-08-02`, EI-19366138707071397): the migration runner only ever applies files matching `*.sql` (`migration-runner.js`’s `.filter(f => f.endsWith('.sql'))` — the same mechanism the pre-existing `NNN-*.sql.PENDING-CODE-DEPLOY` idiom relies on), so a `.DRAFT`-suffixed file is invisible to boot auto-apply, `db:migrate`, and the green-checkpoint preflight while it’s mid-edit — including a deliberate temporary both-ways guard-test mutation (the “prove a guard you haven’t seen fail” house rule), which previously could race a concurrent operator restart and execute half-finished SQL against the live DB (the migration-729/WI-7057 near-miss that prompted this). Once it’s finished and tested, **arm it** with the tool’s printed `arm_command` (`mv <path>.DRAFT <path>`) to land it at `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/<NNN>-<slug>.sql` (NOT the sidecar mirror) — only then does it auto-apply on the next operator restart. It refuses to hand out a number when PG is unreachable (an unreserved number re-opens the race). ## Recommended fix (plan) [Section titled “Recommended fix (plan)”](#recommended-fix-plan) Small, mostly additive; each item is independent: 1. ~~**Add `npm run db:next-migration`.**~~ **DONE (`2026-06-20`)** — `scripts/next-migration.mjs` + the `db:next-migration` npm script. Reservation now works without the MCP client (the highest-leverage gap — it kills the `ls | tail` path at the source). Mirrors the MCP tool via the shared ledger + advisory key. ~~A follow-up could DRY the two onto one exported core~~ — see item 4 below (still open). **Also DONE (`2026-07-03`, EI-6852):** both allocators now read the on-disk max **inside** the advisory-lock transaction instead of before it, closing the TOCTOU window described above. 2. ~~**Gate `lint:migrations`**~~ **DONE for the PG-free checks (`2026-07-04`, EI-6843)** — not via `.github/`/`.husky` but via the vitest suite: `packages/operator-core/lib/lint-migrations.test.ts` scans the real sql/ dir for duplicate numbers + raw tx-control on every `test:affected` / green-checkpoint run. The required “clean first” sequencing was honored by RE-BASELINING instead of editing history: `ENFORCED_FROM` 215→494 grandfathers the applied, ledgered legacy (immutable — recorded checksums), so the gate starts green and only a genuinely NEW violation reds it. Still open: the PG-backed unreserved-number check is not in the gate (needs a live PG; exercised only by the CLI) — backfill the missing reservation rows (e.g. `510` as of `2026-07-05`) before gating it. (Do NOT instead change the boot runner to abort on dup numbers: it currently applies both colliding files by filename, and altering boot-apply semantics — especially the `continueOnError` fleet path — is far riskier than catching the dup at PR time.) 3. **Mark the sidecar mirror.** Since the mirror dir is itself gitignored, a `README` placed in it wouldn’t be tracked — put the “this is a gitignored build mirror; author migrations in the canonical libs dir” note where it’s visible: the canonical dir’s own README, or `migration-drift.ts` (which already owns `resolveSqlDir`). 4. **DRY the allocator** (low priority). Export the allocation core from `next_migration.ts` and have both the MCP tool and `scripts/next-migration.mjs` call it, instead of the two mirroring the ledger contract independently. The `2026-07-03` EI-6852 fix had to be hand-applied to **both** files in lockstep (see above) precisely because they’re still two independent implementations of the same contract — live evidence for why this item matters, not just a hypothetical. Sequencing mattered for the gating item (#2) and was honored via the `2026-07-04` re-baseline; the same rule — clean first, gate second — applies to any future gating of the reservation check.

# Manually-applied migrations must be re-run-safe — guard DDL or the auto-deploy dies on lock timeouts

> The deploy pipeline re-applies every pending sql/<NNN> file on the live DB. A migration already applied by hand on the dev box re-runs at deploy time — and bare ALTER TABLE/CREATE POLICY/GRANT statements take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks that can hit the runner's lock_timeout and roll back the whole deploy. Wrap RLS/policy/grant DDL in existence-guarded DO blocks so a re-run takes zero locks.

## What happened (live, 2026-06-09) [Section titled “What happened (live, 2026-06-09)”](#what-happened-live-2026-06-09) Migration `208-scout-ticks-and-lens-weights.sql` was applied **manually** to the dev box’s native PG (the documented dev chore — native `:5432` has no auto-runner). The auto-deploy pipeline then tried to apply the same file on the live DB at 20:00/20:30/20:45 and **all three deploys failed with `canceling statement due to lock timeout` and auto-rolled back**, stranding the live operator \~5 hours behind staging. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` no-ops cheaply — but the rest of a conventional migration does NOT: * `ALTER TABLE … ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, **every run** * `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS … ; CREATE POLICY …` — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, every run * `GRANT …` — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, every run On a table that’s already live (because the manual apply created it and resolvers/routines are already reading it), any concurrent reader queues those locks past the runner’s `lock_timeout` → the migrate step dies → rollback. ## The rule [Section titled “The rule”](#the-rule) A migration that can ever be **re-applied on a DB where it already ran** (which is every migration on this project, because of the manual-dev-apply + deploy-re-apply pattern) must make its lock-taking statements conditional: 
```sql
DO $$ BEGIN
  IF NOT (SELECT relrowsecurity FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'harness_shared.t'::regclass) THEN
    ALTER TABLE harness_shared.t ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
  END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_policies WHERE schemaname='harness_shared'
                  AND tablename='t' AND policyname='t_workspace_isolation') THEN
    CREATE POLICY t_workspace_isolation ON harness_shared.t USING (…) WITH CHECK (…);
  END IF;
  IF NOT has_table_privilege('harness_app', 'harness_shared.t', 'INSERT') THEN
    GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON harness_shared.t TO harness_app;
  END IF;
END $$;
```
 Guarded = the re-run takes **zero** table locks; the fresh-migrate path (embedded-pg, the `fresh-migrate.integration.test.ts` gate) executes the statements normally. See `208-scout-ticks-and-lens-weights.sql` for the worked fix, and mirror it instead of the older bare-DDL pattern in `202-*.sql`. ## How to recognize it [Section titled “How to recognize it”](#how-to-recognize-it) * `/tmp/papercup-auto-deploy.log` shows `migrate: apply <NNN>-…` then `✖ deploy failed: canceling statement due to lock timeout` then a rollback. * `papercup-release` checkout SHA stops advancing while `origin/main` moves. * The live operator stays healthy (rollback works) — the failure is silent unless you look at the deploy log, so a stalled release SHA is the tell.

# Mobile apps (Android + iOS) — how the monitoring-first phone app works

> The papercup-rust-mobile app, its device API, push, build, and the gotchas that make "why is my phone silent" diagnosable. From mobile-apps-revival-v2-2026-07-13.

The phone app is a **monitoring interface, not a work surface**. The desktop is where the owner works; the phone shows what the fleet is doing and what needs the owner, with **no execute/approve/claim affordances**. Keep that principle when extending it — add read-only tiles and attention producers, not action buttons. ## Where the code lives [Section titled “Where the code lives”](#where-the-code-lives) * **App:** `papercup-rust-mobile/` — a **separate git repo** on branch `master`, **NOT** covered by the papercup git-sync auto-commit. Edits there need a **manual commit**, and the papercup Edit-tool worktree guard refuses it (it can’t tell a separate repo from a stray worktree) — edit via `sed`/`bash` and commit by hand. Rust core (`crates/papercup-core`) + UniFFI bindings, Jetpack Compose (Android), SwiftUI (iOS). * **Server (device API):** `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/device/*` — `defineTool` routes gated by `DEVICE_AUTH` (`{ kind: ['device'] }`). The phone reaches them at `https://api.papercuspai.com/api/device/*`. * **Device auth:** `lib/device-jwt.ts` (HS256, `MOBILE_JWT_SECRET`), `lib/device-store.ts` (paired devices + push tokens), `lib/device-push-dispatcher.ts` (FCM + APNs send). * **Monitoring producers:** `lib/device-monitoring.ts` (fail-soft, dependency-injected). ## The gotchas that cost hours [Section titled “The gotchas that cost hours”](#the-gotchas-that-cost-hours) 1. **The public URL tunnel is Cloudflare-DASHBOARD-managed.** `api.papercuspai.com` is served by `cloudflared` (tunnel `c53515b3`, user unit `cloudflared-papercupai-api.service`) whose ingress config lives in the Cloudflare **dashboard**, not the local `~/.cloudflared/papercupai-api.yml` — editing that local file does **nothing** (and SIGHUP-ing cloudflared after a bad local edit can kill the tunnel → both domains 530). If the public API is down, check the systemd unit is `active` first; don’t touch the local yml. ⚠ **This dev box’s resolver LIES about `papercuspai.com` — never probe prod reachability with a from-box `curl` (2026-07-16, EI-12998).** The machine is on Tailscale; its resolver (`Current DNS 100.100.100.100`, search `*.ts.net`) returns a **stale split-DNS override** for `papercuspai.com` → `18.204.152.241` (a dead old AWS EC2) with a **max-uint TTL (4294967295)** — the signature of a static override. So every `curl https://api.papercuspai.com/...` from this box hits the dead IP and looks like a total prod outage when prod is fine. Two agents burned hours “fixing” a non-existent DNS outage this way. **Verify prod from an EXTERNAL vantage instead:** DNS via DoH (`curl https://dns.google/resolve?name=api.papercuspai.com&type=A` → Cloudflare-proxy IPs when healthy), HTTP via an external fetcher (`curl https://r.jina.ai/https://api.papercuspai.com/api/device/attention` → `200` with the operator’s `{"error":{"code":"unauthorized",...}}` device-auth JSON when healthy). A real phone is not on this tailnet and reaches prod normally. 2. **`/api/health` 404 on the public domain is a red herring** — it routes to a different internal port (`:3057`), not `:3070`. The phone never calls it. Test reachability with a real device route (`/api/device/attention` with a device JWT). 3. **`MOBILE_JWT_SECRET` durability = device-token durability.** Device JWTs are HS256-signed with it; if it’s unset in dev, `getSecret()` mints a **per-process** secret that rotates on every restart → all paired phones silently stop working until they re-pair. It’s set durably in `apps/operator/.env.local` (gitignored, survives deploys, identical in the release + staging trees). `mobileJwtSecretStatus()` reports durability; a one-time boot/first-use warning fires when it’s ephemeral. 4. **Two-port model applies.** Device routes run on the GREEN operator (`:3070`, release checkout). A server-side device-route edit reaches `:3070` only via the deploy pipeline (or a forced `deploy-cli --execute`); `:3170` is staging. Probe where your write actually lands. ## Push (the owner’s remote control) [Section titled “Push (the owner’s remote control)”](#push-the-owners-remote-control) Both providers **mint their auth token in-process** (the old design expected a pre-signed env token refreshed by a job that never existed, so pushes silently no-op’d): * **FCM (Android, LIVE):** `google-auth-library` JWT client signs a service-account JWT from `FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PATH` (default `~/.papercusp/firebase-admin.json`, project `papercusp-mobile`) → OAuth access token → HTTP v1 send. * **APNs (iOS, DORMANT):** `jose` signs an ES256 provider JWT from a `.p8` (`APNS_KEY_PATH`/`APNS_KEY_ID`/`APNS_TEAM_ID`), cached \~50 min, sent over **HTTP/2** (APNs rejects HTTP/1.1). **Blocked on Apple Developer enrollment** — absent creds ⇒ cleanly skipped, so iOS registration is harmless until enrolled. Unconfigured providers are skipped, never thrown — `dispatchPush` returns `PushSendResult[]`. `pushEnabled()` reports which providers are live. ## The monitoring surface (Phase B) [Section titled “The monitoring surface (Phase B)”](#the-monitoring-surface-phase-b) `lib/device-monitoring.ts` exposes fail-soft, dependency-injected producers reused across routes — a failed read returns a `null` tile, never a broken dashboard: * `releaseGateTile()` — reuses `fetchOrientPipeline` (cached). `stale-verdict` is **not** treated as red (load-bearing silence — don’t raise a phantom alarm). * `poolTile()` — `accountStatus` + `accountRoutingExhausted` (inference-pool health). * `fleetsAndPotsTile()` — `listPresence` + `fetchPresenceFleet`, grouped by fleet + pot. * `connectionTile()` — `deviceConnectionSnapshot` (paired? push registered? secret durable?). * `systemAlerts()` — PURE composer: red-gate + pool-exhaustion → owner-attention alerts. Routes: `GET /device/monitoring` (all tiles), and `GET /device/attention` carries `systemAlerts` alongside its existing `groups` + `workItems`. Most owner-attention surfaces (fleet-leader escalations, open owner questions, needs-human) are **already** produced by `plans:attention` (which the device attention route reads) — only the system-health conditions (red-gate, pool-exhaustion) were missing. ## Building [Section titled “Building”](#building) Android: `cd papercup-rust-mobile && export ANDROID_NDK_HOME=$HOME/Android/Sdk/ndk/27.0.12077973 ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Android/Sdk && make tokens bindings-kotlin && tools/build-scripts/build-android.sh` (the last step does the 4-ABI cargo-ndk release cross-compile + `gradlew assembleDebug`; `make build-android` additionally runs `install-and-launch.sh`, which needs an adb device). APK → `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`. iOS: needs the Mac VM (`ssh -p 2222`, `~/.papercusp/build-vms.env`) + `make build-ios`. For automated microphone endurance tests, keep the Android emulator **windowed** even on an Xvfb display. Emulator 36.5.11 and 36.6.11 both exit 139 on the first gRPC `injectAudio` stream when launched with `-no-window`; the same AVD and audio payload remain online when launched with a display, `-grpc 8554`, `-allow-host-audio`, and `-gpu swiftshader_indirect`. Treat one pilot audio injection plus an `adb get-state` check as the rig preflight before a multi-turn soak, so a harness crash cannot masquerade as an app stability failure. ### The working rig (2026-07-16, verified 10/10 STT+TTS) [Section titled “The working rig (2026-07-16, verified 10/10 STT+TTS)”](#the-working-rig-2026-07-16-verified-1010-stttts) A reusable rig lives at `~/.papercusp/scratch/voice-endurance-20260716/` (`injectord.py`, `turns.sh`, `ui.py`, `rig.py`, generated 16 kHz WAVs). Three non-obvious rules cost hours before the soak ran clean — bake them into any future rig: 1. **`injectAudio` crashes the emulator unless a guest recorder is actively consuming the stream.** In the default `MODE_UNSPECIFIED` (blocking) delivery mode the emulator only pulls packets while the app holds an `AudioRecord`; pushing audio (even silence) with no active recorder overflows/SIGSEGVs it within \~4 s. So the injector daemon holds **one** `injectAudio` stream open for the whole campaign but **yields nothing while idle** (never a silence keep-alive) and streams WAV chunks only on command — and it **never closes** the stream (closing it also SIGSEGVs the emulator). Per turn: tap the Voice FAB → `LISTENING` → drop a `play <wav>` command → tap the FAB again to stop and send. Rows land in `harness_shared.operator_turns` (`source` = `voice_stt` / `voice_tts`). 2. **Run the emulator on your own dedicated Xvfb display** (e.g. `:99`), not a shared one. A peer reaping the shared `:90` kills the emulator with `XIO: fatal IO error on X server` mid-run. 3. **Liveness is `adb get-state`, never a `pgrep` for the AVD name.** The running process cmdline is `qemu-system-x86_64 -avd papercusp-test` (no `.avd`), so a `pgrep -f papercusp-test.avd` always misses and reports a healthy emulator as dead. Worse, `pkill -f` with any pattern containing `papercusp-test`, `injectord.py`, or an AVD path **self-matches your own shell** (exit 144) and also matches the unrelated `papercusp-testvm-clean` VM — kill by the exact qemu pid via `pgrep -f "Sdk/emulator/qemu/linux-x86_64"` instead. Pre-grant `RECORD_AUDIO` (`adb shell pm grant … android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO`) so the mic session opens without a dialog mid-soak; the app’s pairing credential survives an `install -r` on the persistent userdata partition, so re-pairing is usually unnecessary across relaunches of the same AVD. ## What stays owner-gated [Section titled “What stays owner-gated”](#what-stays-owner-gated) * **APNs enrollment** — Apple Developer account + `.p8` key (iOS push is dead until then). * **On-device verification** — the owner re-pairs their own phones (`/settings/mobile`) and confirms a push actually lands; can’t be done without their devices. * **Graduating the `mobile-pairing` onboarding item** out of `ONBOARDING_PREVIEW_FEATURES` — wait until pairing + push are owner-verified end-to-end (Android works; iOS pending enrollment), or a fresh install is promised notifications that don’t fire.

# Mobile endpoints are a defineRoute flag, not a separate router

> The mobile API moved off the bespoke _hono/mobile.ts router onto defineRoute under /api/device/* + a `cors: true` flag. Device JWTs resolve through requirePrincipal; isRevoked treats unknown devices as revoked, which bites synthetic test JWTs.

## What changed [Section titled “What changed”](#what-changed) The `/api/mobile/*` routes used to live in a bespoke Hono router (`_hono/mobile.ts`, \~1000 LOC, since deleted) with its own `cors()` block, its own `deviceAuth()` middleware, and lazy DDL. As of the endpoint-unification arc (`endpoint-unification-2026-05-21`) they are ordinary `defineRoute` modules under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/device/*.ts` — the URLs were renamed `/api/mobile/*` → `/api/device/*` (P2b) and the principal kind is `'device'`, not `'mobile'`. Making a route reachable from the paired phone is now one flag: 
```ts
defineRoute({
  method: 'GET',
  path: '/device/whatever',
  auth: DEVICE_AUTH,  // = { kind: ['device'] } — gate on the device-JWT principal
  cors: true,         // mount the shared CORS allowlist
  handler(req, ctx) { /* ctx.principal is the device */ },
});
// (a query-token route adds `tokenIn: ['query']`, e.g. routes/device/sync.ts)
```
 `cors: true` mounts the shared CORS middleware (`corsFor` in `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/cors.ts` — tauri.localhost, localhost:\*, 127.0.0.1:\*, 10.0.2.2:\*) via `corsFor(def.cors?.origins)`. The device-JWT gate is the separate `auth: { kind: ['device'] }` requirement (the reusable `DEVICE_AUTH` constant in `routes/device/_shared.ts`). ## Gotcha 1 — the device JWT is just a bearer [Section titled “Gotcha 1 — the device JWT is just a bearer”](#gotcha-1--the-device-jwt-is-just-a-bearer) A device JWT arrives as `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` — the same header shape as an agent’s `system`/`pi` bearer. The `/api/agent-tools/*` catch-all resolves principals with a **composite** resolver: `resolveBearer` (token\_index → agent) first, then `principalFromDeviceJwt`. One hook reaches both. A phone can therefore call any built-in `defineTool` directly; it no longer needs the `/voice-tool/:name` proxy. ## Gotcha 2 — `isRevoked` treats an unknown device as revoked [Section titled “Gotcha 2 — isRevoked treats an unknown device as revoked”](#gotcha-2--isrevoked-treats-an-unknown-device-as-revoked) `principalFromDeviceJwt` (`packages/operator-core/lib/auth/principal/from-device-jwt.ts`) runs `isRevoked(claims.sub)` (parity with the old `deviceAuth()` middleware). `isRevoked` returns **`true` for any device not present in `harness_shared.mobile_devices`** — a valid signature is not enough; the device must be a known, paired, non-revoked row. Consequence for tests: a synthetic JWT minted with `signDeviceToken` for a device that was never `insertDevice`’d will (correctly) resolve to a **null principal**. Mock it: 
```ts
vi.mock('../device-store', async (orig) => ({
  ...(await orig<typeof import('../device-store')>()),
  isRevoked: async () => false,
}));
```
 ## Gotcha 3 — route-stack auth needs a DB; handler-direct tests don’t [Section titled “Gotcha 3 — route-stack auth needs a DB; handler-direct tests don’t”](#gotcha-3--route-stack-auth-needs-a-db-handler-direct-tests-dont) Driving a `requirePrincipal`-gated route through `registerAllRoutes` + `app.request()` exercises the real resolver chain, which touches PG. In a no-DB test that throws (or flakily 500s). Either mock the auth/DB layer (the `auth.test.ts` pattern) or test the handler directly with a hand-built `RouteContext` (the `agent-tools-catchall.test.ts` pattern) — the latter is cleaner for verifying port fidelity.

# Mock the leaf sink, not the mid-cycle module, for fire-and-forget emits

> A vitest vi.mock over a module reached by a fire-and-forget dynamic import inside a circular graph races the import and leaks the real function; mock the single downstream sink instead.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) A unit test that mocks a module to suppress fire-and-forget lifecycle emits flakes red intermittently (or, on a loaded machine, deterministically), with a `console.warn` from the *real* module the mock was supposed to replace — tripping `vitest-fail-on-console`. The warn often surfaces inside a *later* test than the one that triggered it (the emit is fire-and-forget, so the rejected promise resolves on a subsequent tick). Concrete instance (EI-8413): `work-items-urgent.test.ts` mocked `./work-items-events` (spreading `importOriginal` + overriding the `emit*` functions), yet `[work-items-events] created-event for WI-9001 emit failed: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')` still fired. ## Root cause [Section titled “Root cause”](#root-cause) `createWorkItem` reaches the emit through a **fire-and-forget dynamic** `import('./work-items-events')`, and `work-items-events` statically imports `./work-items` back — a **circular import graph**. An **async** `vi.mock` factory (one that `await importOriginal()`s and spreads the result) does not reliably intercept that dynamic import under the cycle: exactly one call per run resolves to the **real** module, so the real `emitWorkItemCreatedEvent` runs — reaching the real `emitAwaitedEvent`, which (in the test) queries the fake `sql` seam, gets a garbage waiter row whose `pattern` is `undefined`, and crashes on `pattern.startsWith('@')`. The `.catch` fail-soft then `console.warn`s. The mock *looks* correct in isolation (a single-test probe returns the mock), which is why it survives review — the race only manifests when a create runs after the module graph is warm. ## The fix: mock the single downstream SINK [Section titled “The fix: mock the single downstream SINK”](#the-fix-mock-the-single-downstream-sink) Don’t fight the racy mock on the mid-cycle module. Mock the **one leaf function every emit funnels into** — here `emitAwaitedEvent` in `./events/await/engine`, which is NOT in a circular import with the module under test, so the mock is race-free: 
```ts
vi.mock('./events/await/engine', async (importOriginal) => ({
  ...(await importOriginal<Record<string, unknown>>()),
  emitAwaitedEvent: vi.fn(async () => ({ ok: true, key: '', woken: 0, notified: [], msgId: null })),
}));
```
 Even when the real `emitWorkItemCreatedEvent` slips past the module spy, it now hits a no-op engine and never touches the fake DB.
