The one **owner-action** blocker between the current Windows build and a confident **public** release — the exact parallel of the macOS Developer ID blocker ([macos-signing-notarization-runbook](/internal/docs/agent-insights/macos-signing-notarization-runbook)). Everything else (the never-trap setup gate WI-791, the dismissible dogfood banner, the build pipeline) is done in code; this needs an Authenticode certificate an agent cannot obtain. Why it's mandatory for PUBLIC release The alpha installer is **unsigned** (plan `windows-desktop-release-readiness-2026-06-11` D-004 — accepted-as-known for a handful of insiders). For the public it is not acceptable: an unsigned NSIS installer downloaded from the internet triggers **SmartScreen** — a full-screen *“Windows protected your PC … unknown publisher”* with only a buried *More info → Run anyway* escape — plus Defender SmartScreen friction. A large fraction of users click *Don’t run* / delete rather than dig for the override. (Plan `windows-public-release-readiness-2026-06-25` **D-001** retires the alpha deferral.) ## OV vs EV — pick before buying (it changes the SmartScreen experience) [Section titled “OV vs EV — pick before buying (it changes the SmartScreen experience)”](#ov-vs-ev--pick-before-buying-it-changes-the-smartscreen-experience) | | OV (Organization Validation) | EV (Extended Validation) | | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | SmartScreen | reputation builds **slowly** — early downloaders still see the warning until enough clean installs accrue | **instant** trust — no warning from the first download | | Key storage | a `.pfx`/`.p12` file you can import (exportable) | **hardware token (FIPS 140-2) or cloud HSM** — key is non-exportable (CA requirement since June 2023) | | Cost / vetting | cheaper, lighter org vetting | pricier, stricter org vetting | | Automation | sign with the `.pfx` directly (or import → thumbprint) | sign via the token’s CSP or a cloud-HSM signer (e.g. `azuresigntool` against Azure Key Vault / DigiCert KeyLocker) | **Recommendation: EV** if the budget allows — it removes the SmartScreen wall entirely on day one, which is the whole point of signing for a public launch. OV still works and is far better than unsigned, but warn the first wave of users the warning may appear until reputation builds. ## The good news: the pipeline signs automatically — when a cert is present [Section titled “The good news: the pipeline signs automatically — when a cert is present”](#the-good-news-the-pipeline-signs-automatically--when-a-cert-is-present) `bin/build-windows-on-vm.sh` runs `tauri build --bundles nsis` inside the Windows VM. Tauri signs the bundled `.exe` **and** the NSIS `*-setup.exe` via `signtool` **iff** the build is told which cert to use. The script wires this so that **no script edit is needed at release time** — the gate is purely the credentials in env (mirrors the macOS `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` gate). With no cert env set, it builds **unsigned**, exactly as today. ## Pipeline capability — VERIFIED end-to-end (self-signed dry-run, 2026-07-05) [Section titled “Pipeline capability — VERIFIED end-to-end (self-signed dry-run, 2026-07-05)”](#pipeline-capability--verified-end-to-end-self-signed-dry-run-2026-07-05) Every link the pipeline OWNS was exercised on the Windows VM with a throwaway self-signed code-signing cert (WI-2749; the cert + PFX were deleted after) — so the owner’s real cert-drop is a credentials swap, not a debugging session: * **`signtool` present** — Windows SDK `10.0.26100` (`…\Windows Kits\10\bin\10.0.26100.0\x64\signtool.exe`). * **Our actual installer signs** — a self-signed cert signed the real 611 MB `Papercusp GUI_…-setup.exe`: `Successfully signed`, signature attaches (`Get-AuthenticodeSignature` → SignerCertificate populated). (A self-signed cert fails `verify /pa` trust-chain — expected; a real OV/EV cert chains to a public CA.) * **RFC3161 timestamping works** — `signtool /tr … /td sha256` succeeded against `timestamp.digicert.com`, `timestamp.sectigo.com`, and `timestamp.comodoca.com`. * **The config glue is exact** — the in-VM PFX-import → thumbprint-readback → JSON patch produced precisely `bundle.windows.{certificateThumbprint, timestampUrl, digestAlgorithm:"sha256", tsp:true}` (valid JSON, round-trips). * **The final link is confirmed in tauri’s source** — `tauri-bundler` `windows/sign.rs::sign_command_default` reads exactly those fields and runs `signtool sign /fd <digest> /sha1 <thumbprint> /d <product>` plus, when `tsp:true`, `/tr <url> /td <digest>` — i.e. the exact invocation proven above. **Fix shipped from the dry-run:** the pipeline now defaults **`tsp:true`** (`WINDOWS_SIGN_TSP`, RFC3161). Previously `tsp` was unset, so tauri emitted the **legacy `/t` timestamp** — which RFC3161-only CAs (SSL.com eSigner, common for EV) reject. The default is now the modern, verified-working path. Not exercised (needs the owner’s cert): a real public CA trust-chain, and a `tauri build` that actually emits the signed bundle (core tauri behavior, config confirmed byte-exact above). A full signed rebuild is one command once the cert lands — see below. ## What the OWNER must provide (one-time) [Section titled “What the OWNER must provide (one-time)”](#what-the-owner-must-provide-one-time) **OV path** — a code-signing `.pfx`/`.p12` (from DigiCert, Sectigo, SSL.com, …) * its password. That’s it. **EV path** — an EV code-signing cert provisioned on a **hardware token** or a **cloud HSM**. Cloud-HSM is the automatable option: * **Azure Key Vault + `azuresigntool`**: the vault URL, a cert name, and a service-principal (tenant/client id + secret), **or** * **DigiCert KeyLocker / SSL.com eSigner**: the vendor’s signing-tool creds. A physical USB token can’t be used by a headless VM build — choose cloud-HSM (or EV via a vendor cloud-signing service) for automation. ## Per-build env — VM-era shape (see the callout above for the current `build-windows-cross.sh` var names) [Section titled “Per-build env — VM-era shape (see the callout above for the current build-windows-cross.sh var names)”](#per-build-env--vm-era-shape-see-the-callout-above-for-the-current-build-windows-crosssh-var-names) The VM script read these host-side and threaded the signing config into the in-VM build. Set **one** of the two paths: 
```sh
# ── OV path: a PFX + password (importable) ───────────────────────────────────
export WINDOWS_CERT_PFX_BASE64="$(base64 -w0 codesign.pfx)"   # the .pfx, base64
export WINDOWS_CERT_PASSWORD='<pfx-password>'
# optional (sensible defaults shown):
export WINDOWS_SIGN_TIMESTAMP_URL='http://timestamp.digicert.com'
export WINDOWS_SIGN_DIGEST='sha256'
export WINDOWS_SIGN_TSP='true'   # RFC3161 timestamp (default). Set false ONLY for a
                                 # legacy server that lacks RFC3161. tsp=true is required
                                 # by RFC3161-only CAs like SSL.com eSigner (common for EV).


# ── EV / already-in-store path: sign by thumbprint (cert already in the VM's
#    CurrentUser\My store — e.g. installed by the token CSP / cloud-HSM connector)
export WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_THUMBPRINT='<40-hex-sha1-thumbprint>'
export WINDOWS_SIGN_TIMESTAMP_URL='http://timestamp.digicert.com'
export WINDOWS_SIGN_TSP='true'
```
 What the build does with them (no manual steps in the VM): * **OV/PFX**: decodes the PFX in the VM, `Import-PfxCertificate` into `Cert:\CurrentUser\My`, reads back its thumbprint. * Patches the in-VM `src-tauri/tauri.windows.conf.json` → `bundle.windows.{certificateThumbprint, timestampUrl, digestAlgorithm, tsp}` so `tauri build` signs every produced binary + the installer. * **Timestamping** is always set when signing — a timestamped signature stays valid after the cert expires. EV non-exportable keys need a signCommand, not a thumbprint For some cloud-HSM/EV setups the key can’t be reached by plain `signtool` thumbprint signing. In that case use Tauri’s `bundle.windows.signCommand` (a custom command template, `%1` = file) pointed at `azuresigntool sign … %1` (or the vendor tool). Set `WINDOWS_SIGN_COMMAND='azuresigntool sign -kvu <vault> -kvc <cert> -kvt <tenant> -kvi <client> -kvs <secret> -tr http://timestamp.digicert.com -td sha256 %1'` and the build injects it as `signCommand` instead of a thumbprint. (Verify the exact `azuresigntool`/`AzureSignTool` invocation against your vault.) ## Verify the result (in the VM, or on any Windows box) [Section titled “Verify the result (in the VM, or on any Windows box)”](#verify-the-result-in-the-vm-or-on-any-windows-box) 
```powershell
# Authenticode present + chains to a trusted CA, and is timestamped:
signtool verify /pa /v "Papercusp_<ver>_x64-setup.exe"
Get-AuthenticodeSignature "Papercusp_<ver>_x64-setup.exe" | Format-List
#   Status         : Valid
#   SignerCertificate / TimeStamperCertificate populated
```
 A truly fresh Windows machine downloading the signed installer should then: * **EV**: launch with **no** SmartScreen warning. * **OV**: show no warning once reputation builds; until then, *More info → Run anyway* (document this for the first wave). ## Caveats specific to this app [Section titled “Caveats specific to this app”](#caveats-specific-to-this-app) * **Payload trimming.** The Windows payload is trimmed (`code-server`, `bin/omp` excluded — see `build-desktop-sidecar.sh`) to control installer size; signing doesn’t change that, but keep an eye on payload growth. (The VM-era \~2 GiB makensis datablock cap this point originally referenced no longer applies now that Inno Setup, not NSIS, produces the installer — Inno’s own span-slicing handles a large payload instead.) * **Sign the inner `.exe` too, not just the installer.** `build-windows-cross.sh` Authenticode-signs the app `.exe` and the Inno `*-setup.exe` separately (`authenticode_sign`, called at both sites); confirm both are signed (`osslsigncode verify` each) — an unsigned inner binary still triggers Defender on first run. * **Don’t run `release-local.sh` (tag/push/GitHub-release) from an agent** — the outward publish is owner-authority. This runbook covers building a *signed installer*; distribution is a separate owner step. * **Updater `.sig` stays minisign-signed** (host-side, separate from Authenticode) — that already works.

# Windows operator goes down and never respawns — the wsl.exe wrapper-child liveness blind spot

> Why the Papercusp Server app left a durably-dead operator un-respawned on Windows (child_exited stayed false because the wsl.exe wrapper outlived the inner node operator), the decide_serve_respawn fix that makes operator reachability the ground-truth signal, and why Linux CI never caught it. WI-3170, 2026-07-06.

**Symptom (owner-reported, live):** *“the windows app is still very unreliable with the operator going down all the time.”* VM forensics (WI-3141) showed the operator **durably down \~11+ minutes** — `operator.json` recorded a pid that was not running, **no** `serve.mjs`/`sidecar-main` process existed at all, and the health probe returned “fetch failed” — while the **Papercusp Server** app that is supposed to supervise + respawn it was alive the whole time. It was *durably down*, not “restarting frequently.” If you are debugging a Windows operator that dies and stays dead while the Server tray app keeps running, this is the page. ## Root cause: on Windows the supervised `Child` is the `wsl.exe` WRAPPER, not the operator [Section titled “Root cause: on Windows the supervised Child is the wsl.exe WRAPPER, not the operator”](#root-cause-on-windows-the-supervised-child-is-the-wslexe-wrapper-not-the-operator) `spawn_serve` (`papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs`) launches the operator via `make_sidecar_command(via_wsl, …)`. On Windows the operator (`serve.mjs` node process) runs **inside WSL**, so the `std::process::Child` the supervisor stores and polls with `try_wait()` is the **`wsl.exe` wrapper process**, not the node operator itself. The two liveness facts can therefore diverge: * `child_exited` (from `try_wait()` on the stored `Child`) = “did the **wsl.exe wrapper** exit?” * `operator_reachable` (an HTTP health probe on the recorded port) = “is the **actual operator** answering?” When the **inner** WSL node operator dies but the **`wsl.exe` wrapper outlives it** (a very common WSL failure shape — the distro/relay keeps the wrapper up), `child_exited` stays **`false`** even though the operator is gone. ## The bug: the decider short-circuited to Healthy on `!child_exited` [Section titled “The bug: the decider short-circuited to Healthy on !child\_exited”](#the-bug-the-decider-short-circuited-to-healthy-on-child_exited) The old pure decider read (paraphrased): 
```rust
// OLD — buggy
if !child_exited || operator_reachable {
    return ServeRespawnAction::Healthy;
}
```
 `!child_exited` is **first in the OR**, so when the wrapper outlived the dead inner operator (`child_exited == false`), the decider returned `Healthy` and **never consulted `operator_reachable`**. The dead operator was never respawned. `child_exited` — the signal the whole decision hung on — is simply **not a reliable operator-liveness signal on Windows/WSL**. ## The fix: operator **reachability** is the ground-truth liveness signal [Section titled “The fix: operator reachability is the ground-truth liveness signal”](#the-fix-operator-reachability-is-the-ground-truth-liveness-signal) Respawn when the operator is **unreachable past a debounce, REGARDLESS of `child_exited`**. `decide_serve_respawn` now (WI-3170): 
```rust
fn decide_serve_respawn(
    child_exited: bool,
    shutting_down: bool,
    operator_reachable: bool,
    unreachable_respawn_ready: bool,   // ← new: unreachable past debounce (see gating)
    respawns_in_window: usize,
    max_respawns: usize,
) -> ServeRespawnAction {
    if shutting_down { return ServeRespawnAction::Suppressed; }
    if operator_reachable { return ServeRespawnAction::Healthy; }   // reachable ⇒ healthy, full stop
    if child_exited || unreachable_respawn_ready {
        if respawns_in_window >= max_respawns { return ServeRespawnAction::GiveUp; }
        return ServeRespawnAction::Respawn;
    }
    ServeRespawnAction::Healthy
}
```
 Reachability is checked **first and unconditionally**: a reachable operator is healthy; an unreachable one that has been unreachable long enough is respawned whether or not the wrapper `Child` has exited. ### Why the debounce is gated (keeps Linux/macOS byte-identical + avoids double-spawn) [Section titled “Why the debounce is gated (keeps Linux/macOS byte-identical + avoids double-spawn)”](#why-the-debounce-is-gated-keeps-linuxmacos-byte-identical--avoids-double-spawn) `unreachable_respawn_ready` is computed in the supervision loop and armed **only** when all of: * `sup_via_wsl` — the Windows/WSL topology where the wrapper-outlives-inner divergence exists. On Linux/macOS the stored `Child` *is* the operator, so the old `child_exited` path is authoritative and the new path never arms → **behavior there is unchanged.** * `ever_reachable` — the operator came up successfully at least once. This stops a **slow cold boot** (operator not reachable *yet*) from being mistaken for a death and triggering a competing second spawn. * unreachable continuously for `SERVE_UNREACHABLE_DEBOUNCE` (15s) — a brief flap does not trigger a respawn. Crash-loop protection is preserved: `MAX_RESPAWNS_PER_WINDOW` (5 / 300s) → `GiveUp` + `notify_operator_dead`. Shutdown still suppresses respawns. ## Why Linux CI never caught it [Section titled “Why Linux CI never caught it”](#why-linux-ci-never-caught-it) The existing WI-2667 decider tests run on Linux CI, where the stored `Child` **is** the operator — so a dead operator always means `child_exited == true`, and the buggy `!child_exited` branch is never exercised with a live-wrapper / dead-inner combination. **The blind spot is structurally invisible to any test that doesn’t model a wrapper `Child` outliving its inner process.** The regression guard for it is a pure-decider unit test that sets exactly that state: 
```plaintext
child_exited=false, operator_reachable=false, unreachable_respawn_ready=true
  → expect Respawn      (the case the old code returned Healthy for)
```
 (see `serve_respawn_when_operator_unreachable_past_debounce_despite_live_wrapper_child` in `src-tauri/src/main.rs`). `cargo test` in `src-tauri` covers this plus all the pre-existing WI-2667 decider cases. ## VERIFIED LIVE on the Windows VM (2026-07-06, WI-3170 P-004) [Section titled “VERIFIED LIVE on the Windows VM (2026-07-06, WI-3170 P-004)”](#verified-live-on-the-windows-vm-2026-07-06-wi-3170-p-004) Confirmed end-to-end on the QEMU Windows VM against the installed Inno full-seed build (`/api/health` sha `99f2214b3b`). The operator runs inside the **`papercup-runtime`** WSL distro (NOT the default `Ubuntu`; user `papercup`, `/home/papercup/.papercusp/operator.json`) — reach it with `wsl.exe -d papercup-runtime`. Two destructive runs, same Server app (pid 12336) supervising throughout: * **Run 1** (`verify-operator-respawn-vm.sh`): killed operator pid 9 + `pkill serve.mjs` → Server respawned a healthy operator (fresh pid 8207) in **\~15s**. Exit 0 = PASS. * **Run 2** (instrumented, per-second trace): killed pid 8207 → `/api/health` **DOWN continuously for \~15s** (operator.json emptied) → **recovered at t≈17s** (fresh pid 9770). **Why this proves the debounce path (not the old `child_exited` path):** the supervision loop polls every **1.5s** (`main.rs` `sleep(from_millis(1500))`). A `child_exited==true` respawn fires on the *next* poll → recovery in \~3–5s. The observed \~15s dead-window before respawn is `SERVE_UNREACHABLE_DEBOUNCE` (15s) elapsing — i.e. `child_exited` stayed **false** (the `wsl.exe` wrapper outlived the killed inner operator, the exact blind spot) and the new `unreachable_respawn_ready` arming is what triggered the respawn. The owner-reported “operator goes down and stays down” symptom is resolved. > VM gotchas for the next verifier: the operator lives in `papercup-runtime`, not the default distro (probing the default shows a listening 16069 socket via the shared WSL2 netns but **no** process/operator.json — separate PID+mount ns). `tasklist.exe` interop is **off** inside `papercup-runtime`, so read the Windows-side `wsl.exe`/Server pids over SSH (`tasklist /FI ...`), not from within the distro. ## Co-install guard (only the Server role owns the operator) [Section titled “Co-install guard (only the Server role owns the operator)”](#co-install-guard-only-the-server-role-owns-the-operator) VM forensics also found **two** `papercusp-desktop.exe` running — the Server (pid 3832) *and* a stale old-build GUI (pid 6476). Only the **Server** role may spawn/own/supervise the operator; a co-installed GUI must never fight it for ports/PG. This is now pinned by `Role::owns_operator()` (`src-tauri/src/app_role.rs`) * an `assert!(role.owns_operator())` at the Server serve-spawn gate + the `only_server_role_owns_operator` test. (Relates the WI-2902 co-install footgun.) ## Live verification (the unit test is necessary but not sufficient) [Section titled “Live verification (the unit test is necessary but not sufficient)”](#live-verification-the-unit-test-is-necessary-but-not-sufficient) The pure decider is unit-tested, but the *integration* behavior — the supervision loop actually computing `unreachable_respawn_ready` and respawning a real operator — only runs on Windows/WSL and cannot be exercised on Linux CI. Verify it on the QEMU VM with `papercusp-desktop/bin/verify-operator-respawn-vm.sh` (run **inside the VM’s WSL**, with a fixed build installed, and coordinate with whoever owns the VM first — the owner may be live-testing): it reads the live port from `operator.json`, kills **only** the inner `serve.mjs` (leaving the `wsl.exe` wrapper + Server alive — the exact blind-spot repro), waits ≤90s, and confirms the Server respawns the operator within the debounce via `operator.json` port rotation * `/api/health`. ## Pointers [Section titled “Pointers”](#pointers) * Fix: `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` (`decide_serve_respawn` + the supervision loop’s `unreachable_since` / `ever_reachable` / `SERVE_UNREACHABLE_DEBOUNCE` state) and `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/app_role.rs` (`owns_operator`). * Verify script: `papercusp-desktop/bin/verify-operator-respawn-vm.sh`. * Tracking: **WI-3170**, plan `windows-operator-reliability-2026-07-06`. Relates WI-3141 (operator-down forensics), WI-2667 (serve-respawn supervision), WI-2902 (co-install footgun). * **General lesson:** whenever a supervised child process is actually a *wrapper* (WSL, a shell, a launcher, `sudo`, a container runtime), process-exit (`try_wait`/`waitpid`) of the wrapper is **not** liveness of the thing you care about. Health-probe the actual service and treat reachability as ground truth; use process-exit only as a fast-path hint.

# Windows-VM desktop testing — the working recipe and its sharp edges

> How to build, install, launch, observe and tear down the Windows desktop app in the local QEMU Windows 11 VM — schtasks launch, bk.log observation, wsl --exec (never `wsl --`), UNC discovery, and the WSL signal boundary.

⚠ Superseded (WI-5651, 2026-07-20) — the BUILD half of this recipe is retired WI-5651 permanently retired the QEMU Windows 11 VM as a **build** mechanism — `bin/build-windows-on-vm.sh` (named throughout this doc) no longer exists. Windows is now cross-compiled on Linux by `bin/build-windows-cross.sh` (cargo-xwin + Inno Setup under wine; see `papercusp-desktop/SHIPPING.md` § Windows). The **install/launch/teardown testing recipe below** (schtasks launch, `bk.log` observation, `wsl --exec`, UNC discovery, the WSL signal boundary) was written for verifying a build produced BY that VM script, inside that same VM — it is preserved here because the WSL/schtasks/pty sharp edges it documents describe the SHIPPED APP’s real behavior and likely still apply to testing a cross-built artifact, but **no one has re-verified this recipe against a `build-windows-cross.sh` artifact as of this note** (a fresh Windows VM/box would still be needed to install and exercise the cross-built installer — that part of the workflow is unaffected by how the artifact was produced). Treat the recipe below as a strong starting point, not a confirmed-current procedure. ## What [Section titled “What”](#what) The Windows desktop lane (plan `windows-desktop-release-readiness-2026-06-11`) was built and tested entirely on the local QEMU Windows 11 VM (see the superseded-mechanism callout above — the BUILD step has since moved off the VM). The working recipe, assembled over \~14 fix iterations on 2026-06-11, with every sharp edge that cost an hour: ## The recipe [Section titled “The recipe”](#the-recipe) * **Boot the VM**: `~/windows-vm/boot-windows.sh` (detach it — a killed parent session takes QEMU down with it; `setsid … & disown` or a user-level systemd unit). SSH: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -p 2223 user@127.0.0.1`. SPICE viewer on `:5931` for pixels. * **Build**: `papercusp-desktop/bin/build-windows-on-vm.sh` does the whole lane — pack (D-006 exclusions live in its tar step) → scp → clean extract → `npm install` + `npx tauri build --no-bundle` + **ISCC (Inno Setup 6.5.2+)** under vcvars64 → collect → **host-side** `tauri signer sign` (updater `.sig`). It builds BOTH roles (Papercusp GUI + Papercusp Server) and packs each with Inno (template `src-tauri/windows/inno/papercusp.iss`, output collected to `src-tauri/target/windows-vm/bundle/inno/`), NOT Tauri’s bundler. **(Changed 2026-07-06, WI-3172: cut over from Tauri’s NSIS bundle to Inno Setup — see sharp edge §5 for why.)** Authenticode signing is in-VM via `WINDOWS_SIGN_*` / `WINDOWS_CERT_*` env (D-004; unset ⇒ unsigned dev/dogfood build); the minisign updater `.sig` is still minted host-side (the private key never leaves this box), though the Windows auto-updater itself is PENDING REWORK post-Inno-cutover — it expected the NSIS artifact (WI-3172). * **Install silently**: `Start-Process -FilePath …-setup.exe -ArgumentList "/VERYSILENT","/SUPPRESSMSGBOXES","/NORESTART" -Wait`. **NOT `/S`** — see sharp edge §23 (`/S` is the NSIS convention; this is now Inno Setup, and Inno silently ignores the unrecognized switch, launching the full interactive wizard instead of installing headlessly). * **Launch with logs**: `schtasks /run /tn papercusp-e2e` — an *Interactive-only* scheduled task running `papercusp-launch.cmd`, which redirects the app’s stdout+stderr to `C:\Users\user\papercusp-bk.log`. This is the ONLY way to get the GUI app’s output on Windows; launching over a bare ssh session puts the app in the wrong session (no webview) and captures nothing. `papercusp-e2e-direct` launches without the log redirect. * **Observe**: tail `papercusp-bk.log` for the chain `pg: listening` → `migrations` → `[serve] listening` → `wrote operator.json`. Operator health from inside the VM: `Invoke-WebRequest http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/health`. * **Reach into the runtime**: `wsl -d papercup-runtime --user papercup --exec <cmd>` over ssh. Append `| tr -d '\r\0'` host-side — wsl.exe emits UTF-16 (it ignores `WSL_UTF8=1` in some paths; the desktop decodes by sniffing, you must too). ## The sharp edges (each one cost real time) [Section titled “The sharp edges (each one cost real time)”](#the-sharp-edges-each-one-cost-real-time) 1. **`wsl --exec`, NEVER `wsl --`** — the bare `--` separator re-joins everything after it into one string and runs it through the distro’s default shell, shredding multi-word args. A `bash -c '<multiline script>'` arrives re-tokenized and executes garbage. `--exec` preserves the argument vector. (Bit the wizard’s Install Agent Runtime button via pty.rs, found live.) 2. **No Windows console signal crosses the WSL boundary.** The serve child on Windows is only the wsl.exe *relay*; `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` from a console-less GUI app reaches nobody, so the old shutdown hard-killed the relay and embedded PG needed WAL recovery every boot. Graceful shutdown must SIGTERM the **Linux pid** (from the distro-side `operator.json`) through `wsl.exe --exec kill -TERM <pid>` (`kill_sidecar` in main.rs does this now). 3. **WSLENV `HOME/p` does not survive WSL session init** — passwd re-sets HOME after the merge. Serve state lands under `/home/papercup`; the Windows side discovers it via `\\wsl.localhost\papercup-runtime\home\papercup`. 4. **Embedded PG cannot live on DrvFs** (`/mnt/c/...`) — a 0700 data dir is impossible without the metadata mount option; PG data goes on ext4 inside the distro (D-007). Consequence: `wsl --unregister` deletes the database. 5. **NSIS datablock caps at \~2 GiB → this is WHY the build cut over to Inno Setup (WI-3172, 2026-07-06).** The owner-mandated full offline seed (git `super.bundle` + pot corestore) puts the payload at \~3.4 GB and makensis dies packaging it — “Internal compiler error … error mmapping file … out of range” at the signed-32-bit \~2 GiB datablock offset (the corestore alone is > 2 GiB, so no slimming rescues NSIS; MSI caps lower, a 7z-SFX combined `.exe` hits the \~2 GB PE-loader limit). **Inno Setup 6.5.2+ builds a single \~4 GB `setup.exe`** — hence the cutover. *NSIS-era history (preserved):* the old `--bundles nsis` lane shipped without `sidecar/code-server` and `sidecar/bin/omp` (D-006) with zlib compression via `tauri.windows.conf.json`, and that in-VM build was deliberately keyless — it exited 1 with “A public key has been found, but no private key” AFTER the bundle finished (the sanctioned outcome; Windows cannot hold an empty env var, so an empty-passphrase key hung tauri-cli on an ssh stdin prompt forever). The current `--no-bundle` Inno lane no longer produces that failure. 6. **Job objects kill `app.restart()`** — an installer-spawned app (NSIS “run after install”) lives in a job; the relaunched child dies with the parent. Post-onboarding restart spawns with `CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB` (D-010). 7. **WebView2 maps custom protocols onto `http://<scheme>.localhost`** — the raw `papercusp://localhost` form silently no-ops on navigate (D-008). 8. **Stale serve lockfile + Linux pid-reuse** — after `wsl --shutdown` or a host reboot, low Linux pids recycle and can defeat a naive pid-alive check; serve’s lock liveness check matches the owner’s cmdline too. 9. **`schtasks` tasks are session-bound**: `Logon Mode: Interactive only` — the auto-logged-in console session must exist (it does on this VM). `taskkill` without `/F` often cannot close the app (WM\_CLOSE refused); use `taskkill /PID <pid>` first to exercise the graceful path, `/T /F` for teardown. 10. **Never forward PATH through WSLENV** (`PATH/l`) — the translated Windows PATH *replaces* the distro PATH inside the spawned process, so `/usr/bin` et al vanish and every distro-binary spawn from serve (kopia, locale, git) dies ENOENT — while the same binary works from a fresh `wsl --exec` session, which is what makes it maddening to diagnose. Forward specific dirs as their own `/p` vars (`PAPERCUSP_SIDECAR_BIN`) and compose PATH on the Linux side. 11. **Hard-killing the app orphans the entire WSL backend** — `taskkill /T /F` kills the Windows tree (app + wsl.exe relay) but the Linux-side node/PG keep running (and keep the redirected log handle open, so the next launch’s `>` redirect fails and the task silently exits 1). Tolerated by design for the operator itself (next launch `--ensure` reuses it), but tear down test sessions with a WSL-side `kill -TERM <serve-pid>` (clean pg\_ctl stop, removes operator.json), not a Windows-side kill. 12. **Watch for peer churn on the shared tree mid-build** — the sidecar SPA build snapshots whatever the canonical tree holds; an in-flight peer refactor (mid-edit import/export mismatch) fails your build with a MISSING\_EXPORT that has nothing to do with your change. Check `coord:presence` for the file’s owner and just retry once they’re consistent. 13. **The rootfs bake script re-runs at first boot — every step must be idempotent AND prompt-free.** `build-rootfs.sh` ships *itself* as `/opt/papercup/bootstrap`; files it created at image-build time already exist on the re-run. A bare `gpg --dearmor -o <keyring>` hangs FOREVER on an interactive “Overwrite? (y/N)” (wedged the whole Windows first-run live — use `gpg --batch --yes`). Symptom: gate stuck at “Configuring runtime…”, `ps -ef` in the distro shows `bash /opt/papercup/bootstrap` + a stuck child. 14. **You can get full DevTools into the packaged app’s webview**: launch with `set WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS= --remote-debugging-port=9222`, then drive CDP from the VM’s own node (v24 has global WebSocket/fetch): `/json` lists targets; `Runtime.evaluate` reads the DOM; `Log.enable` streams console. This separates “app broken” from “paint broken” instantly. Do NOT add `--disable-gpu`/`--disable-gpu-compositing` — WebView2 creation fails outright and the app exits. 15. **Transient white window with a healthy DOM** — observed twice on schtasks-launched windows: CDP shows the full DOM but the window paints white (WebView2 GPU/compositor init flake under QEMU qxl). It self-resolved after the onboarding-finalize restart. If you see white, check the DOM via CDP (§14) before assuming the app is dead. 16. **Inbox (pre-Store) WSL’s `wsl.exe` wedges FOREVER under a pseudoconsole** — the wizard’s pty-routed installs/logins sit silent with zero output, zero exit, and no distro-side process; the same command via plain pipes works instantly. The VM runs inbox WSL (`wsl --version` is not even a recognized option there). Full diagnosis recipe + the fix set: [wsl-inbox-conpty-pty-hang](/internal/docs/agent-insights/wsl-inbox-conpty-pty-hang). pty.rs now carries a 20s no-output watchdog that kills the wedge and prints a `wsl --update` hint into the pane. 17. **NEVER run `wsl --update` on this VM** — Store WSL (2.7.8) cannot create its utility VM under the nested-QEMU profile (“Nested virtualization is not supported”, `CreateVm/0x800705b4`); every distro boot fails until you `wsl --uninstall` to revert to the inbox engine (state survives the round trip; verified live 2026-06-12). The §16 watchdog hint is for real hardware, not here. 18. **Window/tray observation MUST run inside Session 1 — via an interactive scheduled task that writes a result FILE the Session-0 ssh reads.** A powershell spawned from the WSL operator (or a plain ssh) runs in Session 0 and `EnumWindows` returns zero interactive windows (D-002). Pattern that works (verified P-004 tray / P-008 quit / D-003 focus, 2026-07-04): `schtasks /create /tn <t> /tr "powershell -File C:\...\verify.ps1" /sc ONCE /st 00:00 /it /rl LIMITED /f` then `/run`; the script does the `EnumWindows` P/Invoke (and any `PostMessage WM_CLOSE` / `SetForegroundWindow`) **in-session** and `Set-Content`s the result to a txt Session-0 then reads. The Server tray app shows only a `com.papercusp.server-siw` single-instance window (no user window) — the notification-area icon is not a top-level window, so it never appears in `EnumWindows`; verify the tray by Server-is-windowless + owns-the-sidecar, not by enumerating the icon. 19. **A `schtasks`-relaunched GUI does not reliably persist a debuggable WebView2** — so the CDP path (§14) only works on the *first-boot* GUI or a `Start-Process`-launched one. On a *relaunch* via the `papercusp-e2e` task (after the GUI was closed), the GUI process spawns/attaches the Server then exits, leaving the Server+sidecar up but `:9222` unreachable. This looks like the app “not persisting” but is a Session-1 task-tree artifact, NOT a product second-launch bug (Start-Process launches persist; single-instance PASS\_ALL). For a CDP/button-click E2E, launch the GUI with `Start-Process` (or keep the first-boot GUI alive), don’t relaunch through the task. 20. **Catch `cfg(windows)` Rust errors LOCALLY in \~40 s — don’t spend a 15-25 min VM build to find a typo (WI-2215).** The desktop’s \~68 `#[cfg(windows)]` / `#[cfg(target_os = "windows")]` regions (main.rs, wsl\_setup.rs, native\_console.rs, pty.rs, custom\_protocol.rs, endpoint\_ipc.rs, dev\_bridge.rs, native\_terminal.rs) do NOT compile under a plain `cargo check` on the Linux box — that target builds the `cfg(not(windows))` half, so a Windows-only type/import/borrow error is invisible until the VM build. Run `bin/check-windows-cfg.sh` instead (\~40 s cold, \~4 s warm). It is `cargo xwin check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p papercusp-desktop`. **Why not a bare `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`:** the graph pulls in `ring` (via the TLS stack), whose build SCRIPT compiles C/asm and needs the MSVC librarian `lib.exe`; on Linux cargo aborts at `ring` before ever reaching our crate (`cc-rs: failed to find tool "lib.exe"`). `cargo-xwin` shims clang-cl / llvm-lib / llvm-rc in and downloads the MSVC CRT+SDK (one-time, cached under `~/.cache/cargo-xwin`); `check` is metadata-only so no real linker is needed. One-time setup (the script prints the exact command for any missing piece): `rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, `sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends clang lld llvm`, `cargo install cargo-xwin`. `build-windows-on-vm.sh` runs it as an opt-out pre-flight (`SKIP_WINDOWS_CFG_PRECHECK=1`) and aborts before the VM trip on a compile error; it skips gracefully when the toolchain is absent. It is a COMPILE check, not a build — a runnable `.exe` is still the VM’s job, and this is deliberately not in the green-checkpoint suite (needs the SDK). 21. **`papercup-runtime` periodically wedges: `wsl --exec` silently returns empty output + exit 1 (sometimes 0), no stderr, no diagnostic** — hit live during WI-3080 verification and reproduced again on 2026-07-06 (EI-8163): even a trivial probe (`wsl -d papercup-runtime --user papercup --exec whoami`) came back with zero stdout, empty stderr, exit 1. **Recovery, verified live**: `wsl --terminate papercup-runtime` (exits 0) then immediately retry the same `--exec` call — it succeeds on the very next attempt (no boot delay observed). Root cause not pinned down (stale `wslhost.exe` session / hung distro init / a WSL2 utility-VM hiccup are all plausible); treat it as a transient utility-VM fault, not a broken distro state — `wsl --terminate` does not lose anything persistent inside the distro. **Practical rule**: if your first `--exec` probe in a session comes back empty with a nonzero exit and no stderr, don’t debug the command — `wsl --terminate papercup-runtime` and retry once before looking any further. `papercusp-desktop/bin/wsl-exec-retry.sh` wraps this pattern (detect empty+nonzero on the first attempt, terminate, retry once, surface the second attempt’s real exit code) for scripted/agent use over ssh. 22. **A compound command inlined into `ssh ... 'wsl -d papercup-runtime -- bash -lc "..."'` silently mis-parses across FOUR re-splitting layers** (EI-9100, 2026-07-10) — distinct from the `--exec`-vs-`--` issue in §1 (that one is wsl.exe’s OWN arg handling; this one is everything UPSTREAM of it). The chain is: your local shell → ssh → Windows OpenSSH → **cmd.exe** (the default remote shell) → wsl.exe → bash. Any inline heredoc, pipe, or nested single-quote breaks at one of these boundaries with a confusing, boundary-specific error that never names the real cause: * heredoc content mis-split by cmd.exe before reaching bash: `cat: '# WI-3328...': No such file or directory` * a pipe meant for bash intercepted by cmd.exe instead: `'grep' is not recognized as an internal or external command` * single-quote nesting breaking across the ssh→cmd.exe→wsl→bash boundary: `/bin/bash: -c: line 1: unexpected EOF while looking for matching ''` **The fix is never to inline multi-layer quoting for anything beyond a single bare command.** Instead: (1) write a plain script file locally, (2) `scp` it to the VM using a **Windows-style** destination path (`user@127.0.0.1:C:/Users/User/<file>` — NOT `/mnt/c/Users/User/<file>`, which fails with `scp: dest open "/mnt/c/...": No such file or directory` because the SSH server’s sftp-server is native Windows and does not resolve WSL-mount paths as its own root), (3) execute with ONE clean invocation and zero further nested quoting: `ssh ... wsl -d papercup-runtime --exec bash /mnt/c/Users/User/<script>.sh` (or `node ... .mjs`) — note this is where §1’s `--exec` (not `--`) still applies, one layer downstream of the fix this item is about. 23. **`/S` is a false-silent flag post-Inno-cutover — the installer looks perfectly “hung” instead of erroring** (found live 2026-07-17, WI-5013 Windows P-031/032 E2E). `/S` is the **NSIS** silent switch; this repo’s installer has been **Inno Setup** since WI-3172 (§5/§22 context above), and Inno Setup silently *ignores* any command-line switch it doesn’t recognize — it does not error, it just launches the full interactive setup wizard. Over `Start-Process -Wait` (headless, no one to click “Next”), this looks EXACTLY like a hung/deadlocked installer: the process stays alive and Responding:True, CPU/IO deltas go to zero within seconds, the extraction temp dir (`is-XXXXXX.tmp\…setup.tmp` + `_isetup\_setup64.tmp`) freezes at its fixed SFX-stub overhead size (\~4.3 MB) forever, and the real destination dir (`{app}`) never gets created — because the wizard is sitting on its welcome page, not extracting. Diagnostic tell: a proper Session-1 `EnumWindows` check (§18 pattern) shows a **visible** window titled `Setup - <ProductName> version <x.y.z>` owned by the `…-setup.tmp` child pid. **Fix**: use Inno’s real unattended switches — `/VERYSILENT /SUPPRESSMSGBOXES /NORESTART` (`/SILENT` still shows a progress bar with no wizard pages if you want *some* visual signal). Don’t spend 20+ minutes sampling I/O/Defender/disk-queue looking for a resource-contention cause before checking for a live wizard window — check the window FIRST, it’s a 10-second Session-1 EnumWindows call and rules this whole class out immediately. 24. **A printed `%ERRORLEVEL%` can be a parse-time snapshot, not the installer result** (EI-20110660251227029, 2026-08-10). In a compound command such as: \\$SSH ‘cmd /c ""C:\…\setup.exe” /VERYSILENT & echo SERVER\_EXIT=%ERRORLEVEL%”’ `cmd.exe` expands `%ERRORLEVEL%` while it parses the whole line, before the installer on the left of `&` runs. The echo therefore reports the previous command’s status (often 0 in a fresh `cmd /c`), and a literal `echo INSTALL_EXIT=0` is unconditional. Those values are fake measurements: a probe that cannot fail is not a verification result. Capture the remote command’s real status host-side instead (SSH propagates it; use `EXIT=$?`, or `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` when the SSH output is piped). If the check must stay inline, branch on the actual command (`&& echo OK || echo FAIL`) or enable delayed expansion and read `!ERRORLEVEL!`. Always assert a positive outcome too — for example, that `{app}` and the expected executable exist, the process is running, or its port answers. Never call an install successful from printed `*_EXIT=0` lines alone. ## Where the artifacts live [Section titled “Where the artifacts live”](#where-the-artifacts-live) * VM build dirs: `C:\Users\user\papercup-build-*` (su-44446 = the iteration dir; `papercup-build-release` = the clean lane dir). * Collected host-side: `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/windows-vm/bundle/inno/` (was `bundle/nsis/` pre-WI-3172). * Installed app: `C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Papercusp\`. * Boot log: `C:\Users\user\papercusp-bk.log`. ## Why this is the shape it is [Section titled “Why this is the shape it is”](#why-this-is-the-shape-it-is) D-001..D-010 on `windows-desktop-release-readiness-2026-06-11` carry the full rationale (build-on-VM, bundle-the-rootfs, NSIS-only, unsigned alpha, ext4 PG, payload trims, navigate-after-discovery, statics-pre-operator, breakaway restart).

# How to drive a Windows desktop first-run GUI smoke headlessly on VM :2223

> The Windows 11 QEMU dev VM (:2223 ssh, :5931 SPICE) can be driven for a full first-run GUI smoke WITHOUT a human at the SPICE viewer. Observe the screen with QEMU monitor `screendump`; run PowerShell over SSH via base64 `-EncodedCommand` (dodges cmd/$ quoting hell); launch the GUI on the visible console session and INJECT mouse clicks with an interactive scheduled task (SSH lands in a non-visible session, so Start-Process there shows no window). Includes the clean-reset recipe and the elevated-launch=no-window gotcha.

The Windows 11 dev VM (`~/windows-vm/`, QEMU; **ssh `-p 2223 user@127.0.0.1`** key `~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win`, **SPICE `:5931`**, HMP monitor at `~/windows-vm/qemu-monitor.sock`) is normally driven by a human at a `spicy` viewer. You do **not** need one — a full first-run GUI smoke is drivable headlessly. This is how WI-800 (the 0.0.2 alpha first-run smoke) was done. SSH lands in a NON-visible session OpenSSH on this VM authenticates into a session that is **not** the interactive console (session 1). A GUI launched with `Start-Process` from your SSH PowerShell renders on an invisible window station — `screendump` shows nothing and `MainWindowHandle` is 0. To put a window on the SPICE console (or to inject input there) you must run **in session 1**, which you reach with an **interactive scheduled task** (`schtasks /it`). This is the single biggest gotcha. ## The four primitives [Section titled “The four primitives”](#the-four-primitives) 1. **PowerShell over SSH without quoting hell** — `cmd` mangles `$`. Encode the script UTF-16LE→base64 and run `powershell -EncodedCommand`: 
   ```bash
   B64="$(printf '%s' "$SCRIPT" | iconv -f UTF-8 -t UTF-16LE | base64 -w0)"
   ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -p 2223 user@127.0.0.1 \
     "powershell -NoProfile -EncodedCommand $B64"
   ```
 `-o IdentitiesOnly=yes` is required — a loaded ssh-agent with >5 keys trips “Too many authentication failures” before the `-i` key is tried. 2. **Observe the screen** — QEMU monitor `screendump` writes the framebuffer to PPM; convert with `pnmtopng`: 
   ```bash
   printf 'screendump /tmp/s.ppm\n' | socat - UNIX-CONNECT:~/windows-vm/qemu-monitor.sock
   pnmtopng /tmp/s.ppm > /tmp/s.png   # ~200 bytes ⇒ black/asleep; wake with `sendkey shift`
   ```
 Crop with ImageMagick (`convert s.png -crop WxH+X+Y +repage out.png`) to read button labels and derive pixel coordinates (the framebuffer is 1280×800). 3. **Launch the GUI on the visible console (session 1)** — an interactive task: 
   ```plaintext
   schtasks /create /tn t /tr "<exe-or-wrapper>" /sc once /st 00:00 /it /rl LIMITED /f
   schtasks /run /tn t
   ```
 Use `/rl LIMITED` (non-elevated = the real double-click path). Wrap the exe in a `.cmd` that `set RUST_LOG=info,papercusp=debug` and redirects stdout to a file to capture the Tauri/sidecar boot log (read it back with a FileShare.ReadWrite open — the running app keeps the handle). 4. **Inject mouse clicks into session 1** — a tiny `SetCursorPos` + `mouse_event(0x2/0x4)` PS script, run via an interactive task at the pixel coords you read from the screenshot. (QEMU HMP `mouse_move` is relative and unreliable with `usb-tablet`; `sendkey` works for keyboard but Win32 cursor injection in-session is the robust way to click.) ## Clean-reset recipe (for a genuine *first*-run) [Section titled “Clean-reset recipe (for a genuine first-run)”](#clean-reset-recipe-for-a-genuine-first-run) 
```powershell
Get-Process papercusp-desktop | Stop-Process -Force
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Papercusp\uninstall.exe" /S            # NSIS (per-user)
Start-Process msiexec -ArgumentList '/X{GUID}','/quiet' -Wait # any old MSI install
wsl --unregister papercup-runtime                            # force re-import next boot
Remove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\com.papercusp.desktop","$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Papercusp" -Recurse -Force
```
 ## What a healthy first-run looks like [Section titled “What a healthy first-run looks like”](#what-a-healthy-first-run-looks-like) * `wsl -l -v` shows `papercup-runtime` re-import → **Running**. * Inside the distro: `postgres -D /home/papercup/.papercusp/embedded-pg-data` and `node … serve.mjs --ensure` running; the PG port forwards to Windows `127.0.0.1`. * Tauri stdout: `[serve] listening on http://127.0.0.1:<port> (UI ON)`, `/api/health` → 200, `DBOS launched`. * The dogfood clone **defers gracefully** with no GitHub auth: `[papercusp-pot] not created this boot: clone auth_required: awaiting GitHub sign-in` (never a crash/trap). The `DogfoodBootstrapBanner` is dismissible. ## Gotchas [Section titled “Gotchas”](#gotchas) * **Elevated launch ⇒ no window.** `schtasks /rl HIGHEST` (elevated) boots the backend fine but the Tauri webview window never appears (`MainWindowHandle` stays 0). Use `/rl LIMITED`. Users double-click non-elevated, so this is a test artifact, not a public bug — but it will waste an hour if you don’t know it. * **First-run self-restart.** After the WSL import the app relaunches itself (the PID changes) to spawn the sidecar through the freshly-set-up `wsl.exe` — expected (see `main.rs` / `wsl_setup.rs`). * **Spaces-in-username** is testable without switching console users: create a `First Last` account, grant `SeBatchLogonRight` (secedit), then install + launch the app via a task `/ru "First Last"`. The startup log proves all Windows-side paths resolve with the space (`shared sidecar home: C:\Users\First Last`, `\\?\C:\Users\First Last\…`). The operator boot under the spaces profile needs interactive onboarding (a fresh user has no distro), so it’s a partial test. * **SmartScreen is NOT exercised by an scp’d installer** — it has no Mark-of-the-Web. Testing the “unknown publisher” wall needs a real browser download (and is moot once the installer is Authenticode-signed).

# A work-item's severity is real — but a raw SQL audit checking payload/metadata top-level keys always finds zero

> harness_shared.work_items has no top-level severity column and severity is never a top-level JSON key either — issue-family severity lives at payload->'_ei'->>'severity' (migration 374's engineer_issues compat-view convention), defaulted to 'minor' at write time. A raw audit like `payload ? 'severity'` or `metadata ? 'severity'` silently returns zero rows for every item, reading exactly like 'there are no criticals' when the real severities are sitting one JSON level deeper. Always go through work_items:list/work_items:claimable/the engineer_issues view (or payload->'_ei'->>'severity' directly) instead.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) `harness_shared.work_items` (the true base table since migration 374) has **no `severity` column**, and `severity` is **not a top-level key** in either its `payload` or `metadata` JSON either. For issue-family rows (`item_kind` ∈ `bug`/`change`/`task`), severity is nested one level deeper, inside a `_ei` sub-object the `engineer_issues` compat view/trigger maintains: 
```sql
-- sql-snippet-justified: quotes the real column shape this page exists to warn about.
payload -> '_ei' ->> 'severity'   -- the ACTUAL location, e.g. 'critical'
payload ? 'severity'              -- ALWAYS false — 'severity' is never a top-level key
metadata ? 'severity'             -- ALWAYS false — there is no metadata.severity either
```
 An agent auditing “how many open critical bugs are there” with the natural, un-nested query gets **zero rows every time** — not an error, not a warning, just an empty result that reads exactly like “there are no criticals”. This happened live on 2026-07-27: an agent saw `fleet:leader-brief`’s `unowned_criticals: 7` and, suspecting the metric was broken, “verified” it with a raw `payload->>'severity'='critical'` audit that returned 0 rows — concluded the metric was a false alarm, dismissed it, and **carried that wrong conclusion forward into a loop checkpoint for a successor to inherit**. The 7 real criticals it had dismissed included a live-trading gate and a fleet-wide false-green in `testing:run`/`build:typecheck`, aged up to 433h unowned. The mistake was caught only when the same agent re-derived severity’s real storage location from `374-work-items-unify-base-table.sql` and re-ran the audit correctly. ## Why it’s nested this way [Section titled “Why it’s nested this way”](#why-its-nested-this-way) Migration 374 unified `harness_features_consolidated` + `engineer_issues` into one base table, `harness_shared.work_items`. Feature-family rows never had a `severity` concept; issue-family rows did (an `engineer_issues.severity` column with a `CHECK (severity = ANY (ARRAY['critical','major','minor', 'nit']))` constraint, migration 131). Rather than adding a nullable `work_items.severity` column used only by 3 of the unified kinds, the migration folded every issue-only field (`severity`, `scope`, `source`, `found_during`, `linked_feature_id`, `created_by`, `assigned_by`, `signal_origin`) into a single `payload->'_ei'` sub-object, and the `engineer_issues` compat view projects it back out: 
```sql
-- sql-snippet-justified: the compat view definition itself (374), showing where severity
-- actually lives and its write-time default — not a query to hand-write.
COALESCE(payload->'_ei'->>'severity', 'minor') AS severity
```
 So severity **is** genuinely stored (defaulted to `'minor'` at write time by `createIssue` in `issues-engineer.ts` — `${input.severity ?? 'minor'}` — and again by the compat view’s own `COALESCE` as a belt-and-braces fallback for any legacy row that predates the convention). `work_items:get` / `work_items:list` read it correctly (`issueToWorkItem` maps `severity: i.severity` off the `engineer_issues` view, which already did the `_ei` unwrap). The bug is purely in **raw SQL against the base table** guessing the wrong JSON shape. ## The fix — don’t guess the JSON shape; use the tool or the compat view [Section titled “The fix — don’t guess the JSON shape; use the tool or the compat view”](#the-fix--dont-guess-the-json-shape-use-the-tool-or-the-compat-view) * **Prefer the tools** — `work_items:list { severity }`, `work_items:claimable`, or `improvements`/`issues` search all resolve severity correctly; they never touch `payload` directly. * **Need raw SQL?** Query through the `engineer_issues` compat view (real top-level `severity` column, already unwrapped) — not `work_items` directly: 
  ```sql
  -- sql-snippet-justified: the sanctioned raw-SQL path, via the compat view.
  SELECT issue_id, severity, state FROM harness_shared.engineer_issues
   WHERE scope = 'harness:<slug>' AND severity = 'critical' AND state = 'open';
  ```
 Note `engineer_issues` scopes on **`scope = 'harness:<slug>'`**, not `harness_slug` — it has no `harness_slug` column (that lives one level down, on the real `work_items` row). Copying the `work_items` idiom (`WHERE harness_slug = ...`) either errors (no such column) or, if “fixed” by dropping the predicate, silently spans every harness. * **Querying `work_items` directly anyway?** Reach one level deeper: `payload->'_ei'->>'severity'` — never `payload->>'severity'` or a `payload ? 'severity'` existence check. ## General rule [Section titled “General rule”](#general-rule) A JSON payload column that folds a *compat view’s* only-some-kinds fields under a versioned sub-key (`_ei`, or any similar convention) will never satisfy a top-level `? 'key'` or `->>'key'` check for that field — the absence of rows from that query is not evidence the data doesn’t exist. Before concluding “zero rows ⇒ nothing to find” on any `harness_shared.*` JSON audit, check the relevant compat view’s `CREATE VIEW` definition (or the migration that introduced the payload-folding) for how the field is actually nested, or use the tool that already knows.

# A work-item's tags live in three places — only two are read by the claim path

> Why work_items:tag could return ok, show up in work_items:get.topics, and still leave the item failing fleet admission with fleet_scope_violation — and which field each claim-spec evaluator actually reads.

## The symptom [Section titled “The symptom”](#the-symptom) You tag an existing work-item so a fleet’s claim spec will admit it: 
```plaintext
work_items:tag { id: "WI-5779", topic: "p2p-release" }   → ok: true
work_items:get { id: "WI-5779", detail: true }           → topics: ["p2p-release"] ✓
scheduler:get_next { harness: "papercusp" }              → fleet_scope_violation ✗
work_items:claim { id: "WI-5779" }                       → fleet_scope_violation ✗
```
 The tag persisted, is readable, and the claim path behaves as if it were never set. A NEW item created with the same `topics` *appears* to work — then fails the moment anyone claims it by id. That asymmetry is the tell. ## Why (the part that is not guessable from the tools) [Section titled “Why (the part that is not guessable from the tools)”](#why-the-part-that-is-not-guessable-from-the-tools) One spec language (`view.filter` with a `tags` field) is served by **two different evaluators reading two different data sources**, and `work_items:tag` historically wrote to a **third** store that neither of them reads: | Surface | Where its `tags` come from | | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | feature-family admission (SQL, compiled from the spec) | `harness_features_consolidated.tags` **column** — `FIELD_MAP` in `scheduler/get-next.ts` | | issue-family admission (JS evaluator) | `payload.tags` — `staticTagsOfWorkItem` in `scheduler/claim-spec-match.ts` | | `work_items:tag` / `work_items:get{detail}.topics` | `coord_links` rows with `rel='tagged'` (the coord tag store) | So the tag landed in the coord store, `topics` read it back happily, and the column / `payload.tags` the claim path reads stayed NULL. Confirmed on the live row: WI-5779 had two `tagged` edges in `coord_links` while `harness_features_consolidated.tags` was NULL. The create-time asymmetry has the same shape: `work_items:create`’s admission subject (`createAdmissionSubject`, `agent-tools/work_items/create.ts`) takes `tags` **straight from the requested `topics`**, never from storage — so create+assign passes while a later by-id claim of the same item, which reads storage, refuses. **Do not diagnose this as a stale cache or a materialized view.** That was the first (wrong) guess on the original report; there is no cache involved — the field is simply never written. ## What is true now [Section titled “What is true now”](#what-is-true-now) `work_items:tag` / `untag` / **both create paths** mirror the topic into the claim-visible field for the item’s family (`work-item-topic-tags.ts`), so the three surfaces agree. A tag applied from here on is claim-visible immediately. **Items tagged BEFORE that landed are not backfilled** — if an older item still refuses admission, re-tag it once and it repairs itself. ## Diagnosing it in 30 seconds [Section titled “Diagnosing it in 30 seconds”](#diagnosing-it-in-30-seconds) Don’t infer from `topics`; read the field the evaluator reads. 
```sql
-- feature-family: is the COLUMN populated? (topics can be non-empty while this is NULL)
SELECT feature_id, tags, source_plan_slug
  FROM harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated
 WHERE workspace_id = '<ws>' AND harness_slug = '<h>' AND feature_id = 'WI-nnnn';


-- issue-family: payload.tags is the one that counts
-- sql-snippet-justified: shows the raw payload column BECAUSE the point is that the
-- tool-level view disagrees with it — reading it through the tool would hide the bug.
SELECT issue_id, payload -> 'tags'
  FROM harness_shared.engineer_issues
 WHERE workspace_id = '<ws>' AND issue_id = 'EI-nnnn';
```
 `tags` NULL while `work_items:get{detail:true}.topics` is non-empty ⇒ this class. Belt-and-braces alternative that avoids the `tags` field entirely: link lane items via `targetPlanItem: { slug, itemId }`. That sets `source_plan_slug`, which **both** evaluators’ `plan` clause matches, so a plan-scoped spec admits the item regardless of tags. ## The SQL trap this fix hit (worth stealing) [Section titled “The SQL trap this fix hit (worth stealing)”](#the-sql-trap-this-fix-hit-worth-stealing) The first implementation silently no-op’d on exactly the rows it was written for: 
```sql
-- WRONG: on an untagged row `tags` is NULL, so jsonb_typeof(NULL)='array' is NULL,
-- `NULL AND …` is NULL, and `NOT NULL` is NULL — which is not TRUE, so the UPDATE
-- matched ZERO rows and the tag was never mirrored.
WHERE NOT (jsonb_typeof(tags) = 'array' AND tags ? 'p2p-release')


-- RIGHT: collapse the unknown to a definite boolean.
WHERE NOT COALESCE(jsonb_typeof(tags) = 'array' AND tags ? 'p2p-release', false)
```
 Any `WHERE NOT (<predicate over a nullable jsonb column>)` guarding an idempotent write has this bug. The integration test caught it because it seeded the **NULL** case first — a test that only seeded `tags = '[]'` would have passed while the fix did nothing. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * `packages/operator-core/lib/work-item-topic-tags.integration.test.ts` — the regression guard. * `scheduler/fleet-scope-admission.ts` `itemMatchesScope` — where the family fork lives.

# Work-item writes must resolve the workspace by id, not from ambient activeWorkspaceId()

> Why a work-item mutation deep in a tool call chain can silently no-op (report success, persist nothing) — the WI-5261 lost-ALS-scope class — and the resolve-by-id fix.

## Symptom [Section titled “Symptom”](#symptom) A work-item write “succeeds” but nothing persists. Classic tell: `release {claimHold:true}` returns ok, yet `work_items:get` shows `payload:{}` and the item keeps getting re-served by `scheduler:get_next` (EI-15345 / WI-1281 re-served \~2h apart, twice, despite repeated holds). The scheduler read-side is a red herring — it correctly applies the `_claimHold` feature floor (`claimFloorsWhereSql`). The bug is write-side. ## Root cause — the WI-5261 lost-ALS-scope class [Section titled “Root cause — the WI-5261 lost-ALS-scope class”](#root-cause--the-wi-5261-lost-als-scope-class) `activeWorkspaceId()` resolves the request’s workspace from AsyncLocalStorage. Several `await`s deep in a tool call chain (e.g. release handler → releaseOne → `setWorkItemClaimHold`), the ALS request scope can be **lost**, so `activeWorkspaceId()` silently falls through to the process-global default (`workspace-registry.ts`; “confirmed live for papercusp-workspace, 2026-07-17”). If a write derives its target workspace from that bare `activeWorkspaceId()` (or an item lookup like `getWorkItem`/`getFeatureWorkItemOnly` that PINS to it), and the resolved value doesn’t match the item’s OWN workspace, the `WHERE workspace_id = …` matches zero rows — the write no-ops. With an INSTEAD OF view trigger in the path, `RETURNING` can even echo a “success” payload while the inner table UPDATE matched nothing. `scheduler/get-next.ts` was already hardened against this (WI-5261): it threads the caller’s resolved workspace via `opts.workspaceId` instead of trusting `activeWorkspaceId()`. Sibling write paths that trust the ambient value are still exposed. ## Fix pattern [Section titled “Fix pattern”](#fix-pattern) Resolve the item’s ACTUAL workspace by id, ambient-independent, then scope the write to it: 
```plaintext
-- sql-snippet-justified: IMPLEMENTATION pattern for the write path itself (resolving an
-- item's own workspace before writing) — it is what a tool must do, not a read to run.
SELECT harness_slug, workspace_id
  FROM harness_shared.work_items
 WHERE feature_id = ${id} AND ${harness ? sql`harness_slug = ${harness}` : sql`TRUE`}
 ORDER BY (workspace_id = ${activeWorkspaceId()}) DESC, updated_ts DESC NULLS LAST
 LIMIT 1
```
 The `(workspace_id = active) DESC` primary sort still PREFERS the active-workspace row when present (unchanged healthy behavior + disambiguates a cross-workspace id collision, F-B3), but falls back to the item’s real row when the ambient value is wrong. Then `UPDATE … WHERE workspace_id = <that row's workspace_id> AND feature_id = ${id}`. Never `WHERE workspace_id IN (issuesScopeWorkspace(), activeWorkspaceId())`. ## When you hit this [Section titled “When you hit this”](#when-you-hit-this) Any work-item mutation that keys on `workspace_id` and runs deep in a tool handler. Grep for `activeWorkspaceId()` / `issuesScopeWorkspace()` used directly in a write’s WHERE. If the write can run for an item whose workspace differs from the caller’s window, it’s exposed — resolve by id. ## Test-schema caveat [Section titled “Test-schema caveat”](#test-schema-caveat) `work-items-claim-hold.integration.test.ts` uses an INVERTED schema: `work_items` is the BASE table (PK `(harness_slug, feature_id)`, no workspace column) and `harness_features_consolidated` is a passthrough view — the opposite of production (`work_items` is a UNION view over the two family tables with an INSTEAD OF trigger). So that harness cannot represent the same id in two workspaces; exercise the workspace-mismatch case with the ambient `activeWorkspaceId()` mock set to a workspace that differs from the seeded item’s.

# worker:chunk-loop dark-launch — the metrics surface + ramp gate, and how to run it

> The operator-hosted worker:chunk-loop op routes a coding worker through the operator process instead of the subprocess invoke-once path. Routing is a gated cohort in orchestrator-runner.ts useWorkerChunkLoopOp: the papercusp-worker-chunk-loop-blueprint flag (default-ON), a per-harness workerChunkLoop config knob (default false), and optional workerChunkLoopCohortPercent / workerModeCohortPercent 0..100 feature-stable hashing for the 25→50→100 ramp. To dark-launch you set workerChunkLoop:true plus the current cohort percent on ONE non-critical CODING harness (NOT papercup/papercusp) via its instance config (Blueprint Settings → POST /api/harness/:slug/spec; the keys land in configOverrides and configGet reads them), then dispatch real features. Outcomes are now recorded per-run (migration 397, harness_shared.worker_chunk_loop_outcomes) at the single runWorkerChunkLoop convergence point, labelled by execution path (op vs subprocess). Read them with dev:worker_chunk_loop_metrics (completion-rate + outcome distribution by path + op−subprocess delta); pass rampStep to get the deterministic advance/hold/rollback recommendation (decideRampAdvance). The actual %-advance and the dark-launch RUN are owner-attended.

## What this is [Section titled “What this is”](#what-this-is) The `worker:chunk-loop` op runs the coding worker’s chunk loop **inside the operator process** (a near-port of `runWorkerChunkLoop`) instead of spawning the `invoke-once` subprocess. The value is finer crash-recovery + one execution model on the **coding hot path** — so it ships behind a staged dark → ramp → retire rollout, never a blind cutover. ## Routing — the cohort gate [Section titled “Routing — the cohort gate”](#routing--the-cohort-gate) `orchestrator-runner.ts` `useWorkerChunkLoopOp({ role, flagEnabled, harnessOptIn, cohortPercent, cohortKey })` returns true only when **all four** hold: * `role === 'worker'` * `flagEnabled` — `papercusp-worker-chunk-loop-blueprint` (default-**ON**) * `harnessOptIn` — `configGet(cfg, 'workerChunkLoop', false) === true`, from `readEffectiveHarnessConfig` (blueprint knobs ⊕ the workspace-PG instance config) * `cohortKey`’s stable feature bucket is inside `workerChunkLoopCohortPercent` (or legacy alias `workerModeCohortPercent`). Omitted percent preserves the old `workerChunkLoop:true` behavior: 100%. The knob is set on **zero** harnesses, so every coding worker still runs the subprocess path. Flipping the flag alone changes nothing — the per-harness knob + cohort percent are the real gate. ## Dark-launch a harness (owner-attended) [Section titled “Dark-launch a harness (owner-attended)”](#dark-launch-a-harness-owner-attended) 1. Pick **one non-critical CODING harness** — NOT `papercup`/`papercusp`. (As of 2026-06-24 no live non-critical coding harness exists; stand one up first.) 2. Set `workerChunkLoop: true` and `workerChunkLoopCohortPercent: 25` in its **instance config** — Blueprint Settings panel → `POST /api/harness/:slug/spec`. The keys are not declared blueprint params, but `splitConfigJson` routes any non-typed key into `configOverrides` and `instanceEntryToConfig` spreads it back, so `configGet` reads it. Reversible: set it back to `false` or `0`. 3. Ensure the Brief-15 wiring is **deployed** to the operator running that harness (`:3170` staging, or the green pipeline to `:3070` — the metrics tool + table land via the normal deploy). 4. Dispatch one real coding feature → the op path fires → an outcome row lands. ## Reading the metrics [Section titled “Reading the metrics”](#reading-the-metrics) Every `runWorkerChunkLoop` call (both paths) writes ONE row to `harness_shared.worker_chunk_loop_outcomes` at the convergence point in `run-worker-chunk-loop.ts` (best-effort — a persist hiccup never fails the loop), labelled `execution_path` = `op` | `subprocess` via `InvokeContext.executionPath` (the op runner sets `'op'`; the subprocess path defaults to `'subprocess'`). `dev:worker_chunk_loop_metrics { windowHours?, harnessSlug?, rampStep? }` returns per-path **completion rate** + **outcome distribution** (completed/escalated/planning\_failed/aborted) + avg chunks-committed + avg replan-strikes, plus the **op−subprocess completion-rate delta**. It degrades to a zeroed empty result before any rows exist. ## Deciding a ramp step (owner-gated per step) [Section titled “Deciding a ramp step (owner-gated per step)”](#deciding-a-ramp-step-owner-gated-per-step) Pass `rampStep` (0|25|50|100) and the tool adds a `rampRecommendation` from the pure `decideRampAdvance` (`worker-chunk-ramp.ts`): * **advance** — op has ≥ `minOpSamples` (20) runs AND op completion-rate is within `completionParityTolerance` (0.02) of subprocess AND no op-specific `planning_failed` spike. * **hold** — not enough op samples, or op below parity but not regressed. * **rollback** — op completion-rate is `regressionThreshold` (0.05) below subprocess, OR the op `planning_failed` rate exceeds subprocess by `maxPlanningFailedRateDelta` (0.05). The planning\_failed guard is deliberate: a mis-built operator-side `InvokeContext` (the D-005 risk) shows up as the op path failing to PLAN, which raw completion-rate can mask. The recommendation is advisory — the actual cohort %-advance is the owner’s call per step. To advance, update `workerChunkLoopCohortPercent` one step at a time: 25 → 50 → 100. The feature bucket is keyed by workspace + harness + feature id, so retries for the same feature stay on the same execution path while the cohort grows monotonically. ## Gotcha — migration renumber drift [Section titled “Gotcha — migration renumber drift”](#gotcha--migration-renumber-drift) The table was first authored as `394-worker-chunk-loop-outcomes.sql`, hit a concurrent migration-number collision, and was renamed to `397-…` (reserved via `db:next-migration`). Both filenames are recorded in `schema_migrations`; `db:check_drift` will show `394-worker-chunk-loop-outcomes.sql` as an “extra” (applied-but-file-gone) — **benign**. The migration’s privilege/RLS block is gated on the policy not already existing, so a re-apply on the in-use table is a lock-free no-op (avoids the 2026-06-09 lock\_timeout deploy-wedge class).

# The workspace-domain split (EI-295)

> Presence/activity rows stamp AGENT workspace; plan-store rows stamp DEFAULT. Readers joining both must accept all three workspace IDs (agent, default, global) until axes unify.

## What [Section titled “What”](#what) The Papercusp workspace scoping model uses two distinct domains for row identity: * **Presence rows** (`harness_shared.coord_presence`, read into `harness_shared.fleet_assignment` as `source='presence'`): stamp the **AGENT workspace** — the workspace where the agent is spawned (e.g., `papercusp-workspace`). * **Plan-store rows** (e.g., `plans`, `plan_item_claims`, `plan_items`): stamp the **DEFAULT\_WORKSPACE\_ID** (`'default'`) — the workspace resolved by `resolvePlanScope`. This split exists because agents span workspaces but claims + plans are anchored to a single default scope. It is intentional but sharp: readers that JOIN presence-domain rows with plan-store rows see double the workspace scope until the axes unify. > **Current behavior (2026-07-10).** The `owner_activity` table named below (Bugs 1–3, as of 2026-06-11) no longer exists — presence now lives in `harness_shared.coord_presence`, and the canonical reader is the `harness_shared.fleet_assignment` VIEW (migration 165+, `state-not-chat-fleet-state-2026-06-05`), which UNIONs `plan_item_claims` + `plan_item_assignments` + work-item `taken_by` claims with `coord_presence`, each LEFT-joined to its holder’s liveness. **The rule itself is unchanged and still enforced**: `listFleetAssignments` (`packages/operator-core/lib/fleet/assignments.ts`) still explicitly accepts all three workspace IDs — the caller’s workspace, `DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID`, and `GLOBAL_WORKSPACE` (`'*'`) — with an inline comment citing EI-295 verbatim. Bug 3 (below) is now moot: `defaultSharedResolver` (`packages/operator-core/lib/plan-items/liveness.ts`) was rewritten to decide a harness’s liveness mode from `harness_shared.contributors` (a distinct-GitHub-user count), not from presence/claim rows at all — it no longer touches either domain, so the “wrong domain” failure mode described in Bug 3 cannot recur there. See “The rule for future agents” below — it still applies verbatim to any NEW reader that joins presence with plan-store rows. ## The bugs (2026-06-11) [Section titled “The bugs (2026-06-11)”](#the-bugs-2026-06-11) Three bugs surfaced from this split on 2026-06-11: ### Bug 1: fleet\_assignment reader dropped all claims [Section titled “Bug 1: fleet\_assignment reader dropped all claims”](#bug-1-fleet_assignment-reader-dropped-all-claims) **What**: The `fleet_assignments` reader (`lib/fleet/assignments.ts`) was filtering for only one workspace ID. It would join `owner_activity` (agent workspace) with `plan_item_claims` (default workspace) but accept only one side, dropping claims in the other domain. **Fixed in**: `packages/operator-core/lib/fleet/assignments.ts` — the WHERE clause now accepts rows from all three workspace IDs: the caller’s agent workspace, `DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID` (`'default'`), and `GLOBAL_WORKSPACE` (`'*'`) — and unifies them in the result. ### Bug 2: claim renewal missed default-domain rows [Section titled “Bug 2: claim renewal missed default-domain rows”](#bug-2-claim-renewal-missed-default-domain-rows) **What**: The auto-renewal routine (`renewOwnerActivityClaims` in `lib/plan-items/claims.ts`) refreshed the `owner_activity` side (agent workspace) but did not refresh `plan_item_claims` rows in the default workspace. Claims would show stale in one domain while live in the other. **Fixed in**: `packages/operator-core/lib/plan-items/claims.ts` — the renewal now touches both domains. > *Update (2026-07-10):* `renewOwnerActivityClaims` (the function name is historical) now renews only `plan_item_claims`, filtered by `(workspace_id = <caller's> OR workspace_id = DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID)` — there is no separate `owner_activity` row left to renew, since that table was retired in favor of `coord_presence` (a live heartbeat, not a claim-renewal target). ### Bug 3: shared-resolver counted contributors in the wrong domain [Section titled “Bug 3: shared-resolver counted contributors in the wrong domain”](#bug-3-shared-resolver-counted-contributors-in-the-wrong-domain) **What**: The `defaultSharedResolver` (`lib/plan-items/liveness.ts`) counted work contributors by querying `owner_activity`, but some contributors’ claims were only live in the default-workspace `plan_item_claims` rows. The count was incomplete. **Status**: Still unfixed, but harmless after fix #2. Once claims renew correctly in both domains, the domain mismatch no longer loses data — it just means the counter runs over only one domain instead of unifying both. A full fix would be to join both domains in the counter query. > *Update (2026-07-10):* `defaultSharedResolver` (`packages/operator-core/lib/plan-items/liveness.ts`) has since been rewritten and no longer counts contributors via `owner_activity`/presence at all — it now counts `COUNT(DISTINCT github_user_id)` from `harness_shared.contributors` to decide whether a harness is SHARED (>1 contributor ⇒ `'activity'` liveness mode). This bug’s specific failure mode (undercounting by querying the wrong workspace domain) no longer applies to this function; it is superseded by a different data source entirely. ## The rule for future agents [Section titled “The rule for future agents”](#the-rule-for-future-agents) **Any reader JOINing presence-domain rows (`harness_shared.coord_presence`, `harness_shared.fleet_assignment`) with plan-store rows (like `plan_item_claims`, `plans`, `plan_items`) must accept and return rows from ALL THREE workspace IDs (agent workspace, `DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID`, and `GLOBAL_WORKSPACE='*'`) until the axes are unified.** This is not a bug in your code; it is a property of the schema. If you write a reader that touches both domains: 1. Do not filter by a single workspace ID mid-query. 2. Do not assume one domain “is the right one” — both are valid. 3. If you need a single answer, unify the results on the client side or add a migration to stamp both domains the same way. The workspace split is tracked under [EI-295](/) and the unification plan is in [local-pot-orchestration D-013](/). ## Related [Section titled “Related”](#related) * `lib/fleet/assignments.ts` — reader that correctly handles both domains (still cites EI-295 inline) * `lib/plan-items/claims.ts` — renewal routine for `plan_item_claims` (the plan-store domain) * `lib/plan-items/liveness.ts` — `defaultSharedResolver` no longer touches either domain (see the 2026-07-10 update above) * EI-295 — the issue tracking full unification * local-pot-orchestration D-013 — the unification roadmap

# The PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID pin silently rebinds every workspace

> A host-wide PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID env pins activeWorkspaceId() above registry.current, so every non-request path (background work, spawn envelope, harness-list tool) resolves to the pinned workspace with NO warning — one stray `=default` made papercusp-workspace surface default's whole harness registry. Plus how harness→workspace membership actually works, and the dev-box native-PG substrate.

## The trap [Section titled “The trap”](#the-trap) `activeWorkspaceId()` (`packages/operator-core/lib/workspace-registry.ts`) resolves in three steps: 
```plaintext
1. request-scoped  — currentRequestWorkspaceId()  (x-papercusp-workspace header → ALS)
2. process pin     — process.env.PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID            ← sits ABOVE the default
3. global default  — registry.current ?? workspaces[0] ?? 'default'
```
 Step 2 is meant for a **deliberately single-workspace process** (an orchestrator agent, a durable-pipeline dispatcher). But the `:3070` hono-host is inherently **multi**-workspace — it serves every desktop window. If `PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID` is set on *that* host, it pins **every non-request path** to one workspace: * background work and the operator brain, * the **spawn envelope** (`packages/operator-core/lib/console-launcher.ts` sets `PAPERCUSP_HOME = papercuspPath()`, which resolves against the pinned workspace), * the **harness-list / features** tools whenever a request didn’t stamp `x-papercusp-workspace`. And it does so **silently**: the P-021 “global fallback inside a request” warning (`warnGlobalFallbackInRequest`) only fires when resolution reaches step 3 — the env pin returns at step 2, *before* that guard. So a stray pin leaves no trace in the logs. ### The symptom this actually caused (2026-06-01) [Section titled “The symptom this actually caused (2026-06-01)”](#the-symptom-this-actually-caused-2026-06-01) `apps/operator/.env.local` carried a `# TEMPORARY (gate-fix validation)` line: 
```plaintext
PAPERCUSP_WORKSPACE_ID=default
```
 added so the durable pipeline would resolve `sheets` (which lives in `default`). It was never reverted. Effect: the **`papercusp-workspace`** desktop showed **default’s** entire harness registry (`papercup-org*`, `sheets`, `restart`, …) instead of its own. It also caused the `resolveProject → papercup 404` (the dogfood P-026 blocker): with the active workspace forced to `default`, `papercup` — which is registered only in `papercusp-workspace` — was unreachable. **Fix:** remove the pin, restart the `:3070` host (no hot-reload — it re-sources `.env.local` only on restart: `systemctl --user restart papercup-dev-api.service`). Resolution then falls through to the per-window header, then `registry.current` (`papercusp-workspace`), and each workspace shows its own set again. A boot guardrail now warns loudly when the pin is set (`bin/hono-host.ts`, `serve()` callback) — a bare `# TEMPORARY` comment was not enough to stop it surviving. ## How harness→workspace membership actually works [Section titled “How harness→workspace membership actually works”](#how-harnessworkspace-membership-actually-works) A harness “belongs to” a workspace iff that workspace’s registry row carries its slug. The store is **one JSONB row per workspace** in `harness_shared.harness_registry` (`payload->'projects'[]` = `{slug, path}`): 
```sql
SELECT workspace_id,
       (SELECT string_agg(p->>'slug', ', ' ORDER BY p->>'slug')
          FROM jsonb_array_elements(payload->'projects') p) AS slugs
FROM harness_shared.harness_registry ORDER BY workspace_id;
```
 The harness LIST a workspace shows = its own row’s `projects[]`.
