Runtime Behavior [Section titled “Runtime Behavior”](#runtime-behavior) The Swarm skin is selected by `FLAGS.THE_HIVE` / `papercusp-the-hive`. * Logo components switch from the classic cup marks to The Swarm primary mark via `useLexiconPackId()`. * `HiveThemeBridge` forces `data-theme="honeycomb"`, sets `document.title` to the literal `HIVE_TITLE = 'The Swarm'`, and injects the Hive favicon while the flag is on. * When the flag turns off, `HiveThemeBridge` restores the user’s saved active theme and the classic title `CLASSIC_TITLE = 'Papercusp Operator'`. * The selectable Honeycomb theme is generated from the repo-root `design-tokens/honeycomb.semantic.tokens.json` into `apps/operator/app/_semantic.honeycomb.css` by the repo-root `npm run tokens` script (style-dictionary), which emits the CSS under the `[data-theme="honeycomb"]` selector. * The legacy `hive` selector remains as an implementation-pack alias; new runtime usage should prefer `honeycomb`. * The Swarm desktop icons are parallel exports only. `tauri.conf.json` still points to the classic icon set until packaging explicitly opts into the Swarm pack. ## Lexicon [Section titled “Lexicon”](#lexicon) Both packs are presentation-only — they relabel nouns, not code identifiers, tables, or tools. The **classic / Pot** column is the public-release default (flag OFF); the **the-hive / Swarm** column is the flag-on internal/testing skin. Source of truth: `libs/generic/lexicon/src/packs.ts`. | Concept (term key) | Classic / Pot (default, flag OFF) | the-hive / Swarm (flag ON) | | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------- | | Project / deployable group (`pot`) | Pot | Hive | | Live set of working agents (`fleet`) | Fleet | Colony | | Brain / high-judgment orchestrator (`brain`) | Mug | Queen | | Always-on operator (`operator`) | Papercup | Sentinel | | Health / overwatch monitor (`overwatch`) | Kettle | Overwatch | | Idea-radar scout (`scout`) | Blender | Scout | | AI agent / worker (`contributor`) | Cup | Bee | | Human member (`human`) | Human | Keeper | | Unit of work (`chunk`) | Chunk | Cell | | Shared store (`cupboard`) | Cupboard | Comb | | Machine / deployment instance (`node`) | Node | Swarm | | Collaboration substrate (`substrate`) | Coordination | Hive Mind | | Agent signal / handoff (`signal`) | Signal | Waggle | The agent-role marks map to cup glyphs in the classic pack (matching `apps/tui` `agent_pane_kind.rs`, fixed regardless of pack): **Mug** ☕ (brain/queen), **Kettle** 🫖 (overwatch), **Papercup** 🥤 (operator/sentinel), **Cup** 🍵 (contributor/bee). Nav icons in the GUI use lucide `Coffee` / `Thermometer` / `CupSoda` respectively. Under the flag-on **the-hive** pack: the live agent collective is the **Colony** (term key `fleet`); **Swarm** (term key `node`) is the deployment-to-instance unit — a deployment of a Hive to a single machine. Owner revision D-007 (plan P-009) reassigned `Swarm` from the live-agent row to the deployment row and folded the earlier `Frame` machine/region term into `Swarm`. `Sentinel` was renamed from `Sentinel Bee` by owner directive 2026-06-09 (hive-agent-tabs P-003); the shaping icon file is still named `icons/sentinel-bee.svg`, but the flag-on lexicon term is `Sentinel`. ## Color Tokens [Section titled “Color Tokens”](#color-tokens) There are three distinct The Swarm color sources — do not conflate them: * **Shipped Honeycomb theme tokens** — the values the selectable `honeycomb` theme actually emits at runtime, from `design-tokens/honeycomb.semantic.tokens.json` (muted honey, accent `#C68E24`). Documented in the table below. * **SVG mark palette** — `HIVE_BRAND_COLORS` in `apps/operator/app/_components/HiveVisualIdentity.tsx` (honey `#F6B72F`, deep honey `#B97812`, cream `#FFF2C2`). These are the colors the brand SVGs (`primary-mark.svg`, `queen-mark.svg`, `favicon.svg`) actually render with. * **Prototype demo palette** — the brighter `#EAB308`/`#FDE68A` honey used only in the `/dev/swarm-logos` exploration page (`swarm-logos.module.css`). Not a runtime theme. The shipped Honeycomb token pack is dark-first and WCAG-oriented (values are the runtime CSS variables emitted under `[data-theme="honeycomb"]`): | Token | Value | Use | | ------------------ | --------: | ------------------------- | | Background | `#070704` | app shell base | | Deepest background | `#030303` | maximum depth | | Popover surface | `#11100B` | cards and elevated panels | | Raised surface | `#15130B` | elevated chrome | | Text | `#F4EBD4` | primary foreground | | Muted text | `#9F9378` | secondary foreground | | Primary accent | `#C68E24` | muted honey action color | | Strong accent | `#D6A64A` | hover/focus accent | | Accent ink | `#130D03` | text on honey | Semantic colors remain distinct from the primary honey accent: success green (`#68D391`), danger rose (`#E06F69`), and warning honey (`#D6A64A`). ## Motif Rules [Section titled “Motif Rules”](#motif-rules) Use hexagons as layout structure, not wallpaper. The comb motif works for background texture, dividers, empty states, and swarm/loading states when it is low-contrast and aligned to the UI grid. Do not use cartoon bees, playful yellow-on-white compositions, or random honeycomb decoration. The Swarm should feel like an engineered distributed system. ## Preview And Exports [Section titled “Preview And Exports”](#preview-and-exports) * Preview the system at `/dev/operator-logo` in the operator app. * Editable SVG and raster export notes live in `apps/operator/public/brand/the-hive/README.md`. * Regenerate theme CSS with `npm run tokens` after editing token JSON. * Rebuild docs with `cd apps/operator-docs && npm run build` after changing this page so `apps/operator/public/internal/docs/` is refreshed.

# Build system overview

> Where each piece is built, what produces what, and the one URL that runs all of it.

The operator is Vite now, not Next.js The operator frontend migrated **Next.js → Vite** (`@papercusp/operator-vite`, a TanStack-Router SPA). Read any “Next.js app / Next standalone / `next dev` / `next start`” wording below as the **Vite** SPA (`:3055` dev) served by the `:3070` **Hono host** (`apps/operator/bin/hono-host.ts`). There is no `next.config.js` left in `apps/operator/`, and `next dev`/`next start` are no longer used; running/browsing the old standalone webapp is what’s retired — a `PreToolUse` hook blocks browser nav to `:3055`/`:3070`. (Note: `apps/operator/app/**` is **not** dead code — operator-vite still imports its live page bodies via the `@/app` alias, with the former `next/*` imports rewritten to a re-implemented compat layer under `@/lib/router-compat/*` — `dynamic.tsx`, `link.tsx`, `navigation.tsx` — not `next/*` shims.) See the `operator-next-is-retired` insight. > **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`. ## What “the build system” means here [Section titled “What “the build system” means here”](#what-the-build-system-means-here) Three different things are bundled by three different commands: | Artifact | What it is | Built by | Path | | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Linux `.deb` / `.rpm`** | Tauri desktop installer for Linux | `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` then `npm run build` (`= tauri build`) in `papercusp-desktop/` (runs locally on the dev host) | `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/{deb,rpm}/` | | **macOS `.dmg`** | Tauri desktop installer for macOS — a **universal** binary (x86\_64 + arm64), built with `tauri build --target universal-apple-darwin`; artifact is `Papercusp_*_universal.dmg` | Same flow (via `bin/mac-vm-build.sh`), but executed **inside the macOS VM** over SSH | `~/papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/universal-apple-darwin/release/bundle/dmg/` on the Mac VM (the tree is rsynced into `~/papercup-build-mac`), then `scp`’d back | | **Windows `.msi` + NSIS `.exe`** | Tauri desktop installer for Windows | Same, executed **inside the Windows VM** (via `win-build.ps1`) | `C:\Users\User\papercupai\papercusp-desktop\src-tauri\target\release\bundle\{msi,nsis}\` on the Win VM, then `scp`’d back | | **`:3070` Hono host** | Production Hono host (`apps/operator/bin/hono-host.ts`) serving the built Vite SPA + the `/api` surface + `/internal/docs` (the testing surface) | `bin/prod` in the `papercup/` repo | built `apps/operator-vite/dist/` (served by the Hono host) | | **`:3055` Vite dev server** | The Vite dev server (`@papercusp/operator-vite`, TanStack-Router SPA) used by `tauri dev` AND served directly in the browser for fast iteration | `bin/dev` in the `papercup/` repo (papercup-dev systemd user unit) | live, no artifact | Production Tauri builds are real binaries (\~700MB Linux, \~440MB Mac, \~375MB Windows). They contain a bundled Node.js runtime (v24) plus a single esbuild-bundled `serve.mjs` sidecar that **itself** owns embedded Postgres (start + migrations + the `embedded-pg.json` discovery file) and the Hono operator host. The sidecar also vendors a fuller set of runtime binaries and packages: the GitHub CLI (`gh`), the `@rynfar/meridian` host (with `claude-code` deferred to first launch), the `harness` + `@papercusp/orchestrator` + `papercusp-mcp-server` packages, the `papercup` CLI shim, `pgvector` (copied into the embedded-PG tree), and — on Windows only — MinGit-busybox. The Pi/omp CLI and code-server panel are no longer bundled; they resolve from local installs or retired surfaces instead. See the [Architecture](/internal/docs/build-system/architecture) page for the full bundle inventory. They do **not** depend on `:3055` at runtime. Embedded Postgres is the **only** desktop database — the legacy `pglite-server` (removed 2026-06-01) and `zero-cache-server` (removed SP1 C5, 2026-06-06) fallbacks are no longer bundled, so a failed embedded-PG must fail loud rather than silently degrade. `pgvector` is bundled into the embedded-PG tree and is **required**: the baseline schema creates vector-typed columns, so a fresh-DB boot of a bundle without it dies fatally (`type "public.vector" does not exist`). The sidecar build hard-errors (`exit 1`) on Linux/macOS if `pgvector` is missing. ## The single entry point: `/admin` [Section titled “The single entry point: /admin”](#the-single-entry-point-admin) Open `http://localhost:3055/admin` (no nav link — type the URL). Every build / install / VM-launch command in this system is wired into a button there with a live SSE-streamed log. Four sections: * **Building** — Linux Prod Build · Mac Prod Build · Windows Prod Build · Rebuild 3070 host * **Running** — Install + launch each platform · Launch Linux Desktop DEV · Restart dev stack (3055 + 3070) · Audit prod bundles · Env probe * **Packaged build** — Install wdio deps · Run wdio test against the packaged binary · Check webkit2gtk-driver * **Simulators** — Launch Android emulator · Start macOS VM · Launch iOS simulator · List iOS sim devices The button source-of-truth allow-list lives in `packages/operator-core/lib/admin-commands.ts`. The client only sends a `cmd` id; the server resolves it to the actual shell command — there’s no path that lets the client pass raw shell. See [Admin commands](/internal/docs/build-system/admin-commands) for the full reference. ## How to use this section [Section titled “How to use this section”](#how-to-use-this-section) * **[Architecture](/internal/docs/build-system/architecture)** — the bundle layout, the bootstrap → sidecar handoff, what runs in prod vs dev * **[TypeScript layers](/internal/docs/build-system/layers)** — the core/host/routes/client compile-unit scaffold the operator is migrating toward * **[Admin commands](/internal/docs/build-system/admin-commands)** — every `/admin` button explained: what it runs, what it depends on, what it produces * **[VMs](/internal/docs/build-system/vms)** — SSH targets, sudo passwords, port maps, “the Windows VM crashes constantly” survival kit * **[Privacy audit](/internal/docs/build-system/privacy-audit)** — the V1 ship contract, `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh`, what gets scanned * **[Verification](/internal/docs/build-system/verification)** — smoke tests for each platform, what “the build is good to ship” actually means

# /admin command reference

> Every command wired into the /admin ops dashboard — what it runs, what it depends on, what it produces.

## How the page works [Section titled “How the page works”](#how-the-page-works) `http://localhost:3055/admin` lists every build/install/sim command as a card with Run/Stop buttons and a live log box (5000-line ring, stderr in red). `/admin` is a redirect: the index route (`apps/operator-vite/src/routes/admin/index.tsx`) `redirect`s to `/admin/run`, the actual ops-console route (`run.tsx`), which renders `AdminOps` inside the `AdminShell`. Mechanism: * **Source of truth**: `packages/operator-core/lib/admin-commands.ts` exports `ADMIN_COMMANDS` — the server-side allow-list. Each entry is `{id, label, section, description?, command, cwd?}` where `section` is `'building' | 'running' | 'simulators' | 'packaged-build'`. The client only sends `cmd: <id>`; the server never accepts raw shell. * **Spawning**: `GET /api/admin/run?cmd=<id>` opens an SSE stream (the Hono route `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/admin/run.ts`). It forks `bash -lic <command>` as a detached process group (so closing the stream `process.kill(-pid, 'SIGTERM')`s the whole tree). Output is line-buffered: a `meta` event up front (`{commandId, label, command, cwd?, pid, startedAt}`), `log` events (`{stream: 'stdout'|'stderr', line}`), an `error` event on spawn failure, and an `exit` event on close (`{code, signal}`). The stream also emits an initial heartbeat and a 15s keep-alive heartbeat (`initialHeartbeat: true`, `heartbeatMs: 15_000`) alongside those events. * **Kill escalation**: on Stop / stream-close the kill is escalated — `SIGTERM` to the process group first, then `SIGKILL` after 3s if the process is still alive. * **Why `-lic`**: `-l` sources `.profile`, `-i` makes the shell interactive so `.bashrc`’s non-interactive guard short-circuit doesn’t fire — so the spawn inherits `NVM_DIR`, `BUN_INSTALL`, `COMPOSIO_INSTALL_DIR`, `HINDSIGHT_API_URL`, `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY`, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, etc. exactly as your interactive terminal would. The two cosmetic warnings `-i`-without-TTY emits (`cannot set terminal process group`, `no job control in this shell`) are filtered out server-side. ## Auth [Section titled “Auth”](#auth) Both the run and commands endpoints carry a real principal-trust gate: `auth: { trust: ['verified', 'trusted'] }`. The route-stack runs `requirePrincipal` unconditionally for any trust-object `auth` (no flag bypasses it), and `requirePrincipal` throws `PrincipalCheckError(403)` when the resolved principal’s trust isn’t in the allowlist. * A logged-in **operator session** presents a `verified` cookie principal (`papercusp_session` → `trust: 'verified'`) — this is how a browser tab on `:3055/admin` passes. A logged-out tab does not. * A **device JWT** (`verified`) or a **superuser / agent bearer** (`trusted`) passes for non-browser callers. * A bare unauthenticated **loopback** request (e.g. `curl` to `:3055/api/admin/run` with no auth) resolves to a `loopback` principal with `trust: 'unverified-loopback'` — which is NOT in the allowlist, so it gets a **403**. Loopback-binding alone is no longer the gate. There is no `requireFlag()` check — earlier versions had a page-side gate tied to `papercusp-admin`, removed 2026-05-13. The admin page is still loopback-only (operator binds `127.0.0.1:3055` by default) and intentionally NOT linked from any nav; reach it by typing the URL — but the endpoints behind it now enforce the trust gate above regardless. ## Building section [Section titled “Building section”](#building-section) ### `build-linux-prod` — Linux Prod Build [Section titled “build-linux-prod — Linux Prod Build”](#build-linux-prod--linux-prod-build) Runs locally on the dev host (`cwd` = `papercusp-desktop`). Produces both `.deb` and `.rpm` in one pass, then audits each. 
```plaintext
cd /home/dev/papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop
npm run build              # = tauri build (the sidecar must already be built — see note)
bin/audit-bundle.sh src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb
bin/audit-bundle.sh src-tauri/target/release/bundle/rpm/Papercusp-0.0.1-1.x86_64.rpm
```
 > **Note:** `npm run build` is just `tauri build` (`beforeBuildCommand` is empty). The bundled `serve.mjs` sidecar is produced by a **separate** `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` step — `bin/release-local.sh` runs it before `tauri build`. If you only run `tauri build` you’ll bundle a stale/empty `sidecar/`. \~10 minutes if the Rust target dir is warm, \~30 if cold. **Outputs** (verify via the auditor card afterward, too): * `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb` (\~700 MB) * `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/rpm/Papercusp-0.0.1-1.x86_64.rpm` (\~715 MB) ### `build-mac-prod` — Mac Prod Build [Section titled “build-mac-prod — Mac Prod Build”](#build-mac-prod--mac-prod-build) Rsyncs the canonical repo tree into the Mac VM (`~/papercup-build-mac/papercup`, excluding `.git`/`node_modules`/`target`/`.turbo`/`.next`), copies the updater signing key over, then over SSH builds a **universal** DMG via `bin/mac-vm-build.sh` (not `npm run build`), scps the `*.dmg` back to the dev host, and audits it. The build dir is `~/papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop`, and the DMG lives under the `universal-apple-darwin` target path. 
```plaintext
# 1. rsync the working tree into the VM
rsync -az --delete --exclude .git --exclude node_modules --exclude target --exclude .turbo --exclude .next \
  -e "ssh -i /home/dev/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -p 2222 ..." \
  /home/dev/papercupai-workspace/papercup/ aviweiss@127.0.0.1:papercup-build-mac/papercup/


# 2. copy the updater signing key (if present)
scp -i /home/dev/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -P 2222 \
  /home/dev/.papercusp/signing/papercusp.key aviweiss@127.0.0.1:.papercusp-updater.key


# 3. build the universal DMG inside the VM
ssh -i /home/dev/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -p 2222 aviweiss@127.0.0.1 'bash -lc "
  cd ~/papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop
  NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192 npm install --legacy-peer-deps
  export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH=$HOME/.papercusp-updater.key TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD=
  bash bin/mac-vm-build.sh
"'


# 4. copy the universal DMG back and audit it
scp -i /home/dev/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -P 2222 \
  'aviweiss@127.0.0.1:papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/universal-apple-darwin/release/bundle/dmg/*.dmg' /home/dev/
bin/audit-bundle.sh /home/dev/Papercusp_*_universal.dmg
```
 \~30–45 min. NEEDS the Mac VM running with disk room (≥10 GB free). See [VMs](/internal/docs/build-system/vms). **Hard-coded requirements** (all currently met on the VM): * `--legacy-peer-deps` (workspace install hangs without it — see [VMs](/internal/docs/build-system/vms#npm---legacy-peer-deps-is-required)) * `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192` (without it, npm OOMs on the 16-GB VM) * `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH` pointed at the updater key copied in step 2 (empty passphrase) * `bin/mac-vm-build.sh` (term shim + sidecar + tauri) — the build entry point, **not** a bare `npm run build` ### `build-windows-prod` — Windows Prod Build [Section titled “build-windows-prod — Windows Prod Build”](#build-windows-prod--windows-prod-build) SSHes into the Windows VM (`ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -p 2223 User@127.0.0.1`) and runs `win-build.ps1`. Same shape as Mac. Copies back `.msi` (from `bundle/msi/`) and NSIS `.exe` (from `bundle/nsis/`) to `/home/dev/`, then audits both. 
```plaintext
ssh -i /home/dev/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -p 2223 User@127.0.0.1 \
  "powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File win-build.ps1"
scp -i /home/dev/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -P 2223 User@127.0.0.1:papercupai/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/msi/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi /home/dev/
scp -i /home/dev/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -P 2223 User@127.0.0.1:papercupai/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/nsis/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe /home/dev/
bin/audit-bundle.sh /home/dev/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi /home/dev/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe
```
 \~30–45 min. The Windows VM has crashed 6+ times during builds in past sessions — **expect to retry**. See [VMs / Windows VM crash recovery](/internal/docs/build-system/vms#windows-vm-crashes-routinely). ### `rebuild-3070` — Rebuild 3070 host [Section titled “rebuild-3070 — Rebuild 3070 host”](#rebuild-3070--rebuild-3070-host) Runs `bin/prod` in the papercup repo (`cwd` = the papercup repo). It builds the operator (`npm --workspace @papercusp/web run build` = the `@papercupai/operator-docs` Starlight docs + the `@papercusp/operator-vite` SPA) and restarts the Hono host (`bin/hono-host.ts`) on `:3070`, detached (survives the SSE stream closing). This is **not** the desktop bundle — `:3070` serves the same operator UI/API that the packaged Tauri sidecar runs. 
```plaintext
cd /home/dev/papercupai-workspace/papercup
bin/prod
```
 ## Running section [Section titled “Running section”](#running-section) ### `install-linux-deb` — Install + launch Linux .deb [Section titled “install-linux-deb — Install + launch Linux .deb”](#install-linux-deb--install--launch-linux-deb) Installs the most-recently-built local `.deb` and launches `papercusp` (the installed binary on `/usr/bin/papercusp`). Requires `NOPASSWD` sudo for `dpkg`. 
```plaintext
sudo -n dpkg -i /home/dev/papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/.../Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb
setsid /usr/bin/papercusp >/dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null &
```
 ### `install-mac-dmg` — Install + launch Mac .dmg [Section titled “install-mac-dmg — Install + launch Mac .dmg”](#install-mac-dmg--install--launch-mac-dmg) SSH macOS VM → mount the DMG → copy `Papercusp.app` to `/Applications/` → strip Gatekeeper quarantine → `open`. View via SPICE. 
```plaintext
hdiutil attach ~/Papercusp_0.0.1_x86_64.dmg
rm -rf /Applications/Papercusp.app
cp -R /Volumes/Papercusp/Papercusp.app /Applications/
hdiutil detach /Volumes/Papercusp
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Papercusp.app
open /Applications/Papercusp.app
```
 ### `install-windows-msi` — Install + launch Windows .msi [Section titled “install-windows-msi — Install + launch Windows .msi”](#install-windows-msi--install--launch-windows-msi) SSH Windows VM → `msiexec /i ... /quiet` → `Start-Process Papercusp.exe`. Installs to `C:\Program Files\Papercusp\`. ### `launch-linux-dev` — Launch Linux Desktop DEV [Section titled “launch-linux-dev — Launch Linux Desktop DEV”](#launch-linux-dev--launch-linux-desktop-dev) Detached `npm run dev` in `papercusp-desktop/` (Tauri dev mode against `:3055`). Survives closing the stream. Tails `/tmp/papercusp-desktop-dev.log`. In dev mode the Tauri shell doesn’t spawn the `serve.mjs` sidecar — it expects the operator dev stack (Vite `:3055` + Hono `:3070`) running externally; its `beforeDevCommand` (`bin/dev-operator-ifneeded.sh`) brings that stack up if it isn’t already. ### `restart-3055` — Restart dev stack (3055 + 3070) [Section titled “restart-3055 — Restart dev stack (3055 + 3070)”](#restart-3055--restart-dev-stack-3055--3070) Runs `bin/dev` in the papercup repo. This (re)starts **two** systemd `--user` transient units: `papercup-dev` (the **Vite** SPA dev server on `:3055`, `@papercusp/operator-vite`) and `papercup-dev-api` (the Hono API host on `:3070`, `tsx bin/hono-host.ts`). The `/admin` page goes offline for a few seconds while the Hono host re-imports; the Vite side comes back via HMR almost immediately — you’ll lose your SSE log stream and need to refresh. ### `audit-prod-bundles` — Audit prod bundles for PostHog leaks [Section titled “audit-prod-bundles — Audit prod bundles for PostHog leaks”](#audit-prod-bundles--audit-prod-bundles-for-posthog-leaks) Standalone re-run of `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh` against every prod artifact present on disk — the local `.deb`/`.rpm` plus any `.dmg`/`.msi`/`.exe` in `/home/dev/`. Fails (`exit 1`) if no artifacts are found, or if any contains a real PostHog key. See [Privacy audit](/internal/docs/build-system/privacy-audit) for the full contract. ### `env-probe` — Env probe [Section titled “env-probe — Env probe”](#env-probe--env-probe) Prints whether key env vars are set (NVM, BUN, COMPOSIO, HINDSIGHT\_API\_URL, ELEVENLABS, CLOUDFLARE, ANTHROPIC, OPENAI). Use this to diagnose “command can’t find X” issues — these are sourced from your `.bashrc` and pass through via `bash -lic`. ## Packaged build commands (server-side only — no cards) [Section titled “Packaged build commands (server-side only — no cards)”](#packaged-build-commands-server-side-only--no-cards) These three `section: 'packaged-build'` commands exist in the server allow-list and run server-side (`/api/admin/run?cmd=wdio-test` works), but **they do not render as cards on the page**. `AdminOps` only builds three sections — Building, Running, Simulators — filtering commands by `'building' | 'running' | 'simulators'`; there is no `packaged-build` filter or `<Section>`, so the wdio commands never appear in the UI. Invoke them by hitting the endpoint directly (or add a `packaged-build` section to `AdminOps.tsx` if you want cards). They drive [WebdriverIO](https://webdriver.io) + `tauri-driver` against the **shipped** Tauri binary (not the dev server). All run in `tools/perf-test/wdio` in the papercup repo, which is kept out of the workspace on purpose. ### `wdio-install` — Install wdio deps (one-time) [Section titled “wdio-install — Install wdio deps (one-time)”](#wdio-install--install-wdio-deps-one-time) `npm install` in `tools/perf-test/wdio`. ### `wdio-test` — Run wdio test against packaged binary [Section titled “wdio-test — Run wdio test against packaged binary”](#wdio-test--run-wdio-test-against-packaged-binary) Spawns `tauri-driver` on `:4445` and drives the latest packaged Tauri binary via WebDriver, running `specs/*.spec.ts`. Prereqs: a `Linux Prod Build` artifact exists, `webkit2gtk-driver` is installed (`sudo apt`), and `wdio-install` was run once. ### `wdio-webkit-driver-check` — Check webkit2gtk-driver [Section titled “wdio-webkit-driver-check — Check webkit2gtk-driver”](#wdio-webkit-driver-check--check-webkit2gtk-driver) Reports whether `WebKitWebDriver` is on `PATH` (required for `tauri-driver` on Linux). If missing: `sudo apt install webkit2gtk-driver`. ## Simulators section [Section titled “Simulators section”](#simulators-section) ### `launch-android-emulator` [Section titled “launch-android-emulator”](#launch-android-emulator) `~/Android/Sdk/emulator/emulator -avd papercusp-test -no-snapshot-load -no-audio`, detached, tailing `/tmp/android-emulator.log`. Works on the Linux host directly (no VM needed). After boot, `adb devices` shows `emulator-5554`. ### `start-mac-vm` [Section titled “start-mac-vm”](#start-mac-vm) Idempotent — skips if `qemu.*mac_hdd_ng` is already running. Otherwise `systemctl --user start papercup-vm-mac.service` (which runs `boot-sonoma-durable.sh`) and tails `$HOME/macos-vm/OSX-KVM/logs/qemu-current.log`. View via `remote-viewer spice://127.0.0.1:5930`. \~60–120s to SSH-ready. ### `launch-ios-simulator` [Section titled “launch-ios-simulator”](#launch-ios-simulator) SSH macOS VM → `xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 16"` → `open -a Simulator`. Requires the VM running. View through SPICE. ### `ios-simulator-list` [Section titled “ios-simulator-list”](#ios-simulator-list) Shows all available iOS sim devices on the Mac VM. Use device names from here for custom `simctl boot` runs. ## Adding a new command [Section titled “Adding a new command”](#adding-a-new-command) Edit `packages/operator-core/lib/admin-commands.ts`. Each entry: 
```ts
{
  id: 'my-thing',                  // url-safe, used in /api/admin/run?cmd=
  label: 'Human label',
  section: 'building' | 'running' | 'simulators' | 'packaged-build',
  description: 'What it does + caveats',  // optional
  command: 'set -e; echo hello',   // raw bash, executed via `bash -lic`
  cwd: '/optional/work/dir',       // optional
}
```
 After editing, the new card appears immediately — the page fetches the list via `/api/admin/commands` on mount. (The Hono host runs `tsx` with no file-watch, so a `packages/operator-core` edit needs the host to reload — restart `papercup-dev-api` or reload the Tauri shell — before the new command id resolves server-side.)

# Architecture

> How a production Papercusp binary is laid out, what it spawns at startup, and how the browser webview finds the operator server.

## Two repos, two stages [Section titled “Two repos, two stages”](#two-repos-two-stages) 
```plaintext
~/papercupai-workspace/
├── papercup/                 ← the operator (Vite SPA + Hono host + libs)
│   ├── apps/operator-vite/   ← @papercusp/operator-vite — the TanStack-Router SPA UI (:3055 dev)
│   └── apps/operator/        ← @papercusp/web — the Hono host (bin/hono-host.ts, :3070), serve entry (bin/serve.ts), + lib/app page bodies
└── papercusp-desktop/        ← the Tauri shell (Rust)
    └── src-tauri/            ← main.rs + tauri.conf.json — produces the .deb/.dmg/.msi
```
 `papercusp-desktop` is the wrapper. It bundles the operator as a single esbuild-bundled `serve.mjs` **sidecar** (built by `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` into `src-tauri/sidecar/`) and ships the Rust binary + sidecar in one installer. Per plan `operator-core-headless-serve-2026-06-04`, the desktop is an **embedder of `papercusp serve`**: `serve.mjs` owns the whole operator lifecycle (embedded Postgres, migrations, the Hono host, the discovery files); Rust just spawns it and points the webview at it. ## What a Tauri production build does at startup [Section titled “What a Tauri production build does at startup”](#what-a-tauri-production-build-does-at-startup) `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs` `setup()` (production branch): 1. **Pick a free port hint** (e.g. `19210`) and a separate PG port hint — these are cold-start *hints*; the real ports are resolved later from discovery. 2. **Spawn the `serve.mjs --ensure` sidecar** as one child process. `serve` then owns everything PG/operator: it starts real embedded PostgreSQL (`wal_level=logical`) on its own free port, runs migrations, writes `~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json`, runs `runBootstrap()` (which starts the endpoint-IPC server + writes `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc.json`), and starts the Hono host bound to `127.0.0.1:<port>`. `--ensure` reuses an already-healthy operator under the same HOME instead of double-booting. 3. **Poll `~/.papercusp/operator.json`** (`wait_for_operator`, up to 120s for a first boot that pays `initdb` + full migration replay) until the pid is alive **and** the port accepts TCP. The **real** port comes from this file — `--ensure` reuse may land on a different port than the cold-start hint. 4. **`eval()` an init script into the webview** setting `window.__papercuspBase` / `window.__papercuspAppBase` / `window.__PAPERCUSP_TAURI__` and dispatching a `papercusp:base` event. The webview opens on the bootstrap page (`papercusp-desktop/web/index.html`, referenced by `main.rs`) that: 1. Waits for `window.__papercuspBase` (re-applied if the page-load drops it) 2. Polls `<base>/api/desktop/preflight` until ready 3. Navigates to the real operator UI (`tauri.conf.json`’s `frontendDist` is `http://127.0.0.1:3070` — the initial document the packaged build loads, which nothing serves on a user machine; `main.rs` navigates the window to the app origin immediately, and pre-discovery the custom-protocol handler serves the bundled SPA statics until `serve` is healthy. `frontendDist` is **not** a `../web` path.) With the `papercusp://` **custom protocol** on (default, shipped 2026-06-01), the real app loads from `papercusp://localhost/…` (forwarded to the loopback sidecar), so the webview opens **zero** HTTP connections. With `PAPERCUSP_DESKTOP_CUSTOM_PROTOCOL=0` it falls back to the HTTP `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` origin. Either way, `/api` fetches + EventSource ride **endpoint-IPC** (resolved from `endpoint-ipc.json`) to escape libsoup’s 6-socket pool, falling back to HTTP if the socket isn’t up. Tauri’s IPC (`invoke()`) works alongside because the page is in a Tauri webview. ## What dev mode does instead [Section titled “What dev mode does instead”](#what-dev-mode-does-instead) A debug build (`cfg!(debug_assertions) == true`) makes `main.rs` `setup()`: 1. **Skip the `serve.mjs` spawn entirely** — the developer is expected to run the operator dev stack separately. `beforeDevCommand` brings up this session’s **own working-tree Hono host** on `:3270` (see below); it does **not** start the Vite SPA, and it does **not** touch `:3070` (owned by the systemd green-release operator). 2. **Start the tauri-agent-tools dev bridge** (debug-only, localhost-only, token-authenticated) and, on Linux, auto-grant `getUserMedia` 3. **Open devtools automatically** (WebKitGTK doesn’t reliably wire Ctrl+Shift+I) 4. Webview loads the `devUrl` from `tauri.conf.json` (`http://127.0.0.1:3270`); `/api` fetches ride endpoint-IPC re-read from `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc.json` (written by the externally-run operator), with graceful HTTP fallback while it’s down ### Two dev modes: `npm run dev` (default, nohmr) vs `npm run dev:hmr` [Section titled “Two dev modes: npm run dev (default, nohmr) vs npm run dev:hmr”](#two-dev-modes-npm-run-dev-default-nohmr-vs-npm-run-devhmr) The **default** `npm run dev` is `bin/desktop-dev-nohmr`: it overrides `devUrl` to `http://127.0.0.1:3270` and pins `PAPERCUSP_DEV_API_TARGET=3270`, pointing the webview at this session’s own working-tree Hono host (a static SPA bundle, **no** HMR socket). nohmr is the default deliberately — this checkout is edited by a fleet of agents at once, and a Vite HMR server would reload the webview on every fleet edit / dep re-optimization (the “window constantly refreshes” problem), plus its `ws://localhost:3055/?token=…` HMR socket competes with SSE for libsoup’s 6-connection budget. The cost is a manual reload (Cmd-R / Ctrl-R) to pick up new work. `npm run dev:hmr` is the explicit opt-in: it overrides `devUrl` to `http://localhost:3055`, the bare Vite HMR server (which has **no** operator of its own — its `/api` proxies to the green operator on `:3070`). So a default dev Tauri window is a Tauri webview pointed at the working-tree Hono host on `:3270`; only `dev:hmr` points it at the live Vite dev server on `:3055`. Production is the same UI code but served from the bundled sidecar on a private port. (`papercusp-desktop`’s `beforeDevCommand` runs `bin/dev-operator-ifneeded.sh`, which starts **only** the working-tree Hono host — `bin/hono-host.ts` on `:3270`, PTY WS on `:3274` — if it isn’t already up.) ## Where the operator code lives in a prod bundle [Section titled “Where the operator code lives in a prod bundle”](#where-the-operator-code-lives-in-a-prod-bundle) After `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` (which esbuild-bundles the operator into `src-tauri/sidecar/`) followed by `tauri build` (`= npm run build` in `papercusp-desktop/` — note `beforeBuildCommand` is empty, so the sidecar build is a **separate** step): 
```plaintext
/usr/lib/Papercusp/                          # Linux .deb install root
├── papercusp-desktop                        # main Tauri binary
└── sidecar/                                 # bundled as a Tauri resource (sidecar/**/*)
    ├── serve.mjs                            # one esbuild-bundled ESM operator entry — main.rs spawns `node serve.mjs --ensure`
    ├── db-sql/                              # bundled SQL migration files
    ├── node_modules/                        # externalized native deps only (node-pty, @papercusp/embedded-postgres-server + its @embedded-postgres/<plat> binary, …)
    └── bin/
        ├── node                             # bundled Node v24 runtime (Tauri prepends bin/ to the sidecar's PATH)
        └── gh
```
 Embedded Postgres is no longer a separate sidecar directory — `serve.mjs` resolves the `@papercusp/embedded-postgres-server` package (with its platform binary) out of `sidecar/node_modules/` and runs PG in-process. `zero-cache` is **not** shipped (the desktop sidecar serves SSE itself; `zero-cache-server` bundling was removed 2026-06-06 per SP1 C5, after the operator’s `/api/zero-harness/sse` PG LISTEN/NOTIFY path had already replaced the Zero WS transport on desktop on 2026-05-07). Mac is the same shape inside `Papercusp.app/Contents/Resources/`. Windows under `C:\Program Files\Papercusp\` (where the sidecar is routed through WSL). ## The bundled Node binary (`bundled_path_env`) [Section titled “The bundled Node binary (bundled\_path\_env)”](#the-bundled-node-binary-bundled_path_env) `main.rs` has a `bundled_path_env()` helper that builds a `PATH` with the shipped `sidecar/bin/` directory (containing `node` and `gh`) prepended. **Every node-based spawn runs through it** rather than relying on `which node`, because GUI-launched apps inherit `$PATH = /usr/bin:/bin` on macOS — Homebrew’s `node`, `nvm` Node, etc. won’t be visible. Without this, the packaged process can’t find `node` at all (the Linux clean-room test VM caught exactly this — see [VMs](/internal/docs/build-system/vms)), and `pg_dump`/`libpq` discovery would break on Mac. ## The embedded-PG discovery file [Section titled “The embedded-PG discovery file”](#the-embedded-pg-discovery-file) On boot, **`serve.mjs`** (not `main.rs` anymore) writes `~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json`. The actual shape is a single `url` field (the admin URL) plus diagnostics — there is **no** separate `adminUrl`/`appUrl`, and `startedAt` is epoch milliseconds (`Date.now()`), not an ISO string: 
```json
{
  "url": "postgresql://harness_admin:...@127.0.0.1:20721/papercusp",
  "port": 20721,
  "pid": 877130,
  "startedAt": 1747140960000
}
```
 The generic resolver reads the `url` field (the admin URL); the other fields are diagnostics. It also writes `~/.papercusp/operator.json` (the Hono host pid + port that `main.rs` polls) and `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc.json` (the IPC socket path). Three rules: * The operator reads PG discovery via `getHarnessAdminUrl()` in `packages/operator-core/lib/embedded-pg-discovery.ts`. **Never hard-code `:5432` or `:16534` anywhere** — always resolve through this helper. The central connection resolver in `libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/connection.ts` already does this; new code should call the helper. * The discovery files are **owned by `serve`**: it writes them atomically on boot and removes `operator.json`/`embedded-pg.json` on the way down. `serve --ensure` also makes same-HOME double-launches converge on one operator rather than fighting over the file. * Native PG (`:5432`) is for Restart / paperclip / marketplace **and** is what this dev box’s operator runs against (`apps/operator/.env.local` pins a `:5432/papercusp` `DATABASE_URL`). The **ship** target is embedded-pg, but on the standing dev box there is **no** `papercusp_legacy`/`papercusp_native_backup` rename — `papercusp` on `:5432` is alive and in use. Code must keep working under embedded-pg regardless, so resolve through `getHarnessAdminUrl()` rather than assuming either topology. ## What gets *built* vs. what gets *shipped* [Section titled “What gets built vs. what gets shipped”](#what-gets-built-vs-what-gets-shipped) * **Built** but **not shipped**: the Vite SPA’s intermediate output, `target/debug/`, `node_modules/.cache/`. The auditor (`papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh`) scans the *installer* contents, not the build directory. * **Built and shipped** but **not loaded at runtime in prod**: `web/index.html` only runs during the brief bootstrap; `tauri.conf.json`’s `devUrl` is dev-only and never read in a release binary. * **Built and shipped and active**: everything under `sidecar/`. `serve.mjs` is spawned at boot and owns embedded PG in-process for the lifetime of the Tauri window. ## A note on Linux WebKit quirks [Section titled “A note on Linux WebKit quirks”](#a-note-on-linux-webkit-quirks) WebKitGTK is what wry uses on Linux, and it has a few recurring quirks the desktop works around: * **`localhost` vs `127.0.0.1`** — WebKitGTK may resolve `localhost` to `::1` while the sidecar binds IPv4 loopback, which fails the bootstrap’s preflight fetch. `main.rs` deliberately hands the webview a `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` base, not `localhost`. * **libsoup’s 6-socket pool** — the webview’s `/api` fetch + EventSource are routed over endpoint-IPC (Unix socket) instead of HTTP precisely to escape this limit. See the discovery-file handoff above. * **getUserMedia denied by default** — `main.rs` auto-grants media permission on Linux so the operator’s voice / wake-word / ElevenLabs paths work without a `NotAllowedError`. > Historical note: the old “duplicate dashboard” + “access control checks CORS spam” bugs were Next.js-era artifacts (a Next error overlay double-mounting the layout, and wildcard CORS headers in `next.config.js`). Both that machinery and `next.config.js` are gone now that the operator is a Vite SPA served by the Hono host, so those specific fixes no longer apply.

# TypeScript Layers

> The four-layer model — core / host / routes / client — and the inert tsconfig scaffold under apps/operator/layers/ that names them. The scaffold (Phase 6a) was dropped 2026-06-14; the boundary is now enforced physically by the package split.

Status — dropped 2026-06-14 This scaffold (Phase 6a) was **dropped** per owner decision P-004 in [host-architecture-2026-05-20-v2](https://github.com/papercusp/papercusp/blob/main/apps/operator/docs/plans/host-architecture-2026-05-20-v2.md). Next has been removed and `apps/operator/app/api` is empty (zero `route.ts` files, `_hono/` deleted); the client moved to `apps/operator-vite`. The core/host/client boundary is now enforced **physically** by the package split (`tooldef` / `@papercusp/host-platform` / `operator-core` vs `apps`), so the tsconfig-projects layering described below is no longer planned — a `tsc`-projects scaffold would only fight Vite aliasing and duplicate the package boundary. The tsconfigs under `apps/operator/layers/` remain as inert scaffolding, and the route-migration narrative (Phase 4) below was superseded wholesale. Read the rest as design intent, not a live migration path. ## What this is [Section titled “What this is”](#what-this-is) The original design split `apps/operator/` into four compile units. Each one is a tsconfig with its own `include` glob, and the layers reference each other in a one-directional dependency graph. The build invariant was: nothing in `core` can import from `host`, `routes`, or `client`; nothing in `host` can import from `routes` or `client`; etc. That invariant is now satisfied by the package split rather than by these tsconfigs (see the status banner). The partition is **scaffolded but empty**. The four layer tsconfigs exist under `apps/operator/layers/` with `include: []`. `tsc --build apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.layers.json` resolves cleanly but checks no files. The original plan was for files to migrate into a layer’s `include` glob as the route-migration work (Phase 4) and the layering-enforcement work (Phase 6b) progressed — but **that migration is no longer expected** (see the status banner above). Phase 4 was superseded, and the layering-scaffold phase (6a) was dropped because the boundary is already enforced by the package split. This was by design — the alternative was to glob up the existing tree and lie about which files belong where. The layers describe a **target** that the package split (`tooldef` / `@papercusp/host-platform` / `operator-core` vs `apps`) now realizes directly, without these include globs ever being populated. ## The four layers [Section titled “The four layers”](#the-four-layers) 
```plaintext
                  ┌─────────┐
                  │  core   │
                  └────┬────┘
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼              ▼             ▼
   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌─────────┐
   │  host   │   │  client  │   │ routes  │
   └────┬────┘   └──────────┘   └────┬────┘
        │                            │
        └────────► routes ◄──────────┘
                  (via host)
```
 ### core [Section titled “core”](#core) **What lives here:** typed business logic with no host coupling. `defineTool` handlers (the host-clean ones), the endpoint system’s pipeline + dispatch stack, schemas, pure helpers, type definitions. **What may be imported:** anything from `libs/*`, `packages/*`, and host-clean third-party packages (`zod`, `date-fns`, `postgres`, `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, etc.). **What may NOT be imported:** * `next/*` * `node:fs`, `node:child_process` directly (use `@papercusp/host-platform` instead) * DOM types implicitly * React If you find yourself wanting to reach for `node:fs` in core code, the answer is to take a `HostPlatform` parameter (or call `getHostPlatform()`) — see [host-platform](/internal/docs/build-system/architecture) coverage in the host-platform package source. The `HostPlatform` interface, `getHostPlatform()`, `registerHostPlatform()`, and `desktopHostPlatform` already live in the standalone `@papercusp/host-platform` package (`libs/host-platform/src/`, wired into `apps/operator` as a `file:` dependency), so the host abstraction `core` depends on is a real package boundary today — not a future tsconfig include. That existing physical boundary is precisely why the layer scaffold below was deemed redundant. ### host [Section titled “host”](#host) **What lives here:** host-specific glue that the desktop needs but a future web host might not. `desktopHostPlatform`’s body (which already lives in `libs/host-platform/src/desktop.ts`, not under `apps/operator`), IPC bridge code (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/`), embedded-PG discovery, plugin runtime (`packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-host-runtime.ts`), FS watchers, background sweepers, socket lifecycle. **What may be imported:** `core`, anything in `libs/*` and `packages/*`, Node stdlib (`node:fs`, `node:child_process`, `node:net`, etc.). **What may NOT be imported:** `next/*` (Next-specific request/response shapes); React. ### routes [Section titled “routes”](#routes) **What lives here:** transport-shaped code — thin shims that map an HTTP request into a `core` or `host` function call. As originally drafted this meant Next route handlers (`app/api/.../route.ts`) and the Hono routers. Neither shape survives in the live tree: Next has been removed, `apps/operator/app/api` is empty (zero `route.ts` files), and `_hono/` was deleted — the Hono routers now live under `apps/operator/bin/` (`host-app.ts`, `hono-host.ts`, etc.), referenced internally by the logical name `_hono/app.ts`. The `~245`-route surface this layer was meant to receive no longer exists. **What may be imported:** `core`, `host`, Hono types (and, when Next was still present, `next/*` request/response shapes). **What may NOT be imported:** React; client-only browser APIs. A handler that holds non-transport state (cookies, cost caps, feature locks, transcript persistence) is A1-class — it stays as a substantive shim and doesn’t migrate to a `defineTool` projection. See [agent-policies §endpoint-system migration](/internal/docs/agent-policies) for the audit axes. ### client [Section titled “client”](#client) **What lives here:** React components, hooks, transport-adapter polyfills (`packages/operator-core/lib/transport-adapters/`), Zero client wiring, client-side state. **What may be imported:** `core`, `react`, `next/link`, `next/navigation` (client APIs), DOM types, browser-only third-party packages. **What may NOT be imported:** * `node:fs`, `node:child_process` (server-only) * `next/headers`, `cookies()` (server-only) * Database clients (`postgres`, drizzle) * Anything in `host` (the client doesn’t run on the host) ## How to run the layered build [Section titled “How to run the layered build”](#how-to-run-the-layered-build) 
```bash
npx tsc --build apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.layers.json
```
 Exit code 0 with no output means all four layers’ include globs resolved + every cross-layer reference is satisfied. Today this trivially succeeds because every `include` is empty. Had files moved in (Phase 4, Phase 6b), the build would have started checking them and a violation — say, a file in `client/include` importing `host/some-thing` — would surface as a `tsc --build` error. That migration was dropped (P-004); the include globs stay empty. ## What this scaffold doesn’t do [Section titled “What this scaffold doesn’t do”](#what-this-scaffold-doesnt-do) * **No enforcement.** Phase 6a (this) shipped the structural slots only. Phase 6b would have added ESLint `no-restricted-imports` rules + dependency-cruiser, gated on Phase 4 disentangling routes from `core` first. Both are moot now — 6a was dropped and 6b never started. * **No code moves.** The four `include` arrays are `[]` and stay that way; the boundary is enforced by the package split instead. * **No replacement of the app tsconfig.** `apps/operator/tsconfig.json` is what the IDE consumes; it’s untouched. The layered build is a parallel surface that runs independently. ## How a file would have been added to a layer [Section titled “How a file would have been added to a layer”](#how-a-file-would-have-been-added-to-a-layer) This was the intended procedure before P-004 dropped the scaffold; it never ran at scale. When a route migration (Phase 4) determined that a handler was host-clean and projectable, the worker would: 1. Move the handler file to its target location (often `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/<feature>/<name>.ts` — that directory is real and now holds the migrated handlers). 2. Add the file’s path to the appropriate layer’s `include` glob in `apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.core.json` (or `host.json`, etc.). 3. Run `tsc --build apps/operator/layers/tsconfig.layers.json` locally; address any reported violations before committing. In practice the handler moves (step 1) happened — `agent-tools/<feature>/<name>.ts` is populated — but the include-glob registration (step 2) never did, because the package split already enforces the boundary that step 3 was meant to catch. ## When this was revisited [Section titled “When this was revisited”](#when-this-was-revisited) The original trigger was: when ≥75% of the `app/api/*/route.ts` files had been audited (the Phase 4 milestone), or when an enforcement violation appeared that the scaffold should have caught. Neither happened on that path — Phase 4 was superseded by the endpoint-unification + hono-elimination arcs (`app/api` is now empty), and on 2026-06-14 the owner dropped Phase 6a outright (P-004). The tsconfigs stay as inert scaffolding. Sister doc: the [host-platform](https://github.com/papercusp/papercusp/tree/main/libs/host-platform) interface that `core` and `host` share, and [agent-policies §endpoint-system migration](/internal/docs/agent-policies) for the per-route audit rules.

# Privacy audit (PostHog leak scanner)

> The V1 ship contract, how bin/audit-bundle.sh enforces it, and how to extend it for future leak categories.

## The V1 contract [Section titled “The V1 contract”](#the-v1-contract) A freshly installed production binary must: 1. Make **zero network requests** to `flags.papercuspai.com` under any usage. 2. Resolve every feature flag to its `FLAG_DEFAULTS` ship value with `source: "defaults"` — i.e. the flag-eval server must not reach out to PostHog. The flag *values* themselves are no longer all-off: under the current **alpha flags-default-ON policy** a clean install serves the bundled defaults, and a large majority of them ship `true` (e.g. `papercusp-the-hive`, `papercusp-video-channels`, `papercusp-voice-channels`). What the contract guarantees is that those values come from the baked-in `FLAG_DEFAULTS` with no network call — not that they are uniformly `false`. The deliberately-off subset (unverified / destructive / security / dark) includes `papercusp-cloudflare-publish`, `papercusp-harness-phases`, `papercusp-design`, `papercusp-testing` (which now also gates the Oracle — the separate `papercusp-oracle` key was folded into it by owner ask 2026-06-10), `papercusp-improvement-auto-implement`, and `papercusp-inbox-durable-escalations`. (There is no `papercusp-snapshots` flag — SNAPSHOTS was retired in `retire-snapshots-instance-spec-2026-06-09`; the reproducible clone is now the ungated `InstanceSpec`.) Both must hold without anyone configuring anything post-install. ## How the system already enforces it [Section titled “How the system already enforces it”](#how-the-system-already-enforces-it) `packages/operator-core/lib/posthog-config.ts` resolves the active PostHog configuration in this priority order: 1. **Env vars** — `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_HOST`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_KEY`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_PERSONAL_KEY`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_TESTING_FEATURES` 2. **Discovery file** — `~/.papercusp/posthog.json`. The personal API key is read from the `personalApiKey` field *inside that one file*; there is no separate `posthog-personal.json` discovery file (any prose mention of one is stale). 3. **Default** — testing-features disabled → the `/api/flags/bootstrap` layer returns `source: "defaults"` `packages/operator-core/lib/flag-bus.ts` only initializes the PostHog client when `isTestingFeaturesEnabled() === true`. So on a clean install (no env vars, no discovery files), the PostHog SDK never starts for the **flag-eval path**. **Zero flag-network requests by construction.** ### Two-track design [Section titled “Two-track design”](#two-track-design) Privacy reasoning here has to separate two PostHog consumers: * **Server-side flag evaluation** (`posthog-config.ts` / `flag-bus.ts`) stays `unconfigured` / `null` on a clean install — no SDK, zero outbound flag requests, every flag served from the bundled `FLAG_DEFAULTS`. * **Browser telemetry** (`telemetry-flush.ts`, the desktop `telemetry-config` route) consumes the **bundled public defaults** (`POSTHOG_PUBLIC_DEFAULTS` — see below), so a user’s opt-in *alone* enables forwarding. It only fires after explicit opt-in (default off). `libs/flags/src/types.ts` exports `FLAG_DEFAULTS`, baked into the bundle. Under the alpha **flags-default-ON** policy most flags default `true`; only a deliberate subset (unverified / destructive / security / dark) defaults `false`. On a clean install these baked values are exactly what’s returned — the privacy guarantee is the *absence of a flag-network call*, not a uniform-off value set. ### Bundled public PostHog defaults [Section titled “Bundled public PostHog defaults”](#bundled-public-posthog-defaults) Every public build also bundles `POSTHOG_PUBLIC_DEFAULTS` (`packages/operator-core/lib/posthog-public-defaults.ts`): the public `host` (`https://flags.papercuspai.com`) and an anonymous-capture `phc_` projectKey (`phc_tnwKu5QTgaHi6hyrHwA3EUQFKhskJES4c4zAzHCUrPFv`). This is a deliberate loosening of the original “zero PostHog references in the artifact” V1 contract (`mac-desktop-release-readiness-2026-06-11` D-010): the key is a read-only/anonymous-capture client credential (it cannot read events or mutate flag definitions), shipped so a user’s opt-in is the only step needed to forward telemetry — no “drop a JSON file” dance. The write-side keys (`personalApiKey`, `webhookSecret`) are *never* bundled. Because that one public key now legitimately appears in every artifact, the auditor was patched to mask it before scanning (see below). ## What the auditor scans for [Section titled “What the auditor scans for”](#what-the-auditor-scans-for) `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh` **FAILs** an artifact only if it contains a real PostHog secret — a `phx_` or `phc_` key followed by 30+ alphanumeric/underscore chars: 
```plaintext
phx_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}
phc_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}
```
 These are `REGEX_NEEDLES`. Placeholders like `phx_xxx` or path/prose references (`posthog.json`, `PAPERCUSP_POSTHOG_KEY`) deliberately do **not** match — earlier versions used those literal strings as needles and false-positived on source/docs/code, so the literal `NEEDLES` array is now empty. **The one allowed exception:** the bundled public projectKey (`POSTHOG_PUBLIC_DEFAULTS.projectKey`, kept in the script as `PUBLIC_PROJECT_KEY` and synced to `posthog-public-defaults.ts`) is `sed`-masked out of every candidate file *before* the regex runs. A file whose only `phc_`/`phx_` match is that public key therefore does **not** fail; any **other** `phc_`/`phx_` key — especially a write-side `phx_` personal key — still FAILs. So the contract the auditor now enforces is “no PostHog secret *other than* the deliberately-public anonymous-capture key.” It also has **soft `WARN_NEEDLES`** that surface (but do *not* fail) when the browser SDK is in the bundle: 
```plaintext
node_modules/posthog-js/
posthog-js@
```
 `posthog-js` is dynamic-imported only when the user opts into telemetry (default off), so its presence isn’t a leak per se — but a hostile fork could strip the opt-in gate, so it’s worth flagging. WARN, not FAIL. Documentation paths (`content/docs`, any `/docs/` path segment, `*.mdx`, `*.md`, `*.rsc`, prerendered `app/docs/*.html`) are excluded from the FAIL scan via an `exclude_re` so legitimate prose mentions of the needles don’t trip it. ## Supported artifact formats [Section titled “Supported artifact formats”](#supported-artifact-formats) 
```plaintext
.deb         → dpkg-deb -x
.rpm         → rpm2cpio | cpio -idm  (falls back to 7z)
.dmg         → hdiutil attach  (on Linux: 7z)
.msi         → 7z x
.exe (NSIS)  → 7z x
.AppImage    → ./Artifact --appimage-extract
directory    → copied + scanned in place (useful for an unpacked Papercusp.app or the sidecar/ dir)
```
 If `7z` (or `hdiutil`/`rpm2cpio`) isn’t available for a given format, the script WARNs and scans the artifact as a raw binary blob instead. Extraction goes into a `mktemp -d` and is `rm -rf`’d on exit. ## Usage [Section titled “Usage”](#usage) 
```sh
bin/audit-bundle.sh path/to/Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb
bin/audit-bundle.sh /home/dev/Papercusp_0.0.1_x86_64.dmg \
                    /home/dev/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi \
                    /home/dev/Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe
```
 Exit codes: * `0` — all clean (`OK: N/N artifacts clean`) * `1` — at least one artifact had a match, or a named artifact was not found. A missing/`not found` artifact is counted as a failure (`FAIL: <artifact> (not found)`), and the exit-1 summary line reads `FAIL: N of M artifacts contain PostHog leaks`. * `2` — usage error ## /admin integration [Section titled “/admin integration”](#admin-integration) Three integration points: 1. **Inside each prod-build command** (Linux, Mac, Windows): the build script runs the auditor on its own output before declaring success. A bundled leak fails the build. 2. **Standalone “Audit prod bundles for PostHog leaks” card** — re-runs against the local `papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/{deb,rpm}` artifacts plus any `.dmg`/`.msi`/`.exe` in `/home/dev/`. 3. **CI-equivalent local check** — `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh` can be called from any context; consider adding it to a pre-release script if/when one exists. ## Verified-clean status (2026-05-13) [Section titled “Verified-clean status (2026-05-13)”](#verified-clean-status-2026-05-13) All four currently-built artifacts pass: 
```plaintext
Papercusp_0.0.1_amd64.deb       (700 MB)  OK
Papercusp_0.0.1_x86_64.dmg      (460 MB)  OK
Papercusp_0.0.1_x64_en-US.msi   (375 MB)  OK
Papercusp_0.0.1_x64-setup.exe   (268 MB)  OK
```
 ## Extending the scanner [Section titled “Extending the scanner”](#extending-the-scanner) If a new “must not ship in prod” secret pattern is identified, edit `papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh`. Prefer a **regex** that matches only the real secret (long random suffix), not a placeholder or path reference: 
```sh
REGEX_NEEDLES=(
  'phx_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}'
  'phc_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}'
  # add new secret-shaped patterns here
)
```
 For a literal-string match, add to the (currently empty) `NEEDLES` array — but be careful: literal needles like `posthog.json` false-positive on source/docs/code, which is exactly why they were removed. For a “this code is present but gated” signal that should surface without failing the build, add to `WARN_NEEDLES`. Then run the standalone audit card to verify existing artifacts before declaring the new policy enforced. ## Why this isn’t an AST / behavioral scan [Section titled “Why this isn’t an AST / behavioral scan”](#why-this-isnt-an-ast--behavioral-scan) The bundles are gigabytes of compiled JS, minified output, native binaries, postgres data files, etc. A `grep -rlF`/`grep -rlE` over the extracted tree is fast (\~5–10s per artifact). The auditor uses **regex** needles tuned to match only real secrets (a `phx_`/`phc_` key with a long random suffix) so it doesn’t false-positive on placeholders or prose — rather than parsing the JS, which would be slow and brittle against minification. ## What the auditor does NOT catch [Section titled “What the auditor does NOT catch”](#what-the-auditor-does-not-catch) * **Behavioral leaks**: code that hardcodes `flags.papercuspai.com` and calls `fetch()` regardless of `isTestingFeaturesEnabled()`. The auditor scans for embedded *secrets*, not for the SDK’s runtime behavior. Defense: the build chain validates `flag-bus.ts`’s gating discipline; no code outside that file should touch PostHog endpoints. * **Same-host PostHog instance accidentally pointing prod traffic somewhere it shouldn’t**. Defense: see the V1 contract — even with a wrong host, the client must not start. * **Telemetry from other sources** (Tauri’s auto-update, OS crash reporters). These are separate trust decisions documented elsewhere. If you need to validate behavioral guarantees, see [verification](/internal/docs/build-system/verification) — that page covers the live-run smoke test (`curl /api/flags/bootstrap`, `ss -tnp | grep flags.papercuspai`) that catches behavioral leaks.

# Proposal — shared desktop build kit (@papercusp/tauri-release-kit)

> Abstracting the Linux/Mac/Windows Tauri build+release pipeline into a shared library usable by both papercusp and myapp. Design, seam contract, migration.

## The ask [Section titled “The ask”](#the-ask) Can the cross-platform (Linux / macOS / Windows) desktop build + release pipeline be abstracted into a generalized shared library that **both papercusp and myapp** use? **Short answer: yes — the release *orchestration* generalizes cleanly; the *sidecar build* does not and must stay a per-app injected seam.** That split is the whole design. ## What the pipeline does today [Section titled “What the pipeline does today”](#what-the-pipeline-does-today) The canonical tree is the **`papercup/papercusp-desktop/` git submodule** (v0.0.2). It builds three platform families, all driven from `bin/`: | Layer | Driver | Where it runs | | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Linux `.deb` / `.AppImage` / `.rpm` (x86\_64, opt. arm64) | `bin/release-local.sh` → `tauri build` | dev host, locally | | macOS universal `.dmg` | `bin/mac-vm-build.sh` → `tauri build --target universal-apple-darwin` | macOS VM over SSH (`:2222`) | | Windows Inno Setup `.exe` | `bin/build-windows-cross.sh` (WI-5651, 2026-07-20, retired the VM leg this row originally described) | cross-compiled on THIS Linux host — no VM, no SSH; WSL2 runtime distro from `scripts/build-rootfs.sh` | `bin/release-local.sh` is the spine. Its steps: 1. **Version bump** across `package.json`, `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`, `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`. 2. **Build the sidecar** (`bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh`, \~1,070 lines). 3. **`tauri build`** per target — Tauri does native bundling + minisign signing in one shot, keyed by `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH`. 4. **Generate `latest.json`** (the auto-updater manifest) — maps `{platform → {url, signature}}` against the GitHub release download URL. 5. **Commit + tag + push** (`desktop-vX.Y.Z[-channel]`). 6. **`gh release create/upload`** (idempotent, `--prerelease` for alpha/beta). ## The core insight: two layers, only one generalizes [Section titled “The core insight: two layers, only one generalizes”](#the-core-insight-two-layers-only-one-generalizes) The pipeline is **release orchestration** wrapped around a **sidecar build**, and they generalize very differently: * **Release orchestration is domain-free.** Version bump, the `tauri build` target matrix, signing, `latest.json` generation, `gh release` upload, and the Mac/Windows **VM SSH orchestration** know nothing about what the app *is*. This is the shareable half. * **The sidecar build is wildly app-specific.** Papercusp’s `build-desktop-sidecar.sh` is **\~1,070 lines** bundling the operator UI + harness + orchestrator + MCP server + node-pty + embedded-postgres + pgvector * external binaries (omp, gh, MinGit, node) + a WSL rootfs tarball. MyApp’s `apps/desktop/scripts/build-sidecar.mjs` is **\~42 lines** of esbuild over one `serve.ts`. There is nothing to share here — it must be an **injected step**. So the library owns the *dance*; each app supplies a `buildSidecar()` plugin and a config object. ### Generic vs injected boundary [Section titled “Generic vs injected boundary”](#generic-vs-injected-boundary) | Concern | Generic (in the kit) | Injected per-app (seam) | | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | Version bump | ✅ field-path-driven updater | which files/fields | | `tauri build` matrix | ✅ Linux x64/arm64, Win cross, Mac universal | which targets enabled | | Signing | ✅ already an env-var seam | key path / passphrase | | `latest.json` / updater manifest | ✅ generator | GH download base URL | | `gh release` create/upload | ✅ idempotent driver | owner/repo, tag pattern, channel→prerelease | | Mac/Windows **VM orchestration** | ✅ SSH/SCP/rsync boilerplate | VM host/port/user/key, build dir | | WSL rootfs builder | ✅ Docker bootstrap algorithm | pkg list, output path | | **Sidecar build** | ❌ stays per-app | the whole `buildSidecar()` impl | | App metadata | ❌ | name, id, bundle targets, category, publisher | ## Where it would live, and how it’s consumed [Section titled “Where it would live, and how it’s consumed”](#where-it-would-live-and-how-its-consumed) MyApp already consumes the shared `@papercusp/*` libs (`@papercusp/sse`, `@papercusp/sync`, `@papercusp/ui-primitives`, `@papercusp/embedded-pg-discovery`, …) via workspace `*` deps — and **those `*` deps resolve to git submodules**: myapp’s `workspaces` maps `@papercusp/sync` → its local `libs/sync`, which is a submodule of the shared `Papercusp/sync` repo (the same repo papercup vendors at `libs/generic/sync`). So the kit should follow that **same shared-submodule pattern**: > **`@papercusp/tauri-release-kit`** — a standalone repo (like `Papercusp/sync`) vendored as a submodule by **both** papercup (`libs/generic/tauri-release-kit`) and myapp (`libs/tauri-release-kit`), exposing (a) a typed `TauriReleaseConfig` + programmatic API and (b) a thin `bin/` CLI. Each app adds a small `release.config.ts` + a `bin/release` wrapper. > **Build it in-tree first, extract to a shared repo second.** Per CLAUDE.md a domain-free lib *starts* as `libs/generic/<name>` — which is exactly where it lives now (feature-complete, 56 tests green). Promoting it to a standalone repo > > * submodule (so myapp can vendor it) is the bridge step, and it’s **owner-gated** (it creates a GitHub repo + rewrites two `.gitmodules`). A git-submodule of the whole desktop tree was considered and rejected: myapp deliberately does not submodule papercusp, and the desktop *shells* legitimately differ (myapp builds its own SPA + a tiny sidecar; papercusp serves operator-vite + the heavy sidecar). Sharing the **kit** (logic), not the **shell** (the Tauri app), is the right grain. ### Seam contract (shipped — `libs/generic/tauri-release-kit/src/types.ts`) [Section titled “Seam contract (shipped — libs/generic/tauri-release-kit/src/types.ts)”](#seam-contract-shipped--libsgenerictauri-release-kitsrctypests) The shipped `TauriReleaseConfig` (authoritative source: `types.ts`): 
```ts
export interface TauriReleaseConfig {
  appName: string;              // "Papercusp"
  appId: string;                // "com.papercusp.desktop"
  root: string;                 // desktop app root (where src-tauri/ lives)
  repo: { owner: string; name: string };
  version: string;              // e.g. "0.2.1"
  channel: Channel;             // 'alpha' | 'beta' | 'stable'
  versionFiles: VersionFile[];  // [{path, kind: 'json'|'cargo-toml'}]
  targets: TargetKey[];         // flat array: ['linux-x86_64', 'macos-universal', …]
  signing: SigningConfig;       // { keyPath, passwordEnv? }
  buildSidecar: BuildSidecar;   // ← the injected seam: (ctx: SidecarContext) => Promise<void>
  latestJsonUrl: (a: { tag: string; name: string }) => string;
  tagFor?: (version: string, channel: Channel) => string;   // override default tag scheme
  classifyArtifact?: (path: string) => PlatformKey | null;  // override artifact→platform mapping
  vm?: Partial<Record<TargetKey, VmConfig>>;  // per-target SSH frame (Mac/Windows)
}
```
 `buildSidecar` is the firewall: papercusp wires in its 1,070-line bash; myapp wires in its esbuild. The kit never knows the difference. ## Migration order [Section titled “Migration order”](#migration-order) 1. **Canonicity (resolved — P-002).** Three desktop trees exist: * `papercup/papercusp-desktop/` — **submodule, v0.0.2, CANONICAL** (has the release + VM build scripts). The kit’s papercusp adoption targets this. * `papercupai-workspace/papercusp-desktop/` — standalone, v0.0.1, **stale**; it lives *outside* the papercup repo, so it can’t be retired from here — flagged for owner cleanup. * `papercup/libs/papercusp/apps/desktop/` — a v0.0.1 second app, but `branding.md` references it as a deliberate “secondary in-repo desktop app” (icon-pack mirror), so it is **not** auto-deleted — whether to retire it is an owner judgment call, not a safe autonomous removal. Net: canonical is recorded; no destructive deletes were made (both non-canonical trees are either out-of-repo or referenced). 2. **Extract the kit** behind the seam; **papercusp adopts it first** — its `bin/release-local.sh` becomes a thin wrapper over the kit. Prove byte-identical (or intentionally-improved) artifacts. 3. **MyApp adopts second** — add `release.config.ts` + `buildSidecar` (its esbuild) + a `bin/release`, giving myapp the Linux/Mac/Windows release flow it currently lacks entirely. ## MyApp adoption (ready once the kit is a shared submodule) [Section titled “MyApp adoption (ready once the kit is a shared submodule)”](#myapp-adoption-ready-once-the-kit-is-a-shared-submodule) The kit is already proven app-agnostic — a second-app-shaped config runs through `runRelease` unchanged (proven by the kit’s app-shape test). Once the kit is vendored into myapp as `libs/tauri-release-kit`, myapp adds two files (and nothing in the kit changes): 
```ts
// apps/desktop/bin/release.config.ts (myapp)
export function makeMyAppConfig({ version, channel }): TauriReleaseConfig {
  return {
    appName: 'MyApp',
    appId: 'com.myapp.desktop',
    root: DESKTOP_ROOT,
    repo: { owner: 'my-org', name: 'myapp' },
    version, channel,
    versionFiles: [
      { path: 'package.json', kind: 'json' },
      { path: 'src-tauri/tauri.conf.json', kind: 'json' },
      { path: 'src-tauri/Cargo.toml', kind: 'cargo-toml' },
    ],
    targets: ['linux-x86_64'],            // its tauri.conf ships deb+appimage
    signing: { keyPath: '~/.myapp/signing/myapp.key' },
    buildSidecar: async ({ root, ports }) => {       // the seam: ~42-line esbuild
      await ports.exec.run('npm', ['run', 'build:spa'], { cwd: root });
      await ports.exec.run('node', ['scripts/build-sidecar.mjs'], { cwd: root });
    },
    latestJsonUrl: ({ tag, name }) =>
      `https://github.com/my-org/myapp/releases/download/${tag}/${name}`,
  };
}
```
 `apps/desktop/bin/release.ts` is the *same* thin CLI as papercusp’s. Every difference is config — appId, repo, bundle targets, and the sidecar seam (myapp’s esbuild vs papercusp’s 1,070-line bash). This hands myapp the version-bump + `latest.json` + gh-release + auto-updater flow it has **none** of today. ## Risks & timing [Section titled “Risks & timing”](#risks--timing) * ⚠ **The release scripts are being actively stabilized right now.** The `windows-public-release-readiness-2026-06-25` drive (and the Mac drive) are editing `build-windows-on-vm.sh`, Authenticode signing, and the WSL rootfs as of this writing. Refactoring mid-cut risks destabilizing a live public release. Safest sequencing: extract **after** that release lands, **or** scope a first pass to the **stable Linux x86\_64 core only** (the part not in flux) and prove it on both apps before touching the VM paths. * The sidecar seam must be drawn carefully — papercusp’s bundling pulls \~1GB of external binaries with platform-specific exclusions (omp/code-server dropped on Windows for NSIS size limits); these stay entirely on papercusp’s side of the seam. ## Open questions (for owner) [Section titled “Open questions (for owner)”](#open-questions-for-owner) 1. Go now, or after the public-release drive stabilizes? 2. Full kit (incl. VM orchestration) vs Linux-core-first slice? 3. `libs/generic/` npm package (recommended) vs a standalone `Papercusp/tauri-release-kit` repo?

# Verifying a build

> How to smoke-test each platform end-to-end before declaring the artifact good to ship.

## Naming note: the bundle is now `Papercusp GUI`, and there’s a GUI/Server split [Section titled “Naming note: the bundle is now Papercusp GUI, and there’s a GUI/Server split”](#naming-note-the-bundle-is-now-papercusp-gui-and-theres-a-guiserver-split) `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`’s `productName` is now **`Papercusp GUI`** (`identifier: com.papercusp.gui`, currently `version: 0.0.3`) — was plain `Papercusp`. Tauri derives every bundle filename and the installed `.app`/install directory from `productName`, so **every artifact below now carries a `Papercusp GUI_<version>_…` filename**, the macOS app is `Papercusp GUI.app` (mounted at `/Volumes/Papercusp GUI/`), and the Windows install dir/process is `Papercusp GUI`. The in-window title bar (`app.windows[0].title`) is untouched — it still reads plain **“Papercusp”**. There is now also a **two-bundle GUI/Server split** — one Rust binary, two Tauri roles baked via a distinct `identifier` (`src-tauri/src/app_role.rs` + `tauri.server.conf.json`): **`Papercusp GUI`** (`com.papercusp.gui`, the desktop app covered by this page) and **`Papercusp Server`** (`com.papercusp.server`, a headless-hosting variant — see `bin/mac-vm-build.sh`). This page verifies the **GUI** role only; don’t confuse a `Papercusp Server_*` artifact for the one these steps exercise. The Windows target list also grew an `nsis` bundle (`.exe`) alongside `msi` — a Windows release now ships both. The `0.0.3` in the examples below is illustrative and WILL be stale by the time you read this — confirm the real value with `node -p "require('./papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json').version"` and substitute it (or just glob `Papercusp\ GUI_*_amd64.deb` etc.). ## Pre-flight check (any platform) [Section titled “Pre-flight check (any platform)”](#pre-flight-check-any-platform) Re-run the auditor on every artifact: 
```sh
papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh \
  "papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_amd64.deb" \
  "/home/dev/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_x64.dmg" \
  "/home/dev/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_x64_en-US.msi" \
  "/home/dev/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_x64-setup.exe"
```
 Or click **Audit prod bundles for PostHog leaks** in `/admin`. Should print `OK: 4/4`. If any FAIL, **stop** — the artifact must not ship. (The `.dmg` name now carries the build’s arch, e.g. `_x64`/`_aarch64` — `mac-vm-build.sh` packs per-arch DMGs itself via a direct `hdiutil create` rather than relying on Tauri’s `universal-apple-darwin` dmg bundler; if you build a genuine universal binary through Tauri directly instead, the artifact is still `Papercusp GUI_<version>_universal.dmg`.) *** ## Linux .deb verification [Section titled “Linux .deb verification”](#linux-deb-verification) ### 1. Install + launch [Section titled “1. Install + launch”](#1-install--launch) 
```sh
sudo dpkg -i "papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_amd64.deb"
papercusp-desktop
```
 ⚠ **`papercusp` (bare) no longer launches the app** (WI-2902, 2026-07-05): the postinstall script now writes `/usr/bin/papercusp` as a **setup/tutorial CLI dispatcher** (`papercusp setup` / `papercusp tutorial` / `papercusp onboard` — else it prints usage and exits 2). The actual GUI binary the .deb installs is `papercusp-desktop` (the Cargo `[[bin]]` name) — launch that, or use the installed desktop-menu icon. Or click **Install + launch Linux .deb** in `/admin`. Expected: a brief bootstrap page, then the window navigates to the operator UI within \~5–15s (a first boot pays `initdb` + migrations inside `serve.mjs`, so allow longer). Title bar “Papercusp”. If it stays stuck on the bootstrap page, the sidecar never reached the preflight-ready state → check the serve logs. ### 2. Verify no discovery files leaked [Section titled “2. Verify no discovery files leaked”](#2-verify-no-discovery-files-leaked) 
```sh
sudo useradd -m papercusp-verify
sudo -u papercusp-verify ls -la ~papercusp-verify/.papercusp/ 2>&1
```
 Expected: `No such file or directory`. The bundle never created the file. ### 3. Flag bootstrap silent [Section titled “3. Flag bootstrap silent”](#3-flag-bootstrap-silent) 
```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3055/api/flags/bootstrap | jq
```
 Wait — the prod binary doesn’t serve on `:3055`. The sidecar (`node serve.mjs`) picks a free port, which it records in `~/.papercusp/operator.json` (the authoritative source). Read it from there, or grep the listener. 
```sh
PROD_PORT=$(jq -r .port ~/.papercusp/operator.json)
# Fallback if operator.json isn't present:
# PROD_PORT=$(ss -tnlp | awk '/serve\.mjs|node/{split($4,a,":"); print a[2]}' | sort -u | grep -v 3055 | head -1)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:${PROD_PORT}/api/flags/bootstrap | jq
```
 Expected — a `source: "defaults"` payload whose `flags` object carries the **full** flag map. `getAllFlags` builds it via `resolveWithDefaults`, which spreads every key in `FLAG_DEFAULTS` (libs/flags/src/types.ts), so on a clean install you get **all \~101 flag keys**, not a handful. Many of them legitimately default `true` (51 of the keys default on, 50 off), so a clean install showing lots of `true` flags is correct, not a leak. A representative excerpt: 
```json
{
  "flags": {
```
