    "papercusp-cloudflare-publish": false,
    "papercusp-harness-phases": false,
    "papercusp-design": false,
    "papercusp-testing": false,
    "papercusp-the-hive": true,
    "papercusp-video-channels": true,
    "papercusp-voice-channels": true
    // …all remaining flag keys, each at its FLAG_DEFAULTS value
  },
  "evaluatedAt": 1234567890,
  "source": "defaults"
}
```
 `source` must be `"defaults"` (the only other values are `"posthog"` and `"override"`). A `"posthog"` source on a clean install means PostHog config leaked in. Don’t diff against a fixed key list — verify each value against `FLAG_DEFAULTS` in `libs/flags/src/types.ts` (the authoritative full map). Two things to know when comparing: (1) the payload contains **every** flag key, so a verifier expecting a short fixed list will falsely flag a correct install; (2) `getAllFlags` runs the stored PG override row through `resolveWithDefaults`, which **drops retired/unknown keys** — e.g. `papercusp-oracle` (folded into `papercusp-testing` by owner ask 2026-06-10) and the long-gone `SNAPSHOTS` key (retired in `retire-snapshots-instance-spec-2026-06-09`; the reproducible clone is now the ungated InstanceSpec) will never appear even if the stored row still carries them. (`papercusp-templates` / `papercusp-marketplace` were likewise retired — distribution lives in the ungated Cupboard.) ### 4. No outbound PostHog traffic [Section titled “4. No outbound PostHog traffic”](#4-no-outbound-posthog-traffic) 
```sh
sudo ss -tnp | grep -E "flags.papercuspai|posthog"
```
 Expected: empty. ### 5. Embedded PG discovery [Section titled “5. Embedded PG discovery”](#5-embedded-pg-discovery) 
```sh
cat ~/.papercusp/embedded-pg.json
cat ~/.papercusp/operator.json
```
 Expected: JSON with a non-5432 port (both files written by `serve.mjs`). **Confirms the desktop spawned its own embedded PG, didn’t talk to native `:5432`.** ### 6. Feature data loads [Section titled “6. Feature data loads”](#6-feature-data-loads) In the app, navigate to **Harness → sheets**. The Feature Queue panel should populate with features (not empty). No errors in the DevTools console. ### 7. Closed-flag routes really 404 [Section titled “7. Closed-flag routes really 404”](#7-closed-flag-routes-really-404) 
```sh

(Note: 51 flags default `true`, so a clean install with many `true` flags is **correct** — only a *mismatch* against `FLAG_DEFAULTS` is a leak.) | | A retired key (e.g. `papercusp-oracle`, `papercusp-snapshots`) appears in the payload | `resolveWithDefaults` should have dropped it — stored override row leaking retired keys | | `ss -tnp` shows connection to `flags.papercuspai.com` | App phoning home in clean-install state — leak | | Window stuck on the bootstrap page (never navigates off `web/index.html`) | The sidecar never became ready — check the preflight handshake / serve logs | | `embedded-pg.json` / `operator.json` missing, or app connects to `:5432` | Embedded PG didn’t bootstrap (`serve.mjs` owns this) | | Sheets harness shows 0 features when the API returns features | Feature loading broken | | Window shows the **dev** server’s app (URL has `:3055`) | The webview pointed at the dev server instead of the bundled sidecar — rebuild | *** ## A self-contained checklist [Section titled “A self-contained checklist”](#a-self-contained-checklist) Copy this and run top to bottom: 
```sh
# 1. Auditor pass
papercusp-desktop/bin/audit-bundle.sh \
  "papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_amd64.deb" \
  "/home/dev/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_x64.dmg" \
  "/home/dev/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_x64_en-US.msi" \
  "/home/dev/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_x64-setup.exe"


# 2. Linux install + launch + smoke
sudo dpkg -i "papercupai-workspace/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp GUI_0.0.3_amd64.deb"
setsid /usr/bin/papercusp-desktop >/dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null &
sleep 15
PORT=$(jq -r .port ~/.papercusp/operator.json)
echo "operator port: $PORT"

 (`/usr/bin/papercusp` is now a setup/tutorial CLI dispatcher, not the app launcher — see the callout above. The GUI binary + package name changed to `papercusp-desktop` / `papercusp-gui`; only the bundle/app-directory display name changed to `Papercusp GUI`.) When every line is green, the artifact is ship-ready for that platform.

# VMs (Mac + Windows + Linux test)

> SSH access, sudo credentials, port maps, disk-sizing notes, the Windows-VM survival kit, and the Linux clean-room test VM.

## Inventory [Section titled “Inventory”](#inventory) | VM | Host process | SSH port | Display | Inside-VM repo path | | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **macOS Sonoma** (x86\_64) | `qemu-system-x86_64 ... mac_hdd_ng.img` | `2222` | SPICE on `127.0.0.1:5930` | rsync’d `~/papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop` (the in-VM `~/papercupai/papercusp-desktop` checkout is legacy/broken — see below) | | **Windows 11** | `qemu-system-x86_64 ... windows_hdd.qcow2` | `2223` | SPICE on `127.0.0.1:5931` | `C:\Users\User\papercupai\papercusp-desktop` | | **Linux test** `clean` (Ubuntu 24.04) | `qemu-system-x86_64 … run/<name>/overlay.qcow2` (via `scripts/linux-test-vm/vmctl`) | `2224` | SPICE on `127.0.0.1:5932` | n/a — installs the packaged `.deb` (no checkout) | | **Linux fed** `fed-a`/`fed-b` (Ubuntu 24.04) | same golden image, +2nd NIC on `pcusp-fedbr0` (via `bin/vm-federation.sh`) | `2225`/`2226` | SPICE `127.0.0.1:5933`/`5934` | n/a — two-machine federation testing | The **Mac** and **Windows** VMs exist only to *produce* their platform’s Tauri bundle. The **Linux test** VM is different in kind — it *consumes* the built `.deb`, fresh-installing it on a pristine Ubuntu to validate the shipped artifact (and to act as a separate machine for federation testing). Day-to-day operator dev (`:3055`) and Linux builds still run entirely on the host. ## Linux test VM (clean-room: fresh-install + federation) [Section titled “Linux test VM (clean-room: fresh-install + federation)”](#linux-test-vm-clean-room-fresh-install--federation) Unlike the build VMs, this is a **disposable Ubuntu 24.04 clean-room** for testing the packaged `.deb` in true isolation — driven by **`papercusp-desktop/scripts/linux-test-vm/vmctl`**, not a hand-rolled boot script. It exists for (1) **fresh-install testing** the real `.deb` on a pristine machine, and (2) acting as a **separate machine** for shared-harness / federation testing. Plan: `linux-test-vm-and-federation-2026-06-04`. * **Scripts (versioned):** `papercusp-desktop/scripts/linux-test-vm/` — `vmctl`, `boot-vm.sh`, `cloud-init/`, `lib/common.sh`. * **Images (outside the repo, never committed):** `~/papercup-linux-test-vm/` — `images/golden.qcow2` + per-instance `run/<name>/overlay.qcow2`. SSH key `~/.ssh/papercup-vm-linux` (auto-generated on first `provision`). * **Base:** Ubuntu 24.04 cloud image + a *minimal X stack* (openbox via getty-autologin + `startx`) — deliberately **not** GNOME (which fails to register its session on the qxl GPU) and with **no** preinstalled webkit, so `apt install ./Papercusp.deb` pulls the WebKitGTK runtime from scratch (a truer fresh install). 
```sh
cd papercusp-desktop/scripts/linux-test-vm
./vmctl provision            # one-time: build the golden image (~10–15 min)
./vmctl up clean             # boot a pristine overlay
./vmctl install clean        # scp newest .deb in + apt install (the fresh-install test)
./vmctl verify clean         # assert deps/PG/operator/window + screenshot → PASS/FAIL
./vmctl gui clean            # (run yourself) open a SPICE viewer to click around
./vmctl reset clean          # wipe back to a pristine overlay
./vmctl down clean           # power off
```
 `install` defaults to the newest `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/Papercusp_*_amd64.deb` (pass a path to override). `verify` checks: package installs (dpkg), `apt-get -s check` confirms no missing/broken dependencies, binary `ldd`-resolves, app process up, embedded Postgres running, operator responds **on its dynamic port** (parsed from the app log — *not* a fixed `:3070`), and captures a window screenshot via the qemu monitor (`screendump`). Artifacts land in `run/<name>/verify/`. Tunables: `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_RAM_MB`, `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_CPUS`, `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_DISK`, `PAPERCUSP_TESTVM_HOME`. **It earns its keep.** The first fresh-install run caught that the shipped `.deb` had **no database** on a clean machine: the node-based sidecar spawns in `src-tauri/src/main.rs` used a bare `Command::new("node")` while the packaged process PATH has no `node` — fixed by routing all three spawns through the bundled-node PATH (`bundled_path_env`) like `spawn_sidecar` does. The dev box hides this because it always has `node` on PATH, which is exactly why a clean VM is necessary. (Plan decision D-009.) This is the **historical** (pre-refactor) shape of the bug: the embedded-Postgres + zero-cache process management has since moved **into `serve.mjs`** (`apps/operator/bin/serve.ts`), and `zero-cache-server` is no longer shipped — so the `spawn_embedded_postgres_server` / `spawn_zero_cache_server` functions no longer exist in `main.rs`. The bundled-PATH discipline still applies to the surviving `serve.mjs` spawn. ### Two-machine federation (Phase 2) [Section titled “Two-machine federation (Phase 2)”](#two-machine-federation-phase-2) The same VMs double as **separate machines** for cross-machine federation testing — proving the packaged `.deb` federates (a write on one machine lands in the other’s PG) over a real OS + real network hop, not just loopback. Driven by **`papercusp-desktop/bin/vm-federation.sh`**, which reuses the one-box smokes’ assertion core (`bin/lib/federation-asserts.sh`, D-003) over an SSH driver. 
```sh
cd papercusp-desktop
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=2 --dht=testnet --net=bridge   # primary: fed-a ↔ fed-b
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=1                               # host instance ↔ fed-a VM
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=2 --net=socket                 # rootless (no sudo) fallback
bin/vm-federation.sh --vms=2 --no-reset --skip-install    # fast iteration (reuse overlays)
```
 * **Network (D-016):** every fed VM keeps its slirp NIC (internet/SSH/SPICE) and gets a **second** NIC on host bridge `pcusp-fedbr0` (`10.77.0.0/24`, host `10.77.0.1`) with a static guest IP — no dnsmasq/NAT. The host runs a `hyperdht/testnet` advertised on the bridge IP; both VMs set `PAPERCUSP_DHT_BOOTSTRAP` to it → deterministic discovery over a real hop. `--net=socket` is a rootless dual-NIC fallback (qemu socket L2, exactly two VMs). * **Identities:** `papercupai` / `aviynw` via per-instance `GH_TOKEN` (resolved by `gh-token.ts`); `gh` + `postgresql-client` are apt-installed in each VM as driver prereqs. * **Up-front `.deb` gate (P-011):** a static grep of the packaged `serve.mjs` (the sidecar boot entry; `host.mjs` is retired) asserts it carries `PAPERCUSP_DHT_BOOTSTRAP` support + `[swarm]` logs (landed 2026-06-02), failing fast on an older `.deb` that would silently use the public DHT. **Status (verified 2026-06-07, unattended runs on a current `.deb`):** the harness proves everything up to the holepunch boundary in **both modes** — `--vms=2` *and* `--vms=1` reach fresh-install, clean embedded-PG boot on a fresh `initdb`, write-free share (`state:"booted"` both sides), and **cross-machine swarm-join** (both identities announcing on the same topic + DHT). Neither reaches the bidirectional merge, and the boundary is now fully classified: hyperdht **holepunch does not complete between any two endpoints on ONE physical host** — VM↔VM *and* host↔VM both sit at `conns=0` in raw-hyperswarm tests (same topic, same bridge-advertised bootstrap, working UDP both directions), so neither the single-NIC+NAT candidate nor the host’s no-NAT network position rescues it (plan D-017/D-018). `--dht=public` (P-012) is **INCONCLUSIVE** by same-host NAT hairpin, per the plan’s D-004 best-effort caveat — though both peers do announce on the real public DHT through slirp. The full bidirectional-merge acceptance needs **truly separate machines** — and that gate was **discharged on Hetzner (2026-06-08, plan D-019)**: the Tier-3 p2p-perf suite on two separate Hetzner cpx31 VMs over the public DHT got `peer_connected` on both peers, cross-region append→visible p95 = 950.5 ms, and a real NAT holepunch (`punches=1 relaySuccess=0`) — positively confirming the single-host `conns=0` wall is a topology artifact (no second physical box needed; the cloud-deployment layer provides the separate machines on-demand). It was further confirmed **cross-region** (ash↔hil: append→visible p95 = 1115.5 ms over real transcontinental WAN) and — via `bin/deb-hetzner-federation.sh` — for the **shipped `.deb` itself** (two Hetzner VMs, the `.deb`’s headless sidecar, `peer_connected` + bidirectional `origin=remote` merge over the public DHT). (These last two results are recorded in the agent-insight below; the `linux-test-vm-and-federation-2026-06-04` plan’s decision log ends at D-019, so they have no D-020/D-021 plan citation.) The finding, the clean-machine traps the harness flushed out (slirp-subnet, embedded-PG boot race, the sidecar port-grep race, embedded-pg-refuses-root, and the bundled `pgvector` needing the 24.04 toolchain), and the Hetzner discharge are in the agent-insight [VM federation harness](/internal/docs/agent-insights/vm-federation-separate-machine-proof). ## SSH commands [Section titled “SSH commands”](#ssh-commands) 
```sh
# Mac
ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-mac -p 2222 aviweiss@127.0.0.1
# Windows
ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -p 2223 User@127.0.0.1
```
 Inside the Mac VM, `sudo` password is `aviweiss`. Windows VM has no sudo concept; `User` has admin rights. ## Booting them [Section titled “Booting them”](#booting-them) ### Mac VM [Section titled “Mac VM”](#mac-vm) 
```sh
systemctl --user start papercup-vm-mac.service     # the supported path
```
 The unit runs **`boot-sonoma-durable.sh`** (32 GB RAM, `Type=forking` + `PIDFile=qemu.pid`, QMP control socket at `OSX-KVM/qmp.sock`, logs in `OSX-KVM/logs/qemu-current.log`, graceful QMP `system_powerdown` on stop). \~60–120s to SSH-ready. ⚠ Do **not** launch `boot-sonoma.sh` for routine boots — it is the *installer-media* variant (16 GB, attaches `BaseSystem.img`, currently a macOS Tahoe installer) and was the cause of the 2026-06-11 service crash-loop split-brain. If SSH is dead and the service can’t bind SPICE `:5930`, an orphaned qemu probably holds the ports and may be parked at the OpenCore boot picker — recover it via QMP, never `pkill`: [mac-vm-qmp-recovery](/internal/docs/agent-insights/mac-vm-qmp-recovery). To view the desktop: `remote-viewer spice://127.0.0.1:5930`. ### Windows VM [Section titled “Windows VM”](#windows-vm) 
```sh
cd ~/windows-vm
nohup bash boot-windows.sh > /tmp/win-boot.log 2>&1 &
```
 \~90s to SSH-ready. (To get a desktop window in one shot, `~/windows-vm/launch-vm-and-viewer.sh` boots the VM and opens `remote-viewer spice://127.0.0.1:5931`.) ## Resource specs (current; tunable in the boot scripts) [Section titled “Resource specs (current; tunable in the boot scripts)”](#resource-specs-current-tunable-in-the-boot-scripts) | | macOS VM | Windows VM | | ------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | | RAM | 32 GB (was 16; Xcode + Rust eats RAM) | 32 GiB (was 8 GB pre-2026-05-12) | | vCPUs | 8 (`-smp 8`: 4 cores × 2 threads) | 16 | | Disk | 120 GB qcow2 (grown from 80 on 2026-05-13) | `windows_hdd.qcow2`, \~120 GB qcow2 | | Cache | writeback | writeback | | Net | virtio-net-pci | e1000 | | Storage | AHCI | AHCI | ## Disk discipline [Section titled “Disk discipline”](#disk-discipline) Tauri builds are huge. A clean Mac build typically consumes: * \~5 GB Rust target dir (`papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/`) * \~3 GB npm cache (`~/Library/Caches/`) * \~1.5 GB built node\_modules * \~500 MB intermediate `.dmg` staging * \~10 GB Xcode CoreSimulator runtimes (if you build iOS at all) **Pre-build check** the user reflexively runs: `df -h /` on each VM. If `<10 GB` free, clean up before kicking off a build — mid-build ENOSPC is a hard failure and leaves a broken-half state. The macOS VM has been on the verge of full multiple times. Safe deletes when desperate: 
```sh
# iOS simulator runtimes (recreatable in Xcode → Settings → Platforms)
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices/*    # device instances only
# spm cache
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/SourcePackages/
# Rust target (forces clean rebuild but reclaims ~3-5 GB)
rm -rf ~/papercup-build-mac/papercup/papercusp-desktop/src-tauri/target
```
 The canonical Mac build does **not** use the in-VM `~/papercupai/papercusp-desktop` checkout — that one is a legacy/broken tree (its git was historically corrupt; don’t resurrect it, per the mac-desktop-release-readiness plan). `build-mac-prod` instead `rsync`s the canonical tree into an isolated `~/papercup-build-mac/papercup` and builds there, so that’s the target worth clearing. The Linux host (\~40-50 GB free typical) doesn’t hit ENOSPC during builds but the Rust target dir there does grow to \~5 GB. ## Node version pinning [Section titled “Node version pinning”](#node-version-pinning) Both VMs run **nvm + Node 22** for the build-time `npm install` + `tauri build`. (This is separate from the *bundled* runtime that ships inside the artifact — `bin/build-desktop-sidecar.sh` vendors Node **v24** into `sidecar/bin/node`.) Node 20 hangs / errors during `npm install`. 
```sh
# In either VM:
nvm install 22       # one-time
nvm use 22           # every shell
```
 The **`build-mac-prod`** `/admin` command pins Node 22 via `bin/mac-vm-build.sh` (which sources `~/.nvm/nvm.sh` and runs `nvm use 22`). The **`build-windows-prod`** command instead runs a PowerShell script (`win-build.ps1`) — bash `nvm` doesn’t apply there, so that script handles its own Node pinning. If you SSH into the Mac VM manually, don’t forget `nvm use 22`. ## npm `--legacy-peer-deps` is required [Section titled “npm --legacy-peer-deps is required”](#npm---legacy-peer-deps-is-required) The workspace’s peer-dep tree has unresolvable conflicts that make `npm install` hang **silently with 0% CPU** in modern npm. **Always pass `--legacy-peer-deps`** for installs done in the build context. The /admin scripts do this; if you do manual installs in either VM, you must too. ## Mac VM environment quirks [Section titled “Mac VM environment quirks”](#mac-vm-environment-quirks) * **Bundled-Node PATH**: GUI-launched apps on macOS inherit `$PATH = /usr/bin:/bin` — Homebrew Node, nvm Node, brew-installed `pg_dump` / `libpq` are all invisible. `main.rs:bundled_path_env()` builds a `PATH` with the shipped `sidecar/bin/` (node/gh) prepended, and every node-based spawn (currently the `serve.mjs` sidecar) runs through it. **If you add a new spawn**, route it through the same helper. * **Gatekeeper**: the DMG is unsigned. First launch will be blocked. The install-mac-dmg `/admin` command strips quarantine via `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Papercusp.app`. If launching by hand, you’ll need to do this too. ## Windows VM crashes routinely [Section titled “Windows VM crashes routinely”](#windows-vm-crashes-routinely) The Windows VM crashed **6+ times during a single build session** (2026-05-13). Symptoms: SSH hangs indefinitely, `qemu-system-x86_64` process disappears, `/tmp/win-boot.log` last line is a kernel power error. **Recovery procedure** (this happens often enough it’s worth automating; for now do it manually): 
```sh
# Verify dead
ps -ef | grep -v grep | grep "qemu.*windows_hdd"   # → should be empty


# Restart
cd ~/windows-vm && nohup bash boot-windows.sh > /tmp/win-boot.log 2>&1 &


# Wait ~90s
sleep 90 && ssh -i ~/.ssh/papercup-vm-win -p 2223 User@127.0.0.1 'echo ok'


# Re-run the build (it'll resume from incremental Rust cache if not corrupted)
```
 The Rust target dir in the Windows VM survives crashes — it’s qcow2 + AHCI writeback so a few seconds of write-back data may be lost, but cargo’s atomic incremental graph handles this gracefully. If a build was mid-`tauri build` when the VM crashed, you may need to delete and recreate `C:\Users\User\papercusp-desktop\src-tauri\binaries\embedded-postgres-server-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.exe` — `tauri-bundler` doesn’t always recover cleanly from in-place sidecar binary writes when the process disappears mid-write. Symptom: `failed to remove symlink ... os error 5`. ## Why builds don’t run in containers [Section titled “Why builds don’t run in containers”](#why-builds-dont-run-in-containers) The Tauri team’s MSI tooling (`wix`) requires Windows, and Apple’s code-signing tooling requires macOS. We don’t currently sign builds (the audit pipeline assumes unsigned binaries) but the Mac build does need to be a Darwin host for `cargo` to cross-compile to `x86_64-apple-darwin`. So the VMs aren’t replaceable by Linux containers without a substantial cross-compile setup. ## Build cancellation [Section titled “Build cancellation”](#build-cancellation) The `/admin` build commands run via `bash -lic`. Closing the SSE stream (Stop button or browser close) sends `SIGTERM` to the whole process group — which cleanly terminates the local `npm` and `tauri build` invocations on the host, but the SSH-driven Mac/Windows builds **continue running inside the VM** even after SIGTERM kills the SSH client. To actually cancel a Mac/Windows build mid-flight, SSH in separately and `pkill -f "tauri build\|cargo"`.

# The layered agent-liveness model

> How Papercusp decides an agent is alive — supervision, stream activity, dispatch beats, coord beats — which consumers read which legs, and why the sweep never prods processes directly.

Shipped by `agent-liveness-heartbeat-hardening-2026-06-12` (after the stale-claims sweep and EI-348). This page is the one mental model; the per-module docs live in the source headers it links. ## The four signals, robustness-ordered [Section titled “The four signals, robustness-ordered”](#the-four-signals-robustness-ordered) | # | Signal | Written by | Semantics | Covers a long no-tool-call turn? | | - | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | | 1 | **Supervision heartbeat** — `spawned_agents.heartbeat_at` | The host that OWNS the process: the operator’s nursery loop (`fleet/operator-spawn.ts ensureSpawnHeartbeatLoop`) for cups; the psu launcher’s supervisor beat (`scripts/psu-launcher.mjs startSupervisorBeat` → the bootstrap-su heartbeat endpoint) for interactive sessions | ”I hold this process handle and it is alive” | **Yes** | | 2 | **Stream activity** — `spawned_agents.last_output_at` (cups, mig 233) · pty discovery-file `lastOutputAt` (psu pty sessions) | The runner’s in-process stdout/stderr listeners (`dbos/orchestrator-runner.ts onOutputActivity`); the pty host’s activity tracker (`scripts/psu-pty-host.mjs makeActivityTracker`) | “The agent emitted bytes just now” — *generating*, not merely alive | Yes, and it distinguishes generating from wedged | | 3 | **Dispatch beat** — `coord_presence.last_active_at` AND `.heartbeat_at` via `touchActivity` | The projected-tool dispatch seam (`projected-tool-deps.ts recordInvocationImpl` → `agent-tools/coordination/dispatch-heartbeat.ts`), throttled per owner | ”The agent made ANY platform tool call recently” — the per-edit lock hook traffic alone keeps an actively-editing session warm | No (but such turns also make no edits) | | 4 | **Coord beat** — `coord_presence.heartbeat_at` | `coord:declare-intent`, `coord:inbox` reads | ”The agent touched the coordination layer recently” | No | A projected dispatch IS genuine activity, so leg 3 beats via `touchActivity` (bumps `last_active_at` *and* `heartbeat_at`, presence-v2 D-003) — distinct from the pure keepalive `touchHeartbeat` (leg 1’s 60s supervisor beat) which bumps `heartbeat_at` only. Both are no-ops when no presence row exists, so one-shot HTTP callers never mint roster rows. Two invariants: * **A signal is written by whoever can actually observe it.** The sweep/roster never `kill -0`s processes: it’s same-host-only, session agents have no PID (`coord_presence.pid` is null for HTTP MCP clients), and alive ≠ progressing — a wedged process passes `kill -0` forever. Supervision heartbeats ARE process-prodding, done by the process-owner and projected into PG where every host can read them. * **Annotate, don’t suppress** (plan D-002) — for the badge and for attended / non-cup sessions: stream-activity staleness flags a `possibly_wedged` candidate for humans/the Mug (`fleet:tree`, `isPossiblyWedged` in `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts`) without feeding claim release, so an attended-but-quiet session keeps its claims. **The exception is a supervised local cup under the now-shipped wedge auto-reaper** (D-006, flag `WEDGE_AUTO_REAP` default ON): a cup whose stream is silent past 30min IS reaped — `reapWedgedLocalSpawns` (`fleet/operator-spawn.ts`) durably cancels it via `cancelSubtree`, which DOES release its work-item and plan-item claims (`claimsReleased` / `planClaimsReleased` in `fleet/nursery.ts`) before the local abort. For a wedged cup, then, stream-activity staleness (leg 2) feeds claim release; absence of any observed output is still never treated as a wedge. ## Which consumers read which legs [Section titled “Which consumers read which legs”](#which-consumers-read-which-legs) | Consumer | Legs read | Where | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Stale-claims sweep (releases `taken_by` of dead holders) | 1 + 3/4 (presence OR nursery, alias-aware per mig 225) | `work-items-stale-claims.ts` | | Spawn reclaim (frees ceiling slots of dead-host spawns) | 1, plus same-host pid-alive as a keep-alive override (EI-85) | `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts` | | Colony roster / Sessions view | best of 1 (nursery join, pid-alive definitive) and 3/4 (presence) — EI-348 | `adv-roster.ts mergeRosterEntries` | | Wedge badge (`possibly_wedged`) | 1 fresh AND 2 stale | `fleet:tree` → `isPossiblyWedged` | | Wedge auto-reaper (cancels + releases claims of supervised cups silent past threshold) | 1 fresh AND 2 stale | `fleet/operator-spawn.ts reapWedgedLocalSpawns` (flag `WEDGE_AUTO_REAP`, default ON) | **The rule for new consumers: read the strongest leg available for the agent class, not just presence.** EI-348 was exactly a consumer reading only leg 3/4 for agents whose truth lived in leg 1. For cups, legs 1 and 2 are not two independent timers: the nursery heartbeat loop (`ensureSpawnHeartbeatLoop`) is one tick on `SPAWN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS` that (a) bumps `heartbeat_at`, (b) write-throughs `last_output_at` for streams that moved since the last persist (`GREATEST`-monotonic, P-008 — zero extra write cadence), and (c) runs the wedge auto-reaper. The runner’s `onOutputActivity` only records the in-process stream timestamp; this tick is what persists it. ## The supervisability boundary [Section titled “The supervisability boundary”](#the-supervisability-boundary) Processes our infrastructure launches are fully supervisable: fleet cups (operator children) and psu sessions (the launcher stays parent in both the plain and managed-pty paths; the pty host additionally sees every byte). The remainder — a bare `claude` launched outside psu, remote claude.ai/code sessions, desktop embedded chat — can only be observed through their platform traffic (legs 3/4). That is why the dispatch beat exists and ships enabled. ## Tuning knobs [Section titled “Tuning knobs”](#tuning-knobs) * `DISPATCH_BEAT_INTERVAL_MS` (45s) — `dispatch-heartbeat.ts` * `SUPERVISOR_BEAT_MS` (60s) — `psu-launcher.mjs` * `SPAWN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS` (60s) — `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts` * `ACTIVITY_PERSIST_MS` (15s, pty discovery write-through) — `psu-pty-host.mjs` * `WEDGE_SILENT_MS` (10min, badge threshold) — `fleet/spawn-reclaim.ts` * `WEDGE_REAP_SILENT_MS` (30min, env `PAPERCUSP_WEDGE_REAP_MS`, reaper threshold — distinct from and longer than the badge’s) — `fleet/operator-spawn.ts` * `WEDGE_AUTO_REAP` flag (default ON, D-006) — `libs/flags/src/types.ts` * Liveness windows: `LIVE_MS` 60s / `STALE_MS` 10min (`liveness.ts`) · claim-sweep grace `STALE_CLAIM_GRACE_MS` 10min (`work-items-stale-claims.ts`)

# Checkpoints and facts — the durable carry surfaces

> The memory layers that carry agent state across turns, wakes, compactions, and successors — work-item checkpoints, loop checkpoints, standing facts, and where each is stored and re-injected.

Agents are transient; work is not. Papercusp gives a session four distinct places to park state, each with a different **delivery guarantee** — route by how the state must come back, not by habit. ## The four layers [Section titled “The four layers”](#the-four-layers) | Layer | Verb | Delivery | Use for | | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Work-item checkpoint | `work_items:checkpoint { id, checkpoint }` | Re-injected when the item is next picked up — by you or any successor | In-flight progress on one item: what’s done, what’s left, the next step | | Loop checkpoint | `loop:checkpoint { did, left, insight, next }` | Re-injected on the armed loop’s next wake; a cold wake reconstructs from it | An engine loop’s iteration state | | Standing fact | `facts:assert { scope, scopeRef?, key, body }` | Folded **verbatim** into every relevant orient/brief until retracted (TTL default 7d) | Scoped conclusions future turns must see deterministically (“X is owner-residue — exclude it”) | | Shared memory | `memory:remember` | Semantic recall (orient’s mem0 hit list, `memory:search`) | Fuzzy background worth recalling, not guaranteed delivery | Rules of thumb: a checkpoint is *per unit of work*, a fact is *per conclusion*, memory is *per thing worth knowing*. Live ephemera (intents, handoffs, presence) belong to `coord:*`, not to any of these. ## Where checkpoints actually live [Section titled “Where checkpoints actually live”](#where-checkpoints-actually-live) Work-item, loop, and pot checkpoints are rows in **`harness_shared.carry_notes`**, keyed by scope (`workitem:<harness>:<WI-id>`, `loop:…`, `pot`) — migration 472. Two traps: * `harness_shared.work_item_checkpoints` was the legacy checkpoint table; migration 494 folds any stragglers into `carry_notes` and drops it. * `work_items:get` at the trimmed payload tier does **not** surface an item’s checkpoint — absence of a checkpoint in a `get` is not evidence none exists. Read directly: `select note from harness_shared.carry_notes where scope like 'workitem:%:<id>'`. ## Facts discipline [Section titled “Facts discipline”](#facts-discipline) `facts:list { scope }` before asserting (upsert is by key — don’t fork a second key for the same conclusion). `facts:retract` the moment a fact stops being true: a stale fact delivered verbatim into every future brief is worse than none. Bodies store at ≤500 chars — write tight conclusions, not essays. ## Why this exists [Section titled “Why this exists”](#why-this-exists) Compaction ([context compaction](/internal/docs/agents/compaction)) and session death are routine, not exceptional. State parked on these surfaces survives both losslessly; state carried only in conversation prose degrades into a summary and goes stale. The discipline is: flush first, then let prose point at what was flushed.

# The seat-donation model — fleet-scoped vs pot-scoped agent-seat offers

> How a host donates spawn capacity (agent_slot allotments) to a single fleet or a whole shared pot, why spawn-audience is a grant separate from trust, the host-side honor gates that stay fail-closed either way, and how the spend paths resolve offers. Plan pot-seat-pools-prose-ux-2026-07-18.

## One paragraph [Section titled “One paragraph”](#one-paragraph) A host donates agent-seat capacity — an `agent_slot` allotment, N seats of a given model·effort on one of its gateway accounts — to one of two scopes: a single named **fleet** (`resource:delegate { fleetSlug }`, the original form) or a whole shared **pot** (`resource:delegate { potSlug, audience }`, added by `pot-seat-pools-prose-ux-2026-07-18`). Both forms are spent through the exact same host-side honor gates and the same atomic claim — the pot form only widens **who may spend** a standing offer; it never changes **how** spending is authorized. See also [seat-donation traps found during the live drill](/internal/docs/agent-insights/seat-donation-model-traps) for concrete bugs and non-obvious nuances hit while exercising this model end-to-end. ## Fleet-scoped vs pot-scoped: what changes, what doesn’t [Section titled “Fleet-scoped vs pot-scoped: what changes, what doesn’t”](#fleet-scoped-vs-pot-scoped-what-changes-what-doesnt) | | Fleet-scoped (original) | Pot-scoped (P-001, this plan) | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Grantee arg | `fleetSlug` | `potSlug` + REQUIRED `audience` | | Who may spend | that one fleet’s owner only | any fleet in the pot whose OWNER passes the host’s audience check | | Donate cadence | once per fleet-of-the-day | once per pot — no re-donating for every new fleet | | Offer target | the fleet owner directly | the pot’s shared-hive topic (P2P) | | Spend resolution | `fleet:request_remote_spawn` names/matches the fleet-scoped offer | resolved as a **fallback** when no fleet-scoped offer is named/available (P-004), or pooled alongside fleet-scoped offers by `fleet:launch-on-plan { placement:'remote' }` (P-005) | | Account id | never leaves the host, either way | never leaves the host, either way | | Over-draw safety | Gate 5 atomic claim (below) | same — no separate broker | Both forms persist as a row in `resource_allotments` (`fleetSlug`/`potSlug` exactly one, never both — the store refuses otherwise) and both advertise `model · effort · count · audience` only; the account id is resolved host-side at claim time (Gate 4.6), never published. ## Audience is a grant separate from trust (D-002) [Section titled “Audience is a grant separate from trust (D-002)”](#audience-is-a-grant-separate-from-trust-d-002) `trust:add` already means *“this user’s verified remote work auto-runs”* — reusing that same list to also mean *“may start agents on my box”* would be a silent scope escalation of an existing grant. So a pot-scoped offer declares its **audience** explicitly, at delegate time: * **`'trusted-members'`** — the host’s own local trust list, checked at **claim** time. The recommended default in UI/prose. * **`'whole-pot'`** — a deliberate, wider opt-in: every member of the pot. There is **no silent default** — `resource:delegate` refuses a `potSlug` delegation with no `audience` at the tool boundary (a loud validation error, not a fallback). Because the audience check runs **host-side, at claim time** (the P-003 gate below) rather than at delegate/publish time, a trust **revocation** takes effect on the very next claim attempt — no need to republish or pull the standing offer. ## The host-side honor gates (fail-closed, D-003) [Section titled “The host-side honor gates (fail-closed, D-003)”](#the-host-side-honor-gates-fail-closed-d-003) Every spend — fleet-scoped or pot-scoped — passes through the same gate ladder in `delegated-spawn-honor.ts`. Only Gate 2.5/3.5 is new for the pot form; everything else is unchanged from the original fleet-scoped design. | Gate | Checks | Applies to | | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | `ACCEPT_DELEGATED_SEATS` — the per-host, owner-authority, default-OFF master opt-in | both — the **one** intentionally-silent floor: a host with it off does no work at all, on either offer form | | 2 | Offer resolution/match — a named offer id, a fleet-scoped match, or (P-004) a pot-scoped fallback when nothing fleet-scoped matches | both | | **2.5 / 3.5** | **The audience gate (P-003, new):** fires ONLY when Gate 2 matched a POT-scoped candidate. `'trusted-members'` → the host’s local trust store; `'whole-pot'` → pot membership. Refusal is **loud**: `audience_refused`, receipt threaded by offer id, visible in `p2p:trace` | pot-scoped only | | 4 | Seat-cap pre-check | both | | 4.5 | Can-this-host-actually-run-it probe (`spawnConsole`, WI-5306) | both | | 4.6 | Account resolution against **this host’s own** gateway (WI-5316) — `'auto'` only survives to here; account id never leaves the host | both | | 5 | The atomic claim — exactly one hook invocation spawns; this **is** the over-draw safety (D-001) | both | Every refusal past Gate 1 is loud and threaded by offer id (visible from both sides via `p2p:trace`) — a pot-scoped offer is bookkeeping the host publishes about its own standing intent; the only thing that ever **grants** execution is the host itself, at Gate 5. ## Spend paths [Section titled “Spend paths”](#spend-paths) * **`fleet:request_remote_spawn`** resolves pot-level offers when no fleet-scoped offer is named or available, with deterministic host selection (round-robin) when more than one host offers to the same pot. * **`fleet:launch-on-plan { placement: 'remote' }`** pools pot-scoped seat-offers alongside fleet-scoped ones into one combined pool *before* spreading the requested member count across it — a plan launched into a shared pot sees every donor, not just fleet-specific ones. Both spend paths are **fleet-leader-only**: being a trusted (or whole-pot) member is necessary but not sufficient to spend a delegated seat — you must also be the leader of the fleet doing the spending. This is a third authority axis alongside D-002’s audience and the host-local `ACCEPT_DELEGATED_SEATS` gate; see the traps doc for how this was discovered live. ## Prose-first UX + the allocated-fleet model (D-004 / D-005) [Section titled “Prose-first UX + the allocated-fleet model (D-004 / D-005)”](#prose-first-ux--the-allocated-fleet-model-d-004--d-005) \[owner 2026-07-18] End users never call endpoints directly — they describe intent in prose (*“offer two sonnet seats to the design pot”*, *“launch this plan on remote seats”*, *“why hasn’t the remote member arrived”*) and their chat agent owns the verbs. Concretely: the operator chat surface exposes `fleet:create`, `fleet:request_remote_spawn`, `p2p:trace` (plus the already-exposed `resource:delegate`) with per-tool `guidance` mapping each prose pattern to a call; the plan-launch routing gate (`plans/launch-prompt.ts`) presents the remote-fleet route, naming the exact verb, whenever the plan’s pot is shared **and** seat-offers exist. The precise mental model for a “remote fleet” is an **allocated fleet** — a fleet that runs only on explicitly allocated agent seats. The seat *source* (the user’s own machine via local delegation, or a peer’s via a federated pot/fleet offer) is orthogonal to that, and the code must never assume all seats in an allocated fleet are remote: * The routing gate states available inventory in prose **with donors named** — *“I see 3 agent slots available from these 3 users”* — sourced from the offer projection. An **empty** inventory is not a dead end: the fleet can still be created, and the agent says a peer must allocate seats to it afterward (offering to relay that ask over the hive). * The agent always asks *“would you like to add any of your own agent slots to this remote fleet?”* and, on yes, executes the local delegation itself (`resource:delegate` to that fleet) — local and remote seats are placed uniformly by the same spread logic. ## Where the code lives [Section titled “Where the code lives”](#where-the-code-lives) | File | Role | | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `agent-tools/resource/delegate.ts` | the donate verb — fleet- or pot-scoped allotment + P2P offer publish | | `agent-tools/resource/offers.ts` | the offer-visibility read (`/res` Agent-seats group, `potShared` view) | | `p2p/delegated-spawn-honor.ts` | the host-side honor gate ladder (1 → 2 → 2.5/3.5 → 4 → 4.5 → 4.6 → 5) | | `agent-tools/fleet_registry/request-remote-spawn.ts` | the spend verb — resolves fleet- then pot-scoped offers, deterministic host selection | | `agent-tools/plans/launch-prompt.ts` | the routing-gate prose (inventory disclosure, own-slots ask, exact-verb naming) | | `p2p/capabilities.ts` | the grant/assignment vocabulary v1.5 stays wire-compatible with | | `p2p/pool-broker.ts` | the v2 dual-signature broker (reference only — not used by v1.5) | ## Known limitation — cross-machine spend is currently unverifiable live [Section titled “Known limitation — cross-machine spend is currently unverifiable live”](#known-limitation--cross-machine-spend-is-currently-unverifiable-live) WI-5446 — cross-machine seat-offers do not federate (likely = WI-953) **P-011’s live two-machine verify is blocked on a diagnosed federation bug, not staffing or cooperation.** Staged correctly (donor-side `resource:delegate` fired directly on the peer machine, `hive` passed explicitly — so this is distinct from EI-16667 below): the delegation succeeds locally, and the offer **never reaches the spending machine**. `fleet:request_remote_spawn` on the spender only ever auto-selects its **own** machine’s offer (proof, not just absence-by-silence: the tool refuses and asks the caller to disambiguate whenever 2+ open offers exist, and only auto-selects when exactly one exists — so seeing exactly one confirms the peer’s offer is genuinely absent, not merely deprioritized), and `p2p:trace` returns zero receipts on **both** machines — not a refusal, no traffic at all. Be explicit about the boundary this draws: **every gate and spend path described above is verified — unit- and integration-green, 12 of 14 plan items done.** What is **not** verified is a real cross-machine round trip; that gap is entirely in the P2P federation layer *underneath* this model, not in the seat-donation logic itself. Tracked as **WI-5446**, and — per the pot-seat-pools fleet leader’s diagnosis, linked caused-by — **likely not a new bug at all**: it matches the same publisher-reports-success / receiver-gets-silence shape already open as **WI-953** (“shared-hive directory announce never reaches the joiner”), one layer further down the same federation path. If that linkage holds, a working cross-machine seat-offer is really an **acceptance test for WI-953’s eventual fix**, not a separate investigation — don’t start by re-debugging the seat-offer publish code. Treat any cross-machine seat-donation claim as unverified until one of the two resolves. ## Open question [Section titled “Open question”](#open-question) `resource:offers`’ pot-wide (`potShared`) visibility currently resolves only on a workspace with exactly one shared hive, with no explicit `hive`/`potSlug` disambiguation argument — see [EI-16673](/internal/docs/agent-insights/seat-donation-model-traps) for the concrete failure on a real multi-hive workspace. Left open rather than resolved here: fixing it is a code change to `resource:offers`, out of scope for this docs pass.

# Data Sync overview

> How harness UI panels read from Postgres in real time via the SSE sync-resolver + RichGrid.

Zero is fully decommissioned, not merely retired Zero / zero-cache / ZQL named-queries is **gone from the tree** — `zero-decommission-2026-06-20` (Z-2) removed `@rocicorp/zero` from every `package.json`, deleted the `@papercusp/zero-harness` package (`libs/zero-harness` no longer exists as a directory), and stripped the Zero-specific transport out of `@papercusp/sync`. Zero repo-wide `@rocicorp/zero` deps: **0**. The shipping desktop app uses **SSE-primary** sync (the `:3070` Hono host pushes invalidate/update over Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY` through the v2 sync-resolver registry, described below); zero-cache is not run anywhere. Source of truth: `apps/operator/providers/HarnessSyncProvider.tsx` (transport-selection doc-comment) + the root `CLAUDE.md` deployment-model section. This page describes the current (post-Zero) stack throughout. **How SSE sync works today.** The `:3070` Hono host serves `/api/zero-harness/sse`. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` opens one dedicated PG `LISTEN` on the `sync_invalidate` channel (on the embedded-PG admin URL), fans each `pg_notify` out to subscribers, and bridges PG-trigger `<schema>.<table>.changed` events to the camelCase query names via `queryNamesForTriggerEvent` in `sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts`. **Freshness, restated.** It is not the old \~50ms logical-replication push. Each write fires an invalidate that pushes near-instantly to subscribers; the worst-case staleness for an **unbridged** table is the 180s drift-repair tick (`DEFAULT_SSE_DRIFT_REPAIR_MS` in `HarnessSyncProvider.tsx`), which is a repair sweep, **not** a freshness source. **Degraded fallback.** On sustained SSE failure, `SyncProvider`’s `useTransportFallback` drops SSE → `POLLING` as a last resort. POLLING is intentionally not the default: it re-fetches every subscribed query (\~40 on the dashboard) each interval, saturating the browser’s 6-connection-per-host HTTP/1.1 cap. Default to the data-sync library, not a fresh poll **For any new component that reads server state, default to `useSyncQuery({queryName, args})` from `@papercusp/sync`.** Don’t roll a new `fetch + setInterval` poll. Don’t open a raw `EventSource` for query data. The library is the single audited path: SSE/WS push, payload-on- invalidate, REST refetch fallback, observability shim (`window.__sync_metrics__`), reconnect resilience. Each parallel poll or ad-hoc EventSource forks all of that and accumulates as drift. **Genuine exceptions** (you may roll your own integration): * **Streaming-by-nature payloads** — log tails, terminal output, command-runner progress, LLM token streams. These are byte streams, not query data; raw `EventSource` is the right tool. See the existing uses in `OperatorPanel`, `BranchActionRunner`, `ProvisionStream`, `PiPanel` (pty). * **Pure UI timers** — `setNow(Date.now())` for relative-time refresh, `setInterval` for animation steps. No fetch, not data sync. * **Mobile (`apps/operator-mobile/`)** — uses its own pure-HTTP + EventSource path with `usePolledList` and `sync-stream.ts` for per-device JWT scoping and battery-aware visibility pause. New mobile consumers stay on that pattern. If you think you have another reason to bypass the library, **surface it as a question first** instead of forking quietly. Drift here costs real CPU, battery, and latency that the user only sees as “the app feels sluggish.” **The migration template** (3-line summary): 1. **Read** — add a resolver entry in `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts` (the v2 registry): `'queryName.variant': { argsSchema, resolve }` returning a flat row array. Prefer the structured DB projection if one exists (e.g. read `harness_plans.items` jsonb rather than re-parsing markdown). There is no ZQL path anymore — `libs/zero-harness` doesn’t exist. 2. **Write** — at the write site (the REST route / `defineTool` handler, or a watcher), fire `notifySyncInvalidate('queryName.variant', args)` from `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` after the write commits. For an optimistic write surface use `useSyncMutate('group.verb', restFallback)`; with no WebSocket/Zero client on the operator UI it always takes the REST fallback, and the invalidate above is what pushes the new state back to subscribers. 3. **Component** — `const { data } = useSyncQuery({queryName, args})`. Done. Full recipe in the [Cookbook](/internal/docs/data-sync/cookbook); the v2 registry’s per-entry recipe is in the [adding-a-sync-query](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-sync-query) insight. ## What this section covers [Section titled “What this section covers”](#what-this-section-covers) This is a reference for agents and humans building UI panels in the harness operator (`apps/operator/app/harness/`). Read this **before** you wire a new panel to data. The stack is two layered conventions, not a single library: 1. **The sync-resolver + SSE push** — Postgres is the source of truth. The v2 registry (`packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts`) resolves named queries; `sync-sse.ts` LISTENs on `sync_invalidate` and pushes invalidations to subscribers over Server-Sent Events. Clients call `useSyncQuery(...)` and refetch when the query’s name/args are invalidated — no manual polling loop to write. 2. **RichGrid** (`@papercusp/grid-core`, mirrored at `Papercusp/papergrid`) — the column-driven grid renderer every tabular panel uses. It is a DOM / CSS-grid renderer that virtualizes via `@tanstack/virtual-core` (its sibling `DataGridShell` is the canvas glide-data-grid one). It accepts plain rows + a `ColumnDef[]`, handles sorting, row click, row styling, and (optionally) virtual rendering. It does **not** know about the sync layer — the panel passes `useSyncQuery`’s rows as the `rows` prop. These two are intentionally orthogonal: * A panel can use **sync without RichGrid** (e.g. card or feed UX). * A panel can use **RichGrid without sync** (e.g. data that comes from a one-shot REST call — `ProjectsList` at `apps/operator/app/harness/[slug]/projects/`). * The default for a new tabular panel that displays Postgres-backed data is **both**. ## Why this exists [Section titled “Why this exists”](#why-this-exists) Before this stack was in place, every panel had its own list-rendering code (a `<table>` or a `.map()` over `<div>`s), its own polling loop, its own optimistic-update logic, and its own bug about “stale data after a mutation.” Migrating to RichGrid + the sync library collapses all of that into: 
```tsx
const { data: rows } = useSyncQuery<SnapshotRow>({ queryName: 'snapshotsConsolidated.bySlug', args: { harnessSlug: slug } });
return <RichGrid rows={rows ?? []} columns={columns} getRowId={s => s.id} inline />;
```
 Mutations write directly to Postgres (via a normal `POST /api/...` route). Freshness is invalidate-driven: each write fires a `sync_invalidate` notify that pushes near-instantly to subscribers, and an unbridged table’s worst-case staleness is the 180s drift-repair tick (see the banner above), which is a repair sweep, not the normal freshness path. ## Where each piece lives [Section titled “Where each piece lives”](#where-each-piece-lives) | Concern | Package | Path | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | | RichGrid component + `ColumnDef` types | `@papercusp/grid-core` | `libs/generic/papergrid/grid-core/src/RichGrid.tsx` | | Named-query registry (v2 resolver) | `packages/operator-core` | `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts` | | PG-trigger → query-name bridge | `packages/operator-core` | `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts` | | Sync hooks (`useSyncQuery`, …) | `@papercusp/sync` | `libs/generic/sync/src/SyncContext.ts` | | SSE wiring (LISTEN, invalidate bus) | `packages/operator-core` | `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` | | Sync provider for harness app | local | `apps/operator/providers/HarnessSyncProvider.tsx` | | Postgres database | server | `papercusp` DB on `:5432` | ## Reading order for new contributors [Section titled “Reading order for new contributors”](#reading-order-for-new-contributors) 1. [RichGrid](/internal/docs/data-sync/richgrid) — the renderer; learn this first because it’s the smaller, self-contained surface. 2. [Named queries](/internal/docs/data-sync/named-queries) — the v2 registry: how a row in Postgres becomes a row in your component, and how to add a new query to the shared catalog. 3. [Schema conventions](/internal/docs/data-sync/schema) — per-harness Postgres schemas, `harness_shared` cross-harness views. 4. [Pitfalls](/internal/docs/data-sync/pitfalls) — non-obvious issues that have silently broken every panel in a schema. Read this before debugging. 5. [Cookbook](/internal/docs/data-sync/cookbook) — copy-paste recipes for the most common panel-building tasks. ## Source-of-truth files [Section titled “Source-of-truth files”](#source-of-truth-files) When the docs and the code disagree, the code wins. The docs are kept in sync best-effort, but the canonical references are: * `libs/generic/papergrid/grid-core/src/RichGrid.tsx` — props, `ColumnDef` shape * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts` — every query name and its `argsSchema`/`resolve` (`knownQueryNamesV2()` enumerates them) * `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts` — which Postgres table backs which query name, for the PG-trigger invalidation bridge * `apps/operator/app/adv/harnesses/useHarnessData.ts` — a live consumer reading the consolidated queries via `useSyncQuery` (`featuresConsolidated.bySlug`, `issuesConsolidated.bySlug`, `agentRunsConsolidated.bySlug`)

# Cookbook

> Copy-paste recipes for the most common panel-building tasks.

Zero is fully decommissioned, not merely retired — historical reference Zero / zero-cache / ZQL named-queries is **gone from the tree**, not just off the transport path — `zero-decommission-2026-06-20` removed `@rocicorp/zero` from every `package.json` and deleted the `@papercusp/zero-harness` package (`libs/zero-harness` no longer exists as a directory). The `@papercusp/zero-harness` imports in the recipes below are **illustrative of the old pattern only** and will not resolve if copy-pasted. The shipping app uses **SSE for every runtime** — desktop Tauri shell *and* plain browser — where the operator sidecar’s `:3070` host pushes invalidate/update over Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`; zero-cache is **not run** at all. `POLLING` exists only as a degraded last-resort fallback, and the WebSocket transport still lives in `@papercusp/sync` but Papercusp no longer selects it. Treat this whole page as historical reference for the shape of the old recipes — for the CURRENT recipe (sync-resolver v2 + SSE), see the [Data Sync overview](/internal/docs/data-sync) instead. Source of truth: `apps/operator/providers/HarnessSyncProvider.tsx` (transport-selection doc-comment, hardcoded `syncType="SSE"`) + the root `CLAUDE.md` deployment-model section. ## Recipe 1: New panel reading from an existing Zero table [Section titled “Recipe 1: New panel reading from an existing Zero table”](#recipe-1-new-panel-reading-from-an-existing-zero-table) The 80% case. You want to render an existing per-harness table as a new panel. 
```tsx
'use client';


import { useMemo } from 'react';
import { RichGrid, type ColumnDef } from '@papercusp/grid-core';
import type { SnapshotsConsolidatedRow } from '@papercusp/zero-harness';
import { useSyncQuery } from '@papercusp/sync';


interface Props {
  slug: string;
  onSelect?: (id: string) => void;
}


export default function MySnapshotsPanel({ slug, onSelect }: Props) {
  // `useSyncQuery<T>` types T as the ROW element; `.data` is `T[]`.
  // `args` is a named object, not a positional array. The `bySlug` query's
  // Zod arg schema is `{ harnessSlug: string }` — the key must be
  // `harnessSlug`, not `slug`, or the query receives no filter.
  const { data: rows } = useSyncQuery<SnapshotsConsolidatedRow>({
    queryName: 'snapshotsConsolidated.bySlug',
    args: { harnessSlug: slug },
  });


  const columns = useMemo<ColumnDef<SnapshotsConsolidatedRow>[]>(() => [
    {
      key: 'when', header: 'When', width: 1.3,
      sortKey: 'ts', defaultSortDir: 'desc',
      render: ({ row }) => new Date(Number(row.ts)).toLocaleString(),
    },
    {
      key: 'iter', header: 'Iter', width: 0.4, align: 'right',
      sortKey: 'iterNum',
      render: ({ row }) => row.iterNum,
    },
  ], []);


  return (
    <RichGrid<SnapshotsConsolidatedRow>
      rows={rows}
      columns={columns}
      getRowId={(r) => r.snapshotId}
      onRowClick={(r) => onSelect?.(r.snapshotId)}
      inline
    />
  );
}
```
 ## Recipe 2: Migrating an existing `.map()` list to RichGrid [Section titled “Recipe 2: Migrating an existing .map() list to RichGrid”](#recipe-2-migrating-an-existing-map-list-to-richgrid) Source pattern (anti-pattern in this codebase): 
```tsx
{items.map((item) => (
  <div key={item.id} className="row">
    <span>{item.id}</span>
    <span>{item.name}</span>
    <span>{item.status}</span>
  </div>
))}
```
 Migration: 
```tsx
import { useMemo } from 'react';
import { RichGrid, type ColumnDef } from '@papercusp/grid-core';


const columns = useMemo<ColumnDef<Item>[]>(() => [
  { key: 'id', header: 'ID', width: 1, sortKey: 'id',
    render: ({ row }) => row.id },
  { key: 'name', header: 'Name', width: 3, sortKey: 'name',
    render: ({ row }) => row.name },
  { key: 'status', header: 'Status', width: 1, sortKey: 'status',
    render: ({ row }) => row.status },
], []);


return (
  <RichGrid<Item>
    rows={items}
    columns={columns}
    getRowId={(i) => i.id}
    inline
  />
);
```
 Steps in order: 1. Add `import { RichGrid, type ColumnDef } from '@papercusp/grid-core'`. 2. Build a `columns` array, one entry per visible field. Wrap in `useMemo`. 3. Replace the `.map()` block with `<RichGrid …>`. 4. Move per-row click handler from each row to `onRowClick`. 5. Drop the manual loading + error CSS (RichGrid renders its own header even when rows is empty; provide a sibling empty-state component if you need a friendlier message). ## Recipe 3: Adding a new column to an existing Zero-synced table [Section titled “Recipe 3: Adding a new column to an existing Zero-synced table”](#recipe-3-adding-a-new-column-to-an-existing-zero-synced-table) Per-harness tables are being retired The per-harness-table model below predates the consolidation migrations. The canonical stores are now the `harness_shared.*_consolidated` tables — writers should target those directly (see the `COMMENT ON harness_features_consolidated` in `000-baseline.sql`), and Zero exposes only the `*Consolidated.bySlug` / `*Consolidated.all` queries (the per-harness named queries — `featuresSheets`, `issuesOrg`, … — were removed; see the comment in `libs/zero-harness/src/queries.ts`). Add columns to the consolidated table (Recipe 5) rather than to per-harness tables. The per-harness table names are **not** uniformly `harness_<table>` — several (e.g. `feature_audit`, `agent_runs`) carry no `harness_` prefix. The published per-harness tables are `harness_features`, `feature_audit`, `harness_issues`, `harness_proposals`, `agent_runs`, `harness_snapshots` (plus `messages`, `supervisor_notes`); see the publication list in `bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh` and `libs/zero-harness/src/schema.ts`. 
```sql
ALTER TABLE harness_<slug>.harness_snapshots
  ADD COLUMN new_col text;
```
 For each existing harness, repeat. Then: 1. Update the per-harness template SQL (the file `bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh` `sed`-substitutes `{{SCHEMA}}` into and runs) so future harnesses get it — the column DDL lives in the template, not in the shell script itself. 2. Update `libs/zero-harness/src/schema.ts` — add `new_col: string()` (or the right type — beware TIMESTAMPTZ). 3. The publication already includes the table; the new column flows automatically. 4. Restart `zero-cache-harness`. 5. Update consumers (`useSyncQuery` results now include `new_col`). ## Recipe 4: Adding a new table to all harnesses [Section titled “Recipe 4: Adding a new table to all harnesses”](#recipe-4-adding-a-new-table-to-all-harnesses) Bigger lift. Steps: 1. Add the `CREATE TABLE` DDL to the **per-harness template SQL** (the file `bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh` renders via `sed "s/{{SCHEMA}}/$schema/g"`), and add the table to the publication list in the scaffold script’s `add_to_zero_publication` array. The script itself contains no DDL — it only substitutes the schema name into the template and runs it. 2. Run scaffold against every existing harness: 
   ```bash
   for slug in $(psql -tAc "SELECT nspname FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname LIKE 'harness\_%'" | sed 's/^harness_//'); do
     bin/scaffold-harness-schema.sh "$slug"
   done
   ```
 3. Add the table to `libs/zero-harness/src/schema.ts` (register it in the `createSchema({ tables: [...] })` list). 4. Add a query factory to `queries.ts`. 5. Add a `slugToXxxKey` helper to `queries.ts`. 6. Restart `zero-cache-harness`. ## Recipe 5: Cross-harness consolidated table [Section titled “Recipe 5: Cross-harness consolidated table”](#recipe-5-cross-harness-consolidated-table) When you need to render data across all harnesses (e.g. global feature list). 1. Create a new base table in `harness_shared`: 
   ```sql
   CREATE TABLE harness_shared.harness_<name>_consolidated (
     harness_slug text,
     <column>     <type>,
     -- …
     PRIMARY KEY (harness_slug, <pk>)
   );
   ```
 2. For each per-harness source table, add an `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` trigger that maintains the consolidated table. 3. Add the consolidated table to the `zero_harness` publication. 4. Register a no-arg named query: 
   ```ts
   <name>Consolidated: () => z.query.<name>Consolidated,
   ```
 5. Register the table in `schema.ts` and restart zero-cache. `harness_features_consolidated` is the working example to copy. ## Recipe 6: Mutations that update Zero panels [Section titled “Recipe 6: Mutations that update Zero panels”](#recipe-6-mutations-that-update-zero-panels) You want a button that inserts a row and have every connected client see it appear. 
```tsx
async function addNote() {
  const res = await fetch('/api/harness/<slug>/notes', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ text: 'hello' }),
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    toast.error('add note failed');
    return;
  }
  // No reload, no refetch. Zero will broadcast the new row in <100ms.
}
```
 The API route writes to PG. Zero broadcasts. `useSyncQuery` re-renders. Done. If you want optimistic UI before the round-trip, hold the new row in component state and clear it when the Zero query result reflects the real one. Don’t try to write through Zero — that’s not how this stack works. ## Recipe 7: Per-row action buttons [Section titled “Recipe 7: Per-row action buttons”](#recipe-7-per-row-action-buttons) Buttons inside a column cell that need to **not** trigger the row’s `onRowClick`: 
```tsx
{
  key: 'action',
  header: '',
  width: 0.6,
  align: 'right',
  render: ({ row }) => (
    <button
      onClick={(e) => {
        e.stopPropagation();
        handleDelete(row.id);
      }}
    >
      delete
    </button>
  ),
}
```
 The `e.stopPropagation()` is required. ## Recipe 8: Selected-row highlight [Section titled “Recipe 8: Selected-row highlight”](#recipe-8-selected-row-highlight) `getRowBg` is called with `(row, rowIndex, isSelected)` — RichGrid already tracks whether a row is selected (from its own internal state, or from the controlled `selectedRowIds`/`onSelectedRowIdsChange` pair if you pass them): 
```tsx
const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);


const getRowBg = (row: Row, _rowIndex: number, isSelected: boolean) =>
  row.id === selectedId ? '#1f2937' : undefined;


<RichGrid
  rows={rows}
  columns={columns}
  getRowId={(r) => r.id}
  onRowClick={(r) => setSelectedId(r.id)}
  getRowBg={getRowBg}
  inline
/>
```
 Return `undefined` (not `'transparent'`) to fall back to RichGrid’s own default striping/hover background rather than overriding it outright. For a checkbox-style multi-select rather than a single active row, skip the manual `selectedId` state entirely: pass `selectable` (or a controlled `selectedRowIds`/`onSelectedRowIdsChange` pair) and read the built-in `isSelected` argument in `getRowBg` instead of comparing ids yourself. `apps/operator/app/adv/harnesses/WorkItemsPanel.tsx` is a current live example of RichGrid with this exact `getRowBg` selected-row pattern; the retired `SnapshotsPanel.tsx` (see Reference panels below) shows the older, pre-dock version of the same idea. ## Recipe 9: PG-mirrored filesystem store [Section titled “Recipe 9: PG-mirrored filesystem store”](#recipe-9-pg-mirrored-filesystem-store) Use this when a filesystem JSON file must remain authoritative — e.g. an external CLI writes it, or a runtime loader reads it by path — but you also want cross-harness queries and Zero subscriptions over the same data. The pattern in three parts: **1. The PG table** is a derived index of the JSON. Same schema, plus `updated_at`. Add to the `zero_harness` publication. 
```sql
CREATE TABLE harness_shared.plugin_enables (
  harness_slug   text NOT NULL,
  plugin_slug    text NOT NULL,
  version        text NOT NULL,
  config_hash    text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  enabled_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (harness_slug, plugin_slug)
);
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON harness_shared.plugin_enables TO harness_app;
GRANT SELECT ON harness_shared.plugin_enables TO harness_zero;
ALTER PUBLICATION zero_harness ADD TABLE harness_shared.plugin_enables;
```
 **2. A mirror helper.** Reads the JSON for one harness/scope, upserts matching rows, deletes orphans. This is the function every writer calls. packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-enables-pg.ts 
```ts
import { getOrgPg } from '@papercusp/db-org';


export async function mirrorHarness(harness: string): Promise<void> {
  const file = await readEnabled(harness);                  // read JSON
  const enabled = file?.enabled ?? {};
  const { sql } = getOrgPg();
  for (const [pluginSlug, meta] of Object.entries(enabled)) {
    await sql`
      INSERT INTO harness_shared.plugin_enables
        (harness_slug, plugin_slug, version, config_hash, enabled_at, updated_at)
      VALUES (${harness}, ${pluginSlug}, ${meta.version}, ${meta.configHash},
              ${meta.enabledAt}, now())
      ON CONFLICT (harness_slug, plugin_slug) DO UPDATE
        SET version = EXCLUDED.version,
            config_hash = EXCLUDED.config_hash,
            updated_at = now()
    `;
  }
  // Delete rows for plugins removed from the JSON
  const slugs = Object.keys(enabled);
  if (slugs.length === 0) {
    await sql`DELETE FROM harness_shared.plugin_enables WHERE harness_slug = ${harness}`;
  } else {
    await sql`
      DELETE FROM harness_shared.plugin_enables
      WHERE harness_slug = ${harness} AND plugin_slug NOT IN ${sql(slugs)}
    `;
  }
}
```
 **3. Hook every writer.** After each successful JSON write — direct or via subprocess — call the mirror. Best-effort: a mirror failure logs but does not fail the API call. 
```ts
// in the API route that calls the CLI
const r = await spawn(PAPERCUSP_BIN, ['plugin', 'enable', slug, '--harness', h]);
if (r.code === 0) {
  try { await mirrorHarness(h); } catch (e) {
    console.warn('[plugins/enable] PG mirror failed for', h, e);
  }
}
```
 **4. Backfill + drift recovery.** Provide a script that reads ALL JSONs and re-syncs PG. It runs on a fresh checkout, after a direct CLI run that bypassed the operator API, or whenever you suspect drift. scripts/backfill-plugin-enables.mjs 
```js
// Same logic as mirrorHarness, run for every harness directory.
// Idempotent: re-running on already-synced data is a no-op.
```
 ### When to pick this pattern over PG-canonical [Section titled “When to pick this pattern over PG-canonical”](#when-to-pick-this-pattern-over-pg-canonical) | Pick PG-canonical (Recipe 1-2) when | Pick PG-mirror (this) when | | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | You own every writer | A third-party process or runtime path writes the JSON and you can’t change it | | The data has no on-disk consumer | A loader reads the JSON file at runtime by path | | Atomicity of write matters | The JSON is the operational source of truth and PG is a query-side index | Reference implementations: * `packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-enables-pg.ts` (papercusp CLI is the writer) * `packages/operator-core/lib/plugin-configs-pg.ts` (substrate plugin loader reads JSON at runtime) ## Recipe 10: Where to put a new panel [Section titled “Recipe 10: Where to put a new panel”](#recipe-10-where-to-put-a-new-panel) | Panel scope | Location | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Tabular data for one harness, shown in the harness dashboard | `apps/operator/app/harness/<Name>Panel.tsx` | | Dock panel in the per-harness workbench | A `Real<Name>Panel.tsx` under `apps/operator/app/harness/dock/`, registered with `panelRegistry.register('data:<name>', Real<Name>Panel)` in `dock/sample-panels.tsx` (see `RealFeaturesPanel.tsx` / `RealIssuesPanel.tsx` for the shape) | | Cross-harness panel (global view) | `apps/operator/app/<route>/<Name>Panel.tsx` | The live `apps/operator` harness UI is dock-based (`apps/operator/app/harness/[slug]/HarnessDockShell.tsx`); wire a new panel in as a dock panel rather than into a monolithic tab switcher. There is no single `DepartmentHarnessDashboard.tsx` anymore — that file moved to the **retired** `libs/papercusp/_retired/apps-web/app/harness/` tree when the dock rewrite shipped (the `MemoryEntriesGrid` component it once hosted is gone entirely, not just moved); treat it as historical reference only, not a live extension point. ## Reference panels [Section titled “Reference panels”](#reference-panels) When in doubt, copy the structure from one of these live RichGrid consumers: * `apps/operator/app/adv/harnesses/WorkItemsPanel.tsx` — sortable/filterable RichGrid with `getRowBg` selected-row highlighting and resizable columns. * `apps/operator/app/harness/[slug]/projects/ProjectsList.tsx` — RichGrid with `onRowClick` navigation, a small, focused table. The following now live in the **retired** `@papercusp/web` surface (`libs/papercusp/_retired/apps-web/app/harness/`) but still show the canonical RichGrid + sync wiring from before the dock rewrite: * `…/web/app/harness/SnapshotsPanel.tsx` — small, single per-harness table, sortable + per-row delete. * `…/web/app/harness/issues/IssuesList.tsx` — RichGrid, multi-state row, with `rowProps` legacy-class workaround. * `…/web/app/harness/ProposalsPanel.tsx` — inline mutation actions.

# Named queries

> The shared catalog of queries every panel reads from.

Zero is fully decommissioned — this page is historical reference only The Zero / zero-cache / ZQL named-queries / WebSocket-push stack described below is **gone, not just retiring**: `zero-decommission-2026-06-20` (Z-2) removed `@rocicorp/zero` from every `package.json`, deleted the `@papercusp/zero-harness` package (`libs/zero-harness` — the directory itself no longer exists in the tree), and stripped the Zero-specific WS transport out of `@papercusp/sync`. Zero-repo-wide `@rocicorp/zero` deps: **0**. The shipping desktop app uses **SSE-primary** sync (the `:3070` Hono host pushes invalidate/update over Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY` through the v2 sync-resolver registry described below); zero-cache is not run anywhere. Source of truth: `apps/operator/providers/HarnessSyncProvider.tsx` (transport-selection doc-comment), the root `CLAUDE.md` deployment-model section, and [Adding a query to the Zero-free sync resolver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-sync-query) for the current, authoritative recipe. The “Query does not implement QueryInternals” section further down describes an error that **cannot recur** — it is kept only so an agent that finds an old comment/plan mentioning it isn’t left guessing what it meant. ## Why named queries [Section titled “Why named queries”](#why-named-queries) Every panel read the harness UI does goes through one **named query** — `useSyncQuery({ queryName, args })` — resolved against a single registry, so “what does the harness sync from Postgres?” always has one answer: open the registry. That principle survived the Zero decommission unchanged; only the registry’s *shape* changed. Today the registry is `REGISTRY` in `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts` (the “v2” resolver) — a flat `Record<string, QueryEntry>` (152 entries as of 2026-07-04) keyed by a **dotted string name** (`'featuresConsolidated.bySlug'`, `'snapshotsConsolidated.bySlug'`, `'storage.usage'`, …), each entry pairing a Zod `argsSchema` with an async `resolve(args)` that runs a normal drizzle/PG query and returns a flat row array. There is no `defineQueries` namespace object, no ZQL, and no separate `schema.ts`/publication step — a dotted name is just a registry key, and adding one is a \~15 LOC addition to that one file. **Full recipe, key points, and gotchas:** [Adding a query to the Zero-free sync resolver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-sync-query) — this page won’t duplicate it. ## The current catalog [Section titled “The current catalog”](#the-current-catalog) `knownQueryNamesV2()` (same file) enumerates every registered name — that’s the canonical list; don’t trust an inline copy here to stay in sync with it. The four core per-harness entities are still slug-agnostic consolidated tables in `harness_shared`, each read by a `.bySlug` query keyed on `harnessSlug` (a column, not a schema name): | Query | Returns | Args | | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | ----------------- | | `featuresConsolidated.bySlug` | `FeatureRow[]` | `{ harnessSlug }` | | `issuesConsolidated.bySlug` | `IssueRow[]` | `{ harnessSlug }` | | `agentRunsConsolidated.bySlug` (or `agentRunsConsolidated.recent`) | `AgentRunRow[]` | `{ harnessSlug }` | | `snapshotsConsolidated.bySlug` | `SnapshotRow[]` | `{ harnessSlug }` | | `harnessProjects.lite` | `ProjectRow[]` | (none) | | `harnessWorkspaces.byHarness` | `WorkspaceRow[]` | `{ harnessSlug }` | `featuresConsolidated` also carries `featuresConsolidated.byHive` (cross-member browse, WI-259 P-006/D-010) and `featuresConsolidated.byPlanSlug`. The doc text claiming a `needsReview` variant, a `bySourcePlan` form, or an `all` form is drift — those queries do not exist in the registry. Adding a new harness still doesn’t add a query — the slug is a regular row value, not a schema name. ## Adding a new named query [Section titled “Adding a new named query”](#adding-a-new-named-query) See the full recipe (schema check, registry entry shape, the P-067 PG-trigger bridge, the test-count-assertion gotcha, verification) at [Adding a query to the Zero-free sync resolver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-sync-query). In short, an entry in `REGISTRY` looks like: packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/index.ts 
```ts
'myNewThing.bySlug': {
  argsSchema: z.object({ harnessSlug: z.string() }),
  resolve: async (args) => {
    const { harnessSlug } = args as { harnessSlug: string };
    const { getOrgPg, generated } = await import('@papercusp/db-org');
    const { eq } = await import('drizzle-orm');
    const { db } = getOrgPg();
    return (await db.select().from(generated.myNewThing)
      .where(eq(generated.myNewThing.harnessSlug, harnessSlug))) as unknown[];
  },
},
```
 Then in your panel, read it through the `@papercusp/sync` wrapper. The `useSyncQuery` hook is exported from `@papercusp/sync` (the package lives at `libs/generic/sync`) and is transport-agnostic — it resolves `queryName` + `args` through whichever adapter is active: 
```tsx
const { data: rows } = useSyncQuery<MyNewThingRow>({
  queryName: 'myNewThing.bySlug',
  args: { harnessSlug: slug },
});
```
 The same generic (`libs/generic/sync`) package also exports the companion write hook `useSyncMutate(path, restFallback)` and `useSyncPrefetch()`. On the operator harness UI (SSE transport, no WebSocket client) `useSyncMutate` always takes the `restFallback` — it exists so a call site can adopt the same API a `WEBSOCKETS`-transport consumer of the generic package would use (elsewhere in the monorepo) without a behavior difference on SSE/polling. `useSyncPrefetch()` warms the cache so a later `useSyncQuery` for the same `queryName` + `args` resolves instantly. You also need the PG-trigger bridge entry so writes that bypass app code (raw SQL, MCP-tool writes, migrations) still invalidate the query: add `'harness_shared.your_table': ['myNewThing.bySlug']` to `TABLE_TO_QUERY_NAMES` in `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-resolver/table-to-query-names.ts` — see [Adding a query to the Zero-free sync resolver](/internal/docs/agent-insights/adding-a-sync-query) Step 3. Skip it and the query still works for app-code writes (which call `notifySyncInvalidate` directly) but silently misses out-of-band ones. ## ”Query does not implement QueryInternals” (Zero-era, historical) [Section titled “”Query does not implement QueryInternals” (Zero-era, historical)”](#query-does-not-implement-queryinternals-zero-era-historical) This error meant the panel’s `@rocicorp/zero` package and the one Zero instantiated against were different copies, thrown from every `useQuery` call. It cannot recur — `@rocicorp/zero` has zero `package.json` references left anywhere in the repo (`zero-decommission-2026-06-20` Z-2) — but it’s left here in case an old comment, plan, or search result references it and an agent needs to know it’s inert history, not a live failure mode to reproduce or guard against. ## Cross-harness queries (consolidated tables) [Section titled “Cross-harness queries (consolidated tables)”](#cross-harness-queries-consolidated-tables) `harness_features_consolidated` is the **canonical** base table in `harness_shared` — writers target it directly. The data-flow direction was inverted across two migrations: * **Migration 029** made the consolidated table the source of truth. It had started life as a trigger-mirrored copy of the per-harness `harness_features` tables (writers pumped into per-harness, a trigger fanned out into consolidated), but 029 flipped that so writes go straight to the consolidated table. * **Migration 032** dropped the per-harness physical tables entirely and replaced each with an auto-updatable `VIEW` over the consolidated table, filtered by `harness_slug` (`WITH CHECK OPTION` so a write can’t land under the wrong slug).
