# Delegate fire-and-forget refactor

> Lift the 2-minute ceiling on delegate_to_claude by making it an async dispatch + later contextual update.

> **Implemented (with refinements).** The async race-with-timeout path (Q1 Option B) shipped in `packages/operator-core/lib/commands/defs/delegation.ts`: a sync window races a deadline, and on overrun the handler returns `{ status: 'started', agentSessionId, message }` and drains the SSE stream in the background. The EL voice tool is still `delegate_to_claude` (`response_timeout_secs: 15` in `apps/operator/scripts/el-agent-sync.mjs`). Completion fires two browser events — `operator:delegation-complete` (panel-targeted) and `operator:delegation-async-complete` (voice-targeted) — and the voice-mode listener does the live-session push as **`sendSystem()`** (not the plan’s `sendContextualUpdate`). The ack shape also changed from the draft below: it carries a `message` hint, not `expectedSeconds`, and the session id field is `agentSessionId`, not `claudeSessionId`. > > Two further refinements vs. the draft below: > > * **The per-delegate Haiku summary was NOT shipped.** The contextual update carries a raw `fullText.slice(0, 280)` headline (with an ellipsis when truncated) built in `OperatorDelegationListener.tsx` — there is no model call. So the “Contextual update path” step 1 and the Risk-register “extra Haiku call per delegate” cost concern no longer apply. > * **Q3 resolved to a hindsight-inbox (Option B-style), not the recommended panel-only Option A.** When no live EL session is present, `OperatorDelegationListener.tsx` POSTs the headline to the operator coord-inbox hindsight channel (`/api/agent-mcp/operator-hindsight`, `kind: 'delegate-complete'`). `drainHindsightOnConnect()` in `voice-mode.ts` folds pending items into a single `[While you were away, N update(s)]` `sendSystem()` on the next EL connect (cites “collapse-delegate D-003”). ## Why [Section titled “Why”](#why) EL caps `response_timeout_secs` at **120s** (the API rejects 121+). Real delegates regularly run 30s–2min today, with a long tail past that for file-heavy reasoning. When EL hits its 120s wall, the agent sees “tool errored” even though the SSE stream is still running and the result eventually lands in the panel via `operator:delegation-complete`. Symptoms users have already hit: * Agent says “the delegate timed out” while the SSE stream finishes cleanly seconds later (we hit this; bumped 20s → 120s; still vulnerable to >2min runs). * Agent can’t summarize the result because the tool returned an error instead of the `fullText`. ## What changes [Section titled “What changes”](#what-changes) `delegate_to_claude` returns **immediately** with a small ack and the result lands later via two channels: 1. **The panel** (already wired — `operator:delegation-complete` updates the panel’s lastDelegation; user can read details there). 2. **The agent** — via `sendContextualUpdate(text)` from EL’s SDK, triggered server-side when the SSE stream finishes. The agent gets a system-style note (`[Delegate ID completed] one-sentence summary`) on its NEXT turn, and can speak about it then. ### Tool return shape [Section titled “Tool return shape”](#tool-return-shape) Today (synchronous): 
```js
{ status: 'complete', fullText, claudeSessionId, costUsd }
```
 After (async-by-default for >5s expected runs; sync for short): 
```js
// Returned within ~100ms of the call:
{ status: 'started', claudeSessionId, expectedSeconds: 90 }
```
 The agent’s persona will already speak “looking into that” at the moment the tool returns. No “details in the panel” — that line moves to the contextual-update handler when the result actually lands. ### Contextual update path [Section titled “Contextual update path”](#contextual-update-path) When the SSE stream completes server-side: 1. Build a one-sentence summary of `fullText` (Haiku call, capped at 80 tokens, <$0.001). 2. Stream a contextual update into the active EL session: 
   ```js
   conv.sendContextualUpdate(
     `[Delegate ID-PREFIX completed] SUMMARY. Full text in the panel.`
   );
   ```
 3. The agent’s persona (already updated) tells it: “if a contextual update mentions a delegate completing, speak the summary aloud and say ‘details in the panel’ on the next turn.” So the user hears the update naturally. If the user is mid-conversation (not idle), the contextual update queues until their next turn. EL handles this internally. ## Open design choices (need user input) [Section titled “Open design choices (need user input)”](#open-design-choices-need-user-input) ### Q1: keep a sync path for fast delegates? [Section titled “Q1: keep a sync path for fast delegates?”](#q1-keep-a-sync-path-for-fast-delegates) A small delegate (“what’s a Bell number?”, “summarize this 200-line file”) finishes in 5-15s. Going async for those is dumb — the agent already returns the summary in the same turn, which is the natural UX. **Option A** (always async): one code path, simpler. Adds latency to fast delegates (the user hears “looking into that, hang on” then 30s of nothing then the summary on next turn). **Option B** (race-with-timeout): sync path tries to return within \~10s; if not, the tool returns `{ status: 'started', ... }` and the SSE stream keeps running in the background, completing via the contextual-update path. Best UX, more code complexity. Recommend **B**. \~30 extra lines. ### Q2: what does “started” look like in the panel? [Section titled “Q2: what does “started” look like in the panel?”](#q2-what-does-started-look-like-in-the-panel) Currently the panel shows the delegate row immediately on session creation, then updates with the result. With async-by-default, the row will sit in “running” state for minutes. Today there’s no visual cue for “this is actively in flight.” **Option A** (no UI change): the row shows up in the Delegates tab; you can tell it’s still running because turnCount=0 and there’s no summary yet. **Option B** (running indicator): add a spinner/dot to delegates that haven’t received a `done` event yet. \~10 lines of CSS + one boolean. Recommend **B**. Cheap and visible. ### Q3: failure mode when EL session disconnects mid-flight? [Section titled “Q3: failure mode when EL session disconnects mid-flight?”](#q3-failure-mode-when-el-session-disconnects-mid-flight) If the user’s EL session ends before the SSE stream completes, the contextual update has nowhere to land. The result still goes to the panel — but the agent never speaks about it. **Option A** (panel-only): result hits the panel, agent forgets. The user can reconnect and ask the operator about it (via the existing `delegates.list` + `delegates.get` queries). **Option B** (hindsight memory): write a session-completion record to a small “agent inbox” table; on next session start, EL fetches and surfaces (“you have 2 delegate results waiting from the prior session: \[…]”). Recommend **A** for now. **B** is real work and the panel + voice hint pattern (Q1’s contextual-update + chaining) makes it discoverable enough. ## Implementation order [Section titled “Implementation order”](#implementation-order) Once the above is settled: 1. **`delegation.ts` handler refactor** — pull the SSE consumer into a separate function that runs in the background. Tool handler returns `{ status: 'started', claudeSessionId }` after \~10s of waiting (Q1 Option B). 2. **Background completion path** — when the SSE finishes, build the summary (cheap Haiku call), call `conv.sendContextualUpdate` on the live EL session. Need to thread the live `conv` reference through to the background callback — that’s the trickiest piece; probably an in-process `Map<sessionId, conv>`. 3. **`el-agent-sync.mjs` description update** — `delegate_to_claude` description gets simpler (“returns immediately; result arrives via contextual update”). Drop the timeout knob since we’re not waiting on EL’s tool wall anymore. 4. **Persona update** — current persona says “always summarize after the tool returns.” Becomes “say ‘looking into that’ when the tool returns; when you receive a contextual update about a delegate completing, summarize then.” 5. **Panel running indicator** (Q2 Option B). 6. **Suite scenarios** — at least one for the new “long delegate completes via contextual update” path. Tricky to test in the text-only suite because contextual updates fire on the NEXT turn — would need to send a follow-up user message after the ack and assert the agent speaks the result then. ## Risk register [Section titled “Risk register”](#risk-register) | Risk | Mitigation | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | In-process Map of active EL sessions doesn’t survive server restart | Sessions are per-tab anyway; restart loses the conv ref. Result still hits the panel; agent just won’t speak about it. Acceptable. | | Contextual updates land mid-sentence and confuse the agent | EL queues them until end-of-turn. Tested, documented in their SDK. | | Persona drift — agent could ad-lib the summary before the contextual update arrives | Suite scenario for it; el-tools-check + drift gate stays strict. | | Cost: extra Haiku call per delegate for the one-sentence summary | <$0.001 per call. Probably noise. Could fall back to a regex-extracted first-line if budget gets touchy. | ## What we’re NOT doing in this refactor [Section titled “What we’re NOT doing in this refactor”](#what-were-not-doing-in-this-refactor) * **Multi-tab sessionId routing.** If the user has two tabs both running EL and a delegate completes, the contextual update goes to whichever tab the delegate was originally fired from. That’s the leader tab anyway (focus-follows-tab keeps things consistent), so this is fine. * **Delegate cancellation.** No “cancel running delegate” UI. Add later if asked. * **Multi-delegate contention.** Two delegates running at once (rare) each get their own contextual update on completion. Already works this way today; the panel listener already handles concurrent.

# Design phase — plan

> Add Design as a first-class phase in the feature lifecycle, with a separate Design tab, a generic ecosystem-agnostic engine, and per-ecosystem adapters (React/Tailwind ships first). Designer agents produce JSON-IR specs that implementer agents consume.

This plan turns Design into a first-class phase in the same way Implementation already is — its own gate, its own agent role, its own tab — while keeping papercusp generic enough to design React, Rust, C++, or anything else with a UI. Earlier discussion lived in chat; this doc is the canonical spec for the build. > **Implementation status (partial — kept as the canonical spec).** The spine shipped: lifecycle fields + gate + `needsDesign` heuristic in `packages/operator-core/lib/design-phase.ts` (`DesignStatus = 'pending' | 'accepted' | 'ignored'`, `computeNeedsDesign`, `assertDesignGate`). The lifecycle fields shipped as **columns on the existing `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated` table** (`needs_design`, `design_status`, `design_spec_id`, `discarded_design_work`), keyed by `(harness_slug, feature_id)` — there is no separate `harness_design_phase` table; the orchestrator design gate reads `needs_design` / `design_status` straight from the consolidated (canonical) store. Spec artifacts shipped in `harness_shared.harness_design_artifacts` (columns `id`, `harness_slug`, `feature_id`, `kind`, `payload`, `metadata`, `created_ts`; PK `(harness_slug, id)`). Also shipped: the UI IR JSON Schema (`design-ir/schema.ts`); the designer prompt + DESIGN\_SPEC resolution (`design-spec/`); the first ecosystem adapter (`design-adapter-react-tailwind/` — `registry` / `tokens` / `codeEmit`); the Design tab (`apps/operator/app/design/[slug]/DesignDashboard.tsx`, behind the `papercusp-design` V1 feature flag — `FLAGS.DESIGN`, default off) **with all six panes implemented** (features, memos, registry, tokens, sketch, regressions); **Lost Pixel** visual regression (the `lost-pixel ^3.22.0` dependency, `lostpixel.config.ts`, the `lostpixel-baseline/` directory, the `lostpixel` / `lostpixel:update` npm scripts, and `RegressionPane.tsx` reading its output); and the full §15 MCP surface (12 tools) shipped by the `@papercupai/design-phase` plugin: `validate_spec`, `lint_spec`, `submit_spec`, `list_memos`, `read_memo`, `get_design_spec`, `search_registry`, `get_registry_component`, `list_tokens`, `read_token`, `get_accepted_spec`, `record_review` (snake\_case, not the camelCase names drafted in §15; the `design-phase:` prefix is a su-catalog / test-fixture convention — the plugin manifest itself uses the bare names). The **spec-submission + reviewer-verdict plumbing shipped at the storage + MCP layer**: `submit_spec` persists a `kind='spec'` artifact and flips `design_status`; `record_review` records approved / rejected / changes-requested and flips `design_status` back to `pending` on rejection; `get_accepted_spec` resolves the accepted IR via `design_spec_id`; and the artifacts table carries a `'review'` kind (migration 052). The token pipeline’s repo-level `npm run tokens` build runs on **Style Dictionary v4** (`^4.4.0`, `design-tokens/style-dictionary.config.mjs`; see [design tokens](/internal/docs/design/tokens)); the react-tailwind adapter, separately, ships its own minimal in-house CSS-vars + Tailwind-preset emitter (Terrazzo is not a dependency). Genuinely **aspirational**: `tldraw` (`SketchPane` is a minimal HTML5 canvas — its docstring says “tldraw is a planned upgrade”); the orchestrator’s automatic designer / reviewer **spawn loop** (no `designReady` / `spawn-designer` logic exists in the orchestrator — the verdict plumbing above is wired, but nothing spawns the agents yet); the Plotly / raw / chart sub-IRs; the non-React adapters; the design-crit picker; and the mock-input + export adapters. *** # 1. Why a phase, not a tag [Section titled “1. Why a phase, not a tag”](#1-why-a-phase-not-a-tag) Tags are orthogonal grouping (which features share memory). Phases are sequential states with gates and deliverables. Design has both. Every feature with a user-facing surface needs design *before* implementation, then again as *review* after; that’s a workflow, not a label. A separate Design tab is justified because the working surface is different from the dashboard’s: queues, mocks, tokens, registry, visual diff. The data spine is shared with the dashboard’s Features component (see §6). *** # 2. Lifecycle integration [Section titled “2. Lifecycle integration”](#2-lifecycle-integration) Design reuses the existing card lifecycle vocabulary (`pending / accepted / ignored`). It does not introduce new state names. The phase is the axis of difference, not the state machine. A feature record gains: 
```plaintext
needsDesign:         boolean    // set by orchestrator on creation
designStatus:        Lifecycle  // pending | accepted | ignored
designSpec:          SpecRef|null  // pointer to spec when accepted
discardedDesignWork: boolean    // human force-skipped after work began
```
 `pending` covers both “awaiting designer spawn” and “designer in flight” — the implementation lifecycle treats spawned-but-unfinished the same way. `ignored` is overloaded: it can mean “phase explicitly skipped” (this feature doesn’t need design) or “feature dropped” (no design will happen because the feature is dead). The two are conflated because the gate behavior is identical (no spec required to advance or close). If telemetry needs to distinguish, use the existing feature-lifecycle status to disambiguate. Gate: a feature cannot transition into the implementing phase until `designStatus ∈ { accepted, ignored }`. ## 2.1 Storage [Section titled “2.1 Storage”](#21-storage) > **As shipped:** the lifecycle fields landed as **columns on the existing canonical features table** rather than a new sibling table — `needs_design`, `design_status`, `design_spec_id`, `discarded_design_work` on `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated`, keyed by `(harness_slug, feature_id)`. There is no `harness_design_phase` table; the gate reads the design columns straight from the consolidated store. `needsDesign`, `designStatus`, `designSpec`, `discardedDesignWork` live on the canonical features table `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated` (columns `needs_design`, `design_status`, `design_spec_id`, `discarded_design_work`), keyed by `(harness_slug, feature_id)`, in the harness DB. This matches the existing pattern (per memory: features, issues, proposals, etc., are PG-canonical via Zero sync). Spec artifacts (the IR JSON, sketches, screenshots) live in a sibling table `harness_shared.harness_design_artifacts` with columns `(id, harness_slug, feature_id, kind, payload, metadata, created_ts)`, keyed by `(harness_slug, id)`. (Note the `created_ts` BIGINT timestamp, and the `id` + `metadata` columns the earlier draft omitted.) PG over filesystem so artifacts are queryable, syncable via Zero, and survive harness moves. ## 2.2 Relationship to existing `proposals` [Section titled “2.2 Relationship to existing proposals”](#22-relationship-to-existing-proposals) Design specs are NOT proposals. Proposals (per memory) are implementation alternatives — competing plans for how to build something. Design specs define what to build. Sibling category, new table, no overloading. A proposal MAY reference a design spec; a design spec NEVER references a proposal. *** # 3. The `needsDesign` heuristic [Section titled “3. The needsDesign heuristic”](#3-the-needsdesign-heuristic) Cheap, deterministic, runs at feature creation. Falsy means skip the design phase entirely. The heuristic reads from the *proposal/scope* — feature description, acceptance criteria, plan text, declared file globs — not from actual code diffs (there are none at creation time). 
```plaintext
needsDesign := proposalMentionsUiSurface
            || proposalMentionsUserCopy
            || proposalDeclaresNewRoute
            || proposalDeclaresIconography
            || proposalGlobsMatchUiPaths   // declared file globs
            || flaggedManually
```
 Where `uiPaths` is per-ecosystem-adapter (React-Tailwind: `**/*.tsx / **/*.css`; Qt: `**/*.ui / **/*.qml`; etc.). Adapters declare their UI globs; the orchestrator unions across active adapters. Backend, infra, refactors, and bugfixes skip by default. The orchestrator can override either direction. *** # 4. Roles [Section titled “4. Roles”](#4-roles) ## 4.1 Designer agent [Section titled “4.1 Designer agent”](#41-designer-agent) Output is a *specification*, not edited components. To enforce this, the runtime restricts designer commits to a per-adapter allowlist (default: `design/`, `content/internal-docs/design/`, sketch artifact paths). Commits outside the allowlist are rejected with a clear error and the designer is re-prompted, not killed. If a designer legitimately needs to scaffold something outside the allowlist (e.g., a token JSON proposal in a custom path), the designer requests an allowlist extension via a special spec annotation; orchestrator (or human) approves. Deliverables per feature: * A UI IR document (see §7) describing the surface * Token decisions (which existing tokens, any new ones — §9) * Component contract: which registry components to use, with which variants and props * Copy (labels, empty states, error messages) * Interaction states (hover/focus/disabled/loading/error) * Optional: tldraw sketch, screenshot annotations, references Inputs: * The feature record (description, acceptance criteria) * `DESIGN_SPEC.md` (global rules — §5; with fallback chain) * Component registry (§8) * Token store (§9) * Adjacent design memos under `content/internal-docs/design/` * **For redesigns of existing features:** preview-adapter capture of the current state (screenshot or live preview URL); designer needs to know what exists before proposing changes ## 4.2 Design reviewer (lightweight) [Section titled “4.2 Design reviewer (lightweight)”](#42-design-reviewer-lightweight) After implementation ships, a review pass compares the rendered surface to the spec. Output is either *approved* or a re-opened design card with the diff. If the reviewer rejects, a fresh designer agent is spawned with: the rejected spec, the rendered diff, and the reviewer’s notes as new input. The original designer’s spec is preserved as an artifact for traceability — never overwritten. Reviewer is the same agent persona as the designer with a different prompt; one binary, two roles. ## 4.3 Orchestrator changes [Section titled “4.3 Orchestrator changes”](#43-orchestrator-changes) Concrete trigger for spawning designers: 
```plaintext
designReady := needsDesign
            && designStatus == null
            && dependencies.allMet
            && scope.stable
            && !backoff.active   // see below
```
 After a rejected design, a back-off timer prevents immediate re-spawn (default 1 hour, configurable). Rejection reasons feed the next prompt so the designer doesn’t repeat the mistake. The orchestrator also: * Sets `needsDesign` on creation per heuristic (§3) * Spawns the appropriate number of designers (§20.9) * Honors the gate before promoting to implementing * Schedules the post-ship review pass ## 4.4 Cost / token budget [Section titled “4.4 Cost / token budget”](#44-cost--token-budget) Designers spawn 2–3 per feature (§20.9) and consume tokens on a similar order to implementers. Budget controls are the same as implementers — orchestrator can drop to N=1 for cost-constrained features, and the global per-workspace budget cap covers both designer and implementer spend. No separate budget axis. *** # 5. `DESIGN_SPEC.md` [Section titled “5. DESIGN\_SPEC.md”](#5-design_specmd) A separate doc, sibling to `SPEC.md`, that the designer agent always loads. Contents: * Voice, tone, terminology rules * Token policy (when to use existing vs propose new) * Accessibility minimums * Animation / motion rules (already partially captured in `/docs/design/performance` and `libraries`) * Forbidden patterns (anti-pattern catalog) * Approved component list (links into §8) ## 5.1 Fallback chain [Section titled “5.1 Fallback chain”](#51-fallback-chain) Resolved in order; first hit wins: 1. `<harness root>/DESIGN_SPEC.md` 2. `<workspace root>/DESIGN_SPEC.md` 3. `<papercusp app default>/DESIGN_SPEC.md` (ships with the SDK, minimal — just “use existing tokens, semantic HTML, ARIA roles”) 4. Empty (with a logged warning surfaced as a banner in the design tab: “no DESIGN\_SPEC.md found; using minimal defaults”) Day-1 is unblocked by (3). Harnesses adopt their own as needed. ## 5.2 Per-harness scope [Section titled “5.2 Per-harness scope”](#52-per-harness-scope) This file is per-harness, not per-workspace, so different harnesses (different surfaces, different teams, different ecosystems) carry different design rules without contaminating each other. Designer agent loads the spec from the active harness root. *** # 6. The Design tab [Section titled “6. The Design tab”](#6-the-design-tab) Add a sibling to the Dashboard tab. The existing Features component takes a `mode` parameter; default is `dashboard`, design tab passes `design`. Mode controls: * Which columns render (design adds: design status chip, mock link, token-decision chip, approval state) * Which actions appear (design adds: open spec, open mocks, approve, request changes, mark skipped) * Which sub-filter buckets exist (design uses: needs-design / in-design / approved / skipped / review-pending) ## 6.1 Pane layout [Section titled “6.1 Pane layout”](#61-pane-layout) Three-column layout, mirroring the dashboard’s overall feel: * **Left rail** — Features list (the shared component in `mode=design`), filterable by sub-bucket * **Main column** — the active pane (one of the six below); pane-switcher tabs across the top * **Right rail** — selected feature detail (spec, status, recent events, designer/reviewer assignments) Six panes for the main column: 1. **Features (mode=design)** — shared component (also lives in the left rail; tab repeats it for full-width view) 2. **Design memos** — surface `content/internal-docs/design/*.mdx` as a working backlog with status (open / addressed / wontfix) 3. **Component registry browser** — searchable inventory (§8); humans browse, agents query via MCP 4. **Token inventory** — DTCG store (§9), with per-ecosystem preview of generated outputs 5. **Sketch / annotation canvas** — embedded tldraw, scoped to the selected feature 6. **Visual regression strip** — Lost Pixel screenshots, before/after per route or per component A seventh, deferred: cross-app consistency audit (operator vs papercup vs papercusp). Defer until tokens are unified. ## 6.2 Approval actor model [Section titled “6.2 Approval actor model”](#62-approval-actor-model) * **Reviewer agent** approves or rejects by default after implementation ships * **Human** can approve or reject at any time, including before the reviewer agent runs — explicit human approval bypasses the agent * **Designer agent** never self-approves * Approve / Reject actions are visible on the feature card in both Dashboard and Design tabs ## 6.3 Operator-panel integration [Section titled “6.3 Operator-panel integration”](#63-operator-panel-integration) Design events surface in the OperatorPanel directive cards (per the existing pattern) when they need user attention: * Design crit deadlocked — needs human pick * Designer escalated (failure-mode TBD per §18) * Reviewer rejected, re-spawn requires confirm * New token proposed, awaiting approval In-flight states (designer running, awaiting dependency) stay internal — they go in the design-tab events column, not as operator directives, to avoid card noise. *** # 7. The UI IR — JSON shape, ecosystem-agnostic [Section titled “7. The UI IR — JSON shape, ecosystem-agnostic”](#7-the-ui-ir--json-shape-ecosystem-agnostic) This is the most important architectural decision in the plan. The designer agent emits a *semantic* tree that implementer adapters resolve into their idioms. It must not emit JSX, Tailwind classes, Qt XML, or any ecosystem-specific syntax. ## 7.1 Why JSON, not a custom DSL [Section titled “7.1 Why JSON, not a custom DSL”](#71-why-json-not-a-custom-dsl) We considered copying Slint’s syntax (a real declarative DSL with parser/typechecker/LSP) versus a JSON schema. JSON wins unambiguously because the IR’s primary author and primary consumer are both LLMs: | | DSL (Slint-like) | JSON IR | | -------------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | Time to v0.1 | 3–4 months | 2–3 weeks | | LLM emission quality | Mid; needs many-shot | Native | | Free tooling | None (write parser/LSP/diff) | jq, JSON Patch, JSON Schema, IDE support | | Adapter complexity | Parse → AST → walk | Consume object directly | | Refactoring cost | Touches parser + adapters | Bump `irVersion`, ship transformer | A DSL’s main benefit (human readability) doesn’t apply when humans aren’t the primary authors. Costs (parser, LSP, agent prompt overhead, two-layer adapter parsing) all do. **Hybrid escape hatch (Vega-Lite/Altair pattern):** if a real human-authoring use case ever emerges, ship a thin DSL surface that compiles to the same JSON. We never lose the option. ## 7.2 Schema language: JSON Schema (default), CUE (option) [Section titled “7.2 Schema language: JSON Schema (default), CUE (option)”](#72-schema-language-json-schema-default-cue-option) JSON Schema is universally understood and trivial to validate in every language. **CUE** is stronger — real type system, better constraint expression — and is worth considering once the IR stabilizes. Start with JSON Schema; migrate to CUE if/when limits bite. ## 7.3 Sketch of the shape (illustrative — valid JSON in v0.1 [Section titled “7.3 Sketch of the shape (illustrative — valid JSON in v0.1”](#73-sketch-of-the-shape-illustrative--valid-json-in-v01) examples) 
```jsonc
{
  "irVersion": "0.1",
  "surface": "operator-panel",
  "ecosystem": "*",
  "layout": {
    "kind": "stack",
    "direction": "vertical",
    "gap": { "token": "space.md" },
    "children": [
      { "kind": "header", "title": { "copy": "Operator" } },
      {
        "kind": "list",
        "emptyState": { "copy": "No directives.", "icon": "inbox" },
        "item": {
          "kind": "card",
          "slots": {
            "title":   { "ref": "card.title" },
            "body":    { "ref": "card.body" },
            "actions": { "ref": "card.actions" }
          },
          "interactions": ["hover", "focus", "select"]
        }
      }
    ]
  },
  "components": [
    {
      "id": "btn-accept",
      "registry": "action.primary",
      "props": { "label": "Accept" }
    }
  ],
  "tokens": {
    "uses": ["color.bg.surface", "color.fg.primary", "space.md", "radius.sm"]
  },
  "states": {
    "loading": { "kind": "spinner", "label": { "copy": "Loading…" } },
    "error":   { "copy": "Could not load directives.", "retry": true }
  },
  "a11y": { "landmark": "main", "headingLevel": 2 }
}
```
 Properties of this format: * No DOM assumptions. `kind: "stack"` becomes flexbox, QVBoxLayout, or `Vertical { }` depending on adapter. * No CSS. Visual properties reference tokens, never literals. * No imperative JS. Interactions are declared by name; adapters bind them. * Explicit registry references for non-primitive components. * `kind` values draw from OpenUI vocabulary (`open-ui.org/components`) where possible, so naming aligns with industry usage. ## 7.4 Sub-IR escape hatch — Plotly for charts [Section titled “7.4 Sub-IR escape hatch — Plotly for charts”](#74-sub-ir-escape-hatch--plotly-for-charts) Charts are a domain that already has a mature multi-language declarative spec. We don’t reinvent it. 
```jsonc
{ "kind": "chart", "spec": { /* Plotly JSON */ } }
```
 Designer agent reaches for `kind: "chart"` only when the surface genuinely includes data viz; otherwise compose primitives. **Plotly** chosen over Vega-Lite, ECharts, ApexCharts after survey: * Most language bindings of any chart spec — JS, Python, R, Julia, MATLAB, F#, .NET. Directly serves the cross-ecosystem goal. * Most LLM training data (pervasive in data-science notebooks); agents emit it more reliably. * Verbose but explicit; agents don’t care about character count, and explicit specs are easier to validate and diff. * 18.2k★, large active community. Vega-Lite’s grammar-of-graphics elegance matters when humans compose specs by hand — wrong axis to optimize for an agent-authored format. ## 7.5 No card / form sub-IR [Section titled “7.5 No card / form sub-IR”](#75-no-card--form-sub-ir) Earlier drafts proposed embedding Adaptive Cards as a card sub-IR. On closer look, AC’s unique value is its multi-stack *external* renderer ecosystem (Teams, Outlook actionable messages, Bot Framework). For *our internal* cards/forms/dashboards, embedding AC adds a dependency without saving work and constrains us to AC’s bounded vocabulary. The IR’s general `kind: "card"` / `kind: "form"` is rendered by the ecosystem adapter. Adapters may *implement* their renderer using libraries like JSON Forms, react-jsonschema-form, or Formily — that’s an adapter detail, not an IR-level decision. Adaptive Cards reappears in §13 as an *export adapter*, not a sub-IR. ## 7.6 Iconography [Section titled “7.6 Iconography”](#76-iconography) Icons are a sub-registry under the component registry, with their own schema (`iconId → svgPath / sourcePointer`). Referenced by ID in the IR. As shipped in v0.1 the IR’s icon reference is a **plain string id** (`iconRef = string`): the inline slot-prop form is `"icon": "inbox"`, and the `{ kind: "icon", id: "inbox" }` node form carries the same string under its `icon` field. Adapters scan icon paths declared in their manifest; the React-Tailwind adapter will scan `lucide-react` exports + project-local SVGs. ## 7.7 Copy and i18n [Section titled “7.7 Copy and i18n”](#77-copy-and-i18n) Every user-facing string in the IR uses `{ key, default }`: 
```jsonc
{ "title": { "key": "operator.header.title", "default": "Operator" } }
```
 Adapters that have no i18n runtime treat `default` as the literal. Adapters with i18n (most React apps) wire `key` through their existing translation layer. Designers default to `key`-with-default on every spec — cheap now, prohibitively expensive to retrofit. ## 7.8 Responsive / viewport [Section titled “7.8 Responsive / viewport”](#78-responsive--viewport) Layout nodes accept per-breakpoint overrides keyed by named viewport tokens (`viewport.narrow`, `viewport.medium`, `viewport.wide`) defined in the DTCG store: 
```jsonc
{
  "kind": "stack",
  "direction": "vertical",
  "responsive": {
    "viewport.wide": { "direction": "horizontal" }
  }
}
```
 Container-query semantics — overrides apply when the *container* matches the viewport, not the global window. Adapter resolves to its idiomatic mechanism (CSS container queries, Qt layout policies, etc.). ## 7.9 Theming (light/dark, brand variants) [Section titled “7.9 Theming (light/dark, brand variants)”](#79-theming-lightdark-brand-variants) The IR always references base token IDs. Theme resolution is the adapter’s job, driven by the active DTCG `$themes` group. Designer never thinks about light/dark in the spec; they think about semantic tokens (`color.bg.surface`) that resolve correctly under any theme. ## 7.10 Motion / animation [Section titled “7.10 Motion / animation”](#710-motion--animation) A `motion` field on layout/component nodes declares intent semantically: 
```jsonc
{ "motion": { "enter": "slide-up", "exit": "fade", "duration": "duration.md" } }
```
 Allowed values draw from a small, named vocabulary — the shipped schema enum is `fade / slide-up / slide-down / slide-left / slide-right / scale / none`. Concrete keyframes/easings live in tokens (`duration.*`, `easing.*`). Adapters bind to their motion library (motion / auto-animate / Qt animations / etc.). ## 7.11 A11y — per-element [Section titled “7.11 A11y — per-element”](#711-a11y--per-element) `a11y` lives on every interactive node, not just the surface root: 
```jsonc
{
  "kind": "button",
  "registry": "action.primary",
  "props": { "label": { "key": "...", "default": "Accept" } },
  "a11y": {
    "role": "button",
    "ariaLabel": { "key": "...", "default": "Accept directive" },
    "keyboardShortcut": "Enter"
  }
}
```
 The surface root keeps `landmark` + `headingLevel`. Live regions, focus management, and tab order get dedicated fields as the IR matures (open: do these go in `a11y` or a sibling `interaction` field?). ## 7.12 Composition: surface vs route [Section titled “7.12 Composition: surface vs route”](#712-composition-surface-vs-route) A *surface* is one IR document. A *route* is a thin manifest that lists surfaces (and their layout — split-pane, tabs, modal stack). Route manifests are a separate JSON shape, much smaller than surface IR. Designer authors a route spec when adding/changing navigation; otherwise just surfaces. ## 7.13 Data binding boundary [Section titled “7.13 Data binding boundary”](#713-data-binding-boundary) The IR declares slots and binding points; it does not declare data sources. A list says “this is a list, items repeat, each item gets slots A B C”; the implementer wires the data source. 
```jsonc
{
  "kind": "list",
  "binding": { "slot": "items", "repeats": true, "shape": "DirectiveCard" },
  "item": { /* IR for one item, slots reference DirectiveCard fields */ }
}
```
 `shape` is a named type the implementer maps to its data layer (TypeScript type, Rust struct, etc.). The designer doesn’t pick the data source; the implementer does. ## 7.14 Free-form escape hatch [Section titled “7.14 Free-form escape hatch”](#714-free-form-escape-hatch) When the IR genuinely can’t express something, `kind: "raw"` lets the designer hand off ecosystem-native code: 
```jsonc
{ "kind": "raw", "ecosystem": "react-tailwind", "payload": "<MyJsx/>" }
```
 Linter flags `raw` as a warning (it bypasses the abstraction); crit may reject if used to skip thinking. Always available, never default. ## 7.15 IR linter (anti-pattern checks) [Section titled “7.15 IR linter (anti-pattern checks)”](#715-ir-linter-anti-pattern-checks) A validator says “is this valid JSON matching the schema?”. A linter says “is this *good* IR?”. Both run on every submitted spec. Lint rules (open-ended, expand as patterns emerge): * Maximum nesting depth (default 6) * Every interactive element has an `a11y.role` or maps to a registry component that supplies one * No literal colors / dimensions outside `tokens.uses` references * Every `states.error` has a recovery action (retry, navigate) * Every `states.loading` has an aria-live equivalent * `surface` is unique within the harness * Registry component IDs all resolve in the active registry * Token IDs all resolve in the active DTCG store Linter runs at submit time; warnings flow to the design crit prompt; errors block acceptance until fixed. *** # 8. Component registry — neutral schema + ecosystem adapters [Section titled “8. Component registry — neutral schema + ecosystem adapters”](#8-component-registry--neutral-schema--ecosystem-adapters) shadcn’s registry is React/Tailwind-coupled. We want the *idea* without the coupling. ## 8.1 Neutral schema [Section titled “8.1 Neutral schema”](#81-neutral-schema) 
```jsonc
{
  "id": "action.primary",            // semantic id, ecosystem-free
  "kind": "component",
  "summary": "Primary call-to-action button",
  "inputs": [
    { "name": "label", "type": "string", "required": true },
    { "name": "icon",  "type": "icon",   "required": false }
  ],
  "variants": ["default", "loading", "disabled"],
  "states":   ["hover", "focus", "active"],
  "examples": [{ "inputs": { "label": "Accept" }, "preview": "asset:..." }],
  "ecosystems": {
    "react-tailwind": {
      "sourcePointer": "<adapter-declared-path>/Button.tsx",
      "importHint":    "import { Button } from '...'",
      "propMap":       { "label": "children", "icon": "leftIcon" }
    },
    "qt-widgets":  { "sourcePointer": "...", "importHint": "...", "propMap": {} }
  }
}
```
 Designer agent searches by semantic id / summary / inputs. Implementer agent (which already knows its ecosystem) reads the matching `ecosystems[e]` block to know what to import and how to map props. ## 8.2 Registry adapters [Section titled “8.2 Registry adapters”](#82-registry-adapters) Adapters populate the registry by scanning paths they themselves declare — no global hardcoded path. * `registry-adapter-react-shadcn` — scans the React/TSX path tree declared in the adapter manifest; infers inputs from TS prop types; captures Storybook screenshots as examples. Ships first. For papercusp itself, the declared path is `libs/papercusp/`. * `registry-adapter-qt-widgets` — community * `registry-adapter-egui` — community * `registry-adapter-slint` — community Adapters are papercusp plugins (we already have a plugin system). ## 8.3 Cross-harness sharing [Section titled “8.3 Cross-harness sharing”](#83-cross-harness-sharing) The registry is per-harness because each harness has its own component path tree. For shared design system libraries (e.g., a papercup-org-wide `libs/papercusp/` that multiple harnesses consume), the adapter manifest can declare additional registry sources outside the harness root. Cross-harness registry sharing is opt-in per adapter, not implicit. *** # 9. Tokens — DTCG as canonical, per-ecosystem outputs [Section titled “9. Tokens — DTCG as canonical, per-ecosystem outputs”](#9-tokens--dtcg-as-canonical-per-ecosystem-outputs) The W3C Design Tokens Community Group format (`design-tokens.org`) is the cross-ecosystem standard JSON for tokens. It is deliberately neutral: color, dimension, typography, duration, etc. Adopt DTCG as the canonical token store under `design/tokens/`. As shipped, the canonical DTCG store file is **`design/tokens/base.json`** — the runtime sync-resolver, the `list_tokens` MCP tool, and the Design tab’s Token pane all read it directly. The seeder writes a sibling `design/tokens/seeded-from-harness-css.json` as the input to the manual semantic pass (§20.13), which merges into `base.json`. Per-ecosystem transformers emit: * CSS custom properties for React/Tauri * Tailwind preset * `.qss` for Qt * Theme structs for egui / iced * `.slint` for Slint * Anything the adapter author writes Transformer choice: **Terrazzo** (DTCG-native, modern) or **Style Dictionary** (battle-tested, Amazon). Terrazzo is the recommended default for new code; Style Dictionary remains a fine choice for adapters that need the wider transform ecosystem. > **As shipped:** the repo-level `npm run tokens` build runs on **Style Dictionary v4** (`^4.4.0`, config in `design-tokens/style-dictionary.config.mjs`) — not Terrazzo. The react-tailwind adapter, on a separate path, ships its **own minimal in-house** CSS-vars + Tailwind-preset emitter (its docstring notes Terrazzo “is not yet a dep”). Terrazzo remains the planned long-term transformer but is not currently a dependency. This solves the existing harness.css triplication problem (operator + libs/papercusp + libs/git-graph) as a side effect: single source, generated outputs. ## 9.1 Proposing new tokens [Section titled “9.1 Proposing new tokens”](#91-proposing-new-tokens) When a designer’s spec needs a token that doesn’t exist: 1. Spec annotates `tokens.proposed: [{ id, type, value, reason }]` 2. Linter flags this as a warning, not an error (proposals are normal) 3. Token inventory pane surfaces the proposal as a “review new token” action 4. Approver (human or design crit) promotes the proposal into the DTCG store, optionally renaming for semantic consistency 5. Spec is re-validated; the token ID resolves; gate can advance Auto-promotion is off by default — token names are a human/design-judgment call. ## 9.2 Human authoring paths [Section titled “9.2 Human authoring paths”](#92-human-authoring-paths) * **Tokens Studio for Figma** (Figma plugin) — for designers comfortable in Figma; exports DTCG natively * **Token inventory pane** — custom in-app editor, built into the Design tab (§6.4). DTCG JSON is simple enough that per-type controls (color picker, dimension input, font dropdown) are a small build. There is no mature standalone OSS token editor to adopt. * **tweakcn** — visual editor specifically for the Tailwind output; optional, downstream of DTCG. *** # 10. Preview surface — abstract pane with adapters [Section titled “10. Preview surface — abstract pane with adapters”](#10-preview-surface--abstract-pane-with-adapters) Storybook is web-only. Treat it as the React adapter for a generic *preview pane* concept. Preview adapter contract: 
```plaintext
capturePreview({ componentId, variant, state }) -> ImageAsset
listPrimitives() -> ComponentId[]
livePreviewUrl?({ componentId }) -> URL    // optional, web-style only
```
 Adapters: * `preview-adapter-storybook` — for React (mounts existing Storybook stories, captures via Playwright) * `preview-adapter-binary-screenshot` — for native apps; exec the binary with a flag, capture the window * `preview-adapter-slint-live` — Slint’s own live preview * `preview-adapter-headless-imgui` — captures ImGui frames The Design tab’s preview pane is adapter-agnostic; it just renders whatever asset the active adapter returned. *** # 11. Sketch / annotate [Section titled “11. Sketch / annotate”](#11-sketch--annotate) Embed **tldraw** in the Design tab. Pixels and shapes are ecosystem-neutral; nothing to abstract. Sketches are stored in `harness_design_artifacts` (§2.1) with `kind = "sketch"`, payload = tldraw’s serialized state. They’re keyed to the feature, retrievable across sessions, and Zero-synced to all clients. Designer agent can also drop annotations on screenshots produced by the preview adapter (e.g., “this gap should be space.md”) — stored with `kind = "annotation"`. *** # 12. Visual regression — Lost Pixel [Section titled “12. Visual regression — Lost Pixel”](#12-visual-regression--lost-pixel) **Lost Pixel** is the OSS Percy/Chromatic alternative; it operates on screenshots so it works for any ecosystem that can produce a window. Run on PRs against the previous baseline; surface the diff strip in the Design tab and as a check on the feature card. For native ecosystems: the same `capturePreview` adapter that feeds the preview pane feeds Lost Pixel. ## 12.1 Baseline ownership [Section titled “12.1 Baseline ownership”](#121-baseline-ownership) * Baseline = last main-branch commit * PR diffs against that baseline; the strip surfaces every changed screenshot * Explicit “approve diff” action (human or reviewer agent) updates the baseline at merge time * No silent baseline drift; every change is approved *** # 13. Mock import + external export adapters [Section titled “13. Mock import + external export adapters”](#13-mock-import--external-export-adapters) ## 13.1 Mock-input adapters [Section titled “13.1 Mock-input adapters”](#131-mock-input-adapters) Figma is React-world’s mock-source default but irrelevant to a Qt dev. Treat the **Figma-Context-MCP** shape (selection → semantic tree → component matches) as the *protocol*, with Figma being one implementation. * `mock-adapter-figma` — Figma Dev Mode MCP * `mock-adapter-tldraw` — sketches drawn in the embedded canvas * `mock-adapter-screenshot` — image → semantic tree (uses `screenshot-to-code` style primitive) * `mock-adapter-text` — pure prose spec Each adapter declares its `parse(input)` input shape in the plugin manifest (e.g., Figma adapter expects a Figma node URL; screenshot adapter expects an image asset). All emit into the same UI IR, so the designer agent’s downstream flow is identical regardless of input. ## 13.2 External-surface export adapters [Section titled “13.2 External-surface export adapters”](#132-external-surface-export-adapters) When a feature targets an *external* surface that has its own declarative format and renderer ecosystem, the implementer adapter emits that format directly from the IR. We don’t write renderers for these surfaces. * `export-adapter-adaptive-cards` — emits Adaptive Cards JSON for Teams, Outlook actionable messages, Bot Framework, Cortana Skills * `export-adapter-slack-block-kit` — emits Slack Block Kit JSON for Slack messages and modals * `export-adapter-discord-embeds` — community * (community can add more) One plugin per export target. Optional and opt-in per feature. *** # 14. The Ecosystem Adapter Contract [Section titled “14. The Ecosystem Adapter Contract”](#14-the-ecosystem-adapter-contract) The first concrete artifact to build. Every adapter type listed above (registry, preview, token output, mock input, code emit, export) is a specialization of a single plugin shape: 
```typescript
interface DesignEcosystemAdapter {
  id:          string;     // stable plugin id, e.g. "papercusp-design-react-tailwind"
  displayName: string;     // human-readable, e.g. "React + Tailwind (papercusp)"
  ecosystem:   string;     // machine ecosystem id; matches the IR `ecosystem` field, e.g. "react-tailwind"
  capabilities: AdapterCapability[];
  irVersionsSupported: string[];    // e.g. ["0.x", "1.x"]
  uiPaths: string[];                // globs for needsDesign heuristic


  registry?: {
    sourcePaths: string[];                          // declared scan roots
    listPrimitives(): RegistryEntry[];
    sourceFor(id: string): SourcePointer;
  };
  preview?: {
    capture(spec: PreviewSpec): Promise<ImageAsset>;
  };
  tokens?: {
    emit(dtcg: DtcgDoc): Promise<FileEmit[]>;
  };
  mockInput?: {
    inputShape: JsonSchema;                         // declared input contract
    parse(input: unknown): Promise<UiIr>;
  };
  codeEmit?: {
    /**
     * @param ir   the spec to emit
     * @param target.outDir destination workspace path
     * @param target.mode   "scaffold" | "patch" | "preview"
     */
    fromIR(ir: UiIr, target: CodeEmitTarget): Promise<FileEmit[]>;
  };
  exportTarget?: {
    targetId: string;                               // "adaptive-cards", ...
    fromIR(ir: UiIr): Promise<unknown>;             // target-native payload
  };
}
```
 Ships in the papercusp plugin SDK. The first adapter is `papercusp-design-react-tailwind`, used by papercusp itself (eat-your-own-dogfood). *** # 15. MCP surface for designer agents [Section titled “15. MCP surface for designer agents”](#15-mcp-surface-for-designer-agents) Designers consume the registry, tokens, memos, and live surface state via an MCP server bundled with the design phase. Tools: * `searchRegistry({ query, ecosystem? }) → RegistryEntry[]` * `getRegistryComponent(id) → RegistryEntry` * `readToken(id) → DtcgToken | null` * `listTokens({ category? }) → DtcgToken[]` * `proposeToken({ id, type, value, reason }) → ProposalRef` * `submitSpec(featureId, ir) → { ok, lintIssues, validationErrors }` * `lintSpec(ir) → LintIssue[]` — pre-submit self-check * `validateSpec(ir) → ValidationError[]` — schema-only check * `listMemos({ status?, tags? }) → Memo[]` * `readMemo(slug) → Memo` * `captureCurrentSurface(featureId) → ImageAsset | null` * `getDesignSpec() → string` — the resolved DESIGN\_SPEC.md * `listSiblingSpecs(featureId) → SpecRef[]` — recent accepted specs in the same harness for style consistency Reviewer/crit get a superset that adds `compareSpecs(a, b)`, `acceptSpec(featureId, specId)`, `rejectSpec(featureId, specId, reason)`. *** # 16. Implementer-side IR consumption [Section titled “16. Implementer-side IR consumption”](#16-implementer-side-ir-consumption) Implementer agents are upgraded to consume IR. Two protocol options considered; we ship (b) first. (a) **Code-emit fast path** — adapter’s `codeEmit.fromIR()` produces scaffold files, implementer edits them. Faster but the implementer loses understanding of *why* code looks the way it does. (b) **IR-as-context** — implementer prompt includes the IR JSON + the adapter’s “how to translate IR into this ecosystem” rules. Implementer writes code by hand, referring to IR. Slower per feature but produces higher-quality, idiomatic code; implementer internalizes the design intent. Path (b) is the default. Path (a) is opt-in for high-volume CRUD features where idiomaticity matters less than throughput. The implementer prompt gains a section: “the design spec is the source of truth for what to build; deviations require a new designer pass, not silent edits.” *** # 17. Testing strategy [Section titled “17. Testing strategy”](#17-testing-strategy) * **IR validator** — golden specs that should/shouldn’t validate; per-rule unit tests * **IR linter** — per-rule unit tests with positive + negative examples * **Adapter conformance** — the plugin SDK ships an `assertAdapterConformant()` test harness any adapter plugin must pass (covers: capability declarations, IR version support, source-pointer resolution, registry round-trip, etc.) * **End-to-end (per ecosystem)** — designer emits spec → adapter emits code → Lost Pixel matches expected baseline; runs in CI on every adapter change * **Reviewer regression** — known good/bad spec/render pairs; the reviewer should accept the good and reject the bad * **Designer prompt eval** — small benchmark of “feature description → IR” pairs; track quality across model/prompt changes (reuse the EL suite-test pattern from operator) *** # 18. What we adopt vs build vs skip [Section titled “18. What we adopt vs build vs skip”](#18-what-we-adopt-vs-build-vs-skip) **Adopt:** * **DTCG** — token format * **Terrazzo** (default) or **Style Dictionary** — token transformer * **tldraw** — sketch canvas * **Lost Pixel** — visual regression * **Storybook** — React preview adapter (or **Ladle** if we want faster; revisit) * **Figma Dev Mode MCP** — for the React/Figma mock-input adapter * **Plotly** — chart sub-IR escape hatch * **shadcn/ui registry-template** — as inspiration for the React registry adapter, not as the core schema * **Tokens Studio for Figma** — optional human authoring path for DTCG * **Adaptive Cards / Slack Block Kit** — optional export adapters only (not core sub-IRs) * **OpenUI vocabulary** — as a naming reference for IR `kind` values **Build:** * The phase model + lifecycle gate + designer agent + reviewer agent * The UI IR JSON schema (and v0.1 examples) * The IR linter (§7.6) * The neutral component registry schema * The Ecosystem Adapter Contract + plugin shape * The Design tab + 6 panes * The `needsDesign` heuristic (reads scope text, not diffs) * `DESIGN_SPEC.md` template + fallback chain * React-Tailwind adapter (first; for papercusp itself) * In-app token editor (Token inventory pane) * Token-extraction seeder script (CSS custom properties → DTCG) * Design lifecycle columns on `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated` + `harness_shared.harness_design_artifacts` PG table + Zero sync hookups (the lifecycle fields shipped as columns on the canonical features table, not a separate `harness_design_phase` table) **Skip / defer:** * **Slint syntax adoption** — JSON IR wins on agent DX and effort; reconsider only if humans become primary authors * **Custom DSL parser/LSP** — see above; \~3 months of work avoided * **Adaptive Cards as internal sub-IR** — kept only as export adapter * **Vega-Lite / ECharts / ApexCharts** — Plotly chosen * **rjsf / JSON Forms / Formily as IR concerns** — these are adapter implementation details * **Penpot** — only if humans need a mock canvas later; tldraw covers most of it * **Onlook** — too heavyweight to fork; reference architecture only * **Stagewise** — dev-tool not design-tool; revisit for the review pass if useful * **bolt.new / bolt.diy** — wrong altitude * **Cross-app consistency audit pane** — defer until tokens are unified via DTCG *** # 16. Build order [Section titled “16. Build order”](#16-build-order) Each step is independently shippable. 1. **Schema + lifecycle fields + gate.** Add the design lifecycle columns (`needs_design`, `design_status`, `design_spec_id`, `discarded_design_work`) to the canonical features table `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated`, plus the `harness_shared.harness_design_artifacts` table (with Zero sync). (Shipped as columns on the consolidated table, not a separate `harness_design_phase` table.) Heuristic at creation. Gate before implementing. No UI yet. 2. **Design tab shell** with Features pane only (mode=design). Three-column layout (§6.1). Validates the `mode` parameter abstraction. 3. **`DESIGN_SPEC.md` template + fallback chain** + designer agent prompt rooted in it. Designer can produce a free-form spec (no IR yet). 4. **UI IR v0.1** — minimal JSON Schema, hand-written examples, validator + linter (§7.6). Designer agent emits IR; no consumer yet. 5. **Ecosystem Adapter Contract** + plugin shape. Empty registry of adapters. 6. **`papercusp-design-react-tailwind` adapter**, capabilities: `registry`, `tokens` (Tailwind), `codeEmit`. Implementer agent prompt updated to consume IR. 7. **DTCG token store** under `design/tokens/`. Token-extraction seeder runs once over the operator’s `harness.css` triplets to produce the initial DTCG file (the eat-our-own-dogfood case; community adapters define their own seeders). Adapter emits Tailwind preset + CSS vars. `harness.css` files are migrated incrementally (see §20.13). 8. **Component registry browser pane** (Design tab). Reads from the adapter. 9. **Token inventory pane** + new-token proposal flow (§9.1). 10. **Storybook preview adapter** — captures stories as examples for the registry; powers the preview pane. 11. **tldraw sketch pane** + artifact storage. 12. **Lost Pixel** in CI; visual regression strip pane; baseline-approval action (§12.1). 13. **Design memos pane** — surface existing `.mdx` memos with status; promote-to-feature action (§17.3). 14. **Reviewer agent + post-ship review pass** + design-crit agent role (§20.9). 15. **Mock-input adapters** (Figma, screenshot, tldraw-derived). Optional; opt-in per feature. 16. **Export adapters** (Adaptive Cards, Slack Block Kit). Optional; opt-in per feature. Steps 1–4 are the spine. Steps 5–6 are the abstraction proof. Everything after is panes and adapters that hang off the spine. ## 16.1 Rough effort estimate [Section titled “16.1 Rough effort estimate”](#161-rough-effort-estimate) * Steps 1–4 (spine): \~2–3 weeks each, sequential * Steps 5–6 (abstraction proof): \~3–4 weeks each * Steps 7–13 (panes + DTCG): \~1–2 weeks each, parallelizable * Steps 14–16 (reviewer + adapters): \~2 weeks each Total: \~2–3 months to a working v1 with the spine + React adapter. \~6 months to feature-complete with all panes and the reviewer loop. Add a quarter for the second ecosystem adapter to shake out genuine ecosystem-neutrality bugs in the IR. *** # 20. Resolved decisions [Section titled “20. Resolved decisions”](#20-resolved-decisions) ## 20.1 Model selection per role [Section titled “20.1 Model selection per role”](#201-model-selection-per-role) Configurable per-harness with sensible defaults: * Designer: best available reasoning model (Opus class) * Crit: same family as designer (apples-to-apples comparison) * Reviewer: mid-tier (Sonnet class) — pattern-matching task * Implementer: unchanged from existing config Override via `DESIGN_SPEC.md` frontmatter: `models: { designer: "...", reviewer: "...", crit: "..." }`. ## 20.2 Adapter lifecycle and conflict [Section titled “20.2 Adapter lifecycle and conflict”](#202-adapter-lifecycle-and-conflict) * Adapters activate lazily — on first reference (feature creation triggers heuristic scan; spec submission triggers code-emit) * Manifest declares `claims: ["react-tailwind"]`; if two installed adapters claim the same ecosystem, harness must explicitly pick one in `harness.config.json` (`design.activeAdapters: { ... }`) * Conflict surfaces as an operator directive, not a silent pick ## 20.3 Permission / sandbox model [Section titled “20.3 Permission / sandbox model”](#203-permission--sandbox-model) Reuses papercusp’s existing plugin permission grants. Design-phase permissions: * `read:registry` (always granted) * `read:design-tokens` (always granted) * `write:design-artifacts` (always granted for designer agents) * `read:current-surface` (granted for redesigns) * `propose:tokens` (granted for designer agents) * `external-call:<targetId>` (per-export-adapter; user grants on install) Adapters cannot scan paths outside their declared `sourcePaths` without an additional grant. ## 20.4 Designer-in-flight visibility [Section titled “20.4 Designer-in-flight visibility”](#204-designer-in-flight-visibility) Happy path stays out of operator directives. The feature card shows a small “designing” badge with elapsed time + token count. Operator directive only fires for the cases listed in §6.3 (deadlock, escalation, rejection, new-token proposal). ## 20.5 Concurrent edits / locking [Section titled “20.5 Concurrent edits / locking”](#205-concurrent-edits--locking) * DTCG token store: optimistic locking with `version` field; conflicts surface a “merge needed” operator directive * Registry entries: read-only at the IR layer (only adapters write, during scans, with a global advisory lock per ecosystem) * Design specs: per-feature, no concurrent designers on one feature (the N=2-3 happens *before* any spec is accepted) ## 20.6 Cost telemetry per spec [Section titled “20.6 Cost telemetry per spec”](#206-cost-telemetry-per-spec) Every spec artifact records `tokensIn`, `tokensOut`, `costUsd`, `modelId`, `elapsedMs` — same shape the rest of the runtime uses. Surfaced in the design tab’s right rail per feature; aggregated in the existing budget views. ## 20.7 Lost Pixel intentional-vs-regression [Section titled “20.7 Lost Pixel intentional-vs-regression”](#207-lost-pixel-intentional-vs-regression) Spec acceptance writes a `targetBaselineHash` to the design phase record. Lost Pixel diffs against the baseline; if the new hash matches `targetBaselineHash`, the diff is auto-approved as intended. Mismatches surface for human review. No silent baseline drift; intent is always declared. ## 20.8 Migration of existing UI [Section titled “20.8 Migration of existing UI”](#208-migration-of-existing-ui) * Existing surfaces do NOT retroactively get IR specs (the migration would be bottomless) * New features: must produce IR if they create UI * Touched features: changing an existing surface requires authoring its IR first (one-time cost paid lazily) * The operator’s existing surfaces become ground-truth for designer training data — preview adapter can capture them as reference material ## 20.9 Multi-designer concurrency + design crit [Section titled “20.9 Multi-designer concurrency + design crit”](#209-multi-designer-concurrency--design-crit) Hybrid; not PR-style merge. * Orchestrator spawns 2–3 designers in parallel; each emits a candidate spec * A **design-crit agent** (the reviewer agent’s persona, in “crit” mode) scores candidates against `DESIGN_SPEC.md` rubric and picks ONE as canonical, optionally cherry-picking notes / decisions from runners-up as annotations * Crit can deadlock (no clear winner); deadlock surfaces as an operator directive (§6.3) for human pick * Auto-merging specs is a trap — design choices need a single authorial voice or the result is incoherent * Default N=2; raise to 3 only when feature is high-stakes / orchestrator marks it `exploratory` * Rejected candidates kept as artifacts on the feature for later reference, not deleted ## 20.10 IR versioning [Section titled “20.10 IR versioning”](#2010-ir-versioning) * Schema lives in core papercusp; semver * Every spec carries `irVersion: "0.3"`; runtime ships upgrade transformers between minor versions * Adapters declare `irVersionsSupported: ["0.x", "1.x"]` in plugin manifest; orchestrator refuses to gate-promote a spec into an adapter that doesn’t claim its version * **v1.0 lock criteria:** at least 2 production adapters consuming IR for ≥1 month without a breaking change to the schema. Concrete bar; no fuzzy “mature enough.” * Ownership: core team for v1; lightweight RFC process afterward (the IR should stabilize fast) ## 20.11 Memo ↔ feature linkage [Section titled “20.11 Memo ↔ feature linkage”](#2011-memo--feature-linkage) Promotable, with light coupling. * Memo gets a “promote to feature” action → creates feature with the memo as initial spec source * Memo retains link as `spawnedFeatures: [...]` * Memo `status` (open / addressed / wontfix) lives on the memo regardless of promotion — a promoted memo flips to `addressed` when its feature ships * Don’t auto-promote; humans/orchestrator decide * Un-promoted memos stay advisory and surface in the design tab’s memo pane as backlog ## 20.12 Human override UX [Section titled “20.12 Human override UX”](#2012-human-override-ux) No checkbox at creation (clutter). Surface override via the card itself. * Right-click card → “Skip design” / “Force design” — works in both Dashboard and Design tabs * Keyboard shortcut for the toggle: TBD by operator UX (single-key shortcut conflicts likely; defer naming until Design-tab integration lands) * If designer agent has already spawned, “Skip design” requires confirm + sets `discardedDesignWork: true` for telemetry * Status visible on every card as a small badge (design icon when `needsDesign`, struck-through when manually skipped) — no extra rows or modals * Heuristic should be right >90% of the time; override is an exception path, not first-class chrome ## 20.13 Token migration path [Section titled “20.13 Token migration path”](#2013-token-migration-path) No magic extractor exists; we build a small one. Operator-specific plan; community adapters define equivalents for their CSS-or-not sources. * **Step A — seeder script.** Regex over the three `harness.css` files for `:root` custom properties → DTCG seed file. Tailwind configs (if present) convert almost trivially because they’re already structured. * **Step B — manual semantic pass.** Extracted tokens have technical names (`--color-1`, `--space-md`); a designer (human or agent) renames to semantic (`color.bg.surface`, `space.gutter`) and dedups. This is the hard part; no tool replaces it. * **Step C — flip the imports.** `harness.css` files become thin wrappers that `@import` the generated CSS vars from DTCG. Keep originals committed for one window. * **Step D — Lost Pixel gate.** Run regression across known routes; only delete the originals when the diff is empty. * Estimate: half a day of focused renaming for the operator harness; longer for libs/papercusp due to surface area. *** # 21. Still-open questions [Section titled “21. Still-open questions”](#21-still-open-questions) These remain genuinely undecided and will resolve as we hit them. * **Designer agent failure mode:** if the designer can’t produce a valid IR (validation fails repeatedly), does the orchestrator escalate to a human, fall back to free-form spec, or skip the phase? Probably escalate, but TBD on UI. * **IR ↔ implementation traceability:** do generated files carry back-pointer comments to their source spec, or do we use a source-map-style sidecar (no comment noise in the code)? Lean sidecar. * **Cross-harness design system sharing:** when multiple harnesses share a `libs/papercusp/`-equivalent, do they also share a DTCG store and a registry, or do those stay per-harness with explicit `extends` syntax in the harness’s `DESIGN_SPEC.md`? Lean explicit `extends`, but defer until we hit the case. * **Designer-agent web access:** can designers query the live web for design references (color trends, ux patterns) or are they closed-world to memos + registry + DESIGN\_SPEC.md? Closed-world is safer; web access is a separate capability gate per harness.

Severity / status chips are 9px — same readability concern as proposals [Section titled “R1. Severity / status chips are 9px — same readability concern as proposals”](#r1-severity--status-chips-are-9px--same-readability-concern-as-proposals) Inspected: * `.h-issue-sev.sev-minor`: `font-size: 9px` * `.h-issue-status.st-open`: `font-size: 9.5px` Same family of issue I called out on the proposals tab in round 1 (8.5px sub-labels). The “current state” lifecycle button is `disabled` [Section titled “R2. The “current state” lifecycle button is disabled”](#r2-the-current-state-lifecycle-button-is-disabled) Round 1 asked for clear visual indication of which lifecycle state is current. The fix uses three signals: `aria-pressed`, `is-current` class, AND `disabled`. The first two are right; disabling the current button is a half-step too far. Disabled buttons usually mean “you can’t do this” — but the user *can* meaningfully click on a current-state button (to no-op, or to confirm the state). More importantly, disabled buttons are styled as dimmed/unavailable, which makes the *current* state look LESS prominent than the unselected ones. **Fix:** drop the `disabled` attribute. Keep `aria-pressed` + `is-current`. Style the current state as the most prominent (filled background, white text), not the dimmest. ## R3. Eyebrow chip text concatenates without spaces [Section titled “R3. The DOM has separate `<span>` chips with their own classes, so visually the chips render with CSS spacing — but accessibility tools (and copy-paste) get the run-on string. A separator span (`·`) between sibling chips would help both. **Fix:** use `<span aria-hidden="true">·</span>` or `gap` on the parent flex container with non-zero margins between chips so screen readers + copy-paste hear/get them as separate items. ## R4. The “Feature detail” / “Issue detail” overline [Section titled “R4. The “Feature detail” / “Issue detail” overline”](#r4-the-feature-detail--issue-detail-overline) These overlines appear above the eyebrow strip. Useful orientation but slightly redundant with the page chrome (the user clicked a feature row, so they already know they’re seeing a feature detail). Optional to keep — if the overline goes away, the eyebrow ID + status are still enough. ## R5. The chip color choices [Section titled “R5. The chip color choices”](#r5-the-chip-color-choices) * **Severity `minor`**: white-ish text, transparent background. Reads as “this is informational” — good for minor. * **Status `open`**: rose/red text + rose-tinted background. Reads as “attention needed” — fine, though “open” isn’t necessarily a problem state. Worth verifying that: * `severity: critical` gets the loudest treatment (red bg + white text) * `status: closed` gets a muted gray treatment * `status: wontfix` reads distinctly from `closed` Couldn’t verify in this state; only one issue type was visible. *** # Top-priority list [Section titled “Top-priority list”](#top-priority-list) If the designer ships **one** more thing: > **C9.r2 — issue drawer Recent runs + View timeline.** The only remaining round-1 gap. # Gotchas, performance, and migration anti-patterns

> Sharp edges, perf budgets, and traps caught during the original migration.

This page collects the non-obvious things — “I would have stepped on this if you hadn’t told me” — found during the multi-phase library migration of the harness page. Skim before making UI changes. ## The `data-state` vs `aria-selected` trap (Radix Tabs) [Section titled “The data-state vs aria-selected trap (Radix Tabs)”](#the-data-state-vs-aria-selected-trap-radix-tabs) When you use `@radix-ui/react-tabs` without an associated `<Tabs.Content>` for each trigger, **Radix only sets `aria-selected="true"` on the active trigger — it does NOT set `data-state="active"`.** Reason: with no `<Tabs.Content>`, there’s nothing to “open”; Radix considers the tab semantically selected but not “active”. This bites when you write CSS like: 
```css
.h-tab[data-state="active"] {
  background: var(--bg-3);
}
```
 …and your styling silently never fires. **Fix:** target `aria-selected="true"` instead. 
```css
/* For tabs without Tabs.Content (filter pills + imperative content render) */
.h-tab[aria-selected="true"] {
  background: var(--bg-3);
}


/* For tabs WITH Tabs.Content */
.my-tab[data-state="active"] {
  background: var(--bg-3);
}
```
 `harness.css` has examples of both at the bottom. ## Native `title=` is fine in grid cells, NOT on actions [Section titled “Native title= is fine in grid cells, NOT on actions”](#native-title-is-fine-in-grid-cells-not-on-actions) The “no native title=” rule is a soft rule, not a hard one. **Use `<Tooltip label>` for action elements** — buttons, status badges, IconButtons, anywhere the user might hover for a hint about what clicking does. **Use native `title=` for grid-cell truncation tooltips** — when you have thousands of `<RichGrid>` rows and each cell wants “show full text on hover when truncated”. Wrapping every cell in a Radix Tooltip mounts thousands of portals + listeners and noticeably hits scroll performance. Native `title=` is browser-built-in, free, and accessible-enough for data hover. A tell that you should use native `title=`: the value is dynamic and per-row (`title={row.title}`), not a static label. Static action-button hints almost always belong in `<Tooltip>`. ## Content disclosure: use `LazyDetails` — native `<details>` has been fully migrated [Section titled “Content disclosure: use LazyDetails — native \<details> has been fully migrated”](#content-disclosure-use-lazydetails--native-details-has-been-fully-migrated) *(Updated 2026-07-09 — the old “approved native `<details>` sites” list is gone; every listed site migrated.)* There are **zero native `<details>` blocks left in app UI**. The historical tension — HR6 says use `<Collapsible>`, but Radix Collapsible mounts heavy children eagerly even when collapsed — was resolved by **`app/_components/LazyDetails.tsx`**: a Radix Collapsible wrapper that defers mounting `children` until first open (and keeps them mounted afterward so internal state survives collapse/expand). It is the standard primitive for content disclosure (prose, diagnostic dumps, JSON dumps, debug help text) *and* satisfies HR6, so there is no perf reason to reach for native `<details>` anymore. * Heavy renderer behind a collapsed section (Monaco, MarkdownPreview, JSON tree, long log dump) → `<LazyDetails summary={…}>…</LazyDetails>`. * Interactive disclosure that should start mounted (collapsible form sections, per-row expanders needing shared animation/focus) → plain `<Collapsible.Root>`. * Native `<details>` remains acceptable **only inside rendered markdown content** (content-author markup the React tree can’t reach), same as the native-checkbox markdown carve-out in HR2. Two native-`<details>` niceties are knowingly given up by LazyDetails: Chromium’s find-in-page inside collapsed content (`hidden-until-found`) and auto-expand on print. If a surface genuinely needs those, raise it in review rather than silently reintroducing `<details>` — the direction is zero `<details>` in `.tsx`. ## Native checkbox / radio / range — `accent-color` is the carve-out, NOT the migration [Section titled “Native checkbox / radio / range — accent-color is the carve-out, NOT the migration”](#native-checkbox--radio--range--accent-color-is-the-carve-out-not-the-migration) When a native `<input type="checkbox|radio|range">` legitimately can’t be wrapped, `accent-color` recolors the OS-rendered control’s tint to match the app accent without breaking semantics — a strict improvement, never a workaround. **There is now a global baseline rule** in `globals.css`: 
```css
:where(input[type="checkbox"], input[type="radio"], input[type="range"]) {
  accent-color: var(--accent);
}
```
 so a bare native checkbox/radio/range picks up the app accent automatically — you no longer need to add a per-site scoped rule just to get the tint right. A handful of sites still layer an ADDITIONAL scoped rule on top of the baseline for extra styling (e.g. `.pc-toggle input { accent-color: var(--accent) }`, `.pc-template-manifest-structured input[type="checkbox"]` which also adds a `drop-shadow` glow) — those are refinements, not the thing that makes the color apply at all. **Do not read this as “native checkboxes are fine now.”** HR2 is still absolute for harness UI: use `<Checkbox>`. The wrapper exposes `indeterminate` declaratively, gives us a stable `data-state` hook, and owns focus styling. None of that comes from `accent-color`. The carve-out is narrow: native checkboxes that legitimately can’t be wrapped (markdown task lists rendered via `MarkdownPreview`, low-priority radio groups where a `<RadioGroup>` would be overkill, range sliders that are bespoke per-site anyway). When in doubt, wrap. ## Floating widgets that pin to a viewport corner are NOT centered Modals [Section titled “Floating widgets that pin to a viewport corner are NOT centered Modals”](#floating-widgets-that-pin-to-a-viewport-corner-are-not-centered-modals) The canonical example is the Deck (`OperatorPanel`, the fixed `.operator-panel` HUD whose wordmark reads “Deck”) — a floating, viewport-anchored panel with its own bespoke animations and HUD overlays. It’s not a centered modal (Modal would yank it to screen-center and add a backdrop), not an anchored Popover (no trigger to align to), and not a side Drawer (it doesn’t slide in from the edge). For this shape, the correct pattern is landmark/dialog semantics by hand — an `aria-label`ed container using `role="region"` (non-blocking, always-on-screen HUD) or `role="dialog"` (if it genuinely captures a task) — with positioning + animation owned by the component. HR1 doesn’t apply here; the rule’s intent (“focus management + escape handling come from the wrapper”) doesn’t fit a panel that lives forever on screen and toggles open/closed via its own state machine. Treat the Deck as the canonical exception; if you add a new floating-corner-widget pattern, document it next to it. *(History: `OracleDock` and `OperatorChatSidebar` — the “Papercup chat” web sidebar — were the other two examples of this pattern. Both were retired 2026-07-09 (`_retired/legacy-web-chats/`): the only chat surface is the terminal-native pui chat pane in the zellij dock.)* ## Radix Select doesn’t allow empty-string values [Section titled “Radix Select doesn’t allow empty-string values”](#radix-select-doesnt-allow-empty-string-values) `<Select value="">` is reserved by Radix Select to mean “no value selected” — same as `<Select value={undefined}>`. If your business logic uses `''` as a real value (e.g., “default mode”), Radix Select will display the placeholder when you actually mean to display “default”. **Fix:** translate at the boundary. 
```tsx
<Select
  value={mode || '_default'}
  onChange={(v) => setMode(v === '_default' ? '' : v)}
  options={[{ value: '_default', label: 'default' }, { value: 'ceo', label: 'ceo' }]}
/>
```
 Use a papercup like `'_default'` that’s guaranteed not to collide with a real value, and translate in `onChange`. ## Vaul drawer needs an explicit Title [Section titled “Vaul drawer needs an explicit Title”](#vaul-drawer-needs-an-explicit-title) Radix Dialog’s accessibility check warns if you don’t render a `<Dialog.Title>`. Vaul reuses the Dialog primitive internally and inherits the same check. Always include a sr-only Title: 
```tsx
<Drawer.Title style={{
  position: 'absolute', width: 1, height: 1, padding: 0, margin: -1,
  overflow: 'hidden', clip: 'rect(0,0,0,0)', whiteSpace: 'nowrap', border: 0,
}}>
  Feature {feature.id}
</Drawer.Title>
```
 ## Modal overlay click vs ESC [Section titled “Modal overlay click vs ESC”](#modal-overlay-click-vs-esc) Radix Dialog’s outside-click is implemented as a `pointerdown` event on the overlay, not a `click`. If you’re writing tests that “click outside to close”, dispatch a `pointerdown` event, not a `click`: 
```js
const overlay = document.querySelector('[data-state=open][role!=dialog]');
overlay.dispatchEvent(new PointerEvent('pointerdown', { bubbles: true, pointerType: 'mouse' }));
```
 ESC works as expected via `keydown`. ## Tooltip needs real pointer events to fire [Section titled “Tooltip needs real pointer events to fire”](#tooltip-needs-real-pointer-events-to-fire) When testing tooltips programmatically, synthetic `MouseEvent('mouseenter')` doesn’t trigger Radix Tooltip’s open state. You need real pointer events from a browser-driver (Playwright `page.hover()` works; `verdict hover @e18` works). This is a Radix design choice (focus on real input intent, not synthetic dispatches) — there’s no workaround beyond using a real driver. ## cmdk groups hide automatically when filtering [Section titled “cmdk groups hide automatically when filtering”](#cmdk-groups-hide-automatically-when-filtering) When the user types in `<Command.Input>`, cmdk filters items by their `value` prop. If a `<Command.Group>` ends up with zero matching children, cmdk **hides the entire group, including the heading.** This is the right UX, but if you’re testing or debugging, your group’s heading vanishing is expected behavior, not a bug. Use `<Command.Group hidden={false}>` to force-show, or check the `[hidden]` attr in DevTools. ## Performance budget — what’s reasonable [Section titled “Performance budget — what’s reasonable”](#performance-budget--whats-reasonable) These are the numbers we measured after the original migration. Use them as floors; if your change makes any of these significantly worse, investigate. | Interaction | Dev mode | Production target | | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------- | | Cold page load (HTTP `time_total`) | 0.87 – 1.21s | < 200ms | | Inner tab switch (e.g., Inbox All → Threads) | \~150ms | \~50ms | | Command palette open (Dialog mount + cmdk wiring) | \~314ms | \~100ms | | Modal open/close cycle | \~100ms | \~30ms | | Memory after 10 modal open/close cycles | 0 KB heap growth | 0 KB heap growth | If you’re adding a new modal or a new heavy panel and tab switches start feeling sluggish (>300ms in dev), check: 1.
