principals | `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/agent-mcp/provision.ts` (calls `provisionSystemPrincipal` in `packages/agent-mcp/src/provisioning.ts`) | ## URL spawn params [Section titled “URL spawn params”](#url-spawn-params) Read by `buildHttpSpawnContext` in `http-projection.ts` and the equivalent on the MCP route. | Query param | Header | Field | | -------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | `workspace` | `X-Papercusp-Workspace` | `ctx.workspaceId` | | `harness` | `X-Papercusp-Harness` | `ctx.harnessSlug` (also drives `projectDir` resolution) | | `role` | `X-Papercusp-Role` | `ctx.role` | | `feature` | `X-Papercusp-Feature` | `ctx.featureId` | | `chunk` | `X-Papercusp-Chunk` | `ctx.chunkId` | | `run` | `X-Papercusp-Run` | `ctx.runId` | | `spawn` | `X-Papercusp-Spawn` | `ctx.spawnId` | | `parent_spawn` | `X-Papercusp-Parent-Spawn` | `ctx.parentSpawnId` | | `client` | `X-Papercusp-Client` | `ctx.uiClientId` | Header form takes precedence over query form when both are present. The orchestrator uses query form when writing per-spawn `.mcp.json` because mcp-handler clients don’t have a clean way to attach custom headers. `client` carries the per-session SID used for coordination ownership (locks, plan edits, `agent_chats`). It is required for superuser / power-user identity attribution: a client-less superuser/power-user call reaches `resolveAgentIdentity` with `uiClientId=null` and **throws**, so identity-resolving tools fail for those callers. It follows the same header-first precedence as the others (the `X-Papercusp-Client` header overrides a static `?client=` query value). ## Operations endpoints [Section titled “Operations endpoints”](#operations-endpoints) | Endpoint | Purpose | | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `GET /api/plugins/tools` | List every projected tool. Used by `/settings/plugins/tools`. | | `POST /api/plugins/host/refresh` | Re-run discovery. Returns full host status. | | `GET /api/credentials/search-providers` | Read masked search-provider keys + provider list (UI-only). | | `POST /api/credentials/search-providers` | Update keys (UI-only). | | `POST /api/agent-tools/<scope>/<verb>` | Built-in tool catch-all. | | `POST /api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>` | Plugin tool catch-all (HTTP). | | `GET/POST /api/mcp` | MCP transport (Streamable HTTP). | | `GET /api/sse` | MCP transport (SSE). Same handler. | | `GET /api/operator/state-snapshot` | SSE stream of `state-snapshot` events for the active workspace. Carries `openCards` (from `ctx.askUser`) + `toolState` (from `ctx.publishState`). Session-cookie required (401). | | `POST /api/operator/conversations/:id/card-response` | Resolves a pending `ctx.askUser` card. Body: `{ correlationId, action: 'submit'\|'decline'\|'cancel', workspaceId, payload?, reason? }`. 30 RPS per session user. 404 on cross-workspace replay (defense-in-depth). | | `POST /api/operator/conversations/:id/run-cancel` | Cancels every pending card under a `runId`. Body: `{ runId, workspaceId }`. Same auth + rate limit + cross-workspace gate as `/card-response`. | | `POST /api/workspaces/switch` | Body `{ id }`. Captures `leaving = reg.current`, writes new current, fires `dispatchWorkspaceSwitch(leaving)` — drops state snapshots + cancels every pending card under the leaving workspace. | ## Result envelope [Section titled “Result envelope”](#result-envelope) Tool functions return `ToolResult`: 
```ts
interface ToolResult {
  content: Array<
    | { type: 'text'; text: string }
    | { type: 'image'; data: string; mimeType: string }
    | { type: 'resource'; resource: { uri: string; ...etc } }
  >;
  isError?: boolean;
}
```
 The dispatcher does not inspect `content` — it’s passed through to the transport verbatim. `isError` flips the MCP transport’s `tools/call` error envelope but doesn’t change the HTTP status (HTTP statuses come from `error.code` mapping). For **large outputs** (>50k chars), write to `<stateDir>/scratch/<id>.<ext>` and return: 
```ts
return {
  content: [{
    type: 'text',
    text: JSON.stringify({ path: '/abs/path', sizeBytes, sample: '...' }, null, 2),
  }],
};
```
 The dispatcher records `output_ref` and `output_size` based on the result, so the Intel UI can link directly to scratch files without the response body bloating up.

# Spawn-URL signing

> Per-spawn MCP URLs carry an HMAC signature over their baked params. The dispatcher refuses to honor role claims that don't match. Realistic prompt-injection defence.

> **Webapp retired (2026-05-14).** Any `localhost:3055` or `localhost:3070` URL on this page is only reachable while the **Tauri dev shell** is running. Start it with `cd papercusp-desktop && npm run dev`. ## The problem this solves [Section titled “The problem this solves”](#the-problem-this-solves) Before 2026-05-11 the per-spawn URL bound a worker to `?role=worker&workspace=…&harness=…&run=…&spawn=…`. The dispatcher trusted those params verbatim. A worker that wanted operator-tier tools just rewrote `?role=worker` → `?role=operator` and called. One line, no auth, no audit. Today every per-spawn URL carries an HMAC-SHA256 `sig` plus a Unix-epoch `exp`. The dispatcher’s `tryBuildSpawnContext()` calls `verifySpawnParams()` before honoring any role claim. Forged URLs fail with `invalid_signature` and the attempt lands in `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures` for on-call review. ## How it works [Section titled “How it works”](#how-it-works) Both ends share a 32-byte signing key stored at: 
```sql
SELECT value_b64 FROM harness_shared.operator_secrets WHERE name = 'spawn-signing-key';
```
 The row is auto-minted by the **operator** on first use (`randomBytes(32)` + an `onConflictDoNothing()` insert). The orchestrator’s key loader does **not** mint — if the row is missing it throws (`spawn-signing-key row missing — operator boots mint it on first verify call`), expecting the operator to have minted it already. Both sides cache the key in-process, but with **different invalidation policies**: * **Operator** (`loadOrCreateKey` in `spawn-signing.ts`) re-reads PG and compares `rotated_at` on every call, so a rotation is picked up on the very next signing/verifying call. Its 5-minute TTL is only a fallback for when `rotated_at` can’t be read. * **Orchestrator** (`loadSigningKey` in `spawn-mcp.ts`) checks the 5-minute TTL **first** and returns the cached key without opening a PG pool while inside the window (a deliberate hot-path optimization — it skips the pool-open + `SELECT`). It only re-reads PG (where `rotated_at` then wins) after the TTL lapses. So on the orchestrator side the 5-minute window is the **primary** mechanism, not a fallback: a rotation is not picked up until the TTL expires. ### Mint side — orchestrator [Section titled “Mint side — orchestrator”](#mint-side--orchestrator) `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/spawn-mcp.ts` → `writeSignedSpawnMcp()` is what the orchestrator’s `invoke()` calls when it lays down a per-spawn `.mcp.json`. It: 1. Builds the baked URL params (`harness, workspace, role, run, spawn, [feature], [chunk], [parent_spawn], [client]`). 2. Adds `exp`. **As of the 2026-07-01 owner directive, the default is `exp=0` — PERMANENT, no time-based expiry** (pass `ttlSec > 0` to get the old `now + ttlSec` behavior). The 24h TTL used to force a daily re-mint that churned `.mcp.json` and triggered a Claude Code re-approval prompt, silently darkening unattended sessions; `exp=0` is a papercup the verifier special-cases to skip only the *time* check — the signature still covers `exp`, so a role-escalation rewrite of a permanent URL fails verification exactly as before. Revocation is now **key-rotation only** (see [Coarse revocation](#coarse-revocation)), not expiry. 3. Canonicalizes by sorting + URL-encoding (only the allowlist; duplicates rejected; `sig` itself ignored). 4. HMAC-SHA256 over the canonical string, base64url-encoded, appended as `sig=`. 5. Writes the `.mcp.json` with mode 0600. The per-spawn worktree dir is mode 0700. The same signed, role-scoped URL is also written into a per-spawn **codex** `CODEX_HOME/config.toml` (`writeSignedSpawnCodexHome` → `[mcp_servers.papercusp] url = "<signed URL>"`, mode 0600). Codex doesn’t env-expand inside `config.toml`, so the URL is fully baked including the `sig` — auth is the `sig` query param, no bearer. `invoke()` routes codex backends to `writeSignedSpawnCodexHome` and everything else to `writeSignedSpawnMcp`. Operator-initiated **superuser** spawns are a separate envelope handled *before* the signing branch: when `PAPERCUSP_SPAWN_SU_BEARER` is set, `writeSignedSpawnMcp` writes a `?superuser=1` URL plus an `Authorization: Bearer` header and returns — **no `sig` is minted** for SU spawns (the superuser door is checked before the sig path in the verifier). The orchestrator’s PG DSN is inherited from the operator-set env. If signing fails (DSN missing, row missing on first boot), `writeSignedSpawnMcp` throws — the outer try/catch in `invoke()` logs `spawn-mcp write failed` and the agent boots without an MCP endpoint, making the failure visible. Callers that need the historical soft-warn fallback (emit unsigned + warn) can pass `allowUnsigned: true` AND run the operator with `PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG` unset. ### Verify side — operator [Section titled “Verify side — operator”](#verify-side--operator) `packages/operator-core/lib/spawn-signing.ts` → `verifySpawnParams(url)` runs first thing in `tryBuildSpawnContext()` at `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts`. It: 1. Reads `sig` + `exp`. Missing either → `missing_sig` / `missing_exp`. 2. Rejects past-`exp` URLs as `expired`. 3. Canonicalizes the same way the minter does; rejects duplicates. 4. Computes HMAC over the canonical string with the cached key. 5. `timingSafeEqual` against the provided `sig`. 6. On mismatch → `invalid_signature`. On encoding error → `invalid_sig_encoding`. Any non-`ok` result is persisted to `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures` (reason + claimed role/harness/workspace/spawn + remote\_addr + user\_agent + exp\_claim) and the request is rejected with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_<reason>`. ## Operating modes [Section titled “Operating modes”](#operating-modes) ### Strict (default) [Section titled “Strict (default)”](#strict-default) `PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG=1` in `apps/operator/.env.local`. Unsigned URLs that claim a spawn context (any of `role=`, `spawn=`, `workspace=`) hard-reject with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_missing_sig_required_mode`. Bare URLs with no claims are accepted (tools/list returns the full catalog, tools/call fails on `invalid_request_context` from the dispatcher). Two auth envelopes are checked **before** the signature path and so don’t need a `sig`: `?superuser=1` + loopback + superuser bearer, and `?power_user=1` + loopback + a verified power-user HMAC access token. The power-user path clamps the workspace to the **token’s** claim (any `?workspace=` in the URL is ignored), unlike the superuser path. ### Soft-warn (rollout-only) [Section titled “Soft-warn (rollout-only)”](#soft-warn-rollout-only) `PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG` unset or `!= '1'`. Unsigned-with-claims URLs accepted with a console warning. Was the default during the 2026-05-11 rollout window for in-flight spawn compatibility. ## Coarse revocation [Section titled “Coarse revocation”](#coarse-revocation) If a key may be compromised, or a bad batch of prompts shipped and you want every in-flight spawn to fail closed, rotate. There is **no per-spawn revocation** — rotation invalidates everything. This is now the **only** revocation mechanism for permanent (`exp=0`) URLs — since the 2026-07-01 default dropped time-based expiry, a URL that isn’t explicitly `ttlSec`-scoped never ages out on its own. ### Preferred: admin endpoint (immediate effect) [Section titled “Preferred: admin endpoint (immediate effect)”](#preferred-admin-endpoint-immediate-effect) 
```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/rotate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# → { "ok": true, "rotatedAt": "2026-05-11T04:00:00.000Z" }
```
 The endpoint rotates the PG row **and** bumps the operator’s in-process cache, so revocation takes effect on the very next MCP call (not the 5-minute lazy-cache lag). The route is gated by `auth: { trust: ['trusted'] }`, and `requirePrincipal` maps the failures as follows: * **403** when a principal resolves but its trust isn’t in the `['trusted']` allowlist. A loopback request with a **missing or wrong bearer** falls back to the loopback principal (`trust: 'unverified-loopback'`), which isn’t `trusted` → 403. * **401** only when **no principal resolves at all** — e.g. an off-loopback request with no/invalid bearer (the loopback fallback can’t fire off-loopback). A valid superuser bearer over loopback yields `trust: 'trusted'` → accepted. ### CLI wrapper [Section titled “CLI wrapper”](#cli-wrapper) 
```bash
bun run rotate:spawn-key                # confirmation prompt
bun run rotate:spawn-key -- --yes       # no prompt
```
 (`apps/operator/scripts/rotate-spawn-signing-key.mjs`. Prefers the HTTP endpoint when the operator is reachable; falls back to direct PG when not — the direct `UPDATE` bumps `rotated_at`, so every operator process picks up the new key on its next call, while orchestrator caches expire within 5 minutes. The script itself prints “Operator + orchestrator caches expire within 5 minutes.”) ### Direct PG (only when the operator is down) [Section titled “Direct PG (only when the operator is down)”](#direct-pg-only-when-the-operator-is-down) 
```sql
UPDATE harness_shared.operator_secrets
SET value_b64 = encode(gen_random_bytes(32), 'base64'),
    rotated_at = now()
WHERE name = 'spawn-signing-key';
```
 After rotation: every in-flight `.mcp.json` URL is now invalid. The orchestrator must re-spawn affected workers. Use sparingly. ## Observability [Section titled “Observability”](#observability) ### From the operator admin API [Section titled “From the operator admin API”](#from-the-operator-admin-api) 
```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.papercusp/superuser-token)
curl "http://localhost:3070/api/admin/spawn-signing/failures?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```
 Returns the audit log + a summary count by reason for the configured window (default last 24h). Query params: * `limit` — max rows (default 100, max 1000) * `since` — ISO timestamp; only rows with `ts > since` * `reason` — filter by reason string ### From SQL [Section titled “From SQL”](#from-sql) 
```sql
-- Recent failures by reason (last 24h)
SELECT reason, count(*) FROM harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures
WHERE ts > now() - interval '24 hours'
GROUP BY reason ORDER BY 2 DESC;


-- Most-recently failed spawns
SELECT ts, reason, claimed_role, claimed_harness, claimed_spawn
FROM harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures
ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 20;
```
 A non-zero rate of `invalid_signature` outside explicit test runs is a real signal. Correlate `claimed_spawn` with the orchestrator’s spawn IDs to identify which spawn produced the forgery. ## Reason codes [Section titled “Reason codes”](#reason-codes) | reason | When | | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `missing_sig` | URL has `exp` but no `sig`. Once a URL carries `exp` (or `sig`), `verifySpawnParams` runs and any failure is logged **and** hard-rejected, regardless of strict vs soft-warn mode. (The soft-warn logged-only-accept path only fires when *neither* `sig` nor `exp` is present, and that path emits no reason code.) | | `missing_exp` | URL has `sig` but no `exp` | | `invalid_exp` | `exp` not parseable as a non-negative integer | | `expired` | `exp < now()` — only reachable when the mint used a `ttlSec > 0` override; the default `exp=0` (permanent, since 2026-07-01) skips this check entirely | | `invalid_sig_encoding` | `sig` isn’t valid base64url | | `invalid_signature` | HMAC mismatch — the realistic forgery signal | | `duplicate_param:<k>` | Same allowlisted key appears twice (forger appending `&role=operator` after the signed one) | | `missing_sig_required_mode` | Unsigned URL hit the verifier with `PAPERCUSP_REQUIRE_SPAWN_SIG=1` | ## Threat model [Section titled “Threat model”](#threat-model) ### Defends against [Section titled “Defends against”](#defends-against) * **Prompt-injected worker rewriting URL params.** The HMAC is over the canonical original; the agent doesn’t have the key. Edits produce `invalid_signature`. ### Does NOT defend against [Section titled “Does NOT defend against”](#does-not-defend-against) * **Same-UID code that queries PG for the key.** The agent runs as the operator’s UID and has libpq access. HMAC is friction, not enforcement. * **Replaying another spawn’s `.mcp.json`.** Each URL is a valid bearer for its `exp` window (24h default). `.mcp.json` is 0600 and worktrees are 0700, but same UID means same OS user can read across them. * **The `?superuser=1` door.** Separate envelope (loopback + superuser-bearer); see [Superuser mode](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/superuser-mode). HMAC doesn’t change that surface. * **Editing `~/.papercusp/granted-capabilities.json`.** Plain JSON, same UID, writable. The capability gate trusts what it finds. * **Operator memory dump** (`gcore <pid>`). Key is in the heap. * **Replacing the operator binary or PG client.** Far beyond prompt injection but in scope for same-UID ownership. ### What actually closes the loop [Section titled “What actually closes the loop”](#what-actually-closes-the-loop) OS-level isolation per worker (`bwrap` / `firejail` / a separate UID with file ACLs). Real fix; bigger lift. Eventual landing spot. ## Signed-param allowlist [Section titled “Signed-param allowlist”](#signed-param-allowlist) Only these keys participate in the HMAC. Adding others has no effect on the signature. 
```plaintext
harness, workspace, role, run, spawn, feature, chunk, parent_spawn, client, exp
```
 Reorder, URL-encoding variants, and duplicates are all canonicalized before signing/verification. ## Tests [Section titled “Tests”](#tests) The suites are Vitest, under `packages/operator-core/lib/`. The integration ones need Docker (testcontainers Postgres); run them from the package dir (e.g. `cd packages/operator-core && npx vitest run <name>`): | Test | Kind | What it proves | | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `spawn-signing.test.ts` | unit | sign/verify canonicalization + every reason code | | `__tests__/spawn-signing-e2e.integration.test.ts` | integration | full path through the MCP boundary | | `__tests__/mint-roundtrip.integration.test.ts` | integration | orchestrator’s `writeSignedSpawnMcp` ↔ operator’s verifier agree on HMAC | | `__tests__/admin-rotate.integration.test.ts` | integration | rotation endpoint auth + revocation semantics | | `__tests__/admin-failures.integration.test.ts` | integration | audit-read endpoint (filter + summary) | Run them before promoting any change to the signing pipeline. ## File map [Section titled “File map”](#file-map) 
```plaintext
packages/operator-core/lib/spawn-signing.ts                                 — sign/verify/rotate/log
packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts  — verifier wired into tryBuildSpawnContext
packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/admin/spawn-signing-rotate.ts    — POST: rotate + bump cache
packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/admin/spawn-signing-failures.ts  — GET: audit read
apps/operator/scripts/rotate-spawn-signing-key.mjs                          — CLI wrapper
apps/operator/docs/spawn-signing-threat-model.md                            — long-form threat model
packages/operator-core/lib/__tests__/spawn-signing-e2e.integration.test.ts
packages/operator-core/lib/__tests__/mint-roundtrip.integration.test.ts
packages/operator-core/lib/__tests__/admin-rotate.integration.test.ts
packages/operator-core/lib/__tests__/admin-failures.integration.test.ts


libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/spawn-mcp.ts   — writeSignedSpawnMcp (mint side)
libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/invoke.ts       — calls writeSignedSpawnMcp on every spawn
```
 (The `operator_secrets` + `spawn_sig_verification_failures` tables are defined by SQL migrations under `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/`, not by runtime DDL — the old `ensure-schema.ts` lazy-`CREATE TABLE` path was removed.)

# ctx.publishState — state-shaped tools

> Tools that publish their current state instead of streaming events. Reconnect-resilient by construction; clients see the latest snapshot, never event history.

# `ctx.publishState` — state-shaped tools [Section titled “ctx.publishState — state-shaped tools”](#ctxpublishstate--state-shaped-tools) A **state-shaped tool** publishes its current snapshot rather than streaming events. Clients reconnecting mid-run receive the latest snapshot — never event history. 
```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'search:semantic',
  state: z.object({
    results: z.array(z.object({ id: z.string(), score: z.number() })),
    progress: z.number(),
    phase: z.enum(['embedding', 'querying', 'ranking', 'done']),
  }),
  handler: async (args, ctx) => {
    ctx.publishState({ results: [], progress: 0, phase: 'embedding' });
    const embedded = await embed(args.query);
    ctx.publishState({ results: [], progress: 0.4, phase: 'querying' });
    const results = await query(embedded);
    ctx.publishState({ results, progress: 1, phase: 'done' });
    return results;
  },
});
```
 ## Why state-shaped instead of events? [Section titled “Why state-shaped instead of events?”](#why-state-shaped-instead-of-events) Most streaming tools today emit events (`ctx.emit('progress', …)`, `ctx.emit('text-delta', …)`) and rely on a replay ring buffer (T2.2) to recover from disconnects. That’s the right shape when output is **append-only** (LLM token streams). But for tools whose output is a **current value that supersedes prior values**, replay is the wrong shape: | Aspect | Event-shaped (`ctx.emit`) | State-shaped (`ctx.publishState`) | | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Wire form | typed events on the wire | one `snapshot` SSE event per change (see [Client-side consumption](#client-side-consumption)) | | Replay on reconnect | Last N events from ring buffer | Latest snapshot | | Memory | Linear in stream length | Bounded by state shape | | Long-lived disconnect | Buffer evicts past the tool’s `replayBufferSize` | Snapshot persists across disconnects | | Workspace switch | Buffers cleared | Snapshots cleared | For a search tool with 100 results, state-shape is \~10KB regardless of how many internal updates happened. For a token stream, that same encoding would be lossy. The ring buffer has no universal eviction threshold: the dispatcher’s effective cap is the per-tool `replayBufferSize` and defaults to `0` (no buffer at all) when unset — `const replayCap = tool.state ? 0 : (tool.replayBufferSize ?? 0)`. Several long-stream tools opt into `replayBufferSize: 5000` (`plans:resume`, `plans:launch`, `architect:chat`, `oracle:chat`, `agent_chats:chat`); a tool that sets a different size evicts at that size. State-shaped tools force the cap to `0` and never buffer. The on-the-wire event name differs by transport adapter. The chat-surface route this page directs you to — `GET /api/operator/state-snapshot`, consumed by `useStateSnapshots()` — emits the SSE event named `snapshot`. The voice converse route (`/api/agent-mcp/operator-converse`) is the only adapter that emits an event named `state-snapshot`. ## Declaring a state-shaped tool [Section titled “Declaring a state-shaped tool”](#declaring-a-state-shaped-tool) Add `state: StandardSchemaV1` to `defineTool` — any [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) validator (Zod, Valibot, ArkType, …), not just Zod, since the core stopped being Zod-locked (P-020). The schema is the source of truth for the snapshot shape: 
```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'whatever',
  state: z.object({ /* your shape */ }),
  ...
})
```
 Tools that declare `state` automatically: * Get `ctx.publishState` installed (when the call has both `workspaceId` and `runId` — the HTTP catch-all defaults a `runId` per-request, so plain JSON / SSE callers both work). * Opt **out** of the replay ring buffer (no double-storage — state snapshots replace events on the wire). * Become **streamable** — the HTTP catch-all’s strict-streamable predicate recognizes `tool.state` as a valid trigger for `Accept: text/event-stream`, so the runId-bearing SSE path is reachable even when no `events` are declared. * Persist snapshots for 5 minutes after run-end (reconnect window). ## Handler API [Section titled “Handler API”](#handler-api) 
```ts
ctx.publishState(snapshot)
```
 * **Validated** against `tool.state` at publish time via the schema’s `~standard.validate` (Standard Schema, P-020) — synchronously, since `publishState` is fire-and-forget and can’t await an async validator. Bad shapes throw synchronously. * **Replaces** the run’s current snapshot (v1 is snapshot-only). * **Reactive** — every call bumps the run’s `version` and re-emits to subscribed clients. ### Graceful degradation when there’s no state channel [Section titled “Graceful degradation when there’s no state channel”](#graceful-degradation-when-theres-no-state-channel) `ctx.publishState` is only installed when the call has **both** a `workspaceId` and a `runId`. Handlers MUST guard for its absence rather than assume it exists — the framework-blessed degradation is an `isError` result carrying the code `no_state_channel`: 
```ts
async handler(args, ctx) {
  if (!ctx.publishState) {
    return {
      content: [{ type: 'text', text: JSON.stringify({
        error: 'no_state_channel: <tool> requires a runId-bearing context',
      }) }],
      isError: true,
    };
  }
  // …publish snapshots normally
}
```
 The canonical example tool `dev:state_counter` (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/dev/state_counter.ts`) does exactly this. The HTTP projection surfaces the same `no_state_channel` contract when the JSON path can’t supply a `runId`. ### v1 limitations [Section titled “v1 limitations”](#v1-limitations) * **Snapshot-only.** Passing a JSON-Patch array throws. Deltas are deferred to v1.1 once we measure full-snapshot perf on real tools. * **In-process state.** Snapshots live in the operator’s Node process. The registry is stashed on `globalThis` via a `Symbol.for('papercusp.stateChannelRegistry')` key — the same pattern the replay buffer uses — so dev HMR / module re-imports do **not** lose state. A full Node process (server) restart does drop them. PG-backed persistence is a follow-up. ## Client-side consumption [Section titled “Client-side consumption”](#client-side-consumption) The workspace-scoped SSE stream (`GET /api/operator/state-snapshot`, emitting `snapshot` events) carries `toolState` alongside `openCards`. Use `useStateSnapshots()` to subscribe and `selectToolStates()` to filter: 
```ts
import { useStateSnapshots, selectToolStates } from '@/lib/use-state-snapshots';


function MyComponent() {
  const { cards, connected, byRun } = useStateSnapshots();
  const states = selectToolStates(byRun);
  // cards: flattened OpenCardWithRun[] across all open runs (primary product for card rendering)
  // connected: EventSource open state
  // byRun: Map<runId, SnapshotEnvelope>
  // states is Map<runId, toolState>
}
```
 The `useStateSnapshots` hook owns one EventSource per mount. `selectToolStates` is a pure helper — do not call `useStateSnapshots()` from inside it. ### Reconnect comes from the workspace route, not per-tool replay [Section titled “Reconnect comes from the workspace route, not per-tool replay”](#reconnect-comes-from-the-workspace-route-not-per-tool-replay) A state-shaped tool’s reconnect resilience is delivered by this workspace-scoped `/api/operator/state-snapshot` SSE, **not** by the per-tool streaming SSE’s `Last-Event-ID` replay path. On connect, the route replays `snapshotWorkspace()` — a snapshot of every currently-open run in the workspace — then live-fans-out subsequent changes via `subscribeWorkspace`. The per-tool streaming SSE only replays when `replayBufferSize > 0`, and state tools force their cap to `0`, so it never replays them. ## How state-shape absorbs T4.3 [Section titled “How state-shape absorbs T4.3”](#how-state-shape-absorbs-t43) The original Phase-4 plan had T4.3 “long-lived disconnected tools” as a separate Tier-4 item: detach `AbortSignal` from disconnect, manage the ring buffer’s lifetime, decide when to *actually* abort. State-shape collapses T4.3 to **zero engineering**: * State outlives any single SSE connection. * Reconnect serves the current snapshot — no buffer to evict, no history to replay. * “Long-lived” is the default for state-shaped tools. The tool author opts in by declaring `state`. The framework handles the rest. ## When NOT to use state [Section titled “When NOT to use state”](#when-not-to-use-state) * **LLM token streams** (`runAgentChat` etc.) — those are inherently append-only. Use `ctx.emit('text-delta', …)` with `replayBufferSize` for reconnect. * **One-shot tools** with a final result — no streaming, no need for state. * **Tools that need to emit ordered events** (notifications, log lines) — state collapses ordering into “latest only.” For a tool that mixes a state-shaped result (`results`) with an append-only side stream (`log_lines`), declare `state` AND `events` — both surfaces work together. ## Reference implementation [Section titled “Reference implementation”](#reference-implementation) `dev:state_counter` (`packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/dev/state_counter.ts`) is the in-repo proof-of-concept and E2E verification fixture for `ctx.publishState`. It declares a `state` schema, ticks a counter, and calls `ctx.publishState` once per tick with abort handling (`if (ctx.signal.aborted) break;`) and the `no_state_channel` guard above. It backs the `/dev` demo. ## See also [Section titled “See also”](#see-also) * [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx) — interactive prompts on the same state channel. * Plan: `apps/operator/docs/plans/bespoke-card-improvements-2026-05-13.md` §5

# Superuser mode

> Give an agent shell launched outside Papercusp full access to MCP tools across every workspace and harness, with a single token.

## What this is [Section titled “What this is”](#what-this-is) A way to point any `omp`, `claude`, or `codex` shell — running in any directory, on any of your workspaces — at Papercusp’s MCP server. Plugin tools (Repomix, GitNexus, Firecrawl, Phase 9 spawn primitive, …) and built-ins (intel:*, artifacts:*, …) all become available. The agent picks the workspace per call. This is the opposite of the orchestrator’s per-spawn URL: instead of locking the agent into one (workspace, harness, role, run, spawn), the agent gets superuser access and chooses workspace per tool invocation. Threat model: friction, not enforcement Loopback alone can’t tell a user-shell agent apart from a papercusp-spawned agent — both run on the same machine, same user, same loopback. Superuser requires a bearer token from `~/.papercusp/superuser-token` (mode 0600). A spawned agent that wants to escalate its gates can `cat` the token file. Same way it can `rm -rf` your home directory. Superuser is for *honest* user shells, not for *enforced* isolation. For real isolation, run shell-omp under a different OS user with file ACLs that prevent the orchestrator user from reading the token. (The orchestrator-spawned path has a separate envelope — see [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing). Forging a worker URL into operator-tier fails the HMAC verifier; pasting the superuser token into your own shell does not, by design.) ## One-time setup [Section titled “One-time setup”](#one-time-setup) 
```bash
$ apps/operator/scripts/install-standalone-mcp.sh
✓ Minted ~/.papercusp/superuser-token (mode 0600)
✓ Merged 'papercusp-su' into ~/.omp/agent/mcp.json (mode 0600)
✓ Installed ~/.local/bin/psu (tracked picker launcher)
✓ Endpoint responded 200
```
 The script: 1. Mints a random token — 24 bytes of `/dev/urandom` (192 bits of entropy) base64url-encoded into a **32-character** string (not 32 bytes of token entropy). Only on first install — a re-run **reuses** the existing token so live shells keep working. (The on-disk reader only sanity-rejects tokens shorter than 16 chars.) 2. Writes it to `~/.papercusp/superuser-token` (mode 0600, owned by you) 3. Registers the `papercusp-su` MCP server for OMP (`~/.omp/agent/mcp.json`) and Claude Code (`~/.claude.json`), each with the operator URL + `Authorization: Bearer <token>` 4. Renders the per-client playbooks into `~/.papercusp/` and installs the `psu` launcher (plus the `ptool` defineTool CLI) into `~/.local/bin` (see [below](#the-psu-launcher-and-playbooks)) 5. Verifies the operator is running and accepts the token Re-run any time to refresh the playbooks and launcher — it **reuses** the existing token, so live shells keep working. To rotate the token deliberately, delete `~/.papercusp/superuser-token` first, then re-run; the operator picks up the new token without restart (file mtime triggers a cache refresh). Add `--profile=power` for the power-engineer subset. ## The `psu` launcher and playbooks [Section titled “The psu launcher and playbooks”](#the-psu-launcher-and-playbooks) The MCP registration above makes the SU tools *available* to a raw `omp` / `claude` shell; a second layer — the **engineer-collaborator playbook** — teaches a shell how to use them. That layer is delivered by a single launcher, **`psu`** (the older `omp-su` / `claude-su` / `codex-su` wrappers are retired). Plain `omp` / `claude` / `codex` stay vanilla; only `psu` loads the playbook. `psu` records a tracked `/adv` session, then execs the **raw** agent CLI with the playbook + the `papercusp-su` MCP + the right per-client flags assembled per launch (`buildLaunchSpec`): 
```bash
psu                                                          # interactive picker
psu --no-picker --agent=claude --harness=papercup --no-plan  # scripting
psu --resume                                                 # resume a tracked session
```
 | Agent | Playbook injection | | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `omp` | `--append-system-prompt ~/.papercusp/<profile>-collaborator.md` (+ `-e ~/.papercusp/papercusp-coord.ts` for coordination) | | `claude` | `--append-system-prompt-file ~/.papercusp/<profile>-collaborator.claude.md` | | `codex` | a per-session `CODEX_HOME` whose `AGENTS.md` *is* the playbook | **One base, per-client overlays.** The shared base playbook (`prompts/papercusp-su-<profile>.tools.md`) carries all client-neutral guidance. The client-specific task/workflow tooling — which differs by client (OMP `todo_write` / `omp:sessions`; Claude Code `TodoWrite` / `Task`; Codex `update_plan`) — lives in a small overlay (`papercusp-su.{omp,claude,codex}.md`) that is spliced into the base at a `<!-- PAPERCUSP-SU:CLIENT-TOOLING-OVERLAY -->` marker. This keeps one source of truth for the base and prevents, e.g., OMP-only “don’t use the Claude task tools” guidance from landing in the Claude or Codex playbook. **Codex is special.** Codex has no `--append-system-prompt`; it injects instructions through `AGENTS.md` within its `CODEX_HOME`. So for a Codex launch `psu` mints a dedicated per-session `CODEX_HOME` whose `AGENTS.md` *is* the playbook and whose `config.toml` registers the `papercusp-su` server with the bearer supplied at launch — so plain `codex` (`CODEX_HOME=~/.codex`) never sees the server, and the token is never written into shared config. Re-run `install-standalone-mcp.sh` (optionally `--profile=power`) any time to refresh the playbooks and the launcher. ## How the request flows [Section titled “How the request flows”](#how-the-request-flows) 
```plaintext
omp shell anywhere on the box
  └─ reads ~/.omp/agent/mcp.json
  └─ POST http://localhost:3070/api/mcp?superuser=1
       Authorization: Bearer <token>
       Accept: application/json, text/event-stream


operator
  └─ /api/mcp route detects ?superuser=1
  └─ checks: loopback origin + bearer matches superuser-token file
  └─ on failure: tool-shaped error from tools/call (`request_rejected: superuser_invalid_bearer`).
  │  (initialize + tools/list remain open per MCP spec; the gate fires at dispatch.)
  └─ on success: builds spawn ctx { isSuperuser: true,
                                    workspaceId: '*',
                                    role: 'operator', ... }


projected-tool dispatcher
  └─ ctx.gateBypass (from isSuperuser) → bypass role allowlist
  └─ ctx.gateBypass (from isSuperuser) → bypass capability gate
  └─ ctx.gateBypass (from isSuperuser) → bypass quota window
  └─ tool runs
  └─ tool_invocations row recorded with role='operator',
     run_id='<uuid>' (fresh per request),
     spawn_id='ephemeral-<hex>', window_key='run:<uuid>'
```
 ## Workspace switching [Section titled “Workspace switching”](#workspace-switching) The endpoint URL is workspace-agnostic. Tools that need a workspace take a `workspace` argument; the dispatcher uses `args.workspace ?? ctx.workspaceId`, and `ctx.workspaceId` defaults to `'*'` in superuser mode. To discover what workspaces exist: 
```typescript
papercusp:list_workspaces()
// → { workspaces: [
//      { slug: "default", harnesses: ["sheets","papercup-org"], lastActiveTs: 1778... },
//      { slug: "scratch", harnesses: [], lastActiveTs: 1778... }
//    ],
//    defaultWorkspace: "default" }
```
 Then any subsequent call: 
```typescript
intel.spawn_tree({ harness: "sheets", workspace: "default", limit: 50 })
orchestrator.spawn({ workspace: "default", harness: "sheets",
                     role: "worker", featureId: "F-FILL-001",
                     chunkId: "C-1" })
```
 Tools that don’t care about workspace (`repomix.pack`, `fetch_plus.fetch_clean`, `firecrawl.scrape`, `gitnexus.list_repos`) ignore the missing `workspace` arg — they’re path-driven or URL-driven. ### Scoped-superuser clamp (default OFF) [Section titled “Scoped-superuser clamp (default OFF)”](#scoped-superuser-clamp-default-off) Everything above describes the default behavior, where an unresolved superuser workspace silently becomes the cross-workspace wildcard `'*'`. With the `papercusp-scoped-superuser-clamp` flag **ON** (it defaults **OFF** — a reversible kill-switch the owner flips after an attended verification), a superuser session must either resolve to a **concrete** workspace or **explicitly** opt into unscoped god-mode via `?workspace=*` / `?all_workspaces=1`: * An **unresolved** workspace is no longer silently promoted to `'*'`; it’s rejected with `scoped_superuser_workspace_unresolved`. * A **scoped** session (concrete `workspaceId`) is confined to its workspace. A `crossWorkspace` tool that isn’t on the read-only scoped-safe allowlist is denied with `workspace_forbidden`; `harness: 'all'` / `harness:'*'` (the global escape) and a per-call `harness` that escapes the session’s pot are denied with `harness_forbidden`. * Opting in with `?workspace=*` / `?all_workspaces=1` is the deliberate cross-workspace admin path that lifts the clamp. ## What’s NOT bypassed [Section titled “What’s NOT bypassed”](#whats-not-bypassed) These still apply to superuser: 1. **Per-tool input validation** — invalid args still return `invalid_input` 400. 2. **Per-tool timeout** — long-running tools still get killed at the tool’s `timeoutSec`. 3. **Workspace requirement on first-party tools.** Most first-party tools (`harness:*`, `tasks:*`, `messages:*`, …) need a concrete workspace to open a PG transaction. Pass `?superuser=1&workspace=<slug>` in the URL — the default `workspaceId='*'` doesn’t satisfy them. The projected wrapper throws `UnauthorizedToolError`, which the dispatcher codes `unauthorized` (HTTP 401, **not** `handler_error`/500), with the message `built-in tool "<name>" requires a workspace-scoped call — this session has no workspace transaction. Scope the session to a workspace, or pass a per-call workspace where the host/tool supports one.` 4. **Transport-level server-side deadline.** Independent of the per-tool `timeoutSec` kill, every call also gets the transport deadline (`PAPERCUSP_MCP_DEADLINE_MS`, default **55s**, under the 60s `maxDuration`). A tool that exceeds it returns a clean `request_timeout: tool "..." exceeded <ms>ms (still running server-side...)` to the client — the tool keeps running server-side. Pass a `_meta.idempotencyKey` to make a retry replay the result once it completes instead of re-executing. 5. **Power-profile narrowing (when `?profile=power`).** The power profile narrows **both** the advertised catalog *and* the callable set: a `?profile=power` (or `x-papercusp-profile: power`) superuser session that names an engineer-only (Group A) tool is rejected with `tool_not_available_for_profile: "<tool>" is not available in the power-engineer profile`, mirroring the `tools/list` filter so a direct-name call can’t bypass the listing restriction. What **is** bypassed: role allowlist, capability gate (the dispatcher’s `isSuperuser` short-circuits in both), per-window quota, and the spawn-URL signature check (superuser has its own bearer envelope). ## Troubleshooting [Section titled “Troubleshooting”](#troubleshooting) | Symptom | Cause | Fix | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `request_rejected: superuser_invalid_bearer` on `tools/call` (and an empty `tools/list`) | Token mismatch, token file missing, or `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header not sent | Re-run `install-standalone-mcp.sh`; check the header is set in `~/.omp/agent/mcp.json` / `~/.claude.json` | | `request_rejected: superuser_non_loopback` | Request didn’t originate from loopback (127.0.0.1 / ::1 / localhost) | Call the operator over loopback | | `unknown_tool` 404 | Plugin didn’t load | `curl /api/plugins/host/refresh` to see load errors | | `harness_required` / `workspace required` from a tool | Tool needs a real workspace/harness; `*` doesn’t work for it | Pass `workspace: "default"` (or other slug from `list_workspaces`) explicitly | | `unauthorized` 401 (`built-in tool "..." requires a workspace-scoped call`) | A first-party tool needs a workspace tx and the session is unscoped (`workspaceId='*'`) | Pass `?superuser=1&workspace=<slug>` (or a per-call `workspace` arg) | | `request_timeout: tool "..." exceeded ...ms` | Tool ran past the 55s transport deadline (`PAPERCUSP_MCP_DEADLINE_MS`); it keeps running server-side | Retry with the same `_meta.idempotencyKey` to replay the result, or raise the env deadline | | `tool_not_available_for_profile` | A `?profile=power` session named an engineer-only (Group A) tool | Drop `?profile=power` (full operator surface), or call a power-profile tool | | `scoped_superuser_workspace_unresolved` | `papercusp-scoped-superuser-clamp` is ON and the session resolved to no workspace | Pass `?workspace=<slug>`, or opt into god-mode with `?workspace=*` / `?all_workspaces=1` | | `workspace_forbidden` / `harness_forbidden` | Clamp is ON and a scoped session tried to span workspaces, use `harness:'all'`, or escape its pot | Use an unscoped (`?workspace=*` / `?all_workspaces=1`) session, or name a concrete in-scope harness | ## Telemetry [Section titled “Telemetry”](#telemetry) Every superuser tool call writes a `harness_shared.tool_invocations` row with: * `role = "operator"` * `run_id = "<uuid>"` — a fresh per-request UUID, **not** a fixed `"standalone"` papercup (the shared papercup was dropped to avoid a cross-cancellation hazard) * `spawn_id = "ephemeral-<random hex>"` * `window_key = "run:<uuid>"` Quota is bypassed for superuser, but the invocation row is still recorded — the stable marker for superuser activity is the `ephemeral-` `spawn_id` prefix. ## Revoking access [Section titled “Revoking access”](#revoking-access) 
```bash
$ rm ~/.papercusp/superuser-token
```
 The next `tools/call` is rejected with `request_rejected: superuser_invalid_bearer` (and `tools/list` returns an empty catalog). To replace it with a fresh token instead, delete it and then re-run `install-standalone-mcp.sh` (a plain re-run reuses the existing token).

# Telemetry

> Every tool call lands in `harness_shared.tool_invocations`. Schema, queries, and the Phase 9 spawn-lineage forward-look.

## The single table [Section titled “The single table”](#the-single-table) `harness_shared.tool_invocations` is where every projected-tool call goes. One row per dispatch attempt, regardless of transport, regardless of outcome. The table originally shipped in migration 046 (now folded into the squashed `000-baseline.sql`, with the original at `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/archive/046-tool-invocations.sql`); later migrations added the `args_json` / `transport` / `event_count` / `metadata_json` / `principal_*` columns and two views (below). 
```sql
CREATE TABLE harness_shared.tool_invocations (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  workspace_id    TEXT NOT NULL,
  harness_slug    TEXT NOT NULL,
  plugin_name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  tool_name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  role            TEXT NOT NULL,
  feature_id      TEXT NULL,
  chunk_id        TEXT NULL,
  run_id          TEXT NULL,
  spawn_id        TEXT NOT NULL,
  parent_spawn_id TEXT NULL,                 -- Phase 9 lineage
  window_key      TEXT NOT NULL,             -- 'chunk:<id>' or 'run:<id>'
  invoked_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  duration_ms     INT NULL,
  status          TEXT NOT NULL,             -- enum below
  output_ref      TEXT NULL,                 -- papercusp://scratch/... URI for large outputs
  output_size     BIGINT NULL,
  error_message   TEXT NULL,
  args_json       JSONB NULL,                -- the call's input args (truncated past 32 KB)
  transport       TEXT NULL,                 -- 'http' | 'mcp' | 'ipc' | 'in_process'
  event_count     INT NULL,                  -- number of ctx.emit calls during the run
  metadata_json   JSONB NULL,                -- ctx.metadata() payload + reaction cause-chain
  error_code      TEXT NULL,                 -- dispatcher error CLASS (NULL on success); see below
  principal_kind        TEXT NULL,           -- Principal audit fields (bearer/MCP path only;
  principal_auth_method TEXT NULL,           -- NULL → surfaces as 'unknown' in /dev)
  principal_trust       TEXT NULL
);
```
 The squashed schema also ships two views over the table: `tool_invocations_artifacts` (successful calls that wrote a scratch `output_ref` — feeds the Intel Pack/Diff sub-tabs) and `tool_invocations_spawn_tree` (recursive `parent_spawn_id` lineage, `depth=0` for roots). The spawn-tree view **caps recursion at depth 16** — the recursive join stops at `c.depth < 16`, so a runaway spawn-of-spawn chain can’t blow up the CTE. Four indexes: * `tool_invocations_quota_idx` on `(workspace_id, tool_name, role, window_key) WHERE status='ok'` — partial index, makes the dispatcher’s quota read O(log n) per call. * `tool_invocations_telemetry_idx` on `(workspace_id, harness_slug, invoked_at DESC)` — feed for Intel UI’s recent-activity panel. * `tool_invocations_error_code_idx` on `(error_code, invoked_at) WHERE error_code IS NOT NULL` (migration 205) — partial index over *failing* rows only, backing the improvement-watchdog’s grouped-by-`error_code` scan; success rows (the vast majority, `error_code IS NULL`) are excluded. * `tool_invocations_invoked_at_cov_idx` on `(invoked_at DESC) INCLUDE (tool_name, duration_ms, status)` (migration 315) — covering index leading on `invoked_at` so `dev:telemetry`’s **cross-workspace** 24h rollup runs as an Index-Only Scan instead of broad-scanning the whole table (the quota index leads on `workspace_id`, so it can’t range-scan `invoked_at` across workspaces). ## The status enum [Section titled “The status enum”](#the-status-enum) | Status | Meaning | | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `ok` | Function returned successfully. Counts against quota. | | `error` | Function threw. Doesn’t count against quota. `error_message` populated. | | `timeout` | Dispatcher’s AbortController fired before function returned. | | `quota-exceeded` | Pre-dispatch quota check rejected. Function never ran. | | `role-not-allowed` | Pre-dispatch authorization rejected. Function never ran. Three dispatcher error codes collapse into this status: `role_not_allowed`, `missing_capability`, and `capability_denied` (the resource-authorize / capability-envelope denial). | | `invalid-input` | Function threw a typed input-validation error (`invalid_input`). | Add a new status only by editing the dispatcher; do not let tool functions return arbitrary status values. ### `error_code` — the un-collapsed error class [Section titled “error\_code — the un-collapsed error class”](#error_code--the-un-collapsed-error-class) `status` is a *lossy* collapse: three codes fold into `role-not-allowed`, a handful of distinct failure modes fold into `error`. The `error_code` column (migration 205, `watchdog-robustness`) preserves the dispatcher’s full error CLASS that `status` throws away. It’s a low-cardinality string, `NULL` on success rows (and on legacy rows written before migration 205): `unauthorized` · `handler_error` · `harness_required` · `role_not_allowed` · `missing_capability` · `quota_exceeded` · `timeout` · `invalid_input` · `invalid_args` `recordTelemetry` already computes this code to pick the `status`; persisting it means the **improvement-watchdog** can separate a deterministic config bug (an `unauthorized` that recurs identically — a real bug, fire on few) from a transient crash (`timeout` under load — volume-gated) without fragile `error_message LIKE` matching. The watchdog scans `error_code` grouped by tool, backed by the partial `tool_invocations_error_code_idx`. ## Reading the table [Section titled “Reading the table”](#reading-the-table) The table has RLS — every read needs `app.workspace_id` set first: 
```sql
SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', 'default', false);
SELECT tool_name, role, status, duration_ms, error_message
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE invoked_at > now() - interval '1 hour'
ORDER BY invoked_at DESC;
```
 `harness_admin` is `BYPASSRLS` and sees every workspace; `harness_app` is RLS-bound and sees only the configured workspace. ## Useful queries [Section titled “Useful queries”](#useful-queries) ### Per-tool success rate this run [Section titled “Per-tool success rate this run”](#per-tool-success-rate-this-run) 
```sql
SET app.workspace_id = 'default';
SELECT
  tool_name,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='ok') AS ok,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='error') AS errors,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='timeout') AS timeouts,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='quota-exceeded') AS quota_hits
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE run_id = 'r-2026-05-10-001'
GROUP BY tool_name
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;
```
 ### What did role X do in this run [Section titled “What did role X do in this run”](#what-did-role-x-do-in-this-run) 
```sql
SELECT invoked_at, plugin_name, tool_name, status, duration_ms
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE run_id = 'r-2026-05-10-001' AND role = 'architect'
ORDER BY invoked_at;
```
 ### Quota near-limits (architect at 4/5) [Section titled “Quota near-limits (architect at 4/5)”](#quota-near-limits-architect-at-45) 
```sql
SELECT tool_name, role, window_key, count(*) AS used
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status = 'ok' AND window_key LIKE 'run:%'
GROUP BY tool_name, role, window_key
HAVING count(*) >= 4;
```
 ### Slowest calls [Section titled “Slowest calls”](#slowest-calls) 
```sql
SELECT tool_name, role, duration_ms, output_size, invoked_at
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status = 'ok' AND duration_ms > 5000
ORDER BY duration_ms DESC
LIMIT 20;
```
 ### Failed calls with messages [Section titled “Failed calls with messages”](#failed-calls-with-messages) 
```sql
SELECT invoked_at, tool_name, role, status, substring(error_message, 1, 200)
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status IN ('error', 'timeout')
ORDER BY invoked_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```
 ## Output reference for large results [Section titled “Output reference for large results”](#output-reference-for-large-results) Tools that produce a large result write it to the scratch tree at `~/.papercusp/scratch/<workspace>/<toolName>/<runId>/<basename>` and return `outputRef` as a `papercusp://scratch/<workspace>/<toolName>/<runId>/<basename>` URI (see `scratch-uri.ts`); the dispatcher persists it to the `output_ref` column. The body of the tool result still includes a small sample + the ref. Repomix uses this pattern; expect code2prompt and any future packing tools to do the same. This keeps the table queryable without bloating it with 1MB+ payloads. ## `parent_spawn_id` lineage [Section titled “parent\_spawn\_id lineage”](#parent_spawn_id-lineage) `parent_spawn_id` captures the spawn-of-spawn relationship: a child call’s rows reference the parent’s `spawn_id`. It is **now populated** (not the always-`null` placeholder it once was) on two paths: * The `parent_spawn` spawn-URL param, parsed into `ctx.parentSpawnId` by the MCP transport (`routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts`). The fleet spawner (`fleet/operator-spawn.ts` + `fleet/parent-wake.ts`) is what threads it through — superseding the never-installed, now-retired `@papercupai/orchestrator-spawn` plugin. * The event-reaction cause chain (`lib/events/dispatch-reaction.ts` sets `parentSpawnId` to the triggering call’s `spawnId`). The `harness_shared.tool_invocations_spawn_tree` view (recursive CTE over `parent_spawn_id`, `depth=0` for roots) already exists for querying this lineage. ## How the row is written [Section titled “How the row is written”](#how-the-row-is-written) `recordTelemetry` runs in the `finally` of `runDispatchStack` (`dispatch-stack.ts`) on every termination path and calls the host-injected `deps.recordInvocation` — whose Papercusp implementation is `recordInvocationImpl` in `packages/operator-core/lib/projected-tool-deps.ts`. Each terminal path produces a row: * After every successful tool execution: `(status='ok', duration_ms, output_size, ...)`. * After every thrown error: `(status='error', duration_ms, error_message, error_code)`. * After a quota check rejection: `(status='quota-exceeded')` with `error_message` of the form `Tool "<toolName>" exceeded quota (<count>/<limit>) in window "<windowKey>"` (and `error_code='quota_exceeded'`). Function did not run. * After an authorization rejection: `(status='role-not-allowed')` with the dispatcher’s `error_code` (`role_not_allowed` / `missing_capability` / `capability_denied`). Function did not run. ### Deferred, batched writes (P-003) [Section titled “Deferred, batched writes (P-003)”](#deferred-batched-writes-p-003) `recordInvocationImpl` does **not** `INSERT` synchronously. `recordTelemetry` is *awaited* in the dispatcher’s `finally`, so a per-call PG round-trip (\~10–50ms) was the dominant overhead on a tight `capability:bash` loop. Since `route-everything-through-definetool` P-003 the write moves off the hot path: * **Snapshot + enqueue.** `recordInvocationImpl` calls `buildTelemetryRow` to snapshot the row synchronously (just a `JSON.stringify` of args), pushes it onto an in-process `telemetryQueue`, and returns in microseconds. No `await` of PG on the dispatch path. * **Debounced background flush.** A 10ms-debounced flusher (`flushPendingTelemetry`) drains the queue in **batched, per-workspace transactions** of up to 200 rows each: it groups the batch by `workspace_id`, then runs one `BEGIN` / `set_config('app.workspace_id', …)` / many-`INSERT`s / `COMMIT` per workspace group. So the GUC is set **once per batch transaction grouped by workspace** — not once per row. * **Bounded queue.** The queue is hard-capped at 5000 rows (`TELEMETRY_MAX_PENDING`); if the producer outruns PG (a stall), it sheds **oldest** rows so a PG outage can never OOM the host. * **Quota correctness.** `readQuotaState` calls `flushPendingTelemetry()` *first*, draining any queued `ok` rows before counting — so a quota’d tool never under-counts despite the deferral. Tests and telemetry consumers needing synchronous visibility can `await flushPendingTelemetry()`. Best-effort throughout. `recordTelemetry`’s own `catch` in `dispatch-stack.ts` is silent — a snapshot/enqueue failure never breaks the dispatcher. The warnings come from the background flusher, not any HTTP catch-all: a failed batch logs `[projected-tool-deps] telemetry flush batch failed (<n> rows): …` and the row is dropped; queue overflow logs `[projected-tool-deps] telemetry queue overflow — dropped <n> row(s)` (rate-limited to the first drop and every 1000th after). The `app.workspace_id` GUC inside each batch transaction is set via `SELECT set_config('app.workspace_id', $1, true)` (the local/`true` form) — never `SET LOCAL = $1` (PG doesn’t accept binds in `SET`, audit-2 silently broke this for two days before we caught it). ### `args_json` / `metadata_json` serialization gotchas [Section titled “args\_json / metadata\_json serialization gotchas”](#args_json--metadata_json-serialization-gotchas) * **NUL bytes are stripped.** Both JSONB columns are serialized through `jsonbSafeStringify`, which removes NUL bytes (`U+0000`) from every string value. Postgres `jsonb` cannot represent `U+0000` and rejects the whole `::jsonb` cast — before this fix a single NUL in a tool’s args (binary-ish payloads, truncated file reads, terminal output) silently dropped that call’s *entire* telemetry row. * **Large `args_json` becomes a papercup.** When the serialized args exceed 32768 bytes (32 KB), `args_json` is replaced with the papercup object `{"_truncated": true, "_size": <byteLen>}` — not a truncated string. Queries against `args_json` on large calls should expect that shape, not the original args. * **`metadata_json` reaction chain.** On a reaction-triggered call, `metadata_json` carries `metadata.reaction = { depth, chain, ruleId, rootRunId }` (the cause-chain from `event-reaction-system` D-010, so “why did this fire?” is answerable). When `ctx.uiClientId` is present it is also injected into `metadata_json` (via `finalizeMetadata`). ## Where to read in code [Section titled “Where to read in code”](#where-to-read-in-code) * Schema: `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/000-baseline.sql` (original at `archive/046-tool-invocations.sql`) * Quota read + insert (shared across all three transports): `packages/operator-core/lib/projected-tool-deps.ts` — the single `PROJECTED_DEPS` object (`readQuotaStateImpl` + `recordInvocationImpl`), passed to the plugins / agent-tools / transport Hono routes under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/` (and the IPC server `libs/generic/ipc-endpoint-server/src/server.ts`) * Telemetry orchestration: `recordTelemetry` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-stack.ts` * Window-key + ceiling computation: host-injected `computeQuotaWindow` (engine default `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-types.ts:defaultComputeQuotaWindow`; Papercusp policy `packages/agent-mcp/src/quota-policy.ts:papercuspComputeQuotaWindow`) ## Future Intel-tab queries [Section titled “Future Intel-tab queries”](#future-intel-tab-queries) The planned `/harness/<slug>?tab=intel` page reads `tool_invocations` for the four sub-tabs: * **Spawns** — tree of `spawn_id → parent_spawn_id` to visualize agent lineage * **Pack** — recent `repomix.pack` / `code2prompt.pack` calls per feature * **Diff** — `code2prompt.diff` results linked from feature panel * **Graph** — gitnexus query/context/impact (when the GitNexus bridge ships) The current schema supports all of these without modification — and some already shipped: the `tool_invocations_spawn_tree` and `tool_invocations_artifacts` views back the Spawns / Pack / Diff data, with read routes under `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/harness/` (`intel-spawn-tree.ts`, `intel-artifacts.ts`). The remaining work is query views, not new tables.

# Transports

> How HTTP, MCP, and in-process callers all reach the same function. The dispatcher is one; only the framing differs.

## The three transports [Section titled “The three transports”](#the-three-transports) | Transport | Used by | Path | | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **HTTP** (plugin) | Dashboard fetches, agent HTTP fallback | `POST /api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>` | | **HTTP** (built-in) | Dashboard fetches with bearer | `POST /api/agent-tools/<scope>/<verb>` | | **MCP** | Spawned agents over `mcp-handler` Streamable-HTTP | `POST /api/mcp` | | **In-process** | Direct TS imports, server actions | `dispatchProjectedTool(...)` (gated) or `tool.fn(input, ctx)` (ungated) | The HTTP, MCP, and gated in-process paths all go through the same `dispatchProjectedTool` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-projected.ts` (`dispatchProjectedToolStream` for the in-process streaming variant). The same role/capability/quota/timeout/telemetry behavior applies. The raw `tool.fn(input, ctx)` call is the one exception — it bypasses the dispatcher entirely (see [In-process callers](#how-in-process-callers-reach-a-function) below). > **mcp-handler’s SSE transport is disabled.** Only `/api/mcp` (Streamable-HTTP) is live; `mcp-handler` is configured with `disableSse: true`, so a request to `/api/sse` short-circuits to HTTP 404. SSE was turned off because mcp-handler’s SSE transport requires Redis (`REDIS_URL` / `KV_URL`) for cross-process pub/sub, which the operator doesn’t run. Streamable-HTTP needs no Redis. (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts`.) ## How HTTP requests reach a function [Section titled “How HTTP requests reach a function”](#how-http-requests-reach-a-function) The catch-all routes are stupidly simple: 1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts` receives the request (the Hono host catch-all — migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/plugins/[...path]/route.ts`). It’s a **two-step** catch-all: it first tries the in-memory plugin-`apiRoutes` registry (`dispatchPluginApiRoute`) — a plugin can register bespoke handlers outside the projected-tool system; a registry hit returns that plugin’s `Response` directly and skips everything below. A registry miss (`null`) falls through to projected-tool dispatch. 2. Looks up the tool by `lookupByHttpPath(req.pathname)` — if not found, 404 (a 404 on a path that matches a *registered* route under a different HTTP method is upgraded to 405-with-`Allow`, since the catch-all shadows the global method-not-allowed hook) 3. Validates the HTTP method against the manifest’s `expose.http.methods` (default `['POST']`) — if not allowed, 405 4. Builds a `UnifiedToolContext` from URL spawn params + headers + the host’s resolver impls (spawn, secret, projectDir resolver). If no `run` param/header was supplied, a fresh `runId` is generated server-side so `ctx.askUser` / `ctx.publishState` can install — they gate on `workspaceId + runId`. SSE callers had this since T2.2; the JSON path got parity in the pass-9 audit. 5. If `Authorization: Bearer ...` present, resolves it to a principal and tx (no-op for plugins; required for built-ins) 6. Hands off to `dispatchProjectedTool` 7. Maps the resulting `DispatchProjectedResult` to status code + JSON body The streaming path is the same except step 7 — when `Accept: text/event-stream` is on the request, the response is a `ReadableStream` of SSE events. Each `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` call from the function emits one event. **Replay-on-reconnect** (Last-Event-ID + X-Papercusp-Run-Id) is handled in `handleHttpToolRequestStreaming` (http-projection.ts): when both headers are present and the tool has a replay-buffer hit, it serves the buffered tail, emits `event: done` with `{resumed: true, replayed: N}`, and closes the sink — no re-dispatch (the original run already aborted on disconnect, by design). ## How MCP requests reach a function [Section titled “How MCP requests reach a function”](#how-mcp-requests-reach-a-function) Slightly more involved because we use `mcp-handler` as a transport library. 1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/index.ts` (Hono `/api/:transport`, migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/[transport]/route.ts`) wires a `createMcpHandler` server (Streamable-HTTP only, SSE disabled) with `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list` etc. 2. `tools/list` iterates `listMcpProjections(role)` — projection registry filtered by the calling role from URL params. Returns `{ name, description, inputSchema }` for every visible tool. 3. `tools/call` looks up by `lookupByMcpName(name)`, builds a `UnifiedToolContext` (similar to HTTP, but the spawn context comes from the connection URL), and calls `dispatchProjectedTool`. 4. The dispatcher returns; the MCP SDK serializes the result into the JSON-RPC envelope. Streaming on MCP works via `notifications/progress` — when the client sent a `progressToken` in `_meta`, every `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` becomes one notification. mcp-handler routes those over the open Streamable-HTTP response stream. **Write idempotency / result replay.** Passing `_meta.idempotencyKey` on a `tools/call` persists the result under that key (`storeMcpResult`) and replays the stored outcome (`lookupStoredMcpResult`) on any retry with the same key, instead of re-firing the tool. This is recovery for a write whose response died on a dropped connection — opt-in per call. **Per-call keepalive + deadline.** A long/blocking `tools/call` holds the Streamable-HTTP event-stream open but silent, which would otherwise trip the \~60s tunnel/client idle timers. The transport emits a spec-legal SSE comment keepalive on a cadence well under that (default 20s, `PAPERCUSP_MCP_KEEPALIVE_MS`) to reset both timers, and enforces a server-side deadline (default 55s, `PAPERCUSP_MCP_DEADLINE_MS`, set under the 60s `maxDuration`) that returns a clean JSON-RPC error rather than a silent tunnel drop. Both ride the per-request stream — not the disabled Redis-backed SSE transport. ## Slash exposure — the tool catalog as slash commands [Section titled “Slash exposure — the tool catalog as slash commands”](#slash-exposure--the-tool-catalog-as-slash-commands) `expose.slash` is a third exposure key next to `expose.mcp` / `expose.http` — but unlike those it is **a catalog projection, not a dispatch transport** (plan `slash-exposure-tool-catalog-2026-06-12`, D-001). It projects every MCP-exposed tool onto the MCP **prompts** primitive, so agent clients that render MCP prompts as slash commands (Claude Code, OMP) surface the whole session-visible catalog as `/papercusp:tool:<name>` commands. There is no fifth framing adapter and no new `tool_invocations.transport` value: the rendered prompt *instructs the agent* to invoke the tool over the session’s existing MCP connection, so role gates, quota, audit, and result formatting are all inherited from the normal `tools/call` path. * **Default ON for every MCP-exposed tool** (owner-ratified D-003). Opt out per tool with `expose: { slash: false }`, or override naming/description/ args with an object (`{ slash: { name, description, args } }`). The `papercusp-slash-exposure` flag (default enabled) is the global lever. * **`prompts/list`** serves the static `definePrompt` catalog **plus** one dynamic `tool:<mcp-name>` prompt per visible tool — derived from the *same role/profile/manifest/allowlist walk `tools/list` uses* (the shared `resolveVisibleToolListings` in `_mcp-handler.ts`), so the slash surface mirrors the tool surface by construction. The `tool:` prompt-name namespace is reserved; `registerPrompt` rejects static prompts there. * **Arguments**: top-level scalar input fields become MCP prompt arguments (advertised `required: false` on the wire so a bare `/command` is always invokable; required-ness is annotated in the description). The rendered instruction embeds the full input JSON Schema and directs the agent to **elicit missing required fields from the user before invoking**, and to confirm first for high-tier tools. * **`prompts/get`** on a `tool:*` name re-checks session visibility, renders the instruction, and writes a `slash.prompt_get` row to `harness_shared.audit_log` (slash-origin telemetry; the subsequent tool call audits through normal dispatch). * **Codex** doesn’t render MCP prompts as slash commands, so Codex launches materialize the same projection as prompt **files** in `$CODEX_HOME/prompts/tool-<name>.md` (`packages/operator-core/lib/slash-tool-prompts-codex.ts`), with `$ARGUMENTS` in the supplied-args slot. Those files carry their own managed marker, deliberately disjoint from the saved-prompts marker, so the two emitters sharing the flat dir never prune each other’s files. Per-tool mechanics (naming, argument derivation, the instruction render) live in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/slash-projection.ts`. ## How in-process callers reach a function [Section titled “How in-process callers reach a function”](#how-in-process-callers-reach-a-function) The projection registry is exported. Any TypeScript module on the server can do: 
```ts
import { lookupByMcpName } from '@papercusp/agent-mcp';


const tool = lookupByMcpName('repomix.pack');
if (!tool) throw new Error('not registered');
const result = await tool.fn(
  { target_dir: '/some/path' },
  {
    workspaceId: 'default',
    harnessSlug: 'sheets',
    role: 'architect',
    runId: 'R',
    spawnId: 'inproc',
    log: console.log,
    progress: () => {},
    signal: new AbortController().signal,
    spawn: pluginSpawnImpl,
    secret: secretImpl,
    projectDir: '/some/project',
    stateDir: '/some/project/.papercusp',
  },
);
```
 This bypasses the dispatcher — no role check, no quota, no telemetry. Use when you genuinely want to call the function as a function, not as a tool. For consistency, prefer routing through `/api/plugins/...` even from server-side code so gating + telemetry stay uniform. ## The signed URL params [Section titled “The signed URL params”](#the-signed-url-params) When a request hits an HTTP plugin route or the MCP transport, the framework reads these query params (or equivalent `X-Papercusp-*` headers): | Param | Required for | Purpose | | -------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `workspace` | Always | RLS scoping; `app.workspace_id` GUC | | `harness` | Path-resolving tools | Looks up `projectDir` / `stateDir` via `loadHarnessRegistry()` | | `role` | Plugin-tool role gate | A canonical `AGENT_ROLES` id (`worker`, `validator`, `scoper`, `architect`, `reviewer`, `debugger`, `operator`, `documenter`, `curator`, `oracle`, `cup`, `mug`, `planner`, `orchestrator`, … through `judge`). The set is **open** — plugins contribute namespaced `<plugin>:<role>` ids (`role-config.ts`). | | `run` | All non-worker quotas | `window_key = 'run:<id>'` | | `chunk` | Worker quotas | `window_key = 'chunk:<id>'` | | `spawn` | Telemetry attribution | Unique per orchestrator spawn | | `feature` | Optional context | Passed to `tool_invocations.feature_id` for Intel UI | | `parent_spawn` | Optional Phase 9 lineage | Captured for spawn-of-spawn telemetry | | `client` | Optional coordination | Per-session coordination / lock owner id (the operator’s stable `s-…` spawnId); part of the signed envelope | | `exp` | **Signature envelope** | Unix epoch seconds; URLs past `exp` are rejected | | `sig` | **Signature envelope** | HMAC-SHA256 over the canonical sorted other params, base64url-encoded | The orchestrator bakes these into the per-spawn `.mcp.json` it writes before launching an agent process. The signed-param allowlist (`SIGNED_PARAM_ALLOWLIST` in `spawn-signing-core.ts`) is **nine data params plus `exp`**: `harness`, `workspace`, `role`, `run`, `spawn`, `feature`, `chunk`, `parent_spawn`, `client`. The orchestrator always bakes the five mandatory params (`harness`, `workspace`, `role`, `run`, `spawn`) and conditionally adds up to four optional ones (`feature`, `chunk`, `parent_spawn`, `client`), then **HMAC-signs whatever it baked plus `exp`** so the dispatcher refuses to honor a rewritten role. The agent’s MCP client then carries them on every request without the agent ever having to know about them. See [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing) for the full scheme; the minting end lives at `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/spawn-mcp.ts:writeSignedSpawnMcp()`. ## Default exposure [Section titled “Default exposure”](#default-exposure) If a manifest entry omits `expose.*`, the framework picks defaults: * `expose.mcp.name` → `<short-pluginName>.<tool.name>` (drops `@scope/` prefix) * `expose.http.path` → `/api/plugins/<short-pluginName>/<tool.name>` So `@papercupai/repomix` plugin’s `pack` tool gets `repomix.pack` over MCP and `/api/plugins/repomix/pack` over HTTP. You only declare `expose.*` to override these — for instance, to host the same tool at a non-default URL for backwards compat. If you only set `expose.mcp` and not `expose.http`, the tool is MCP-only. If only `expose.http`, HTTP-only. The framework requires at least one. ## Streaming progress [Section titled “Streaming progress”](#streaming-progress) Both transports thread `ctx.progress(pct, msg?)` through: 
```ts
// Tool function
ctx.progress(0,   'starting');
ctx.progress(25,  'fetched manifest');
ctx.progress(75,  'transformed');
ctx.progress(100, 'done');
```
 On MCP (when client passed `_meta.progressToken`): 
```plaintext
notifications/progress { progressToken, progress: 25, total: 100, message: 'fetched manifest' }
```
 On HTTP (when client sent `Accept: text/event-stream`): 
```plaintext
event: progress
data: {"progress":25,"total":100,"message":"fetched manifest"}
```
 The function code is identical for both. Tools that don’t call `ctx.progress` work fine — the receiver just gets the final result. `ctx.progress` is a thin alias over the more general `ctx.emit` primitive described next. ## Typed event streams [Section titled “Typed event streams”](#typed-event-streams) For tools that need richer streaming than `progress(pct, msg)` — LLM token deltas, mid-stream tool-call announcements, parsed sub-results — declare a typed event vocabulary in the manifest and emit via `ctx.emit(name, data)`: 
```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'architect.chat',
  args: z.object({ message: z.string() }),
  events: {
    delta:     z.object({ text: z.string() }),
    tool_call: z.object({ name: z.string(), input: z.unknown() }),
    cost:      z.object({ usd: z.number() }),
  },
  requirePrincipal: false,
  roles: ['operator'],
  timeoutSec: 600,
  idleTimeoutSec: 120,
  capability: 'harness:write',
  handler: async (input, ctx) => {
    for await (const ev of runAgentChat({ promptText: input.message })) {
      if (ev.type === 'delta')     ctx.emit('delta', { text: ev.text });
      else if (ev.type === 'tool_call') ctx.emit('tool_call', { name: ev.name, input: ev.input });
      else if (ev.type === 'result')    ctx.emit('cost', { usd: ev.costUsd });
    }
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: 'turn complete' }] };
  },
});
```
 ### Projection table [Section titled “Projection table”](#projection-table) | Wire | When emit(‘delta’, payload) is called | When handler returns | When handler throws | | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | **HTTP/SSE** (`z.string()` schema) | `event: delta\ndata: <payload as raw text>` (one or more `data:` lines per SSE spec for multi-line) | `event: done\ndata: <ToolResult.content as JSON>` | `event: error\ndata: { code, message }` | | **HTTP/SSE** (object schema) | `event: delta\ndata: <JSON.stringify(payload)>` | same | same | | **MCP** | `notifications/papercusp/event { progressToken, event: 'delta', data: payload }` (always JSON-encoded — JSON-RPC carries strings as quoted strings inside the params object) | `tools/call` response with ToolResult | `tools/call` response with `isError: true` | | **In-process (`dispatchProjectedToolStream`)** | `{ kind: 'event', name: 'delta', data: payload }` (handler-supplied; no transcoding) | `{ kind: 'done', result }` | `{ kind: 'error', error: { code, message } }` | ### Wire format per event — schema-inferred [Section titled “Wire format per event — schema-inferred”](#wire-format-per-event--schema-inferred) The framework inspects each declared event’s Zod schema at registration time and picks the on-the-wire encoding: * `z.string()` → **raw text**. The payload is the text; multi-line content gets split into multiple `data:` lines per SSE spec, joined back by `parseSseStream`. Use for high-frequency token streams (LLM deltas, log lines) — no JSON.stringify on emit, no JSON.parse on consume, smaller bytes per frame. * Any object/union/etc. → **JSON-encoded**. Use for structured events (suggestions, tool\_calls, cost summaries). 
```ts
events: {
  delta:      z.string(),                              // raw on the wire
  tool_call:  z.object({ name: z.string(), input: z.unknown() }),  // JSON
  cost:       z.object({ usd: z.number() }),           // JSON
  suggestion: SuggestionSchema,                        // JSON
}
```
 The MCP transport always JSON-encodes (JSON-RPC doesn’t have a raw-text channel inside a notification’s `params`); the classification only affects the SSE wire. Clients consuming over MCP see `data: '<the text>'` as a string field; over SSE for the same event, they see `data: <the text>` without quotes. ### Content-type hints via `.describe()` [Section titled “Content-type hints via .describe()”](#content-type-hints-via-describe) Any text-based format works through `z.string()` — XML, CSV, YAML, NDJSON, Markdown, plain logs are all just text-shaped on the wire; the framework doesn’t care what the bytes inside the string represent. The producer formats, the consumer parses. When a tool wants to advertise *which* text format it emits, attach a `.describe()` annotation.
