# Generated API & lib reference (projection site)

> The operator HTTP/tool API and the libs/generic TypeDoc API rendered as a browsable human site, projected directly from code. Built on demand via npm run docs:preview; additive to the hand-written docs, replacing none of them.

Two parts of this reference are **projected directly from code**, not hand-written — so they never drift. They are **additive**: they document surfaces that never existed as hand-authored pages, and they replace none of the conceptual, spec, design, or runbook docs in this site. * **Operator API** — every HTTP-exposed `defineTool` projected into an OpenAPI 3.1 spec (`npm run gen:openapi`) and rendered with [`starlight-openapi`](https://starlight-openapi.vercel.app/). * **Lib API** — the borrowable `libs/generic/*` libraries’ public TypeScript API, rendered with [`starlight-typedoc`](https://starlight-typedoc.vercel.app/) from the same entry points `npm run gen:lib-api` resolves. This is the human half of the “two independent projections of one source” design (`docs-and-memory-as-projections-2026-06-05` D-004): the agent form is served directly from code over the `docs:*`/MCP surface, and this site is the parallel human view of the **same** artifacts. ## Building & browsing it [Section titled “Building & browsing it”](#building--browsing-it) The render is **generated on demand**, behind a `DOCS_PREVIEW` build, so it is not baked into the default docs build (which stays fast and free of the operator-core registry import + the multi-lib TypeDoc run). To build and browse it: 
```bash
# from the repo root
npm run docs:preview          # gen:openapi + DOCS_PREVIEW=1 astro build -> dist-preview
npm run docs:preview:serve    # serve it; open the printed URL
```
 Then browse: * **`/internal/docs/preview/api`** — the Operator API reference (one page per operation). * **`/internal/docs/preview/lib-api`** — the libs/generic TypeScript API. ## Don’t hand-edit it [Section titled “Don’t hand-edit it”](#dont-hand-edit-it) These pages are a **projection**. Edits go to the source — the code (for the API/lib surface) or the plans/insights (for rationale) — never to the generated output, which is overwritten on every build.

# Role & persona registry

> The built-in agent roles (AGENT_ROLES) joined with their spawn personas. Generated from role-config.ts + the harness persona files.

> **Generated — do not edit by hand.** Run `npm run gen:doc-projections` (or `npm run gen:doc-role-registry`). Source: `scripts/gen-doc-role-registry.ts`. Part of `starlight-projection-generators-2026-06-05` (Brief 29). # Role & persona registry [Section titled “Role & persona registry”](#role--persona-registry) A **role** is what kind of agent a spawn is. `AGENT_ROLES` is the runtime source of truth for the built-in role ids (tool `roles:` allowlists, `byRole` guidance, quotas); a role’s **persona** is its spawn prompt at `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/<id>/prompts/<role>.md` (the `base` library is the universal one). Not every role has a persona (operator/oracle are chat surfaces), and many personas are blueprint deciders/helpers that are not themselves `AGENT_ROLES` entries. Sources: `packages/agent-mcp/src/role-config.ts` (54 built-in roles) + `libs/papercusp/packages/harness/blueprints/*/prompts/*.md` (58 personas). ## Built-in roles (`AGENT_ROLES`) [Section titled “Built-in roles (AGENT\_ROLES)”](#built-in-roles-agent_roles) These ids appear in tool `roles:` allowlists, `rolesQuota` keys, and `byRole` guidance overrides. # Distribution trust posture

> The v1 trust model for distributing harnesses, blueprints, plugins, tool-packs, and knowledge-packs through the Cupboard — why forking/installing pulls a supply-chain surface, how capability-gating + install-consent contain it, why instruction-carrying kinds are review-gated, what we defer, and what's out of scope.

The **Cupboard** is one storefront with six listing kinds, each with a different consumer action and a different trust surface: | Kind | Action | Pulls code? | Trust surface | | ---------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `harness` | **join** | No — joins a Hypercore swarm by topic | Peer/membership trust ([shared harnesses](/internal/docs/security/shared-harnesses)) | | `blueprint` | **fork** | **Yes** — clones the project remote + any bundled plugin code | Supply chain + review gate (this page) | | `plugin` | **install** | **Yes** — installs a distributable plugin (a pack *with* a runtime) | Supply chain (this page) | | `pack` | **install** | **Yes** — installs a runtime-less code-tool pack, registering MCP tools | Supply chain (this page) | | `knowledge-pack` | **install** | No code — seeds curated learnings into a pot’s shared memory | Injected agent context + review gate (this page) | | `template` | **install** | **Yes** — clones a first-party app-template repo + materializes an app scaffold | Supply chain (first-party author) | > The runtime-less code-tool pack is the `pack` kind (briefly named `tool-pack` by migration 008, then renamed back by `cupboard-public-release-2026-07-12`); `knowledge-pack` was `learning-pack` before migration 011. Both superseded values still parse as normalized wire aliases (`normalizeListingKind`), so older clients keep publishing/browsing. > The `snapshot` kind was **retired** (`retire-snapshots-instance-spec-2026-06-09`, D-005). It is no longer in `LISTING_KINDS`, `normalizeListingKind` returns `null` for it, and Cupboard migration 008 deletes every snapshot row and drops `snapshot` from the `listing_kind` CHECK constraint — no current worker code can serve a snapshot listing. References below are to its successors (blueprint for the fork path). This page is the trust posture for the kinds that either **pull code** — forking a blueprint, installing a plugin or pack, materializing a template — or **inject agent context** — a knowledge-pack. It records the v1 decision (`harness-blueprint-distribution-2026-06-03`, **P-009 / D-007 / D-009**) and, importantly, what is **deferred** and what is **out of scope**. ## The supply-chain surface [Section titled “The supply-chain surface”](#the-supply-chain-surface) Forking a blueprint pulls the project remote *and any plugin code it bundles*; installing a plugin or pack pulls code directly. A `pack` is a runtime-less code-tool pack that registers MCP tools (`provides_tools`), so it sits on the same supply-chain surface as a plugin. Plugin code runs in the operator’s plugin host with access to host services (tasks, secrets, fetch, compute). **Unconstrained, that is a classic supply-chain risk** — a published listing could ship a plugin that reads secrets or exfiltrates over the network. A `knowledge-pack` pulls *no executable code*, but it injects curated learnings into a pot’s shared memory — i.e. content that lands in agent context. That is a different risk (prompt injection), addressed by the review gate below rather than by capability-gating. ## v1 posture: capability-gate + install-consent [Section titled “v1 posture: capability-gate + install-consent”](#v1-posture-capability-gate--install-consent) The v1 containment for the **code-pulling** kinds is the **existing two-tier plugin capability model** — we reuse it rather than inventing a distribution-specific mechanism (D-009). A plugin capability is usable **iff it is in BOTH tiers**: 1. **Tier 1 — manifest.** The plugin’s `capabilities[]` (manifest) declares what it *could* use. Format `namespace:action[:resource]` (`tasks:read`, `http:fetch:*.youtube.com`, `secrets:read:YT_API_KEY`). 2. **Tier 2 — install-consent.** At install/enable the operator presents those caps to the user, who grants a subset. The grant set is stored in `harness_shared.plugin_capability_grants` (originally Migration 051, now in `000-baseline.sql`) and loaded at plugin init. The gate is `hasCapability(ctx, cap)` in [`packages/plugin-loader/src/capabilities.ts`](https://github.com/Papercusp/plugin-loader) — it ANDs the manifest set with the granted set (both wildcard-aware). The grants store + loader live in the operator core (`lib/plugin-grants.ts` · `getGrantsForPluginInHarness`, and `lib/plugin-host-runtime.ts` · `loadGrantedCapsSafe`; post-carve these are `@papercusp/operator-core`). Caution `loadGrantedCapsSafe` returns `undefined` — not an empty array — when there are **zero** grants for a `(plugin@version, harness)` pair (no consent flow has run yet, or Postgres is unreachable with no legacy file present) and on any read error. That `undefined` is stored verbatim into the runtime’s grant state, and `hasCapability` treats `granted === undefined` as the **legacy single-tier (manifest-only)** path. So the operator runtime is *not* unconditionally on the two-tier path: until grants exist for a plugin, or if the grants read fails, it falls back to manifest-only for that plugin. The deliberate revoke path deletes specific caps (leaving a non-empty set), so an explicit user-revoke is *not* confused with “no grants yet”. The dangerous egress surfaces are gated at the boundary a forked plugin actually hits: `makeFetchProxy` rejects any host not covered by an `http:fetch:<host>` capability, and `makeSecretsProxy` rejects any `secrets:read:<NAME>` not granted. ### Fork inherits the parent’s grants [Section titled “Fork inherits the parent’s grants”](#fork-inherits-the-parents-grants) Forking does **not** silently re-prompt or degrade a plugin to manifest-only on first invocation. `copyGrantsToNewHarness` (`lib/plugin-grants.ts`) copies every `(plugin, version, capability)` grant from the source harness to the new one under the target slug, `granted_by='system'`, `reason='fork from <sourceSlug>'` (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so a re-fork doesn’t duplicate). The fork inherits its parent’s capability decisions rather than starting from no grants. ### Backfill for already-enabled plugins [Section titled “Backfill for already-enabled plugins”](#backfill-for-already-enabled-plugins) At operator boot, `backfillGrantsFromEnabledPluginsAndLegacyFile` **silently grants** each currently-enabled plugin its full manifest-declared cap set (`granted_by='system'`, `reason='enabled-plugins.json backfill'`) so existing harnesses don’t break on first reload after the two-tier rollout. A legacy `~/.papercusp/granted-capabilities.json` file is a **read-only fallback** that is also replayed verbatim. The practical consequence: the consent prompt is for *new* installs — already-enabled plugins are backfilled with their declared caps rather than re-prompted retroactively. Users can revoke any backfilled cap from the consent UI afterward. ### Server-capability invocation (palette) [Section titled “Server-capability invocation (palette)”](#server-capability-invocation-palette) The desktop palette’s server-capability path (`lib/capabilities/invoke.ts` · `paletteInvokeGuard` → `invokeServerCapability`; post-carve `@papercusp/operator-core`) runs **with no gate bypass for trust/role**: it is a plain loopback `operator` principal, a server-side §3 admission re-check refuses non-eligible tools, and destructive/high-risk tools require an explicit `confirmed:true`. Every call is audited. (See D-007 in the source.) ## Review gate for instruction-carrying kinds [Section titled “Review gate for instruction-carrying kinds”](#review-gate-for-instruction-carrying-kinds) Capability-gate + install-consent covers **code-egress** risk (fetch/secrets) — it does **not** cover **prompt-injection** risk from content that lands in agent context. So the two **instruction-carrying** kinds now carry a **pre-publication review gate**: * A **knowledge-pack** injects curated learnings into a pot’s shared memory. * A **blueprint** runs agent roles. `REVIEW_POLICY_KINDS = ['knowledge-pack', 'blueprint']`. At publish, a listing of one of these kinds lands `review_status='pending'` (every other kind, and every pre-008 row, is `'approved'`). Pending/rejected listings are **excluded from public list and read** — only the publisher can read their own pending listing (via `GET /:id` with auth), and operators triage them through `/admin`. A non-owner request for a non-approved listing returns 404. An operator approval (or rejection, with a surfaced reason) flips the status. Pure code kinds — `plugin` and `pack` — are **not** review-gated; they keep install-consent + reactive moderation (reports → unlist). The split is by risk type: code kinds are contained by the capability gate at runtime; instruction kinds have no analogous runtime gate, so they’re held for human review before they’re publicly visible. ## Publisher trust signals (Cupboard worker) [Section titled “Publisher trust signals (Cupboard worker)”](#publisher-trust-signals-cupboard-worker) The Cupboard worker (`apps/operator-public`) surfaces *advisory* publisher signals on each listing — they inform, they do not hard-gate (a provisional listing is **not** an ownership claim): * **Publisher-collaborator signal** — the publisher’s GitHub permission on the bound repo at publish time (`publisher_permission`, Migration 002; `derivePublisherPermission`). The browse card shows “collaborator” vs “not a collaborator”. A non-collaborator who can merely read a public repo reads as `read`. * **Channel-2 device attestation** — an optional device-key to GitHub-login gist binding (Migration 003), verified/revoked by the hourly indexer. * **Operator ban-list** — `banned_publisher_pubkeys`; a banned publisher device pubkey’s listings are filtered from browse and 404 on detail. * **Private repos are rejected** at publish; all listings are public. These are the same signals harness listings already carried — the storefront merge applies them uniformly across all listing kinds (every kind is project-remote-backed in v1). ## Deferred (D-009) — acceptable because there are no users yet [Section titled “Deferred (D-009) — acceptable because there are no users yet”](#deferred-d-009--acceptable-because-there-are-no-users-yet) * **Plugin signing.** No cryptographic signature on plugin code. Note that a **review gate is no longer fully deferred**: the instruction-carrying kinds (blueprint, knowledge-pack) are now pre-publication review-gated (above). What remains deferred is review/curation for the **pure code kinds** (plugin, pack), which keep install-consent + reactive moderation as their floor, and cryptographic signing for all kinds. Capability-gate + install-consent (code kinds) and the review gate (instruction kinds) are the floor; signing raises it later. Revisit before there are real users installing third-party listings. ## Out of scope here (D-012) [Section titled “Out of scope here (D-012)”](#out-of-scope-here-d-012) * **Producer-side trust** — collaborator push-access to the papercupai project remote (who may *publish/contribute to* a project), as opposed to consumer-side trust (what a *forked/installed* plugin may *do*, this page). That surface is owned by the [project-centric rethink](/internal/docs/spec) and the distributed-coordination plans (`distributed-coordination-shared-harness-2026-06-04`). ## Summary [Section titled “Summary”](#summary) | Concern | v1 | | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Live listing kinds | `harness`, `blueprint`, `plugin`, `pack`, `knowledge-pack`, `template` (snapshot retired; `tool-pack`/`learning-pack` parse as normalized aliases) | | Forked/installed plugin capability | manifest ∩ user-consented grant (`hasCapability`) when grants present; manifest-only fallback when grants absent/unreadable | | Consent record | `plugin_capability_grants` (baseline.sql; was Migration 051) | | Fork capability inheritance | parent grants copied `granted_by='system'` (`copyGrantsToNewHarness`) | | Already-enabled plugins | manifest caps backfilled at boot (`granted_by='system'`); legacy JSON read-only fallback | | Network / secret egress | per-host / per-name capability via fetch+secrets proxies | | Instruction-carrying kinds | pre-publication review gate (`blueprint`, `knowledge-pack` land `pending`, hidden until operator-approved) | | Palette server-capability | §3 re-check, confirm-for-destructive, no trust bypass, audited | | Publisher trust | advisory signals (collaborator perm, device attestation, ban-list); private repos rejected | | Signing | deferred (D-009); review deferred only for pure code kinds | | Producer-side push trust | out of scope (D-012) |

# Shared harnesses

> The trust and security model for peer-to-peer shared harnesses — how identity, authorization, membership, and revocation work, what we borrow from other P2P systems, and the tradeoffs we accept intentionally.

Partially built — model is being implemented in phases This page records the security model for **shared harnesses** (the peer-to-peer, multi-engineer sync substrate), the research it rests on, and the tradeoffs we are choosing **intentionally**. The model below is the agreed direction, tracked in the design memo `apps/operator/docs/plans/papercusp-trust-model-2026-05-31.md`. Sections marked **Today** describe the original (2026-05-31) insecure state; **Recommended** describes the target. **Build-state update (2026-06-13).** The substrate trust layer is now substantially built: **per-log admission** (signed announce + GitHub-anchored `verifyBinding` attestation), **revocation** (`revoked_pubkeys` projection drop-list, gated on a live GitHub repo-admin check), and **identity attestation** (`verifyAttestation`) are all wired. Crucially, a confirmation audit (P-017, plan `shared-pot-hardening-2026-06-13`) verified that the model’s load-bearing invariant — **every decision-bearing fact re-derives from GitHub at the point of action** — holds across all current call sites. See [The advisory-vs-trusted boundary](#the-advisory-vs-trusted-boundary) for the verified call-site table. Per-op signing (Phase 2 below) remains a defense-in-depth future enhancement, not a shipped gate — the shipped model is **per-log** admission, so an admitted peer’s ops are trusted wholesale (the accepted equivocation tradeoff), which is why the GitHub re-derivation invariant is what actually carries the safety. **Build-state update (2026-06-25).** Read admission is intentionally **not** a repo-collaborator permission gate. The pure decider in `sync/hyperbee/read-admission.ts` admits a log only after announce signature verification, GitHub-gist attestation verification, and the `revoked_pubkeys` veto. Boot adds two Pot-specific scope wideners: an already-known Pot member can be admitted from the local `hive_members` projection via `trustedHiveMemberDeviceAdmission`, and a same-Pot cross-member announce whose membership has not federated yet is buffered as `pending` and retried within the boot grace window. GitHub collaborator/admin permission remains the authority for repo binding, revocation actions, push/PR/merge, and shipped verification; it is not the swarm read-admission allow-list. ## What a shared harness is [Section titled “What a shared harness is”](#what-a-shared-harness-is) A shared harness lets several engineers collaborate on one coding project. Shared state — the **feature queue, pull-request status, the contributor list, and feature “claims”** — syncs peer-to-peer over the Holepunch stack and is projected into each peer’s local Postgres: * **Hyperswarm** — DHT peer discovery. The swarm **topic = `sha256("papercusp-substrate-v1:gh:<github_repository_id>")`**, derived from the *public* GitHub repo id, so it is **discoverable, not a secret**. `gh:<repository_id>` is only one of several topic bindings: the shipped multi-engineer (**Pot**) substrate is keyed by **`pot:<hive_pubkey>`**, which *replaces* the per-repo slug as the top-level federation unit (a Pot’s Swarms all join this one topic), with `local:<workspace_id>/<slug>` for pre-binding/private dev and an explicit `topic:<hex>` carrier so a link-joiner lands on the owner’s exact Pot topic rather than re-deriving a `gh:` topic that wouldn’t match. * **Hypercore** — one Ed25519-signed append-only log per device. * **Model B peer-log** — one single-writer Ed25519 log per device + a read-merge over the others (`sync/hyperbee/peer-log.ts`). This **replaced** the earlier multi-writer **Autobase** design; Autobase mentions below are the historical survey/analysis, not the shipped substrate (P-024 truth fix). Identity is anchored to **GitHub**: each device holds an Ed25519 keypair in the OS keychain. The OAuth `GET /user` channel is a **local self-attestation only — it is never part of remote admission**. Remote admission (post write-free-join) proves the `device_pubkey ↔ github_user_id` binding entirely from a **device-signed announce** plus `verifyAttestation` on a **public GitHub gist** — the gist pins `owner.id === github_user_id`, the body’s `device_pubkey`, and a device signature. There is **no device-signed commit** anywhere in the code: the old shared-repo contributor-file channel was removed in the write-free-join work. The single most important fact: **the authority for the one thing that truly matters — merging code — is GitHub itself.** PRs merge through the GitHub REST API with a real user token, so GitHub’s write-access and branch-protection rules are enforced regardless of anything that happens on the swarm. ## The trust problem [Section titled “The trust problem”](#the-trust-problem) Original 2026-05-31 state: the substrate was wide open Replicated Autobase ops were **not signed, authenticated, or authorized on receipt** — the only admission check was a schema-version filter. Because the swarm topic is derivable from the public repo id, **any peer who could reach the DHT could join and write forged feature/PR/contributor/claim rows into every other peer’s local database.** The designed defenses (an admission step gated on the two-channel binding, a `revoked_pubkeys` drop-list) existed on paper but had **no production callers**. **Update (2026-06-13):** admission is now wired (Model B per-log: signed announce + GitHub-anchored `verifyBinding` + `revoked_pubkeys` veto — see `packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/read-admission.ts`), so a peer is admitted only on a verified GitHub-anchored attestation, not by mere DHT reachability. What remains **intentionally** unbuilt is **per-op** signature verification at projection time: once a peer is admitted, its ops are projected wholesale (the accepted equivocation tradeoff). The forged-advisory-row surface is therefore narrowed to *already-admitted* peers and, per the verified invariant below, **no decision-bearing action acts on those rows without re-deriving from GitHub**. Keep two threat models separate: * **Untrustworthy local user** — every local API route is `auth: 'public'` (127.0.0.1 only). It trusts whoever is on the desktop. Fine for a single-user desktop; not a shared-machine model. * **Untrustworthy swarm peer** *(the serious one)* — public topic + unsigned ops means a peer can poison every other peer’s local DB/UI. This is what the security layer exists to contain. A code audit (2026-05-31) confirmed that **GitHub is the only authorization actually enforced today.** Everything Papercusp layers on top — the feature state machine, the PR “trusted authors” gate, the `completion_ref` “shipped ✓” verifier, contributor identity signatures, and substrate op-auth — is currently dead code, unwired, or self-asserted. ## How other systems solve it [Section titled “How other systems solve it”](#how-other-systems-solve-it) A three-pass survey of production P2P / local-first / decentralized systems. They converge on a small primitive set: **sign every replicated write and verify it on receipt; gate membership cryptographically; anchor identity to keys or an external authority; and accept that true deletion is impossible in an append-only log.** | System | Identity anchor | Per-op authorization | Membership / removal | Verdict for Papercusp | | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Hypercore** | per-device Ed25519 key (our model) | signed merkle tree per log (integrity, single-writer) | — | **Maps** — proves you authored *your* log, not that you’re allowed | | **Autobase** | — | **none built in**; *“optimistic blocks should self-verify in the apply handler”* | `addWriter`/`removeWriter` are app calls inside `apply` | **Maps / confirms the gap** — per-op verification is the app’s job | | **Hyperswarm / HyperDHT** | connecting peer’s Noise key | Noise authenticates the *connection*, not ops | only `firewall(remotePublicKey)` | **Maps / confirms threat** — public topic; connection-auth ≠ op-auth | | **blind-pairing** (Keet) | invite secret | candidate signs with invite key; member verifies | admit-by-invite; app-evaluated `userData` | **Partial** — a ready admission handshake; put the GitHub proof in `userData` | | **Radicle** *(closest analog)* | self-sovereign `did:key` (opposite of ours) | **signs every write** (`refs/rad/sigref`); **rejects invalid before storing**; signed collaborative objects | delegate threshold/quorum | **Mechanism maps, anchor doesn’t** — proves the sign-and-verify-before-store pattern | | **Radicle COBs** | content-addressed | exposes each change’s author → filter a bad author at view-build | filter at materialization | **Maps** — our `revoked_pubkeys` is this *local projection filter*, not network rejection | | **Kleppmann (BFT-CRDT)** | — | **signatures necessary but NOT sufficient** — a signed *equivocation* breaks version vectors | a replicated ACL must itself be a BFT CRDT | **Decisive** — don’t try to make advisory state Byzantine-trustworthy | | **Keyhive / BeeKEM** (Ink & Switch) | **deliberately excludes** identity binding | capability chains + per-op Ed25519 sig; BeeKEM needs only **causal** order → fits Autobase | coordination-free removal with **real post-compromise security** | **Authz maps; complements (≠ replaces) the GitHub binding** — see [Keyhive](#does-keyhivebeekem-fit-our-stack) | | **MLS / RFC 9420** | — | TreeKEM epoch chain | needs **one linear chain of agreed Commits**; concurrent commits fork a DAG it can’t merge | **Does not map** over Autobase’s concurrent merge | | **Keybase** *(two-channel analog)* | per-user signed **sigchain**; key↔GitHub via a GitHub-hosted signed proof | each link signed, `seqno` + `prev` hash | revocation = a **signed revoke link**; sibkeys for device-loss recovery | **Maps — improves the binding**: model two-channel as a signed link; revoke-as-signed-statement beats a side-list | | **Sigstore / SLSA / in-toto** | short-lived **OIDC** identity (Fulcio) | keyless sig + **Rekor transparency log**; in-toto/DSSE | no revocation (short-lived certs); compromise caught by **monitoring** | **Partial — provenance pattern**: a signature proves *authenticated-at-a-time*, **not** authorization or “good.” Confirms “shipped” must be **GitHub-derived** | | **AT Proto `did:plc`** | hybrid: self-cert keys + a directory | signed repo commits | **rotation-key priority list + 72h recovery window** | **Partial — recovery lesson**: for us, GitHub *is* the recovery anchor | | **Nostr NIP-05** | pubkey ↔ `name@domain` via a `.well-known` file | per-event Schnorr sig | — | **Partial** — a GitHub-hosted well-known file is a lighter binding variant | | **Secure Scuttlebutt** | per-identity signed append-only feed (≈ Hypercore) | every message signed | **invite + follow-graph** bounds replication & Sybils | **Partial — admission analog**: Pot membership + revocation bounds shared-pot replication; GitHub permission is reserved for decision-bearing actions | ### The decisive constraints [Section titled “The decisive constraints”](#the-decisive-constraints) 1. **Autobase will not authenticate ops for us** — per-op signing and `addWriter` gating are *our* code, in the `apply`/projection seam. 2. **Signatures are necessary but not sufficient** (Kleppmann) — a validly-admitted-then- malicious writer can sign false or *equivocating* rows. Full Byzantine resilience needs a hash-DAG causal layer we are **not** going to build. 3. **True removal / post-compromise security is impossible in an append-only multi-writer log** — a revoked writer’s signed ops persist and replicate; “removal” means every honest peer drops them at projection time. 4. **A provenance signature proves authentication-at-a-time, not authorization or quality** (Sigstore) — so the trustworthy “shipped” signal must come from GitHub’s *merge state*, not a self-reported receipt. 5. **GitHub already enforces the only hard authorization that matters.** This is the escape hatch from the unsolved Byzantine-CRDT access-control problem. ## Does Holepunch provide its own solution? [Section titled “Does Holepunch provide its own solution?”](#does-holepunch-provide-its-own-solution) Mostly the **building blocks**, not a turnkey access-control product: * **Hypercore** signs each log for free. * **Autobase** gives a writer set with `addWriter`/`removeWriter`, but **you** write the per-op check and the admission policy in `apply`. * **blind-pairing-core** (what Keet actually uses) is a real cryptographic invite/pairing handshake — admit-by-possession-of-invite-secret. This is Holepunch’s native admission answer. * **Hyperswarm** gives Noise-encrypted connections + a coarse `firewall(remotePublicKey)` reject hook. What Holepunch deliberately leaves to the app: fine-grained capabilities (read/write/admin), **identity binding** (always app-layer — our GitHub anchor), and **post-compromise security on removal** (`removeWriter` stops new appends; it is not key-rotation/PCS). Of those, the only one we actually need is identity binding — which no library provides. **So the plan builds on Holepunch’s native primitives**: per-op signature verification + GitHub-anchored `addWriter` (via blind-pairing, GitHub proof in `userData`) + a `revoked_pubkeys` projection drop-list. ## Does Keyhive/BeeKEM fit our stack? [Section titled “Does Keyhive/BeeKEM fit our stack?”](#does-keyhivebeekem-fit-our-stack) Compatible *in principle*, but **not native and arguably overkill**: * **It fits the ordering model** — BeeKEM needs only a *causal* order, which Autobase provides. It’s the only post-compromise-secure option that works over a concurrent-merge log (MLS does not). * **But it’s an Automerge-ecosystem Rust library** (the `beekem` crate), not a Holepunch component. Adopting it means embedding that crate and running its control ops over Autobase — an unsupported combination, and it is **pre-alpha, unaudited, BeeKEM not formally proven**. * **It couples authorization with *encryption*** (it’s a continuous group key agreement). Our substrate data is plaintext to swarm members today; BeeKEM means encrypting group state with key rotation — a large shift that *buys* post-compromise security but is more than advisory data needs. * **It still doesn’t solve identity** — Keyhive defers human-identity binding to “a future layer above,” i.e. our GitHub anchor regardless. ## Recommended model — GitHub is the authority of record [Section titled “Recommended model — GitHub is the authority of record”](#recommended-model--github-is-the-authority-of-record) 1. **Authority of record = GitHub.** Every *decision-bearing* fact (did it merge, who has write access, real PR status, who is a contributor) is **re-derived from GitHub at the point of action** — never trusted from a peer. 2. **Peer-synced rows = advisory cache** (fast/offline UI), explicitly untrusted. 3. **Per-op Ed25519 signing + verify-on-receipt** in the Autobase `apply`/projection path — *defense-in-depth / UX integrity*, not the authority of record. **Sign sequence + freshness, not just content** (Radicle’s 2026 replay-CVE lesson). 4. **GitHub-anchored log admission** — signed announce + GitHub gist attestation verifies the device identity; `revoked_pubkeys` denies known-bad devices. Pot scope is then narrowed/widened by signed `harness_slug`, local `hive_members`, and pending retry for membership propagation. This is not a collaborator permission gate. 5. **Identity binding = a Keybase-style signed link** — the GitHub-hosted device-signed proof is the cross-check that lets any peer detect a rewritten identity; revocation is a *signed* statement, not just a side list. 6. **Device-key rotation/recovery is GitHub-rooted** — losing a device means re-running the two-channel binding from the new device; the old key goes on `revoked_pubkeys`. GitHub (the account) plays `did:plc`’s “higher-authority key” recovery role. 7. **“Shipped”/provenance = GitHub-derived** — read merge state from GitHub; optionally record it as a signed in-toto-style attestation. Do **not** build a Rekor-style transparency log — GitHub already is the authority and stores attestations. (This also means the `completion_ref` “shipped” signal should be GitHub-derived, not a self-reported peer receipt.) 8. **Sybil/admission = verified GitHub identity plus Pot membership/revocation.** The swarm topic is public, so unauthenticated devices are filtered by signed announce + gist attestation; shared-Pot cross-member scope is filtered by `hive_members`; and `revoked_pubkeys` is the hard local blocklist. The GitHub collaborator graph is still consulted at decision points that need repo authority, but it is not the read-admission allow-list. 9. **Do not** adopt MLS or build a Byzantine-CRDT ACL. ### The advisory-vs-trusted boundary [Section titled “The advisory-vs-trusted boundary”](#the-advisory-vs-trusted-boundary) The central decision: which synced surfaces are advisory vs must-re-derive-from-GitHub. | Synced surface | Advisory (peer-supplied cache)? | Decision-bearing → re-derive from GitHub? | | ------------------------ | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Feature queue / status | yes — display & coordination | a “shipped” decision → GitHub merge state | | PR status | yes — display | merge / approval authority → GitHub | | Contributor list | yes — display | ”is X a real contributor / has write access” → GitHub collaborators | | Feature claims | yes — coordination/UX only | (advisory by nature; no hard authority needed) | | Completion / “shipped ✓“ | no | **GitHub-derived only** | Anything in the right column must never be acted on from peer state alone. ### Confirmation pass — 2026-06-13 (P-017): every decision-bearing fact re-derives [Section titled “Confirmation pass — 2026-06-13 (P-017): every decision-bearing fact re-derives”](#confirmation-pass--2026-06-13-p-017-every-decision-bearing-fact-re-derives) The shipped substrate uses **per-log** admission: a peer is admitted on a verified signed-announce + GitHub-anchored attestation, after which its ops are trusted **wholesale** into the projection (no per-op authz — the accepted equivocation tradeoff). That is safe **iff** every decision-bearing fact re-derives from GitHub at the point of action. A call-site audit (plan `shared-pot-hardening-2026-06-13`, P-017) confirmed this invariant holds across **all** authorization-bearing consumers of peer-synced state — there is **no gap**. The federated tables are `contributors`, `queue` / `features-by-id` (→ `harness_features_consolidated`), `working-set`/`claims`, `presence`, plans, and coord; the table below enumerates every site that *acts* on one (display-only reads omitted). PR state is **not** federated: `harness_feature_prs` was reclassified `sync:'none'` (EI-479) — it is GitHub-derived and re-polled per-machine, so Postgres is the local store-of-record and federation is redundant; it has no projection producer and is not a registered projection tag. (This is why the auto-merge row below correctly reads the `Pr` object from a live GitHub poll, not from a federated row.) | Call-site | Authorization decision | Reads | Re-derives from GitHub? | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `harness/binding-service.ts` · `claimBinding` | claim a repo binding (needs maintain/admin) | local cache + **live** `getRepoPermission` | **Yes** — `getRepoPermission(owner,repo,login)` at point of action | | `harness/binding-service.ts` · `supersedeBinding` | supersede a binding (needs admin) | local cache + **live** `getRepoPermission` | **Yes** — live permission check, admin required | | `harness/binding-service.ts` · claimant re-verify sweep | demote a claimant who lost write access | cached claimants | **Yes** — per-claimant live permission check | | `sync/hyperbee/revoke-contributor.ts` | revoke a contributor’s device key | `contributors` row | **Yes** — `repos.get → permissions.admin` gate before any write | | `sync/hyperbee/read-admission.ts` (+ `boot.ts`) | admit a peer’s log to the substrate | signed announce + local Pot membership projection | **Yes** — announce-sig verify + `verifyBinding` (GitHub-hosted attestation); `revoked_pubkeys` veto; same-Pot scope uses `hive_members` / pending retry, not repo collaborator permission | | `harness/fork-pr-on-feature-pass.ts` | fork-PR vs direct-push mode on feature pass | local pipeline pass event | **Yes** — **live** `getPermission` (fork iff `read`/`none`) | | `pr-host/auto-merge.ts` · `tryAutoMerge` → `host.merge` | merge a PR | `Pr` object from **GitHub** poll (`PrHost`/`github.ts`) | **Yes** — PR state read live from GitHub; merge enforced by GitHub write-access + branch protection | | `pr-host/auto-approve.ts` · `tryAutoApprove` | post an approving review | **local** `trusted_authors` + GitHub PR author | **N/A** — trust list is local config (not federated); approval still doesn’t bypass GitHub’s merge authority | | `harness/completion-ref-verifier.ts` | stamp the “shipped ✓” verified tier | `completion_ref` on the feature row | **Yes** — `git ls-remote <remote> <sha>` (GitHub native auth) confirms the SHA is on the remote | | `dbos/orchestrator-finalize.ts` · `reconcileDoneStatus` | flip a feature `validating`/`in_progress → passed` | `harness_features_consolidated.status` (federated) | **N/A — advisory.** Fires only from the **local** orchestrator’s own pipeline reaching an unblocked DONE (`outcome==='done'`); a peer’s forged row cannot make the local pipeline run a feature to DONE. `passed` is internal pipeline coordination, **not** a “shipped”/authz fact — every downstream effect (push/PR/merge) is independently GitHub-gated. (Completion-integrity update, `fleet-backlog-lessons-2026-07-01` P-001/WI-1542: the same local-only write now also stamps `terminal_owner='system:dbos-orchestrator-finalize'` and a `terminal_completion_ref` — an auditability fix for the genuine-completions metric, not a change to who may write or to the trust boundary.) | | `contributors` / `claims` / `queue` / `working-set` readers (claim avatars, status badges, queue UI) | display & coordination only | federated rows | **N/A** — advisory by design; gate no action | **Why the federated feature `status` is not a gap (the one row worth tracing).** `harness_features_consolidated.status` *is* a federated projection target (tag `features-by-id`), so an admitted peer can write a `status` value into another peer’s PG. But no authorization decision acts on it: a forged `status='shipped'` does not earn the verified ✓ badge (that re-derives via `git ls-remote`), and `reconcileDoneStatus` only closes the `validating`/`in_progress`→`passed` loop (the `in_progress` case was added 2026-06-17 for coding-harness cups that skip the validator step) as the **local** pipeline’s own terminal verdict on a feature it actually executed — it cannot be driven by a peer-supplied row; terminal-failure states (failing/deprecated) are left untouched. The real “did it ship” authority remains GitHub’s merge state, and code only lands through GitHub’s write-access + branch-protection. This is the security doc’s own placement of “feature queue / status” in the **advisory** column, confirmed at the code level. **Verdict:** the wholesale-trust-of-admitted-peer model is sound **because** the re-derivation invariant is universal. No remediation needed; P-017 closed `done`. ### Revocation chokepoints (built) [Section titled “Revocation chokepoints (built)”](#revocation-chokepoints-built) Two revocation mechanisms are wired beyond the `revoked_pubkeys` admission drop-list: * **PR auto-approve and auto-merge refuse a revoked contributor’s PR up front.** A PR whose author is a revoked Pot contributor is denied (action `skipped_revoked`) **before** the trust / checks / approval gates — the strongest deny, **overriding the trust list** (it holds even for an author otherwise in `trusted_authors`). The live chokepoint resolves it via `isHiveContributorRevoked` and passes it into both `tryAutoApprove` and `tryAutoMerge`. * **Owner-revocation of another contributor** (`revokeContributorViaGithub`) is gated on a **live GitHub repo-admin** check (`repos.get → permissions.admin`) — the harness-owner authority. It works by unioning the target’s device pubkeys into the **owner’s own** contributor-row `revoked_pubkeys` and publishing it (the old “delete the `user/<id>` branch” lever became a no-op under write-free join, and an admin cannot delete another user’s attestation gist). Because `load-revoked-pubkeys` **unions `revoked_pubkeys` across all contributor rows** for the harness, that block federates via the owner’s log and is honored by every peer’s admission union. ## Accepted-insecurity tradeoffs [Section titled “Accepted-insecurity tradeoffs”](#accepted-insecurity-tradeoffs) Under this model we **deliberately accept**: 1. **Public, discoverable topic** — swarm spam/DoS is *mitigated* (firewall + admission), not prevented. 2. **Advisory rows can be injected by an admitted identity** — read admission proves identity and Pot membership, not truth. An admitted-then-malicious writer can still inject signed-but-false advisory rows (equivocation). Mitigation: nothing decision-bearing acts on it without GitHub re-derivation. 3. **No true removal / no post-compromise security** in the append-only log — revocation is best-effort projection filtering; the data persists and replicates. 4. **Sybil resistance is mostly delegated to GitHub identity plus Pot membership** — identity = GitHub account, bounded by the gist attestation and GitHub’s account-creation friction; cross-member shared-Pot writes also require a current `hive_members` device row or they remain pending/dropped. 5. **Per-op signatures don’t defeat a signed equivocator** (Kleppmann) — accepted because state is advisory and GitHub-re-derived; we explicitly do not build a BFT-CRDT ACL. 6. **Identity binding inherits GitHub account integrity** — a compromised GitHub account is a compromised identity (the same trust root as the merge authority, so not a new exposure). 7. **Local API stays loopback-trusted** — a single-user-desktop model, not a shared machine. ## Phased implementation [Section titled “Phased implementation”](#phased-implementation) * **Phase 1 — make peer state advisory + re-derive from GitHub.** Highest value, lowest risk; neutralizes the forgery surface for anything that matters. Resolves `completion_ref` as a GitHub-derived “shipped” signal. * **Phase 2 — per-op Ed25519 signing + verify-on-receipt** in the `apply`/projection path (sign seq + content); drop unverifiable ops at projection. * **Phase 3 — GitHub-anchored `addWriter` admission** (two-channel proof in blind-pairing `userData`) + `revoked_pubkeys` projection drop-list; model the binding as a signed link. * **Phase 4 — only if a threat model demands real PCS** — Keyhive/BeeKEM membership. ## Sources & method [Section titled “Sources & method”](#sources--method) Three deep-research passes (web search → fetch primary sources → adversarial verification), \~9M tokens. Passes 1–2 (50 claims verified): Holepunch repos, Radicle (Heartwood + `radicle-cob` + LWN), ForgeFed, Kleppmann (PaPoC’22 + keynote), Ink & Switch Keyhive notebook, RFC 9420/9750 + DMLS drafts. Pass 3 (Keybase, Sigstore/SLSA, `did:plc`, Nostr, SSB): primary-sourced but the workflow’s vote-tally step crashed, so those rows are extracted-not-triple-verified; the two most decision-relevant (Sigstore threat model, `did:plc` recovery) were re-confirmed by direct fetch. Full per-claim detail lives in the design memo `apps/operator/docs/plans/papercusp-trust-model-2026-05-31.md`.

# Sharable infrastructure plan

> The design — now largely shipped — for letting plugin configuration carry reproducible share semantics and arbitrary infrastructure provisioning, so a fork can stand up a complete working stack.

## What problem this solves [Section titled “What problem this solves”](#what-problem-this-solves) The snapshot export/fork system has been retired This section’s premise — that a harness snapshot is **exported** and **forked** as a tarball — is no longer current. The snapshot-EXPORT/fork system (`@papercusp/export-state`, the `snapshots:*` tools, `/api/snapshots/*`, and the Cupboard `kind=snapshot` fork-source) was retired on **2026-06-09** to `_retired/snapshot-system/`, and migration `libs/papercusp/libs/db/sql/199-drop-snapshot-index.sql` dropped the `snapshot_index` table (verified applied to the live database). The one job that survived — the *reproducible clone* — is now a lightweight **InstanceSpec** descriptor `{ blueprintRef, repoSha, deploymentConfig, genome }` (`packages/operator-core/lib/instance-spec/`, with `instance:capture|boot|clone` tools), **not** a forkable tarball. The share-semantics and provisioning mechanisms described below still shipped (into the plugin SDK + substrate); read the captured-state list and the “fork a snapshot” flow as the *historical* motivation that produced them, not as a live tarball pipeline. The original motivation: a harness snapshot used to capture — * The harness’s project files (code, docs, prompts) * The harness’s database state (the `harness_<slug>` schema name is still correct — see `packages/operator-core/lib/scaffold-harness-schema.ts` — but it is no longer captured/restored by a snapshot export) * Per-harness plugin configs (raw JSON in `~/.papercusp/harnesses/<slug>/plugin-configs/`) * The set of enabled plugins (`enabled-plugins.json`) When a user **forked** that snapshot, they got a fully working harness — *as long as* the underlying infrastructure already existed. Concretely: * If the original harness deployed to a Cloudflare Pages project, the forker has to manually create their own Cloudflare account + token + Pages project + paste credentials before the `cloudflare-pages` plugin’s actions work. * If the original harness pushed to a GitHub repo, the forker has to manually create a PAT + a target repo before `github-repo` works. * If the original harness used a hypothetical `aws-lambda` plugin to deploy serverless functions, the forker has to manually create the Lambda + IAM role + API gateway… none of which is captured by today’s snapshot. This makes “publish a working harness template” significantly harder than it should be. Two changes close the gap: 1. **Per-field share semantics** — plugins declare which config fields are sharable (default), which are private to the publisher (must be re-supplied), and which are credentials (must be re-authorized via OAuth or paste). The snapshot exporter respects these flags. 2. **Build scripts** — plugins can ship an executable `setup` script that the substrate runs (with full visibility) on the fork-er’s host to provision the plugin’s required infrastructure. Symmetric `teardown` and `verify` scripts cover uninstall and health-check. Both changes preserve the snapshot system’s current safety properties (no secret leakage; no silent code execution) while extending what a snapshot can encapsulate. ## Vision: standing up a complex clone [Section titled “Vision: standing up a complex clone”](#vision-standing-up-a-complex-clone) The user-visible flow the share-semantics + provisioning pieces were built to enable — illustrated here against a complex stack like `ecommerce-stripe-aws-cloudflare`. (The “fork a snapshot tarball” entry points named below predate the [snapshot-export retirement](#what-problem-this-solves); the connect-accounts and approve-provisioning steps are the parts that shipped.) 
```text
Forking ecommerce-stripe-aws-cloudflare → my-store
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────


  1.  Fork project files       …………………………………………………………… ✓ done (instant)
  2.  Restore harness DB schema ……………………………………………………… ✓ done (1.2s)
  3.  Apply redacted plugin configs ……………………………………………… ✓ done (instant)
  4.  Connect external accounts:


      ☐ GitHub      [ Connect with GitHub ]      ←  OAuth, no token paste
      ☐ Stripe      [ Connect with Stripe ]      ←  OAuth
      ☐ AWS         [ Paste access keys… ]       ←  no OAuth — paste
      ☐ Cloudflare  [ Paste API token… ]         ←  no OAuth — paste


  5.  Approve and run provisioning scripts:


      ☐ aws-lambda          provision-aws.sh   [Review ▶]
            Creates: 1 Lambda function, 1 API Gateway, 1 IAM role
            Estimated cost: $0–5/mo
      ☐ stripe-webhooks     provision-stripe.sh   [Review ▶]
            Creates: 1 webhook endpoint, 1 Stripe restricted-key
      ☐ cloudflare-pages    provision-cloudflare.sh   [Review ▶]
            Creates: 1 Pages project, 1 custom domain binding


      ☐ I trust this snapshot's publisher (papercupai)


      [ Approve all & run ]    [ Run one at a time ]
```
 After step 5, the harness is genuinely ready to run. Every credential the user provided is theirs; every cloud resource was provisioned with their explicit approval; the audit log preserves what ran. ## Two-part proposal [Section titled “Two-part proposal”](#two-part-proposal) This plan is split across two complementary mechanisms. They’re orthogonal — either could ship without the other — but together they’re what unlocks shareable arbitrary infrastructure. | Part | What it does | Read more | | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | **Build scripts** | Plugins declare `provision.{setup,teardown,verify}` scripts that the substrate runs on the host with full visibility, capturing output and tracking created resources for cleanup. | [Build scripts](./build-scripts) | | **Share semantics** | Plugins flag each `configSchema` field as `secret` (credential, stripped on snapshot) / `shareable: false` (publisher-specific identifier, stripped) / default (config that travels with the snapshot). | [Share semantics](./share-semantics) | | **OAuth integration** | The substrate provides a generic OAuth helper so plugins can mark a credential field as `oauth: { provider, scopes }` and users get a “Connect” button instead of a paste field. | [OAuth integration](./oauth-integration) | ## Implementation status [Section titled “Implementation status”](#implementation-status) The two-part proposal above is **largely shipped**. What landed, where it lives, and which proposed fields stayed design-only: **Build scripts / provision lifecycle — shipped.** The runner and OS-level sandbox live at `packages/operator-core/lib/provision/` (`runner.ts`, `sandbox.ts` for bwrap, plus `audit-log.ts`, `trust-store.ts`, `network-policy.ts`, `single-user.ts`, `hashes.ts`, a WAL `state-store.ts`, and the `runtime/lib.sh` `papercusp_record_resource` FIFO bridge). It runs as a durable DBOS workflow (`packages/operator-core/lib/dbos/provision-workflow.ts`, gated by `PAPERCUSP_DBOS_PROVISION`, default-on), and three first-party plugins ship `provision/` scripts (`cloudflare-stack` and `github-repo` ship the full `{setup,teardown,verify}.sh` trio; `cloudflare-pages` ships only `verify.sh`). Per \[\[plugin-system-pot-port-2026-06-11]] P-010, the shipped `ProvisionScript` type carries `path` / `timeoutSec` / `runAt` plus consent-dialog fields `displayName` / `description`; the proposed `network`, `writesState`, and `requiresInteractive` fields **stay design-only** and are not in the SDK. `PluginProvision` additionally carries `cloudProvider`, `allowedHosts`, `skipReprovisionOnPatch`, and `auditLogCapMb`. **OAuth integration — shipped.** The substrate lives at `packages/operator-core/lib/oauth/` (`state.ts` for HMAC-signed URL state + single-use nonce, `providers.ts` with the hand-written GitHub provider, `token.ts` with the `getOAuthToken` Promise-cache that dedupes concurrent refreshes and retries once on 401, `storage-fs.ts`), exposes `/api/oauth/start|callback|verify-paste`, and offers `ctx.oauth.token(provider)` (refreshing \~5 minutes before expiry). See `packages/operator-core/lib/oauth/README.md`. OAuth was rolled in-house — the `arctic` library mentioned below was **not** adopted as a dependency. Additional providers (Slack/Linear/Notion/Jira) remain V2 (`// V2: slack, linear, notion, jira providers.` in `providers.ts`). **Share semantics — shipped at the SDK contract.** The plugin SDK declares the per-field flags `secret` / `snapshotPolicy` / `shareable` / `oauth` / `aliases` on `configSchema`, plus top-level `provision`, `oauth`, and `versionPin` (`packages/plugin-sdk/src/index.ts`). Note the exporter that *consumed* these flags rode the now-retired snapshot-export system; the flags themselves remain the live contract. ## What this plan does NOT change [Section titled “What this plan does NOT change”](#what-this-plan-does-not-change) To set scope expectations: * **The plugin loader contract** — plugins still ship as a manifest + JS entry + capability declaration. Scripts are an *additional* lifecycle surface, not a replacement. * **The capability gate** — actions and hook handlers still run inside the DI sandbox with `secrets:read:*` / `http:fetch:*` enforcement. Build scripts are a separate, opt-in escape hatch with their own consent flow, not a backdoor around the gate. * **The harness contract** (§3 of the spec) — fresh-context roles, structured state, atomic checkout, etc. all unchanged. * **The CLI surface** — `papercusp install` (live — `libs/papercusp/packages/cli/src/papercusp.ts`) and `papercusp plugin enable` (live — `plugin-cli.ts`, `cmdPluginEnable`) keep their current commands; new flags get added without renames. Stale: the snapshot tarball format and \`papercusp snapshot fork\` This section originally also promised an **additive snapshot tarball format** (a manifest `requiresProvisioning: true` flag and per-plugin `.shape.json` companion files) and that `papercusp snapshot fork` would keep working. Both are now stale: * There is no longer a live snapshot tarball/fork format to extend — the export-and-fork system was retired on 2026-06-09. The named identifiers `requiresProvisioning` and `.shape.json` were **never implemented** in executable code: they appear only in docs (this page — and for `.shape.json`, also `cloudflare-stack`’s `README.md`), never wired into `packages/`/`libs/`/`apps/` source. * `papercusp snapshot fork` no longer reaches a working fork-source. The `snapshot-cli.ts` command still dispatches from `papercusp.ts`, but its backend (`snapshots:*` tools, `/api/snapshots/*`, Cupboard `kind=snapshot`) was retired, so `fork` fetches a marketplace catalog entry that no longer exists. Use the InstanceSpec replacement (`instance:capture|boot|clone`) for reproducible clones. ### Known gap, explicitly acknowledged [Section titled “Known gap, explicitly acknowledged”](#known-gap-explicitly-acknowledged) * **Marketplace moderation** — the current marketplace publish flow has no human-review gate. Any service-token holder can publish. Build scripts make this gap more consequential (an unsigned script from an unverified publisher is now a code-execution vector, not just a misbehaving REST integration). The mitigations in this plan — sandbox-by-default, consent dialog, static-analysis warnings, quarantine-invalidates-trust — are designed assuming the marketplace ships *without* moderation initially. A separate spec doc covering a moderation/review layer is forthcoming and is **not** part of this plan. ## High-level phasing [Section titled “High-level phasing”](#high-level-phasing) | Phase | Scope | Approx LOC | Sequencing | | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **V1 (share-semantics + OAuth)** | Per-field share flags (`secret` / `shareable` / `snapshotPolicy`) + snapshot-export filtering + schema-evolution aliases (rename + removal) + plugin-version pinning + security-advisory consultation. Plus OAuth substrate, GitHub provider, `ctx.oauth.token()` helper with concurrent-refresh Promise cache, paste-PAT scope verification. | \~600 | Single PR. The two were originally split A → B but ship together because OAuth-acquired tokens depend on the `secret` flag for snapshot stripping. | | **V1 (build-scripts)** | Build-script lifecycle: SDK types, provision-runner service, OS-level sandboxing (bwrap-bundled with smoke test on Linux; sandbox-exec + signed-only on macOS), `papercusp_record_resource` helper, audit logging with per-plugin cap override, PG-based recovery contract, idempotency with scriptHash + configHash + pluginVersion, consent flow, fork-time review UI, cloudProvider presets, network-policy floor (IMDS/RFC1918), trust per-(publisher, plugin) with ownership-transfer + key-rotation handling, hook queue-and-replay, single-user-host detection. | \~1,400–1,500 | After share-semantics + OAuth. | | **V1.1** | github-repo dogfood (re-implement repo creation as build script), `runAt` scheduling for hooks/routines/webhooks, `budgetCap` + AWS-Budgets helper, `compute:exec:*` vs build-scripts docs, plugin “host activity” tile, skip-teardown banner, marketplace moderation layer (separate spec). | \~500 | Fast-follow once V1 has shipped to a vetted-publisher alpha and a real plugin author has used it. | | **V1.1+** | cloudflare-pages-via-github mode, additional OAuth providers (Slack/Linear/Notion/Jira), per-tenant OAuth multi-tenancy. | \~300 per provider | Demand-driven. | | **V2** | macOS Tauri-sidecar with restricted entitlements, layer-7 network-policy proxy with TLS interception, encrypted-at-rest token storage, per-cloud `budgetCap` helpers (GCP/Azure/Cloudflare), Windows sandboxing. | TBD | Separate workstreams. | V1 LOC honest total: **\~2,000–2,100 LOC** across substrate + UI. The earlier “\~1,500 LOC” estimate was sloppy math; this version reflects each subsystem’s real footprint after rounds 3–6 added defensive features (PG lock, smoke test, helper library, advisory checks). Adopting `arctic` for OAuth (subject to supply-chain audit, see [OAuth integration](./oauth-integration#library-decision-arctic-vs-roll-our-own)) trims \~150 LOC. The V1 / V1.1 / V2 split is explicit per item in [Open Questions](./open-questions). ### Snapshot tarball format change (never shipped) [Section titled “Snapshot tarball format change (never shipped)”](#snapshot-tarball-format-change-never-shipped) The original plan proposed an additive snapshot tarball change: per-plugin `.shape.json` companion files describing what was redacted, ignored gracefully by older substrates. This was **never implemented** — `.shape.json` exists only in the rendered copies of this doc, not in source — and there is no longer a snapshot tarball to extend, since the export/fork system was retired on 2026-06-09 (see [What problem this solves](#what-problem-this-solves)). The per-field redaction *intent* survives in the SDK’s `secret` / `snapshotPolicy` / `shareable` flags; the tarball companion-file format does not. ## Why this is a good fit for snapshots specifically [Section titled “Why this is a good fit for snapshots specifically”](#why-this-is-a-good-fit-for-snapshots-specifically) A common alternative would be: “let plugins call `terraform apply` from inside their action handlers.” That doesn’t work because: * Action handlers run inside the DI sandbox with capability gates; they can’t shell out to arbitrary binaries (only ones explicitly capability-granted via `compute:exec:<bin>`). * Action handlers have no watch-able execution surface in the UI — they return a result and a log slice, not a streamed, step-by-step run the user can follow. * Action handlers fire on every invocation; provisioning should fire once per harness lifecycle (setup at fork, teardown at uninstall, verify on boot). The `provision.{setup,teardown,verify}` shape matches what infrastructure genuinely is: a one-shot lifecycle event with a long-running, watch-able execution. As shipped, that execution is rendered by `ProvisionStream` (`apps/operator/app/_components/ProvisionStream.tsx`) as a **structured step list** on the shared `StructuredStreamView` — each provision step is a typed row with status (✓/✗/running) and duration, with a raw-output drawer one click away for steps whose tool spew you genuinely want. (It is no longer a live xterm pane; the xterm-only viewer was replaced per \[\[structured-streams-not-terminals-2026-06-05]].) The model also matches Homebrew’s formula model, Tauri’s window-trust model, and `npm install` scripts (with the security mitigations the latter *should* have had). ## Where to file feedback [Section titled “Where to file feedback”](#where-to-file-feedback) Comments on individual sections of this plan should land in the harness’s `docs/` directory as separate `review-<topic>.md` files, or as inline comments on the eventual PR. Once the plan is signed off, this directory becomes the implementation reference.

# Authoring a build script

> How publishers ship `provision.setup` / `teardown` / `verify` scripts that work end-to-end with snapshot fork — manifest extensions, runtime helpers, project-file templating, reference plugins.

This page is the publisher-facing guide for the build-script lifecycle — the substrate primitive that lets a forked snapshot provision real infrastructure (Cloudflare, AWS, GitHub, etc.) on the forker’s host. It deliberately points outward. Most of what you need to know about declaring inputs and templating files is **standard JSON Schema and POSIX envsubst** — read those upstream docs first; this page only covers the small papercusp-specific delta. ## Prerequisites — read these once [Section titled “Prerequisites — read these once”](#prerequisites--read-these-once) If you’ve never authored anything that prompts users for config and runs a script with their answers, read: * [JSON Schema getting-started](https://json-schema.org/learn/getting-started-step-by-step) (\~30 min) — the format we use for `configSchema`. Covers `type`, `description`, `default`, `pattern`, `enum`, `required`. * [POSIX shell parameter expansion](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/V3_chap02.html#tag_18_06_02) or the [GNU envsubst manpage](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/envsubst.1.html) (\~5 min) — the templating syntax we use for `*.tmpl` files. Covers `${VAR}`, `${VAR:-default}`, `${VAR:?error}`. * [react-jsonschema-form `ui:*` hints](https://rjsf-team.github.io/react-jsonschema-form/docs/usage/widgets/) (\~10 min) — how the fork-time form picks widgets. We use rjsf to render your `configSchema` + `uiSchema`. * [Heroku `app.json` env generators](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/app-json-schema#env) (\~5 min, only for the names) — we adopt their `generator: "secret"` / `"secret-base64"` / `"secret-hex"` etc. naming verbatim. These are the only external dependencies. Total onboarding: \~50 min once. ## Mental model [Section titled “Mental model”](#mental-model) A snapshot is a tarball of project files + DB state + plugin configs. When someone forks it, the substrate: 1. Restores project files + DB schema into the forker’s harness dir. 2. Reads each enabled plugin’s `configSchema` and prompts the forker for any field marked `secret: true` or `shareable: false` — the publisher’s values were stripped at publish time. 3. For each plugin that declares `provision.setup`, the substrate: * Shows a consent dialog (script hash, allowed hosts, cloud provider). * On approve, runs the script in a sandbox with the forker’s config in env vars. * Streams stdout/stderr to a live terminal pane. * Persists `papercusp_record_resource` calls so teardown can clean up. Your job as a publisher is to: * Declare your variables in `configSchema` with the right share-semantics flags so the right values are stripped at publish time. * Author `provision/setup.sh` (and optional `teardown.sh`/`verify.sh`) that read those values from env and provision your platform’s resources idempotently. * Author `*.tmpl` files in your harness’s project dir so post-provision, the harness’s code knows the new resource IDs. ## Manifest extensions — the four flags you need [Section titled “Manifest extensions — the four flags you need”](#manifest-extensions--the-four-flags-you-need) Standard JSON Schema covers `type`, `description`, `default`, `pattern`, `enum`, etc. The substrate adds four extensions to drive snapshot redaction and form rendering: ### `secret: true` [Section titled “secret: true”](#secret-true) Marks a field as a credential. By default, **secret fields are stripped from snapshots** at publish time and the forker is prompted for a fresh value at fork time. 
```json
"byoCloudflareToken": {
  "type": "string",
  "secret": true,
  "snapshotPolicy": "strip",
  "description": "API token with Pages:Edit + R2:Edit scopes."
}
```
 ### `snapshotPolicy: "strip" | "include" | "warn-and-prompt"` [Section titled “snapshotPolicy: "strip" | "include" | "warn-and-prompt"”](#snapshotpolicy-strip--include--warn-and-prompt) Override snapshot behavior for `secret: true` fields: * `"strip"` (default) — value never travels with the snapshot * `"include"` — declares that the value *may* travel (e.g. a demo Slack webhook) * `"warn-and-prompt"` — flags the field for a per-snapshot prompt Policy is declarative only today `snapshotPolicy` is a share-semantics declaration on the field — the `papercusp snapshot publish` CLI does not yet consume it. The publish command tars `.papercusp/` with only `--name` / `--note` / `--icon` / `--include-project` / `--include-logs`; there is no `--include-secrets` flag or per-secret redaction step wired in. Until that lands, do not rely on `"include"` / `"warn-and-prompt"` to gate what leaves your host — strip secrets yourself before publishing. ### `shareable: false` [Section titled “shareable: false”](#shareable-false) Marks a field as a publisher-specific identifier (account ID, org name, region) — different per forker, also stripped from snapshots. 
```json
"accountId": {
  "type": "string",
  "shareable": false,
  "pattern": "^[a-f0-9]{32}$",
  "description": "Cloudflare account UUID."
}
```
 ### `generator: "<name>"` (planned — not yet wired) [Section titled “generator: "\<name>" (planned — not yet wired)”](#generator-name-planned--not-yet-wired) Not implemented yet The `generator` field is a design target — the fork/instantiate path does **not** auto-fill generated values today. Until it lands, generate these values inside `setup.sh` (e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`) and record them with `papercusp_state_set`. Substrate auto-fills the field at fork time. Adopted from Heroku’s [app.json env generators](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/app-json-schema#env); same names so publishers transferring from Heroku recognize them. | Generator | What it produces | | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | | `secret-256` | 32 random bytes, base64url | | `secret-base64-256` | Same, explicit base64 | | `secret-hex-256` | 32 random bytes, hex | | `uuid` | RFC 4122 v4 UUID | | `random-name` | Memorable two-word name (`bold-meadow-7`) | | `slug-of:harness_slug` | The forking harness’s slug | 
```json
"sessionSecret": {
  "type": "string",
  "secret": true,
  "generator": "secret-256",
  "description": "Session signing secret, auto-generated at fork."
}
```
 ### `uiSchema` block (sibling to `configSchema`) [Section titled “uiSchema block (sibling to configSchema)”](#uischema-block-sibling-to-configschema) rjsf-style hints. We don’t reinvent these — read [rjsf widgets docs](https://rjsf-team.github.io/react-jsonschema-form/docs/usage/widgets/). 
```json
"uiSchema": {
  "byoCloudflareToken": {
    "ui:widget": "password",
    "ui:help": "Create at dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens."
  }
}
```
 ## Env vars `setup.sh` receives [Section titled “Env vars setup.sh receives”](#env-vars-setupsh-receives) The runner sets three namespaces of env vars before invoking your script: ### `$USER_VAR_*` — flattened config scalars [Section titled “$USER\_VAR\_\* — flattened config scalars”](#user_var_--flattened-config-scalars) Every top-level scalar (`string`/`number`/`boolean`) in your plugin’s config becomes `USER_VAR_<UPPER_SNAKE>`. lowerCamelCase is converted to UPPER\_SNAKE\_CASE. Nested objects/arrays remain accessible via `$PAPERCUSP_CONFIG` parsed with jq. Mirrors the [Dev Container Features `options`-to-env mapping](https://containers.dev/implementors/features/#options-property) — same convention plus a `USER_VAR_` prefix to disambiguate from arbitrary script env. 
```bash
# config: { "accountId": "abc", "r2BucketName": "demo-assets" }
# env:    USER_VAR_ACCOUNT_ID=abc, USER_VAR_R2_BUCKET_NAME=demo-assets
```
 ### `$OUTPUT_*` — your script’s outputs [Section titled “$OUTPUT\_\* — your script’s outputs”](#output_--your-scripts-outputs) Set via `papercusp_state_set` (see [helpers](#runtime-helpers) below), which folds the value into `state.json`’s `outputs` object. The runner does **not** currently re-inject those values as `$OUTPUT_*` env vars on later phases — `teardown.sh` / `verify.sh` instead read the full state JSON from `$PAPERCUSP_PLUGIN_STATE`. For `papercusp_render_templates`, the values an output `${OUTPUT_<key>}` template sees are whatever the *same* script has `export`ed into its own env; the helper does not auto-source `state.json`. ### `$PAPERCUSP_*` — substrate [Section titled “$PAPERCUSP\_\* — substrate”](#papercusp_--substrate) | Variable | What | | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | | `$PAPERCUSP_CONFIG` | Full plugin config as JSON (parse with jq if needed) | | `$PAPERCUSP_HARNESS_SLUG` | The harness slug — useful as a default name | | `$PAPERCUSP_PLUGIN_NAME` | The plugin slug | | `$PAPERCUSP_PROJECT_DIR` | RW-mounted harness project dir (templates target) | | `$PAPERCUSP_PLUGIN_DIR` | RO-mounted plugin source dir | | `$PAPERCUSP_SCRATCH_DIR` | RW-mounted scratch dir; also `$HOME` and CWD | | `$PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_LIB` | Path to lib.sh — source it for helpers | | `$PAPERCUSP_RECORD_FIFO` | Record-bridge file the helpers append to (see below) | | `$PAPERCUSP_PLUGIN_STATE` | Full `state.json` — injected on `teardown`/`verify` only | | `$PAPERCUSP_PROGRESS_FD` | fd the progress/warn/error markers write to (default 2) | | `$PAPERCUSP_PHASE` | One of `setup` / `teardown` / `verify` | ## Runtime helpers (`lib.sh`) [Section titled “Runtime helpers (lib.sh)”](#runtime-helpers-libsh) Source the helper library at the top of every script: 
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
. "$PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_LIB"
```
 Then use: | Helper | Purpose | | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `papercusp_progress <step> <message>` | Emit a structured progress event. UI shows progress bar. | | `papercusp_warn <message>` | Surface a yellow warning indicator. | | `papercusp_error <message>` | Surface a red error indicator (script may continue). | | `papercusp_record_resource <kind> <id> [<json-meta>]` | Record a resource for teardown. Idempotent on `(kind, externalId)` — re-recording the same resource collapses rather than duplicating. | | `papercusp_state_set <key> <json-value>` | Set a `state.json` output. Becomes `$OUTPUT_<key>`. | | `papercusp_render_templates` | Walk `$PAPERCUSP_PROJECT_DIR` for `*.tmpl`, render each. | Resource kinds (`cloudflare.d1.database`, `aws.lambda.function`, `github.repo`) are **plugin-author vocabulary**, not substrate-defined. Your `teardown.sh` is the dispatcher that knows how to delete each kind. Under the hood, `papercusp_record_resource` writes newline-JSON to the `$PAPERCUSP_RECORD_FIFO` bridge, which the substrate folds into the durable store. That store is PG-backed (a single JSONB row per `(workspace, harness, plugin)`) — not an on-disk append-only WAL — so recording is a transactional read-modify-write that dedupes on `(kind, externalId)`. ## Project-file templating (the `.tmpl` convention) [Section titled “Project-file templating (the .tmpl convention)”](#project-file-templating-the-tmpl-convention) The substrate doesn’t dictate templating — we use plain envsubst. Publishers commit `*.tmpl` files in the harness project dir; setup calls `papercusp_render_templates` after creating resources, which: 1. Walks `$PAPERCUSP_PROJECT_DIR` for `*.tmpl` (skips `.git/`, `node_modules/`, `dist/`, `.next/`, `.papercusp/`, `target/`, `build/`, `.turbo/`). 2. Runs `envsubst` on each, with `$USER_VAR_*` + `$OUTPUT_*` + `$PAPERCUSP_*` in env. 3. Writes the rendered file to the same path without `.tmpl`. 4. Removes the `.tmpl` source. Example `wrangler.toml.tmpl`: 
```toml
name           = "${OUTPUT_workerName}"
account_id     = "${USER_VAR_ACCOUNT_ID}"
compatibility_date = "2026-04-01"


[[d1_databases]]
binding       = "DB"
database_name = "${OUTPUT_d1DatabaseName}"
database_id   = "${OUTPUT_d1DatabaseId}"


[vars]
SESSION_SECRET = "${USER_VAR_SESSION_SECRET}"
PUBLIC_API_URL = "${OUTPUT_workerUrl:-https://${OUTPUT_workerName}.workers.dev}"
```
 Add the rendered output (`wrangler.toml`) to your harness’s `.gitignore` — only the `.tmpl` is committed. ## Reference plugins (fork these to start) [Section titled “Reference plugins (fork these to start)”](#reference-plugins-fork-these-to-start) The substrate ships canonical reference plugins. To scaffold a new plugin from one: 
```bash
papercusp plugin init my-stack --template cloudflare-stack
cd my-stack
# edit provision/setup.sh, configSchema, etc.
```
 Local-dir install is not a wired command Both this guide’s older drafts and `plugin init`’s own next-steps print `papercusp install --from-path .`, but that flag does **not** exist. `papercusp install` only recognizes `--from-lock`, `--harness`, and `--accept-capabilities[=current|=all]`; an unknown `--from-path` token falls through to the positional slug and fails slug validation. Installing a locally-edited plugin from a directory is a documented concept, not an implemented install path — develop and test against your in-place copy (e.g. `papercusp plugin verify`) until it lands. Available templates: | Template | What it provisions | Use when… | | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | | `cloudflare-stack` | Pages + Workers + D1 + R2 + KV (mega-plugin) | Your harness deploys to Cloudflare | | `cloudflare-pages` | Cloudflare Pages only (lighter reference) | You only need a Pages site, not the full stack | | `github-repo` | GitHub repo (single resource) | Your harness pushes code to GitHub | | *(more coming)* | *aws-stack, fly-stack, render-stack, vercel-stack* | *As they ship* | The `cloudflare-stack` source is the most complete worked example — read its [setup.sh](https://github.com/Papercusp/papercusp/blob/main/plugins/cloudflare-stack/provision/setup.sh) and [README](https://github.com/Papercusp/papercusp/blob/main/plugins/cloudflare-stack/README.md) side-by-side with this guide. ## Sandbox restrictions [Section titled “Sandbox restrictions”](#sandbox-restrictions) Your script runs in a substrate-bundled bwrap (Linux) or sandbox-exec (macOS) sandbox. Constraints: * **Filesystem**: RO access to `/usr`, `/lib`, `/bin`, `/etc`, your plugin dir; RW access to `$PAPERCUSP_SCRATCH_DIR`, `$PAPERCUSP_PROJECT_DIR`, `/tmp`. `$HOME` is set to the RW scratch dir (and CWD is `chdir`’d there too), so writes under `$HOME` land in scratch — everything else is RO. * **Network**: outbound only to `provision.allowedHosts` (or the declared `cloudProvider` preset’s allowlist). The substrate hard-blocks IMDS (`169.254.0.0/16`), RFC1918, and loopback regardless of declared hosts. See [build-scripts § Network policy floor](/internal/docs/snapshots/build-scripts#network-policy-floor). * **No interactive subprocesses**. Scripts that try to read from stdin or open browsers mid-run are killed. Use OAuth via `ctx.oauth.token()` in your action handlers, not `aws sso login` from setup. Sandbox bypass escape hatches Two env vars let the runner skip the sandbox — useful to know when debugging why a script behaves differently across machines: `PAPERCUSP_DISABLE_SANDBOX=1` (CI/test) skips sandboxing entirely, and `PAPERCUSP_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX=1` (dev fallback) runs scripts unsandboxed after a failed bwrap smoke test, recording a `sandbox-bypass` audit event per run. Neither is set in normal operation; assume your script is fully sandboxed unless you’ve opted out. ## Idempotency [Section titled “Idempotency”](#idempotency) `setup.sh` runs once per `(harness, plugin)` per `(configHash, scriptHash, pluginVersion)` tuple. Re-runs are blocked unless the user explicitly clicks Re-provision OR one of the hashes changes. How each hash decides a re-provision (the conservative defaults): * **configHash** — by default every config field is hashed, so *any* config change re-provisions.
